lab.title: Build a first LAN and verify a saved configuration
lab.intro:
Build a two-PC LAN, test communication, and practice the IOS configuration workflow. You will then make a controlled unsaved change and observe which configuration returns after a reload. Use a new Packet Tracer project for this exercise.

The commands target the Packet Tracer 2960. Interface names, messages, and timing can differ on other models or software versions. Output examples are representative; compare their meaning with your result.
lab.topology:
```diagram
{ "type": "topology", "title": "Two PCs on one switch",
  "caption": "Both PCs use the same /24 subnet. No router or default gateway is needed for this local exchange.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "PCA", "kind": "pc", "label": "PC-A", "sub": "192.168.10.10/24", "x": 2, "y": 3 },
    { "id": "S1", "kind": "switch", "label": "S1", "sub": "2960", "x": 6, "y": 3 },
    { "id": "PCB", "kind": "pc", "label": "PC-B", "sub": "192.168.10.20/24", "x": 10, "y": 3 }
  ],
  "links": [
    { "from": "PCA", "to": "S1", "fromLabel": "Fa0", "toLabel": "Fa0/1" },
    { "from": "S1", "to": "PCB", "fromLabel": "Fa0/2", "toLabel": "Fa0" }
  ] }
```

| Connection | Cable |
|---|---|
| PC-A FastEthernet0 to S1 FastEthernet0/1 | Copper straight-through |
| PC-B FastEthernet0 to S1 FastEthernet0/2 | Copper straight-through |

| Device | IPv4 address | Subnet mask | Default gateway |
|---|---|---|---|
| PC-A | 192.168.10.10 | 255.255.255.0 | Leave blank |
| PC-B | 192.168.10.20 | 255.255.255.0 | Leave blank |
| S1 | No management address in this lab | — | — |

The mask places these two addresses in the same subnet. Chapters 04 and 05 explain how to calculate that boundary. Here, enter the values as given so you can concentrate on the device workflow.

steps.title: Prepare the project
steps.body:
Install and sign in to Packet Tracer using the chapter's setup guide. Place one 2960 and two PC-PT devices in a blank Logical workspace. Set their display names to S1, PC-A, and PC-B.

Save the project as **00-first-lan.pkt** in your lab folder. The display name is a workspace label; setting it does not necessarily configure the IOS hostname.

:::expected
The workspace contains three separately named devices, and you know where the project file is saved. No network communication has been tested yet.
:::

steps.title: Cable and inspect the ports
steps.body:
Connect the devices using the connection table. Select each endpoint explicitly. If you use automatic cable selection, inspect the resulting ports and correct the connections to match the table.

Allow the simulation to advance while the links become ready. If a link remains unavailable, check the selected device, port, cable, and device power. Do not assume that every delay has the same cause.

:::expected
Each PC is attached to the intended switch port. Once the ports are operational, the link indicators show readiness. The switch can provide Layer 2 forwarding without a management IP address.
:::

steps.title: Address the PCs and test the LAN
steps.body:
On each PC, open **Desktop → IP Configuration**, select static addressing, and enter the address and mask from the table. Leave the default gateway blank. Open PC-A's **Desktop → Command Prompt** and enter:

```text
ping 192.168.10.20
```

Repeat from PC-B toward **192.168.10.10**. If an initial request times out, repeat once after the links are ready. Address resolution or convergence can affect an initial attempt, but persistent loss requires investigation.

:::expected
Both PCs receive replies from the other PC. This establishes working ICMP communication between these two addresses at this time. It does not test access to another subnet or an application service.
:::

steps.title: Enter IOS and set the hostname
steps.body:
Open S1's CLI. If an initial configuration dialog appears, answer **no**. Press Enter as needed to reach the command prompt. Enter the following commands without copying the prompt text:

```ios S1
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname S1
S1(config)# interface FastEthernet0/1
S1(config-if)# exit
S1(config)# end
S1# show running-config
```

Find the hostname in the running configuration. If output pauses at **--More--**, use Space for another page or **q** to stop.

:::expected
The prompt changes to S1, and running configuration contains `hostname S1`. The interface command selected a configuration context; it did not assign an IP address or save the configuration.
:::

steps.title: Practice help and interpret interface status
steps.body:
At privileged EXEC, enter **show ?**, then **show ip ?**. Read the choices before clearing the unfinished line with Ctrl+U or Backspace. Run:

```ios S1
S1# show ip interface brief
S1# configure terminal
S1(config)# do show ip interface brief
S1(config)# no ip domain-lookup
S1(config)# end
```

Locate FastEthernet0/1 and FastEthernet0/2. Both should report operational states once the connected links are ready. Unused ports can remain down. An unassigned IP address on these Layer 2 switch ports is expected.

The final configuration command disables this isolated switch's DNS lookup behavior. There is no need to deliberately start a long lookup to complete the exercise.

:::expected
You can run the interface summary from EXEC and, using `do`, from configuration mode. You can explain the difference between an unused down port and an administratively disabled port.
:::

steps.title: Introduce and correct a controlled fault
steps.body:
Disable the switch port connected to PC-B:

```ios S1
S1# configure terminal
S1(config)# interface FastEthernet0/2
S1(config-if)# shutdown
S1(config-if)# end
S1# show ip interface brief
```

Try PC-A's ping again after the simulated state updates. Record the affected port's status and the ping result. Restore the port:

```ios S1
S1# configure terminal
S1(config)# interface FastEthernet0/2
S1(config-if)# no shutdown
S1(config-if)# end
```

Allow the port to become ready, then repeat the same ping and interface check.

:::expected
The disabled port reports **administratively down**, and PC-A cannot successfully ping PC-B through it. After restoration and any required convergence, the port operates again and the ping receives replies. The corrective command belongs on the affected interface.
:::

steps.title: Save and verify
steps.body:
Save the restored configuration and inspect the result:

```ios S1
S1# copy running-config startup-config
```

Accept the destination filename with Enter and wait for the save to complete. Then run:

```ios S1
S1# show startup-config
```

Find **hostname S1** in startup configuration, and confirm that FastEthernet0/2 is not configured with `shutdown`. Save the Packet Tracer project as well.

:::expected
You have verified the saved device configuration, and you have separately saved the topology file. You can identify the command that saves the device and the menu action that saves the project.
:::

steps.title: Observe an unsaved reload
steps.body:
Change only the hostname to **TEMP** and leave the change unsaved:

```ios S1
S1# configure terminal
S1(config)# hostname TEMP
TEMP(config)# end
TEMP# show running-config
TEMP# show startup-config
TEMP# reload
```

Before reloading, the running hostname should be TEMP while the saved hostname remains S1. If prompted to save the modified configuration, answer **no**; then confirm the reload. Read each prompt because wording varies.

After boot, enter privileged EXEC, check the hostname and interface summary, and repeat the PC-to-PC test. If you accidentally saved TEMP, configure S1 again and save it to restore the intended result. Finish by saving the project as **00-first-lan-complete.pkt**.

:::expected
With the unsaved change discarded, the device returns as S1. Communication works after the connected ports become ready. You can explain the result using running and startup configuration, rather than the workspace display label.
:::

lab.troubleshooting:
| Symptom | Evidence to collect | Appropriate next action |
|---|---|---|
| No replies between PCs | Both PC address/mask settings; cable endpoints; switch port states | Correct the specific mismatch and repeat the same test. |
| Administratively down on Fa0/2 | Configuration for FastEthernet0/2 | Apply `no shutdown` to that interface, then wait for readiness and verify. |
| Invalid command | Full prompt and caret location | Check mode and syntax with context help; confirm command support. |
| Apparent freeze after a mistyped word | Lookup message or pager prompt | Distinguish DNS lookup from paging; interrupt or wait as appropriate. |
| Wrong name after reload | Running and startup hostname lines | Configure the intended name, save in the correct direction, and inspect startup configuration. |
lab.challenge:
Add PC-C to S1 FastEthernet0/3 with **192.168.10.30**, mask **255.255.255.0**, and no gateway. Verify communication with both existing PCs. Then disable only FastEthernet0/3 and predict which pairs should still communicate.

**Check your result:** PC-A and PC-B should continue communicating; PC-C loses its switch connection. Restore FastEthernet0/3, verify all three PCs again, save the device configuration, and save the project. Explain why the switch did not need a management IP address to forward this traffic.

Switch> show running-config

questions.prompt: Why is this command rejected on a default lab switch?
options: The switch has no IP address.
The running configuration must be saved first.
The command requires privileged EXEC on this device.
The hostname must be configured first.
questions.explanation: The > prompt indicates user EXEC. Enter enable to reach privileged EXEC, then run show running-config. Check the prompt before treating a parser error as a spelling problem.

whyWrong.0: A management IP is not needed to inspect the configuration through the local CLI.
whyWrong.1: The active configuration can be displayed before it is saved.
whyWrong.3: The default hostname does not prevent the command.

questions.prompt: At S1(config-if)#, which command returns directly to privileged EXEC?
options: end
exit
enable
configure terminal
questions.explanation: end leaves configuration mode and returns to S1#. From interface configuration, exit returns only to global configuration.

whyWrong.1: exit moves from interface configuration to global configuration.
whyWrong.2: enable is used to enter privileged EXEC from user EXEC.
whyWrong.3: configure terminal enters global configuration from privileged EXEC.

questions.prompt: You configure hostname S1 and see S1# before a reload. After declining to save and reloading, the prompt is Switch#. What best explains the result?
options: The workspace display name overrode IOS.
Hostname changes take effect only after two reloads.
Switches cannot retain hostnames.
The hostname change was not saved.
questions.explanation: The running configuration contained S1, but the saved configuration used at startup did not. A changed prompt proves that a setting is active; it does not prove that the setting was saved.

whyWrong.0: A workspace label and IOS hostname are separate settings.
whyWrong.1: The hostname takes effect immediately in this lab.
whyWrong.2: A saved hostname can be retained across reloads.

questions.prompt: Which command saves the active configuration to the normal startup configuration?
options: copy startup-config running-config
copy running-config startup-config
show startup-config
configure terminal
questions.explanation: The copy command names the source first and destination second. Copy running configuration to startup configuration, accept the intended destination, and verify the saved setting.

whyWrong.0: This is the reverse direction and can merge saved commands into the active configuration.
whyWrong.2: show displays information; it does not save the running configuration.
whyWrong.3: This enters configuration mode without saving.

questions.prompt: On an isolated practice switch, which setting prevents EXEC hostname lookups after some mistyped input?
options: shutdown
no ip domain-lookup
no hostname
copy running-config startup-config
questions.explanation: no ip domain-lookup disables this device's DNS lookup behavior. It is appropriate here because the practice switch does not need hostname resolution; it is not a general command to disable DNS for network clients.

whyWrong.0: shutdown disables an interface when entered in the relevant context.
whyWrong.2: Removing a hostname does not disable name resolution.
whyWrong.3: Saving a configuration does not itself change lookup behavior.

questions.prompt: The CLI displays --More-- during show running-config. Which two actions normally help you navigate this paged output? Choose two.
options: Press Space to display another page.
Enter configure terminal to save the output.
Press q to stop displaying the remaining output.
Reload the device to release the prompt.
Type no shutdown to resume the display.
questions.explanation: The output pager is waiting for navigation input. Space advances a page, Enter advances a line, and q normally stops the display.

whyWrong.1: configure terminal is not a pager navigation key and does not save output.
whyWrong.3: A reload is unnecessary and would interrupt the device.
whyWrong.4: no shutdown is an interface command, not a pager control.

questions.prompt: On the classic IOS lab device, which two statements correctly distinguish running and startup configuration? Choose two.
options: Leaving configuration mode automatically copies all settings to startup configuration.
Running configuration represents the currently active settings.
A .pkt filename is the name of the switch's running configuration.
Startup configuration is the saved configuration used at startup.
show running-config saves the configuration it displays.
questions.explanation: The active configuration and the saved startup configuration serve different purposes. Leaving configuration mode or displaying a configuration does not copy it. The Packet Tracer project is another separate item.

whyWrong.0: end or exit does not save the configuration.
whyWrong.2: The .pkt file is a simulator project containing the topology and project state.
whyWrong.4: show is a display command.

questions.prompt: Startup configuration contains hostname S1. You change only the running hostname to TEMP, enter reload, and answer no when asked to save. Which hostname should the device use after a normal boot from that startup configuration?
options: TEMP
A randomly generated hostname
No hostname because reload erases startup configuration
S1
questions.explanation: Declining to save leaves the startup configuration unchanged. A normal restart using that configuration restores hostname S1.

whyWrong.0: TEMP was the unsaved running change.
whyWrong.1: IOS does not choose a random name in this situation.
whyWrong.2: reload restarts the device; it does not inherently erase startup configuration.

exhibit.title: Context help
exhibit.text:
S1# show ip interface brief ?
  |     Output modifiers
  <cr>

questions.prompt: What does `<cr>` in this context-help response mean?
options: The command has already executed.
A required argument is still missing.
Pressing Enter can complete this command at this position.
The command is unavailable on this image.
questions.explanation: The `<cr>` marker represents a carriage return. It indicates that the command can be completed by pressing Enter; other listed choices may be optional continuations.

whyWrong.0: Context help lists syntax choices without executing the command.
whyWrong.1: A command requiring another argument would not be complete at this point.
whyWrong.3: The response indicates valid completion, not lack of support.

questions.prompt: IOS reports % Ambiguous command after you enter a short abbreviation. What should you do next?
options: Use more characters or context help.
Disable the interface.
Save and reload before trying again.
Change the device's management address.
questions.explanation: An ambiguous abbreviation matches more than one command at that point. Supply enough characters to distinguish your intended command.

whyWrong.1: Interface state does not resolve an ambiguous keyword.
whyWrong.2: The parser ambiguity is a syntax issue, not evidence that a restart is needed.
whyWrong.3: A management address is unrelated to command abbreviation.

questions.prompt: You are at S1(config)# and want the interface summary without leaving configuration mode. Which command is appropriate on the supported lab image?
options: show ip interface brief
configure show interfaces
copy running-config startup-config
do show ip interface brief
questions.explanation: The do prefix runs the EXEC verification command from configuration mode on the lab image. You could also use end and run the normal show command from privileged EXEC.

whyWrong.0: The plain EXEC command is not the expected form at this configuration prompt.
whyWrong.1: This is not the syntax for displaying interface status.
whyWrong.2: This saves configuration rather than displaying interface states.

exhibit.title: Representative show ip interface brief excerpt
exhibit.text:
Interface         IP-Address   Status                  Protocol
FastEthernet0/1    unassigned   up                      up
FastEthernet0/2    unassigned   administratively down   down
FastEthernet0/3    unassigned   down                    down

questions.prompt: Which two conclusions are supported by the displayed interface summary? Choose two.
options: Fa0/1 reports an operational physical and line-protocol state.
All applications on the attached PC are working.
Fa0/3 must have an incorrect IP mask.
The switch cannot forward traffic because its ports are unassigned.
Fa0/2 has been disabled administratively.
questions.explanation: The summary supports local interface-state conclusions: Fa0/1 is up/up, while Fa0/2 is administratively down. It does not validate host addressing or applications.

whyWrong.1: Up/up does not test an application.
whyWrong.2: Down/down alone does not identify an IP-mask error.
whyWrong.3: Layer 2 access ports can forward traffic without individual IP addresses.

exhibit.title: Representative fresh-switch output
exhibit.text:
S1# show startup-config
startup-config is not present

questions.prompt: You have verified the intended active settings on this fresh lab switch. Given the output, what is the appropriate next step?
options: Save to startup-config and inspect it.
Erase running configuration.
Change every switch port to a routed port.
Close the terminal because saving is unsupported.
questions.explanation: A fresh device may not yet have a saved startup configuration. Save the verified running configuration and check that the required settings appear in the saved result.

whyWrong.1: Erasing the desired active settings does not create the intended saved configuration.
whyWrong.2: Port mode is unrelated to the absence of a startup configuration.
whyWrong.3: The message does not establish that saving is unsupported.

questions.prompt: Which key sequence is commonly used to interrupt an IOS operation such as an ongoing ping or hostname lookup?
options: Space
Ctrl+Shift+6
Ctrl+S
The Enter key twice
questions.explanation: Ctrl+Shift+6 is a common IOS escape sequence. The terminal or simulator must deliver the keys correctly; if a lookup does not interrupt, allow it to time out before correcting the input.

whyWrong.0: Space is commonly a pager control, not the general IOS interrupt sequence.
whyWrong.2: Ctrl+S may pause terminal output in some environments.
whyWrong.3: Enter is not the general operation-interrupt sequence.

questions.prompt: You saved the Packet Tracer project after changing a switch hostname. Which check directly verifies that the hostname is in the device's saved startup configuration?
options: The project filename contains the new hostname.
The switch's workspace label is correct.
show startup-config contains the intended hostname.
The current prompt contains the intended hostname.
questions.explanation: Inspect startup configuration to verify the saved device setting. The prompt verifies the active name, while the file and workspace names describe the simulator project.

whyWrong.0: A filename does not establish the contents of startup configuration.
whyWrong.1: The workspace label is separate from the IOS hostname.
whyWrong.3: The prompt alone does not distinguish saved from unsaved settings.

cards.front: Which IOS prompts identify user EXEC, privileged EXEC, global configuration, and interface configuration?
cards.back: Device>, Device#, Device(config)#, and Device(config-if)#, respectively. Read the prompt before deciding which commands are available.

cards.front: From interface configuration, how do exit and end differ?
cards.back: exit returns one level to global configuration. end returns directly to privileged EXEC. In EXEC mode, exit can end the session.

cards.front: How do you save and verify a conventional IOS startup configuration?
cards.back: Use copy running-config startup-config, accept the intended destination, then inspect show startup-config for the required settings.

cards.front: What is the operational difference between running and startup configuration?
cards.back: Running configuration is active now. Startup configuration is the saved configuration used at startup. Classic IOS commonly uses RAM for running configuration and NVRAM for startup configuration; storage varies by platform.

cards.front: What does --More-- mean, and how do you navigate it?
cards.back: The terminal pager has paused the display. Space normally advances a page, Enter a line, and q stops the remaining output. It is not evidence that the device has frozen.

cards.front: What does no ip domain-lookup change?
cards.back: It disables this device's DNS lookup behavior, including lookups triggered by some unrecognized EXEC input. It does not disable DNS for all clients. Use it only where the device does not need that lookup behavior.

cards.front: How do invalid, incomplete, and ambiguous command errors differ?
cards.back: Invalid input points to syntax, mode, or support to check. Incomplete means a required argument is missing. Ambiguous means the abbreviation matches multiple choices. Context help narrows the issue.

cards.front: What does startup-config is not present mean on a fresh lab device?
cards.back: The expected startup configuration file is absent. Verify the desired active settings, save running configuration to startup configuration, and inspect the saved result.

cards.front: What happens to an unsaved hostname change if you reload and decline to save?
cards.back: Under a normal boot using the existing startup configuration, the device returns to the saved hostname. The unsaved running change is lost.

cards.front: What does `<cr>` mean in IOS context help?
cards.back: Pressing Enter can complete the command at this position. Displaying help has not executed the command.

cards.front: Why should you use output filters carefully?
cards.back: Filters such as | include hostname make a line easier to find, but they can hide relevant surrounding configuration. Use the full relevant section when diagnosing a problem.

cards.front: How can you run a common EXEC verification command from configuration mode?
cards.back: On a supporting IOS image, prefix it with do, for example do show ip interface brief. Alternatively, use end and run the command from privileged EXEC.

cards.front: When is an IOS command abbreviation usable?
cards.back: When the characters entered uniquely identify the command in that context. A different software image can offer additional choices, making the same abbreviation ambiguous.

cards.front: Does end save the settings you just configured?
cards.back: No. end leaves configuration mode. Commands in these labs take effect when accepted, but you must separately copy running configuration to startup configuration to save them.

cards.front: Which common IOS key sequence interrupts an ongoing operation?
cards.back: Ctrl+Shift+6. Behavior depends on how the terminal or simulator handles the keys; some operations may need to time out.

cards.front: Does an unassigned IP address on a Layer 2 switch port prevent normal frame forwarding?
cards.back: No. Layer 2 access ports do not need individual IP addresses to switch frames. A management interface serves a different purpose, and a Vlan1 status line does not describe every physical port.

cards.front: How does a console connection differ from a remote terminal session?
cards.back: A console provides local device-management access without depending on the device's IP reachability. A remote terminal session uses network connectivity and the configured remote-access method, such as SSH.

cards.front: What three kinds of saved work should you distinguish in this course?
cards.back: The device's startup configuration, the Packet Tracer .pkt project, and the app's browser study progress. Save the device, save the project, and use progress export/backup for study records.

lab.title: Follow an IPv4 exchange across two LANs
lab.intro:
Build two Ethernet LANs connected by one router. Observe address resolution and packet forwarding, then introduce a return-path fault. PC-B fills the destination-host role called Server-B in the lesson; no application server is needed for an ICMP test.

Use a new project with the listed device models. The commands assume their interface names. Record the actual MAC addresses assigned by your simulator: they will differ from the illustrative addresses in the lesson. Event order, packet counts, and timing may also vary.
lab.topology:
```diagram
{ "type": "topology", "title": "Two LANs joined by R1",
  "caption": "SW1 and SW2 provide separate Layer 2 LANs. R1 has one interface in each subnet.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "PCA", "kind": "pc", "label": "PC-A", "sub": "192.168.10.10/24", "x": 1, "y": 3 },
    { "id": "SW1", "kind": "switch", "label": "SW1", "x": 3.5, "y": 3 },
    { "id": "R1", "kind": "router", "label": "R1", "sub": "2911", "x": 6, "y": 3, "highlight": true },
    { "id": "SW2", "kind": "switch", "label": "SW2", "x": 8.5, "y": 3 },
    { "id": "PCB", "kind": "pc", "label": "PC-B", "sub": "192.168.20.20/24", "x": 11, "y": 3 }
  ],
  "links": [
    { "from": "PCA", "to": "SW1", "fromLabel": "Fa0", "toLabel": "Fa0/1" },
    { "from": "SW1", "to": "R1", "fromLabel": "Fa0/24", "toLabel": "Gi0/0" },
    { "from": "R1", "to": "SW2", "fromLabel": "Gi0/1", "toLabel": "Fa0/24" },
    { "from": "SW2", "to": "PCB", "fromLabel": "Fa0/1", "toLabel": "Fa0" }
  ] }
```

Use copper straight-through cables for all four PC-to-switch and router-to-switch links shown. Select the ports explicitly.

| Device | Interface | IPv4 address | Mask | Gateway |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| PC-A | FastEthernet0 | 192.168.10.10 | 255.255.255.0 | 192.168.10.1 |
| R1 | GigabitEthernet0/0 | 192.168.10.1 | 255.255.255.0 | — |
| R1 | GigabitEthernet0/1 | 192.168.20.1 | 255.255.255.0 | — |
| PC-B | FastEthernet0 | 192.168.20.20 | 255.255.255.0 | 192.168.20.1 |

The switches use their default access VLAN for these separate LANs. They need no management IP address for this exercise. R1 needs no static or default route to reach its two directly connected subnets.

steps.title: Build and label the topology
steps.body:
Place and cable the devices as shown. Set their workspace display names. Open each network device's CLI and decline the initial configuration dialog if it appears. Configure the hostnames:

```ios R1
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R1
R1(config)# end
```

On SW1 and SW2, use the same sequence with `hostname SW1` and `hostname SW2`, respectively. Inspect the cable endpoints before continuing. Router interfaces may initially remain administratively disabled.

:::expected
There are two separate switch LANs with R1 between them. The CLI hostnames match the labels, and you can identify R1's interface toward each subnet.
:::

steps.title: Configure the router interfaces
steps.body:
```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface GigabitEthernet0/0
R1(config-if)# description LAN-A
R1(config-if)# ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# interface GigabitEthernet0/1
R1(config-if)# description LAN-B
R1(config-if)# ip address 192.168.20.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip interface brief
R1# show ip route
R1# copy running-config startup-config
```

Accept the save command's default destination. Once links are ready, verify that both configured interfaces report **up/up** and that the routing table contains connected routes for **192.168.10.0/24** and **192.168.20.0/24**. Some IOS versions also display local /32 routes for the router's own addresses.

:::expected
R1 has an operational interface and a connected route for each LAN. No route learned from another router is required in this topology. If a connected route is absent, check the address and interface state before adding unrelated routing commands.
:::

steps.title: Configure the hosts and record the baseline
steps.body:
On each PC, use **Desktop → IP Configuration** to enter the table's address, mask, and gateway. Read the settings back to catch typing errors.

Save each switch's configuration, then save the project as **01-models-ready.pkt**. Do not initiate test traffic yet: the next step is intended to capture the first exchange. Normal background traffic or earlier tests may already have populated some tables; that is an observation to record, not an error.

Before starting the ping, predict:

- Which IPv4 address PC-A will resolve through ARP for a packet destined for PC-B.
- The source and destination IPv4 addresses of the request.
- Which device will replace the Ethernet header and decrement the IPv4 TTL.

:::expected
Your prediction is: PC-A uses gateway 192.168.10.1 as its next hop; the request's IP addresses are 192.168.10.10 and 192.168.20.20; R1 performs the routed forwarding step.
:::

steps.title: Observe the first remote exchange
steps.body:
Switch to **Simulation** mode. Open the event filters and select **ARP** and **ICMP** to keep the display manageable. From PC-A's Command Prompt, run:

```text
ping 192.168.20.20
```

Use **Capture/Forward**, or the equivalent step control in your version, to advance events. Open the event or PDU details at PC-A, R1's incoming side, and R1's outgoing side. Inspect the available Layer 2 and Layer 3 fields.

Record the request's source MAC, destination MAC, source IP, destination IP, and TTL on both sides of R1. Also record the ARP target addresses if requests appear. A cached mapping can eliminate an ARP exchange; do not invent a missing packet or assume that every ping must generate fresh ARP.

:::expected
On LAN-A, the ICMP request frame is addressed to R1's LAN-A MAC. On LAN-B, the outgoing frame uses R1's LAN-B MAC as source and PC-B's MAC as destination. The request's IP addresses remain unchanged, and normal forwarding through R1 reduces its TTL by one. Any necessary ARP on LAN-B is a separate local exchange initiated there.
:::

steps.title: Compare local and remote delivery
steps.body:
Allow the first test to finish, then use Realtime mode for a repeat ping from PC-A to PC-B. Also test PC-A to **192.168.10.1**, its local gateway address. Return to Simulation mode if needed to inspect that local request.

Compare the two packets. Their outgoing frames can use the same destination MAC, but their destination IP addresses differ. A packet addressed to 192.168.10.1 is for R1 itself; a packet addressed to 192.168.20.20 is to be forwarded toward PC-B.

:::expected
Both tests receive replies after the topology is ready. You can distinguish “using the router as next hop” from “addressing the router as the IP destination.” A gateway MAC in a frame does not imply that the packet's destination IP is the gateway.
:::

steps.title: Read the three tables
steps.body:
Collect the following evidence:

```ios R1
R1# show ip route
R1# show arp
```

```ios SW1
SW1# show mac address-table
```

```ios SW2
SW2# show mac address-table
```

On each PC, run `arp -a`. Match actual MAC addresses to the devices using the tables and the device interface information. Write down what each table associates: prefix with forwarding information, IP with MAC, or VLAN/MAC with switch port.

:::expected
SW1 learns PC-A's MAC on Fa0/1 and R1's LAN-A MAC on Fa0/24 when it receives frames from them. SW2 makes the equivalent local observations. R1 can hold ARP mappings for neighbors on both LANs. PC-A normally needs the local gateway mapping for the remote test, not PC-B's MAC.
:::

steps.title: Introduce a return-path fault
steps.body:
In PC-B's IP Configuration, change only the gateway from **192.168.20.1** to the unused address **192.168.20.254**. Keep its address and mask unchanged. Allow existing tests to finish.

From PC-B, ping its local router interface, **192.168.20.1**. Then, from PC-A, ping PC-B again. If helpful, inspect ICMP and ARP events in Simulation mode.

:::expected
PC-B can still reach 192.168.20.1 directly because that destination is local. The remote PC-A-to-PC-B exchange fails: PC-B's reply to 192.168.10.10 needs an off-subnet next hop, and its configured gateway is unavailable. A request arriving at PC-B does not guarantee a reply can return.
:::

If your results differ, verify that no extra routes, gateways, devices using .254, or previous topology changes exist. Compare the actual host settings and event details before drawing a conclusion.

steps.title: Restore and verify
steps.body:
Restore PC-B's gateway to **192.168.20.1**. Test PC-A to PC-B and PC-B to PC-A. Inspect the addressing settings and router interface summary once more. Save the completed project as **01-models-complete.pkt**.

:::expected
Both remote tests receive replies, and the configuration matches the original plan. Your lab record identifies the fault, the evidence that isolated it, the single setting corrected, and the successful retest.
:::

lab.troubleshooting:
| Symptom | Useful checks |
|---|---|
| Router link stays down | Actual cable endpoints, peer port, interface address context, and `no shutdown`; inspect `show ip interface brief`. |
| A connected subnet is missing | Verify the address/mask and operational state of that subnet's router interface. |
| Local gateway replies but the remote host does not | Check both hosts' settings, both LANs, R1's routes, and the return path. |
| No ARP request appears during a later ping | Inspect existing ARP entries; cached mappings can be reused. |
| Packet details differ from the lesson | Use your actual MACs and initial TTL; compare the forwarding changes, not fixed sample values. |
| One early timeout followed by replies | Note the timing and resolution events; investigate if loss persists instead of treating the first timeout as a diagnosis. |
lab.challenge:
Add PC-C on SW1 Fa0/2 with **192.168.10.30/24** and gateway **192.168.10.1**. Predict the ARP target and frame destination for PC-A sending to PC-C, then compare them with PC-A sending to PC-B.

**Check your result:** for PC-C, PC-A resolves 192.168.10.30 and sends directly to PC-C's MAC. For PC-B, it resolves or reuses the gateway mapping. Temporarily remove PC-A's gateway and repeat both tests: communication with PC-C should remain possible, while PC-A has no route to PC-B in this simple host configuration. Restore the gateway and verify both tests before saving.

questions.prompt: PC-A has one interface and only the connected and default routes shown. After resolving the required MAC, which destination addresses belong in its ICMP request to PC-B?
questions.explanation: PC-B is outside PC-A's /24, so the local frame goes to the gateway interface on LAN-A. The enclosed packet still names PC-B as its destination.

whyWrong.0: That MAC is on the remote LAN, not the local next hop.
whyWrong.2: The request would then be addressed to the router itself.
whyWrong.3: This is R1's interface on the remote LAN, not PC-A's local gateway.

questions.prompt: For TCP over IPv4 over Ethernet, which PDU names correspond to Layers 4, 3, and 2, in that order?
options: Packet, frame, bits
Segment, frame, packet
Frame, packet, segment
Segment, packet, frame
questions.explanation: A TCP segment is carried in an IP packet, which is carried in an Ethernet frame. UDP uses the term datagram at the transport layer.

whyWrong.0: These begin at Layer 3 and continue downward.
whyWrong.1: A frame carries the packet, not the reverse.
whyWrong.2: This lists the requested layers in reverse order.

questions.prompt: A router forwards an ordinary IPv4 packet between two Ethernet LANs. No NAT, tunnel, or fragmentation is involved. Which two actions describe normal forwarding? Choose two.
options: It decrements TTL by one and updates the IPv4 header checksum.
It changes the source IPv4 address to its outgoing interface address.
It creates a new Ethernet frame using its outgoing interface's MAC as source.
It replaces the destination IPv4 address with the next-hop IPv4 address.
It sends the incoming Ethernet frame unchanged onto the second LAN.
questions.explanation: The router performs a new link-layer encapsulation for the outgoing Ethernet LAN. Normal IPv4 forwarding reduces TTL and updates the affected header checksum, while preserving the source and destination IP addresses under these assumptions.

whyWrong.1: Ordinary routing in this example does not translate the source address.
whyWrong.3: The route identifies a forwarding action without replacing the packet's final destination address.
whyWrong.4: The outgoing link needs a frame addressed for that link.

exhibit.title: Representative R1 show arp excerpt
exhibit.text:
Protocol  Address          Age (min)  Hardware Addr   Type  Interface
Internet  192.168.10.1            -   0001.9641.7a01  ARPA  GigabitEthernet0/0
Internet  192.168.10.10           2   0060.2f3e.1b22  ARPA  GigabitEthernet0/0
Internet  192.168.20.1            -   0001.9641.7a02  ARPA  GigabitEthernet0/1
Internet  192.168.20.20           1   00d0.ba2c.5e01  ARPA  GigabitEthernet0/1

questions.prompt: R1 is configured with 192.168.10.1/24 and 192.168.20.1/24 on the interfaces shown. What does this ARP output support?
options: The .1 entries are R1's addresses; the others are neighbors.
The entries with a dash have expired.
The 192.168.10.10 entry is an IP route.
Every entry was learned from the switch's MAC table.
questions.explanation: The known interface configuration identifies the .1 entries as R1's local addresses. The numbered ages identify dynamic neighbor mappings in this excerpt. A dash alone does not distinguish all possible static and local entries.

whyWrong.1: A dash does not mean expired.
whyWrong.2: An ARP entry maps an IPv4 address to a link-layer address; it is not a route.
whyWrong.3: ARP and switch source-MAC learning populate separate tables.

questions.prompt: A host uses 172.16.5.77/24 and gateway 172.16.5.1, with no additional routes. It has no cached next-hop mapping and needs to send to 172.16.6.9. Which IPv4 address should it resolve with ARP?
questions.explanation: The /24 places the host in 172.16.5.0/24 and the destination outside that subnet. The default route selects 172.16.5.1 as the local next hop.

whyWrong.0: The destination is remote under the configured mask.
whyWrong.1: This address is not the host's configured local next hop.
whyWrong.3: The ARP request is a link-layer broadcast, but its target IPv4 address is the required gateway.

exhibit.title: Representative SW1 show mac address-table excerpt
exhibit.text:
Vlan  Mac Address       Type     Ports
1     0060.2f3e.1b22    DYNAMIC  Fa0/1
1     0001.9641.7a01    DYNAMIC  Fa0/24

questions.prompt: A frame in VLAN 1 arrives on Fa0/1 with destination MAC 0001.9641.7a01. All shown ports are forwarding. What is the normal Layer 2 forwarding action?
options: Send through Fa0/24, preserving the source and destination MAC addresses.
Flood because the remote destination IP is not in the MAC table.
Replace the destination MAC with the switch's management MAC.
Drop because a switch cannot forward a frame to a router.
questions.explanation: The destination MAC is known on Fa0/24 in VLAN 1. Ordinary Layer 2 forwarding selects that eligible port and preserves the endpoint MAC addresses; it does not perform an IP routing hop.

whyWrong.1: This lookup uses the destination MAC and VLAN, not the remote IP address.
whyWrong.2: Ordinary bridging does not rewrite the frame to the switch's management MAC.
whyWrong.3: A router interface can be the next Ethernet destination.

questions.prompt: A packet from 192.168.10.10 to 192.168.20.20 crosses one router without NAT, tunneling, or fragmentation. Which values remain the same in the forwarded IPv4 packet?
options: TTL and IPv4 header checksum
Incoming and outgoing Ethernet source MAC addresses
Source and destination IPv4 addresses
The reply packet's source and destination addresses
questions.explanation: Ordinary routing preserves the request's source and destination IP addresses. TTL and its header checksum change, and the outgoing Ethernet encapsulation is new.

whyWrong.0: TTL is decremented and the checksum must reflect the changed header.
whyWrong.1: The outgoing frame uses the outgoing interface's source MAC.
whyWrong.3: A reply is a separate packet whose IP source and destination reverse direction.

questions.prompt: A capture at the sender records an IPv4 packet with TTL 128. The same packet arrives with TTL 126. Assume ordinary forwarding, one decrement per routed hop, and no other TTL changes. How many routers forwarded it?
questions.explanation: The observed reduction is 128 − 126 = 2. The initial TTL is explicitly known here; a received TTL by itself is insufficient for an exact hop count.

whyWrong.0: There was a reduction of two.
whyWrong.1: One decrement would leave 127.
whyWrong.2: 126 is the remaining TTL, not the number of forwarding hops.

questions.prompt: Which two statements describe a normal ARP request and solicited reply on an Ethernet LAN? Choose two.
options: The request is carried in a UDP datagram.
The request normally uses the Ethernet broadcast destination.
A router forwards the original Ethernet broadcast into every connected subnet.
The solicited reply is normally unicast to the requester.
An ARP reply supplies the entire route to a remote network.
questions.explanation: ARP uses Ethernet directly to resolve an IPv4 next-hop address on the local link. A normal request is broadcast and its solicited reply is unicast; it does not distribute a remote route.

whyWrong.0: ARP is not carried in UDP or IPv4.
whyWrong.2: The Layer 2 broadcast remains in its broadcast domain; a router can initiate a separate ARP exchange on another link.
whyWrong.4: ARP supplies a local IP-to-MAC mapping, not an end-to-end path.

exhibit.title: Capture after R1
exhibit.text:
Ethernet source: R1 GigabitEthernet0/1 MAC
Ethernet destination: PC-B MAC
IPv4 source: 192.168.10.10 (PC-A)
IPv4 destination: 192.168.20.20 (PC-B)

questions.prompt: R1 routes between LAN-A and LAN-B without NAT. A capture on LAN-B shows the request below. Which explanation fits?
options: PC-A changed its own MAC to match R1.
R1 replaced the link-layer encapsulation.
SW2 changed the source IPv4 address.
The frame must be invalid because its MAC and IP source belong to different devices.
questions.explanation: On the outgoing LAN, the link-layer sender is R1, but the packet still identifies PC-A as its original IP source. This is normal routed forwarding.

whyWrong.0: The router supplies a new local-link encapsulation; PC-A's NIC address does not need to change.
whyWrong.2: The source IP remains PC-A, and ordinary Layer 2 forwarding is not IP translation.
whyWrong.3: Layer 2 and Layer 3 addresses describe different scopes, so this combination is expected.

questions.prompt: Which layer of the four-layer TCP/IP model covers IP addressing and routing?
options: Application
Transport
Internet
Link
questions.explanation: The TCP/IP Internet layer provides IP addressing and packet forwarding functions, corresponding broadly to OSI Layer 3.

whyWrong.0: Application protocols provide application-level services.
whyWrong.1: Transport includes TCP and UDP services to application endpoints.
whyWrong.3: Link handles communication across the local link.

questions.prompt: A router interface reports up/up. Which statement is justified by this output alone?
options: The local physical and line-protocol states are operational.
The connected host's default gateway is correct.
All destination applications are available.
The remote host has a working return route.
questions.explanation: Up/up describes the local interface's operational states. Host settings, routes, policy, and applications require additional evidence.

whyWrong.1: The status does not inspect the host's gateway configuration.
whyWrong.2: No application has been tested by this status display.
whyWrong.3: The output does not validate the remote return path.

questions.prompt: For HTTP carried over TCP, what is the encapsulation order as data moves from the application toward an Ethernet link?
options: HTTP data → Ethernet frame → TCP segment → IP packet
HTTP data → TCP segment → IP packet → Ethernet frame
IP packet → HTTP data → TCP segment → Ethernet frame
TCP segment → Ethernet frame → HTTP data → IP packet
questions.explanation: The specified application uses TCP, which is carried in IP and then Ethernet. The question explicitly specifies HTTP over TCP; HTTP can also use other transport arrangements, such as HTTP/3 over QUIC.

whyWrong.0: The frame is the outer link-layer unit in this example.
whyWrong.2: The application data is created before this encapsulation sequence.
whyWrong.3: This mixes the layer order.

questions.prompt: PC-A is 192.168.10.10/24 and PC-C is 192.168.10.30/24 on the same VLAN. PC-A has no additional routes and no cached mapping for PC-C. What does it normally do before sending an IPv4 packet to PC-C?
options: Resolve the remote router's WAN MAC.
Send the IPv4 packet with the subnet broadcast address as destination IP.
Send the packet to its gateway because any configured gateway must handle all traffic.
Resolve PC-C's MAC using ARP, then send directly to that MAC.
questions.explanation: The destination is on the connected /24. PC-A resolves the destination host's MAC and sends directly on the LAN. The configured gateway is not needed for this exchange.

whyWrong.0: A remote router's MAC is not the next hop for a local destination.
whyWrong.1: The packet retains PC-C's unicast destination IP.
whyWrong.2: A default gateway is used when the selected route calls for it, not for every packet.

questions.prompt: PC-A's remote ping reaches PC-B, but PC-B has an unused address configured as its default gateway. PC-B can still ping its actual local router interface. Which explanation best fits?
options: PC-B's remote reply uses an unavailable gateway.
The switch must decrement TTL twice.
The local test proves that PC-B's default gateway is correct.
ICMP requires a TCP connection before replying.
questions.explanation: A local router-interface ping uses direct delivery on PC-B's subnet. Replying to remote PC-A requires the selected off-subnet next hop, so a wrong gateway can prevent the return traffic even when the request arrives.

whyWrong.1: Ordinary switching does not decrement IP TTL.
whyWrong.2: A local destination does not require the default gateway.
whyWrong.3: ICMP Echo does not use TCP.

cards.front: Name the seven OSI layers from Layer 7 to Layer 1.
cards.back: Application, Presentation, Session, Transport, Network, Data link, Physical. Use the names to describe functions; a real device or protocol can involve several layers.

cards.front: What PDU names are commonly used for TCP, UDP, IP, and Ethernet?
cards.back: TCP segment, UDP datagram, IP packet, and Ethernet frame. The upper-layer data is carried inside the lower-layer unit in the stated protocol stack.

cards.front: How does the four-layer TCP/IP model relate to OSI?
cards.back: TCP/IP Application broadly groups OSI Layers 5–7; Transport corresponds to Layer 4; Internet to Layer 3; Link groups Layers 1–2. A five-layer teaching model splits Link into Data link and Physical.

cards.front: How do a MAC address, an IP address, and a transport port differ?
cards.back: A MAC identifies a link-layer endpoint on Ethernet; IP supports logical addressing across networks; a TCP or UDP port identifies a transport endpoint. Common field sizes are 48-bit Ethernet MAC, 32-bit IPv4, 128-bit IPv6, and 16-bit port.

cards.front: What is the relationship between an Ethernet frame, its payload, and MTU?
cards.back: An Ethernet frame carries a network-layer packet plus link-layer information and an FCS. In ordinary untagged Ethernet, a 1500-byte IP MTU fits within a frame of up to 1518 bytes counted from destination MAC through FCS. Tags and other formats can alter frame size.

cards.front: Are IPv4 and TCP headers always 20 bytes?
cards.back: No. Twenty bytes is the minimum for each; options can make them larger. The UDP header is eight bytes. Read the actual header length when interpreting a capture.

cards.front: What changes during ordinary IPv4 routing between Ethernet LANs without NAT or tunneling?
cards.back: The router creates a new Ethernet encapsulation for the outgoing link, normally decrements TTL by one, and updates the IPv4 header checksum. The packet's source and destination IP addresses remain the same.

cards.front: Can the TTL shown by a ping reply reveal the exact number of routers crossed?
cards.back: Only if the reply's starting TTL and forwarding assumptions are known. The displayed value is remaining TTL in the received reply, not automatically the request's hop count. Do not substitute a guessed operating-system default.

cards.front: How does a simple host with a connected route and default gateway choose a next hop?
cards.back: For a destination on its connected subnet, it sends directly to the destination host. Otherwise it uses the default gateway. Hosts with additional routes must select the appropriate route rather than relying only on this simplified rule.

cards.front: Does ordinary Layer 2 switching rewrite endpoint MAC addresses or decrement IP TTL?
cards.back: No. It normally preserves source and destination MAC addresses and does not create an IP routing hop. Features such as VLAN tagging can affect frame format, so do not claim that every transmitted bit must remain identical.

cards.front: Which commands display ARP mappings on IOS and a Windows or Packet Tracer PC?
cards.back: show arp on the IOS lab router; arp -a on the Windows or Packet Tracer PC command prompt. These display IP-to-MAC mappings, not routes or switch forwarding ports.

cards.front: Does an empty ARP cache prove that communication never occurred?
cards.back: No. Entries can age out, be cleared, or change. An ARP snapshot describes the mappings present at that time; combine it with configuration and current tests.

cards.front: What does up/up in show ip interface brief establish?
cards.back: The interface reports operational physical and line-protocol states. It does not independently prove correct host addressing, an end-to-end route, or application availability.

cards.front: Why can a Layer 3 switch still appear in a discussion of Layer 2 forwarding?
cards.back: A device can perform functions at multiple layers. A Layer 3 switch may bridge frames within a VLAN and route packets between IP networks. Identify the function being used for the specific traffic.

cards.front: What does a dynamic switch MAC-table entry associate?
cards.back: A VLAN and learned source MAC address with an incoming port. The switch uses destination-MAC lookups in that VLAN to select forwarding ports; the entry does not establish the host's IP configuration.

cards.front: What does the Ethernet FCS do?
cards.back: It detects corruption in a received frame; it does not correct the data. A frame rejected for an FCS error is not repaired by the FCS mechanism. Any recovery depends on other relevant mechanisms or protocols.

cards.front: Does IPv4 ping use TCP or UDP ports?
cards.back: Neither. It uses ICMP Echo Request and Echo Reply messages carried directly in IPv4. A successful ping does not prove that a TCP or UDP application is available.

cards.front: Which address does ARP resolve before a correctly configured host sends to a remote subnet through its default gateway?
cards.back: The local gateway's IPv4 address. The Ethernet frame is addressed to that gateway's MAC, while the enclosed IP packet keeps the remote destination IP.

cards.front: What limits the scope of a normal Ethernet ARP request?
cards.back: It is a local Layer 2 broadcast. Switches flood it to eligible forwarding ports in the same VLAN except the incoming port; routers do not route the original Ethernet broadcast into other subnets.

cards.front: Why must you consider the return path when troubleshooting a ping?
cards.back: The source needs an Echo Reply, not just delivery of the request. A destination with an incorrect gateway can receive a request yet fail to return its reply to a remote subnet.

commands.task: Display R1's IPv4-to-MAC mappings.
commands.note: Read the address, MAC, interface, and age together. An entry does not test an application.

commands.task: Display the switch's MAC address table.
commands.note: This table associates VLAN/MAC entries with switch ports. Command spelling varies on older images.

commands.task: Display IPv4 addresses and a brief summary of router interface states.
commands.note: Check both Status and Protocol, then investigate the relevant interface if needed.

commands.task: Display the IPv4 routing table.
commands.note: In the two-LAN lab, expect connected routes for both operational, addressed router interfaces.

commands.task: Display this PC's ARP cache.
commands.note: This is a Windows/Packet Tracer PC command, not an IOS command. Cached entries may be reused without new ARP requests.

commands.task: Inspect detailed status and counters for R1's LAN-A interface.
commands.note: Use the actual interface name on your model. A counter is evidence to interpret, not a complete diagnosis by itself.

commands.task: Assign 192.168.10.1/24 to the selected R1 Ethernet interface.
commands.note: Confirm you selected GigabitEthernet0/0 for LAN-A, then enable and verify the interface.

commands.task: Trace the route toward 192.168.20.20 from IOS.
commands.note: Probe types and displayed responses vary. A missing response is not proof that the hop cannot forward traffic.

commands.task: Trace toward 192.168.20.20 from a Windows or supported Packet Tracer PC command prompt.
commands.note: Windows uses tracert; IOS uses traceroute. If the simulator lacks the command, use its supported event inspection.

commands.task: Enable the selected router Ethernet interface after configuring its address.
commands.note: Administrative enablement is necessary here; verify the actual physical and line-protocol states afterward.

commands.task: Test ICMP reachability from R1 toward PC-B at 192.168.20.20.
commands.note: Interpret the result for this source, destination, and time. A router-originated ping can use a different source address from a PC-originated test.
