lab.title: Follow traffic through switches and a router
lab.intro:
Build two small Ethernet LANs and use a router to connect them. You will identify the job of each device, test a local service, and observe which communication stops when one router interface is shut down.

This is a first look at routing, not a routing configuration course. Follow the supplied addresses exactly; later chapters explain how to calculate networks and choose addresses yourself. No Internet connection, DNS server, DHCP service, VLAN configuration or static route is required. The router learns these two networks from its own active interfaces.
lab.topology:
Start a new Packet Tracer file. Choose the **2911** router and **2960** switches from the device palette; the named interfaces below belong to those models. Use the standard **PC** and **Server** end devices. If your installation uses different labels, select the equivalent Ethernet interface and record the change.

```diagram
{"type":"topology","title":"Fig 02.L1 — Two LANs joined by R1","caption":"PC-A reaches Server-A through SW1; reaching PC-B also requires R1 and SW2.","nodes":[{"id":"A","kind":"pc","label":"PC-A","sub":"192.0.2.10","x":0.5,"y":1},{"id":"S","kind":"server","label":"Server-A","sub":"192.0.2.20","x":0.5,"y":5},{"id":"SW1","kind":"switch","label":"SW1","x":3,"y":3},{"id":"R1","kind":"router","label":"R1","x":6,"y":3},{"id":"SW2","kind":"switch","label":"SW2","x":9,"y":3},{"id":"B","kind":"pc","label":"PC-B","sub":"198.51.100.10","x":11.5,"y":3}],"links":[{"from":"A","to":"SW1","toLabel":"Fa0/1"},{"from":"S","to":"SW1","toLabel":"Fa0/2"},{"from":"SW1","to":"R1","fromLabel":"Gi0/1","toLabel":"Gi0/0"},{"from":"R1","to":"SW2","fromLabel":"Gi0/1","toLabel":"Gi0/1"},{"from":"SW2","to":"B","fromLabel":"Fa0/1"}]}
```

| Device and interface | Address | Mask | Default gateway |
|---|---|---|---|
| PC-A FastEthernet0 | `192.0.2.10` | `255.255.255.0` | `192.0.2.1` |
| Server-A FastEthernet0 | `192.0.2.20` | `255.255.255.0` | `192.0.2.1` |
| R1 GigabitEthernet0/0 | `192.0.2.1` | `255.255.255.0` | Not entered on this interface |
| R1 GigabitEthernet0/1 | `198.51.100.1` | `255.255.255.0` | Not entered on this interface |
| PC-B FastEthernet0 | `198.51.100.10` | `255.255.255.0` | `198.51.100.1` |

The switches need no management IP address for this exercise. Their default access ports can already switch frames within VLAN 1. The two switches are not directly cabled together.

steps.title: Place, label and cable the devices
steps.body:
Change each device's display name to match the diagram. Select **Copper Straight-Through** and make these five connections. Check the port names at both ends before clicking.

| First end | Second end | Cable |
|---|---|---|
| PC-A FastEthernet0 | SW1 FastEthernet0/1 | Copper straight-through |
| Server-A FastEthernet0 | SW1 FastEthernet0/2 | Copper straight-through |
| SW1 GigabitEthernet0/1 | R1 GigabitEthernet0/0 | Copper straight-through |
| R1 GigabitEthernet0/1 | SW2 GigabitEthernet0/1 | Copper straight-through |
| SW2 FastEthernet0/1 | PC-B FastEthernet0 | Copper straight-through |

:::expected
All five cables connect the intended ports. Endpoint-to-switch links can take time to become usable as switch ports initialize. Router-facing links may remain down until Step 3 enables the router interfaces. A red router link at this point is not a reason to change the IP addresses or replace every cable.
:::

steps.title: Name the switches and inspect their connections
steps.body:
Open SW1's **CLI** tab. Press Enter if necessary; if an initial configuration dialog appears, answer `no`. Enter the following commands. A `>` prompt is user EXEC mode; `enable` reaches the privileged `#` prompt. `configure terminal` enters configuration mode, and `end` returns to privileged EXEC.

```ios SW1
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname SW1
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# description PC-A
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if)# interface fastethernet0/2
SW1(config-if)# description Server-A
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# description R1-GigabitEthernet0/0
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show interfaces status
```

Repeat on **SW2**, using its own block.

```ios SW2
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname SW2
SW2(config)# interface fastethernet0/1
SW2(config-if)# description PC-B
SW2(config-if)# no shutdown
SW2(config-if)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW2(config-if)# description R1-GigabitEthernet0/1
SW2(config-if)# no shutdown
SW2(config-if)# end
SW2# show interfaces status
```

:::expected
The prompts identify the correct switches, and the listed port descriptions match the cables. The PC and server ports should reach `connected` once their endpoints are powered on. Router-facing ports may still show `notconnect`. If `show interfaces status` is unavailable in your simulator version, inspect each port with `show interfaces fastethernet0/1` or its corresponding interface name and check its state.
:::

steps.title: Address and enable the router and endpoints
steps.body:
Open R1's CLI and decline the initial configuration dialog if offered. Configure one address on each router interface. These addresses will be the PCs' default gateways: the next device used to reach the other LAN.

```ios R1
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R1
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# description LAN-A-to-SW1
R1(config-if)# ip address 192.0.2.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# description LAN-B-to-SW2
R1(config-if)# ip address 198.51.100.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip interface brief
```

On **each PC and Server-A**, open **Desktop → IP Configuration**, select **Static**, and enter its address, mask and gateway from the table. Leave DNS blank. On Server-A, open **Services → HTTP** and set HTTP to **On**. You do not need to edit the supplied web page.

:::expected
R1's GigabitEthernet0/0 has `192.0.2.1` and GigabitEthernet0/1 has `198.51.100.1`; both should become `up/up`. Recheck the actual IP Configuration window on each endpoint rather than assuming an entry saved correctly. The router's address belongs in the gateway field; the endpoint's own address does not.
:::

steps.title: Test the local server
steps.body:
On PC-A, open **Desktop → Command Prompt** and enter `ping 192.0.2.20`. Repeat once if the first attempt loses an initial request while addresses are resolved. Then open **Desktop → Web Browser** and visit `http://192.0.2.20`. Use the numeric address so this test does not depend on name resolution.

Write the device path for this traffic. PC-A and Server-A share the same LAN, so their frames pass through SW1 without needing to pass through R1. Do not disconnect anything yet.

:::expected
The repeated ping receives replies and the browser displays Server-A's page. The forwarding path is PC-A → SW1 → Server-A. If ping works but the page does not load, check HTTP service and the URL before changing the switch configuration. A successful ping checks IP reachability; it does not prove that an application is running.
:::

steps.title: Test the other LAN
steps.body:
From PC-A's command prompt, ping `192.0.2.1`, then `198.51.100.10`. From PC-B, ping `198.51.100.1` and `192.0.2.20`. On PC-B's browser, visit `http://192.0.2.20`.

Inspect the router:

```ios R1
R1# show ip route
R1# show ip interface brief
```

:::expected
Repeated tests reach the other LAN. R1's routing table contains connected networks for `192.0.2.0/24` through GigabitEthernet0/0 and `198.51.100.0/24` through GigabitEthernet0/1. IOS may also show local /32 routes for the router's own addresses. You did not need to add static routes because both networks are directly attached and active.

The path from PC-A to PC-B is PC-A → SW1 → R1 → SW2 → PC-B. A missing default gateway can leave the Step 4 local test working while this remote test fails. Check both the sender's gateway and the return path from the destination.
:::

steps.title: Shut one router interface and observe the effect
steps.body:
Save a working copy of the Packet Tracer file as `02-components-working.pkt` before introducing the fault. On **R1 only**, disable the interface toward SW2.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip interface brief
```

Leave the fault in place while you test. From PC-A, repeat `ping 192.0.2.20` and `ping 198.51.100.10`. Refresh Server-A's page from PC-A and attempt a new request from PC-B. Record which tests work before proceeding.

:::expected
R1's GigabitEthernet0/1 shows `administratively down` with protocol down. PC-A can still reach Server-A through SW1, but PC-A cannot reach PC-B. PC-B has lost its path through R1 to Server-A. Use fresh ping requests as the clearest check; a browser may retain a page that it downloaded earlier.

The failure affects the path that uses the disabled interface. It does not stop SW1 from switching local frames, and it does not prove that Server-A's HTTP service has failed.
:::

steps.title: Restore and verify service
steps.body:
Return the failed interface to its working state.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip interface brief
R1# show ip route
```

:::expected
GigabitEthernet0/1 returns to `up/up` after the link initializes, and its connected network returns to the routing table. Repeat PC-A's ping to PC-B and PC-B's ping and HTTP request to Server-A. Both remote tests and the local test from Step 4 must work again. Recovery is complete when communication is restored, not merely when the command is accepted.
:::

steps.title: Save the restored configurations
steps.body:
On each device, save its running configuration. These are interactive commands: after each one, accept the displayed destination filename by pressing Enter. Do not paste the next device's commands into that prompt.

```ios R1
R1# copy running-config startup-config
```

```ios SW1
SW1# copy running-config startup-config
```

```ios SW2
SW2# copy running-config startup-config
```

:::expected
Each device reports that the copy completed; wording varies by IOS simulation. Use **File → Save As** to save the restored project as `02-components-complete.pkt`. Saving the Packet Tracer project preserves the topology and endpoint settings as well as device state. The completed file must contain the restored `no shutdown` state, not the Step 6 fault.
:::

steps.title: Explain the roles and a proposed expansion
steps.body:
Without changing the topology, answer these three questions in your notes.

1. Which device supplies the local Layer 2 forwarding role, which supplies routing, and which supplies a web service?
2. If the office adds Wi-Fi, which function is missing? If it adds policy enforcement between the LAN and Internet, which security function should the design consider?
3. A proposed PoE switch has a 120 W budget. Each compatible AP is allocated 30 W, and each selected port supports that allocation. Can four APs fit? Can five?

:::expected
SW1 and SW2 supply Layer 2 switching, R1 routes between the two LANs, and Server-A supplies HTTP. Wi-Fi needs an access point; a larger deployment may also use a controller. A firewall supplies traffic-policy enforcement, potentially with IPS capabilities depending on the required design.

Four 30 W allocations total 120 W and fit the stated budget exactly; five total 150 W and do not. Real selection must also account for the switch's available budget under its actual power supplies, other powered devices, and the APs' supported power requirements. This is a paper allocation exercise, not a claim that the Packet Tracer 2960 models PoE.
:::

lab.troubleshooting:
- **A router port remains administratively down:** identify the correct R1 interface with `show ip interface brief`, enter that interface, and apply `no shutdown`.
- **A router port is down but not administratively down:** inspect the cable endpoints, the far switch port and device power. An IP address cannot repair a disconnected cable.
- **PC-A cannot reach Server-A:** verify `192.0.2.10` and `192.0.2.20` with mask `255.255.255.0`, inspect SW1's endpoint ports, and retry after link initialization.
- **Local traffic works but remote traffic fails:** compare each endpoint's gateway with the address on its local R1 interface. Verify that both router interfaces are up.
- **Ping works but HTTP fails:** check that HTTP is on, use `http://` and the correct numeric address, and generate a new browser request.
- **The CLI rejects a command:** check the device and prompt first. Do not enter router `ip address` commands on a 2960 physical switch port. Inspect `?` for available syntax when a display command differs.
lab.challenge:
Add PC-C to SW2 FastEthernet0/2 using copper straight-through. Assign it the unused address `198.51.100.20` and choose its mask and gateway from the existing design. Without copying a routing configuration, make PC-C reach both PC-B and Server-A's web page.

Then predict what happens to PC-C → PC-B and PC-C → Server-A if R1 GigabitEthernet0/1 is shut down again. Test your prediction, restore the interface, retest, and save a separate challenge file.

:::expected
PC-C uses mask `255.255.255.0` and gateway `198.51.100.1`. No extra route or switch management address is needed. PC-C reaches PC-B through SW2 and reaches Server-A through SW2 → R1 → SW1. With R1 GigabitEthernet0/1 shut down, the local PC-B test continues to work while the remote server test fails. Restore R1 GigabitEthernet0/1 with `no shutdown`, confirm `up/up`, and verify both tests before saving.
:::

questions.prompt: A PC must send an IP packet to a different IP network. Which function selects the next hop using the destination IP address?
options: A Layer 2 switch forwarding within one VLAN
An access point accepting a wireless association
A router consulting its IP routing table
A hub repeating the received electrical signal
questions.explanation: Routing selects an outgoing path using the destination IP network and the routing table. A router or a Layer 3 switch with routing configured can supply this function.

whyWrong.0: Layer 2 forwarding uses MAC addresses within the local VLAN rather than selecting an IP next hop.
whyWrong.1: Wireless association establishes a client's connection to an AP; it does not by itself choose routes between IP networks.
whyWrong.3: A hub repeats signals and does not inspect an IP routing table.

exhibit.title: Documented forwarding behavior — teaching evidence, not CLI output
exhibit.text:
SW3 forwards frames between local ports in each VLAN.
SW3 is configured with IP routing and serves as gateway for two IP networks.
Traffic between those networks is routed by SW3.

questions.prompt: Which device role best matches the documented behavior of SW3?
options: A Layer 2 switch providing management access
A wireless controller managing radio settings
A hub connecting a shared Ethernet segment
A Layer 3 switch performing routing and switching
questions.explanation: SW3 both forwards Ethernet frames within each LAN and routes between the IP networks. Those documented functions justify identifying a Layer 3 switching role; the label on a diagram alone would not establish that routing is configured.

whyWrong.0: A management IP address alone would not provide the documented forwarding between networks.
whyWrong.1: The evidence describes wired switching and IP routing, not AP management.
whyWrong.2: A hub neither learns destination MAC forwarding entries nor makes IP routing decisions.

questions.prompt: Which two statements accurately describe a next-generation firewall and an inline IPS? (Choose two.)
options: An NGFW can add application-aware policy to stateful traffic inspection.
An inline IPS can reject traffic it identifies as malicious under its policy.
An NGFW replaces the need for routing decisions on connected networks.
An inline IPS must allow a detected attack through before reporting it.
An NGFW can inspect every encrypted payload without decryption access.
questions.explanation: An NGFW combines traffic-policy enforcement with capabilities such as application visibility and intrusion prevention. An inline IPS sits in the traffic path and can block a detected threat, subject to its configuration and inspection capability.

whyWrong.2: Security inspection and routing solve different problems; a design still needs a forwarding path.
whyWrong.3: Inline placement permits a prevention action before forwarding; alert-only behavior is a policy choice, not a requirement.
whyWrong.4: Encrypted payload visibility depends on decryption capability, policy and the actual traffic; it is not automatic.

questions.prompt: A company wants a consistent wireless configuration across many access points. What is the main role of a wireless LAN controller?
options: Coordinate AP configuration, operation and monitoring
Replace every Ethernet switch that connects the APs
Supply electrical power to all APs through a radio link
Store the web content requested by wireless clients
questions.explanation: A wireless LAN controller provides centralized coordination for supported APs, including configuration and monitoring. The traffic-forwarding path depends on the wireless deployment; controller management does not mean every data frame follows the same path.

whyWrong.1: APs commonly still need a wired network connection and the switching infrastructure behind it.
whyWrong.2: PoE comes through a compatible wired power source, not the controller's radio coordination.
whyWrong.3: A web server supplies web content; that is a different role.

questions.prompt: An office adds compatible controller-managed access points on PoE switch ports. Which two statements describe the design correctly? (Choose two.)
options: The AP must provide a separate IP router function for every associated client.
The AP connects wireless clients to the wired network through its uplink.
The controller makes a sufficient switch power budget unnecessary.
The switch can supply power and Ethernet connectivity on the AP's cable.
The controller must carry all user traffic in every supported deployment.
questions.explanation: The AP supplies wireless access, while a compatible PoE switch can supply both its wired connection and electrical power. A controller coordinates AP operation, but forwarding and power requirements still depend on the chosen design.

whyWrong.0: Wireless access does not require a distinct routing function for every client; integrated devices may offer additional functions.
whyWrong.2: A controller does not create additional electrical power in the switch's PoE budget.
whyWrong.4: Some deployments switch traffic locally, so controller management does not imply universal centralized forwarding.

questions.prompt: Which IEEE PoE option supplies up to 30 W at the power-sourcing port?
options: 802.3af Type 1
802.3bt Type 4
802.3at Type 2
802.3bt Type 3
questions.explanation: 802.3at, often called PoE+, supplies up to 30 W at the power source. The power available to the attached device is lower after cable losses; do not confuse source and device-side ratings.

whyWrong.0: 802.3af supplies up to 15.4 W at the source.
whyWrong.1: 802.3bt Type 4 supports a higher source rating, up to 90 W.
whyWrong.3: 802.3bt Type 3 supports a higher source rating, up to 60 W.

exhibit.title: PoE allocation worksheet — supplied values
exhibit.text:
Available budget: 120 W
Existing allocations: 90 W
Remaining budget: 30 W
Each proposed AP allocation: 30 W

questions.prompt: Each additional AP needs a 30 W allocation, and each selected port supports it. Based on the stated total budget, how many more such APs can the switch support?
options: Three additional APs
Two additional APs
No additional APs
One additional AP
questions.explanation: The remaining allocation budget is 120 − 90 = 30 W, enough for one more 30 W AP. Per-port capability and aggregate available power must both be sufficient.

whyWrong.0: Three APs would require 90 W of additional available budget.
whyWrong.1: Two APs would require 60 W, more than the stated remainder.
whyWrong.2: The given 30 W remainder does fit one compatible 30 W allocation.

exhibit.title: Campus design notes
exhibit.text:
Access switches connect users and APs.
Their uplinks reach a redundant pair of switches.
That pair performs both distribution and core functions.
There is no separate core layer.

questions.prompt: Which campus architecture matches the described design?
options: A two-tier design with a collapsed distribution/core layer
A three-tier design with a separate core between distribution blocks
A spine-leaf design with every endpoint attached directly to a spine
A WAN hub-and-spoke design using one office as the provider
questions.explanation: A two-tier campus combines distribution and core functions into a collapsed layer above access. Redundant devices can exist within that layer without turning the architecture into three tiers.

whyWrong.1: The description explicitly combines distribution and core rather than separating them.
whyWrong.2: Spine-leaf has different roles, and endpoints normally attach to leaves in the basic design.
whyWrong.3: This is an internal campus hierarchy, not a description of WAN site connections.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of the core in a three-tier campus design?
options: Attach desks and phones directly to their local network
Provide a resilient, high-capacity path between distribution blocks
Convert each client's radio signal into an Ethernet frame
Host the office's application databases and shared files
questions.explanation: The core interconnects distribution blocks and provides a reliable transport path across the campus. Access connects endpoints; distribution aggregates access and commonly provides routing or policy boundaries.

whyWrong.0: Endpoint attachment is the access layer's principal role.
whyWrong.2: An access point supplies the wireless-to-wired access function.
whyWrong.3: Application hosting is a server role, not the defining purpose of a campus core.

exhibit.title: Basic spine-leaf plan
exhibit.text:
Spines: S1, S2
Leaves: L1, L2, L3
Each leaf connects to S1 and S2.
Servers attach to leaf ports.

questions.prompt: Which two statements describe the basic two-tier spine-leaf design shown in the notes? (Choose two.)
options: Each leaf has a link to each spine.
Each server connects directly to both spines.
Endpoints normally attach to leaf switches.
Leaves must form a chain before reaching a spine.
Adding a spine eliminates the need to configure forwarding.
questions.explanation: In the basic spine-leaf pattern, endpoints connect to leaves and each leaf connects to every spine. These physical paths support a scalable design, but routing and other forwarding choices still require an appropriate configuration.

whyWrong.1: The basic pattern attaches servers to leaves rather than directly to spines.
whyWrong.3: A leaf chain is not the described basic spine-leaf connection pattern.
whyWrong.4: A cable creates a physical path; usable forwarding requires correct configuration.

questions.prompt: Three branches reach headquarters through separate WAN links. Each branch's only path to the others passes through headquarters. What is the effect of losing the headquarters transit function?
options: Only local switching inside headquarters must fail.
All branch LAN interfaces must lose their physical link.
Communication between branches loses its only designed path.
Each branch automatically becomes a full-mesh transit point.
questions.explanation: In this hub-and-spoke design, interbranch communication depends on the hub's transit role. A failure there removes that path even if each branch's local LAN continues operating.

whyWrong.0: The impact includes traffic using headquarters as transit; local switching may remain operational.
whyWrong.1: A remote transit failure does not imply that every branch's local physical interface goes down.
whyWrong.3: A new full mesh does not appear automatically; alternate connectivity and forwarding would need to exist.

questions.prompt: A computer supplies web pages to other computers on the network. Which description is most accurate?
options: It becomes a router because several clients use it.
It is a switch because it has an Ethernet address.
It ceases to be an endpoint when HTTP is enabled.
It is an endpoint performing a server role.
questions.explanation: A server supplies a service such as HTTP to clients and is also an endpoint on the network. Server and endpoint describe compatible roles, not mutually exclusive hardware categories.

whyWrong.0: Serving application data is different from forwarding IP packets between networks.
whyWrong.1: An Ethernet address does not make a device an Ethernet switch.
whyWrong.2: Enabling a service does not remove the machine's role as a traffic endpoint.

questions.prompt: On a home device combining routing, switching and an AP, wired clients still reach the Internet. Nearby wireless clients cannot find the configured network name. Which function should be investigated first?
options: The WAN routing function that the wired clients are using
The wireless access-point function and its radio configuration
The Ethernet switching function serving the wired clients
The remote Internet server used by both kinds of client
questions.explanation: The symptom is failure to discover the wireless network, while the wired forwarding path works. Start with the AP's radio, network-name settings and wireless environment before changing a working wired path.

whyWrong.0: Successful wired Internet use is evidence that the WAN path is working for those clients.
whyWrong.2: The failed step is wireless discovery rather than the wired clients' Ethernet attachment.
whyWrong.3: Clients must first discover and join the local wireless network before reaching a remote server.

questions.prompt: A hosted application automatically adds capacity as demand grows and releases it when demand falls. Which cloud characteristic does this illustrate?
options: Rapid elasticity
A fixed on-premises capacity limit
A shared Ethernet collision domain
A separate physical server for every request
questions.explanation: Rapid elasticity is the ability to expand and reduce provisioned resources in response to demand. It differs from simply hosting a server in someone else's building.

whyWrong.1: The scenario changes resource capacity rather than remaining at a fixed installed amount.
whyWrong.2: Collision domains describe Ethernet media behavior, not resource scaling.
whyWrong.3: Elasticity does not require a separate physical machine for each request.

questions.prompt: Developers deploy their own application to a provider-managed runtime. The provider maintains the operating system and platform, while the developers control their application. Which service model best fits?
options: Software as a Service, with the provider's finished application
Infrastructure as a Service, with customer-managed guest operating systems
Platform as a Service, with a managed application environment
On-premises hosting, with the customer's own physical facilities
questions.explanation: Platform as a Service supplies a managed environment on which customers deploy their applications. The key distinction is the division of responsibility, not the fact that users reach the application over a network.

whyWrong.0: SaaS supplies an application to use rather than a runtime for the customer's own application deployment.
whyWrong.1: IaaS normally gives the customer responsibility for its guest operating system and application stack.
whyWrong.3: The stated runtime and operating system are maintained by the provider, not described as customer-owned on-premises equipment.

cards.front: What addresses guide Layer 2 switching and IP routing?
cards.back: Layer 2 switching uses destination MAC addresses within a VLAN. Routing uses the destination IP address and a routing table.

cards.front: What makes a switch a Layer 3 switch?
cards.back: It supports IP routing as well as Ethernet switching. Routing must be configured; a management IP alone does not establish a forwarding role.

cards.front: 802.3af Type 1: maximum power supplied at the source port?
cards.back: 15.4 W. Device-side available power is lower because of cable losses.

cards.front: 802.3at Type 2: maximum power supplied at the source port?
cards.back: 30 W; commonly called PoE+. Distinguish supplied power from power available at the powered device.

cards.front: 802.3bt Types 3 and 4: maximum source-port power?
cards.back: Type 3: up to 60 W. Type 4: up to 90 W. Check the actual switch and powered-device capabilities.

cards.front: What two power limits must a PoE design satisfy?
cards.back: The selected port must support the device's required allocation, and the total allocations must fit the switch's available power budget.

cards.front: What are PSE and PD, and why does PoE detection matter?
cards.back: The PSE supplies power; the PD receives it. Standards-based detection checks for a compatible powered device before normal operating power is supplied.

cards.front: Which commands inspect, allow and disable PoE on supported Cisco ports?
cards.back: show power inline inspects it. In interface configuration, power inline auto allows detection/allocation; power inline never disables PoE.

cards.front: What does a next-generation firewall add to stateful filtering?
cards.back: Capabilities such as application-aware policy and intrusion prevention. Inspectable traffic and enforcement depend on configuration and visibility.

cards.front: How do IDS and inline IPS differ?
cards.back: IDS detects and reports suspicious activity. An inline IPS can block traffic as it passes, according to policy; detection is not a guarantee against every attack.

cards.front: Cisco DNA Center (Catalyst Center) versus a WLC: main roles?
cards.back: Catalyst Center provides management, automation and health information for supported campus devices. A wireless LAN controller coordinates its APs; client forwarding depends on the deployment.

cards.front: Campus access, distribution and core: primary roles?
cards.back: Access attaches endpoints; distribution aggregates access and often supplies routing/policy boundaries; core interconnects distribution blocks.

cards.front: Two-tier versus three-tier campus design?
cards.back: Two-tier combines distribution and core functions. Three-tier separates access, distribution and core; device count alone does not define the tiers.

cards.front: Why do two physical uplinks not automatically guarantee redundancy?
cards.back: Both paths need a compatible design and forwarding configuration. Identify shared devices, power and other failure dependencies before claiming resilience.

cards.front: What connects to what in a basic spine-leaf design?
cards.back: Endpoints normally attach to leaves. Each leaf connects to every spine. This is the basic reference pattern, not a universal rule for every fabric variant.

cards.front: What must be available when adding a leaf to a basic spine-leaf fabric?
cards.back: A connection to each spine, suitable ports and capacity, and the required forwarding configuration; adding cables alone is insufficient.

cards.front: What distinguishes a WAN from a local LAN?
cards.back: A WAN connects networks across a wider geographic area, often through provider services. Local switching can remain operational when the WAN path fails.

cards.front: Can a server also be an endpoint?
cards.back: Yes. An endpoint originates or receives traffic; a server is an endpoint supplying a service such as HTTP to clients.

cards.front: Which functions can one SOHO wireless router combine?
cards.back: Ethernet switching, wireless access, IP routing and security functions. Diagnose the failed function rather than treating the whole enclosure as one role.

cards.front: How do on-premises hosting and cloud services differ?
cards.back: On-premises describes a local deployment location. Cloud describes a service model with characteristics such as on-demand resources and elasticity; a private cloud can also be on premises.

commands.note: Hardware command recognition. The Packet Tracer 2960 lab does not require or promise PoE simulation.

commands.task: Display the switch's compact table of port state, VLAN, duplex and speed.
commands.note: Compare the named ports with the physical cable table. This is a read-only check.

commands.note: Supported PoE hardware only. This removes power from a connected powered device; it is not a routine requirement for PC ports.

commands.task: On a supported PoE port, allow automatic powered-device detection and allocation.
commands.note: Allocation still depends on compatible devices, per-port capability and the available budget.

commands.task: Enter configuration for GigabitEthernet0/0 on the 2911 router.
commands.note: Confirm the physical cable reaches this interface before changing it.

commands.task: Show interface IP addresses and their status and protocol states in one summary.
commands.note: Verify the address and both state columns. Up/up does not by itself prove an application works.

commands.task: Display the router's IPv4 routing table.
commands.note: In this introductory lab, identify the two directly connected networks; no static routes are needed.

commands.task: Enable the router interface you have already selected.
commands.note: Then check its operational state and test traffic. The far end and cable must also be operational.

commands.task: Set the selected interface's descriptive label to LAN-A-to-SW1.
