commands.task: Save the running router configuration to its startup configuration.
commands.note: This command prompts for a destination filename. Press Enter to accept it, wait for completion, then save the Packet Tracer project separately.

tickets.title: A third-floor switch loses its path when another floor reboots
tickets.scenario: The building uses access switches and a collapsed distribution/core pair. Users on A3 can reach their local printer, but lose access to the server network whenever A2 is powered off. A cable inspection confirms the connections below. There are no unlisted links or wireless alternatives.

exhibits.title: Verified physical connection record
exhibits.text:
A1 uplink 1 → CC1
A1 uplink 2 → CC2
A2 uplink 1 → CC1
A2 uplink 2 → CC2
A3 uplink 1 → A2
A3 uplink 2 → no cable
Server network → collapsed distribution/core layer

exhibits.title: Tests while A2 is powered off
exhibits.text:
A3 user → printer attached to A3: succeeds
A3 user → server network: fails
A1 user → server network: succeeds

tickets.question: Which dependency explains A3's loss of server access?
options: A3 cannot switch local traffic while the collapsed core operates.
A3's only path to the server network passes through A2.
Every access-switch reboot must disable the whole campus.
The server application must stop whenever any access switch fails.
tickets.explanation: The verified cable record gives A3 only one uplink, and it leads through A2. Local traffic on A3 can continue, but traffic toward the server network loses its path while A2 is off. This is a specific single-path dependency; it does not establish that every access-switch chain is forbidden or that an unused port is administratively shut down.
tickets.fix: Record A3's dependency in the diagram and restore A2 to recover the existing path. Verify local and server tests again. For a planned improvement, connect A3 to the intended distribution/core layer using a reviewed design that supplies appropriate independent paths and forwarding configuration. Do not create extra Layer 2 links casually: later switching chapters explain loop prevention. After an approved redesign, update the port records and test each intended failure separately; two cables alone do not prove resilience.

tickets.title: Two compatible phones receive no PoE power
tickets.scenario: Two compatible IEEE PoE phones remain dark on a supported PoE Catalyst switch. A controlled test confirms both phones power on through a known-good cable on another compatible port. The switch has sufficient remaining budget for both phones. The following excerpts are representative teaching evidence, not a claim of a completed hardware test.

exhibits.title: Selected running configuration
exhibits.text:
interface GigabitEthernet1/0/7
 description Conference-phone-A
 power inline never
!
interface GigabitEthernet1/0/8
 description Conference-phone-B
 power inline never

exhibits.title: Power allocation worksheet
exhibits.text:
Remaining switch budget: 120 W
Required allocation for each phone: 15.4 W or less
Both selected ports support the required standard and allocation
PoE administration on Gi1/0/7 and Gi1/0/8: disabled

tickets.question: Which finding directly explains why the switch is not supplying power on these ports?
options: The two phones require more power than the 120 W remainder.
An IP address must be assigned before IEEE PoE can supply power.
Power delivery is disabled by power inline never.
A wireless controller must authorize each wired phone's power.
tickets.explanation: Both selected interfaces explicitly disable PoE. The supplied compatibility and budget information rule out those two constraints in this exercise, so the administrative setting must be corrected. Standard power detection does not require the phone to have an IP address first.
tickets.fix:
On the supported PoE switch, restore automatic power detection on each intended port:
```ios ASW1
ASW1# configure terminal
ASW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet1/0/7
ASW1(config-if)# power inline auto
ASW1(config-if)# interface gigabitethernet1/0/8
ASW1(config-if)# power inline auto
ASW1(config-if)# end
ASW1# show power inline
```
Check that each port detects its phone and supplies an appropriate allocation without exhausting the budget. Allow the devices to boot and verify their operation; do not expect a specific watt reading or boot time from this exercise. If detection still fails, test the affected cable paths and ports independently. This is hardware command recognition; PoE behavior is not required of the Packet Tracer 2960 lab.

lab.title: Establish a baseline and diagnose Ethernet link faults
lab.intro:
Build one small LAN in Packet Tracer, verify it, and introduce one interface fault at a time. You will compare both ends of the same link, restore service between tests, and finish with supplied fiber and cable-test evidence.

Packet Tracer does not reproduce every hardware counter, physical cable defect or optical power measurement. The configured speed/duplex and administrative states are the main observations in this lab. If the simulated traffic or error counters do not behave like hardware, record that limit and use the lesson's representative examples to explain the real mechanism. The optical exercise is paper-based; no optical meter or transceiver is required.
lab.topology:
Use two **2960** switches, named SW1 and SW2, and two standard **PC** end devices, named PC-A and PC-B. Start a new file. The interswitch link deliberately uses FastEthernet ports so the 10/100 duplex exercise applies.

```diagram
{"type":"topology","title":"Fig 03.L1 — One LAN with a testable interswitch link","caption":"Both PCs share one subnet; the tests require switching but no router or default gateway.","nodes":[{"id":"A","kind":"pc","label":"PC-A","sub":"10.0.30.11/24","x":1,"y":3},{"id":"S1","kind":"switch","label":"SW1","x":4,"y":3},{"id":"S2","kind":"switch","label":"SW2","x":8,"y":3},{"id":"B","kind":"pc","label":"PC-B","sub":"10.0.30.12/24","x":11,"y":3}],"links":[{"from":"A","to":"S1","toLabel":"Fa0/1","label":"straight-through"},{"from":"S1","to":"S2","fromLabel":"Fa0/24","toLabel":"Fa0/24","label":"crossover"},{"from":"S2","to":"B","fromLabel":"Fa0/1","label":"straight-through"}]}
```

| Device and interface | Connection or address | Cable or mask |
|---|---|---|
| PC-A FastEthernet0 | SW1 FastEthernet0/1 | Copper straight-through |
| SW1 FastEthernet0/24 | SW2 FastEthernet0/24 | Copper crossover |
| SW2 FastEthernet0/1 | PC-B FastEthernet0 | Copper straight-through |
| PC-A | `10.0.30.11` | `255.255.255.0` |
| PC-B | `10.0.30.12` | `255.255.255.0` |

Leave both PCs' default gateway and DNS fields blank. No switch management IP, trunk, VLAN change or route is needed. The switch ports remain in their default VLAN 1. Do not add a second interswitch link.

steps.title: Cable, name and address the network
steps.body:
Connect the three cables exactly as listed. On each PC, open **Desktop → IP Configuration**, choose **Static**, and enter its address and mask. Clear any leftover gateway or DNS address if you reused a device.

Open SW1's CLI, press Enter and decline the initial configuration dialog if present. Enter its baseline configuration.

```ios SW1
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname SW1
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# description PC-A
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if)# interface fastethernet0/24
SW1(config-if)# description To-SW2
SW1(config-if)# speed auto
SW1(config-if)# duplex auto
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if)# end
```

Configure SW2 separately.

```ios SW2
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname SW2
SW2(config)# interface fastethernet0/1
SW2(config-if)# description PC-B
SW2(config-if)# no shutdown
SW2(config-if)# interface fastethernet0/24
SW2(config-if)# description To-SW1
SW2(config-if)# speed auto
SW2(config-if)# duplex auto
SW2(config-if)# no shutdown
SW2(config-if)# end
```

:::expected
The device prompts and cable endpoints match the diagram. After the switch ports initialize, all three links should be usable. A crossover is specified so the lab does not depend on auto-MDIX support during forced-setting tests. Do not deliberately use a wrong cable and assume it must fail; supported auto-MDIX can make either copper arrangement work.
:::

steps.title: Record the working baseline
steps.body:
On PC-A's **Desktop → Command Prompt**, enter `ping 10.0.30.12`. Retry once if initial address resolution loses a first request. Repeat the test from PC-B to `10.0.30.11`. Then inspect the interswitch port at both ends.

```ios SW1
SW1# show interfaces status
SW1# show interfaces fastethernet0/24
SW1# show running-config
```

```ios SW2
SW2# show interfaces status
SW2# show interfaces fastethernet0/24
SW2# show running-config
```

Write down each end's administrative state, operational speed, duplex and displayed error counters. Find the FastEthernet0/24 stanza in each running configuration. Default automatic settings may be omitted from that display.

:::expected
Both PCs receive replies on a repeated test. Both interswitch ends should operate at 100 Mbps full duplex, with the compact display commonly showing `a-full` and `a-100`. Detailed output should show an up physical and line-protocol state. If a compact display command is unavailable, use the detailed interface output.

Save the working topology as `03-interfaces-baseline.pkt`. Keep your first counter readings; later comparisons need a baseline. No conclusion should depend on all counters being exactly zero or on one particular simulator output layout.
:::

steps.title: Introduce a controlled duplex mismatch
steps.body:
This is an isolated lab fault, not a recommended production configuration. Force **SW1** FastEthernet0/24 to 100 Mbps half duplex.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/24
SW1(config-if)# speed 100
SW1(config-if)# duplex half
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show interfaces fastethernet0/24
```

Now force **SW2** FastEthernet0/24 to 100 Mbps full duplex.

```ios SW2
SW2# configure terminal
SW2(config)# interface fastethernet0/24
SW2(config-if)# speed 100
SW2(config-if)# duplex full
SW2(config-if)# end
SW2# show interfaces fastethernet0/24
```

Leave both settings in place while you inspect them. Repeat pings in each direction and compare new counter readings with Step 2. Do not assume a few small ping requests provide enough traffic to expose every performance symptom.

:::expected
The two configurations and operational displays should show matching speed but opposing duplex settings. A real Ethernet link can remain up in this condition. Under traffic, the half-duplex end may accumulate collisions or late collisions, while the other end may see receive errors.

The simulator may show successful pings and unchanged counters. That does not make the mismatch correct. The decisive evidence is the half/full disagreement on the two ends of this one connection. Record the actual behavior rather than inventing a target counter value.
:::

steps.title: Restore duplex agreement and test again
steps.body:
Restore automatic settings on each switch, using the block for that device.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/24
SW1(config-if)# speed auto
SW1(config-if)# duplex auto
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show interfaces fastethernet0/24
```

```ios SW2
SW2# configure terminal
SW2(config)# interface fastethernet0/24
SW2(config-if)# speed auto
SW2(config-if)# duplex auto
SW2(config-if)# end
SW2# show interfaces fastethernet0/24
```

:::expected
Both ends return to 100 Mbps full duplex after the link settles, and repeated pings work in both directions. Old error totals need not disappear: they are historical counters. Compare new readings over a new test interval. If the display still shows half duplex, inspect the configuration at both physical ends before proceeding.
:::

steps.title: Introduce a speed mismatch
steps.body:
Force **SW1** FastEthernet0/24 to 10 Mbps full duplex.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/24
SW1(config-if)# speed 10
SW1(config-if)# duplex full
SW1(config-if)# end
```

Force **SW2** FastEthernet0/24 to 100 Mbps full duplex.

```ios SW2
SW2# configure terminal
SW2(config)# interface fastethernet0/24
SW2(config-if)# speed 100
SW2(config-if)# duplex full
SW2(config-if)# end
SW2# show interfaces fastethernet0/24
```

Inspect SW1 with `show interfaces fastethernet0/24` and repeat PC-A's ping. Keep the failure in place long enough to note the state at each end.

:::expected
The configured rates disagree. A physical 10/100 link with these forced rates cannot establish a compatible Ethernet connection, so expect a down link and failed cross-switch communication. Record any simulator limitation if its state differs. Matching duplex alone is insufficient when the speeds do not match. The PCs' IP addresses have not changed, so readdressing them is not a justified repair.
:::

steps.title: Restore speed negotiation and verify recovery
steps.body:
Return both interswitch interfaces to their baseline settings.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/24
SW1(config-if)# speed auto
SW1(config-if)# duplex auto
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show interfaces fastethernet0/24
```

```ios SW2
SW2# configure terminal
SW2(config)# interface fastethernet0/24
SW2(config-if)# speed auto
SW2(config-if)# duplex auto
SW2(config-if)# end
SW2# show interfaces fastethernet0/24
```

:::expected
The operational rates and duplex agree again, both ends return to an up state, and repeated pings succeed. If they do not, check that the crossover still connects FastEthernet0/24 to FastEthernet0/24 and that you entered both recovery blocks on the intended switches.
:::

steps.title: Identify an administrative shutdown
steps.body:
Disable **SW1's** interswitch port without touching the cable.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/24
SW1(config-if)# shutdown
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show interfaces fastethernet0/24
```

Inspect the far end separately.

```ios SW2
SW2# show interfaces fastethernet0/24
SW2# show running-config
```

:::expected
SW1 should identify its interface as `administratively down`. SW2 loses the link but has not been administratively shut down; its configuration still lacks `shutdown` on this port. A down state at SW2 therefore does not tell you whether SW1 was disabled, disconnected or powered off. Inspecting both ends resolves that ambiguity. PC-A's ping to PC-B fails while the port is disabled.
:::

steps.title: Restore, retest and save the final state
steps.body:
Enable SW1's port again.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/24
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show interfaces fastethernet0/24
```

Check SW2's state and repeat the ping in both directions. Once the baseline is restored, save each switch with its own interactive copy command.

```ios SW1
SW1# copy running-config startup-config
```

At the destination-filename prompt, press Enter and wait for completion. Then use SW2's CLI:

```ios SW2
SW2# copy running-config startup-config
```

:::expected
Both interfaces are up at matching full-duplex speed, and communication works. Accept SW2's destination filename with Enter as well. Save the Packet Tracer project as `03-interfaces-complete.pkt`. Do not save a faulty state as your final working configuration.
:::

steps.title: Diagnose supplied physical-layer evidence
steps.body:
These cases are paper exercises. Use the module facts in the lesson and the readings supplied here; do not attempt to generate optical measurements in Packet Tracer.

| Case | Evidence | Decision to make |
|---|---|---|
| A | A 350 m OM3 path with 10GBASE-SR modules at both ends; the documented OM3 limit is 300 m | Is this path within the specified reach? |
| B | Compatible duplex modules are documented, but strand 1 connects Tx to Tx and strand 2 connects Rx to Rx | What connection must be corrected? |
| C | Receive reading −16 dBm; supplied acceptable range −12 through −1 dBm | Is received power within range, and what should be investigated? |
| D | A basic continuity tester passes pins 1–8, but a better tester reports a split pair | Why does the basic result not clear the cable? |
| E | A new 1 Gbps copper run measures 130 m including patch leads | What should be checked before blaming the IP configuration? |

:::expected
A exceeds the supplied OM3 reach; use a design whose fiber and optics support the distance, such as suitable OM4 within the stated SR specification, after verifying the whole installation. B requires Tx at each end to reach Rx at the other. C is below the low limit: inspect the transmitter, path, connectors, polarity and compatibility rather than naming one unproven cause. D has the wrong physical pairing despite pin continuity, which can harm signal performance. E exceeds the normal 100 m channel design limit; verify measurement and redesign the physical path or select suitable fiber.
:::

lab.troubleshooting:
- **No baseline ping:** verify PC addresses and masks, device power and all three cable endpoints. These PCs are on the same LAN and do not need a gateway.
- **A CLI command is rejected:** verify the prompt and port. Use the 2960 FastEthernet0/24 interfaces for these 10/100 tests, not a fixed-speed fiber interface.
- **A port is up but pings fail:** inspect the other ports in the path and endpoint settings. Local link-up is only one part of reachability.
- **Counters do not change during the mismatch:** record the simulator result. A mismatch is identified by comparing duplex at both ends, not by waiting for a specific synthetic error total.
- **Recovery commands seem ineffective:** inspect both switches' running configurations and detailed interface state. Changing only one end can leave the previous fault in place.
- **A physical optical link remains down after a repair:** recheck compatible module part numbers, supported ports, fiber grade, distance, polarity and measured receive levels. A successful command cannot prove an optical path is healthy.
lab.challenge:
On paper first, predict the result of setting SW1 FastEthernet0/24 to `speed 100` and `duplex full` while leaving SW2 automatic. Which end may operate half duplex on a real 10/100 link, and why?

Test this optional variation in a copy of your Packet Tracer file. Compare the two operational displays, document any simulator limitation, then restore both ends to `speed auto` and `duplex auto`. Finish by proving communication works. Do not change the PCs' addresses or cable type during this test.

:::expected
The automatic SW2 end can detect 100 Mbps but cannot infer full duplex from the nonnegotiating forced end, so it can use half duplex. SW1 remains full duplex. The link can be up despite disagreement. After both ends are restored to automatic settings, they should agree on 100 Mbps full duplex and repeated pings should succeed. If Packet Tracer does not model that fallback, the correct written explanation still distinguishes the documented hardware behavior from what the simulation displayed.
:::

exhibit.title: Representative: SW1# show interfaces status
exhibit.text:
Port      Name          Status       Vlan       Duplex  Speed Type
Fa0/3     Appliance     connected    1          a-half  a-100 10/100BaseTX

questions.prompt: The appliance is manually set to 100 Mbps full duplex. Its connected switch port is automatic and shows the following state. What has been established?
options: The cable is too long for a 100 Mbps connection.
The ends disagree on duplex despite matching speed.
The appliance and switch both operate at full duplex.
The switch port is administratively shut down.
questions.explanation: The appliance is full duplex while the switch displays half duplex, so their operational settings disagree. In this 10/100 case, an automatic end can detect the forced end's speed without learning its duplex.

whyWrong.0: The display does not measure cable length or prove a distance fault.
whyWrong.2: The exhibit explicitly shows half duplex on the switch.
whyWrong.3: The switch port is connected, not administratively disabled.

questions.prompt: A conventional 10/100 Ethernet crossover exchanges the transmit and receive pairs. Which pin mapping describes that exchange?
options: Pins 1↔2 and 3↔6, without moving pairs
Pins 1↔3 and 2↔6 between the ends
Pins 1↔1 through 8↔8 between the ends
questions.explanation: A conventional 10/100 crossover swaps the pair using pins 1–2 with the pair using pins 3–6. This connects the intended transmit and receive arrangements where crossover wiring is required.

whyWrong.0: Reversing all pins describes a rollover arrangement used by some serial console cables.
whyWrong.1: Exchanging conductors within each pair is not the required transmit/receive pair crossover.
whyWrong.3: Keeping each pin number unchanged describes a straight-through cable.

spec.title: One switch and a shared hub segment
spec.caption: PC-C and PC-D share the hub segment; all switch ports belong to VLAN 1.

questions.prompt: All switch ports are in VLAN 1, and there are no routers or additional links. How many Ethernet collision domains and broadcast domains are represented?
options: One collision domain and three broadcast domains
Four collision domains and one broadcast domain
Three collision domains and three broadcast domains
Three collision domains and one broadcast domain
questions.explanation: Each of the switch's three connected ports separates an Ethernet segment, giving three collision domains. The two PCs behind HUB1 share one of those segments, and all devices remain in one VLAN and therefore one broadcast domain.

whyWrong.0: The switch separates the segments; one VLAN does not create three broadcast domains.
whyWrong.1: The two PCs attached to the hub share one collision domain rather than having one each.
whyWrong.2: Switch ports do not create separate broadcast domains when they share the same VLAN.

questions.prompt: On the half-duplex end of a 10/100 duplex mismatch, which two observations are consistent with its collision-handling behavior? (Choose two.)
options: A collision counter increases during simultaneous traffic.
A late-collision counter increases during the test.
The port must operate at a different speed from its peer.
The interface must be administratively down throughout the test.
The two ends must display the same duplex setting.
questions.explanation: The half-duplex end applies collision handling while the full-duplex peer does not. Collisions and late collisions can result; compare the two duplex settings because counters alone do not exclude cable or hardware faults.

whyWrong.2: A duplex mismatch can exist at matching speed, such as 100 Mbps at both ends.
whyWrong.3: The link can remain up and carry traffic despite the mismatch.
whyWrong.4: A mismatch means the ends disagree on duplex.

exhibit.title: Representative counter comparison — same interface
exhibit.text:
Start of test: 4 input errors, 4 CRC
End of test:   89 input errors, 89 CRC
Both ends: 1000 Mbps, full duplex

questions.prompt: Both ends of a copper link show 1 Gbps full duplex. During a controlled transfer, received CRC errors increase on the switch. What is the best next action?
options: Force the switch to half duplex to enable collision detection.
Change the host's default gateway to clear the CRC counter.
Test the cable path and compare the far-end error readings.
Treat the CRC total as proof that the routing table is wrong.
questions.explanation: Rising CRC errors establish that received frames are failing their error check. With the documented speed and duplex agreement, investigate the physical path and endpoint hardware while collecting far-end evidence; the counter does not identify one unique failed component.

whyWrong.0: Forcing half duplex is not a justified repair for a link whose ends agree on full duplex.
whyWrong.1: A default gateway change does not repair corruption of received Ethernet frames.
whyWrong.3: A routing table chooses paths; CRC errors concern received frame integrity.

questions.prompt: A 350 m path will use 10GBASE-SR modules. The supported reaches are 300 m on OM3 and 400 m on OM4. Which choice meets the stated distance?
options: OM4 multimode fiber within the specified SR design
OM3 multimode fiber because both ends use SR
Single-mode fiber because its core is smaller
Cat6A copper because the connectors can be adapted
questions.explanation: The 350 m path exceeds the supplied OM3 reach but is within the 400 m OM4 specification. Module compatibility and the actual fiber path still need verification.

whyWrong.1: Matching modules do not extend OM3 beyond the stated 300 m reach.
whyWrong.2: SR is specified here for multimode fiber; a different fiber type is not automatically supported.
whyWrong.3: SR is optical, and this distance exceeds the normal copper channel limit.

questions.prompt: Which Cisco switch command provides a compact table of port status, VLAN, duplex, speed and media type?
options: show ip route
show running-config
show power inline
show interfaces status
questions.explanation: The switch's `show interfaces status` command provides the compact port overview. Use the detailed interface command for the named port's counters or physical and line-protocol state.

whyWrong.0: The routing table does not provide the requested switch-port status columns.
whyWrong.1: The running configuration shows configured commands rather than this operational table.
whyWrong.2: PoE status describes electrical power allocation rather than the requested Ethernet state.

exhibit.title: Supplied optical measurements — teaching example
exhibit.text:
Receive power: -16.0 dBm
Acceptable range for this exercise: -12.0 to -1.0 dBm
Link state: down

questions.prompt: The optical receiver's supplied acceptable range is −12 through −1 dBm. What conclusion is supported by a receive reading of −16 dBm?
options: The signal exceeds the receiver's upper power limit.
The receive power is below the supplied lower limit.
The fiber polarity is definitely the only fault.
Both transmit modules are confirmed healthy.
questions.explanation: −16 dBm is less received power than the −12 dBm lower limit. Investigate the optical path and far-end transmitter; the receive value alone does not isolate the cause.

whyWrong.0: A value above −1 dBm would exceed the supplied upper limit.
whyWrong.2: Polarity, distance, connectors, incompatible modules or a transmitter fault can contribute.
whyWrong.3: A receive reading at one end does not establish the health of both transmitters.

questions.prompt: Which comparison of single-mode and multimode fiber is accurate?
options: Multimode supports longer links because it has a larger core.
Either fiber type is interchangeable when the connector is LC.
Single-mode has a smaller core and is common on longer links.
Jacket color alone proves the installed fiber's speed and reach.
questions.explanation: Single-mode fiber has a smaller core and is commonly used by longer-distance optical systems. Reach depends on the compatible module-and-fiber design, not the core description alone.

whyWrong.0: A larger core does not mean longer reach; multimode light paths can limit supported distance.
whyWrong.1: Matching connectors do not establish fiber and optical-standard compatibility.
whyWrong.3: Use cable markings and verified specifications; color alone is insufficient.

questions.prompt: A duplex fiber patch connects Switch A Tx to Switch B Tx and Switch A Rx to Switch B Rx. Both modules are otherwise compatible. What should be corrected first?
options: Connect each transmitter to the far receiver.
Force one interface to half duplex before testing.
Change both IP masks so receivers detect light.
Increase route preference for the optical path.
questions.explanation: A duplex optical link requires each transmitter to connect to the other end's receiver. The documented arrangement is a polarity fault; correct the physical path, then verify light levels and link state.

whyWrong.1: Ethernet duplex configuration does not rearrange the physical fiber connections.
whyWrong.2: IP masks do not determine which optical receiver a strand reaches.
whyWrong.3: Routing preference cannot repair an incorrect physical optical path.

questions.prompt: Assume traditional 10/100 MDI/MDI-X ports with no auto-MDIX. Which two connections require a crossover cable? (Choose two.)
options: PC to switch
Switch to switch
Router Ethernet port to switch
PC to router Ethernet port
Server Ethernet port to switch
questions.explanation: Two switch MDI-X ports need a crossover, as do a PC and router whose ports both use MDI. PC, server and router connections to a switch use unlike arrangements and therefore straight-through wiring in this stated case.

whyWrong.0: A PC-to-switch connection pairs MDI with MDI-X, so straight-through is appropriate.
whyWrong.2: A router-to-switch connection pairs MDI with MDI-X.
whyWrong.4: A server-to-switch connection uses straight-through under the stated assumptions.

exhibit.title: Representative selected interface states
exhibit.text:
Fa0/1 status: connected
Fa0/2 status: notconnect
FastEthernet0/3 is administratively down, line protocol is down
Fa0/4 status: err-disabled

questions.prompt: Which interface is explicitly disabled by its local administrative configuration?
options: Fa0/1, because connected means the cable is removed
Fa0/2, because notconnect always identifies shutdown
Fa0/4, because err-disabled identifies manual shutdown
Fa0/3, because its state is administratively down
questions.explanation: `Administratively down` identifies a local shutdown state. Enabling it may be part of an authorized repair, but cable, far-end state and other configuration still determine whether service returns.

whyWrong.0: Connected describes a local operational link, not a removed cable.
whyWrong.1: Notconnect does not identify one unique cause; the cable or far end could be down.
whyWrong.2: Err-disabled indicates a protection mechanism whose cause must be investigated.

questions.prompt: A 10/100 link has a forced 100/full endpoint and an automatic switch port operating at 100/half. Both support autonegotiation. What is the preferred starting repair?
options: Leave the disagreement because both ends have the same speed.
Return both ends to auto and verify negotiated speed and duplex.
Force the switch to 10/half and keep the endpoint at 100/full.
Change the endpoint's address before either interface setting.
questions.explanation: Returning both supported ends to automatic settings lets them agree on compatible speed and duplex. Verify the result and traffic afterward; matching manual settings at both ends are another deliberate option where required.

whyWrong.0: Matching speed does not make opposing duplex settings correct.
whyWrong.2: That introduces a speed mismatch as well as retaining incompatible duplex settings.
whyWrong.3: The evidence identifies an interface-setting disagreement, not an addressing error.

questions.prompt: An office plans 90 m of installed cable plus 10 m of patch leads for supported 10GBASE-T switch ports. Which category supports that full 100 m channel?
options: Cat6A
Cat5
Cat3
Cat5e
questions.explanation: Cat6A supports a 100 m 10GBASE-T channel on suitable interfaces. The permanent link and patch leads together consume the channel distance, and actual module reach must still be checked.

whyWrong.1: Cat5 is not the specified category for a full-distance 10GBASE-T channel.
whyWrong.2: Cat3 is associated with much lower-speed twisted-pair Ethernet.
whyWrong.3: Cat5e is a normal 1 Gbps choice, but not the full-distance 10GBASE-T requirement.

exhibit.title: Representative: SW1# show interfaces fastethernet0/3
exhibit.text: FastEthernet0/3 is administratively down, line protocol is down

questions.prompt: A printer port is administratively down. The intended design says it should be enabled. What is the best next action?
options: Replace the patch cable without changing the port configuration.
Change the switch's default gateway before inspecting the port.
Enable the intended port and verify link state and reachability.
Force a lower speed without changing the shutdown state.
questions.explanation: The known local shutdown must be removed before the interface can carry traffic. Verify the intended port, apply `no shutdown`, then check local state and communication; command acceptance alone does not prove recovery.

whyWrong.0: Replacing a cable does not remove the administrative shutdown.
whyWrong.1: A gateway change does not enable the disabled interface.
whyWrong.3: Speed changes cannot override an administrative shutdown.

questions.prompt: What does a late collision on a half-duplex 10/100 Ethernet link mean?
options: A frame was dropped because the output queue had filled.
A normal full-duplex transmission ended after a timer expired.
The cable has been proved defective without more inspection.
A collision occurred beyond the permitted collision window.
questions.explanation: A late collision occurs later than the allowed collision-detection window. Investigate duplex agreement and physical or hardware conditions; it does not independently prove one specific defect.

whyWrong.0: Output queue drops and collision timing are different measurements.
whyWrong.1: Full-duplex Ethernet does not normally use collision detection.
whyWrong.2: A duplex mismatch or other hardware condition can contribute, so the cable is not proved to be the cause.

cards.front: What is the usual copper Ethernet channel limit, and what must you check?
cards.back: 100 m for the specified category on supporting ports, commonly 90 m installed plus 10 m patch leads. Some copper modules have shorter limits.

cards.front: Cable choices for 1 Gbps and for a full 100 m 10GBASE-T channel?
cards.back: Cat5e or better is the normal new 1 Gbps choice. Use Cat6A for 10GBASE-T at 100 m on supporting interfaces.

cards.front: Which pin groups form the four physical twisted pairs?
cards.back: 1–2, 3–6, 4–5 and 7–8. A split pair can pass simple pin continuity while using the wrong physical pairing.

cards.front: Which pairs does a conventional 10/100 crossover exchange?
cards.back: Pins 1–2 exchange with pins 3–6: 1↔3 and 2↔6. This is the 10/100 crossover mapping, not a complete rule for every four-pair interface.

cards.front: Without auto-MDIX, when is crossover used on traditional 10/100 ports?
cards.back: Between like electrical arrangements: switch–switch or PC–router, for example. PC/router/server–switch uses straight-through.

cards.front: How does a rollover console cable differ from an Ethernet cable?
cards.back: A traditional rollover reverses pins for a serial console connection. Connect it to the Console port; similar-looking connectors do not make it Ethernet.

cards.front: Cisco 1000BASE-SX and LX/LH SFPs: typical fiber and reach?
cards.back: SX uses 850 nm MMF, with reach dependent on grade and commonly up to 550 m. Cisco LX/LH supports 1310 nm SMF up to 10 km; check the exact module.

cards.front: 10GBASE-SR versus LR: common supported distances?
cards.back: SR: 300 m on OM3, 400 m on OM4. LR: 10 km on specified SMF. The modules, fiber and ports must be compatible.

cards.front: How do single-mode and multimode fiber differ?
cards.back: Single-mode has a smaller core and commonly supports longer-distance optical designs. Multimode has a larger core and commonly serves shorter links; use specifications, not jacket color alone.

cards.front: What do common 1 Gbps SFP and 10 Gbps SFP+ examples teach about module choice?
cards.back: Match form factor, supported port speed, Ethernet optical standard and fiber. Physical fit and matching connectors alone do not establish compatibility.

cards.front: Is −16 dBm within a supplied receive range of −12 through −1 dBm?
cards.back: No. −16 dBm is lower power than the −12 dBm limit. Check transmitter, path, connectors, distance and compatibility; the reading alone does not isolate the cause.

cards.front: What are runts and giants?
cards.back: Runts are undersized Ethernet frames. Giants exceed the permitted frame size for that interface and encapsulation; tags and larger configured frames affect the limit.

cards.front: What does a late collision suggest on a half-duplex 10/100 link?
cards.back: A collision occurred beyond the permitted window. Investigate duplex agreement and physical/hardware conditions; it is not proof of one specific defect.

cards.front: Hub versus switch: collision and broadcast domains?
cards.back: A hub's devices share one collision domain. A switch separates port segments, while ports in one VLAN share a broadcast domain. Full-duplex Ethernet has no normal collisions.

cards.front: What can an automatic 10/100 end do when its peer is forced to 100/full?
cards.back: Detect 100 Mbps but not the forced duplex setting, then operate at half duplex. The resulting link can be up with a duplex mismatch.

cards.front: What evidence supports a duplex-mismatch diagnosis?
cards.back: Opposing operational duplex settings at the two ends. Collisions/late collisions or received-frame errors may support it, but counters alone are not conclusive.

cards.front: How do you restore automatic speed and duplex in interface configuration?
cards.back: speed auto and duplex auto on both supported ends. Verify the resulting operation and traffic; reset counters only after preserving a baseline.

cards.front: What does the a- prefix in a-full or a-100 mean?
cards.back: The setting was selected automatically, rather than explicitly forced. It can reflect negotiation or sensed/defaulted behavior, so compare both ends.

cards.front: What do connected, notconnect, administratively down and err-disabled mean?
cards.back: Connected: local link up. Notconnect: no operational link. Administratively down: local shutdown. Err-disabled: a protection mechanism disabled the port; investigate its cause.

cards.front: How should you interpret output drops and low optical receive power?
cards.back: Output drops often indicate an egress queue problem. Low receive power means a reading below the module's supplied limit; investigate the optical path rather than assuming one cause.

commands.task: Label the selected interface Uplink-DSW1.
commands.note: A description records intent. Verify the actual cable before relying on the label.

commands.task: On the 2960 FastEthernet lab port, set the speed to 100 Mbps.
commands.note: A deliberate manual configuration must match the peer. Do not assume auto-MDIX will compensate during forced-setting tests.

commands.task: On the 2960 FastEthernet lab port, set full duplex.
commands.note: Compare the peer's setting. A forced 100/full end with an automatic 10/100 peer can produce a mismatch.

commands.task: Return the selected 2960 FastEthernet port's speed to automatic selection.
commands.note: Restore automatic duplex as well on both ends, then verify operation.

commands.task: Return the selected 2960 FastEthernet port's duplex to automatic selection.
commands.note: A default automatic setting may be omitted from the running configuration.

commands.task: On a supported Catalyst copper port, enable automatic MDI/MDI-X detection.
commands.note: Cisco's 2960 procedure uses speed auto and duplex auto as well. This command is platform dependent; it is not required for the explicitly cabled Packet Tracer lab.

commands.task: Show the switch's compact port-state, VLAN, duplex, speed and media table.
commands.note: Compare the two ends of the same connection, especially a-half versus full.

commands.task: Show the detailed state and counters for FastEthernet0/1.
commands.note: Record a baseline and compare changes during traffic. Counters suggest causes; they do not automatically identify a failed cable.

commands.task: On supported Catalyst hardware, display the error-counter table for FastEthernet0/3.
commands.note: If this display is unavailable in Packet Tracer, inspect show interfaces fastethernet0/3 instead. The drill practices documented hardware syntax.

commands.task: After preserving the readings, reset counters for FastEthernet0/1 only in the isolated lab.
commands.note: Answer the confirmation prompt separately. Do not use bare clear counters, which affects other interfaces.

commands.task: On supported optical hardware, display transceiver measurements for TenGigabitEthernet1/1/1.
commands.note: Use the platform's detail option for supported thresholds. Virtual devices and Packet Tracer do not substitute for real optical measurement.

tickets.title: Backups slow down after an endpoint replacement
tickets.scenario: An appliance's replacement NIC is manually set to 100 Mbps full duplex. The connected switch interface supports 10/100/1000 and remains automatic. Pings work, but larger transfers are slow. You identify the exact two ends, collect a baseline and repeat a transfer. The excerpts are representative IOS-style diagnostic evidence.

exhibits.title: Representative: ASW2# show interfaces status
exhibits.text:
Port      Name               Status       Vlan       Duplex  Speed Type
Gi1/0/12  Backup-appliance   connected    1          a-half  a-100 10/100/1000BaseTX

exhibits.title: Counter comparison on Gi1/0/12
exhibits.text:
Before transfer: 10 collisions; 0 late collisions
After transfer:  420 collisions; 180 late collisions
Operational speed: 100 Mbps
Operational duplex: half

exhibits.title: Verified endpoint settings
exhibits.text:
Adapter mode: manually configured
Speed: 100 Mbps
Duplex: full

tickets.question: Which fault has the evidence established?
options: The cable is defective because every late collision proves cable damage.
The two ends use opposite duplex settings at the same speed.
The endpoints use different speeds and have no physical connection.
The IP default gateway is incorrect because larger transfers are slow.
tickets.explanation: The switch operates at 100/half while the endpoint is set to 100/full. That direct comparison establishes a duplex mismatch, and the increasing collision counters are consistent with it. The counters do not independently prove or exclude a cable fault; the operational settings are the decisive evidence here.
tickets.fix:
Coordinate the endpoint change so its NIC returns to automatic speed and duplex. Then restore the switch side:
```ios ASW2
ASW2# configure terminal
ASW2(config)# interface gigabitethernet1/0/12
ASW2(config-if)# speed auto
ASW2(config-if)# duplex auto
ASW2(config-if)# end
ASW2# show interfaces gigabitethernet1/0/12
```
Verify matching operational speed and full duplex on both ends. Record current counters, repeat the same transfer and compare new increments and completion time. Old totals do not disappear when the cause is fixed. If the endpoint must remain manually configured for a documented reason, deliberately match both ends instead; do not force only one and assume the peer follows. Save the working configuration only after verification.

tickets.title: An optical uplink uses incompatible module types
tickets.scenario: A new 180 m OM3 multimode path joins DSW1 and CORE1. Both intended interfaces are administratively enabled, but the link is down. You inspect the module labels and verify the fiber record. These are supplied inventory and measurement observations, not fabricated output from an executed switch session.

exhibits.title: Verified component record
exhibits.text:
DSW1 optical port: 10GBASE-SR, 850 nm, supported by DSW1
CORE1 optical port: 10GBASE-LR, 1310 nm, supported by CORE1
Installed path: OM3 multimode, 180 m
Both interfaces: administratively enabled

exhibits.title: Specification comparison
exhibits.text:
10GBASE-SR over OM3: up to 300 m for the specified modules
10GBASE-LR: specified for single-mode fiber
Connector shape at both ends: LC
No completed end-to-end optical qualification test is available

tickets.question: Which confirmed incompatibility should be corrected before further link testing?
options: The OM3 path is 120 m longer than the stated SR reach.
Matching LC connectors prove the two optics form a compatible pair.
The design combines SR over MMF with an LR module intended for SMF.
The enabled interfaces must be shut down permanently to protect the fiber.
tickets.explanation: The inventory identifies incompatible optical designs: SR over OM3 at one end and LR at the other. The 180 m path is within the supplied SR-on-OM3 distance, but distance alone does not make the module pair compatible. Connector fit does not prove that a supported optical link exists.
tickets.fix:
For the intended OM3 design, select a compatible 10GBASE-SR module supported by CORE1 so both ends use the appropriate SR design. Follow the equipment's module replacement and fiber-handling procedure. Alternatively, an LR design requires a correctly specified single-mode path and compatible modules at both ends; changing a label does not change the installed fiber.

After the component correction, verify transmit-to-receive polarity, inspect and clean connectors using approved equipment, and measure received power against each actual module's permitted range. Never look into a live fiber. On supported hardware, use the interface and transceiver displays, then test traffic and watch for new errors. Do not predict an exact receive dBm value or declare both transmitters healthy from one reading; other faults may remain after the confirmed mismatch is corrected.

lab.title: Configure two LANs and isolate address, mask, and gateway faults
lab.intro:
Build two separate LANs using /26 and /27 masks. You will verify each field, test a local peer and a remote peer, then create and repair a gateway fault. The switches can stay at their default settings; no VLAN or routing protocol configuration is needed.

This procedure has been checked against the address plan and Cisco command documentation, but was not executed in Packet Tracer during this review. Output excerpts are representative. Compare addresses, prefixes, and interface state rather than exact spacing, message timing, or TTL values.
lab.topology:
```diagram
{ "type": "topology", "title": "Two LANs with one router", "caption": "PC-A and PC-C share LAN-A; PC-B is reached through R1 on LAN-B.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "A", "kind": "pc", "label": "PC-A", "sub": "192.168.44.130/26", "x": 1, "y": 1 },
    { "id": "C", "kind": "pc", "label": "PC-C", "sub": "192.168.44.150/26", "x": 1, "y": 5 },
    { "id": "S1", "kind": "switch", "label": "SW1", "x": 3.5, "y": 3 },
    { "id": "R", "kind": "router", "label": "R1 · 2911", "x": 6, "y": 3 },
    { "id": "S2", "kind": "switch", "label": "SW2", "x": 8.5, "y": 3 },
    { "id": "B", "kind": "pc", "label": "PC-B", "sub": "192.168.44.194/27", "x": 11, "y": 3 }
  ],
  "links": [
    { "from": "A", "to": "S1", "fromLabel": "Fa0", "toLabel": "Fa0/1" },
    { "from": "C", "to": "S1", "fromLabel": "Fa0", "toLabel": "Fa0/2" },
    { "from": "S1", "to": "R", "fromLabel": "Fa0/24", "toLabel": "Gi0/0" },
    { "from": "R", "to": "S2", "fromLabel": "Gi0/1", "toLabel": "Fa0/24" },
    { "from": "S2", "to": "B", "fromLabel": "Fa0/1", "toLabel": "Fa0" }
  ] }
```

Use copper straight-through for all five links. The Packet Tracer automatic connection tool is an alternative. Gi0/2 on R1 remains unused during the required exercise.

| Device/interface | IPv4 address | Mask | Default gateway |
|---|---|---|---|
| R1 Gi0/0 | `192.168.44.129` | `255.255.255.192` | Not needed for these connected LANs |
| R1 Gi0/1 | `192.168.44.193` | `255.255.255.224` | Not needed for these connected LANs |
| PC-A Fa0 | `192.168.44.130` | `255.255.255.192` | `192.168.44.129` |
| PC-C Fa0 | `192.168.44.150` | `255.255.255.192` | `192.168.44.129` |
| PC-B Fa0 | `192.168.44.194` | `255.255.255.224` | `192.168.44.193` |

LAN-A is `192.168.44.128/26`: hosts .129–.190, broadcast .191. LAN-B is `192.168.44.192/27`: hosts .193–.222, broadcast .223. These ranges do not overlap.

steps.title: Build and name the devices
steps.body:
Start a new Packet Tracer file and place the specified models. Rename the workspace labels so the devices match the diagram. Connect each listed port. On the router's CLI tab, decline the initial configuration dialog if it appears, then press Enter to obtain `Router>`.

```ios R1
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R1
R1(config)# end
```

:::expected
You are at `R1#`. Switch links may initially be amber while ports transition to forwarding. Router-facing links may stay down until you enable R1's interfaces. Device labels and port connections match the diagram.
:::

steps.title: Address R1's two interfaces
steps.body:
Configure one LAN at a time. `exit` returns from interface configuration to global configuration; `end` returns to privileged EXEC mode.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# description LAN-A
R1(config-if)# ip address 192.168.44.129 255.255.255.192
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# description LAN-B
R1(config-if)# ip address 192.168.44.193 255.255.255.224
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip interface brief
```

:::expected
Gi0/0 displays .129 and Gi0/1 displays .193. With the cables and switch ports ready, both interfaces become up/up. If either remains administratively down, return to that interface and check `no shutdown`. An enabled interface that remains down needs a link check.
:::

steps.title: Address the PCs
steps.body:
For each PC, open **Desktop → IP Configuration**, select **Static**, and enter all three values from the table. Read the mask field after entering the address; replace any automatically supplied value with the planned mask. DNS is not needed because this exercise uses IP addresses directly.

On each PC, open **Desktop → Command Prompt** and run:

```text
ipconfig
```

:::expected
PC-A and PC-C show mask 255.255.255.192 and gateway 192.168.44.129. PC-B shows mask 255.255.255.224 and gateway 192.168.44.193. All three host addresses are unique and lie within the appropriate usable range.
:::

steps.title: Verify the masks with the right commands
steps.body:
On R1, inspect both the operational prefix and the configured dotted mask.

```ios R1
R1# show ip interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1# show ip interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1# show running-config
R1# show ip route
```

:::expected
The detailed interface output identifies .129/26 and .193/27. In the full running configuration, find each interface heading and its `ip address` line. Representative connected-route lines are:
```output R1# show ip route
C        192.168.44.128/26 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0  ← LAN-A
C        192.168.44.192/27 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/1  ← LAN-B
```
Additional local /32 routes may appear. If your image omits a detailed command, use the running configuration for the mask and the routing table for the resulting subnet.
:::

steps.title: Test local and remote communication
steps.body:
On PC-A, test its gateway, its local peer, and the remote host, in that order.

```text PC-A
ping 192.168.44.129
ping 192.168.44.150
ping 192.168.44.194
```

Then test the return direction from PC-B.

```text PC-B
ping 192.168.44.193
ping 192.168.44.130
```

:::expected
After links settle, repeated tests receive replies. Initial ARP resolution can delay an early reply; repeat once before diagnosing persistent loss. PC-A reaches PC-C directly on LAN-A, while traffic between PC-A and PC-B crosses R1. A successful echo request and reply tests both forward and return paths for that exchange.
:::

steps.title: Observe rejection of an invalid address
steps.body:
Use unused Gi0/2 to try the network address of another /27. This isolates the test from the working LANs. Read the router's response, then inspect the interface.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/2
R1(config-if)# ip address 192.168.44.224 255.255.255.224
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show running-config
R1# show ip interface brief
```

:::expected
The proposed address has all host bits zero. IOS should reject it as an invalid host address; exact error wording varies by image. Gi0/2 should remain unassigned, and Gi0/0 and Gi0/1 retain their working addresses. Do not interpret a prompt returning as proof that the command succeeded.
:::

steps.title: Introduce a gateway fault and record the symptoms
steps.body:
On PC-A only, change the default gateway to `192.168.44.190`. Leave its address and /26 mask unchanged. No device in this topology uses .190, although it is a valid address within LAN-A. Do not change R1 or either other PC.

```text PC-A
ipconfig
ping 192.168.44.150
ping 192.168.44.129
ping 192.168.44.194
```

:::expected
The local peer .150 and the router's actual local address .129 should still respond. The remote PC .194 should fail because the configured next hop .190 is unused. This shows why merely pinging the actual router address does not prove that the default-gateway field is correct. Record your results before proceeding.
:::

steps.title: Restore the gateway and check mask decisions
steps.body:
Restore PC-A's gateway to `192.168.44.129`. Confirm the mask remains `255.255.255.192`, then repeat the same local and remote tests.

```text PC-A
ipconfig
ping 192.168.44.150
ping 192.168.44.194
```

On paper, now consider a /24 mask on PC-A without applying it: would .194 be local or remote? Which address would PC-A try to resolve with ARP?

:::expected
Remote communication works again after the gateway correction. Under the hypothetical /24, .194 would appear local, so PC-A would ARP for .194 rather than its gateway. Whether that incorrect configuration happens to work can depend on proxy ARP. The required lab does not rely on Packet Tracer implementing that optional behavior.
:::

steps.title: Restore and save
steps.body:
Confirm all three PCs match the original address table and the unused Gi0/2 has no address. Save the router configuration, then save the Packet Tracer file.

```ios R1
R1# copy running-config startup-config
```

:::expected
Accept the default destination filename when prompted. Save as `ipv4-two-lans.pkt`. Run the local and remote PC-A tests once more. The saved file is your known working baseline for later exercises.
:::

lab.troubleshooting:
- A local gateway fails: check cable and port assignments, R1's state, and the PC's address and mask before changing routes.
- Local hosts respond but a remote host fails: inspect both gateway fields and both masks. Read the fields even if they look familiar.
- A connected route is absent: verify the address and mask, then confirm that its interface and line protocol are up.
- A command is rejected: record the message and check the retained configuration; do not continue on the assumption that it took effect.
- One initial echo is lost: allow links to settle and repeat. Persistent failure needs investigation.
- A device model has different interface names: use the specified 2911 and 2960 models or adapt the port table before configuring anything.
lab.challenge:
Add a third 2960 switch and one PC-PT to the unused R1 Gi0/2, using straight-through cables from Gi0/2 to switch Fa0/24 and from switch Fa0/1 to PC Fa0. The new LAN must contain `10.7.19.77/21`. Calculate its network, broadcast, usable range, and first usable gateway. Configure the PC with the given host address and the router with that gateway. Test the new gateway and PC-A.

Before testing, decide whether `10.7.23.250` and `10.7.24.1` are members of the new subnet.

:::expected
Mask: `255.255.248.0`. Network: `10.7.16.0/21`. Broadcast: `10.7.23.255`. Usable range: `10.7.16.1–10.7.23.254`, or 2,046 addresses. Configure Gi0/2 with `ip address 10.7.16.1 255.255.248.0` and `no shutdown`. The PC uses `10.7.19.77`, the same mask, and gateway `10.7.16.1`. Address .23.250 is inside; `10.7.24.1` is the first usable address of the next /21. With links up and the correct host settings, R1 has the new connected prefix and routes between the three LANs.
:::

questions.prompt: What is the network address containing 10.1.1.77/27?
questions.explanation: A /27 mask is 255.255.255.224, giving an increment of 32 in the fourth octet. The address .77 lies in the .64–.95 block, whose network is 10.1.1.64.

whyWrong.0: The .32/27 block ends at .63.
whyWrong.2: The host address contains nonzero host bits; clear them to obtain the network.
whyWrong.3: The .96/27 block begins after this host.

questions.prompt: What is the broadcast address for 172.16.200.9/21?
questions.explanation: The /21 mask is 255.255.248.0, with third-octet increments of 8. The network starts at 200 and the next one starts at 208, so setting all host bits gives 172.16.207.255.

whyWrong.0: This ends a /24, before the /21 block ends.
whyWrong.1: Third-octet value 208 is in the next /21.
whyWrong.2: This would end a /16 rather than the given /21.

questions.prompt: A LAN needs five workstations and one router interface, with no growth allowance. Which mask gives the smallest subnet that fits?
questions.explanation: Six usable addresses are needed. A /29 provides eight total addresses, of which six are usable on this LAN.

whyWrong.1: A /30 has only two usable addresses.
whyWrong.2: A /28 has 14 usable addresses and works, but is larger than required.
whyWrong.3: A /27 has 30 usable addresses and is also larger than required.

questions.prompt: Which is a usable host address in 192.168.10.64/26?
questions.explanation: The /26 block spans .64–.127. The network and broadcast are reserved, leaving .65–.126 for interfaces.

whyWrong.0: This is the network address.
whyWrong.1: This is the subnet broadcast.
whyWrong.3: This starts the next /26 subnet.

exhibit.title: Recorded PC settings
exhibit.text:
IPv4 address:    10.10.20.130
Subnet mask:     255.255.255.128
Default gateway: 10.10.20.1

questions.prompt: The intended LAN is 10.10.20.128/25 and its router interface is 10.10.20.129/25. Which field in the PC record is inconsistent with that plan?
options: Its .130 host address is outside the intended /25.
Its /25 mask is shorter than the intended mask.
Its .130 host address is the subnet broadcast.
Its .1 gateway is outside the intended subnet.
questions.explanation: The PC's .130 address and /25 mask match 10.10.20.128/25. The intended local router is .129; .1 belongs to the other /25, so the gateway setting must be corrected.

whyWrong.0: The upper /25 has usable addresses .129–.254.
whyWrong.1: The configured 255.255.255.128 is exactly /25.
whyWrong.2: The broadcast is .255, not .130.

exhibit.title: Proposed interface configuration
exhibit.text:
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 172.16.5.64 255.255.255.192

questions.prompt: Why is the proposed address unsuitable for an ordinary routed LAN interface?
options: The mask contains a zero between network bits.
The address is the network boundary of this /26.
The address is the broadcast of the lower /26.
The mask leaves too few addresses for any LAN.
questions.explanation: A /26 has fourth-octet boundaries at 0, 64, 128, and 192. The proposed .64 address has all host bits zero; the first usable address is .65.

whyWrong.0: 192 is binary 11000000, so this mask is contiguous.
whyWrong.2: The lower block's broadcast is .63.
whyWrong.3: A /26 provides 62 usable addresses and is a valid LAN size.

exhibit.title: Existing configuration excerpt
exhibit.text:
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 10.0.0.1 255.255.255.128

questions.prompt: Gi0/0 serves the lower half of 10.0.0.0/24. Which command assigns Gi0/1 a usable address in the separate upper half?
questions.explanation: The upper half is 10.0.0.128/25, with usable addresses .129–.254. Address .129 with mask 255.255.255.128 fits that subnet and does not overlap the lower /25.

whyWrong.1: A /24 would include the lower /25 already assigned to Gi0/0.
whyWrong.2: Address .128 is the upper /25 network address.
whyWrong.3: Address .2 belongs to Gi0/0's lower /25.

questions.prompt: A server is 172.20.77.210/20. Which two listed addresses are usable in the same subnet? Choose two.
questions.explanation: The /20 network is 172.20.64.0 and the broadcast is 172.20.79.255. Both .79.1 and .64.200 are inside its usable range.

whyWrong.1: Third-octet value 80 starts the next /20.
whyWrong.3: This is outside the subnet and is the previous block's broadcast.
whyWrong.4: Third-octet value 96 starts a later /20.

questions.prompt: Which two statements correctly describe /31 and /32 prefixes? Choose two.
options: A /31 allocates two endpoints and an extra broadcast.
A /31 can use both addresses on a point-to-point link.
A /30 allocates four usable endpoint addresses.
A /32 identifies one address and is common on loopbacks.
A /32 reserves its only address as a subnet broadcast.
questions.explanation: RFC 3021 permits both addresses of a /31 on a supported point-to-point link. A /32 describes one address; it is commonly used for loopbacks or host routes, but not every loopback must use /32.

whyWrong.0: A /31 contains only two total addresses.
whyWrong.2: A /30 contains four total addresses but only two ordinary usable addresses.
whyWrong.4: A /32 is a single-address prefix, not an ordinary broadcast LAN.

questions.prompt: How many addresses are usable by hosts in the ordinary subnet 10.8.0.0/22?
questions.explanation: A /22 leaves ten host bits, so there are 2^10 = 1,024 addresses. Removing network 10.8.0.0 and broadcast 10.8.3.255 leaves 1,022 usable addresses.

whyWrong.0: 510 is the ordinary usable count for /23.
whyWrong.1: 1,024 is the total before subtracting the two reserved addresses.
whyWrong.2: 2,046 is the ordinary usable count for /21.

questions.prompt: What decimal value results from the bitwise AND shown?
questions.explanation: AND retains a 1 only where both inputs have a 1. The result is 10000000, which is decimal 128 and forms the network's final octet in this /26 example.

whyWrong.0: 173 is the original address octet, before host bits are cleared.
whyWrong.1: 192 is the mask octet, not the AND result.
whyWrong.3: 64 is the block increment, not the network octet for this address.

questions.prompt: Which prefix and block increment correspond to mask 255.255.254.0?
options: /22; increment 4 in the third octet
/23; increment 2 in the third octet
/24; increment 1 in the third octet
/25; increment 128 in the fourth octet
questions.explanation: The mask contains 8 + 8 + 7 = 23 ones. Its partial third octet is 254, so the increment there is 256 − 254 = 2.

whyWrong.0: A /22 uses 252 in the third octet.
whyWrong.2: A /24 has three complete 255 octets.
whyWrong.3: A /25 uses 128 in the fourth octet.

questions.prompt: Which two commands let you verify the configured mask on R1's Gi0/0? Choose two.
options: show ip interface brief
show ip interface gigabitethernet0/0
show running-config
show ip arp
show cdp neighbors
questions.explanation: Detailed IP interface output identifies the address and prefix. The running configuration contains the interface's ip address command with its dotted mask.

whyWrong.0: The brief table omits the mask.
whyWrong.3: ARP maps IPv4 addresses to MAC addresses; it does not record this interface's configured mask.
whyWrong.4: CDP neighbor discovery is not a view of this interface's IPv4 mask.

exhibit.title: Representative R1# show ip interface brief excerpt
exhibit.text:
Interface              IP-Address      OK? Method Status                Protocol
GigabitEthernet0/0      192.168.44.129  YES manual up                    up
GigabitEthernet0/1      192.168.44.193  YES manual administratively down down

questions.prompt: LAN-B uses Gi0/1. Which action directly addresses the condition shown?
options: Enter no shutdown under Gi0/1.
Change Gi0/1 to a /24 mask.
Remove the IPv4 address from Gi0/1.
Change LAN-B's host gateway values.
questions.explanation: Administratively down indicates that the interface is shut down in configuration. Enter no shutdown under Gi0/1, then verify the physical link and protocol become up.

whyWrong.1: This output does not show the mask and gives no reason to change it.
whyWrong.2: Removing the address would not enable the interface.
whyWrong.3: Host settings do not explain an administrative shutdown on R1.

exhibit.title: Recorded diagnostic facts
exhibit.text:
PC-A: 192.168.44.130/24; intended LAN: 192.168.44.128/26
Remote host: 192.168.44.194/27, on R1's other LAN
R1 has a connected route to that remote LAN.
Proxy ARP is enabled on R1's PC-A-facing interface.
PC-A's ARP entry for .194 contains R1's local MAC.

questions.prompt: PC-A incorrectly uses /24 on a /26 LAN. It reaches a host on R1's other LAN, and its ARP entry for that remote host contains R1's local MAC. What explains the observed behavior?
options: The switch forwarded the ARP broadcast through R1.
PC-A changed its mask after receiving an ICMP reply.
R1 answered the request on behalf of the remote host.
The remote host joined PC-A's subnet during the ping.
questions.explanation: The described mapping is consistent with proxy ARP: R1 answers with its own MAC and then routes the packet. The observation explains why a ping can work with a wrong mask; it does not make that mask correct.

whyWrong.0: A router does not ordinarily bridge the LAN's ARP broadcast to its other LAN.
whyWrong.1: An ICMP echo reply does not automatically correct a workstation's mask.
whyWrong.3: A ping does not change the remote host's configured subnet.

exhibit.title: Representative R1# show ip interface Gi0/1 excerpt
exhibit.text:
GigabitEthernet0/1 is up, line protocol is up
  Internet address is 10.55.128.1/18

questions.prompt: What is the last usable host address in the interface's subnet?
questions.explanation: The /18 mask is 255.255.192.0. Third-octet values 128–191 belong to this block, ending at broadcast 10.55.191.255; the last usable address is one less.

whyWrong.1: This is the subnet broadcast.
whyWrong.2: This extends beyond the /18's third-octet boundary.
whyWrong.3: This is usable, but many addresses remain before the /18 ends.

cards.front: What are the bit values in an IPv4 octet?
cards.back: Left to right: 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. Add the values whose bits are 1.

cards.front: Which values can appear in a contiguous subnet-mask octet?
cards.back: 0, 128, 192, 224, 240, 248, 252, 254, 255. Across the whole mask, ones must precede zeros.

cards.front: How do you find the increment in a partial mask octet?
cards.back: 256 minus that mask octet. For 192 the increment is 64; network boundaries are multiples of 64 in that octet.

cards.front: What masks and usable counts correspond to /25, /26, and /27?
What masks and usable counts correspond to /28, /29, and /30?
What are the third-octet mask values for /20, /21, /22, and /23?
cards.back: 240, 248, 252, 254. Their third-octet increments are 16, 8, 4, and 2.

cards.front: How many total and usable addresses do h host bits provide?
cards.back: 2^h total; normally 2^h − 2 usable through /30. Treat /31 point-to-point and /32 separately.

cards.front: How do network and broadcast calculations differ?
cards.back: Network: retain network bits and clear host bits. Subnet broadcast: retain network bits and set host bits to one.

cards.front: How are the two addresses of a /31 point-to-point subnet used?
cards.back: Both identify endpoints under RFC 3021. Neither is reserved as that subnet's directed broadcast.

cards.front: What does /32 identify?
cards.back: Exactly one address. It is common on loopbacks and in host routes; other loopback masks are possible.

cards.front: When does bitwise AND produce a 1?
cards.back: Only when both input bits are 1. ANDing an address with its mask clears the host bits.

cards.front: What does a basic workstation ARP for when the destination is remote?
cards.back: Its reachable next-hop gateway's IPv4 address, unless another route applies. The packet keeps the remote destination IP.

cards.front: Must a gateway use the first usable address in a subnet?
cards.back: No. It must be a valid, unique local router address for the ordinary LAN setup; first or last usable is a convention.

cards.front: How many usable addresses are needed for 62 PCs plus one gateway?
cards.back: 63. A /26 has only 62 usable addresses, so it is too small; /25 supplies 126.

cards.front: Can an IPv4 host address end in .0 or .255?
cards.back: Yes. In 10.4.8.0/22, 10.4.9.0 and 10.4.8.255 are usable. Calculate the full network and broadcast first.

cards.front: Configure 192.168.44.129/26 on the current router interface.
cards.back: `ip address 192.168.44.129 255.255.255.192`, then `no shutdown`. Verify the link becomes up/up.

cards.front: Which interface summary omits masks, and where can you find them?
cards.back: `show ip interface brief` omits them. Detailed `show ip interface` shows a prefix; `show running-config` shows the dotted mask.

cards.front: What should you check after IOS rejects an ordinary subnet's host address?
cards.back: Check whether the proposed address is the network or broadcast, then inspect the retained configuration. Do not assume the command was applied.

cards.front: What does an overlap rejection tell you to examine?
cards.back: Calculate the subnet ranges on both the proposed interface and the named existing interface. Check both addresses and masks.

cards.front: Why might a host with an overly broad mask still reach a remote subnet?
cards.back: Proxy ARP may answer its direct ARP request with a router MAC. A successful ping does not prove that the mask is correct.

tickets.title: One workstation cannot reach a nearby routed subnet
tickets.scenario: SALES-07 belongs on 10.20.30.0/24. R1 uses 10.20.30.1/24 on Gi0/0 and connects the file-server LAN 10.20.40.0/24 on Gi0/1. Other sales PCs reach file server 10.20.40.10. SALES-07 reaches its gateway and a routed server at 10.30.0.10, but fails to reach 10.20.40.10. The administrator has confirmed proxy ARP is disabled on Gi0/0 and no extra host routes exist.

exhibits.title: R1 configuration excerpt
exhibits.text:
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 10.20.30.1 255.255.255.0
 no ip proxy-arp

tickets.question: Which configuration error explains the destination-specific failure?
options: The gateway address is outside SALES-07's configured subnet.
The PC's /16 mask incorrectly treats the file server as local.
R1 requires a default route to reach its directly connected LAN.
The file-server address is the broadcast of its /24 subnet.
tickets.explanation: The PC's /16 makes all of 10.20.0.0–10.20.255.255 appear local, including 10.20.40.10. It tries to resolve the file server directly on the sales LAN, while the file server is behind R1 and proxy ARP is disabled. The 10.30.0.10 destination lies outside the mistaken /16 and is sent to the gateway. Gateway 10.20.30.1 is inside both the intended /24 and mistaken /16; the router has a connected path to the file-server LAN; and 10.20.40.10 is a usable /24 address.
tickets.fix: Restore SALES-07 to address `10.20.30.50`, mask `255.255.255.0`, and gateway `10.20.30.1`. Keep the administrator's proxy-ARP setting unchanged. Read the corrected settings, then repeat tests to the gateway, 10.20.40.10, and 10.30.0.10. Success should follow from the correct local/remote decision, not from enabling a workaround.

tickets.title: Local communication works with an invalid gateway setting
tickets.scenario: LAN-B is 192.168.44.192/27, with R1 at 192.168.44.193. PC-B can reach local PC-C at .200 and R1 at .193, but cannot reach LAN-A host 192.168.44.130. PC-C reaches LAN-A successfully. R1's two LAN interfaces are up/up and their masks match the plan.
tickets.question: What is wrong with PC-B's configuration?
options: Its /27 mask must be /24 to allow any remote communication.
Its .194 address is the subnet broadcast and must be removed.
Its gateway is the network address, not the router interface.
Its .193 local ping proves the gateway field is already correct.
tickets.explanation: The subnet spans .192–.223; .192 is the network address, while R1 actually owns .193. The host's own .194 address and /27 mask are valid. Local pings use local delivery and do not establish that the default-gateway field is correct, so the successful ping to .193 does not contradict the fault.
tickets.fix: Set PC-B's default gateway to `192.168.44.193`, retaining address `192.168.44.194` and mask `255.255.255.224`. Verify the values and retry both PC-C and `192.168.44.130`. Do not widen the LAN mask or duplicate R1's address.
