lab.title: Build a VLSM branch and correct a growth plan
lab.intro:
Allocate three LANs inside `10.44.8.0/24`, reserve a future router link, and compare your calculations with a working configuration. Then assess a larger Operations requirement and move that LAN into additional authorized space.

No Packet Tracer execution was available during this review. The addressing and command sequence have been checked against the plan and documentation. Output below is representative, not captured; your version may differ in spacing, extra routes, and messages.
lab.topology:
```diagram
{ "type": "topology", "title": "Three routed LANs", "caption": "Each LAN has a dedicated interface on R1; the future WAN /30 is reserved on paper and is not connected.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "R1", "kind": "router", "label": "R1 · 2911", "x": 6, "y": 1 },
    { "id": "SU", "kind": "switch", "label": "SW-USERS", "x": 2, "y": 3 },
    { "id": "SO", "kind": "switch", "label": "SW-OPS", "x": 6, "y": 3 },
    { "id": "SD", "kind": "switch", "label": "SW-DEV", "x": 10, "y": 3 },
    { "id": "PU", "kind": "pc", "label": "PC-USERS", "sub": "10.44.8.10/25", "x": 2, "y": 5.5 },
    { "id": "PO", "kind": "pc", "label": "PC-OPS", "sub": "10.44.8.140/26", "x": 6, "y": 5.5 },
    { "id": "PD", "kind": "pc", "label": "PC-DEV", "sub": "10.44.8.200/27", "x": 10, "y": 5.5 }
  ],
  "links": [
    { "from": "R1", "to": "SU", "fromLabel": "Gi0/0", "toLabel": "Gi0/1" },
    { "from": "R1", "to": "SO", "fromLabel": "Gi0/1", "toLabel": "Gi0/1" },
    { "from": "R1", "to": "SD", "fromLabel": "Gi0/2", "toLabel": "Gi0/1" },
    { "from": "SU", "to": "PU", "fromLabel": "Fa0/1", "toLabel": "Fa0" },
    { "from": "SO", "to": "PO", "fromLabel": "Fa0/1", "toLabel": "Fa0" },
    { "from": "SD", "to": "PD", "fromLabel": "Fa0/1", "toLabel": "Fa0" }
  ] }
```

Use copper straight-through for all six links. The 2911 provides the three named Ethernet interfaces without additional modules. The 2960 switches use their default VLAN 1 access ports; they need no management addresses for this exercise.

| Device/interface | Address | Mask | Gateway |
|---|---|---|---|
| R1 Gi0/0 | `10.44.8.1` | `255.255.255.128` | — |
| R1 Gi0/1 | `10.44.8.129` | `255.255.255.192` | — |
| R1 Gi0/2 | `10.44.8.193` | `255.255.255.224` | — |
| PC-USERS Fa0 | `10.44.8.10` | `255.255.255.128` | `10.44.8.1` |
| PC-OPS Fa0 | `10.44.8.140` | `255.255.255.192` | `10.44.8.129` |
| PC-DEV Fa0 | `10.44.8.200` | `255.255.255.224` | `10.44.8.193` |

steps.title: Allocate the block on paper
steps.body:
Users require 100 usable addresses, Operations 50, and Devices 20. These totals include each LAN's router interface. Reserve a /30 for a future two-endpoint router link. Starting with an empty `10.44.8.0/24`, choose the smallest suitable subnet for each requirement and allocate largest first. Record network, mask, usable range, broadcast, gateway, and test PC.

:::expected
| Allocation | Prefix | Usable range | Broadcast |
|---|---|---|---|
| Users `10.44.8.0` | /25 | `.1–.126` | `.127` |
| Operations `10.44.8.128` | /26 | `.129–.190` | `.191` |
| Devices `10.44.8.192` | /27 | `.193–.222` | `.223` |
| Reserved link `10.44.8.224` | /30 | `.225–.226` | `.227` |

The allocations consume `128 + 64 + 32 + 4 = 228` addresses. The free range .228–.255 contains 28 addresses and can be represented as `.228/30`, `.232/29`, and `.240/28`. The reserved link will not appear in the routing table because no interface uses it.
:::

steps.title: Cable the topology and address the router
steps.body:
Place and connect the specified devices. Decline the initial setup dialog on R1 if it appears. Configure the interfaces from the original table; explicitly return to global configuration between interfaces.

```ios R1
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R1
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# description Users LAN
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.44.8.1 255.255.255.128
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# description Operations LAN
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.44.8.129 255.255.255.192
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/2
R1(config-if)# description Devices LAN
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.44.8.193 255.255.255.224
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip interface brief
```

:::expected
With the switch links ready, Gi0/0, Gi0/1, and Gi0/2 are up/up and show the three gateway addresses. Switch ports may take time to enter forwarding. The brief table does not show masks; do not treat it as the complete verification.
:::

steps.title: Address the PCs with dotted masks
steps.body:
On each PC, use **Desktop → IP Configuration → Static**. Enter its address, the exact dotted mask, and its gateway from the table. Replace any automatic mask entry. Then use **Desktop → Command Prompt** to check and test.

```text PC-USERS
ipconfig
ping 10.44.8.1
```

```text PC-OPS
ipconfig
ping 10.44.8.129
```

```text PC-DEV
ipconfig
ping 10.44.8.193
```

:::expected
Each PC reports the table's values and reaches its own gateway after any initial resolution delay. The correct masks are /25, /26, and /27 respectively. A mask of 255.0.0.0 is not correct merely because the address begins with 10.
:::

steps.title: Read the plan back from the routing table
steps.body:
Compare the router's connected prefixes with the paper plan. Use the detailed interface command to inspect the Operations mask directly.

```ios R1
R1# show ip route
R1# show ip interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1# show running-config
```

:::expected
Representative connected routes:
```output R1# show ip route
C        10.44.8.0/25 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0  ← Users
C        10.44.8.128/26 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/1  ← Operations
C        10.44.8.192/27 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/2  ← Devices
```
The detailed Gi0/1 output identifies `10.44.8.129/26`. Additional local /32 routes may be present. If a detailed command is unavailable in your simulator image, read the interface's dotted mask in `show running-config` and compare its calculated subnet with the connected route.
:::

steps.title: Test every pair
steps.body:
Run all six tests. This checks each PC's ability to send traffic through its configured gateway and receive replies from both other LANs.

```text PC-USERS
ping 10.44.8.140
ping 10.44.8.200
```

```text PC-OPS
ping 10.44.8.10
ping 10.44.8.200
```

```text PC-DEV
ping 10.44.8.10
ping 10.44.8.140
```

:::expected
All destinations respond after links and address resolution settle. R1 needs no static routes for these directly connected LANs. Record success or failure for each pair; repeat an initial failed echo rather than assuming a precise number of replies or a particular TTL.
:::

steps.title: Check a proposed Operations expansion
steps.body:
Operations now requires 70 total usable addresses. Work out its minimum prefix, then test the proposed change below. Do not change the PCs yet.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.44.8.129 255.255.255.128
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show running-config
R1# show ip route
```

:::expected
A /26 has only 62 usable addresses, so 70 requires a /25. However, `10.44.8.128/25` covers .128–.255 and overlaps the Devices subnet .192–.223. IOS should reject the command and report an overlap; verify that Gi0/1 retains its /26. Users /25 plus Operations /25 already consumes the entire /24, leaving no space for Devices and the reserved link.
:::

Stop here long enough to record the rejected change and its reason. The next step implements a different, valid plan rather than repeating the failed command.

steps.title: Move Operations into additional allocated space
steps.body:
Assume the address administrator has now assigned `10.44.9.0/24` to this site as well. Use its lower /25 for Operations. Users, Devices, and the reserved link keep their original allocations. Update the address table before changing R1.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.44.9.1 255.255.255.128
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1# show ip route
```

On PC-OPS, enter address `10.44.9.10`, mask `255.255.255.128`, and gateway `10.44.9.1`. Both addresses lie in `10.44.9.0/25`. Do not carry the old host number 140 into this plan: `10.44.9.140/25` belongs to the upper /25 and would put the PC outside its gateway's subnet.

```text PC-OPS
ipconfig
ping 10.44.9.1
ping 10.44.8.10
ping 10.44.8.200
```

:::expected
R1's Operations connected route changes from `10.44.8.128/26` to `10.44.9.0/25`. The other two connected routes are unchanged. PC-OPS reaches its new gateway and both other LANs. From PC-USERS and PC-DEV, test the new Operations address `10.44.9.10`, not the retired .8.140 address.
:::

steps.title: Verify the final plan and save
steps.body:
The final Operations mask remains /25; do not restore its old /26. Read each PC's settings and compare them with the updated plan. From PC-USERS, run the two remote tests below, then save R1.

```text PC-USERS
ping 10.44.9.10
ping 10.44.8.200
```

```ios R1
R1# show ip interface brief
R1# show ip route
R1# copy running-config startup-config
```

:::expected
All three LANs work under the updated plan. Accept the default startup-config filename and save the Packet Tracer file as `vlsm-branch.pkt`. The rejected overlap has been resolved by obtaining and using suitable space, not by weakening the mask checks.
:::

lab.troubleshooting:
- An interface is administratively down: enable the intended port, then check whether the cable and peer allow it to become up/up.
- An overlap is reported: calculate the ranges on both the proposed and named existing interface. The existing mask may be the error.
- A gateway ping fails: inspect that PC's actual address, mask, gateway, and physical connection. An overly broad mask alone does not necessarily prevent reaching a local gateway.
- Local gateway tests pass but a remote pair fails: check both endpoint configurations and R1's connected routes.
- After the move, Operations fails: confirm PC-OPS is .9.10/25 with gateway .9.1, and that other PCs target the new address.
- A successful ping conflicts with an incorrect mask: correct the mask from the plan. Proxy ARP or other host behavior can hide some errors; it is not a substitute for verification.
lab.challenge:
On paper, allocate `192.168.72.0/24` for four LANs requiring 60, 28, 12, and 6 total usable addresses, plus one /30 router link. Use the smallest suitable subnet for each and allocate largest first. List all broadcasts and the exact remaining free blocks.

Save your existing file, then create a separate challenge copy. Reuse only R1 Gi0/0 and Gi0/1 with the two largest new LANs, and shut Gi0/2. Choose the first usable gateway and the next usable address for each test PC. Configure the matching masks and gateways, then verify the two connected prefixes and bidirectional PC pings.

:::expected
| Requirement | Network | Gateway | Test PC | Broadcast |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 60 | `192.168.72.0/26` | `.1` | `.2` | `.63` |
| 28 | `192.168.72.64/27` | `.65` | `.66` | `.95` |
| 12 | `192.168.72.96/28` | `.97` | — | `.111` |
| 6 | `192.168.72.112/29` | `.113` | — | `.119` |
| Link | `192.168.72.120/30` | Two endpoints .121 and .122 | — | `.123` |

Free blocks are `192.168.72.124/30` and `192.168.72.128/25`. Configure Gi0/0 with `ip address 192.168.72.1 255.255.255.192`, and Gi0/1 with `ip address 192.168.72.65 255.255.255.224`; keep both enabled. Use the matching masks on PCs .2 and .66 and their listed gateways. Under Gi0/2, enter `shutdown`. The active connected routes should be `192.168.72.0/26` and `192.168.72.64/27`; the two PCs should reach each other.
:::

questions.prompt: Which network and broadcast contain 172.16.77.210/20?
questions.explanation: The /20 mask has third-octet increment 16. The containing aligned block is 64–79, with the entire fourth octet available as host bits.

whyWrong.0: This treats the address like a /24 and does not start on a /20 boundary.
whyWrong.1: 72 is not a multiple of 16 and is not a /20 network boundary.
whyWrong.3: The block beginning at 80 does not contain third-octet value 77.

questions.prompt: A LAN needs 70 workstations and one gateway. Which prefix gives the smallest suitable subnet?
options: /26, providing 62 usable addresses
/25, providing 126 usable addresses
/27, providing 30 usable addresses
/24, providing 254 usable addresses
questions.explanation: The requirement is 71 usable addresses. A /26 is too small, while /25 is the smallest ordinary subnet with enough usable addresses.

whyWrong.0: 62 is less than 71.
whyWrong.2: A /27 supplies only 30 usable addresses, fewer than the required 71.
whyWrong.3: A /24 fits but consumes more space than necessary.

questions.prompt: 172.16.0.0/16 is divided into equal /23 subnets. How many subnets result, and how many ordinary usable addresses does each provide?
options: 256 subnets; 254 usable each
64 subnets; 1022 usable each
128 subnets; 512 usable each
128 subnets; 510 usable each
questions.explanation: The new prefix adds seven bits: 2^7 = 128 subnets. Each /23 has nine host bits, giving 512 total addresses and 510 usable addresses.

whyWrong.0: These values describe dividing /16 into /24s.
whyWrong.1: These values describe dividing /16 into /22s.
whyWrong.2: 512 is the total per /23, before removing network and broadcast.

questions.prompt: Which network and broadcast belong to 10.4.200.77/20?
questions.explanation: The third-octet increment is 16. Address 200 lies in the aligned 192–207 block, and the fourth octet runs through 255.

whyWrong.1: 200 is not an aligned /20 boundary.
whyWrong.2: 196 is not an aligned /20 boundary.
whyWrong.3: 208 begins the next /20 and excludes the given host.

questions.prompt: Allocate from the bottom of an empty 192.168.40.0/24, largest first. Requirements are 120, 55, and 25 total usable addresses including gateways, plus two /30 links. Which two placements are correct?
options: First router link: 192.168.40.192/30
Second router link: 192.168.40.224/30
questions.explanation: The /25 occupies .0–.127, then the /26 occupies .128–.191, and the /27 occupies .192–.223. The two /30 links follow at .224/30 and .228/30.

whyWrong.1: This overlaps the 55-address LAN.
whyWrong.3: This overlaps the 25-address LAN.
whyWrong.4: This is the first link's allocation; the second starts at .228.

questions.prompt: Three LANs require 100, 100, and 50 total usable addresses. Can all three fit in one /24 using ordinary subnets?
options: Yes; the host totals are below 256.
Yes; allocate the /26 before the /25s.
No; the required blocks total 320 addresses.
Yes; a summary removes duplicate space.
questions.explanation: The two 100-address LANs each require /25, and the 50-address LAN requires /26. Their blocks consume 128 + 128 + 64 = 320 addresses, exceeding a /24's 256.

whyWrong.0: Allocation includes the power-of-two block sizes, not just the requested usable-address totals.
whyWrong.1: Changing the order cannot increase the parent's capacity.
whyWrong.3: A summary changes route representation; it does not free allocated addresses.

questions.prompt: Which one prefix covers exactly the four listed /24 networks?
questions.explanation: The networks cover third-octet values 8–11, an aligned group of four. A /22 covers that exact 1,024-address range.

whyWrong.0: A /23 at .8 covers only .8 and .9.
whyWrong.1: This covers .0 through .3, not the listed networks.
whyWrong.2: This also includes .12 through .15.

questions.prompt: Which is the smallest single containing prefix for 10.44.9.0/24 through 10.44.12.0/24?
questions.explanation: The four /24s cross a /22 boundary. Their smallest single containing prefix is 10.44.8.0/21, covering .8 through .15 and therefore including additional networks.

whyWrong.0: This covers .12–.15 and misses .9–.11.
whyWrong.2: This covers .8–.11 and misses .12.
whyWrong.3: This contains the range but is larger than the required /21.

questions.prompt: Which two addresses are within RFC 1918 private space? Choose two.
questions.explanation: The 172.16.0.0/12 private block ends at 172.31.255.255, and all of 10.0.0.0/8 is private. Thus the listed .31 address and 10 address qualify.

whyWrong.0: 172.32 is beyond the RFC 1918 172 range.
whyWrong.2: 100.64.0.0/10 is shared address space, a separate designation.
whyWrong.4: The private block is 192.168.0.0/16, not 192.169.0.0/16.

exhibit.title: Recorded workstation configuration
exhibit.text:
Address configuration: automatic
IPv4 address:           169.254.42.18
Subnet mask:            255.255.0.0
Default gateway:        none

questions.prompt: This workstation is set to obtain an address automatically. Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: Check why normal DHCP configuration was not obtained.
Add NAT so this RFC 1918 address becomes public.
Use the provider's shared-space gateway for this address.
Change the mask to /24 without checking the LAN plan.
questions.explanation: The record is consistent with IPv4 link-local fallback rather than a normal DHCP lease for the intended LAN. Check connectivity, VLAN membership, and DHCP availability; this snapshot alone does not identify the exact failure.

whyWrong.1: 169.254.0.0/16 is link-local, not RFC 1918 space.
whyWrong.2: Provider shared space is 100.64.0.0/10, not this range.
whyWrong.3: An arbitrary mask change does not restore the intended DHCP configuration.

exhibit.title: Existing and proposed configuration
exhibit.text:
Existing Gi0/0: ip address 10.44.8.1 255.255.255.128
Proposed Gi0/1: ip address 10.44.8.140 255.255.255.0

questions.prompt: Why does the proposed Gi0/1 address conflict with the existing Gi0/0 subnet?
options: The proposed .140 address is the /24 broadcast.
The 10/8 private block permits only one interface.
The interface must be shut before assigning an address.
The proposed /24 includes Gi0/0's entire /25.
questions.explanation: Gi0/0 occupies 10.44.8.0–10.44.8.127. Gi0/1's proposed /24 covers .0–.255, so the two routed interface subnets would overlap.

whyWrong.0: The /24 broadcast is .255.
whyWrong.1: The private parent block can be subnetted across many interfaces.
whyWrong.2: Shutdown state does not remove the address overlap.

exhibit.title: Recorded router interfaces
exhibit.text:
Gi0/1: 10.44.8.129/26, connected to PC-OPS
Gi0/2: 10.44.8.193/27, connected to host 10.44.8.200

questions.prompt: PC-OPS uses 10.44.8.140/25, but its intended LAN is the /26 shown. How does that wrong mask affect its initial decision for destination 10.44.8.200?
options: It treats its .129 gateway as outside the local subnet.
It computes the same local range as R1's /26.
It treats .200 as local and tries ARP for .200.
It changes the router's connected route to a /25.
questions.explanation: The PC's /25 says .128–.255 is local, so .200 appears local and is an ARP target. With the intended /26, .200 is remote and should be sent through the gateway.

whyWrong.0: Both .129 and .140 lie in the PC's mistaken upper /25.
whyWrong.1: The router's /26 ends at .191; the PC's /25 ends at .255.
whyWrong.3: A host's configured mask does not rewrite R1's interface configuration.

exhibit.title: Recorded PC-DEV settings
exhibit.text:
IPv4 address:    10.44.8.200
Subnet mask:     255.255.255.224
Default gateway: 10.44.8.129

questions.prompt: PC-DEV belongs on 10.44.8.192/27 and R1's LAN interface is .193. Which change brings the shown PC settings into line with the plan?
options: Change the mask to 255.255.255.192.
Change the default gateway to 10.44.8.193.
Change the host address to 10.44.8.223.
Change the host address to 10.44.8.193.
questions.explanation: The host .200 and /27 mask match the intended LAN, but gateway .129 does not. Use the actual local router interface .193.

whyWrong.0: This changes the planned subnet without correcting the gateway value.
whyWrong.2: Address .223 is this /27's broadcast.
whyWrong.3: Address .193 is already used by the router, creating a duplicate address.

questions.prompt: Which two existing subnets overlap a proposed 10.20.4.0/22 allocation? Choose two.
questions.explanation: The proposed /22 spans 10.20.4.0–10.20.7.255. The .6.128/25 is contained inside it, while .0.0/21 contains the entire proposed block.

whyWrong.1: This begins after the proposed block.
whyWrong.3: This ends before the proposed block.
whyWrong.4: This is a separate /22 covering third-octet values 12–15.

questions.prompt: Divide 192.168.5.0/24 into at least 12 equal subnets, maximizing the usable capacity of each. Which choice meets both requirements?
options: 255.255.255.240; 16 subnets of 14 usable
255.255.255.224; 8 subnets of 30 usable
255.255.255.248; 32 subnets of 6 usable
255.255.255.192; 4 subnets of 62 usable
questions.explanation: Four extra prefix bits produce 16 subnets, so /28 is the first prefix that meets the minimum of 12. Its four host bits provide 16 total and 14 usable addresses per subnet.

whyWrong.1: Eight subnets do not meet the required 12.
whyWrong.2: This meets the subnet count but reduces capacity unnecessarily.
whyWrong.3: Four subnets do not meet the required 12.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes RFC 1918 addresses?
options: They require translation between every pair of internal LANs.
They can be routed internally but are not globally unique public space.
They become globally unique whenever assigned by DHCP.
They provide firewall protection through their private designation.
questions.explanation: Private addresses can be routed within an organization's network. Separate organizations may reuse the same ranges, so they are not globally unique public allocations.

whyWrong.0: Ordinary routing between nonoverlapping private LANs does not require NAT.
whyWrong.2: DHCP assigns configuration; it does not change the address range's designation.
whyWrong.3: The private designation does not enforce a security policy.

cards.front: Which three blocks are RFC 1918 private space?
Where does 172.16.0.0/12 end? Are 172.32.1.1 and 192.169.1.1 private?
cards.back: It ends at 172.31.255.255. Neither example is RFC 1918; being outside RFC 1918 alone does not prove public usability.

cards.front: What is the block increment in a partial mask octet?
cards.back: 256 minus the mask value. Find the aligned boundary at or below the host's value in that octet.

cards.front: What increments correspond to mask values 128 through 254?
How do /20, /26, and octet-aligned /24 boundaries differ?
cards.back: /20 varies within the third octet; /26 within the fourth. /24 has three full network octets and one full host octet.

cards.front: How do you count equal-size child subnets and usable addresses?
cards.back: Parent /p to child /q: 2^(q−p) subnets. Each ordinary child through /30: 2^(32−q) − 2 usable addresses.

cards.front: How many ordinary usable addresses do /24 through /30 provide?
Compare /30, /31, and /32.
cards.back: /30: four total, two ordinary usable. /31 point-to-point: two endpoints. /32: one address.

cards.front: How many /23s fit in a /16, and how many usable addresses are in each?
cards.back: 2^7 = 128 subnets, each with 2^9 − 2 = 510 usable addresses.

cards.front: How many /20s fit in a /8, and how many usable addresses are in each?
cards.back: 2^12 = 4,096 subnets, each with 2^12 − 2 = 4,094 usable addresses.

cards.front: What checks make a VLSM allocation valid?
cards.back: Enough capacity, correct boundary, containment in the parent, and no overlap. Allocate larger blocks first in empty space.

cards.front: How do you find a single containing summary?
cards.back: Find the shared leading bits of the full address range. Use them as the prefix and clear the remaining bits; check extra covered space.

cards.front: Summarize .8/24–.11/24 versus .9/24–.12/24 under 10.44.
cards.back: 10.44.8.0/22 exactly covers the first group. 10.44.8.0/21 contains the second but also covers four additional /24s.

cards.front: What does an automatically assigned 169.254.x.x address suggest?
cards.back: IPv4 link-local fallback. Investigate why normal DHCP configuration was not obtained; the address alone does not identify the cause.

cards.front: Do modern subnet counts exclude subnet zero and the all-ones subnet?
cards.back: No. All 2^s subnet numbers are available after adding s prefix bits. Do not confuse this with reserving host network/broadcast addresses.

cards.front: Which IPv4 blocks identify loopback and multicast addresses?
cards.back: 127.0.0.0/8 is loopback; 224.0.0.0/4 is multicast. Neither is ordinary unicast addressing for a workstation LAN.
0.0.0.0 can mean unspecified; 0.0.0.0/0 is the default-route prefix. 255.255.255.255 is the limited broadcast.

cards.front: How do invalid host addresses differ from overlapping allocations?
cards.back: Network/broadcast selection makes the host address unsuitable. Overlap means two proposed routed subnet ranges share addresses; inspect the relevant masks.

cards.front: What should you verify when local pings work but remote pings fail?
cards.back: Both endpoints' masks and gateways, followed by router routes. A too-wide mask can make remote addresses appear local.

cards.front: Are private addresses routable, and does NAT replace a firewall?
cards.back: Private traffic can be routed internally. NAT translates addresses; firewall policy is a separate function.

tickets.title: The Devices subnet overlaps an existing interface
tickets.scenario: The approved plan is Users 10.44.8.0/25 on Gi0/0, Operations 10.44.8.128/26 on Gi0/1, and Devices 10.44.8.192/27 on Gi0/2. While configuring Devices, IOS reports an overlap with Gi0/1. Its exact message is not needed: the configuration below shows the relevant evidence.

exhibits.title: Existing Gi0/1 configuration excerpt
exhibits.text:
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 ip address 10.44.8.129 255.255.255.128

exhibits.title: Proposed Gi0/2 configuration
exhibits.text:
interface GigabitEthernet0/2
 ip address 10.44.8.193 255.255.255.224

tickets.question: Which correction follows the approved plan?
options: Move the Devices gateway to .192 but retain its /27 mask.
Change Operations from its configured /25 to the planned /26.
Change Devices to /24 so it includes the Operations interface.
Remove Operations because a /24 can contain only two LANs.
tickets.explanation: Operations was configured as 10.44.8.128/25, spanning .128–.255 and including the proposed Devices range .192–.223. The intended /26 ends at .191, so correcting that mask removes the overlap. Address .192 is not a valid Devices gateway, widening Devices would worsen the overlap, and a /24 can contain more than two smaller nonoverlapping subnets.
tickets.fix:
```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.44.8.129 255.255.255.192
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/2
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.44.8.193 255.255.255.224
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip route
```
With both links operational, verify C prefixes `10.44.8.128/26` and `10.44.8.192/27`. Also compare Operations clients with the planned /26; the router correction does not update their static masks.

tickets.title: A broad host mask sends ARP onto the wrong LAN
tickets.scenario: PC-OPS belongs on 10.44.8.128/26, gateway 10.44.8.129. R1 also connects Users 10.44.8.0/25 and Devices 10.44.8.192/27. The PC reaches its gateway and a remote server at 10.10.20.5, but fails to reach Users printer 10.44.8.20 and Devices scanner 10.44.8.200. Proxy ARP is disabled on the Operations-facing router interface, and there are no extra host routes.

exhibits.title: R1 configuration excerpt
exhibits.text:
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 ip address 10.44.8.129 255.255.255.192
 no ip proxy-arp

tickets.question: Which diagnosis accounts for the observed pattern?
options: R1 needs static routes for its two directly connected LANs.
R1's /26 should be widened to match the incorrect host mask.
The host's /24 treats the printer and scanner as local destinations.
The .129 gateway lies outside the PC's configured /24 subnet.
tickets.explanation: The host's /24 covers .0–.255, so both .20 and .200 appear local even though they are on R1's other LANs. The PC tries ARP on Operations, where those hosts cannot answer and R1 is not acting as a proxy. Server 10.10.20.5 is outside the mistaken /24 and is sent through the valid gateway. R1 already has connected LAN routes, the approved /26 should be retained, and .129 is within both masks.
tickets.fix: Set PC-OPS to `10.44.8.140`, mask `255.255.255.192`, gateway `10.44.8.129`. Verify those settings and repeat tests to .129, `10.44.8.20`, `10.44.8.200`, and `10.10.20.5`. Keep the router's planned subnet and proxy-ARP policy unchanged.

lab.title: Watch a TCP handshake and a UDP lookup in Simulation mode
lab.intro: Build a local LAN, enable HTTP and DNS, and compare a TCP opening with a UDP query. Then disable one service and use separate tests to identify what still works. These are guided simulator observations, not a claim that a particular Packet Tracer release was manually tested; record the actual ports, sequence values, labels, and behavior shown by your installed version.
lab.topology:
```diagram
{ "type": "topology", "title": "TCP and UDP on one subnet",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "A", "kind": "pc", "label": "PC-A", "sub": "192.168.40.10/24", "x": 2, "y": 3 },
    { "id": "S", "kind": "switch", "label": "SW1", "sub": "2960 · VLAN 1", "x": 6, "y": 3 },
    { "id": "V", "kind": "server", "label": "SRV1", "sub": "192.168.40.20/24", "x": 10, "y": 3 }
  ],
  "links": [
    { "from": "A", "to": "S", "fromLabel": "Fa0", "toLabel": "Fa0/1" },
    { "from": "S", "to": "V", "fromLabel": "Fa0/2", "toLabel": "Fa0" }
  ], "caption": "HTTP and DNS share one server address; ports and transport identify the requested service." }
```

| Device | Interface / peer | IP address / mask | DNS / gateway |
|---|---|---|---|
| PC-A | FastEthernet0 to SW1 Fa0/1 | `192.168.40.10`, `255.255.255.0` | DNS `192.168.40.20`; gateway blank |
| SRV1 | FastEthernet0 to SW1 Fa0/2 | `192.168.40.20`, `255.255.255.0` | DNS not needed; gateway blank |
| SW1 | Fa0/1 and Fa0/2 | No management address required | No routing required |

Use copper straight-through cables for both host-to-switch links. Start with new devices rather than a reused switch with unknown configuration. All traffic stays within one IPv4 subnet, so a router and default gateway are unnecessary. The `.test` names below are lab examples, not public sites.

steps.title: Cable, address and name the switch
steps.body:
Place the devices and connect the exact ports in the table. On each host, open **Desktop → IP Configuration**, select **Static**, and enter its address and mask. Set PC-A's DNS server to `192.168.40.20`. On SW1, open the CLI, decline an initial configuration dialog if offered, press Enter to reach the prompt, and enter:

```ios SW1
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname SW1
SW1(config)# interface range fastethernet0/1 - 2
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport access vlan 1
SW1(config-if-range)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if-range)# end
SW1# show interfaces status
```

Wait for both links to become operational and for the switch ports to forward. On PC-A, use **Desktop → Command Prompt**:

```text PC-A
ipconfig /all
ping 192.168.40.20
```

:::expected
The host settings match the table and the ping obtains replies. An initial timeout can occur while address resolution or port initialization completes; repeat the ping after checking link state. Persistent failure is not an expected result: inspect addresses, masks, cables, and port status before continuing. Do not assign an IP address to the switch merely to make local Layer 2 forwarding work.
:::

steps.title: Turn on the services and load the page in Realtime mode
steps.body:
On SRV1, open **Services → HTTP** and set **HTTP On**. This lab uses `http://` and does not require HTTPS. Open **Services → DNS**, select **On**, and add an A record with Name `www.lab.test` and Address `192.168.40.20`; click **Add** and confirm that the record appears.

On PC-A, open **Desktop → Web Browser**, enter `http://192.168.40.20`, and select **Go**. Then run a name lookup from its Command Prompt and browse to `http://www.lab.test`:

```text PC-A
nslookup www.lab.test
```

:::expected
The address-based request displays the server's configured HTTP page. The lookup returns `192.168.40.20`, and the name-based URL displays the same page. Page wording and lookup formatting can vary; the success criteria are the returned address and the loaded content, not an exact welcome message. If name lookup fails while address-based browsing works, check the DNS service, record, and PC-A's DNS setting.
:::

steps.title: Capture the three-way handshake
steps.body:
Enter **Simulation** mode and open **Edit Filters**. Clear unrelated protocols and select ARP, TCP, HTTP, DNS, and UDP if UDP has a separate entry in your version. Clear the event list with **Reset Simulation** if needed; this is not a promise that application or ARP caches are erased. Close and reopen PC-A's browser, request `http://192.168.40.20`, and use **Capture/Forward** to advance the exchange.

Click TCP event envelopes and inspect **OSI Model** and **Inbound/Outbound PDU Details**. Record the following for a new connection: source/destination IP, source/destination port, SYN/ACK flags, sequence number, and acknowledgment number. If an existing connection is reused, finish forwarding it and start another browser session; look for a SYN before calling the capture a new opening.

:::expected
For a new ordinary TCP connection, the opening is client SYN to server port `80`, server SYN/ACK from port `80` to the client's selected port, then client ACK. ARP can appear first if a host needs a MAC mapping. The client port and displayed initial sequence values are observations, not fixed lab requirements. A simulator or analyzer may use relative numbering; check that each SYN is acknowledged with its sequence plus one in the displayed numbering system.
:::

Continue forwarding events until the HTTP request and response complete. Record any FIN or RST events if the simulator exposes them. Do not fail the lab because a close uses a different number of segments, occurs later, or is not visible in the event list: the learning target is the handshake and application data exchange.

steps.title: Capture a DNS lookup over UDP
steps.body:
Leave Simulation mode active, clear the event list, and run `nslookup www.lab.test` from PC-A. Advance the resulting events and inspect the DNS query and reply. If no new query appears, add a new A record `lookup.lab.test` pointing to `192.168.40.20` on SRV1 and look up that fresh name instead. This gives you a new test without assuming a particular cache-clearing command.

```text PC-A
nslookup www.lab.test
```

After creating the optional fresh record, replace `www.lab.test` in that command with `lookup.lab.test`.

:::expected
The small ordinary lookup modeled here uses UDP: the query targets server port `53`, and the reply comes from port `53` to the client's query port. There is no UDP SYN/SYN-ACK/ACK exchange before it. You may also see ARP or retries, so count the DNS messages separately from all event-list rows. A successful uncomplicated lookup normally has a query and a reply; that observation does not mean real DNS uses UDP exclusively.
:::

Write a comparison in your notes: TCP established state before exchanging the HTTP data; UDP carried the DNS request without a UDP connection opening. Do not conclude that UDP could recover a lost query by itself. Any retry of the lookup is behavior of the application using UDP.

steps.title: Look at the socket table with netstat
steps.body:
Return to **Realtime** mode, request the HTTP page again, and immediately open PC-A's Command Prompt:

```text PC-A
netstat
```

If your Packet Tracer version does not implement the command or shows no connection by the time you inspect it, use the captured endpoints from Step 3 as the required evidence. An optional comparison on a real Windows PC is `netstat -an`, which includes numeric endpoints and listening sockets. Do not expect that PC's addresses or ports to match this isolated simulator topology.

:::expected
Any visible TCP connection should be interpreted as a local endpoint, a remote endpoint, and a state. A short HTTP connection may already have closed; an empty snapshot does not contradict the completed HTTP request. Identify the client port and server `80` from a captured connection even if the simulator's socket table provides no usable row. There is no requirement to install another operating system or packet analyzer for this step.
:::

steps.title: Prove that ping and a listening port are different questions
steps.body:
Save a working copy as `tcp-udp-baseline.pkt`. On SRV1, change **Services → HTTP → Off**, leaving DNS On and all addressing unchanged. Start a fresh browser session and attempt `http://192.168.40.20`; use Simulation mode if needed to ensure you are observing a new request rather than previously displayed content. Then compare:

```text PC-A
ping 192.168.40.20
nslookup www.lab.test
```

:::expected
HTTP fails while ping still obtains replies and DNS can still return `192.168.40.20`. The controlled change identifies HTTP service availability as the fault in this lab. Depending on simulator behavior, the TCP attempt may receive a reset or no useful reply; neither an exact error message nor exact retry count is required. On an unknown production network, the same symptom would justify further service and filtering checks, not an automatic claim that the server process was stopped.
:::

steps.title: Restore the service and save
steps.body:
Set SRV1's **HTTP On** again. Return to Realtime mode and retry both `http://192.168.40.20` and `http://www.lab.test` from a fresh browser request. Confirm name lookup and reachability, then save the switch configuration:

```text PC-A
ping 192.168.40.20
nslookup www.lab.test
```

```ios SW1
SW1# copy running-config startup-config
```

Accept the default destination filename when prompted. Save the Packet Tracer topology as `tcp-udp-lab.pkt`; simulator host addresses, service settings, and cables are stored in the topology file, not just in the switch startup configuration.

:::expected
Both forms of HTTP request work again and name lookup returns the server address. Keep notes showing the TCP endpoints, three handshake flags, UDP DNS ports, failed-service observations, and recovery. Those observations should explain the result rather than merely list commands you typed.
:::

lab.troubleshooting:
- **Repeated ping failure:** compare both IP addresses and masks with the table, verify the chosen cables/ports, and wait for forwarding state. A persistent timeout requires investigation.
- **HTTP by address works but by name fails:** confirm PC-A's DNS address, DNS On, the exact A-record name, and the record's address. Avoid adding unrelated routes.
- **No visible SYN:** the browser may be reusing a connection; observe a new session and advance all pending simulation events.
- **No visible DNS event:** run an explicit lookup, use a fresh record, and check the filter selection. Do not infer transport behavior from an empty filtered list.
- **Simulation appears stalled:** pending events need Capture/Forward or automatic playback; a waiting application is not necessarily broken.
- **A CLI display is unsupported:** use the stated PDU inspection alternative and record the limitation. Do not memorize unverified simulator constants.
lab.challenge:
Add `intranet.lab.test` with address `192.168.40.20`. Predict and inspect a lookup of that name, then explain why the answer does not itself establish an HTTP connection. On paper, calculate the cumulative ACK after receiving in-order data beginning at sequence `8001` with length `1200`. Finally, predict the ACK for a SYN at sequence `8001` carrying no data.

:::expected
For the uncomplicated lookup in this lab, expect a UDP query to destination `53` and reply from source `53`, plus possible address-resolution or retry traffic. There is no UDP handshake. The answer supplies the address; a later browser request separately opens or uses a transport connection for HTTP. The data occupies bytes `8001–9200`, so the next expected byte is `9201`. A SYN consumes one sequence number and is acknowledged with `8002`. Real DNS can also use TCP, so describe your observation without turning it into a universal DNS restriction.
:::

questions.prompt: Which interpretation of this representative TCP opening is correct?
options: The client listens on port 51514 and the server initiates the exchange.
The server’s initial sequence is 3001 and its service uses port 9000.
The client requests port 22; the server acknowledges the client’s SYN.
The server accepts data before completing a separate UDP opening.
questions.explanation: The first segment requests TCP port 22 from client port 51514. The server’s SYN/ACK supplies its own sequence 9000 and acknowledges 3001, one beyond the client’s SYN. The final ACK completes this ordinary opening.

whyWrong.0: The initial SYN travels from the client’s selected port to the server service port, not in the reverse direction.
whyWrong.1: 3001 is an acknowledgment number and 9000 is a sequence number; neither is the service port.
whyWrong.3: This is a TCP handshake; UDP has no separate opening in this exchange.

questions.prompt: A TCP data segment starts at sequence 20001 and contains 1460 data bytes, with no SYN or FIN. Every earlier byte has arrived in order and no later data is buffered. What cumulative acknowledgment follows?
questions.explanation: The data occupies bytes 20001 through 21460 inclusive. The next byte expected is 21461, calculated as starting sequence plus data length.

whyWrong.1: 21460 is the last byte received, not the next byte expected.
whyWrong.2: 20002 advances by one rather than by 1460 data bytes.
whyWrong.3: 1461 ignores the starting sequence number.

questions.prompt: Which two fields are present in the UDP header? Choose two.
options: Length
Sequence number
Checksum
Receive window
Acknowledgment number
questions.explanation: UDP has four 16-bit header fields: source port, destination port, length, and checksum. Its length includes the UDP header and data; application data may contain additional fields of the application’s own design.

whyWrong.1: UDP has no sequence-number header field; an application can add its own numbering inside the payload.
whyWrong.3: The advertised receive window is a TCP feature, not a UDP header field.
whyWrong.4: UDP has no acknowledgment header field, although an application can exchange acknowledgment messages.

questions.prompt: A DHCPv4 client has no usable IPv4 address and begins discovery. Which description matches its initial transport exchange?
options: It opens TCP from client port 68 to server port 67 before discovery.
It sends a UDP discovery from server port 67 to client port 68.
It sends ICMP discovery and uses UDP only after receiving an address.
It can broadcast UDP from client port 68 to server port 67.
questions.explanation: Initial DHCPv4 discovery can use source 0.0.0.0 and destination 255.255.255.255, with UDP ports 68 to 67. It does not require a TCP connection opening; later DHCP traffic is not necessarily broadcast.

whyWrong.0: DHCPv4 uses UDP, so no TCP handshake precedes this discovery.
whyWrong.1: The client and server port roles are reversed in this option.
whyWrong.2: DHCP discovery is not an ICMP exchange.

spec.title: Representative ordinary TCP close
spec.caption: Each direction sends a FIN; no application data accompanies the segments shown.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly explains the TCP close shown?
options: The higher server sequence proves that the server closed its direction first.
The client’s FIN consumes sequence 700 and is acknowledged with 701.
The server’s FIN carries one application byte because its ACK advances by one.
The server must stop sending immediately when it acknowledges the client FIN.
questions.explanation: Each TCP direction closes separately. A FIN consumes one sequence number even with no application data, so the client FIN at 700 is acknowledged with 701. The server can still send before issuing its own FIN.

whyWrong.0: Sequence numbers belong to separate directions and do not indicate which endpoint initiated closing.
whyWrong.2: The extra sequence position accounts for FIN, not an application byte.
whyWrong.3: Acknowledging the client’s FIN does not close the server’s sending direction.

questions.prompt: A client uses temporary source port 52340. Which statement about the IANA ranges is correct?
options: 52340 is in dynamic/private 49152–65535; OS selection ranges may differ.
52340 is in user/registered 1024–65535; applications register all such ports.
52340 is in system/well-known 0–65535; transport determines the category.
52340 is outside the usable port field; a TCP port cannot exceed 49151.
questions.explanation: 52340 lies in IANA’s dynamic/private range, 49152–65535. That registry classification does not imply that every operating system chooses temporary client ports from exactly that range.

whyWrong.1: The user/registered range ends at 49151.
whyWrong.2: System/well-known ports occupy 0–1023, not the whole 16-bit field.
whyWrong.3: The port field can represent values through 65535.

exhibit.title: Application behavior
exhibit.text:
First write: 200 bytes
Second write: 300 bytes
Both writes use the same established TCP connection.

questions.prompt: An application makes the two writes shown. What must its receiving application assume?
options: Each TCP segment corresponds to exactly one of the application writes.
TCP supplies a byte stream; the application must identify message boundaries.
The PSH flag separates the two writes into distinct application records.
The TCP receive window identifies where the first application message ends.
questions.explanation: TCP preserves ordered byte delivery rather than application-write boundaries. The application needs its own message framing, such as lengths or delimiters. Neither segment boundaries nor PSH defines application records.

whyWrong.0: TCP can combine or split application writes when forming segments.
whyWrong.2: PSH is not an application-record marker.
whyWrong.3: The receive window describes receive capacity, not message length.

exhibit.title: Representative Windows netstat -an
exhibit.text:
Proto  Local Address         Foreign Address        State
TCP    0.0.0.0:22            0.0.0.0:0              LISTENING
TCP    172.16.5.20:22        172.16.5.99:50210       ESTABLISHED
TCP    172.16.5.20:50344     198.51.100.10:443       ESTABLISHED
TCP    172.16.5.20:50351     198.51.100.10:443       TIME_WAIT
UDP    0.0.0.0:161           *:*

questions.prompt: Assume the administrator confirms SSH uses local port 22 and HTTPS uses remote port 443. Which interpretation of this representative Windows snapshot is correct?
options: The host has two established HTTPS connections and initiates the SSH session.
The UDP 161 row is a TCP listening socket awaiting an SNMP connection.
The TIME_WAIT row means that the remote peer rejected the TCP opening.
The host accepts one SSH connection and has one established HTTPS connection.
questions.explanation: The local port-22 listener and established port-22 row identify an incoming SSH connection. The local temporary port 50344 connects to remote 443, while 50351 is in TIME_WAIT rather than ESTABLISHED. The UDP entry has no TCP connection state.

whyWrong.0: Only one port-443 row is ESTABLISHED, and the local host is the SSH server.
whyWrong.1: The row is explicitly UDP, so TCP listening-state interpretation is inappropriate.
whyWrong.2: TIME_WAIT is associated with TCP closing; it does not show a rejected opening.

questions.prompt: Which statement separates TCP flow control from congestion control?
options: Flow control responds to link capacity; congestion control sets receiver buffers.
Flow control respects receiver capacity; congestion control responds to the path.
Flow control orders bytes; congestion control assigns application port numbers.
Flow control checks message boundaries; congestion control checks TCP checksums.
questions.explanation: The advertised receive window limits traffic according to receiver capacity. Congestion control limits the sender according to network-path conditions. Sending must respect both limits; neither mechanism identifies application messages.

whyWrong.0: This reverses the receiver-capacity and network-path concerns.
whyWrong.2: Byte ordering and port identification are separate functions from these controls.
whyWrong.3: Message boundaries are application-defined, and checksum validation is error detection.

questions.prompt: Which two services conventionally use TCP in the CCNA examples? Choose two.
options: TFTP file transfer
SMTP mail transfer
DHCPv4 address assignment
SSH remote management
NTP time synchronization
questions.explanation: SMTP server-to-server transfer conventionally uses TCP 25, and SSH uses TCP 22. They use TCP’s ordered stream for their application exchange; that does not make UDP applications incapable of implementing their own reliability.

whyWrong.0: TFTP uses UDP and supplies acknowledgments and retransmission in TFTP itself.
whyWrong.2: DHCPv4 uses UDP ports 67 and 68.
whyWrong.4: Conventional NTP uses UDP port 123.

questions.prompt: A client captures the representative exchange shown while attempting Telnet. What can this capture establish without additional device evidence?
options: The connection attempt received an active reset; no TCP opening completed.
The destination process is certainly stopped; no firewall could cause this reply.
The client completed TCP and then failed Telnet username authentication.
The request was silently dropped; a reply could not reach the client.
questions.explanation: A reset in response to the SYN rejects the opening, so the ordinary handshake did not complete. A closed destination port can cause this, but a security device can also generate a reset. The client-side capture alone does not identify the responsible process or device.

whyWrong.1: The reset is evidence of active rejection, not unique proof of a stopped destination service.
whyWrong.2: There is no SYN/ACK and completed opening before an application login.
whyWrong.3: The capture contains a reply, so this attempt was not simply silent at the client.

questions.prompt: One client address opens two separate simultaneous TCP connections to the same server address on TCP 443. How can the client distinguish these connections?
options: The server must use destination ports 443 and 8443 for the two connections.
The initial sequence numbers alone select which socket receives each reply.
The IP header contains a browser-tab identifier for each of the connections.
The local source ports differ, producing distinct pairs of TCP endpoints.
questions.explanation: With TCP, the addresses and ports identify the connection. Because the same client and server addresses and server port are used here, distinct client ports distinguish the two connections. This is a statement about separate connections, not a rule requiring one connection per browser tab.

whyWrong.0: Separate clients or connections can share the same server listening port.
whyWrong.1: Sequence numbers order data within an identified connection; they do not replace its endpoint identity.
whyWrong.2: The IP header has no browser-tab identifier.

questions.prompt: A PC can ping a server address, but its browser cannot open the HTTPS site. Which conclusion is justified?
options: The TCP handshake succeeded, so only certificate validation remains to test.
UDP works to the server, because ping uses a UDP transport endpoint.
ICMP echo can make a round trip; HTTPS needs separate transport and service tests.
The server permits every port from this PC, because its echo reply returned.
questions.explanation: Ping uses ICMP echo and does not establish a TCP connection. Its replies provide reachability evidence for that test, while DNS, TCP, TLS, policy, and the application may still need investigation. A port test and the actual application exchange answer different questions.

whyWrong.0: Ping does not perform the HTTPS TCP or TLS opening.
whyWrong.1: ICMP echo is not carried in UDP.
whyWrong.3: Policy can permit ICMP and deny another protocol or port.

exhibit.title: Representative receive state
exhibit.text:
1001–1100: received
1101–1200: missing
1201–1300: received and retained

questions.prompt: The receiver has the data ranges shown and all earlier data. Which cumulative acknowledgment should remain until the gap is filled?
options: 1301, because the latest arriving segment ended at byte 1300.
1201, because the third segment starts at byte 1201.
1101, because it is the first missing byte in the stream.
1001, because acknowledgments always repeat the first segment’s sequence.
questions.explanation: Cumulative acknowledgment cannot advance past a missing earlier range. With 1101–1200 absent, 1101 remains the next byte needed for an uninterrupted stream. Once the gap is filled and the later range is retained, the ACK can advance to 1301.

whyWrong.0: 1301 would acknowledge the missing middle bytes as already received.
whyWrong.1: 1201 skips over the missing 1101–1200 range.
whyWrong.3: Bytes 1001–1100 arrived, so the receiver need not request 1001 again.

spec.title: Three-way handshake
spec.caption: An ordinary opening with no application data in the SYN segments.

questions.prompt: What sequence and acknowledgment values belong in the client’s third segment?
questions.explanation: Each SYN consumes one sequence number. The client’s next sequence is therefore 12001, and the next server sequence it expects is 45001.

whyWrong.0: Both SYN sequence positions have been omitted.
whyWrong.1: The server’s SYN also consumes one sequence position.
whyWrong.2: The client’s SYN also consumes one sequence position.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes DNS transport on port 53?
options: Both UDP and TCP carry DNS queries; a truncated UDP answer can lead to TCP retry.
UDP carries all client queries; TCP is restricted to server zone-transfer traffic.
TCP becomes mandatory whenever an answer exceeds 512 bytes, regardless of extensions.
UDP serves same-subnet clients; TCP is selected when the lookup must cross a router.
questions.explanation: DNS supports both UDP and TCP for queries. Retrying over TCP after a truncated UDP response is one common use, and full zone transfers also use TCP. DNS extensions permit UDP messages larger than 512 bytes, so that historical size is not a universal transport boundary.

whyWrong.1: TCP also supports ordinary client queries.
whyWrong.2: DNS extensions allow larger UDP responses; a fixed universal 512-byte rule is incorrect.
whyWrong.3: Crossing a router does not itself determine DNS transport choice.

cards.front: What are the three IANA port ranges?
cards.back: System/well-known 0–1023; user/registered 1024–49151; dynamic/private 49152–65535. OS ephemeral selection ranges can differ.

cards.front: What are the TCP minimum and UDP header sizes?
cards.back: TCP: 20 bytes minimum, with options able to extend it. UDP: 8 bytes, containing ports, length, and checksum.

cards.front: What do SYN, ACK, FIN, and RST indicate?
cards.back: SYN synchronizes sequence numbers; ACK marks an acknowledgment. FIN closes one sending direction; RST resets or rejects a connection.

cards.front: TCP opening with client ISN 1000 and server ISN 5000?
cards.back: SYN seq 1000; SYN/ACK seq 5000 ack 1001; ACK seq 1001 ack 5001. Each SYN consumes one sequence number.

cards.front: Must an ordinary TCP close contain exactly four segments?
cards.back: No. Each direction closes with FIN and acknowledgment, but an ACK and FIN can be combined. FIN consumes one sequence number.

cards.front: TCP flow control versus congestion control?
cards.back: Flow control respects the receiver’s advertised capacity. Congestion control limits the sender according to conditions on the network path.

cards.front: What identifies a transport flow?
cards.back: The five-tuple: transport protocol, source IP, source port, destination IP, and destination port. A socket is an application endpoint.

cards.front: Can an application use UDP and still recover lost data?
cards.back: Yes. The application can add numbering, acknowledgments, and retries, as TFTP does. UDP itself does not provide that recovery.

cards.front: Does a successful ping verify HTTP or HTTPS?
cards.back: No. ICMP echo success is round-trip reachability evidence; it does not verify DNS, a TCP port, TLS, or the web application.

cards.front: FTP control and data connections?
cards.back: Control uses TCP 21. Active data traditionally comes from server TCP 20; passive data uses a server-selected destination port.

cards.front: Which ports identify conventional SSH and Telnet?
cards.back: SSH uses TCP 22; Telnet uses TCP 23. SSH protects the management session; Telnet carries it without that protection.

cards.front: Which transports does ordinary DNS support on port 53?
cards.back: UDP and TCP. Small lookups often use UDP; TCP also handles normal queries and retry after a truncated UDP response.

cards.front: What are the DHCPv4 client and server ports?
cards.back: UDP 68 is the client port; UDP 67 is the server port. Initial discovery can be broadcast; later exchanges are not all broadcasts.

cards.front: What does UDP port 69 mean in TFTP?
cards.back: It receives the initial read/write request. The server selects a transfer identifier port used for the remaining exchange.

cards.front: Conventional HTTP and HTTPS ports, and the HTTP/3 exception?
cards.back: HTTP commonly uses TCP 80 and HTTPS TCP 443. HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP, commonly UDP 443.

cards.front: Conventional NTP, SNMP, and UDP syslog ports?
cards.back: NTP UDP 123; SNMP agent UDP 161 and notification receiver UDP 162; conventional UDP syslog 514.

cards.front: Conventional RADIUS and TACACS+ ports?
cards.back: RADIUS uses UDP 1812 for authentication and 1813 for accounting. TACACS+ uses TCP 49.

cards.front: What is the central TCP-versus-UDP comparison?
cards.back: TCP supplies a reliable ordered byte stream. UDP sends separate datagrams without its own delivery, ordering, or retransmission guarantee.

cards.front: Does TCP preserve application-write or message boundaries?
cards.back: No. The application must define its message format within the byte stream. Neither a TCP segment boundary nor PSH is a message marker.

cards.front: What does cumulative TCP acknowledgment 1301 mean?
cards.back: All preceding stream bytes through 1300 have been received, with no earlier gap remaining. Byte 1301 is next expected. Earlier out-of-order arrival does not prevent the ACK advancing once the gap is filled.

commands.task: From a PC command prompt, send ICMP echo requests to 192.168.40.20.
commands.note: ICMP replies are reachability evidence, not a test of a TCP/UDP service.

commands.task: In a Packet Tracer version that supports it, display the PC's TCP connection snapshot.
commands.note: A short connection may already have closed. If this display is unavailable, use Simulation-mode PDU endpoints.

commands.task: On Windows, display numeric TCP/UDP endpoints, including listening TCP sockets.
commands.note: LISTENING and ESTABLISHED are TCP states. This is a Windows command; simulator switches may differ.

commands.task: Resolve www.lab.test using the PC's configured DNS server.
commands.note: Inspect the returned address. A small query often uses UDP 53, but DNS also supports TCP.

commands.task: On Windows, resolve www.lab.test by asking 192.168.40.20 explicitly.
commands.note: The second argument selects the server. Use the configured-server form in a simulator that lacks this argument.

commands.task: From an elevated command prompt on an isolated Windows lab PC, delete all entries in its ARP cache.
commands.note: The wildcard deletes all ARP entries on that PC, not only dynamic ones. This changes the host's ARP state, not the switch MAC table. Packet Tracer cache-clear syntax can differ; check its help.

commands.task: On IOS, summarize TCP connections for which the router itself is an endpoint.
commands.note: This is not a list of every TCP flow being routed. Add all on supported IOS to include listening endpoints.

commands.task: From a supported IOS router, attempt a TCP connection to 10.1.1.10 port 443 using the Telnet client.
commands.note: A successful opening tests TCP acceptance, not TLS or HTTPS content. Use only an authorized lab target; do not send credentials or expect a Telnet login on HTTPS.

commands.task: Display the PC's full IP settings before troubleshooting the lab connection.
commands.note: Compare address, mask, and DNS server with the addressing table.

commands.task: In Windows PowerShell, test whether a TCP connection to 192.168.40.20 port 80 succeeds.
commands.note: Read TcpTestSucceeded. Success alone does not establish that the HTTP page works; this is not a Packet Tracer PC command.

tickets.title: HTTP fails while ping and DNS still work
tickets.scenario: PC-A and SRV1 share a working VLAN and IPv4 subnet. The PC successfully loaded http://www.lab.test before a technician changed one service setting on SRV1. A fresh HTTP request now fails. The exhibits describe the controlled lab state, not a captured production diagnosis.

exhibits.title: PC-A test results
exhibits.text:
ping 192.168.40.20: replies received
nslookup www.lab.test: returns 192.168.40.20
Fresh request to http://192.168.40.20: fails
Fresh request to http://www.lab.test: fails

exhibits.title: SRV1 Services settings
exhibits.text:
HTTP: Off
DNS: On
A record www.lab.test: 192.168.40.20

tickets.question: Which diagnosis is directly supported by all the evidence?
options: The PC needs a default gateway to reach the server in its own subnet.
DNS returns the wrong server address and must be changed to TCP-only.
The HTTP service is disabled even though other traffic still succeeds.
The working ICMP exchange proves that the HTTP response reached the browser.
tickets.explanation: The service setting explicitly shows HTTP Off, while the successful DNS answer and address-based ping support the other tests. ICMP reachability does not establish that an HTTP listener is available. The same failed-browser symptom without the service-setting exhibit would require further investigation rather than an automatic diagnosis.
tickets.fix: On SRV1, open Services → HTTP and set HTTP On. Start fresh requests to both http://192.168.40.20 and http://www.lab.test, verify that the page loads, then save the restored Packet Tracer topology. Do not change addressing or routing to repair a deliberately stopped service.

tickets.title: The server address works but its name does not
tickets.scenario: The isolated LAN contains PC-A at 192.168.40.10/24 and SRV1 at 192.168.40.20/24. No device uses 192.168.40.99. HTTP and DNS are enabled on SRV1, and its www.lab.test A record correctly points to 192.168.40.20. The technician checks a fresh browser request and the PC configuration.

exhibits.title: PC-A configured settings
exhibits.text:
IPv4 address: 192.168.40.10
Subnet mask: 255.255.255.0
DNS server: 192.168.40.99

exhibits.title: Observed tests
exhibits.text:
http://192.168.40.20: page loads
nslookup www.lab.test using configured DNS: fails
http://www.lab.test: name cannot be resolved

tickets.question: Which correction addresses the demonstrated cause?
options: Configure PC-A to use DNS server 192.168.40.20, then repeat the name lookup.
Change SRV1 HTTP to TCP port 53, then repeat the name-based request.
Disable UDP on PC-A so that every browser operation must use TCP.
Add a default route on SW1 because the two addresses use different host numbers.
tickets.explanation: The PC points its DNS queries at an unused address. The successful address-based HTTP request already demonstrates a working HTTP exchange with the intended server. Correcting the DNS setting targets the evidenced fault without confusing DNS port 53 with the web service port.
tickets.fix: Open PC-A Desktop → IP Configuration, change DNS Server to 192.168.40.20, and run nslookup www.lab.test. Confirm the returned address, open http://www.lab.test, and save the repaired topology. Leave the working server IP, subnet mask, and HTTP service unchanged.
