lab.title: Watch a switch learn, flood and forget
lab.intro: Build a small LAN and follow the switch's table as hosts transmit. Separate host ARP state from switch MAC state, then move two hosts behind another switch and diagnose a deliberately incorrect static entry. Output below is representative teaching output, not a record of an executed Packet Tracer session; use the MAC addresses and supported commands shown by your installed version.
lab.topology:
```diagram
{ "type": "topology", "title": "Initial topology: one switch and three PCs",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "A", "kind": "pc", "label": "PC-A", "sub": "192.168.90.10/24", "x": 2, "y": 1 },
    { "id": "B", "kind": "pc", "label": "PC-B", "sub": "192.168.90.20/24", "x": 2, "y": 5 },
    { "id": "S1", "kind": "switch", "label": "S1", "sub": "2960 · VLAN 1", "x": 6, "y": 3 },
    { "id": "C", "kind": "pc", "label": "PC-C", "sub": "192.168.90.30/24", "x": 10, "y": 3 }
  ],
  "links": [
    { "from": "A", "to": "S1", "fromLabel": "Fa0", "toLabel": "Fa0/1" },
    { "from": "B", "to": "S1", "fromLabel": "Fa0", "toLabel": "Fa0/2" },
    { "from": "S1", "to": "C", "fromLabel": "Fa0/3", "toLabel": "Fa0" }
  ], "caption": "All three hosts initially use VLAN 1 on S1; S2 is added in Step 7." }
```

| Host | IPv4 / mask | Initial port | Port after Step 7 |
|---|---|---|---|
| PC-A FastEthernet0 | `192.168.90.10 / 255.255.255.0` | S1 Fa0/1 | S1 Fa0/1 |
| PC-B FastEthernet0 | `192.168.90.20 / 255.255.255.0` | S1 Fa0/2 | S2 Fa0/2 |
| PC-C FastEthernet0 | `192.168.90.30 / 255.255.255.0` | S1 Fa0/3 | S2 Fa0/3 |
| Switch link added in Step 7 | No IP address | Not connected | S1 Fa0/24 ↔ S2 Fa0/24 |

Use straight-through copper for PCs. Use copper crossover or Packet Tracer's automatic connection tool for the switch-to-switch link. No host needs a default gateway or DNS server because the entire exercise stays in one subnet. Begin with new switches; do not add a second inter-switch link, which would introduce a spanning-tree exercise beyond this lab.

steps.title: Cable, address and record the MAC addresses
steps.body:
Create S1 and the three PCs, connect their initial ports, and set each static address under **Desktop → IP Configuration**. Open each PC's **Desktop → Command Prompt** and record its physical/MAC address alongside its name and IP:

```text Each PC
ipconfig /all
```

On S1, decline an initial setup dialog if offered, enter the CLI, and configure the host ports explicitly:

```ios S1
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname S1
S1(config)# interface range fastethernet0/1 - 3
S1(config-if-range)# switchport mode access
S1(config-if-range)# switchport access vlan 1
S1(config-if-range)# no shutdown
S1(config-if-range)# end
S1# show interfaces status
S1# show vlan brief
```

:::expected
The selected ports belong to VLAN 1 and the cabled links become operational. Wait until the ports are forwarding before beginning captures. Record real MAC values from your PCs; the sample addresses used later are illustrations. Link initialization can take time, but no exact color-change timer is a success criterion.
:::

steps.title: Start from an empty table
steps.body:
Before generating test traffic, inspect and clear S1's dynamic table. This clears learned forwarding state on the switch, not the PCs' ARP caches. Do not clear or change configuration on any other device.

```ios S1
S1# show mac address-table
S1# clear mac address-table dynamic
S1# show mac address-table
```

:::expected
The dynamic host entries have been removed. Reserved/static rows can differ by platform and simulator; do not require a completely blank display. If a host transmits background traffic, a dynamic row can reappear immediately. Identify it by the source MAC you recorded and clear again just before the next controlled test if necessary.
:::

steps.title: One ping, one frame at a time
steps.body:
Enter **Simulation** mode and use **Edit Filters** to select ARP and ICMP. On PC-A, inspect `arp -a`; because this is a fresh topology, PC-B's mapping should be absent. If it is already present, restart with a fresh PC or clear that PC's ARP cache using its supported command (`arp -d` in versions that support it), and verify absence with `arp -a`. Clear S1's dynamic table again after any preparatory traffic.

Start the ping on PC-A and use **Capture/Forward** to follow events:

```text PC-A
ping 192.168.90.20
```

After the ARP request reaches S1, pause and inspect the table. Continue through the reply and inspect again. Return to Realtime mode to finish any remaining ping events.

```ios S1
S1# show mac address-table
```

:::expected
The ARP request teaches A on Fa0/1 and is flooded to Fa0/2 and Fa0/3. B replies; the source teaches B on Fa0/2, and the reply is forwarded only to A's known port. Subsequent ICMP request/reply frames use the learned ports. PC-C does not answer an ARP request for B's address, so receiving that request alone does not teach C's MAC.

Representative host rows after A and B communicate:
```output Representative S1# show mac address-table
Vlan    Mac Address       Type        Ports
----    -----------       --------    -----
   1    00aa.aaaa.aaaa    DYNAMIC     Fa0/1  ← use PC-A's actual recorded MAC
   1    00bb.bbbb.bbbb    DYNAMIC     Fa0/2  ← learned from B's source traffic
```
:::

steps.title: Bring PC-C into the table
steps.body:
From PC-A, ping C and then display the table. A successful reply requires C to transmit, providing a source from which the switch can learn.

```text PC-A
ping 192.168.90.30
```

```ios S1
S1# show mac address-table
S1# show mac address-table count
```

:::expected
C appears as a dynamic address on Fa0/3, and A and B may remain if their entries have not aged out. Count the three recorded host addresses rather than assuming all table rows are host rows. If `count` is unsupported, the plain display is sufficient; it is the MAC-to-port mapping that proves the result.
:::

steps.title: Prove unknown-unicast flooding
steps.body:
In Realtime mode, ping B once to refresh A's ARP entry, then use `arp -a` on A to confirm that `192.168.90.20` maps to B's recorded MAC. Clear only S1's dynamic table immediately before the next ping. Do not clear A's ARP cache.

```ios S1
S1# clear mac address-table dynamic
S1# show mac address-table
```

Switch to Simulation mode, clear old events, and start another ping from A to B. Inspect the first ICMP frame's Ethernet destination and the switch's outgoing copies. Then continue through B's reply and a second request.

```text PC-A
ping 192.168.90.20
```

:::expected
A already knows B's MAC, so it can send an ICMP frame addressed to that unicast MAC without a new ARP exchange. S1 learns A but does not know B's location; the first request is copied to both Fa0/2 and Fa0/3. Its destination remains B's unicast MAC. B's reply teaches B, allowing the following request to use Fa0/2 alone. If you instead observe ARP first, refresh A's mapping and repeat: the ARP reply would teach B before the ICMP request, defeating this demonstration.
:::

steps.title: Aging and a static entry
steps.body:
This timer exercise depends on simulator support. First record the current timer. The reference Catalyst 2960 default is 300 seconds, but use the value the device reports. Temporarily select 60 seconds, then stop generating host traffic and wait beyond the configured interval while watching the table.

```ios S1
S1# show mac address-table aging-time
S1# configure terminal
S1(config)# mac address-table aging-time 60
S1(config)# end
S1# show mac address-table aging-time
S1# show mac address-table
```

If the command or aging behavior is not implemented, record that limitation and use the clear/relearn demonstration from Step 5 as your practical evidence. Do not conclude that real dynamic entries are permanent. Next, configure a static entry for PC-A using **A's actual MAC in place of `00aa.aaaa.aaaa`**:

```ios S1
S1# configure terminal
S1(config)# mac address-table static 00aa.aaaa.aaaa vlan 1 interface fastethernet0/1
S1(config)# end
S1# clear mac address-table dynamic
S1# show mac address-table
```

:::expected
On an implementation that models aging, inactive dynamic entries eventually disappear; background transmissions can refresh them. The configured A entry displays as STATIC and survives the dynamic clear. If static configuration is unsupported in your simulator, treat its remaining static-entry steps as paper exercises and complete the dynamic-learning steps normally. A static entry containing the example MAC rather than A's actual address does not test A's forwarding, so correct the substitution before continuing.
:::

steps.title: Add a second switch and watch one port learn two MACs
steps.body:
Add a new 2960 named S2. Connect S1 Fa0/24 to S2 Fa0/24, then move B to S2 Fa0/2 and C to S2 Fa0/3. Keep A on S1 Fa0/1. Both ends of the inter-switch link are deliberately access ports in VLAN 1; this exercise carries one VLAN and does not require a trunk.

```ios S1
S1# configure terminal
S1(config)# interface fastethernet0/24
S1(config-if)# switchport mode access
S1(config-if)# switchport access vlan 1
S1(config-if)# no shutdown
S1(config-if)# end
```

```ios S2
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname S2
S2(config)# interface range fastethernet0/2 - 3
S2(config-if-range)# switchport mode access
S2(config-if-range)# switchport access vlan 1
S2(config-if-range)# no shutdown
S2(config-if-range)# exit
S2(config)# interface fastethernet0/24
S2(config-if)# switchport mode access
S2(config-if)# switchport access vlan 1
S2(config-if)# no shutdown
S2(config-if)# end
S2# show interfaces status
```

Wait for the links to forward. Clear dynamic entries on each switch, ping B and C from A in Realtime mode, and inspect both tables immediately afterwards. If a dynamic entry ages out while you work, repeat the relevant ping.

```ios S1
S1# clear mac address-table dynamic
```

```ios S2
S2# clear mac address-table dynamic
```

```text PC-A
ping 192.168.90.20
ping 192.168.90.30
```

```ios S1
S1# show mac address-table
```

```ios S2
S2# show mac address-table
```

:::expected
S1 reaches B and C through Fa0/24, so their two different MACs appear on that one port. A remains STATIC on S1 Fa0/1. S2 learns A through its Fa0/24, B on Fa0/2, and C on Fa0/3. Check the three known host addresses rather than predicting every control-plane entry the simulator may show.
:::

steps.title: Restore the defaults and save
steps.body:
Remove the static A entry using the same actual MAC used in Step 6. Restore the documented default timer on this new lab switch, inspect the table, and save the working two-switch baseline. If you used a reused device with an intentional nondefault timer, restore the recorded original value instead.

```ios S1
S1# configure terminal
S1(config)# no mac address-table static 00aa.aaaa.aaaa vlan 1 interface fastethernet0/1
S1(config)# no mac address-table aging-time
S1(config)# end
S1# show mac address-table aging-time
S1# show mac address-table
S1# copy running-config startup-config
```

```ios S2
S2# copy running-config startup-config
```

:::expected
The A static entry is gone and the aging configuration is restored. Ping B and C again to verify dynamic operation. Accept the default save filename when prompted and save the topology as `switching-baseline.pkt`. Keep this known-working copy before the controlled fault.
:::

steps.title: Introduce one incorrect static entry
steps.body:
In this isolated lab only, point B's MAC at S1 Fa0/1, which actually leads to A. Substitute **B's actual MAC for `00bb.bbbb.bbbb`**. This is one deliberate change; do not change addresses, cabling, or VLANs.

```ios S1
S1# configure terminal
S1(config)# mac address-table static 00bb.bbbb.bbbb vlan 1 interface fastethernet0/1
S1(config)# end
S1# show mac address-table
S1# clear mac address-table dynamic
S1# show mac address-table
```

From A, retry a ping to B and then to C. If supported, inspect B's unicast request in Simulation mode after address resolution. Read the STATIC row before attempting any repair.

```text PC-A
ping 192.168.90.20
ping 192.168.90.30
```

:::expected
Traffic for B is directed by the incorrect static row. In particular, a B-destined unicast frame arriving from A on Fa0/1 has a destination mapped to that same ingress port, so S1 filters it rather than forwarding toward S2. A-to-B ping fails while A-to-C can still work. Clearing dynamic entries does not remove this fault because the offending entry is static. If the simulator rejects static configuration, use this as a paper diagnosis from the displayed command rather than claiming to have reproduced the failure.
:::

steps.title: Recover the fault and confirm the baseline
steps.body:
Remove only the B static entry created in Step 9. Generate traffic again to relearn the correct path and verify both hosts. Do not save until the correct behavior has returned.

```ios S1
S1# configure terminal
S1(config)# no mac address-table static 00bb.bbbb.bbbb vlan 1 interface fastethernet0/1
S1(config)# end
S1# clear mac address-table dynamic
```

```text PC-A
ping 192.168.90.20
ping 192.168.90.30
```

```ios S1
S1# show mac address-table
S1# copy running-config startup-config
```

:::expected
B is learned dynamically through Fa0/24, both pings succeed, and the wrong static row is absent. Save the repaired topology as `switching-lab.pkt`. Your notes should connect the symptom, incorrect entry, failed dynamic clear, precise removal, and successful retest.
:::

lab.troubleshooting:
- **Host absent from the MAC table:** verify the link and VLAN, generate traffic from that host, then inspect promptly. Merely connecting or receiving is insufficient evidence of learning.
- **ARP appears before the intended unknown-unicast test:** A lacks a current mapping for B; refresh ARP, clear only S1's dynamic entries, and repeat immediately.
- **Multiple hosts appear on Fa0/24:** compare with the final topology; this is expected for B and C behind S2.
- **Aging or a display keyword is unsupported:** record the simulator limitation; use the full table and controlled dynamic clear. CML images also differ, so do not assume every virtual image implements every hardware command.
- **Failure persists after clearing dynamic entries:** check for the deliberately configured STATIC row and remove its exact configuration.
- **Ping fails after moving cables:** check final port assignments, VLAN 1 on both inter-switch ends, and forwarding state. Do not add a second switch link to troubleshoot the first.
lab.challenge:
Using the restored two-switch topology, clear the dynamic tables on S1 and S2. Ensure B's ARP cache has no entry for C so that B's first ping to C begins with ARP; use a supported cache clear or a fresh host if necessary. Predict which switch learns B and which learns C during that ARP request/reply. Then move A from S1 Fa0/1 to S1 Fa0/4, configure Fa0/4 as an enabled VLAN 1 access port, and predict where S1 learns A when it sends again.

:::expected
B's ARP broadcast reaches C and the inter-switch link, so S2 learns B on Fa0/2 and S1 learns B on Fa0/24. C's reply goes only toward B on S2 Fa0/2 because B is already known. S1 does not learn C from a reply it never receives. After A moves and transmits, its dynamic entry is learned on Fa0/4; do not wait for an old aging timer to permit the update. Restore A to Fa0/1 when finished and confirm successful pings before saving the original baseline layout.
:::

questions.prompt: Fa0/1–Fa0/4 and Fa0/24 are VLAN 1 forwarding ports with no filtering policy. A valid frame from 00aa.aaaa.aaaa to 00bb.bbbb.bbbb enters Fa0/1. Which egress choice follows?
options: Fa0/2 only, using the known destination entry.
Fa0/2, Fa0/3, Fa0/4, and Fa0/24, flooding the frame.
Fa0/2 and Fa0/24, using every port with an entry.
No egress, because the source already has an entry.
questions.explanation: The source refreshes A’s entry on Fa0/1. The destination B is already known on a different forwarding port, Fa0/2, so ordinary unicast forwarding selects that port.

whyWrong.1: The destination is known, so unknown-unicast flooding is unnecessary.
whyWrong.2: Other learned addresses do not make their ports destinations for this frame.
whyWrong.3: A known source is normal; same-port filtering concerns the destination.

questions.prompt: With normal dynamic learning enabled, C (00cc.cccc.cccc) sends its first valid frame on VLAN 1 Fa0/3 to B (00bb.bbbb.bbbb). Fa0/2 is forwarding and no policy blocks the frame. What does SW1 do?
options: Learns B on Fa0/3 and floods toward all other forwarding ports.
Rejects C’s frame until an administrator adds C to the table.
Learns C on Fa0/3 and forwards only toward B on Fa0/2.
Learns C on Fa0/3 and floods because C was previously unknown.
questions.explanation: Source learning and destination lookup are separate decisions. The frame teaches C’s location, while the existing B entry directs forwarding to Fa0/2. An unfamiliar valid source is not by itself a reason to flood or reject ordinary traffic.

whyWrong.0: The switch learns the source C, not the destination B, from this arrival.
whyWrong.1: Normal dynamic learning does not require a preconfigured host entry.
whyWrong.3: Unknown-unicast flooding depends on an unknown destination, not an unknown source.

questions.prompt: A second switch sends a flooded copy from 00dd.dddd.dddd to 00ee.eeee.eeee into SW1 Fa0/24 in VLAN 1. With the table shown and ordinary bridging, what is SW1’s decision?
options: Send the copy back through Fa0/24 because E is reached there.
Flood the copy through other ports because Fa0/24 is an uplink.
Refresh D on Fa0/24 and filter the same-port destination copy.
Remove D and E because a forwarding port can learn one address.
questions.explanation: The arrival refreshes the source D on Fa0/24. The known destination E is associated with that same ingress port, so SW1 does not send the frame back onto the segment from which it arrived. This same-port filtering is normal bridging behavior.

whyWrong.0: Ordinary bridging does not return the frame through the same ingress port.
whyWrong.1: An uplink still uses the destination lookup; its role does not force flooding.
whyWrong.3: Several distinct MAC addresses on one uplink are expected.

questions.prompt: An ordinary broadcast arrives on VLAN 10 Fa0/1. No storm-control or filtering policy applies. Which ports transmit a copy?
options: Fa0/2 and Fa0/4, because both physical links are operational.
Fa0/2 only, because it is the other forwarding port in VLAN 10.
Fa0/2 and Fa0/5, because both are in a forwarding state.
Fa0/1 and Fa0/2, because broadcast includes its ingress port.
questions.explanation: Flooding is limited to eligible forwarding ports in the same VLAN and excludes the ingress port. Fa0/3 is down, Fa0/4 is not forwarding for VLAN 10, and Fa0/5 belongs to VLAN 20. Only Fa0/2 qualifies.

whyWrong.0: An operational link is insufficient when it is not forwarding for the VLAN.
whyWrong.2: Fa0/5 is in another VLAN and is not an egress for this broadcast.
whyWrong.3: The switch does not send the ordinary flooded copy back through its ingress port.

questions.prompt: With normal dynamic learning enabled, which two observations create a learned MAC-to-port association within the frame’s VLAN? Choose two.
options: The source MAC address in the received frame
The destination MAC address in the received frame
The interface on which the frame arrived
The destination IP address inside the payload
The output interface selected after the lookup
questions.explanation: The switch observes a source address arriving through a particular ingress port in a VLAN. That evidence establishes a path toward the source. The destination is looked up separately and does not reveal its own location from this frame.

whyWrong.1: The current destination is not evidence of where that destination is connected.
whyWrong.3: An IP address is not the key used for ordinary dynamic MAC learning.
whyWrong.4: The egress interface is a result of forwarding, not the source-location observation.

questions.prompt: An untagged Ethernet II frame carries a 28-byte ARP message. What is its minimum frame length, counted from destination MAC through FCS, with ordinary Ethernet padding?
options: 42 bytes
46 bytes
60 bytes
64 bytes
questions.explanation: Padding extends the data area to 46 bytes. Adding the 14-byte untagged header and 4-byte FCS gives 64 bytes. Preamble, start frame delimiter, and interframe gap are excluded from this count.

whyWrong.0: 42 counts only the header and unpadded ARP message.
whyWrong.1: 46 is the padded data area, not the complete frame.
whyWrong.2: 60 leaves out the four-byte FCS required by the stated counting scope.

questions.prompt: What identifies 0100.5e01.0203 as an Ethernet group address?
options: The organizational prefix proves that one individual NIC owns it.
The low-order bit of the first octet is set, indicating a group.
The final octet is odd, indicating a locally administered address.
The first octet differs from 00, making the address a broadcast.
questions.explanation: The individual/group bit is the least-significant bit of the first octet. In 01 that bit is set, so the address is a group address; this example is an IPv4 multicast MAC. The Ethernet broadcast address is the separate all-ones value.

whyWrong.0: A group address is not an individual NIC’s ordinary unicast identifier.
whyWrong.2: The relevant classification bits are in the first octet, not the last.
whyWrong.3: Many valid unicast/group addresses do not begin with 00; broadcast is ffff.ffff.ffff.

questions.prompt: The switch’s dynamic aging timer is explicitly set to 300 seconds. B sends no frames for six minutes, while A continues sending toward B. No link or topology event occurs. Why can B’s dynamic entry disappear?
options: No source frame from B refreshed its learned location before the timer expired.
A’s traffic replaced B’s entry because the table keeps one source per VLAN.
The timer converted B into a static entry after receiving traffic for five minutes.
The switch required a TCP acknowledgment from B to retain its Ethernet entry.
questions.explanation: A received source frame is evidence of the sender’s location. Sending frames toward B does not provide new source evidence from B, so its inactive dynamic entry can age out. Subsequent traffic for an unknown B is flooded within the eligible VLAN ports until it is relearned.

whyWrong.1: A VLAN can contain entries for many distinct source MAC addresses.
whyWrong.2: Ordinary dynamic aging removes an entry rather than configuring it as static.
whyWrong.3: MAC learning is not maintained by TCP acknowledgment tracking.

questions.prompt: On the reference Catalyst 2960 IOS, which command sets the global MAC aging timer to 600 seconds?
options: SW1(config)# mac address-table aging-time 600
SW1(config)# mac address-table aging 600 vlan all
SW1# mac address-table aging-time 600
SW1(config)# mac address-table timeout 600
questions.explanation: The supported global configuration command is mac address-table aging-time 600. Verify the result with show mac address-table aging-time. This changes learned-entry aging, not the host’s ARP timer.

whyWrong.1: The keyword is aging-time; vlan all is not the global syntax shown.
whyWrong.2: This configuration command requires global configuration mode.
whyWrong.3: timeout is not the supported keyword for this setting.

questions.prompt: After the representative display, an administrator enters clear mac address-table dynamic. No new host frame arrives before the next display. Which host entry remains?
options: No host entry remains because clear removes configured and learned entries.
Only A remains because it is learned in the switch’s default VLAN.
Only 0050.56be.1a2b remains because its entry is configured as STATIC.
All three remain because clear changes only their aging countdowns.
questions.explanation: The dynamic clear removes the two learned entries while leaving the configured static entry. Static configuration requires its matching removal command; ordinary dynamic aging or clearing is insufficient. Reserved platform entries are omitted from this exhibit.

whyWrong.0: The command is restricted to dynamic entries.
whyWrong.1: VLAN 1 does not exempt a dynamic entry from the clear.
whyWrong.3: The clear deletes dynamic entries rather than merely resetting countdowns.

questions.prompt: Which two statements distinguish store-and-forward from cut-through forwarding? Choose two.
options: Cut-through waits for the complete frame before beginning its transmission.
Store-and-forward can check the complete frame’s FCS before forwarding.
Store-and-forward identifies the destination using the source MAC address.
Cut-through can begin forwarding before the complete frame and FCS arrive.
Cut-through replaces damaged payload bits using information in the FCS.
questions.explanation: Store-and-forward has the full frame available for checking before forwarding it. Cut-through can begin earlier and therefore cannot wait for the entire frame’s FCS result before that initial transmission. Hardware behavior varies; family names alone are insufficient to select a mode.

whyWrong.0: Waiting for the complete frame describes store-and-forward rather than the defining early-start behavior.
whyWrong.2: Destination MAC is used for the destination lookup in either forwarding method.
whyWrong.4: The FCS detects corruption; it is not an error-correction code that repairs payload bits.

spec.title: All switch ports are in VLAN 1
spec.caption: Two routed interfaces attach separate LANs; all switch ports share VLAN 1 and the hub is one shared segment.

questions.prompt: The router’s two Ethernet interfaces are routed interfaces in separate LANs. SW1’s three PC links and router link are separate switch ports; the hub connects two PCs and the other router interface. Under introductory domain-counting conventions, what is the count?
options: 7 collision domains and 2 broadcast domains
5 collision domains and 1 broadcast domain
4 collision domains and 3 broadcast domains
5 collision domains and 2 broadcast domains
questions.explanation: SW1 creates four separate link domains: three PC links plus the router link. The hub and everything on its shared segment form one more, giving five collision domains by the diagram convention; correctly operating full-duplex switch links do not actually collide. The routed interfaces separate the two broadcast domains.

whyWrong.0: Hub ports do not each separate the shared collision domain.
whyWrong.1: The two distinct routed LANs do not share one broadcast domain.
whyWrong.2: This misses a link/shared segment and adds a broadcast domain not present in the topology.

questions.prompt: A technician clears a PC’s IPv4 ARP cache. Before the PC sends new traffic, what direct effect does this have on the access switch’s MAC table?
options: The switch removes the PC’s entry because its ARP mapping was removed.
No direct effect; the host’s ARP state and switch’s MAC state are separate.
The switch clears all entries associated with the PC’s access VLAN.
The switch converts the PC’s dynamic entry to a configured static entry.
questions.explanation: The ARP cache on the PC maps IPv4 next-hop addresses to MACs. The switch’s separate table maps MACs within VLANs to ports, so clearing the host cache does not directly delete switch entries. The PC’s later frames can refresh or establish its learned source location.

whyWrong.0: A host-cache deletion is not a switch MAC-table removal operation.
whyWrong.2: Deleting host ARP entries does not request a VLAN-wide switch clear.
whyWrong.3: Host ARP state does not create static switch configuration.

questions.prompt: An inventory shows Gi0/1 connects to another access switch. The representative table has several VLANs and 38 distinct source MACs on Gi0/1. What is the appropriate first interpretation?
options: The table proves an attack and requires immediately disabling the uplink.
The uplink can legitimately learn many downstream hosts; compare the inventory.
The number proves duplicate MAC addresses are moving between two ports.
The entry type proves the switch has disabled dynamic aging on this port.
questions.explanation: An uplink carries frames whose sources are downstream hosts, so many distinct MACs on it are normal. The inventory supports that explanation. A count alone neither proves an attack nor proves that all traffic is benign; investigate additional evidence if the behavior differs from expectations.

whyWrong.0: Distinct learned hosts behind an expected uplink are not by themselves proof of attack.
whyWrong.2: These are different addresses on one port, not evidence of one address alternating between ports.
whyWrong.3: DYNAMIC identifies learned entries; it does not display or prove an aging configuration.

questions.prompt: In an untagged Ethernet II frame, which EtherType identifies an IPv4 payload?
options: 0x86DD
questions.explanation: EtherType 0x0800 identifies IPv4. It tells the receiving protocol stack what payload follows; it is distinct from the destination MAC used for basic forwarding.

whyWrong.0: 0x0806 identifies ARP.
whyWrong.1: 0x86DD identifies IPv6.
whyWrong.3: 0x8100 identifies an 802.1Q tag, not an untagged IPv4 payload.

questions.prompt: A switch receives ordinary user IPv4 multicast in VLAN 1. The destination is not a reserved link-local group. Snooping and multicast restrictions are disabled, and all listed VLAN 1 ports are forwarding. Which behavior matches ordinary multicast flooding?
options: Drop the frame because a group address cannot be dynamically learned as a host source.
Deliver only to the switch CPU because every group address is control-plane traffic.
Select receiver ports from membership information despite snooping being disabled.
Copy to the other eligible VLAN 1 ports, excluding the ingress port.
questions.explanation: With the stated restrictions absent, ordinary multicast is flooded within the VLAN, excluding ingress. Group delivery can differ when snooping, multicast forwarding state, policy, or reserved control addresses apply. The assumptions in the question make the forwarding decision unambiguous.

whyWrong.0: Lack of a learned unicast-source entry does not by itself require discarding ordinary multicast.
whyWrong.1: Only particular control addresses receive special handling; multicast as a whole is not CPU-only.
whyWrong.2: The question excludes the receiver-membership restrictions that would support this selection.

cards.front: What is the basic untagged Ethernet frame size, and what is counted?
cards.back: 64–1518 bytes for the basic 1500-byte-payload framing, destination MAC through FCS. Preamble, SFD, and interframe gap are excluded.

cards.front: What is the data-area size in the basic untagged Ethernet II frame?
cards.back: 46–1500 bytes including any minimum-size padding. The 1500-byte payload limit is distinct from the total Ethernet frame length.

cards.front: What are the Ethernet II header and FCS sizes?
cards.back: Destination MAC 6 + source MAC 6 + EtherType 2 = 14-byte untagged header; FCS adds 4 bytes.

cards.front: Which EtherTypes identify IPv4, ARP, and IPv6?
cards.back: 0x0800 is IPv4; 0x0806 is ARP; 0x86DD is IPv6. They identify the payload protocol.

cards.front: Is every frame longer than 1518 bytes invalid?
cards.back: No. VLAN tags and supported larger-frame configurations change valid sizes. Interpret size/error counters against the platform and interface configuration.

cards.front: How long is a MAC address, and what does an OUI identify?
cards.back: 48 bits, or 12 hexadecimal digits. An OUI identifies an organizational allocation; locally assigned MACs and other IEEE allocation sizes also exist.

cards.front: How do you identify an Ethernet group address and broadcast address?
cards.back: The low-order bit of the first octet is set for group addresses. The all-ones broadcast address is ffff.ffff.ffff.

cards.front: What information does ordinary switching learn and look up?
cards.back: Learn source MAC + VLAN → ingress port. Look up destination MAC in the VLAN to forward, filter, or flood.

cards.front: Does unknown-unicast flooding change the destination MAC?
cards.back: No. It copies the unicast frame to eligible forwarding ports in the same VLAN, excluding the ingress port.

cards.front: What refreshes a dynamic MAC entry, and what is the reference 2960 timer?
cards.back: Frames received from that source refresh its location. The documented 2960 IOS 15.0(2)SE default is 300 seconds; verify the actual device.

cards.front: How do you configure a 600-second MAC aging timer on the reference IOS?
cards.back: In global configuration: mac address-table aging-time 600. Verify with show mac address-table aging-time.

cards.front: What creates a static MAC entry for a VLAN and interface?
cards.back: mac address-table static H.H.H vlan N interface X. It does not age or disappear in a dynamic-table clear; remove the matching configuration to undo it.

cards.front: How do you clear learned MAC entries without removing static entries?
cards.back: At privileged EXEC: clear mac address-table dynamic. Hosts sending new frames can be learned again immediately.

cards.front: Which columns matter in show mac address-table?
cards.back: VLAN, MAC address, entry type, and port. Read the VLAN first; a dynamic row gives the learned path toward the source.

cards.front: Store-and-forward compared with cut-through?
cards.back: Store-and-forward receives the whole frame and checks FCS before forwarding. Cut-through can start before the complete frame/FCS arrives.

cards.front: How do switch ports and VLANs separate Ethernet domains?
cards.back: Switch ports separate collision domains; full-duplex links have no collisions. A VLAN is a broadcast domain that can span multiple switches.

cards.front: Why can a Layer 2 loop carry repeated flooded traffic?
cards.back: Ordinary Ethernet has no hop-count field to stop circulation. Spanning tree creates a loop-free forwarding topology.

cards.front: MAC address table versus ARP table?
cards.back: MAC table: MAC + VLAN → port. IPv4 ARP table: on-link IP → MAC. Clearing either table does not directly clear the other.

cards.front: Do many MAC addresses on one port prove a fault?
cards.back: No. An uplink can carry many hosts. Compare the topology; repeated moves of one MAC warrant investigation but do not alone identify the cause.

cards.front: Can the Ethernet FCS repair a corrupted frame?
cards.back: No. The CRC detects corruption; it is not error correction. A store-and-forward switch discards a frame that fails its FCS check.

commands.task: Display the whole MAC address table.
commands.note: Columns: Vlan, Mac Address, Type (DYNAMIC/STATIC), Ports.

commands.task: Display only the dynamically learned MAC entries.
commands.note: Hides the STATIC and CPU rows.

commands.task: Find the learned or configured path toward MAC 0050.56be.1a2b.
commands.note: An uplink is a path toward the host, not proof of direct attachment. Check the VLAN as well.

commands.task: Display MAC table entries associated with FastEthernet0/24.
commands.note: Several distinct source MACs on an uplink are normal. Correlate the output with the topology.

commands.task: Show only the MAC entries that belong to VLAN 10.
commands.note: The table is keyed by MAC and VLAN.

commands.task: On a reference IOS switch supporting the keyword, display MAC table entry counts.
commands.note: Displayed counters and capacity fields vary. Use the full MAC table if the simulator lacks count; counts alone do not prove an attack.

commands.task: Display the MAC aging timer currently in force.
commands.note: The referenced Catalyst 2960 IOS default is 300 seconds. Verify the actual platform and configuration.

commands.task: Remove every dynamically learned entry from the MAC address table.
commands.note: Removes dynamic entries; static entries remain. New source traffic can repopulate the table immediately.

commands.task: On the reference IOS switch, set the global MAC aging timer to 600 seconds.
commands.note: Verify with show mac address-table aging-time. Per-VLAN settings and platform support require checking the device.

commands.task: Create a static path for MAC 0050.56be.1a2b in VLAN 10 through FastEthernet0/5.
commands.answer: mac address-table static 0050.56be.1a2b vlan 10 interface fastethernet0/5
accept: mac address-table static 0050.56be.1a2b vlan 10 interface fa0/5
commands.note: Assumes VLAN 10 and the port are configured appropriately. A wrong static entry can misdirect traffic and survives a dynamic clear.

commands.task: Remove the explicit global MAC aging timer and restore the platform default.
commands.note: The referenced 2960 default is 300 seconds; removing a command differs from explicitly configuring that value.

tickets.title: A dynamic clear does not repair the wrong path
tickets.scenario: In VLAN 1, PC-A is directly attached to S1 Fa0/1. PC-B, MAC 00bb.bbbb.bbbb, is attached to S2; S1 reaches S2 through Fa0/24. Both links are forwarding. A can ping another host behind S2 but cannot ping B. The table was inspected after clearing dynamic entries and before new source traffic.

exhibits.title: Representative S1# show mac address-table
exhibits.text:
Vlan    Mac Address       Type        Ports
   1    00bb.bbbb.bbbb    STATIC      Fa0/1

exhibits.title: S1 configuration excerpt
exhibits.text: mac address-table static 00bb.bbbb.bbbb vlan 1 interface FastEthernet0/1

tickets.question: What explains the failed ping and persistence after a dynamic clear?
options: The static entry directs B’s traffic toward A’s port and survives the dynamic clear.
S1 must keep only one learned MAC per VLAN and therefore removes downstream hosts.
B cannot be reached through a switch uplink without changing its IP subnet.
The ARP cache on A permanently prevents S1 from learning B’s Ethernet source.
tickets.explanation: The configured B entry points to Fa0/1 rather than the actual path through Fa0/24. A B-destined unicast arriving from A on Fa0/1 is subject to same-port filtering. The offending entry is static, so clearing dynamic entries cannot remove it; deleting that exact configuration permits normal source learning to establish B’s path.
tickets.fix:
```ios S1
S1# configure terminal
S1(config)# no mac address-table static 00bb.bbbb.bbbb vlan 1 interface fastethernet0/1
S1(config)# end
S1# clear mac address-table dynamic
```
Ping B from A, then run `show mac address-table` on S1. Confirm B is learned dynamically on Fa0/24 and connectivity returns before saving. On a different topology, substitute the actual host MAC and configured interface rather than copying this example blindly.

tickets.title: A third PC receives the first unicast copy
tickets.scenario: A, B, and C use S1 Fa0/1, Fa0/2, and Fa0/3 respectively. All three ports are forwarding in VLAN 1 with no filtering policy. A retains B’s ARP mapping, but a technician clears only S1’s dynamic MAC entries. In Simulation mode, the first ICMP request for B reaches both B and C; later requests reach B alone.

exhibits.title: PC-A ARP mapping before the test
Representative first ICMP Ethernet header
exhibits.text:
Source MAC: 00aa.aaaa.aaaa (PC-A)
Destination MAC: 00bb.bbbb.bbbb (PC-B)
Ingress: Fa0/1
Copies: Fa0/2 and Fa0/3

exhibits.title: Representative learned host rows after B replies
exhibits.text:
Vlan    Mac Address       Type        Ports
   1    00aa.aaaa.aaaa    DYNAMIC     Fa0/1
   1    00bb.bbbb.bbbb    DYNAMIC     Fa0/2

tickets.question: Which explanation fits this sequence?
options: A changed the destination to Ethernet broadcast when it sent the first ICMP request.
The switch learned B’s destination address from A before selecting both output ports.
Clearing S1’s table also deleted A’s ARP mapping and forced a new broadcast request.
The first destination was unknown to S1; B’s source reply then established its port.
tickets.explanation: A knows B’s MAC, so it can send an ordinary unicast frame immediately. S1 lacks B’s entry and floods within the eligible VLAN ports while learning A from the request. B’s reply teaches B on Fa0/2, so later requests use known-unicast forwarding; the frame never needs a broadcast destination.
tickets.fix: No repair is required for this controlled clear/relearn behavior. Confirm the destination MAC stays unicast, observe B’s reply creating the Fa0/2 entry, and verify subsequent requests use that port. If flooding continues unexpectedly, investigate why source learning is not retained rather than assuming the host ARP table and switch MAC table are the same.

lab.title: Configure local accounts and SSH, diagnose a refusal, and restore access
lab.intro: Build this as a new Packet Tracer project. You will verify two privilege levels, restrict remote access to SSH, create a controlled transport fault, and recover through the console. All credentials shown are for this isolated exercise. Outputs are representative excerpts; record what your installed simulator actually reports.
lab.topology:
```diagram
{"type":"topology","title":"SSH access lab","caption":"The laptop's console connection is independent of the PC's Ethernet management path.","nodes":[{"id":"L","kind":"laptop","label":"CONSOLE","sub":"RS-232 terminal","x":2,"y":1},{"id":"P","kind":"pc","label":"ADMIN","sub":"10.8.0.10/24","x":2,"y":5},{"id":"S","kind":"switch","label":"SW1","sub":"2960-24TT","x":6,"y":5},{"id":"R","kind":"router","label":"R1","sub":"2911 · 10.8.0.1/24","x":10,"y":3}],"links":[{"from":"L","to":"R","fromLabel":"RS-232","toLabel":"Console","style":"dashed"},{"from":"P","to":"S","fromLabel":"Fa0","toLabel":"Fa0/1"},{"from":"S","to":"R","fromLabel":"Gi0/1","toLabel":"Gi0/0","accent":true}]}
```

| Connection or device | Setting |
|---|---|
| CONSOLE RS-232 → R1 Console | Console cable |
| ADMIN Fa0 → SW1 Fa0/1 | Copper straight-through |
| SW1 Gi0/1 → R1 Gi0/0 | Copper straight-through |
| ADMIN IPv4 | `10.8.0.10`, mask `255.255.255.0`, gateway `10.8.0.1` |
| R1 Gi0/0 | `10.8.0.1/24` |
| SW1 | Default access VLAN for this single-LAN exercise; no management IP required |

The gateway is recorded for a complete host configuration; this lab's SSH destination is on ADMIN's own subnet. DNS is not needed because the SSH test uses an IP address.

steps.title: Open a console and identify the device
steps.body:
Place and cable the devices. On CONSOLE, open Desktop → Terminal and accept the displayed serial settings, using 9600 baud, 8 data bits, no parity and 1 stop bit for the 2911. Press Enter if needed. Decline the initial configuration dialog if it appears. Keep this terminal open throughout the exercise.

```ios R1
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R1
R1(config)# no ip domain-lookup
R1(config)# end
R1# show version
R1# show line
```

:::expected
The prompt is `R1#`. Record the model, image description and available console/VTY lines. `no ip domain-lookup` avoids accidental hostname lookups from mistyped commands; it does not prevent local RSA-key generation or change ADMIN's DNS settings. If the terminal is blank, check the console cable endpoints before investigating Ethernet.
:::

steps.title: Establish the IP path
steps.body:
On ADMIN, use Desktop → IP Configuration to enter the address table. Configure R1 through the console.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# description Management lab LAN
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.8.0.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip interface brief
R1# show running-config
```

On ADMIN, open Desktop → Command Prompt:

```text
ping 10.8.0.1
```

:::expected
Gi0/0 should have `10.8.0.1` and become `up/up` after the link is operational. Repeat an initial ping if address resolution was still in progress. If repeated tests fail, verify cabling, address/mask and interface state. Record every VTY range shown in the running configuration; later steps must apply the intended policy to all available lines.
:::

steps.title: Create users and an enable secret
steps.body:
Configure one administrator and one lower-privilege account. Do this before making a line depend on the local database.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# enable secret EnableLabSecret8
R1(config)# username admin privilege 15 secret AdminLabSecret8
R1(config)# username trainee secret TraineeLabSecret8
R1(config)# end
R1# show running-config | include username
R1# show running-config | include enable
```

:::expected
Both usernames and the enable secret appear. The stored verifier strings and their type numbers may differ by image; do not compare them character for character with an example hash. The configuration explicitly gives `admin` privilege 15 and leaves `trainee` at the default local-user level of 1. If a filter is unsupported, inspect the full running configuration.
:::

steps.title: Protect the console line
steps.body:
Keep the existing console session open. Do not log out until a separate remote session has been tested.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# line console 0
R1(config-line)# login local
R1(config-line)# exec-timeout 5 0
R1(config-line)# logging synchronous
R1(config-line)# end
R1# show running-config | section line con
```

:::expected
The console line uses `login local` and a five-minute idle timeout. The existing session remains available; the next console login will need one of the accounts from Step 3. A missing user entry must be corrected now, before that session ends.
:::

steps.title: Configure the SSH server and VTY policy
steps.body:
Use the conventional RSA-key workflow. If your image rejects the complete key-generation command, inspect `crypto key generate rsa ?`; a supported alternative may prompt for the modulus after `crypto key generate rsa`. Enter `2048` at that prompt. Do not paste an interactive answer as a separate configuration command.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip domain-name lab.test
R1(config)# crypto key generate rsa general-keys modulus 2048
R1(config)# ip ssh version 2
R1(config)# line vty 0 4
R1(config-line)# login local
R1(config-line)# transport input ssh
R1(config-line)# exec-timeout 5 0
R1(config-line)# end
R1# show ip ssh
```

If Step 2 showed VTY 5–15, apply the same policy to that range as well. Run this additional block only when those lines exist:

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# line vty 5 15
R1(config-line)# login local
R1(config-line)# transport input ssh
R1(config-line)# exec-timeout 5 0
R1(config-line)# end
```

:::expected
`show ip ssh` reports the server enabled for version 2.0. Inspect the VTY sections and confirm local authentication and SSH transport on every range. If the simulator lacks SSH support for the chosen device/image, use a supported router/image; reading an output example does not count as a successful login test.
:::

steps.title: Test both users from a new session
steps.body:
On ADMIN, enter:

```text
ssh -l trainee 10.8.0.1
```

Enter `TraineeLabSecret8` when prompted. Inside that remote session:

```ios R1
R1> show privilege
R1> enable
```

Enter `EnableLabSecret8` at the password prompt, then:

```ios R1
R1# show privilege
R1# exit
```

Open a new SSH session as `admin` using `AdminLabSecret8`, then check it:

```text
ssh -l admin 10.8.0.1
```

```ios R1
R1# show privilege
R1# show users
R1# exit
```

Finally try `telnet 10.8.0.1` from ADMIN.

:::expected
`trainee` initially reports privilege 1 and reaches 15 after the enable secret is accepted. `admin` begins at privilege 15. Telnet must not open an authenticated terminal session. Exact rejection wording varies; the result and the VTY configuration matter. If your simulator does not expose `show privilege`, record the prompts and check the username privilege in the configuration.
:::

steps.title: Introduce a remote-transport fault
steps.body:
Confirm that ADMIN has exited its SSH session. On the still-open console, replace the incoming transport with `none` on every VTY range you configured. Do not save this fault.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# line vty 0 4
R1(config-line)# transport input none
R1(config-line)# end
```

If VTY 5–15 exists, apply `transport input none` to that range too. From ADMIN, run the ping and SSH tests again.

```text
ping 10.8.0.1
ssh -l admin 10.8.0.1
```

:::expected
The IP interface remains operational and ping should still succeed. A new SSH terminal session is refused because the VTY lines accept no incoming transport. On the console, `show ip ssh` can still report an enabled SSH server. This combination demonstrates why server status, IP reachability and line policy must be checked separately.
:::

steps.title: Restore the intended transport
steps.body:
Use the console to restore SSH on every VTY range. Keep the fault and recovery as separate observations in your notes.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# line vty 0 4
R1(config-line)# transport input ssh
R1(config-line)# end
```

Apply the same recovery to VTY 5–15 if present. Open a new SSH session from ADMIN as `admin`.

:::expected
The new login succeeds with privilege 15. Telnet remains disallowed. If SSH still fails, compare all VTY ranges, user entries and the SSH server state before changing the interface address or regenerating keys.
:::

steps.title: Verify the complete access policy
steps.body:
From the console, inspect the active sessions while ADMIN's SSH session is open.

```ios R1
R1# show users
R1# show ssh
R1# show ip ssh
R1# show running-config | section line vty
```

Record the user, line and any displayed client address. Keep ADMIN's proven SSH session open while you test a fresh console login. At the console, enter `exit` from privileged EXEC (`R1# exit`), then press Enter to start a new session and sign in with a local account. Closing and reopening the terminal window alone may leave the existing console session active. After both paths have been verified, log out of the SSH session on ADMIN.

:::expected
The commands provide different evidence: terminal users, SSH sessions, SSH server state, and line configuration. The console login accepts a valid local account. A successful test on one VTY does not replace reviewing the other VTY ranges. On images with limited filters/session commands, inspect the full configuration and record the limitation instead of inventing missing output.
:::

steps.title: Save the verified configuration
steps.body:
Save only after the fault has been removed and both access paths work.

```ios R1
R1# copy running-config startup-config
R1# show startup-config
```

Press Enter at the destination filename prompt. Save the Packet Tracer project as `08-secure-device-access.pkt`.

:::expected
The saved configuration includes the intended username, interface, SSH and line settings. It must not contain `transport input none` on the VTY lines. The device save and project save are both complete. A reload is unnecessary for this exercise; if you later test one, retain the verified credentials and console path.
:::

lab.troubleshooting:
- **No console prompt:** check the serial connection and terminal settings; the Ethernet IP address is not the first check.
- **Repeated ping failure:** check host addressing, cable endpoints and R1 Gi0/0 before changing user accounts.
- **SSH server disabled:** check support, RSA-key configuration and SSH settings.
- **Server enabled but session refused:** inspect every VTY range and its accepted transports; a reachable server can still reject terminal access.
- **Password rejected:** check exact username, secret and line authentication method. Do not assume an enable secret is the login password.
- **Unexpected privilege:** inspect the user entry and `show privilege`; an authenticated level-1 session is different from a failed login.
- **Change disappears after restart:** inspect the saved configuration and boot state rather than assuming the earlier save succeeded.
lab.challenge:
Create a user `auditor` with a lab secret of your choice who begins at privilege 1. Prove the account's initial privilege in a new SSH session without using `enable`. Then explain why a successful `ping` and an enabled SSH server would still not prove that `auditor` can sign in.

:::expected
Use `username auditor secret` followed by your chosen lab secret in global configuration mode; omit `privilege 15`. The existing `login local` policy makes the account usable. A new login reports privilege 1. Ping tests ICMP reachability, while `show ip ssh` reports server state; valid credentials and an accepting VTY policy are additional requirements. Save again if you want to retain the new account.
:::

questions.prompt: R1 uses ordinary local enable authentication. An enable secret and a different enable password both exist at privilege 15. Which credential permits the transition from `>` to `#`?
options: The password configured as the enable password
Either configured credential, tried in sequence
The password configured as the enable secret
The shared password under the console line
questions.explanation: For the same privilege level, the enable secret takes precedence over the enable password. This question assumes local enable authentication, with no AAA method list changing that behavior.

whyWrong.0: The enable secret takes precedence for the same level.
whyWrong.1: This local configuration does not fall back to the enable password.
whyWrong.3: Line authentication and the enable transition are separate.

questions.prompt: On traditional IOS, what does `service password-encryption` do to applicable cleartext password fields?
options: Stores those fields using reversible type 7 obfuscation
Replaces those fields with type 9 password verifiers
Encrypts terminal traffic for existing Telnet sessions
Converts the enable secret into a stronger hash
questions.explanation: The command obscures applicable cleartext password fields in the configuration. Type 7 is reversible, and removing the command does not automatically reveal plaintext for fields already converted.

whyWrong.1: That command does not select the scrypt algorithm for those fields.
whyWrong.2: Stored configuration formatting does not protect a Telnet session.
whyWrong.3: It does not upgrade the algorithm used by an enable secret.

exhibit.title: R1 configuration attempt
exhibit.text:
R1(config)# crypto key generate rsa general-keys modulus 2048
% Please define a domain-name first.

questions.prompt: R1 uses the conventional hostname/domain/RSA workflow shown. Which missing configuration is identified by the device?
options: A DNS server that can resolve the router hostname
A default route pointing to the DNS server
A username assigned to privilege level fifteen
A local domain name for the key-generation workflow
questions.explanation: Configure a domain name, then retry the supported RSA-key generation command. The error identifies that prerequisite; it is not evidence that a DNS server must be reachable.

whyWrong.0: The named local domain is configuration data; generating the key does not require a DNS lookup.
whyWrong.1: The error is about device identity configuration, not routing.
whyWrong.2: A user is needed for login but does not resolve this key-generation error.

questions.prompt: Which two identity settings are used by the conventional unnamed RSA-key workflow taught in this chapter? Choose two.
options: An available public DNS resolver
A configured nondefault hostname
An established Telnet session from the client
A successful lookup of the management subnet
A configured local domain name
questions.explanation: The conventional workflow uses a configured hostname and domain name for the device key identity. Other key-management forms exist, so this is a scoped workflow rather than a claim about every possible RSA command.

whyWrong.0: The identity settings do not require a live DNS query.
whyWrong.2: A Telnet session is not a key-generation prerequisite.
whyWrong.3: Subnets are not resolved to generate the local key pair.

exhibit.title: Abbreviated VTY configuration
exhibit.text:
line vty 0 4
 login local
 transport input ssh
line vty 5 15
 password 7 0822455D0A16
 login
 transport input telnet

questions.prompt: A device has VTY 0–15. Which problem is demonstrated by this abbreviated configuration?
options: The SSH server needs a separate key pair for each VTY range
The two VTY ranges enforce different transport and authentication policies
The local username database is limited to the first five VTY lines
The second range inherits SSH-only access from the first range
questions.explanation: VTY 5–15 still permits Telnet with shared-line authentication. Apply the intended local-user and SSH policy to every available range; do not assume the policy on VTY 0–4 covers the rest.

whyWrong.0: One server key configuration can serve multiple VTY lines.
whyWrong.2: The database is not limited by line number; each line selects its authentication policy.
whyWrong.3: Each configured range retains its own transport settings.

questions.prompt: With local authentication and no custom authorization, which account and line combination begins a session at privilege 15?
options: A default-privilege local user on a line using `login local`
A shared line password with `login` and an enable secret
A local user with `secret` but no configured privilege
A privilege-15 local user on a line using `login local`
questions.explanation: Local user privilege and line authentication work together. A user configured with privilege 15 begins at privileged EXEC when authenticated by this local method.

whyWrong.0: The default local-user privilege is 1.
whyWrong.1: The existence of an enable secret does not by itself make line login start at privilege 15.
whyWrong.2: The secret controls password storage, not the initial privilege level.

questions.prompt: A client cannot obtain ping replies from R1, but a new SSH login to R1 succeeds. What does this evidence establish?
options: SSH access works even though this ICMP test did not receive replies
The successful SSH login proves ICMP is enabled on every interface
The failed ping proves the SSH session is connected to another subnet
The client must regenerate R1’s SSH host keys before continuing
questions.explanation: A service test answers a different question from a ping. Record the failed ICMP result separately; do not treat it as proof that all IP communication is broken.

whyWrong.1: SSH and ICMP are separate protocols and can be treated differently.
whyWrong.2: The ping result does not identify the subnet of an authenticated SSH session.
whyWrong.3: A successful session provides no basis for replacing the server keys.

exhibit.title: R1# show ip ssh — legacy image
exhibit.text:
SSH Enabled - version 1.99
Authentication timeout: 120 secs; Authentication retries: 3

questions.prompt: A legacy IOS image reports the SSH version shown. Which configuration restricts that server to SSHv2?
options: `transport input telnet` under the VTY lines
`service password-encryption` in global configuration mode
`ip ssh version 2` in global configuration mode
`login local` under the console and VTY lines
questions.explanation: On an image reporting this compatibility mode, version 1.99 indicates support for SSHv1 and SSHv2. Explicitly select version 2; do not assume every current image starts in this legacy mode.

whyWrong.0: That permits Telnet rather than selecting the SSH version.
whyWrong.1: That affects applicable stored passwords, not the SSH version.
whyWrong.3: That selects local authentication, not an SSH protocol version.

questions.prompt: Which two statements correctly distinguish management access methods? Choose two.
options: A direct serial console can work without a configured IP interface
SSH always proves that a physically separate management network is used
An HTTP management page protects credentials in the same way as HTTPS
TACACS+ and RADIUS support AAA decisions rather than replacing SSH
Cloud management requires every product to disable local access
questions.explanation: Console access does not depend on the device’s IP forwarding path. Central AAA can support authentication and authorization while the administrator still uses SSH for the terminal session.

whyWrong.1: Whether management is in-band or out-of-band depends on the network design.
whyWrong.2: HTTPS adds TLS; ordinary HTTP does not provide that protection.
whyWrong.4: Local access and recovery capabilities vary by product.

questions.prompt: An IOS configuration contains `enable secret 5` followed by a stored verifier. What does the number identify?
options: The privilege level assigned to the enable session
The type of password verifier stored in the configuration
The number of failed logins permitted before disconnection
The minimum number of characters in the original password
questions.explanation: Type 5 identifies the legacy MD5-based verifier format. A one-way hash is still vulnerable to password guessing; do not describe it as impossible to crack or as a universal current default.

whyWrong.0: The type marker is not the requested privilege level.
whyWrong.2: Authentication retry settings are separate configuration.
whyWrong.3: The marker does not encode the original password length.

exhibit.title: Abbreviated VTY configuration
exhibit.text:
line vty 0 4
 login local
 transport input ssh

questions.prompt: The console review confirms that no `username` entries or AAA method lists exist. SSH reaches authentication but every local login fails. What is missing?
options: A shared VTY password that overrides `login local`
A new management subnet with a different mask
An enable password matching the SSH password
A local user matching the credentials being supplied
questions.explanation: The VTY lines request local-user authentication, but the local database has no accounts. Create the intended account through the working console, then verify a new remote session.

whyWrong.0: A shared line password is not the fallback for the local-user method.
whyWrong.1: The session already reaches authentication; the evidence identifies the local database.
whyWrong.2: The enable transition does not supply a missing login identity.

questions.prompt: Which command saves the verified running configuration for the normal next boot?
options: `copy running-config startup-config`
`copy startup-config running-config`
`show startup-config`
`configure terminal`
questions.explanation: The direction of the copy matters: active configuration is the source, startup configuration the destination. The device’s persistent storage implementation may vary, but the active-versus-saved distinction remains.

whyWrong.1: That loads saved settings into the active configuration rather than saving active changes.
whyWrong.2: That displays the saved configuration without updating it.
whyWrong.3: That enters configuration mode without saving changes.

exhibit.title: Terminal sessions — representative excerpt
exhibit.text:
Line       User       Host(s)   Idle       Location
*  0 con 0                idle      00:00:00
   2 vty 0     admin      idle      00:00:05   10.8.0.10

questions.prompt: Which command most directly provides the terminal-session table shown, including the Location column?
options: `show ip ssh`
`show privilege`
`show users`
`show ip interface brief`
questions.explanation: The terminal-session table identifies active lines and users; remote sessions can include a client address under Location. The asterisk marks the session issuing the command.

whyWrong.0: That reports SSH server settings rather than this terminal-line table.
whyWrong.1: That reports the current session’s privilege level.
whyWrong.3: That reports interface addresses and state, not the users of terminal lines.

exhibit.title: VTY configuration
exhibit.text:
line vty 0 4
 login local
 transport input telnet

questions.prompt: R1’s SSH server is enabled and the client can reach its IP address. The only available VTY range has the configuration shown. Which change permits SSH while disallowing Telnet?
options: Replace `login local` with a shared line password and `login`
Replace `transport input telnet` with `transport input ssh`
Create another local username at privilege level fifteen
Save the current running configuration to startup configuration
questions.explanation: The VTY range currently accepts Telnet only. Selecting SSH corrects the transport policy; verify a new session after the change and inspect any additional VTY ranges.

whyWrong.0: Changing the authentication method does not make this range accept SSH transport.
whyWrong.2: An additional user does not change the accepted transport.
whyWrong.3: Saving preserves the existing policy; it does not correct it.

questions.prompt: A powered, normally running router has no usable IP interface. Which access method can still be used by an authorized technician with working credentials and the correct cable?
options: An SSH session to its previous interface address
An HTTPS session to its previous interface address
A Telnet session to its default gateway address
A direct connection to its serial console
questions.explanation: A direct serial console does not require a configured IP interface. Authentication and the console’s own operational state still matter, so this is not a claim that physical access bypasses credentials.

whyWrong.0: SSH requires an IP path to a currently reachable server address.
whyWrong.1: Web management also requires IP reachability.
whyWrong.2: The gateway is not a substitute for a reachable router management address.

questions.prompt: With ordinary IOS privilege assignments, which two actions belong to privileged EXEC or require entering it first? Choose two.
options: Send a basic ping permitted in user EXEC
Read the device hostname from its prompt
Inspect the full running configuration
Enter a username at a login prompt
Enter global configuration mode
questions.explanation: Privileged EXEC provides access to configuration inspection and the entry point for configuration mode. Custom privilege or AAA policies can alter command access; this question uses the ordinary lab assignments.

whyWrong.0: A basic ping is normally available before privileged EXEC.
whyWrong.1: The prompt is visible without privileged access.
whyWrong.3: Logging in is separate from privileged EXEC.

cards.front: What do `>`, `#`, `(config)#` and `(config-line)#` identify?
cards.back: User EXEC, privileged EXEC, global configuration and line configuration. Check the mode before applying a command.

cards.front: How do `exit` and `end` differ in configuration mode?
cards.back: `exit` leaves the current configuration level; `end` returns to privileged EXEC.

cards.front: Running configuration versus startup configuration?
cards.back: Running is the active configuration; startup is the saved configuration read during normal boot. Traditional IOS exposes startup configuration through NVRAM; storage details vary.

cards.front: How do you save active changes for the next normal boot?
cards.back: `copy running-config startup-config`; `write memory` is a familiar alternative on supporting IOS devices. Erasing startup configuration is not a universal factory reset.

cards.front: How should you determine which VTY lines to protect?
cards.back: Inspect `show line`, VTY sections in the configuration, and contextual help. Apply the intended policy to every available range; do not assume a fixed count by device family.

cards.front: What does `exec-timeout 5 0` configure?
cards.back: A five-minute idle EXEC timeout on the selected line. `exec-timeout 0 0` disables the idle timeout; choose settings deliberately.

cards.front: `login` with a line password versus `login local`?
cards.back: The former uses a shared line password; `login local` checks the local username database. Create the account before making the line depend on it.

cards.front: Enable secret and enable password at the same level: which is used?
cards.back: In the basic local enable configuration, the enable secret takes precedence. It is separate from the password used to log in to the line.

cards.front: What do password types 0, 7, 5, 8 and 9 represent?
cards.back: 0: cleartext. 7: reversible obfuscation. 5: legacy MD5-based verifier. 8: PBKDF2-SHA-256. 9: scrypt. Supported defaults depend on the image.

cards.front: Does `service password-encryption` secure Telnet?
cards.back: No. On traditional IOS it obscures applicable stored password fields with type 7. It does not encrypt the terminal session or upgrade an enable secret.

cards.front: What completes the conventional IOS SSH configuration?
cards.back: Reachable IP interface; hostname/domain and supported host keys; SSHv2; a valid user/authentication method; and accepting VTY transport. Verify a new login.

cards.front: What does SSH version 1.99 mean on an image reporting it?
cards.back: Legacy compatibility with SSHv1 and SSHv2. Use `ip ssh version 2` to require v2; do not assume 1.99 is the default on current software.

cards.front: Default ports for Telnet, SSH, HTTP and HTTPS?
cards.back: TCP 23, TCP 22, TCP 80 and TCP 443, respectively. A port number is distinct from authentication or privilege.

cards.front: Does a direct serial console require a working IP interface?
cards.back: No. It is a separate local management path, but the correct cable/settings and configured authentication are still required.

cards.front: `show users`, `show ssh`, and `show ip ssh`: different purposes?
cards.back: Terminal users/lines; SSH-session information; SSH-server configuration and state. Displayed fields vary by image.

cards.front: Default local-user privilege and the effect of `privilege 15`?
cards.back: Default is 1. With basic local authentication, privilege 15 starts at privileged EXEC. `show privilege` verifies the current level.

cards.front: Which VTY command accepts SSH and excludes Telnet?
cards.back: `transport input ssh`. Apply and verify it on all intended VTY ranges.

cards.front: What should an unexpected SSH host-key change prompt you to do?
cards.back: Verify the server identity through a trusted record or management process before accepting the change. A key warning is not fixed by blindly trusting a new key.

cards.front: Does an enabled SSH server prove a user can log in?
cards.back: No. The IP path, compatible client/server algorithms, accepting VTY policy and valid authentication must also work. Test a new session.

cards.front: What does an IOS banner provide?
cards.back: An access notice or message. It does not authenticate the user; the chosen delimiter ends the text, and display timing can differ by protocol.

commands.task: Create local user admin at privilege 15 with lab secret AdminLabSecret8.
commands.note: The privilege setting and the line authentication method jointly determine the initial session access.

commands.task: On traditional IOS, obscure applicable cleartext password fields in the configuration.
commands.note: This uses reversible type 7 for applicable fields; it does not encrypt Telnet traffic.

commands.task: Set the local domain to lab.test for the conventional RSA-key workflow.
commands.note: The device does not need to resolve this domain through DNS to generate its keys.

commands.task: Generate a 2048-bit RSA key pair using the supported general-keys form.
commands.answer: crypto key generate rsa general-keys modulus 2048
commands.note: Use contextual help on images with different syntax; an interactive modulus response is not a separate IOS command.

commands.task: Configure the SSH server to use version 2.
commands.note: Verify the reported version; older compatibility output and modern defaults may differ.

commands.task: Use local usernames to authenticate this line.
commands.note: Create a working user before making the line depend on the local database.

tickets.title: SSH server enabled, but remote sessions are refused
tickets.scenario: A change on an isolated lab router leaves its directly connected management PC able to ping 10.8.0.1. A new SSH session is refused. The account and key configuration are unchanged, and the console remains available. The complete VTY range is 0–4.

exhibits.title: R1# show ip ssh — excerpt
exhibits.text: SSH Enabled - version 2.0

exhibits.title: R1 VTY configuration
exhibits.text:
line vty 0 4
 login local
 transport input none

tickets.question: Which configuration is responsible for refusing new terminal sessions?
options: The interface is missing an IP address
The VTY range accepts no incoming transport
The admin account needs a shared line password
The SSH server must be changed to version 1.99
tickets.explanation: The VTY range explicitly selects transport input none. A running SSH server and a reachable interface do not override that line policy. Restore SSH transport through the console, then verify a new connection.
tickets.fix:
```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# line vty 0 4
R1(config-line)# transport input ssh
R1(config-line)# end
R1# show running-config | section line vty
```
Open a new SSH session from the management PC and verify its privilege. Save after the intended access works.

tickets.title: Local-user cleanup prevents every new SSH login
tickets.scenario: A technician removes all username entries from a lab router. Existing console access remains open. New SSH connections reach authentication, but no supplied local account is accepted. No AAA method lists are configured.

exhibits.title: Complete username check
exhibits.text:
R1# show running-config | include username
R1#

exhibits.title: R1 VTY configuration
exhibits.text:
line vty 0 4
 login local
 transport input ssh

tickets.question: Which change restores the intended named-user authentication?
options: Replace SSH with Telnet on the VTY lines
Set an enable password matching the old username
Create the intended local username and secret
Set a default route to the directly connected PC
tickets.explanation: login local depends on the local username database. With no accounts present, no local credentials can match. Restore the intended account through the working console, then test a separate login before ending that console session.
tickets.fix:
```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# username admin privilege 15 secret AdminLabSecret8
R1(config)# end
```
Use this example secret only in the isolated lab. Verify a new SSH login, check show privilege, and save the corrected configuration.

sections.title: Create and verify the VLAN database
Carry voice and data on a phone port
Check PoE capability and the power budget
Choose the port from the endpoint requirements

lab.title: Build data and voice VLANs, identify assignment faults, and verify power requirements
devices: 1 × Cisco 7960 IP phone with its external power adapter
lab.intro: The required switching work uses a new Packet Tracer project. The PoE budget exercise uses supplied evidence, with an optional supporting-switch observation. No router, DHCP server or call-control server is needed. You will verify switching and port configuration; this lab does not claim to establish a working voice call.
lab.topology:
```diagram
{"type":"topology","title":"Data and voice access lab","caption":"PC-A connects through the powered phone; PC-A and PC-B use VLAN 10, while PC-C and the printer use VLAN 20.","nodes":[{"id":"A","kind":"pc","label":"PC-A","sub":"192.168.10.11/24","x":1,"y":1},{"id":"PH","kind":"phone","label":"Phone","sub":"External power","x":4,"y":1},{"id":"B","kind":"pc","label":"PC-B","sub":"192.168.10.12/24","x":1,"y":5},{"id":"S","kind":"switch","label":"SW1","sub":"2960-24TT","x":7,"y":3},{"id":"C","kind":"pc","label":"PC-C","sub":"192.168.20.13/24","x":11,"y":1},{"id":"PR","kind":"printer","label":"Printer","sub":"192.168.20.20/24","x":11,"y":5}],"links":[{"from":"A","to":"PH","toLabel":"PC"},{"from":"PH","to":"S","fromLabel":"Switch","toLabel":"Fa0/1"},{"from":"B","to":"S","toLabel":"Fa0/2"},{"from":"S","to":"C","fromLabel":"Fa0/3"},{"from":"S","to":"PR","fromLabel":"Fa0/4"}]}
```
