Use copper straight-through cables for every connection. On PC-A, PC-B and PC-C, enter the addresses below under Desktop → IP Configuration. On Printer-PT, use its Config interface/IP settings. Leave gateways and DNS unset for this isolated local-subnet exercise.

| Endpoint | Switch path | Address and mask | Intended VLAN |
|---|---|---|---|
| PC-A Fa0 | Phone PC port → phone Switch port → SW1 Fa0/1 | `192.168.10.11`, `255.255.255.0` | 10 |
| PC-B Fa0 | SW1 Fa0/2 | `192.168.10.12`, `255.255.255.0` | 10 |
| PC-C Fa0 | SW1 Fa0/3 | `192.168.20.13`, `255.255.255.0` | 20 |
| Printer Fa0 | SW1 Fa0/4 | `192.168.20.20`, `255.255.255.0` | 20 |
| Phone | SW1 Fa0/1 | No voice IP service is configured | Voice VLAN 30 |

steps.title: Build and inspect the physical setup
steps.body:
Place the devices and connect the cables. The 2960-24TT in this lab does not supply PoE. Open the phone's Physical tab and connect its external power adapter using the model's power socket. If the interface differs in your Packet Tracer version, inspect the available power module rather than treating the absence of a phone display as a VLAN fault.

Name the switch through its CLI. Decline an initial setup dialog if one appears.

```ios SW1
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname SW1
SW1(config)# no ip domain-lookup
SW1(config)# end
SW1# show interfaces status
```

:::expected
Fa0/1–Fa0/4 should report physical connectivity once the devices and links are ready. The phone must have power for its internal data path to operate. Wait for ordinary forwarding state to settle; do not assume an exact number of seconds across simulator versions. No voice registration is expected.
:::

steps.title: Create the VLANs
steps.body:
```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# vlan 10
SW1(config-vlan)# name USERS
SW1(config-vlan)# exit
SW1(config)# vlan 20
SW1(config-vlan)# name PRINTERS
SW1(config-vlan)# exit
SW1(config)# vlan 30
SW1(config-vlan)# name VOICE
SW1(config-vlan)# end
SW1# show vlan brief
```

:::expected
VLANs 10, 20 and 30 appear as active. Merely creating them has not yet reassigned the connected data ports. If the new VLANs are missing, correct their creation before moving on to host tests.
:::

steps.title: Assign access ports and test local peers
steps.body:
```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface range fastethernet0/1 - 2
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport access vlan 10
SW1(config-if-range)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if-range)# exit
SW1(config)# interface range fastethernet0/3 - 4
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport access vlan 20
SW1(config-if-range)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if-range)# end
SW1# show vlan brief
```

On PC-A, run `ping 192.168.10.12`. On PC-C, run `ping 192.168.20.20`. Then try `ping 192.168.20.13` from PC-A. Inspect the learned addresses:

```ios SW1
SW1# show mac address-table
SW1# show interfaces fastethernet0/2 switchport
```

:::expected
Same-subnet peers in the same VLAN should communicate after address resolution and forwarding are ready. The cross-VLAN test has no router or configured gateway to carry it and should fail. PC-A and PC-B's source addresses should be learned in VLAN 10 after they send traffic; PC-C and the printer's in VLAN 20. Record actual MAC addresses rather than copying invented values.
:::

steps.title: Configure the voice VLAN
steps.body:
```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# description Phone and PC-A
SW1(config-if)# switchport voice vlan 30
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show interfaces fastethernet0/1 switchport
SW1# show vlan brief
```

Repeat PC-A's ping to PC-B. Inspect the phone's displayed network settings if your simulator exposes them.

:::expected
Fa0/1 should show access VLAN 10 and voice VLAN 30. PC-A's ordinary data connectivity remains in VLAN 10. Some image output lists the port under both VLANs. This verifies the switch configuration, not a voice lease, call registration or tagged voice payload: those have not been generated by this lab's absent voice services. Record any observed phone VLAN setting separately from that conclusion.
:::

steps.title: Remove a data VLAN and observe the fault
steps.body:
Delete only the lab's VLAN 20, leaving its access-port assignments in place.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# no vlan 20
SW1(config)# end
SW1# show vlan brief
SW1# show interfaces fastethernet0/3 switchport
```

Repeat PC-C's ping to the printer. Also repeat PC-A's ping to PC-B.

:::expected
The missing VLAN 20 prevents normal data forwarding for its assigned ports, even if their physical links stay connected. Switchport output may label access VLAN 20 as inactive. VLAN 10's local data test should continue working. Do not change the hosts' IP addresses: the deliberate fault is the missing VLAN.
:::

steps.title: Restore the deleted VLAN
steps.body:
```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# vlan 20
SW1(config-vlan)# name PRINTERS
SW1(config-vlan)# end
SW1# show vlan brief
SW1# show interfaces fastethernet0/3 switchport
```

Repeat PC-C's ping to the printer and record fresh MAC-table entries.

:::expected
VLAN 20 is active again; its existing port assignments become usable. The local PC-C-to-printer test should recover when forwarding is ready. This demonstrates the difference between deleting the VLAN and removing an interface's configured VLAN assignment.
:::

steps.title: Move a port into the wrong VLAN
steps.body:
Leave PC-B at `192.168.10.12/24`, but move its port to VLAN 20.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/2
SW1(config-if)# switchport access vlan 20
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show interfaces fastethernet0/2 switchport
```

Try PC-A's ping to PC-B again. Then send a ping from PC-B to PC-A and inspect SW1:

```ios SW1
SW1# show mac address-table interface fastethernet0/2
```

:::expected
The physical link and VLAN 20 can both be active, but PC-B is now in the wrong broadcast domain for its intended peer. Its newly generated source traffic is learned in VLAN 20. Existing ARP entries do not provide a bridge between the two VLANs, so cached addresses do not repair the fault.
:::

steps.title: Restore membership and verify the endpoint plan
steps.body:
```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/2
SW1(config-if)# switchport access vlan 10
SW1(config-if)# description PC-B user workstation
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show interfaces fastethernet0/2 switchport
SW1# show vlan brief
```

Repeat both same-VLAN tests. In your notes, list each endpoint's physical port, data VLAN, optional voice VLAN, address and power source. Explain why this setup needs neither a trunk nor an LACP bundle.

:::expected
PC-A/PC-B and PC-C/printer communication recover independently. Fa0/1 retains data VLAN 10 plus voice VLAN 30; Fa0/2 uses data VLAN 10; Fa0/3–Fa0/4 use data VLAN 20. The lab has one switch and individual host links, so its required tasks stop at access and voice configuration.
:::

steps.title: Interpret a PoE allocation problem
steps.body:
Use this supplied evidence as a paper exercise. A PoE+ switch has a usable allocation budget of 370 W. Ten phones each reserve 6.3 W; ten APs each require 30 W of PSE allocation. A further AP requests 30 W. All cables, per-port limits and device compatibility have already been checked.

Predict the remaining budget before the additional request, whether the request fits, and a suitable correction that does not underpower an existing device.

If your Packet Tracer version supports PoE reporting on a 3650-24PS, you may add SW2 and a compatible powered endpoint to a separate lab segment. Use a supported port such as Gi1/0/1 and inspect:

```ios SW2
SW2> enable
SW2# show power inline
```

Do not expect this extra device's actual budget or draw to match the paper example. If the command is unavailable, finish the paper exercise without claiming a live power measurement.

:::expected
Phones reserve 63 W and the ten APs reserve 300 W, leaving `370 − 63 − 300 = 7 W`. The additional 30 W allocation does not fit. A suitable change is to move an endpoint to a compatible PSE with enough available budget, or provide supported additional power capacity. Do not lower a real 30 W requirement to 7 W merely to make the allocation fit.
:::

steps.title: Save the corrected setup
steps.body:
```ios SW1
SW1# copy running-config startup-config
SW1# show vlan brief
SW1# show running-config
```

Press Enter at the copy destination prompt, and save the project as `09-data-voice-vlans.pkt`.

:::expected
The final setup contains active VLANs 10, 20 and 30 and the intended port assignments. Neither deliberate fault remains. The configuration save and Packet Tracer project save serve different purposes; keep both.
:::

lab.troubleshooting:
- **Phone and attached PC both lack a working link:** check the phone's external power and both Ethernet cables first.
- **Connected port, inactive VLAN:** compare the access VLAN with the VLAN database. Restore the intended VLAN before changing IP settings.
- **Active VLAN, but a moved PC cannot reach its peers:** compare documented membership, switchport output and freshly learned source MAC addresses.
- **PC data works through the phone:** this establishes the data path, not phone registration or voice addressing.
- **Different VLANs cannot communicate here:** expected; no Layer 3 forwarding path was configured.
- **PoE command unavailable:** check the model and image. A non-PoE 2960-24TT cannot supply power through configuration.
- **Power denied:** inspect the actual administrative setting, device requirement, per-port capability and remaining shared allocation before choosing a correction.
lab.challenge:
Add PC-D on SW1 Fa0/5 with `192.168.20.25/24`, no gateway, and a straight-through cable. Configure only the settings needed for it to reach PC-C and the printer. Predict whether it can reach PC-A. Then explain what would happen if you changed only PC-D's switchport to VLAN 10 while leaving its address unchanged.

:::expected
Set Fa0/5 to static access mode in VLAN 20 and ensure it is not shut down. PC-D should reach PC-C and the printer after forwarding and address resolution are ready; it has no routed path to PC-A. Moving only its port to VLAN 10 leaves the host's IP configuration inconsistent with the intended VLAN 20 subnet. Restore the port to VLAN 20, verify its learned source address in that VLAN, and save if retaining the extension.
:::

exhibit.title: SW1# show vlan brief — excerpt
exhibit.text:
10 USERS    active Fa0/1
20 PRINTERS active Fa0/2

questions.prompt: PC-A is 192.168.10.11/24 on Fa0/1; PC-B is 192.168.10.12/24 on Fa0/2. Both links are up, and no routing or VLAN translation is configured. Why can they not communicate?
options: Their host addresses belong to different IPv4 subnets
The peers occupy different Layer 2 broadcast domains
The switch needs a management IP to learn either MAC address
Their VLAN names must match their hostnames for ARP to work
questions.explanation: The masks make each peer appear local, but ARP and ordinary switching remain within the assigned VLAN. Correct the mistaken VLAN membership rather than inventing a gateway requirement for same-subnet peers.

whyWrong.0: Both addresses belong to 192.168.10.0/24.
whyWrong.2: Layer 2 forwarding does not require a switch management IP.
whyWrong.3: Hostnames and VLAN labels do not establish local ARP reachability.

questions.prompt: Which set identifies the default, nondeletable VLANs on the Catalyst lab platform?
options: VLAN 0 and VLANs 1006–1009
VLAN 1 and all VLANs from 2–1001
VLAN 4095 and VLANs 1002–1005
VLAN 1 and VLANs 1002–1005
questions.explanation: VLAN 1 and the legacy reserved VLANs 1002–1005 are present on the referenced Catalyst platform. The user VLANs created in this chapter are separate from that default set.

whyWrong.0: VLAN 0 is not an ordinary configured user VLAN, and 1006–1009 are extended-range IDs.
whyWrong.1: Ordinary user VLANs in 2–1001 are not all precreated or nondeletable.
whyWrong.2: 4095 is reserved, not the factory-default VLAN.

exhibit.title: SW1# show interfaces fa0/4 switchport — excerpt
exhibit.text:
Administrative Mode: static access
Operational Mode: static access
Access Mode VLAN: 20 (Inactive)

questions.prompt: A printer’s address and cable have not changed. Which correction addresses the condition shown for its data VLAN?
options: Recreate VLAN 20 after confirming that it is the intended VLAN
Change the switch hostname to match the printer subnet
Set a new default gateway on the switch for VLAN 20
Convert the printer port to a trunk carrying all VLANs
questions.explanation: The port retains an access-VLAN assignment, but that VLAN is inactive. Restore the intended VLAN and verify the local data path; do not change host addressing to hide the switch-side fault.

whyWrong.1: The hostname does not make an inactive VLAN forward traffic.
whyWrong.2: A gateway setting does not recreate the missing Layer 2 VLAN.
whyWrong.3: Changing to a general trunk does not correct the intended access-VLAN database entry.

questions.prompt: A phone is provisioned to tag voice traffic with VLAN 30. Its attached PC sends ordinary untagged data. The switchport has access VLAN 10 and voice VLAN 30. How are those two traffic types classified?
options: Both traffic types enter VLAN 30 because the phone is the physical neighbor
PC data enters VLAN 30; tagged voice enters VLAN 10
PC data enters VLAN 10; tagged voice enters VLAN 30
Both traffic types enter VLAN 10 because the port remains access mode
questions.explanation: The ordinary PC traffic uses the access VLAN, while correctly tagged phone voice traffic uses the configured voice VLAN. This describes the stated provisioning; it does not claim that every phone automatically obtains those settings.

whyWrong.0: The configured access VLAN still classifies ordinary untagged PC data.
whyWrong.1: This reverses the data and voice assignments.
whyWrong.3: The voice-VLAN feature permits the stated tagged voice behavior on an access port.

questions.prompt: Which two checks help establish the intended switch-side data/voice configuration? Choose two.
options: Confirm that the switch’s hostname contains the voice VLAN ID
Verify that both configured VLANs exist and are active
Treat successful PC data traffic as proof of voice registration
Read the port’s access VLAN and voice VLAN settings
Require the phone port to negotiate a general-purpose trunk
questions.explanation: Start with the VLAN database and the port’s actual data/voice settings. Phone power, provisioning, IP services and registration require their own checks.

whyWrong.0: The hostname is unrelated to port VLAN classification.
whyWrong.2: PC traffic does not verify voice addressing or call-control registration.
whyWrong.4: The access-plus-voice feature does not require a general-purpose trunk.

questions.prompt: An AP requires 25 W available at the powered device. Considering the standard limits below, what is the lowest listed PoE standard that can supply it?
options: IEEE 802.3at, with up to 25.5 W available at the PD
IEEE 802.3af, with up to 12.95 W available at the PD
IEEE 802.3bt Type 3, as the first standard above 25 W at the PD
IEEE 802.3bt Type 4, as the first standard above 25 W at the PD
questions.explanation: Compare power needed at the device with device-side capability, not just the switch-port source rating. 802.3at supplies up to 25.5 W at the PD under its specified conditions.

whyWrong.1: The requirement exceeds the device-side capability of 802.3af.
whyWrong.2: Type 3 can supply more power, but 802.3at already meets 25 W.
whyWrong.3: Type 4 is not the lowest standard that meets this requirement.

questions.prompt: A switch has a usable 370 W PoE allocation budget and 24 powered ports. Ten phones reserve 6.3 W each. Each additional AP requires 30 W of allocation at the PSE. How many APs fit within the remaining power and port capacity?
options: 9 APs, because every phone reserves a full 15.4 W
11 APs, because 307 divided by 30 rounds to eleven
14 APs, because fourteen physical ports remain free
10 APs, using 300 W of the remaining 307 W
questions.explanation: The phones reserve 63 W, leaving 307 W. Ten 30 W allocations fit, and there are enough ports; eleven require 330 W. This calculation uses the stated allocations rather than momentary measured consumption.

whyWrong.0: The problem explicitly supplies a 6.3 W reservation per phone.
whyWrong.1: Capacity must be rounded down; eleven allocations would exceed the remaining budget.
whyWrong.2: Available port count does not override the shared power limit.

exhibit.title: PoE allocation evidence — representative excerpt
exhibit.text:
Available: 370.0 W
Allocated: 345.0 W
Remaining:  25.0 W
Requested allocation on Gi1/0/13: 30.0 W
Operational state: power-deny

questions.prompt: A compatible AP requests 30 W of PSE allocation on a port whose configured maximum is 30 W. Its cable and hardware capability pass checks. What best explains the denial shown?
options: The requested allocation is below the port’s supported power limit
The AP requires a different VLAN ID before power can be supplied
The shared budget has only 25 W remaining for a 30 W request
The switch must reserve less power than the AP actually requires
questions.explanation: The per-port requirement is supported, but the shared remaining budget is insufficient. Provide supported capacity or move an endpoint to a compatible PSE with enough budget; verify actual requirements before changing limits.

whyWrong.0: A request within the per-port maximum can still exceed the shared budget.
whyWrong.1: Changing VLAN membership does not add available power allocation.
whyWrong.3: Underpowering a device is not a sound correction for a genuine requirement.

questions.prompt: Which command directly displays a port’s administrative mode, operational mode, access VLAN and voice VLAN?
options: `show mac address-table interface fastethernet0/1`
`show interfaces fastethernet0/1 switchport`
`show ip interface brief`
`show power inline`
questions.explanation: The switchport view puts intended mode, operating mode and VLAN assignments together. Use VLAN and MAC-table commands alongside it for a fuller diagnosis.

whyWrong.0: That shows learned MAC entries rather than all the listed switchport settings.
whyWrong.2: That reports IP/interface state rather than the full data/voice VLAN configuration.
whyWrong.3: That reports PoE information, not all of these VLAN and mode fields.

questions.prompt: A virtual host presents tagged traffic for several VLANs over one physical uplink. Which connectivity choice fits that requirement?
options: A single access VLAN selected from the host’s management address
A voice-VLAN command for each of the virtual machines
An unconfigured port chosen only because its speed matches
A trunk with VLAN tagging and an allowed list matching the host
questions.explanation: Several tagged VLANs on one uplink call for compatible trunking at both ends. Chapter 10 teaches the configuration; a virtual host does not automatically imply LACP or a particular edge-protection policy.

whyWrong.0: One ordinary access VLAN does not carry all the stated tagged VLANs.
whyWrong.1: The voice feature is not a general list of VM VLANs.
whyWrong.2: Physical speed alone does not establish VLAN tagging and membership.

questions.prompt: An AP’s design uses one untagged management VLAN; client traffic is tunneled to its controller rather than locally presented as separate VLANs. Which port choice fits the stated uplink?
options: An access port in the AP management VLAN, with suitable power
A trunk whose native VLAN is chosen from a wireless client subnet
A voice port with the AP management VLAN used as voice VLAN
A routed port that removes the AP’s Layer 2 management VLAN
questions.explanation: Use the traffic actually presented by the AP. The stated tunneled design can use a single access VLAN; APs that locally present multiple VLANs require a different configuration.

whyWrong.1: The stated uplink presents only its untagged management network.
whyWrong.2: An AP management uplink does not require the phone voice-VLAN feature.
whyWrong.3: That changes the stated Layer 2 attachment rather than implementing it.

exhibit.title: SW1# show interfaces fa0/7 switchport — excerpt
exhibit.text:
Operational Mode: static access
Access Mode VLAN: 10 (USERS)
Voice VLAN: 30 (Inactive)

questions.prompt: The port is intended to provide data VLAN 10 and voice VLAN 30. What switch-side defect is visible, without making assumptions about the phone’s fallback behavior?
options: The phone is proven to have registered in the data VLAN
The data VLAN is inactive because the voice VLAN is missing
The configured voice VLAN is inactive on this switch
The port must be a trunk because a voice VLAN is configured
questions.explanation: The switchport excerpt identifies an inactive voice VLAN. Verify the VLAN database, create or restore the intended VLAN, and then check the phone’s separate power/provisioning/IP state.

whyWrong.0: This output does not establish phone addressing or registration.
whyWrong.1: The excerpt identifies the inactive voice VLAN separately.
whyWrong.3: Access-plus-voice operation does not require general trunk mode.

questions.prompt: Which statement about VLAN 1 is accurate for the Catalyst lab defaults?
options: Its existence means the switch already has secure remote management
It is the default access VLAN and the default native VLAN for trunks
It automatically routes packets between newly created VLANs
It is deleted automatically when another access VLAN is created
questions.explanation: VLAN 1 has default roles on the referenced Catalyst platform. Do not confuse those defaults with static access mode on every port or a complete, secure management configuration.

whyWrong.0: VLAN existence does not create an IP address, SSH service or authentication policy.
whyWrong.2: A VLAN is a Layer 2 domain and does not by itself enable inter-VLAN routing.
whyWrong.3: Creating another VLAN does not delete VLAN 1.

questions.prompt: Which endpoint calls for particular care before reusing assumptions from a single-PC access-port design?
options: A single printer specified to send one untagged data network
A single workstation with one untagged Ethernet interface
A standalone sensor specified to use one untagged data VLAN
A transparent firewall that bridges frames from other devices
questions.explanation: A bridging appliance can carry other devices’ source addresses and participate in a wider Layer 2 path. Review its forwarding role and VLAN requirements before selecting edge protections or MAC limits, which are taught later.

whyWrong.0: That stated requirement fits ordinary access-port selection.
whyWrong.1: That stated requirement fits the basic host-port example.
whyWrong.2: That stated requirement alone does not imply a bridging role.

questions.prompt: After erasing startup configuration on the referenced Catalyst platform, a technician still finds normal-range user VLANs. Which two statements explain how to verify this state? Choose two.
options: VLAN information can persist in the separate VLAN database
Erasing startup configuration guarantees deletion of every switch file
An interface description recreates a VLAN with the same number
A remaining VLAN proves a router is still forwarding between subnets
Check VLAN definitions and interface assignments separately
questions.explanation: The VLAN database can persist independently of the startup configuration. VTP mode and platform influence how definitions are stored; inspect the actual VLAN database and running interface assignments instead of assuming a universal reset result.

whyWrong.1: Other persistent files can remain.
whyWrong.2: Descriptions are labels and do not create VLAN database entries.
whyWrong.3: A VLAN database entry says nothing by itself about routing.

questions.prompt: A supporting PoE switch accepts `power inline auto max 7000`. What maximum allocation is specified?
options: 7000 W, because the value uses whole watts
70 W, because the value uses hundredths of watts
7 W, because the argument is in milliwatts
7 mW, because the value uses microwatts
questions.explanation: 7000 milliwatts equals 7 watts. Supported ranges and the consequences of a limit depend on the platform and device requirement; do not use a low maximum to force an incompatible power budget.

whyWrong.0: The command argument in this supported form is milliwatts.
whyWrong.1: The supplied form does not use hundredths of watts.
whyWrong.3: The argument is already expressed in milliwatts.

cards.front: Normal and extended VLAN ranges on the lab Catalyst platform?
cards.back: Normal: 1–1005. Extended: 1006–4094. VLAN 0 carries priority-tag semantics rather than ordinary membership; 4095 is reserved.

cards.front: Which VLANs are present by default and cannot be deleted in this lab?
cards.back: VLAN 1 and legacy VLANs 1002–1005 on the referenced Catalyst platform.

cards.front: Does default VLAN 1 imply secure management or static access mode?
cards.back: No. VLAN 1 is a default access/native VLAN, but port mode, IP management and authentication are separate configuration.

cards.front: Why inspect both the VLAN database and interface configuration?
cards.back: The database defines VLANs; interface configuration assigns ports. Normal-range VLAN data may persist separately from startup configuration, with VTP/platform-dependent storage behavior.

cards.front: Create VLAN 10 named USERS: commands and modes?
cards.back: At global configuration, enter `vlan 10`; at VLAN configuration, enter `name USERS`. The number identifies the VLAN; the name is a label.

cards.front: Should a lab rely on assigning an absent VLAN to create it?
cards.back: No. Some supporting images create a missing VLAN as a side effect, but explicitly create and verify the VLAN before assigning the port.

cards.front: What happens to a port’s data-VLAN assignment when that VLAN is deleted?
cards.back: The configured assignment remains, but the data VLAN becomes inactive. Recreate the VLAN or deliberately assign the port to the correct active VLAN.

cards.front: Two commands for a fixed access port in VLAN 10?
cards.back: `switchport mode access` and `switchport access vlan 10`. Verify operational mode and that VLAN 10 is active.

cards.front: Access VLAN 10 plus voice VLAN 30: ordinary PC data and tagged voice?
cards.back: Untagged PC data enters VLAN 10; correctly provisioned phone voice tagged with 30 enters VLAN 30. The port can remain in access mode.

cards.front: How can a phone obtain voice-VLAN policy?
cards.back: Supported CDP or LLDP-MED discovery, or device provisioning/manual settings. Missing CDP alone does not prove every phone uses a particular fallback VLAN.

cards.front: Does successful PC traffic through a phone prove voice service works?
cards.back: No. Verify voice VLAN, power, provisioning and IP/call services separately. Switch-side voice configuration is not proof of a registered call endpoint.

cards.front: Does a missing data VLAN prove all traffic on a phone port must fail?
cards.back: No. A separate configured voice VLAN has its own forwarding context; investigate each traffic type and VLAN.

cards.front: PoE source versus powered-device maximums: af, at, bt Type 3 and 4?
cards.back: af: 15.4/12.95 W; at: 30/25.5 W; bt Type 3: up to 60/51 W; Type 4: up to 90/71.3 W. Required capability and cabling conditions must be met.

cards.front: Can configuration add PoE capability to a non-PoE Ethernet port?
cards.back: No. The PSE hardware must support it. Then check per-port capability, PD requirements, cabling, administrative state and shared allocation.

cards.front: On a supporting PoE switch, what do `auto`, `never`, and `max 7000` mean?
cards.back: `auto`: detection/allocation enabled; `never`: PoE disabled; `auto max 7000`: 7 W maximum in the supported milliwatt form. Limits and behavior vary by model.

cards.front: What should you check after a power-denied indication?
cards.back: Requested allocation, remaining shared budget, configured per-port limit, device compatibility and cabling. Do not infer a unique cause from one status label.

cards.front: 370 W budget, ten 6.3 W reservations, then 30 W AP allocations: capacity?
cards.back: 307 W remains; ten 30 W AP allocations fit, leaving 7 W. Check port count separately and use allocations rather than momentary draw.

cards.front: Port-selection starting point for one untagged PC, printer or IoT network?
cards.back: A static access port in the intended VLAN. Add suitable PoE only when required; apply later security features after reviewing the endpoint’s behavior.

cards.front: AP with one untagged management VLAN versus several locally presented VLANs?
cards.back: The first can use an access port. Several VLANs presented on the uplink require compatible trunk tagging. Verify the AP’s actual forwarding design.

cards.front: Which questions guide a virtual-host or appliance uplink?
cards.back: Which VLANs are tagged or untagged? Does it bridge other devices? Is LACP actually configured and supported? Choose the port from these requirements.

commands.note: Verify its state in the VLAN database before assigning endpoints.

commands.task: Name the current VLAN USERS.
commands.note: The name labels the VLAN; its numeric ID is the forwarding identity.

commands.task: Fix this ordinary host-facing port in access mode.
commands.note: The configured mode and access VLAN are separate settings.

commands.task: Assign this access port’s data traffic to existing VLAN 10.
commands.note: Create and verify the intended VLAN before assigning the port.

commands.task: Configure voice VLAN 30 on this phone-facing access port.

commands.task: Display the VLAN database summary and port membership.
commands.note: Use switchport and trunk commands for operational details beyond the summary.

commands.note: Read both VLAN status and actual operational mode.

tickets.title: Voice VLAN missing after a switch configuration change
tickets.scenario: A switchport is intended to provide data VLAN 10 and voice VLAN 30. The attached PC can still reach its same-VLAN peer. Phone power has been verified. You have the following switch evidence; no assumption about the phone’s fallback addressing is required.

exhibits.title: SW1 switchport excerpt
exhibits.text:
Name: Fa0/7
Operational Mode: static access
Access Mode VLAN: 10 (USERS)
Voice VLAN: 30 (Inactive)

exhibits.title: SW1# show vlan brief — relevant user VLANs
exhibits.text:
10 USERS active Fa0/1, Fa0/7
20 PRINTERS active Fa0/3, Fa0/4

tickets.question: Which switch-side correction follows directly from this evidence?
options: Change the PC to a voice-VLAN address
Disable CDP on every host-facing port
Convert the phone port to a routed interface
Restore the intended VLAN 30 in the VLAN database
tickets.explanation: The port references voice VLAN 30, but the VLAN is inactive and missing from the relevant database entries. Restore it, then verify port state and the phone’s separate provisioning and IP services. Data connectivity in VLAN 10 does not establish that voice works.
tickets.fix:
```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# vlan 30
SW1(config-vlan)# name VOICE
SW1(config-vlan)# end
SW1# show vlan brief
SW1# show interfaces fastethernet0/7 switchport
```
Confirm that voice VLAN 30 is active. Then check the phone’s actual VLAN settings and required IP/call services; the VLAN correction alone does not prove registration.

tickets.title: A workstation joins the wrong VLAN after a desk move
tickets.scenario: A workstation at 192.168.10.55/24 moves to a jack patched to SW1 Fa0/18. Its intended peers, including 192.168.10.60/24, remain in VLAN 10. The workstation cannot reach those peers. Its address and cable have been verified; no VLAN translation or alternate link connects the VLANs.

exhibits.title: SW1# show interfaces fa0/18 switchport — excerpt
exhibits.text:
Administrative Mode: static access
Operational Mode: static access
Access Mode VLAN: 20 (PRINTERS)

exhibits.title: Fresh source traffic learned on Fa0/18
exhibits.text:
Vlan  Mac Address     Type     Ports
20    0050.0f77.4a19   DYNAMIC  Fa0/18

tickets.question: What is the cause of the failed same-subnet communication?
options: The workstation’s port is assigned to VLAN 20 instead of VLAN 10
The switch needs the workstation’s IP address as its management address
The peer must be changed to another IPv4 subnet to accept ARP
The physical port must be a trunk to carry one ordinary PC
tickets.explanation: The host addresses place the peers in the same IPv4 subnet, but the actual Layer 2 assignments separate them. The MAC-table entry confirms where fresh source traffic is learned. Restore the documented VLAN assignment and verify the local path.
tickets.fix:
```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/18
SW1(config-if)# description User workstation
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if)# switchport access vlan 10
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show interfaces fastethernet0/18 switchport
```
Generate fresh traffic, verify the MAC entry in VLAN 10, and retest the peer. Save the corrected configuration after verification.

sections.title: Why one link must carry many VLANs
Trunks to APs and virtual hosts

lab.title: Build and diagnose a static trunk
devices: Optional: 2 additional PC-PT for the challenge
lab.intro:
Build two working VLANs across one trunk. Then remove one allowed VLAN and introduce a native mismatch, recording each fault before restoring it. A final disconnected-port exercise applies trunk settings to an AP design.

Use a fresh Packet Tracer file and the devices' CLI tabs, which provide console access independent of the trunk. If the initial configuration dialog appears, answer `no` and press Enter. These instructions use the Packet Tracer 2960 model's `FastEthernet0/1`, `FastEthernet0/2` and `GigabitEthernet0/1` interfaces. Inspect the selected model before wiring. The examples were checked against Cisco documentation; this exact lab has not been executed in Packet Tracer. Treat shown output as representative and use the stated configuration and connectivity checks if the display differs.
lab.topology:
```diagram
{"type":"topology","title":"Lab 10 — Four PCs across one static trunk","caption":"Each VLAN has one PC on each switch. No router or default gateway is needed for same-subnet tests.","nodes":[{"id":"a","kind":"pc","label":"PC-A","sub":"192.168.10.11","x":1,"y":1},{"id":"b","kind":"pc","label":"PC-B","sub":"192.168.20.11","x":1,"y":5},{"id":"s1","kind":"switch","label":"SW1","x":4,"y":3},{"id":"s2","kind":"switch","label":"SW2","x":8,"y":3},{"id":"c","kind":"pc","label":"PC-C","sub":"192.168.10.12","x":11,"y":1},{"id":"d","kind":"pc","label":"PC-D","sub":"192.168.20.12","x":11,"y":5}],"links":[{"from":"a","to":"s1","toLabel":"Fa0/1"},{"from":"b","to":"s1","toLabel":"Fa0/2"},{"from":"s1","to":"s2","fromLabel":"Gi0/1","toLabel":"Gi0/1","label":"trunk 10,20,99"},{"from":"s2","to":"c","fromLabel":"Fa0/1"},{"from":"s2","to":"d","fromLabel":"Fa0/2"}]}
```

| Device / port | Peer / port | VLAN | Address / mask |
|---|---|---|---|
| PC-A FastEthernet0 | SW1 Fa0/1 | 10 | `192.168.10.11 / 255.255.255.0` |
| PC-B FastEthernet0 | SW1 Fa0/2 | 20 | `192.168.20.11 / 255.255.255.0` |
| PC-C FastEthernet0 | SW2 Fa0/1 | 10 | `192.168.10.12 / 255.255.255.0` |
| PC-D FastEthernet0 | SW2 Fa0/2 | 20 | `192.168.20.12 / 255.255.255.0` |
| SW1 Gi0/1 | SW2 Gi0/1 | Trunk 10,20,99; native 99 | No IP address |

Use copper straight-through cables for PC-to-switch links and a copper crossover cable for the switch-to-switch link. Packet Tracer's automatic connection tool is an alternative if it selects the intended ports. Leave every PC's gateway and DNS fields blank. VLAN 99 has no host; it is the agreed unused native VLAN.

steps.title: Cable, address and name the devices
steps.body:
Place and connect the devices as listed. On each PC, open Desktop → IP Configuration, select Static, and enter its address and mask. Open Desktop → Command Prompt and run `ipconfig` to check your entries.

Name the switches from their CLI tabs. A new switch initially displays `Switch>`.

```ios SW1
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname SW1
SW1(config)# end
SW1# show interfaces status
```

```ios SW2
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname SW2
SW2(config)# end
SW2# show interfaces status
```

:::expected
The three cabled ports on each switch should establish a physical connection. Initial amber indicators may reflect spanning-tree startup; allow the simulator to advance before testing. Confirm that the port names match the table. Do not expect the default interswitch connection to carry VLANs 10 and 20 yet.
:::

steps.title: Create the VLANs and access ports
steps.body:
Create the same three VLANs locally on both switches. Explicit access mode removes dependence on default negotiation settings at the PC ports.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# vlan 10
SW1(config-vlan)# name USERS10
SW1(config-vlan)# exit
SW1(config)# vlan 20
SW1(config-vlan)# name USERS20
SW1(config-vlan)# exit
SW1(config)# vlan 99
SW1(config-vlan)# name UNUSED-NATIVE
SW1(config-vlan)# exit
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if)# switchport access vlan 10
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if)# exit
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/2
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if)# switchport access vlan 20
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show vlan brief
```

```ios SW2
SW2# configure terminal
SW2(config)# vlan 10
SW2(config-vlan)# name USERS10
SW2(config-vlan)# exit
SW2(config)# vlan 20
SW2(config-vlan)# name USERS20
SW2(config-vlan)# exit
SW2(config)# vlan 99
SW2(config-vlan)# name UNUSED-NATIVE
SW2(config-vlan)# exit
SW2(config)# interface fastethernet0/1
SW2(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW2(config-if)# switchport access vlan 10
SW2(config-if)# no shutdown
SW2(config-if)# exit
SW2(config)# interface fastethernet0/2
SW2(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW2(config-if)# switchport access vlan 20
SW2(config-if)# no shutdown
SW2(config-if)# end
SW2# show vlan brief
```

:::expected
Each switch lists VLAN 10 with Fa0/1 and VLAN 20 with Fa0/2. VLAN 99 exists and is active, with no PC access port. VLAN names are helpful labels; matching VLAN IDs are what preserve membership across the trunk.
:::

steps.title: Configure the trunk at both ends
steps.body:
Enter the complete settings on SW1, then SW2. Use the console tabs throughout; transient differences while configuring the two ends will not disconnect your console.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# description Trunk-to-SW2-Gi0/1
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk native vlan 99
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,99
SW1(config-if)# switchport nonegotiate
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show interfaces trunk
```

```ios SW2
SW2# configure terminal
SW2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW2(config-if)# description Trunk-to-SW1-Gi0/1
SW2(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
SW2(config-if)# switchport trunk native vlan 99
SW2(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,99
SW2(config-if)# switchport nonegotiate
SW2(config-if)# no shutdown
SW2(config-if)# end
SW2# show interfaces trunk
```

:::expected
Gi0/1 is an operational 802.1Q trunk with native VLAN 99 at both ends. The allowed list is 10,20,99. After startup convergence, those active VLANs should also appear in the forwarding list for this single interswitch path. The 2960 does not need an encapsulation-selection command. If your simulator rejects a command, record the model and rejection; do not substitute dynamic mode for the static trunk.
:::

steps.title: Prove a working baseline
steps.body:
From PC-A's Command Prompt, ping PC-C. From PC-B, ping PC-D. Repeat after initial address resolution if the first echo is lost.

```text PC-A
ping 192.168.10.12
```

```text PC-B
ping 192.168.20.12
```

After generating traffic, inspect both switches:

```ios SW1
SW1# show interfaces trunk
SW1# show mac address-table
```

```ios SW2
SW2# show interfaces trunk
SW2# show mac address-table
```

:::expected
Both same-VLAN pairs communicate. SW1 learns PC-A and PC-B on their local access ports and remote PC-C and PC-D through Gi0/1, in their respective VLANs. A ping from PC-A to 192.168.20.12 is expected to fail: the destination is off subnet and there is no gateway. Record the successful tests and save the Packet Tracer file as `10-trunk-working.pkt` using File → Save As. This is a working checkpoint, not yet a startup-configuration save.
:::

steps.title: Remove VLAN 20 and record the fault
steps.body:
Save a separate working copy as `10-trunk-experiments.pkt`. On SW1 only, remove VLAN 20 from the trunk. Do not repair it until you have collected evidence.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan remove 20
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show interfaces trunk
```

Repeat the two successful pings from step 4 and inspect SW2's trunk list.

```ios SW2
SW2# show interfaces trunk
```

:::expected
PC-A to PC-C still works; PC-B to PC-D fails. SW1's allowed list is now 10,99, while SW2 still allows 10,20,99. The link can remain up and trunking. Record those three facts together: physical operation, a VLAN-specific failure, and different allowed lists. A successful VLAN 10 ping does not prove VLAN 20 is permitted.
:::

steps.title: Restore VLAN 20 without replacing the list
steps.body:
Add VLAN 20 back on SW1. Predict the final list before entering the command.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan add 20
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show interfaces trunk
```

:::expected
The list again contains 10,20,99. After the VLAN is forwarding, both same-VLAN ping pairs succeed. `add 20` preserves VLANs 10 and 99; a bare `allowed vlan 20` would remove them. Check both pairs before moving to the next fault.
:::

steps.title: Introduce a native mismatch and inspect both ends
steps.body:
Change SW2's native VLAN to 999 while leaving SW1 at 99. Create VLAN 999 locally and allow it so its local existence is not an additional fault. This exercise observes a configuration mismatch; no endpoint uses the native VLAN, so a particular ping failure is not required.

```ios SW2
SW2# configure terminal
SW2(config)# vlan 999
SW2(config-vlan)# name TEMP-NATIVE-FAULT
SW2(config-vlan)# exit
SW2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW2(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan add 999
SW2(config-if)# switchport trunk native vlan 999
SW2(config-if)# end
SW2# show interfaces gigabitethernet0/1 switchport
SW2# show interfaces trunk
```

```ios SW1
SW1# show interfaces gigabitethernet0/1 switchport
SW1# show interfaces trunk
```

:::expected
The explicit evidence is native VLAN 99 on SW1 versus 999 on SW2. If CDP warnings or spanning-tree protection appear, record them; their exact behavior is platform dependent. Tagged VLAN tests may continue working or be affected by protective behavior. Explain the fundamental fault: an ordinary untagged frame sent as VLAN 99 by SW1 would be classified into VLAN 999 by SW2. Do not disable spanning tree to make the symptom disappear.
:::

steps.title: Restore the native agreement
steps.body:
Restore the intended native VLAN and allowed list on SW2. Remove the temporary VLAN only after the port no longer uses it.

```ios SW2
SW2# configure terminal
SW2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW2(config-if)# switchport trunk native vlan 99
SW2(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan remove 999
SW2(config-if)# exit
SW2(config)# no vlan 999
SW2(config)# end
SW2# show interfaces trunk
```

:::expected
Both ends again use native VLAN 99 and allow 10,20,99. Allow convergence and repeat both successful baseline pings. If either pair still fails, compare both ends and PC settings with the working checkpoint before adding any new configuration.
:::

steps.title: Prepare a disconnected AP port
steps.body:
Leave SW1 Gi0/2 uncabled and administratively shut down. Configure only the switch side of an AP design: untagged management VLAN 100 and tagged client VLANs 110 and 120. This is a configuration inspection exercise; it does not simulate a FlexConnect AP.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# vlan 100
SW1(config-vlan)# name AP-MANAGEMENT
SW1(config-vlan)# exit
SW1(config)# vlan 110
SW1(config-vlan)# name WIRELESS-STAFF
SW1(config-vlan)# exit
SW1(config)# vlan 120
SW1(config-vlan)# name WIRELESS-GUEST
SW1(config-vlan)# exit
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/2
SW1(config-if)# shutdown
SW1(config-if)# description Prepared-AP-untagged100-tagged110-120
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk native vlan 100
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan 100,110,120
SW1(config-if)# switchport nonegotiate
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show interfaces gigabitethernet0/2 switchport
SW1# show running-config
```

:::expected
The administrative configuration is trunk, native 100, allowed 100,110,120, with DTP disabled. The disconnected, shut port is not an operational trunk. Write down the AP-side requirements: management untagged in 100, staff clients tagged 110, guests tagged 120. None of those VLANs has been extended over Gi0/1 or given a gateway, so the prepared port alone cannot deliver a wireless service. For a virtual host that tags all three VLANs, use an agreed unused native VLAN instead; leave this AP exercise unchanged.
:::

steps.title: Save the restored configuration
steps.body:
Verify the main trunk and both baseline pings once more. Save each switch from privileged EXEC mode, completing the interactive prompt before moving to the next device.

```ios SW1
SW1# copy running-config startup-config
```

If asked `Destination filename [startup-config]?`, press Enter. Wait for the completion message and the `SW1#` prompt.

```ios SW2
SW2# copy running-config startup-config
```

Complete the same destination prompt. Then save the Packet Tracer file as `10-trunk-complete.pkt`.

:::expected
The saved configuration has a working Gi0/1 trunk on each switch and a deliberately shut, disconnected AP preparation port on SW1. No temporary native mismatch remains. Keep your fault observations alongside the file so you can explain why the repairs worked without looking at the commands.
:::

lab.troubleshooting:
- No physical connection: inspect exact ports, cable type, power and administrative shutdown before VLAN settings.
- One VLAN fails across the trunk: compare its access membership, allowed list, local VLAN existence and forwarding at both switches.
- Gi0/2 is missing from operational trunks: expected in step 9 because it is shut and uncabled; inspect its administrative configuration.
- Pings between different VLANs fail: expected in this lab because no inter-VLAN gateway exists.
- First ping partly fails: repeat after ARP resolution and spanning-tree startup. Persistent failure needs investigation.
- A native mismatch produces a different warning or state: rely on the demonstrated settings at both ends, not a memorized message.
lab.challenge:
Add PC-E on SW1 Fa0/3 and PC-F on SW2 Fa0/3 using straight-through cables. Put them in VLAN 30 with `192.168.30.11/24` and `192.168.30.12/24`, leaving gateways blank. Extend VLAN 30 over the existing trunk without removing any current VLAN. Prove all three same-VLAN pairs communicate, then save a separate challenge file.

:::expected Answer key
Create VLAN 30 and assign Fa0/3 on **both** switches. Add 30 to both existing allowed lists; leave native VLAN 99 unchanged.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# vlan 30
SW1(config-vlan)# name USERS30
SW1(config-vlan)# exit
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/3
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if)# switchport access vlan 30
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if)# exit
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan add 30
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show interfaces trunk
```

```ios SW2
SW2# configure terminal
SW2(config)# vlan 30
SW2(config-vlan)# name USERS30
SW2(config-vlan)# exit
SW2(config)# interface fastethernet0/3
SW2(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW2(config-if)# switchport access vlan 30
SW2(config-if)# no shutdown
SW2(config-if)# exit
SW2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW2(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan add 30
SW2(config-if)# end
SW2# show interfaces trunk
```

Both allowed lists become 10,20,30,99. PC-E should ping 192.168.30.12 after convergence; the original VLAN 10 and 20 pairs must still pass. VLAN 30 does not need a router for these same-subnet tests.
:::

exhibit.title: Representative excerpt — SW1# show interfaces trunk
exhibit.text:
Port        Mode         Encapsulation  Status        Native vlan
Gi0/1       on           802.1q         trunking      99

Port        Vlans allowed on trunk
Gi0/1       10,20,30,99

Port        Vlans allowed and active in management domain
Gi0/1       10,20,99

Port        Vlans in spanning tree forwarding state and not pruned
Gi0/1       10,20,99

questions.prompt: VLAN 30 cannot cross SW1's trunk. Which local condition does the exhibit establish?
options: VLAN 30 is allowed but is not active locally.
VLAN 30 is missing from the configured allowed list.
VLAN 30 is active but held out of forwarding by STP.
VLAN 30 is the trunk's untagged native VLAN.
questions.explanation: The first list includes VLAN 30, while the active list does not. Check the local VLAN database for an absent or inactive VLAN before changing the allowed list.

whyWrong.1: VLAN 30 is explicitly present in the allowed list.
whyWrong.2: It is absent from the active list, so the exhibit does not isolate STP as the cause.
whyWrong.3: The configured native VLAN is 99, not 30.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes the VLAN identifier in an ordinary 802.1Q tag?
options: It is 16 bits, providing VLAN IDs 1 through 65534.
It is 12 bits, with usable VLAN identifiers 1 through 4094.
It is 8 bits, providing VLAN IDs 1 through 254.
It is 32 bits, with one separate identifier for each IP subnet.
questions.explanation: The VID is a 12-bit field. Values 0 and 4095 have special or reserved meaning, leaving identifiers 1–4094; individual platforms can impose additional restrictions.

whyWrong.0: The 16-bit TPID identifies the tag format, not the VLAN.
whyWrong.2: The VID has 12 bits, not eight.
whyWrong.3: The complete tag is 32 bits; VLAN identification is only part of it.

questions.prompt: Two operational Cisco switch ports are explicitly set to dynamic auto, with no other trunk-forcing configuration. What does their DTP interaction normally produce?
options: A trunk because each side advertises willingness to trunk.
An error-disabled link caused by a negotiation conflict.
A nontrunking link because neither side initiates trunk negotiation.
A trunk carrying only the common native VLAN.
questions.explanation: Dynamic auto is a passive negotiation mode. Auto paired with auto does not initiate the exchange needed to make the link a trunk.

whyWrong.0: Willingness alone is insufficient when both sides are passive.
whyWrong.1: This combination is a normal nontrunking outcome, not an error-disable trigger.
whyWrong.3: A single native VLAN is not the result of a partly negotiated trunk.

questions.prompt: A compatible Cisco peer is in dynamic auto with DTP enabled. Which two local modes can make that link become a trunk through DTP? (Choose two.)
options: Static access
Dynamic auto
Static trunk with DTP enabled
Dynamic desirable
Static access with VLAN 99
questions.explanation: Dynamic desirable actively negotiates. Static trunk with DTP running advertises a trunking state that a compatible auto peer can accept; manual trunk mode on both ends remains the clearer operational design.

whyWrong.0: Static access keeps the local port nontrunking.
whyWrong.1: Two auto ports are both passive.
whyWrong.4: Changing an access VLAN does not change the port into a trunk.

exhibit.title: Configuration excerpts from the two trunk ports
exhibit.text:
SW1 Gi0/1:
 switchport mode trunk
 switchport trunk native vlan 99
 switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,99,999

SW2 Gi0/1:
 switchport mode trunk
 switchport trunk native vlan 999
 switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,99,999

questions.prompt: The intended unused native VLAN is 99 at both ends. Which single change restores that agreement?
options: On SW1, change its allowed list to VLAN 999 only.
On SW2, add VLAN 99 as an access VLAN.
On SW1, change its switchport mode to dynamic auto.
On SW2, set switchport trunk native vlan 99.
questions.explanation: Native membership is configured per trunk port. Restoring SW2's native value to 99 makes its treatment of ordinary untagged data agree with SW1 and the stated design.

whyWrong.0: An allowed-list change does not set the intended native VLAN.
whyWrong.1: An access-VLAN command does not select the operational trunk's native VLAN.
whyWrong.2: Changing negotiation mode does not repair native VLAN agreement.

questions.prompt: Gi0/1 currently allows VLANs 10,20,99. Which command adds VLAN 30 while preserving that list?
options: switchport trunk allowed vlan add 30
switchport trunk allowed vlan 30
switchport access vlan 30
switchport trunk native vlan 30
questions.explanation: The add keyword modifies the existing list. A bare allowed-vlan list replaces the current selection, potentially interrupting existing users.

whyWrong.1: This replaces the list with only VLAN 30.
whyWrong.2: This selects access-port membership, not the trunk's allowed list.
whyWrong.3: This changes the native VLAN and does not add VLAN 30 to the allowed list.

exhibit.title: Representative older-platform configuration rejection
exhibit.text:
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
Command rejected: An interface whose trunk encapsulation is "Auto" can not be configured to "trunk" mode.

questions.prompt: On this older interface, command help confirms an encapsulation selector is supported. Which command addresses the displayed rejection before retrying static trunk mode?
options: switchport trunk native vlan 1
switchport trunk encapsulation dot1q
switchport nonegotiate
switchport access vlan 10
questions.explanation: An interface that supports an encapsulation choice may require a fixed encapsulation before static trunk mode. This is a platform-specific selector; a 2960's 802.1Q-only interface does not need it.

whyWrong.0: The native VLAN does not select the trunk encapsulation.
whyWrong.2: Suppressing DTP does not choose the encapsulation required by this rejection.
whyWrong.3: Access membership does not resolve an encapsulation choice.

questions.prompt: A trunk uses default native-VLAN treatment with native VLAN 99. It receives an ordinary untagged data frame. How does the switch classify that frame?
options: Into VLAN 1 because the frame has no explicit VID.
Into whichever VLAN last sent a frame on the link.
Into VLAN 99 according to the receiving trunk's native setting.
Into every VLAN in the trunk's allowed list.
questions.explanation: Under the specified default behavior, the native VLAN supplies the membership for ordinary untagged data. The receiving port's configuration determines that classification.

whyWrong.0: VLAN 1 is a default native value, not an override of a configured native VLAN.
whyWrong.1: Classification does not depend on the previous frame.
whyWrong.3: A frame is not assigned simultaneously to all allowed VLANs.

exhibit.title: Configured trunk settings
exhibit.text:
SW1 Gi0/1: mode trunk; native 99; allowed 10,99
SW2 Gi0/1: mode trunk; native 99; allowed 10,20,99

questions.prompt: VLANs 10 and 20 exist and are active on both switches, and the PC access assignments are correct. VLAN 10 works across the link, but VLAN 20 does not. What does this configuration show?
options: SW1's native VLAN must be changed to 20.
SW2 needs an IP address on the physical trunk.
The two switches must use dynamic desirable.
SW1's trunk omits VLAN 20 from its allowed list.
questions.explanation: The two ends do not both permit VLAN 20. Add 20 to SW1's existing list, then verify forwarding and repeat the VLAN 20 traffic test.

whyWrong.0: Tagged VLAN 20 does not need to become native.
whyWrong.1: A Layer 2 trunk does not need an IP address to extend the VLAN.
whyWrong.2: Both ports are already static trunks; negotiation is not the missing element.

questions.prompt: Which two statements correctly describe switchport nonegotiate on a supported statically configured trunk? (Choose two.)
options: It suppresses DTP messages sent by the port.
It removes 802.1Q tags from all transmitted frames.
It requires both ends to use the same access VLAN.
It changes the native VLAN to VLAN 1.
It leaves the static trunk able to carry tagged VLAN traffic.
questions.explanation: The command controls DTP transmission, not the data-plane tag format. A static trunk can continue carrying its configured VLANs without negotiating them with a peer.

whyWrong.1: Disabling DTP does not disable 802.1Q tagging.
whyWrong.2: A trunk's allowed and native VLAN settings matter; matching access VLANs is not this command's requirement.
whyWrong.3: The native VLAN remains whatever the trunk configuration specifies.

questions.prompt: A standard untagged Ethernet frame is 1,518 bytes from destination MAC through FCS. What is its length after one four-byte 802.1Q tag is added, with the payload unchanged?
options: 1,522 bytes
1,514 bytes
1,526 bytes
1,500 bytes
questions.explanation: Adding one four-byte tag produces 1,522 bytes. The IP payload does not become four bytes larger, and the count given excludes preamble and start delimiter.

whyWrong.1: The tag adds bytes instead of removing four.
whyWrong.2: That adds eight bytes rather than the single tag's four.
whyWrong.3: 1,500 bytes describes the usual maximum payload in this example, not the complete frame.

questions.prompt: An ordinary PC should use only untagged VLAN 10 traffic and must not negotiate a trunk. Which port configuration fits?
options: switchport mode dynamic desirable; switchport access vlan 10
switchport mode access; switchport access vlan 10
switchport mode trunk; switchport trunk native vlan 10
switchport mode dynamic auto; switchport trunk allowed vlan 10
questions.explanation: Static access mode defines a nontrunking port, and the access-VLAN command assigns ordinary data to VLAN 10. This matches the PC's single untagged network requirement.

whyWrong.0: Desirable actively attempts to form a trunk.
whyWrong.2: A trunk remains a trunk even if its native VLAN matches the PC's intended VLAN.
whyWrong.3: Dynamic auto leaves trunk negotiation possible with a suitable peer.

questions.prompt: An engineer removes VLAN 1 from a Catalyst trunk's allowed list. Which conclusion is justified?
options: All Cisco discovery and negotiation messages stop on the link.
The trunk's native VLAN automatically becomes the lowest allowed VLAN.
VLAN 1 user forwarding is restricted, but some link-control protocols can still operate.
The trunk becomes an access port in its configured native VLAN.
questions.explanation: The allowed list controls VLAN forwarding eligibility. Cisco documents continued operation of several link-control protocols when VLAN 1 is removed; use each feature's own configuration to control it.

whyWrong.0: Removing a user VLAN does not disable every control protocol.
whyWrong.1: Native VLAN selection is a separate setting.
whyWrong.3: An allowed-list modification does not change static trunk mode.

exhibit.title: AP requirements and switch port configuration
exhibit.text:
AP: management untagged in VLAN 100; staff tagged 110; guests tagged 120.
Switch interface:
 switchport mode trunk
 switchport trunk native vlan 99
 switchport trunk allowed vlan 100,110,120
 switchport nonegotiate

questions.prompt: The AP requires untagged management VLAN 100 and tagged local client VLANs 110 and 120. Which switch-side change fixes the shown configuration?
options: Set the port to access VLAN 100.
Remove VLAN 100 from the allowed list.
Set the native VLAN to 110.
Set the native VLAN to 100.
questions.explanation: The port already permits all required VLANs, but ordinary untagged management traffic must be classified into VLAN 100. Client VLANs 110 and 120 remain tagged.

whyWrong.0: One access VLAN would not carry the two specified tagged client VLANs.
whyWrong.1: Removing management VLAN eligibility would not correct its classification.
whyWrong.2: That would classify untagged management traffic into the staff client VLAN.

exhibit.title: Virtual-host uplink requirements supplied by its administrator
exhibit.text:
Management interface: VLAN 100 tagged
VM group A: VLAN 110 tagged
VM group B: VLAN 120 tagged
No service uses untagged traffic; unused native VLAN 999 agreed.

questions.prompt: A virtual host expects management VLAN 100 and VM VLANs 110 and 120 to remain tagged on its uplink. With default native treatment, which matching switch profile avoids untagging a required VLAN?
options: Allow 100,110,120 and use an agreed unused native VLAN 999.
Allow 100,110,120 and make management VLAN 100 native.
Use access VLAN 110 because the virtual switch handles all VLANs.
Allow only VLAN 999 and make management VLAN 100 native.
questions.explanation: The host explicitly expects all three required VLANs tagged. Keeping the native VLAN outside that set preserves their tagging under the specified default behavior.

whyWrong.1: Management frames in the native VLAN would leave the switch untagged.
whyWrong.2: A single access VLAN cannot transport the required three tagged networks.
whyWrong.3: The required VLANs are absent from that allowed list.

questions.prompt: A firewall's Ethernet interface is configured with logical interfaces for tagged VLANs 10 and 20. It does not use DTP. What should you configure on the connected switch port?
options: Dynamic auto with access VLAN 10.
A static trunk permitting VLANs 10 and 20, with matching native treatment.
An access port in VLAN 20 with an additional allowed list.
A routed switch port with no switchport and no IP address.
questions.explanation: The peer requires multiple tagged VLANs, so the switch must provide a compatible static trunk. The appliance's documented tagging requirements determine the profile; its product category alone does not.

whyWrong.0: Auto relies on negotiation that this peer does not provide.
whyWrong.2: An allowed list does not turn an access port into a trunk.
whyWrong.3: A routed port is not the Layer 2 trunk required by the peer's tagged logical interfaces.

cards.front: Size and position of an ordinary 802.1Q tag?
cards.back: 4 bytes, after the source MAC and before the original EtherType field.

cards.front: What identifies an ordinary 802.1Q tag in the Ethernet frame?
cards.back: The 16-bit TPID value 0x8100.

cards.front: Sizes of the PCP, DEI and VID fields?
cards.back: PCP: 3 bits (values 0–7); DEI: 1 bit; VID: 12 bits.

cards.front: Usable VLAN identifiers in the 12-bit VID field?
cards.back: 1–4094. VID 0 supports priority tagging without a VLAN ID; 4095 is reserved. Platforms can impose additional restrictions.

cards.front: Length of a 1,518-byte Ethernet frame after one tag is added?
cards.back: 1,522 bytes, counting destination MAC through FCS. The payload stays the same.

cards.front: Default native VLAN in the Catalyst examples, and how to select VLAN 99?
cards.back: VLAN 1. Under the trunk interface, use switchport trunk native vlan 99.

cards.front: Under default native treatment, how is ordinary untagged trunk data classified?
cards.back: Into the receiving port's native VLAN. Ordinary data from that native VLAN is sent untagged.

cards.front: What is the most direct evidence of a native VLAN mismatch?
cards.back: The two trunk ports show different native VLAN IDs. Warnings or protective states may also appear; exact behavior depends on the platform.

cards.front: Default allowed VLAN selection in the cited Catalyst guides?
cards.back: All supported VLANs are initially allowed. Verify the actual list; permission alone does not mean each VLAN exists or forwards.

cards.front: allowed vlan 30 versus allowed vlan add 30?
cards.back: The first replaces the list with 30. The second preserves the current list and adds 30.

cards.front: What do the three VLAN lists in show interfaces trunk distinguish?
cards.back: Configured allowed VLANs; VLANs allowed and active locally; VLANs forwarding in spanning tree and not pruned.

cards.front: What is the documented DTP default in the cited Catalyst 2960 guide?
cards.back: Dynamic auto. Verify the actual interface; do not assume that default for every Catalyst model.

cards.front: DTP outcomes: auto with auto, and desirable with auto?
cards.back: With compatible operational DTP peers: auto/auto stays nontrunking; desirable/auto can form a trunk.

cards.front: Purpose of switchport nonegotiate on a static trunk?
cards.back: Suppress DTP messages while retaining the static trunk and its configured 802.1Q traffic.

cards.front: 802.1Q versus DTP?
cards.back: 802.1Q identifies VLANs in frames. DTP negotiates trunk formation on supporting Cisco switch ports.

cards.front: Does removing VLAN 1 from a trunk disable every link-control protocol?
cards.back: No. Cisco documents continued operation of several control protocols; configure each feature explicitly.

cards.front: Where do you inspect a configured port absent from show interfaces trunk?
cards.back: Use `show interfaces <port> switchport` to compare administrative and operational settings, then check link and shutdown state.

cards.front: When does an AP's wired connection need multiple VLANs?
cards.back: When its actual forwarding design carries multiple local VLANs over that link, such as locally switched client VLANs. Multiple SSIDs alone do not prove it.

cards.front: An AP sends management untagged in VLAN 100. What must its trunk peer match?
cards.back: The peer must classify that untagged traffic into VLAN 100 and allow the required management/client VLANs.

cards.front: A host expects all required VLANs tagged. Should one of them be native by default?
cards.back: No. With default untagged-native treatment, use an agreed unused native VLAN so required VLANs retain their tags.

commands.task: Make the selected switch port a static trunk.
commands.note: Configure the peer compatibly; this command does not create or route VLANs.

commands.task: Set the selected trunk's native VLAN to the agreed VLAN 99.
commands.note: Under default treatment, ordinary VLAN 99 data is untagged.

commands.task: Replace the selected trunk's allowed list with exactly 10,20,99.
commands.note: This is a replacement. Use the explicit approved list, particularly on a live trunk.

commands.task: Add VLAN 30 to the selected trunk without removing existing allowed VLANs.
commands.note: Verify the resulting list and the other end.

commands.task: Remove only VLAN 20 from the selected trunk's allowed list.
commands.note: This intentionally interrupts VLAN 20 over this port; the lab observes it before recovery.

commands.task: Suppress DTP messages on the selected statically configured trunk.
commands.note: This leaves the static 802.1Q trunk configured.

commands.task: On this older interface whose help offers a trunk encapsulation selector, explicitly choose 802.1Q.
commands.note: A 2960's 802.1Q-only interface does not need this platform-specific selector.

commands.task: On an isolated exercise trunk, restore permission for all supported VLANs.
commands.note: This expands eligibility; it does not create every VLAN or force forwarding. Keep approved explicit lists on the main lab trunk.

commands.task: List operational trunks and their native, allowed, active and forwarding VLAN information.
commands.note: Inspect both ends; a local display cannot prove the peer's configuration.

commands.task: Inspect administrative and operational switchport settings for GigabitEthernet0/1.
commands.note: Useful when a configured port is absent from the operational trunk list.

commands.task: Keep the selected PC-facing port nontrunking; its intended access VLAN is already set.
commands.note: Static access mode does not depend on DTP to establish the intended role.

commands.task: Display local VLAN existence, activity and ordinary access-port membership.
commands.note: Use this when a VLAN is allowed on a trunk but absent from its active list.

tickets.title: Existing VLANs fail after VLAN 30 is added
tickets.scenario: SW1 Gi0/1 connects to SW2 Gi0/1. Each switch has one correctly addressed PC in VLAN 10 (192.168.10.0/24), VLAN 20 (192.168.20.0/24) and VLAN 30 (192.168.30.0/24). Same-VLAN communication across the link worked for VLANs 10 and 20 before a change intended to add VLAN 30. Now only the new VLAN 30 pair communicates across it. Both switch consoles are available. The following excerpts are representative teaching evidence.

exhibits.title: SW1 trunk summary
exhibits.text:
Port        Mode   Encapsulation   Status      Native vlan
Gi0/1       on     802.1q          trunking    99

Vlans allowed on trunk: 30
Vlans allowed and active: 30
Vlans forwarding and not pruned: 30

exhibits.title: Recorded configuration of SW1 Gi0/1
exhibits.text:
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 switchport mode trunk
 switchport trunk native vlan 99
 switchport trunk allowed vlan 30
 switchport nonegotiate

exhibits.title: Checks completed on both switches
exhibits.text:
VLANs 10,20,30,99 exist and are active locally.
PC access-port assignments and /24 addresses match the design.
SW2 Gi0/1 is trunking, native 99, with 10,20,30,99 allowed and forwarding.

tickets.question: Which diagnosis fits all the evidence?
options: Creating VLAN 30 replaced VLAN 20 in the VLAN database.
The allowed list on SW1 was replaced by 30 instead of extended.
The link changed into an access connection in VLAN 30.
The native VLAN on SW1 changed from 99 to 30.
tickets.explanation: SW1 remains an operational trunk with native VLAN 99. Its allowed list contains only 30, even though the original VLANs still exist. That selective filter explains why the new pair works and the old same-VLAN pairs fail.
tickets.fix:
Use SW1's console to restore the required VLANs while retaining 30.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan add 10,20,99
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show interfaces trunk
```

The allowed list should become 10,20,30,99. Verify local activity and forwarding, then repeat each same-VLAN pair's test in both directions. Do not assume the list alone proves host connectivity. Save after verification and correct the change instructions to distinguish replacement from add.

tickets.title: Native VLAN agreement is missing on a replacement switch
tickets.scenario: The intended native VLAN between SW1 Gi0/1 and SW2 Gi0/1 is 99. A test PC on each switch uses an access port in VLAN 99, with addresses 10.99.0.11/24 and 10.99.0.12/24 and no gateway. Their same-subnet test stopped working after SW2 was replaced. Separate tagged VLAN 10 tests still work in this reported incident. The displays below are representative configuration evidence, not a guarantee of identical protection behavior on every platform.

exhibits.title: SW1 Gi0/1 configuration
exhibits.text:
switchport mode trunk
switchport trunk native vlan 99
switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,99
switchport nonegotiate

exhibits.title: Replacement SW2 Gi0/1 configuration
exhibits.text:
switchport mode trunk
switchport trunk native vlan 1
switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,99
switchport nonegotiate

exhibits.title: Completed local checks
exhibits.text:
Both physical uplink ports are connected and configured as trunks.
VLAN 99 exists and is active on each switch.
The two test PC ports are static access VLAN 99 and linked.
PC addresses and masks match the stated 10.99.0.0/24 design.

tickets.question: What configuration defect must be repaired?
options: The test PCs need default gateways for their same-subnet traffic.
The switches must negotiate DTP before native frames can pass.
The replacement switch's native VLAN is 1 instead of the agreed 99.
VLAN 99 must be removed from both allowed lists.
tickets.explanation: The native settings differ explicitly. Under default treatment, an ordinary untagged frame sent from SW1 as VLAN 99 is not classified as VLAN 99 by SW2. Native mismatches may also trigger spanning-tree protection; neither a working tagged VLAN nor the absence of a particular warning makes this configuration correct.
tickets.fix:
Restore the documented native VLAN on the replacement switch through its console.

```ios SW2
SW2# configure terminal
SW2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW2(config-if)# switchport trunk native vlan 99
SW2(config-if)# end
SW2# show interfaces trunk
```

Compare both native and allowed settings, allow any protective state to recover, and repeat the VLAN 99 and VLAN 10 tests. If a state remains nonforwarding, inspect its evidence rather than disabling spanning tree. Update the replacement template and save the verified configuration.

lab.title: Build two inter-VLAN gateway designs
devices: Part B: 1 × 3650 multilayer switch, 1 × 2911 router, 2 × PC-PT
Optional: 1 additional PC-PT for the challenge
lab.intro:
Use two separate Packet Tracer files to compare router-on-a-stick with SVI routing. In each design you will verify the baseline, introduce one clearly defined fault, observe it, and restore it. The second file also includes a directly connected routed-port test.

Open device CLI tabs for console access. Answer `no` to an initial configuration dialog if offered. Interface names below match the selected Packet Tracer models; inspect yours before cabling. These instructions and representative outcomes were reviewed against Cisco documentation, but this exact lab has not been executed in Packet Tracer. Command support, output formatting and state transitions can vary by simulator release. A 2960 is used as a Layer 2 switch here; the SVI-routing portion specifically requires a multilayer model.
