steps.title: Build Part A and configure the switch
steps.body:
Create a fresh file. Cable the four devices as listed and enter the PC settings through Desktop → IP Configuration → Static. Check each PC with `ipconfig` in its Command Prompt. Configure SW1:

```ios SW1
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname SW1
SW1(config)# vlan 10
SW1(config-vlan)# name USERS10
SW1(config-vlan)# exit
SW1(config)# vlan 20
SW1(config-vlan)# name USERS20
SW1(config-vlan)# exit
SW1(config)# vlan 99
SW1(config-vlan)# name UNUSED-NATIVE
SW1(config-vlan)# exit
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if)# switchport access vlan 10
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if)# exit
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/2
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if)# switchport access vlan 20
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if)# exit
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk native vlan 99
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,99
SW1(config-if)# switchport nonegotiate
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show vlan brief
SW1# show interfaces gigabitethernet0/1 switchport
```

:::expected
The PC ports belong to VLANs 10 and 20. Gi0/1 has the intended administrative trunk configuration. Its physical connection may remain down until R1 Gi0/0 is enabled in step 2. Hosts cannot reach gateways that have not yet been configured.
:::

steps.title: Configure R1's gateway subinterfaces
steps.body:
Enable the parent, then configure the two addressed subinterfaces and explicit unused native subinterface. The encapsulation command must identify the correct VLAN; matching the subinterface number is only a naming convention.

```ios R1
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R1
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# no ip address
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0.10
R1(config-subif)# encapsulation dot1Q 10
R1(config-subif)# ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-subif)# no shutdown
R1(config-subif)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0.20
R1(config-subif)# encapsulation dot1Q 20
R1(config-subif)# ip address 192.168.20.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-subif)# no shutdown
R1(config-subif)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0.99
R1(config-subif)# encapsulation dot1Q 99 native
R1(config-subif)# no shutdown
R1(config-subif)# end
R1# show ip interface brief
R1# show ip route
```

:::expected
Once the link is operational, Gi0/0 and its enabled subinterfaces should be up/up. The parent and native subinterface remain unassigned, intentionally. R1 has connected routes for 192.168.10.0/24 and 192.168.20.0/24. Modern IOS also shows local /32 routes for its own gateway addresses; do not diagnose an older simulator's lack of separate L entries as a fault.
:::

steps.title: Verify both local gateways and routed traffic
steps.body:
First test PC-A to its own gateway, then PC-B to its own gateway. Finally test both directions between PCs.

```text PC-A
ping 192.168.10.1
ping 192.168.20.12
```

```text PC-B
ping 192.168.20.1
ping 192.168.10.11
```

Allow spanning-tree startup and ARP resolution; repeat an initial partially successful test. Then collect:

```ios SW1
SW1# show interfaces trunk
SW1# show mac address-table
```

```ios R1
R1# show ip arp
R1# show ip route
```

:::expected
All four tests succeed after resolution. R1's ARP information associates PC-A with its VLAN 10 interface and PC-B with its VLAN 20 interface. In Packet Tracer Simulation mode, filter for ARP and ICMP and repeat a ping to inspect the addresses; cached ARP entries may mean no new ARP appears. Identify the destination MAC on each side of R1 and the unchanged destination IP of the request. Save the file as `11A-router-stick-working.pkt` before introducing a fault.
:::

steps.title: Break one VLAN's tag mapping
steps.body:
Use File → Save As to create `11A-router-stick-experiment.pkt`. On R1 only, change subinterface .20 to expect tagged VLAN 200. Do not change SW1 or repair the router yet.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0.20
R1(config-subif)# encapsulation dot1Q 200
R1(config-subif)# end
R1# show ip interface brief
R1# show running-config
```

Repeat the gateway and cross-VLAN tests from step 3.

:::expected
PC-A can still reach 192.168.10.1, but PC-B cannot reach 192.168.20.1 and inter-VLAN traffic fails. The subinterface may remain up/up because the parent link is operational. The decisive mismatch is encapsulation VLAN 200 on R1 versus the client's VLAN 20 on SW1, not the .20 suffix. Record the running configuration and test results before recovery. If the selected image rejects changing encapsulation, record the rejection rather than claiming the intended fault was installed.
:::

steps.title: Restore the correct encapsulation
steps.body:
Restore VLAN 20 on the affected subinterface.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0.20
R1(config-subif)# encapsulation dot1Q 20
R1(config-subif)# end
R1# show running-config
R1# show ip route
```

:::expected
The encapsulation again matches VLAN 20. Repeat all four pings from step 3; they should succeed after any needed resolution. Confirm that VLAN 10 was not altered. The repair changes the actual VLAN mapping, not the subinterface's name.
:::

steps.title: Save Part A
steps.body:
Save each restored running configuration. Complete the destination prompt before moving to the other device.

```ios SW1
SW1# copy running-config startup-config
```

Press Enter at `Destination filename [startup-config]?` if offered and wait for completion.

```ios R1
R1# copy running-config startup-config
```

Complete the same prompt, then save the Packet Tracer file as `11A-router-stick-complete.pkt`.

:::expected
Part A is a separate, working file with correct tags and successful tests. Keep it closed or set aside while creating Part B; do not connect the two designs or reuse the configured router in the next topology.
:::

steps.title: Build Part B with SVIs but no forwarding
steps.body:
Create a **new** file containing a 3650 multilayer switch named DSW1, two fresh PCs, and a fresh 2911 router named R2. For now leave R2 uncabled. On a 3650 model that requires a power supply in the Physical tab, install the available compatible power supply and power it on before using the CLI.

| Part B device / port | Peer / port | Address / mask | Gateway |
|---|---|---|---|
| PC-A FastEthernet0 | DSW1 Gi1/0/1 | `192.168.10.11 / 255.255.255.0` | `192.168.10.1` |
| PC-B FastEthernet0 | DSW1 Gi1/0/2 | `192.168.20.12 / 255.255.255.0` | `192.168.20.1` |
| DSW1 Vlan10 | Logical VLAN 10 gateway | `192.168.10.1 / 255.255.255.0` | — |
| DSW1 Vlan20 | Logical VLAN 20 gateway | `192.168.20.1 / 255.255.255.0` | — |
| DSW1 Gi1/0/24, connected in step 11 | R2 Gi0/0 | `10.0.12.2 / 255.255.255.252` | — |
| R2 Gi0/0, connected in step 11 | DSW1 Gi1/0/24 | `10.0.12.1 / 255.255.255.252` | — |

Use straight-through cables from each PC to its switch port. Enter the PC addresses, masks and gateways. Explicitly disable IPv4 forwarding temporarily so the next step demonstrates what `ip routing` changes.

```ios DSW1
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname DSW1
DSW1(config)# no ip routing
DSW1(config)# vlan 10
DSW1(config-vlan)# name USERS10
DSW1(config-vlan)# exit
DSW1(config)# vlan 20
DSW1(config-vlan)# name USERS20
DSW1(config-vlan)# exit
DSW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet1/0/1
DSW1(config-if)# switchport mode access
DSW1(config-if)# switchport access vlan 10
DSW1(config-if)# no shutdown
DSW1(config-if)# exit
DSW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet1/0/2
DSW1(config-if)# switchport mode access
DSW1(config-if)# switchport access vlan 20
DSW1(config-if)# no shutdown
DSW1(config-if)# exit
DSW1(config)# interface vlan 10
DSW1(config-if)# ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0
DSW1(config-if)# no shutdown
DSW1(config-if)# exit
DSW1(config)# interface vlan 20
DSW1(config-if)# ip address 192.168.20.1 255.255.255.0
DSW1(config-if)# no shutdown
DSW1(config-if)# end
DSW1# show ip interface brief
DSW1# show vlan brief
DSW1# show ip route
```

:::expected
With both PC links up and forwarding, the two SVIs should be operational. Each PC should reach its own local SVI address. PC-A to PC-B must not be treated as a working routed service while IPv4 forwarding is disabled. This is the distinction being tested: assigning an IP address to the switch does not itself enable it to route user packets. Record actual model behavior if your simulator differs from the documented feature behavior.
:::

steps.title: Enable and verify SVI routing
steps.body:
Enable IPv4 routing, then repeat the own-gateway and cross-VLAN tests from step 3.

```ios DSW1
DSW1# configure terminal
DSW1(config)# ip routing
DSW1(config)# end
DSW1# show ip route
DSW1# show ip interface brief
DSW1# show ip arp
```

:::expected
The two connected subnet routes are present and PC-A and PC-B communicate in both directions. No router trunk, static route or default route is needed between these directly connected VLANs. Save `11B-svi-working.pkt` as the working checkpoint. The uncabled R2 is not involved.
:::

steps.title: Remove VLAN 20's only active member link
steps.body:
Save a separate `11B-svi-experiment.pkt`. Shut DSW1 Gi1/0/2, the only connected Layer 2 port in VLAN 20. Do not shut the SVI or delete the VLAN; isolating one change makes the observation useful.

```ios DSW1
DSW1# configure terminal
DSW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet1/0/2
DSW1(config-if)# shutdown
DSW1(config-if)# end
DSW1# show interfaces status
DSW1# show vlan brief
DSW1# show ip interface brief
DSW1# show ip route
```

:::expected
PC-B loses its link. Under normal SVI autostate behavior, Vlan20's line protocol goes down because there is no eligible forwarding member port, and its connected route is withdrawn. VLAN 20 still exists and the SVI is not administratively shut down. PC-A should still reach its own VLAN 10 gateway. Record actual status fields; do not insist that every image use the same up/down versus down/down wording.
:::

steps.title: Restore the access link and route
steps.body:
Re-enable the port, allow its startup forwarding transition, then recheck the SVI and routes.

```ios DSW1
DSW1# configure terminal
DSW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet1/0/2
DSW1(config-if)# no shutdown
DSW1(config-if)# end
DSW1# show ip interface brief
DSW1# show ip route
```

:::expected
Vlan20 becomes operational and its connected route returns once its member port is forwarding. Repeat PC-A to PC-B and the reverse ping. Both should work. Applying `no shutdown` to Vlan20 would not have fixed the physical member port that you actually shut down.
:::

steps.title: Add a routed connection to R2
steps.body:
Connect DSW1 Gi1/0/24 to fresh R2 Gi0/0 using a copper straight-through cable. Configure the two ends in separate CLI tabs. This step tests only those directly connected link addresses.

```ios DSW1
DSW1# configure terminal
DSW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet1/0/24
DSW1(config-if)# description Routed-link-to-R2-Gi0/0
DSW1(config-if)# no switchport
DSW1(config-if)# ip address 10.0.12.2 255.255.255.252
DSW1(config-if)# no shutdown
DSW1(config-if)# end
DSW1# show interfaces gigabitethernet1/0/24 switchport
```

```ios R2
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R2
R2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R2(config-if)# ip address 10.0.12.1 255.255.255.252
R2(config-if)# no shutdown
R2(config-if)# end
R2# ping 10.0.12.2
```

```ios DSW1
DSW1# ping 10.0.12.1
DSW1# show ip route
```

:::expected
The switch reports that Gi1/0/24 is not a switchport, and its table includes connected network 10.0.12.0/30. The two link-address pings succeed. R2 has no routes to the PC subnets in this exercise, so a PC-to-R2 ping is not an expected success test: R2 would need a return route. Do not add an unrelated default gateway command to DSW1 to conceal that missing routing design.
:::

steps.title: Save Part B and compare the designs
steps.body:
Save the restored configurations one device at a time.

```ios DSW1
DSW1# copy running-config startup-config
```

Press Enter at the destination filename prompt if offered and wait for completion.

```ios R2
R2# copy running-config startup-config
```

Complete that prompt and save `11B-svi-complete.pkt`. Write two short packet walks for PC-A to PC-B: one through R1's subinterfaces in Part A, the other through DSW1's SVIs in Part B.

:::expected
Both designs use the same host subnets and gateway addresses, and both route between VLANs. Part A sends tagged traffic over a router trunk; Part B makes the routing decision within DSW1. Part B's routed port is a separate Layer 3 connection, not the mechanism that joins its local VLANs.
:::

lab.troubleshooting:
- Own gateway fails on router-on-a-stick: check the PC mask/access VLAN, switch trunk, router parent state, subinterface tag and IP address.
- Subinterface is up/up but the gateway is unreachable: check tag mapping and delivery; up/up alone is insufficient.
- SVI protocol is down: verify the VLAN exists, the SVI is enabled and an eligible member port is linked and forwarding.
- Local SVI replies but cross-VLAN traffic fails: verify `ip routing`, both connected routes and both PC gateways.
- Routed-port neighbor ping fails: compare masks and addresses, check `no switchport` and administrative state at both ends.
- Some commands are absent in a simulator: record the exact model and limitation. Use the lesson's documented evidence for interpretation rather than treating a simulated omission as an IOS rule.
lab.challenge:
In a copy of Part B, add PC-C on unused DSW1 Gi1/0/3 using a straight-through cable. Create VLAN 30 and gateway `192.168.30.1/24`. Give PC-C `192.168.30.11/24` and that gateway. Prove that all three PCs communicate in both directions while the routed-port neighbor test still passes. Do not add a trunk or a default route.

:::expected Answer key
The new VLAN needs its Layer 2 membership, an operational SVI, and the correct host settings. IPv4 routing is already enabled from step 8.

```ios DSW1
DSW1# configure terminal
DSW1(config)# vlan 30
DSW1(config-vlan)# name USERS30
DSW1(config-vlan)# exit
DSW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet1/0/3
DSW1(config-if)# switchport mode access
DSW1(config-if)# switchport access vlan 30
DSW1(config-if)# no shutdown
DSW1(config-if)# exit
DSW1(config)# interface vlan 30
DSW1(config-if)# ip address 192.168.30.1 255.255.255.0
DSW1(config-if)# no shutdown
DSW1(config-if)# end
DSW1# show ip interface brief
DSW1# show ip route
```

Once PC-C's port forwards, Vlan30 is operational and 192.168.30.0/24 appears as connected. PC-C should ping 192.168.10.11 and 192.168.20.12, and both existing PCs should ping 192.168.30.11. DSW1 should still ping 10.0.12.1. R2 still lacks return routes to the PC subnets, so do not use PC-to-R2 success as this challenge's completion criterion.
:::

questions.prompt: The router rejects an IP address on a new Ethernet subinterface because VLAN encapsulation has not been configured. The intended VLAN is 30. What should you do?
options: Enable the switch's VLAN 30 SVI and leave the router unchanged.
Assign the same IP address to the physical parent interface.
Enter encapsulation dot1Q 30, then re-enter the rejected address.
Rename the subinterface from .30 to .300 and repeat the address.
questions.explanation: Configure the subinterface's VLAN encapsulation before its address. An address command that was rejected is not queued for later application; enter it again after correcting the prerequisite.

whyWrong.0: This would change the gateway design rather than complete the router subinterface.
whyWrong.1: The intended service uses tagged VLAN 30 on a subinterface, not untagged parent addressing.
whyWrong.3: The suffix does not configure a VLAN association.

questions.prompt: R1 routes an echo request from PC-A (192.168.10.11) to PC-B (192.168.20.12), without NAT. What is in the outgoing Ethernet frame toward PC-B?
options: Source MAC R1's VLAN 20 interface; destination MAC PC-B; destination IP 192.168.20.12.
Source MAC PC-A; destination MAC PC-B; destination IP 192.168.20.12.
Source MAC R1's VLAN 20 interface; destination MAC PC-B; destination IP 192.168.20.1.
Source MAC PC-A; destination MAC R1's VLAN 10 interface; destination IP 192.168.20.12.
questions.explanation: R1 builds a new Ethernet frame for the outgoing VLAN. Ordinary routing keeps the packet's destination IP while changing the Layer 2 addressing for the next link.

whyWrong.1: PC-A's original Ethernet source is not retained across the routed boundary.
whyWrong.2: The destination IP remains PC-B's address, not R1's outgoing address.
whyWrong.3: This describes the incoming frame toward R1, not the outgoing one.

questions.prompt: With ordinary Catalyst SVI autostate behavior and the SVI administratively enabled, which two conditions are required for Vlan20 to operate? (Choose two.)
options: IPv4 routing is enabled globally.
VLAN 20 exists and is active locally.
At least one other switch is connected by a trunk.
An eligible Layer 2 port in VLAN 20 is linked and STP forwarding.
A default route points toward an external router.
questions.explanation: The VLAN must exist and have an eligible forwarding member link. Neither IPv4 forwarding nor an external route determines whether an ordinary management SVI can be operational.

whyWrong.0: An SVI can be operational for switch management while IPv4 routing is disabled.
whyWrong.2: A connected forwarding access port is sufficient; a trunk is not mandatory.
whyWrong.4: Default routing is unrelated to the local VLAN's SVI line-state prerequisites.

show vlan brief:

questions.prompt: VLAN 20 is active, Vlan20 is not shut down, and Gi1/0/2 is its only member port. What best explains the unusable SVI?
options: The SVI needs the same IP address as Gi1/0/2.
The SVI needs a default route to VLAN 10.
The VLAN must be changed to the native VLAN.
Its only eligible Layer 2 member port is down.
questions.explanation: The supplied evidence shows no linked forwarding port in VLAN 20. Restore the intended member link, then allow forwarding convergence and verify the SVI and connected route.

whyWrong.0: An access port does not take the SVI's IP address.
whyWrong.1: A default route cannot bring a local VLAN member link up.
whyWrong.2: An SVI can serve a VLAN with an ordinary access port; native status is not required.

questions.prompt: A 2960 port toward a router-on-a-stick is explicitly dynamic auto. The router uses Ethernet subinterfaces and sends no DTP. What is the correct switch-side remedy?
options: Assign the router's gateway address to the switch's access port.
Configure a static trunk with the required VLANs and native treatment.
Enable dynamic auto on each router subinterface.
Change the switch's access VLAN to every routed VLAN in turn.
questions.explanation: This peer will not negotiate the trunk. Configure the switch port explicitly as a trunk and match the subinterfaces' VLAN requirements.

whyWrong.0: A Layer 2 switchport address is not the missing trunk configuration.
whyWrong.2: The stated router subinterfaces do not provide DTP negotiation.
whyWrong.3: One access-VLAN assignment cannot carry multiple tagged VLANs.

exhibit.title: Representative host-mode routing display
exhibit.text:
Default gateway is not set

Host               Gateway           Last Use    Total Uses  Interface
ICMP redirect cache is empty

questions.prompt: SW2 is intentionally operating without IP routing. Its management SVI is 192.168.99.10/24, and reachable router 192.168.99.1 has the necessary remote routes. Remote SSH packets arrive, but SW2 lacks a return next hop. Which command supplies it?
options: ip default-gateway 192.168.99.1
interface vlan 99 followed by shutdown
switchport trunk native vlan 99
questions.explanation: A non-routing switch uses ip default-gateway for its own traffic to remote subnets. The prompt establishes the other connectivity and routing prerequisites, isolating this missing host-style next hop.

whyWrong.1: A routing-table static default is not the host-mode gateway setting being used here.
whyWrong.2: Shutting the management interface would remove working local connectivity.
whyWrong.3: Native tagging does not supply a next hop for the switch's IP replies.

questions.prompt: On a supporting multilayer switch, which sequence converts Gi1/0/24 from Layer 2 to an enabled physical Layer 3 interface at 10.0.12.2/30?
options: interface vlan 24 → ip address 10.0.12.2 255.255.255.252 → no shutdown
interface gi1/0/24 → switchport mode trunk → ip address 10.0.12.2 255.255.255.252
interface gi1/0/24 → no switchport → ip address 10.0.12.2 255.255.255.252 → no shutdown
interface gi1/0/24 → switchport access vlan 24 → ip default-gateway 10.0.12.2
questions.explanation: No switchport changes the supported physical interface's role. It can then receive an IP address directly and be enabled with no shutdown.

whyWrong.0: That configures a logical SVI, not the physical port.
whyWrong.1: Trunk mode remains Layer 2 and is not converted by adding an address command.
whyWrong.3: Access membership and a host-mode gateway do not create a routed port.

exhibit.text:

GigabitEthernet0/0.10    192.168.10.1    YES manual  up                    up
GigabitEthernet0/0.20    192.168.20.1    YES manual  administratively down down
GigabitEthernet0/1       unassigned      YES unset   administratively down down

questions.prompt: VLAN 10 works. The switch trunk carries VLANs 10 and 20, and R1's running configuration has correct encapsulation and addresses. Which change directly addresses the displayed VLAN 20 fault?
options: Add an IP address to the parent Gi0/0.
Enable unused Gi0/1 as a return interface.
Replace the VLAN 20 address with the VLAN 10 gateway.
Enter no shutdown under Gi0/0.20.
questions.explanation: The subinterface is explicitly administratively down. Enable that subinterface, then verify its connected route and VLAN 20 gateway reachability.

whyWrong.0: An unaddressed parent is intentional in this subinterface design.
whyWrong.1: The VLANs use Gi0/0; an unused physical port is not their return path.
whyWrong.2: The address is correct and changing it would introduce another fault.

questions.prompt: Which two statements about ip default-gateway on a Cisco switch are correct? (Choose two.)
options: It supplies a host-style next hop while IP routing is disabled.
It installs an S* default route in the IPv4 routing table.
It supports the switch's own traffic toward other subnets.
It enables forwarding of user packets between SVIs.
It must be configured separately under every SVI.
questions.explanation: The command is a global host-style setting used when the switch is not routing. A switch with IP routing enabled uses its routing table instead; directly connected VLANs do not require a default route.

whyWrong.1: The host-mode gateway command is not a static routing-table entry.
whyWrong.3: Enabling user packet forwarding requires the relevant routing functionality.
whyWrong.4: The command is global, not a per-SVI configuration.

questions.prompt: A switch must provide gateways for several local VLANs without sending all inter-VLAN traffic over a separate router trunk. Which design meets that requirement?
options: A router-on-a-stick with one shared trunk.
One access uplink with all hosts configured in different VLANs.
A Layer 2 trunk with every VLAN allowed.
SVIs on a multilayer switch with IPv4 routing enabled.
questions.explanation: SVIs can provide the local VLAN gateways while the multilayer switch routes internally. Actual forwarding capacity and supported features still depend on the selected platform.

whyWrong.0: This design explicitly depends on the separate shared router trunk.
whyWrong.1: An access uplink does not supply gateways for several VLANs.
whyWrong.2: A trunk extends VLANs but does not perform the required routing.

exhibit.title: Representative abbreviated interface status
exhibit.text:
Port       Status       Vlan     Duplex  Speed
Gi1/0/1    connected    10       a-full  a-100
Gi1/0/2    connected    20       a-full  a-100

questions.prompt: What does the routed entry for Gi1/0/24 establish?
options: It is a Layer 3 physical interface rather than a VLAN switchport.
It is a trunk that carries every VLAN with an SVI.
It is an access port in VLAN 24 with a gateway.
It is a VLAN 1 port forwarding only management traffic.
questions.explanation: The port is operating as a routed interface, normally configured with no switchport on this platform. It can use Ethernet and ARP for its IP neighbor while remaining outside Layer 2 VLAN membership.

whyWrong.1: A trunk is a Layer 2 switchport and would be identified as a trunk.
whyWrong.2: An access port would show its VLAN membership.
whyWrong.3: A routed port does not become a management access port in VLAN 1.

questions.prompt: Vlan30 is configured with an address and no shutdown, but is not operational. The complete local VLAN list does not contain VLAN 30, while the intended access port remains assigned to VLAN 30. What should be corrected first?
options: Enable a default route for the SVI.
Create and activate VLAN 30 in the VLAN database.
Change the SVI's suffix to the access-port number.
Enable DTP on the access port.
questions.explanation: The missing VLAN database entry is established by the supplied evidence. Restore VLAN 30, then check that an eligible port is connected and forwarding; the SVI state alone would not uniquely prove this cause.

whyWrong.0: A remote route cannot restore a missing local VLAN.
whyWrong.2: SVI identification follows the VLAN, not the physical port number.
whyWrong.3: Trunk negotiation is not the missing VLAN database entry.

questions.prompt: SW1 sends ordinary native VLAN 99 traffic untagged to R1. Which subinterface command explicitly associates that untagged traffic with VLAN 99 on the router?
options: encapsulation dot1Q 99
switchport trunk native vlan 99
encapsulation dot1Q 99 native
switchport access vlan 99
questions.explanation: The native keyword selects the subinterface's handling of untagged native-VLAN traffic. Whether that VLAN also needs a gateway IP address depends on the design.

whyWrong.0: Without native, the subinterface identifies tagged VLAN 99 traffic.
whyWrong.1: This is a switchport command rather than a router subinterface command.
whyWrong.3: An access-port VLAN command does not configure router subinterface encapsulation.

questions.prompt: PC-A (192.168.10.11/24, gateway 192.168.10.1) starts a ping to 192.168.20.12. Its ARP cache is empty and no other traffic is involved. What is the destination MAC of its initial ARP request?
options: The gateway's MAC, already inferred from its IP address.
PC-B's MAC, obtained from the remote destination IP.
The local switch port's burned-in MAC address.
The broadcast address ffff.ffff.ffff.
questions.explanation: PC-A needs the local gateway's MAC for this off-subnet destination. It first broadcasts an ARP request within its VLAN; after the reply, it can send the echo request to the gateway's MAC.

whyWrong.0: An empty ARP cache means the gateway's MAC must first be resolved.
whyWrong.1: An IP address does not reveal a remote Ethernet MAC.
whyWrong.2: Ordinary switching does not make the local switch port the IP next hop.

exhibit.text:
Vlan10   192.168.10.1   YES manual   up   up
Vlan20   192.168.20.1   YES manual   up   up

show ip route:
Default gateway is not set

questions.prompt: DSW1 has operational, correctly addressed SVIs for VLANs 10 and 20. Both hosts reach their own SVI, but the complete configuration contains no ip routing and the display is host mode. What is missing for forwarding between the two connected subnets?
options: A static default route toward the other SVI.
The global ip routing command.
An address on each Layer 2 access port.
A trunk connecting the two SVIs internally.
questions.explanation: The switch has local IP interfaces but is not forwarding IPv4 between them. Enable IP routing, then verify the connected routes and host-to-host tests.

whyWrong.0: A default route does not replace enabling forwarding and is unnecessary between these connected VLANs.
whyWrong.2: The gateway addresses belong on the SVIs, not the access ports.
whyWrong.3: SVIs do not require an internal trunk cable.

questions.prompt: DSW1 routes connected VLANs 10 and 20 successfully. It has no default route. Which conclusion follows?
options: The VLAN traffic is being switched without a Layer 3 decision.
The hosts must use the routed uplink address as their gateway.
Connected routes are sufficient for those destinations; other destinations need matching routes.
The absence of a default route is hidden by the SVI MAC addresses.
questions.explanation: Each destination subnet already has a connected route, so a default route is unnecessary for that exchange. A default or more specific route may be needed for other destinations, with a valid return path as well.

whyWrong.0: Cross-subnet communication still involves Layer 3 forwarding.
whyWrong.1: Each host uses a reachable gateway in its own subnet.
whyWrong.3: MAC addressing does not replace routing-table selection.

cards.front: When does a host use its default gateway?
cards.back: For a destination outside its local subnet, when the gateway is its selected next hop. It resolves the gateway's local MAC.

cards.front: What changes when an IPv4 packet is routed between two Ethernet VLANs?
cards.back: The router builds a new Ethernet frame and reduces TTL, updating the IPv4 checksum. Source and destination IPs remain unchanged in ordinary routing without NAT.

cards.front: Initial ARP destination when the gateway MAC is unknown?
cards.back: Broadcast ffff.ffff.ffff within the local VLAN, asking for the gateway's MAC. The later data frame uses the resolved gateway MAC.

cards.front: What is router-on-a-stick?
cards.back: Multiple VLAN gateway subinterfaces share one physical router link to a switch trunk.

cards.front: What binds Gi0/0.10 to VLAN 10?
cards.back: encapsulation dot1Q 10. The .10 suffix is a useful naming convention, not the VLAN binding.

cards.front: An address was rejected because subinterface encapsulation was missing. Next step?
cards.back: Configure the correct encapsulation, then enter the IP address again. A rejected command is not saved for later.

cards.front: How does a router subinterface explicitly handle untagged native VLAN 99?
cards.back: encapsulation dot1Q 99 native. Add an IP address only if that VLAN needs a routed service.

cards.front: Why statically trunk the switch port toward ordinary router subinterfaces?
cards.back: Those router subinterfaces do not negotiate DTP. Configure compatible trunk, allowed and native settings directly.

cards.front: Must the parent have an IP address in the lesson's router-on-a-stick design?
cards.back: No; its subinterfaces hold the gateway addresses. The parent must be enabled and physically operational.

cards.front: What is an SVI?
cards.back: A switch virtual interface represents a VLAN at Layer 3, providing switch management addressing or a gateway on a routing switch.

cards.front: What enables IPv4 forwarding between SVIs on a supporting switch?
cards.back: The global ip routing command. Operational SVIs alone do not prove that forwarding is enabled.

cards.front: Ordinary SVI autostate prerequisites?
cards.back: The VLAN exists and is active; the SVI is enabled; at least one eligible Layer 2 member is linked and STP forwarding.

cards.front: An enabled SVI has protocol down. What must you check?
cards.back: VLAN existence/activity and eligible member-port forwarding. Nonadministrative up/down and down/down states do not uniquely identify one cause across platforms.

cards.front: How do you convert a supported physical switch port to Layer 3?
cards.back: Use no switchport, assign the IP address and mask, and enable the interface with no shutdown.

cards.front: Does a routed Ethernet port still use MAC addresses and ARP?
cards.back: Yes. It has its own IP link but is not an access/trunk VLAN switchport. Verify Switchport: Disabled.

cards.front: ip default-gateway versus routing-table routes?
cards.back: The gateway setting supports a non-routing switch's own remote traffic. With IP routing enabled, destination-matching routes apply; a default route is not always needed.

cards.front: What do C and L represent in modern IOS routing output?
cards.back: C is a connected subnet; L is a local host route to the device's own address. Older images may omit separate IPv4 L entries.

cards.front: Where should an IP address go when a physical port is still a Layer 2 switchport?
cards.back: Use the appropriate SVI, or first convert a supported port with no switchport if a physical routed link is intended.

cards.front: Main connection trade-off: router-on-a-stick versus SVIs?
cards.back: Router-on-a-stick shares a separate router trunk across VLANs. SVIs route within a multilayer switch. Features and capacity depend on the platform.

cards.front: What does one physical router interface per VLAN require?
cards.back: A separate addressed router interface and an access link for each VLAN. It consumes more ports than a shared router trunk.

commands.task: Enter the Gi0/0 subinterface conventionally numbered for VLAN 20.
commands.note: The suffix is a name; configure encapsulation separately.

commands.task: Associate the current router subinterface with tagged VLAN 10.
commands.note: Enter encapsulation before assigning the subinterface's gateway address.

commands.task: Associate the current subinterface with untagged native VLAN 99.
commands.note: Match the intended untagged VLAN at the switch; an address is needed only for a routed service.

commands.task: Enable IPv4 packet forwarding on this supporting multilayer switch.
commands.note: Then verify connected routes, local gateway tests and traffic between hosts.

commands.task: Create or enter the logical SVI for VLAN 10.
commands.note: Explicitly create VLAN 10 separately with vlan 10, then verify a forwarding member port.

commands.task: Convert the current supported physical switch port from Layer 2 to Layer 3.
commands.note: Address and enable it after conversion; this is different from configuring an SVI.

commands.task: Set next hop 192.168.99.1 for this non-routing switch's own remote IP traffic.
commands.note: The next hop must be reachable in its connected management subnet.

commands.task: Show interface addresses and status/protocol states in a concise table.
commands.note: State is a starting point, not proof that tags and remote addressing agree.

commands.task: Inspect the detailed state and hardware address of the VLAN 10 SVI.
commands.note: Use the device's actual MAC and state rather than assuming all logical interfaces differ.

commands.task: Display directly connected IPv4 routing entries.
commands.note: Check the connected destination subnets. Use the full routing display when comparing connected and local entries.

commands.task: Verify the switchport role of physical GigabitEthernet1/0/24.
commands.note: Switchport: Disabled identifies the routed-port role in this example.

commands.task: Check the switch's operational trunk VLAN information toward the router.
commands.note: A missing router-facing trunk requires inspection of its mode, link and administrative state.

tickets.title: VLAN 30 loses its gateway after a cleanup
tickets.scenario: DSW1 is a 3650 multilayer switch with IPv4 routing enabled. It serves VLANs 10,20,30 through SVIs. PC-C is 192.168.30.11/24, gateway 192.168.30.1, on Gi1/0/5. After a VLAN cleanup, PC-C cannot reach its gateway. VLANs 10 and 20 still route successfully. Read the representative excerpts and the complete VLAN-presence check before deciding why Vlan30 is unavailable.

exhibits.title: DSW1 SVI configuration excerpt
exhibits.text:
interface Vlan30
 ip address 192.168.30.1 255.255.255.0
 no shutdown

exhibits.title: Completed VLAN and port checks
exhibits.text:
show vlan brief: VLANs 1,10,20 and the model's reserved VLANs appear; VLAN 30 is absent from the complete list.
Gi1/0/5 remains configured with switchport mode access and switchport access vlan 30.
Its switchport display identifies Access Mode VLAN: 30 (Inactive).

exhibits.title: Representative abbreviated IP interface display
exhibits.text:
Vlan10   192.168.10.1   YES manual   up     up
Vlan20   192.168.20.1   YES manual   up     up
Vlan30   192.168.30.1   YES manual   down   down

tickets.question: Which root cause is established by the evidence?
options: The Vlan30 SVI was administratively shut down.
VLAN 30 was removed from the local VLAN database.
PC-C's correct /24 mask needs to become /16.
IPv4 routing was disabled on every SVI.
tickets.explanation: The complete VLAN check proves that VLAN 30 is missing, while its SVI and access assignment remain configured. The interface's nonadministrative down state supports the investigation but does not uniquely prove the cause by itself. Restore the missing VLAN and then verify its forwarding membership.
tickets.fix:
Re-create VLAN 30 without changing the already-correct SVI address.

```ios DSW1
DSW1# configure terminal
DSW1(config)# vlan 30
DSW1(config-vlan)# name USERS30
DSW1(config-vlan)# end
DSW1# show vlan brief
DSW1# show interfaces status
DSW1# show ip interface brief
DSW1# show ip route
```

Confirm Gi1/0/5 is linked and forwarding in VLAN 30. Vlan30 should become operational and its connected route should return. Test PC-C to 192.168.30.1, then to a known host in another routed VLAN, and verify the reply path. Save after tests pass.

tickets.title: A new subinterface has no gateway configuration
tickets.scenario: R1 is a 2911 router-on-a-stick connected to SW1's static trunk. PC-C uses VLAN 30, address 192.168.30.11/24 and gateway 192.168.30.1. VLANs 10 and 20 work, but PC-C cannot reach its new gateway. The change record says a subinterface was added; the running configuration is the authoritative evidence of what actually exists.

exhibits.title: Representative excerpt — R1# show ip interface brief
exhibits.text:
GigabitEthernet0/0       unassigned      YES unset   up   up
GigabitEthernet0/0.10    192.168.10.1    YES manual  up   up
GigabitEthernet0/0.20    192.168.20.1    YES manual  up   up
GigabitEthernet0/0.30    unassigned      YES unset   up   up

exhibits.title: Complete configuration of the new subinterface
exhibits.text:
interface GigabitEthernet0/0.30
!
No encapsulation or IP address is configured under this subinterface.

exhibits.title: SW1 verification worksheet
exhibits.text:
VLAN 30 exists and is active.
PC-C's connected access port belongs to VLAN 30.
The router-facing Gi0/1 trunk is operational.
VLAN 30 is allowed, active and forwarding on Gi0/1.
PC-C's address, /24 mask and gateway match the stated design.

tickets.question: Why is the router not providing the VLAN 30 gateway?
options: The new subinterface lacks both VLAN encapsulation and its gateway IP address.
SW1's allowed list excludes VLAN 30 despite its forwarding display.
The suffix .30 automatically selects VLAN 300 on a 2911.
The gateway must be placed on the unaddressed physical parent.
tickets.explanation: Creating a subinterface name does not supply its VLAN mapping or address. Up/up can follow the operational parent without proving a usable gateway service. The evidence does not prove whether a paste failed or commands were omitted; it proves the two required settings are absent.
tickets.fix:
Complete the new subinterface, setting encapsulation before addressing.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0.30
R1(config-subif)# encapsulation dot1Q 30
R1(config-subif)# ip address 192.168.30.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-subif)# no shutdown
R1(config-subif)# end
R1# show ip interface brief
R1# show ip route
```

Confirm the address is assigned, the interface is operational, and 192.168.30.0/24 appears as connected. Test PC-C's own gateway and a known reachable host in another VLAN. Older images may not show a separate local /32 entry; gateway and forwarding verification matter more than reproducing an exact display.

sections.title: Read local and remote fields correctly
Verify state, lifetime, and reachability separately

lab.title: Discover neighbors and correct a link inventory
lab.intro:
Build one small management LAN, collect neighbor evidence from both switches, and correct a deliberately inaccurate connection record. Then create one-way LLDP visibility and restore it without changing IP addressing.

This procedure was checked against the address plan and Cisco documentation, but was not executed in Packet Tracer during this review. Output is representative. Some Packet Tracer images omit LLDP or individual show commands. Complete CDP on the specified models; if LLDP is unavailable, use the clearly identified paper observations in Steps 6–9 or a supporting Catalyst image in CML/hardware. Do not treat a missing simulator command as a cabling fault.
lab.topology:
```diagram
{ "type":"topology", "title":"Discovery across three network devices", "caption":"Record local and remote ports separately; all links use the default VLAN 1 for this isolated exercise.", "nodes":[{"id":"P","kind":"pc","label":"PC-A","sub":"192.168.12.100/24","x":1,"y":3},{"id":"S1","kind":"switch","label":"SW1","x":4,"y":3},{"id":"S2","kind":"switch","label":"SW2","x":8,"y":1},{"id":"R","kind":"router","label":"R1","x":8,"y":5}], "links":[{"from":"P","to":"S1","fromLabel":"Fa0","toLabel":"Fa0/1"},{"from":"S1","to":"S2","fromLabel":"Gi0/1","toLabel":"Gi0/2"},{"from":"S1","to":"R","fromLabel":"Gi0/2","toLabel":"Gi0/0"}] }
```

| Connection | Cable |
|---|---|
| PC-A Fa0 → SW1 Fa0/1 | Copper straight-through |
| SW1 Gi0/1 → SW2 Gi0/2 | Copper crossover, or automatic selection with ports verified |
| SW1 Gi0/2 → R1 Gi0/0 | Copper straight-through |

| Device/interface | Address/mask | Gateway |
|---|---|---|
| SW1 VLAN 1 | 192.168.12.11 / 255.255.255.0 | 192.168.12.1 |
| SW2 VLAN 1 | 192.168.12.12 / 255.255.255.0 | 192.168.12.1 |
| R1 Gi0/0 | 192.168.12.1 / 255.255.255.0 | None required for this connected LAN |
| PC-A Fa0 | 192.168.12.100 / 255.255.255.0 | 192.168.12.1 |

These management addresses support a separate IP test; discovery itself does not require them. The default VLAN is used only to keep this lab focused. Do not copy it as an organization's management-VLAN policy.

steps.title: Build, name, and address the devices
steps.body:
Start a new project, select the exact models, and connect the listed ports. Decline initial configuration dialogs if shown. Type commands after the prompts.

```ios SW1
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname SW1
SW1(config)# cdp run
SW1(config)# interface range gigabitethernet0/1 - 2
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport access vlan 1
SW1(config-if-range)# cdp enable
SW1(config-if-range)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if-range)# exit
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if)# switchport access vlan 1
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if)# exit
SW1(config)# interface vlan 1
SW1(config-if)# ip address 192.168.12.11 255.255.255.0
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if)# exit
SW1(config)# ip default-gateway 192.168.12.1
SW1(config)# end
```

```ios SW2
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname SW2
SW2(config)# cdp run
SW2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/2
SW2(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW2(config-if)# switchport access vlan 1
SW2(config-if)# cdp enable
SW2(config-if)# no shutdown
SW2(config-if)# exit
SW2(config)# interface vlan 1
SW2(config-if)# ip address 192.168.12.12 255.255.255.0
SW2(config-if)# no shutdown
SW2(config-if)# exit
SW2(config)# ip default-gateway 192.168.12.1
SW2(config)# end
```

```ios R1
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R1
R1(config)# cdp run
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ip address 192.168.12.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# cdp enable
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
```

Set PC-A using **Desktop → IP Configuration → Static**, including the exact mask and gateway in the table.

:::expected
After the ports become operational, each switch SVI can become up/up because VLAN 1 has active forwarding members. R1 Gi0/0 is enabled. Check `show ip interface brief` on each network device and PC-A's `ipconfig` before continuing.
:::

steps.title: Read the CDP tables from both ends
steps.body:
Run the following on SW1, then run the same three show commands on SW2 and R1 at their privileged prompts.

```ios SW1
SW1# show cdp
SW1# show cdp interface
SW1# show cdp neighbors
```

:::expected
Allow periodic advertisements to arrive. SW1 should identify SW2 on its Gi0/1, remote Gi0/2, and R1 on its Gi0/2, remote Gi0/0. SW2 should identify SW1 on its Gi0/2, remote Gi0/1. R1 should identify SW1 on its Gi0/0, remote Gi0/2. PC-A is not expected to advertise CDP. If a row is absent, check both device-wide and interface CDP state before changing addresses.
:::

steps.title: Correct an inaccurate drawing
steps.body:
Treat this as the inherited record: **SW1 Gi0/1 → R1 Gi0/0**, and **SW1 Gi0/2 → SW2 Gi0/1**. Create a correction table with the old claim, your observation, the reverse observation, and the proposed connection. Keep the command's device name attached to each local interface.

:::expected
Both records are wrong. The supported corrections are **SW1 Gi0/2 → R1 Gi0/0** and **SW1 Gi0/1 → SW2 Gi0/2**. Your table includes evidence from both ends, rather than merely copying the workspace drawing.
:::

steps.title: Separate advertised addresses from reachability
steps.body:
Inspect detailed records, then test the management address independently.

```ios SW1
SW1# show cdp neighbors detail
SW1# ping 192.168.12.12
```

From PC-A, ping `192.168.12.11`, `.12`, and `.1` using the full addresses. Record whether the detailed record advertises the address you configured; optional fields and address selection may vary.

:::expected
With the given address plan and operational VLAN, repeated pings should receive replies. That is additional IP evidence. Discovery could still work if you introduced a management-address error, so the neighbor table is not the reason the ping succeeds.
:::

steps.title: Inspect the configured timers and cached lifetime
steps.body:
```ios SW1
SW1# show cdp
SW1# show cdp neighbors
```

Repeat the neighbor view after a short interval and record changes. Also inspect `show cdp` on SW2 to identify the timer and holdtime SW2 advertises. Do not change timers merely to make the observed number match the lesson.

:::expected
The referenced defaults are 60-second advertisements and 180-second holdtime. Remaining holdtime commonly decreases and refreshes when an advertisement arrives. A displayed value is not an exact packet timestamp; the relevant lifetime comes from the neighbor. Clearing SW1's local CDP table, if used for an additional experiment, does not instantly force SW2 to advertise again.
:::

steps.title: Enable LLDP explicitly and compare identities
steps.body:
Use these commands where supported. If `lldp run` is unavailable, read the subsequent observations as a paper exercise instead of entering guessed alternatives.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# lldp run
SW1(config)# lldp timer 30
SW1(config)# lldp holdtime 120
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# lldp transmit
SW1(config-if)# lldp receive
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show lldp
SW1# show lldp neighbors detail
```

```ios SW2
SW2# configure terminal
SW2(config)# lldp run
SW2(config)# lldp timer 30
SW2(config)# lldp holdtime 120
SW2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/2
SW2(config-if)# lldp transmit
SW2(config-if)# lldp receive
SW2(config-if)# end
SW2# show lldp
SW2# show lldp neighbors detail
```

:::expected
After advertisements arrive, each switch learns the other. A representative SW1 observation is **system name SW2, local Gi0/1, remote port Gi0/2, bridge capability B**. CDP may use capability S for the same switching function. LLDP IDs can differ in format; use the actual advertised IDs and descriptions. These stated observations are also the starting facts for the paper fallback.
:::

steps.title: Create one-way LLDP visibility
steps.body:
Stop only SW2's advertisements toward SW1. Leave SW2 receiving and leave all settings on SW1 unchanged.

```ios SW2
SW2# configure terminal
SW2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/2
SW2(config-if)# no lldp transmit
SW2(config-if)# end
SW2# show lldp interface gigabitethernet0/2
SW2# show lldp neighbors
```

On SW1, inspect `show lldp neighbors detail` and `show cdp neighbors` over time. If a detail/interface form is unsupported, inspect the running configuration for the configured directions.

:::expected
SW1 can no longer refresh its LLDP entry for SW2; it disappears after any retained lifetime, or earlier if a shutdown advertisement is processed. SW2 can continue learning SW1. CDP remains independently configured. In the paper exercise, write these directional conclusions and identify which one setting caused them; do not report an unobserved simulator result. Record the fault before Step 9 restores it.
:::

steps.title: Limit discovery on the ordinary PC port
steps.body:
This lab PC has no phone or policy dependency. Disable unnecessary discovery on SW1 Fa0/1. Omit only the LLDP lines if that feature is unavailable in the image.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# no cdp enable
SW1(config-if)# no lldp transmit
SW1(config-if)# no lldp receive
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show cdp interface
```

:::expected
The policy affects the PC-facing port, not the interswitch uplink. PC-A can still ping the management addresses; removing discovery does not shut the port or implement a traffic-filtering policy. Record this intentional final difference from the original default configuration.
:::

steps.title: Restore the uplink and save the verified map
steps.body:
```ios SW2
SW2# configure terminal
SW2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/2
SW2(config-if)# lldp transmit
SW2(config-if)# end
SW2# show lldp neighbors
SW2# copy running-config startup-config
```

Complete SW2's save prompt: if `Destination filename [startup-config]?` appears, press Enter and wait for the `SW2#` prompt. On a supporting image, verify fresh two-way LLDP learning. In the paper fallback, state why reenabling SW2 transmission restores SW1's ability to refresh the entry. Save SW1 and R1 with `copy running-config startup-config`, accepting the destination filename if prompted. Save the project as `12-discovery-complete.pkt` and keep your corrected link table with it.

:::expected
Both uplink directions are restored, the PC-port policy remains intentional, and the corrected map identifies both endpoints of each link. The record distinguishes actual CDP/LLDP observations from any paper-only LLDP work.
:::

lab.troubleshooting:
- Missing neighbor: check link state, device-wide process, local receive policy, remote transmit policy, and cache lifetime.
- LLDP absent but CDP present: inspect LLDP settings independently; CDP does not enable it.
- Neighbor present but management ping fails: check SVI state, VLAN, address, mask, and source reachability.
- Unexpected port ID: compare from the far device and inspect the cable before changing documentation.
- Unsupported command: use the documented full-table/configuration alternative, or the marked paper workflow; do not claim the simulator executed it.
lab.challenge:
In a separate copy, move only SW2's cable end from Gi0/2 to Gi0/1. Configure the new SW2 interface as an enabled VLAN 1 access port with CDP, LLDP transmit, and LLDP receive where supported. Predict which fields change in both switches' neighbor tables. Verify them, revise the link record, and save this variation separately.

:::expected
The physical connection becomes **SW1 Gi0/1 → SW2 Gi0/1**. In SW1's row for SW2, the local port remains Gi0/1 and the remote port changes to Gi0/1. In SW2's row, the local port changes to Gi0/1 and the remote port remains SW1 Gi0/1. Management IPs do not need to change because both ports still serve VLAN 1. Allow stale entries to clear and fresh advertisements to arrive before calling the map verified.
:::

exhibit.title: Representative SW1# show cdp neighbors
exhibit.text:
Device ID  Local Intrfce  Holdtme  Capability  Platform    Port ID
SW2        Gig 0/1       172      S I         WS-C2960-   Gig 0/2
R1         Gig 0/2       156      R S I       CISCO2911   Gig 0/0

questions.prompt: Which link record correctly interprets both rows?
options: SW1 Gi0/2 → SW2 Gi0/1; SW1 Gi0/0 → R1 Gi0/2
SW1 Gi0/1 → SW2 Gi0/1; SW1 Gi0/2 → R1 Gi0/2
SW1 Gi0/1 → SW2 Gi0/2; SW1 Gi0/2 → R1 Gi0/0
SW2 Gi0/1 → R1 Gi0/0; SW1 Gi0/2 has no neighbor
questions.explanation: The command ran on SW1. Local Intrfce belongs to SW1; Port ID is the interface advertised by the neighbor in that row. Record both device names and both ports.

whyWrong.0: This reverses local and remote port ownership and invents an SW1 Gi0/0 observation.
whyWrong.1: The remote ports are Gi0/2 on SW2 and Gi0/0 on R1, not copies of the local port numbers.
whyWrong.3: The table reports two SW1 adjacencies; it does not report a link between SW2 and R1.

questions.prompt: On the Cisco IOS CDP implementation documented in this chapter, the timers have not been changed. What are the default advertisement interval and advertised holdtime?
options: 60 seconds and 180 seconds
30 seconds and 120 seconds
60 seconds and 120 seconds
180 seconds and 60 seconds
questions.explanation: The referenced IOS guide specifies an advertisement every 60 seconds and an advertised holdtime of 180 seconds. A receiver ages its entry when advertisements stop; these values can be configured.

whyWrong.1: These are the LLDP interval and holdtime documented for the chapter’s Catalyst platform.
whyWrong.2: The first number is the CDP default interval, but the default CDP holdtime is 180 seconds.
whyWrong.3: This reverses the interval and holdtime. A timer value is not a count of neighbors.

questions.prompt: A Catalyst 2960 uses the documented LLDP default timer values. Which row is correct?
options: Interval 60 s; holdtime 180 s; reinitialization 2 s
Interval 30 s; holdtime 90 s; reinitialization 2 s
Interval 30 s; holdtime 120 s; reinitialization 5 s
Interval 30 s; holdtime 120 s; reinitialization 2 s
questions.explanation: The referenced Catalyst 2960 guide lists 30 seconds for advertisements, 120 seconds for holdtime, and 2 seconds for reinitialization. Use show lldp to check the actual device; global and interface enablement are separate configuration questions.

whyWrong.0: 60/180 is the CDP timer pair in the chapter’s IOS reference.
whyWrong.1: The documented LLDP holdtime is 120 seconds, not 90.
whyWrong.2: The documented reinitialization delay is 2 seconds, not 5.

exhibit.title: Representative SW1# show lldp neighbors
exhibit.text:
Capability codes: (R) Router, (B) Bridge, (T) Telephone, (S) Station
Device ID   Local Intf  Hold-time  Capability  Port ID
DIST1       Gi0/24     120        B           Te1/0/1

questions.prompt: Which interpretation is supported by this LLDP output?
options: DIST1 is advertising the LLDP station capability.
DIST1 advertises bridge capability and remote port Te1/0/1.
B means the receiving local port is blocked by STP.
The B code proves that DIST1 cannot also support routing.
questions.explanation: Read the legend belonging to this protocol. LLDP B means bridge, which includes Ethernet switching. The row maps the local Gi0/24 to the advertised remote Te1/0/1; it does not establish all configured features on DIST1.

whyWrong.0: The legend uses S for station, not B.
whyWrong.2: The capability field describes the neighbor’s advertised capability, not the local STP state.
whyWrong.3: A bridge capability does not rule out other capabilities or prove how every feature is configured.

questions.prompt: LLDP is globally enabled on two connected switches and the link is up. Which two interface actions are required for SW1 to learn new advertisements from SW2? Choose two.
options: Enable LLDP receive on SW1’s connected interface.
Enable LLDP transmit on SW1’s connected interface.
Enable LLDP receive on SW2’s connected interface.
Enable LLDP transmit on SW2’s connected interface.
questions.explanation: The sender is SW2 and the receiver is SW1. SW2 must transmit and SW1 must receive. The opposite two directions are needed for SW2 to learn SW1, which is a separate observation.

whyWrong.1: SW1 transmit sends SW1 information toward SW2; it does not receive SW2’s advertisements.
whyWrong.2: SW2 receive lets SW2 learn its neighbor; it does not send SW2’s advertisement.

questions.prompt: You must disable CDP only on SW1 Gi0/2 while retaining it on other intended ports. Which command belongs under interface Gi0/2?
options: no cdp run
no lldp transmit
no cdp enable
cdp timer 0
questions.explanation: no cdp enable disables CDP on the selected interface. Keep the global cdp run setting if CDP is still needed elsewhere.

whyWrong.0: no cdp run is a global command and disables CDP device-wide.
whyWrong.1: This affects LLDP transmission, a different discovery protocol.
whyWrong.3: A timer adjustment is not the per-interface enable/disable control.

exhibit.title: Representative SW1# show cdp neighbors
exhibit.text:
Device ID  Local Intrfce  Holdtme  Capability  Platform   Port ID
SW2        Gig 0/1       175      S I         WS-C2960-  Gig 0/2

questions.prompt: An old drawing shows SW1 Gi0/1 connected to SW2 Gi0/1. The cable labels and fresh neighbor observations agree with the exhibit. What should the corrected link record say?
options: SW1 Gi0/2 → SW2 Gi0/1
SW1 Gi0/1 → SW2 Gi0/2
SW1 Gi0/1 → SW2 Gi0/1, because matching numbers are required
SW1 Gi0/2 → SW2 Gi0/2
questions.explanation: The local column belongs to SW1 and Port ID belongs to SW2. Corroborated fresh evidence supports correcting the remote port to Gi0/2 while keeping the local port as Gi0/1.

whyWrong.0: This reverses the ports between devices.
whyWrong.2: Neighbor ports do not have to use matching interface numbers; the evidence contradicts the old drawing.
whyWrong.3: This changes the local port even though the observation still identifies SW1 Gi0/1.

exhibit.title: Recorded interface state on the connected ports
exhibit.text:
SW1 Gi0/1: LLDP Tx enabled; Rx enabled
SW2 Gi0/2: LLDP Tx disabled; Rx enabled

questions.prompt: LLDP runs globally on both switches, the cable is correct, and old entries have expired. What is the expected neighbor-table result?
options: Neither switch learns the other because LLDP requires bidirectional transmission.
Both switches learn each other because global enablement overrides interface settings.
SW1 learns SW2, but SW2 cannot learn SW1.
SW2 learns SW1, but SW1 cannot learn SW2.
questions.explanation: SW1 transmits, so SW2 can receive and learn SW1. SW2 does not transmit, so SW1 receives no new SW2 advertisement. Receive and transmit controls are independent.

whyWrong.0: One-way LLDP learning is possible when the corresponding sender and receiver are enabled.
whyWrong.1: Global enablement does not override a disabled per-interface transmit direction.
whyWrong.2: This reverses the direction: SW2 is the device with transmission disabled.

questions.prompt: A fresh CDP detail entry advertises SW2 management address 192.168.12.12, but SW1 cannot ping it. Which conclusion is justified?
options: Discovery works; IP reachability requires separate checks.
CDP used IP routing, so the failed ping is a command defect.
The management address must be on the port facing SW1.
CDP authenticated SW2 and verified its SSH service.
questions.explanation: CDP operates at Layer 2 and can advertise an address that is not on the facing interface. The entry is discovery evidence, not proof of IP reachability, identity authentication, or a working SSH service.

whyWrong.1: CDP does not depend on an IP route between the devices.
whyWrong.2: A device can advertise a management address from another interface.
whyWrong.3: Ordinary CDP advertisements do not authenticate the neighbor or test a management service.

questions.prompt: Which two privileged EXEC commands help inspect CDP advertisement/holdtime settings on the local IOS device? Choose two.
options: show cdp neighbors detail
show cdp
show cdp interface
show ip route
questions.explanation: show cdp reports local global settings; show cdp interface reports CDP status and timing for participating local interfaces. Neighbor detail is a record about received neighbors, not a substitute for inspecting the local sender settings.

whyWrong.0: Neighbor detail can include the remaining lifetime of a received entry, but the task asks for local CDP timer settings.
whyWrong.3: The IP routing table does not report CDP timer configuration.

questions.prompt: A policy prohibits discovery on an untrusted provider-facing Ethernet port. Internal switch and phone links still require their approved discovery features. Which change best matches the policy?
options: Disable all discovery globally and assume phones are unaffected.
Change the provider port’s advertised hostname to hide every detail.
Disable both discovery protocols on that port and verify internal dependencies.
Disable IP routing; CDP and LLDP will stop automatically.
questions.explanation: Apply the boundary policy to the selected interface. Review both discovery protocols, because disabling one does not disable the other. Preserve approved dependencies on other ports and verify their behavior.

whyWrong.0: A global change exceeds this port-specific policy and can remove needed discovery or phone provisioning information.
whyWrong.1: Changing a hostname does not disable discovery or remove all advertised information.
whyWrong.3: Layer 2 discovery can operate without IP routing.

questions.prompt: An IOS switch supports LLDP but show lldp reports that it is not enabled. You want discovery only on the approved Gi0/1 uplink. What is the appropriate next configuration?
options: Enter cdp run; LLDP automatically shares CDP’s state.
Enable lldp run, Gi0/1 transmit/receive, and verify port policy.
Add a default route; the LLDP process starts when a gateway is reachable.
Only enter lldp receive on Gi0/1; the global process can remain disabled.
questions.explanation: Enable the LLDP process and the intended interface directions. Inspect other interface states rather than assuming a universal default across models or releases.

whyWrong.0: CDP and LLDP have independent configuration.
whyWrong.2: LLDP is Layer 2 and does not need a default route.
whyWrong.3: An interface direction setting cannot make a globally disabled LLDP process operate.

questions.prompt: The sender advertises a 180-second CDP holdtime. A receiver’s countdown is now approximately 174 seconds. What does that indicate?
options: The link has been down for exactly 174 seconds.
The sender will transmit its next advertisement in 174 seconds.
The neighbor was discovered for the first time 174 seconds ago.
About 6 seconds have elapsed since the advertisement that last refreshed this entry.
questions.explanation: 180 − 174 = 6 seconds. The countdown describes the entry’s remaining lifetime after its last refresh; rounding and display timing make this an approximate observation. It does not establish physical link uptime.

whyWrong.0: The countdown is time remaining, not downtime.
whyWrong.1: The receiver’s cache countdown is separate from the sender’s advertisement schedule.
whyWrong.2: A refresh restarts the lifetime of an existing entry, so this is not an age-since-first-discovery value.

questions.prompt: Global configuration explicitly contains `no cdp run`, but Gi0/1 contains `cdp enable`. What should you conclude?
options: CDP remains disabled globally; the interface command does not override that.
Gi0/1 operates CDP while every other interface stays disabled.
Only CDP reception works on Gi0/1.
The device automatically changes to LLDP on Gi0/1.
questions.explanation: CDP needs the global process and the interface enabled. Global disablement prevents CDP operation even where the interface has cdp enable.

whyWrong.1: Per-interface enablement does not override the global state.
whyWrong.2: CDP does not use LLDP-style independent transmit and receive controls here.
whyWrong.3: One discovery protocol does not automatically substitute for the other.

questions.prompt: A supported IP phone uses LLDP-MED network-policy information from its switch. What can that information help the phone learn?
options: The OSPF router ID used for the phone’s default route.
The switch’s complete IPv4 routing table.
The intended voice VLAN and associated traffic-priority policy.
The administrator password required to manage the switch.
questions.explanation: LLDP-MED extends discovery for media endpoints, including network-policy information such as voice VLAN and priority. Advertisement does not replace configuring the required VLAN, power, and data path.

whyWrong.0: LLDP-MED is not an OSPF routing exchange.
whyWrong.1: LLDP-MED does not distribute a full IP routing table.
whyWrong.3: Management passwords are not the purpose of its network-policy advertisement.

questions.prompt: Two devices appear as CDP neighbors, but inspection finds an Ethernet hub between them. What is the correct documentation conclusion?
options: The hub must have an IP address in the CDP table before the observation can be valid.
Document the speakers and hub; discovery does not prove a single cable.
The hub is necessarily the Device ID shown in each CDP row.
Every unmanaged switch must forward LLDP in exactly the same way.
questions.explanation: A hub repeats the received signal and does not identify itself through CDP. Neighbor discovery can therefore omit an intermediate nonparticipating component. Record observed speakers separately from verified physical infrastructure.

whyWrong.0: A hub does not need an IP address or CDP identity to repeat signals.
whyWrong.2: The Device ID belongs to the advertising speaker, not automatically to an intermediate device.
whyWrong.3: Do not generalize this CDP/hub case to all bridges or to LLDP forwarding behavior.

cards.front: What is CDP, and what default state does the referenced Cisco IOS guide document?
cards.back: CDP is Cisco’s Layer 2 discovery protocol. The referenced IOS guide enables it globally and on supported interfaces by default. Inspect the actual platform and configuration; this is not a promise about every Cisco product.

cards.front: What are the documented IOS CDP advertisement interval and holdtime defaults?
cards.back: 60 seconds and 180 seconds. A received advertisement refreshes the neighbor entry; without refresh it ages out. show cdp displays the local settings.

cards.front: How do you enable LLDP on the intended Catalyst uplink?
cards.back: Enable lldp run globally, then explicitly configure lldp transmit and lldp receive on the intended interface. The referenced 2960 guide documents disabled initial LLDP states; verify other ports rather than assuming universal defaults.

cards.front: What LLDP timer defaults does the referenced Catalyst 2960 guide list?
cards.back: Advertisement interval 30 seconds; holdtime 120 seconds; reinitialization delay 2 seconds. show lldp checks the actual local settings.

cards.front: How do cdp run and cdp enable differ?
cards.back: cdp run controls the global process; cdp enable controls the selected interface. Both must permit CDP. A globally disabled process is not overridden by interface enablement.

cards.front: Which LLDP directions allow SW1 to learn SW2?
cards.back: SW2 transmits on its connected port and SW1 receives on its connected port, with LLDP globally running. The reverse directions let SW2 learn SW1.

cards.front: What are LLDP and LLDP-MED?
cards.back: LLDP is IEEE 802.1AB vendor-neutral link discovery. LLDP-MED adds information useful to media endpoints, including voice-network policy, power, and inventory. It does not replace building the VLAN and data path.

cards.front: What practical information can CDP version 2 add?
cards.back: The referenced IOS guide documents version 2 as enabled and includes information such as native VLAN and duplex. A mismatch warning is evidence to investigate, not an instruction to change either side without checking the design.

cards.front: How do the switch/bridge capability codes differ between CDP and LLDP?
cards.back: CDP S means switch. LLDP B means bridge; LLDP S means station. Read each output’s legend rather than transferring letters between protocols.

cards.front: How are phone capabilities commonly labeled in CDP and LLDP?
cards.back: CDP P means phone; LLDP T means telephone. Read the displayed legend and capability set; advertised capabilities do not prove every feature is currently configured.

cards.front: In show cdp neighbors, who owns Local Intrfce and Port ID?
cards.back: Local Intrfce belongs to the device where you ran the command. Port ID is advertised by the neighbor. Record local device/port → remote device/port.

cards.front: Why use show cdp neighbors detail after the brief table?
cards.back: It can expose advertised addresses, software/platform details, and additional TLVs that help identify the neighbor. Available fields depend on what the neighbor advertises and the image displays.

cards.front: Which commands inspect local CDP timing and interface participation?
cards.back: show cdp reports global state/timers; show cdp interface reports participating interfaces and their CDP information. These are separate from a received neighbor’s remaining lifetime.

cards.front: What if show cdp or show lldp reports that the protocol is not enabled?
cards.back: Check global configuration first: cdp run or lldp run as appropriate. Then verify the intended interface settings and the peer’s corresponding protocol. Discovery protocols have independent state.

cards.front: Which LLDP commands inspect neighbor details and per-interface directions?
cards.back: show lldp neighbors detail shows received details; show lldp interface identifies local transmit/receive state on supporting IOS images. Inspect the actual fields and use the lesson’s paper fallback if the simulator omits LLDP.

cards.front: What does a discovery entry’s remaining lifetime tell you?
cards.back: How much longer the receiver may retain that entry without refresh. It is not link uptime or a guarantee that the neighbor is still connected. LLDP field labels/brief-display behavior vary; use detail output and the applicable command reference.

cards.front: Does an advertised management address prove that you can ping or SSH to it?
cards.back: No. CDP/LLDP receive advertisements at Layer 2. Verify IP addressing, VLANs, routing, policy, and the intended service separately; the address may belong to another interface on the neighbor.

cards.front: How do you troubleshoot a missing discovery neighbor?
cards.back: Confirm the actual cable/ports and link state, shared protocol support, global enablement, and the required interface directions. Observe refresh/expiry using actual timer settings; inspect both ends. An empty table alone does not prove a broken cable.

cards.front: How should discovery be controlled at a network boundary?
cards.back: Follow the approved policy per port. Disable CDP and LLDP directions where discovery is prohibited; preserve verified dependencies such as approved phone network policy on trusted links. Disabling one protocol does not disable the other.

cards.front: Why might a CDP table omit a hub between its two speakers?
cards.back: A hub repeats signals and does not advertise a CDP identity. The speakers can be discovered across it. Document the inspected physical path separately; do not generalize this to every unmanaged bridge or to LLDP forwarding.

commands.task: Enable the global CDP process on this supporting IOS device.
commands.note: The intended interfaces must also permit CDP.

commands.task: Disable CDP only on the currently selected untrusted interface.
commands.note: This does not disable LLDP; apply the separate LLDP policy if required.

commands.task: Enable the global LLDP process.
commands.note: Then explicitly configure and verify transmit/receive on the intended interfaces; global state alone is not the complete check.

commands.task: Disable LLDP advertisements sent by the selected interface while leaving its receive setting unchanged.
commands.note: The remote device stops receiving new advertisements from this port; an existing record may remain until it is removed or expires.

commands.task: Disable LLDP reception on the selected interface while leaving its transmit setting unchanged.
commands.note: This stops learning new peer information on this port; it does not stop the peer learning your advertisements.

commands.task: Display the brief CDP neighbor table, including local and advertised remote ports.
commands.note: Local Intrfce belongs to SW1; Port ID belongs to the advertising neighbor.

commands.task: Display detailed received CDP information for all current neighbors.
commands.note: Advertised addresses and other fields depend on the peer; their presence does not prove IP reachability.

commands.task: Display the local CDP process state and timer settings.
commands.note: Inspect the actual interval and holdtime; do not confuse these local settings with received cache age.

commands.task: Display local interface participation and CDP information.
commands.note: This is a local interface check; show cdp neighbors displays received peer records.

commands.task: Display the brief LLDP neighbor table on a supporting IOS image.
commands.note: Read local and remote port columns and this protocol’s capability legend; LLDP B means bridge.

commands.task: Display detailed LLDP information received about current neighbors on a supporting IOS image.
commands.note: Read the actual advertised identity, port, and optional management fields. The simulator may omit this command.

commands.task: Display the local LLDP process and timer settings.
commands.note: A disabled global process must be enabled before intended interface directions can operate.

tickets.title: The uplink monitoring record points at the wrong port
tickets.scenario: The documentation and monitoring configuration claim that SW1 Gi0/1 connects to SW2 Gi0/1. The technician has just inspected the cable labels and sees its SW2 end on Gi0/2. Fresh CDP observations were collected at both ends. The exhibits are representative records, not live output from this app.

exhibits.title: SW1 discovery record
exhibits.text:
Device ID  Local Intrfce  Holdtme  Port ID
SW2        Gig 0/1       176      Gig 0/2

exhibits.title: SW2 discovery record
exhibits.text:
Device ID  Local Intrfce  Holdtme  Port ID
SW1        Gig 0/2       175      Gig 0/1

exhibits.title: Existing documentation
exhibits.text:
Link: SW1 Gi0/1 ↔ SW2 Gi0/1
Monitor interface: SW2 Gi0/1

tickets.question: Which correction follows from the corroborated evidence?
options: Change SW1’s documented port to Gi0/2 and leave the SW2 port alone.
Change SW2’s documented and monitored uplink port to Gi0/2 after reviewing the monitoring target; retain SW1 Gi0/1.
Renumber the switch interfaces so both ends are Gi0/1.
Disable CDP because the table is incompatible with the drawing.
tickets.explanation: Both directions and the physical inspection identify SW1 Gi0/1 ↔ SW2 Gi0/2. The stale record uses the wrong SW2 port. Reversing the columns would move the error to SW1; interface numbers need not match. The observations support correcting this link record, but they do not prove that every VLAN or management service works.
tickets.fix:
Update the local documentation to `SW1 Gi0/1 ↔ SW2 Gi0/2`, record when and how it was checked, and correct the intended monitoring interface using the monitoring system’s approved edit flow. This exercise does not change any real monitoring service. Preserve the original record in the change history.

```ios SW1
SW1# show cdp neighbors
SW1# show cdp neighbors detail
SW1# show interfaces gigabitethernet0/1
```

```ios SW2
SW2# show cdp neighbors
SW2# show interfaces gigabitethernet0/2
```

Verify refreshed observations and both physical port states. Test the required VLAN or management path separately before declaring the service healthy. If hostname or cable evidence disagrees, investigate identity and cache freshness instead of automatically overwriting the drawing.

tickets.title: CDP works, but the new uplink has no LLDP neighbor
tickets.scenario: SW1 Gi0/1 is connected to SW2 Gi0/2. The link is up, CDP is receiving current entries in both directions, and both images support LLDP. SW1 has LLDP enabled globally and has explicitly enabled transmit and receive on Gi0/1. SW2’s recorded global output is below. Old entries have expired.

exhibits.title: SW1 configuration excerpt
exhibits.text:
lldp run
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 lldp transmit
 lldp receive

exhibits.title: SW2# show lldp
exhibits.text: % LLDP is not enabled

exhibits.title: Link inspection
exhibits.text: SW1 Gi0/1 ↔ SW2 Gi0/2; link up; fresh CDP observations in both directions

tickets.question: What is the most direct correction?
options: Enable the LLDP global process on SW2 and explicitly enable its intended Gi0/2 transmit/receive directions.
Add a default route on SW2 because CDP has consumed the local subnet.
Disable CDP globally so LLDP can use the same Ethernet cable.
Change SW1 Gi0/1 to Gi0/2 so the local interface numbers match.
tickets.explanation: SW2 reports that its LLDP process is disabled. CDP working does not enable LLDP. A default route and matching physical interface numbers are irrelevant, and both discovery protocols can operate on the same link.
tickets.fix:
On the supporting SW2 image:

```ios SW2
SW2# configure terminal
SW2(config)# lldp run
SW2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/2
SW2(config-if)# lldp transmit
SW2(config-if)# lldp receive
SW2(config-if)# end
SW2# show lldp
SW2# show lldp interface gigabitethernet0/2
SW2# show lldp neighbors
```

```ios SW1
SW1# show lldp interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW1# show lldp neighbors
```

Wait for an actual advertisement opportunity according to the configured timers, then verify each device receives the intended peer and remote port. Review interface discovery policy on other ports after globally enabling LLDP. Save the intended configuration after verification. If a simulator lacks LLDP, use these records as the paper exercise and do not label it an executed protocol test.

sections.title: Build Layer 2 and Layer 3 port channels
Read the bundle and partner state

lab.title: Build, fault, and restore Layer 2 and Layer 3 LACP bundles
devices: 2 × Catalyst 3560-24PS (D1, D2) for a separate Layer 3 topology
lab.intro: Build a two-member Layer 2 trunk, verify each member, and observe a member failure separately from a negotiation failure. Then create a routed port channel in a second file. These instructions and representative states have been checked against Cisco configuration guidance; this exercise has not been executed in Packet Tracer during this review.
lab.topology:
