tickets.title: The faster root uplink is not forwarding
tickets.scenario: DSW1 has a direct 10 Gbps link Te1/1 to CORE, the verified root for VLAN 100. DSW1 also has Gi1/1 to DSW2, whose root path cost is 2 through its own 10 Gbps CORE link. The network uses short costs. The following are representative abbreviated teaching exhibits from the stated configuration.

exhibits.title: DSW1# show spanning-tree vlan 100 — excerpt
exhibits.text:
Root path cost: 6 through GigabitEthernet1/1
Te1/1               Altn BLK 19        128.49   P2p
Gi1/1               Root FWD 4         128.25   P2p

exhibits.title: DSW1 running configuration excerpt
exhibits.text:
interface TenGigabitEthernet1/1
 switchport mode trunk
 spanning-tree vlan 100 cost 19

tickets.question: Which cause explains the current path selection?
options: The local port number on Gi1/1 is lower, so it overrides the cost comparison.
The manual direct-link cost 19 loses to the indirect path cost 4 + 2 = 6.
The root is selected by physical interface speed rather than the configured bridge ID.
The 10 Gbps link cannot participate in Rapid PVST+ without being a shared link.
tickets.explanation: CORE is explicitly established as root, and the worksheet gives DSW2's cost as 2. DSW1 adds its Gi1/1 cost 4 for a total of 6, which beats the manually assigned 19 on Te1/1. The cost comparison is decided before port IDs matter; the port's speed is not increased by changing its STP cost.
tickets.fix:
Remove the unintended per-VLAN override, then verify the displayed automatic cost and root path. With the stated short-cost method, Te1/1 should use cost 2 and become root port.
```ios DSW1
DSW1# configure terminal
DSW1(config)# interface tengigabitethernet1/1
DSW1(config-if)# no spanning-tree vlan 100 cost
DSW1(config-if)# end
DSW1# show spanning-tree vlan 100
```
Retest traffic and save only after confirming the intended root and path. Interface names in this worksheet belong to its example platform; do not paste them into an unrelated 2960 lab.

tickets.title: A replacement restores classic behavior on an interswitch link
tickets.scenario: The intended topology runs Rapid PVST+. After ASW3 is replaced, the transit link from ASW1 toward ASW3 uses legacy behavior during link changes. Host-edge configuration is unchanged. The following representative excerpts show the peer compatibility state and replacement mode.

exhibits.title: ASW1# show spanning-tree vlan 10 — excerpt
exhibits.text:
Spanning tree enabled protocol rstp
Gi0/1               Desg FWD 4         128.25   P2p Peer(STP)

exhibits.title: ASW3# show spanning-tree summary — excerpt
exhibits.text: Switch is in pvst mode

tickets.question: What does the evidence identify as the mismatch?
options: ASW3 uses classic PVST+, causing classic interoperability on the link facing it.
The ASW1 transit port lacks PortFast, so it can never form a rapid handshake.
A low MAC address automatically disables Rapid PVST+ on neighboring switches.
The P2p label establishes half-duplex operation and a shared physical segment.
tickets.explanation: ASW3's mode and ASW1's Peer(STP) indication identify the classic neighbor. The effect is on compatibility behavior of the connecting link; this does not prove that every host port in the network now waits 30 seconds. P2p is the point-to-point link type, not shared.
tickets.fix:
Configure the intended mode on ASW3, then verify the local mode and ASW1 peer behavior after negotiation.
```ios ASW3
ASW3# configure terminal
ASW3(config)# spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst
ASW3(config)# end
ASW3# show spanning-tree summary
ASW3# show spanning-tree vlan 10
```
If a peer remains in legacy compatibility, confirm that no legacy bridge remains and consult that platform's protocol-migration procedure. Do not enable PortFast on the transit link as a workaround or promise a fixed number of seconds for the Peer(STP) indication to disappear.

lab.title: Configure, trigger, and recover STP protection
devices: Optional licensed CML or hardware switches for the loop-guard fault
lab.intro:
Build a new project with the complete configuration below; no saved file from another chapter is required. You will protect a host port, reject a superior downstream root, and interpret missing-BPDU protection. The base topology is deliberately a line, so the controlled loop-guard demonstration has no redundant physical path that could form a data loop if the feature is unavailable.

These instructions and expected results are authored from Cisco's documented behavior, not a claim of manual Packet Tracer execution. Run the PortFast/BPDU-guard/root-guard exercises where the simulator supports them. Run the BPDU-suppression fault only on an isolated CML/hardware setup after confirming loop guard is operational; Packet Tracer learners use the included prediction and representative evidence. Command acceptance alone does not establish complete simulation support.

steps.title: Build the complete baseline
steps.body:
Cable the four permanent links, open each switch CLI, decline the initial setup dialog if shown, and apply its block. Record the actual Bridge ID MACs after configuration. The differing priorities make VLAN 10 root placement independent of MAC ordering.

```ios SW1
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname SW1
SW1(config)# vlan 10
SW1(config-vlan)# name STUDY
SW1(config-vlan)# exit
SW1(config)# vlan 999
SW1(config-vlan)# name UNUSED_NATIVE
SW1(config-vlan)# exit
SW1(config)# spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst
SW1(config)# spanning-tree vlan 10 priority 32768
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/24
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk native vlan 999
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,999
SW1(config-if)# spanning-tree vlan 10 cost 19
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if)# exit
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk native vlan 999
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,999
SW1(config-if)# spanning-tree vlan 10 cost 4
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if)# exit
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/5
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if)# switchport access vlan 10
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if)# exit
SW1(config)# interface vlan 10
SW1(config-if)# ip address 10.0.10.1 255.255.255.0
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show spanning-tree vlan 10
```

```ios SW2
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname SW2
SW2(config)# vlan 10
SW2(config-vlan)# name STUDY
SW2(config-vlan)# exit
SW2(config)# vlan 999
SW2(config-vlan)# name UNUSED_NATIVE
SW2(config-vlan)# exit
SW2(config)# spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst
SW2(config)# spanning-tree vlan 10 priority 24576
SW2(config)# interface fastethernet0/24
SW2(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
SW2(config-if)# switchport trunk native vlan 999
SW2(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,999
SW2(config-if)# spanning-tree vlan 10 cost 19
SW2(config-if)# no shutdown
SW2(config-if)# exit
SW2(config)# interface fastethernet0/5
SW2(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW2(config-if)# switchport access vlan 10
SW2(config-if)# no shutdown
SW2(config-if)# exit
SW2(config)# interface vlan 10
SW2(config-if)# ip address 10.0.10.2 255.255.255.0
SW2(config-if)# no shutdown
SW2(config-if)# end
SW2# show spanning-tree vlan 10
```

```ios SW3
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname SW3
SW3(config)# vlan 10
SW3(config-vlan)# name STUDY
SW3(config-vlan)# exit
SW3(config)# vlan 999
SW3(config-vlan)# name UNUSED_NATIVE
SW3(config-vlan)# exit
SW3(config)# spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst
SW3(config)# spanning-tree vlan 10 priority 28672
SW3(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW3(config-if)# switchport mode trunk

SW3(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,999
SW3(config-if)# spanning-tree vlan 10 cost 4
SW3(config-if)# no shutdown

SW3(config-if)# end
SW3# show spanning-tree vlan 10
```

:::expected
SW2 displays `This bridge is the root` for VLAN 10 and priority 24586 including the VLAN ID. SW1's Fa0/24 is root port at total cost 19; SW1 Gi0/1 is designated. SW3's Gi0/1 is root port at cost 19 + 4 = 23. No VLAN 10 interswitch port needs to be alternate in this nonredundant topology. Record VLAN 10 only; VLAN 999 has its own election.
:::

steps.title: Configure PCs and protected edge ports
steps.body:
Enter each PC address and mask using Desktop → IP Configuration → Static; leave gateway and DNS blank. Run `ping 10.0.10.12` and `ping 10.0.10.3` from PC-A after convergence. Then configure PortFast and BPDU guard on SW1's specific host port; on SW2 demonstrate the equivalent global defaults for its nontrunking host ports.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/5
SW1(config-if)# spanning-tree portfast
SW1(config-if)# spanning-tree bpduguard enable
SW1(config-if)# shutdown
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show spanning-tree interface fastethernet0/5 detail
```

```ios SW2
SW2# configure terminal
SW2(config)# spanning-tree portfast default
SW2(config)# spanning-tree portfast bpduguard default
SW2(config)# end
SW2# show spanning-tree summary
SW2# show spanning-tree interface fastethernet0/5 detail
```

:::expected
PC-A can reach PC-B and SW3's SVI. SW1 Fa0/5 becomes forwarding as an edge after the controlled bounce; BPDU guard is configured and no violation exists with PC-A attached. SW2's global defaults apply to Fa0/5 but not its trunk Fa0/24. If an optional detailed show command is unsupported, use `show spanning-tree vlan 10`, `show running-config`, and interface status. Record the actual port behavior instead of assuming an exact delay.
:::

steps.title: Trigger BPDU guard with the third switch
steps.body:
Disconnect SW3 Gi0/1 from SW1 Gi0/1 first. Verify that SW3 now has no interswitch cable. Disconnect PC-A from SW1 Fa0/5. Prepare SW3 Fa0/1 as an access port in VLAN 10, then connect it to SW1 Fa0/5 using a crossover cable. This temporary connection has no alternate physical return path.

```ios SW3
SW3# configure terminal
SW3(config)# interface fastethernet0/1
SW3(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW3(config-if)# switchport access vlan 10
SW3(config-if)# no shutdown
SW3(config-if)# end
```

```ios SW1
SW1# show interfaces status
SW1# show logging
```

:::expected
SW3 sends BPDUs; the configured interface BPDU guard causes SW1 Fa0/5 to become err-disabled. SW3 does not need priority zero: any received BPDU is sufficient. Look for the actual `bpduguard` cause in the log. The following shortened lines are representative, not a recorded simulator transcript:

```output Representative SW1 evidence
%SPANTREE-2-BLOCK_BPDUGUARD: Received BPDU on port FastEthernet0/5 with BPDU Guard enabled. Disabling port.
%PM-4-ERR_DISABLE: bpduguard error detected on Fa0/5, putting Fa0/5 in err-disable state
```

If the port stays up, check which physical port received the cable, the SW3 port state, and the presence of BPDU guard. If the simulator does not implement the feature, record that limitation and interpret the evidence above; do not count the exercise as an observed trigger.
:::

steps.title: Remove the BPDU source and recover the host port
steps.body:
Delete the temporary SW3 Fa0/1 cable. Reconnect PC-A to SW1 Fa0/5 with a straight-through cable, and restore SW3 Gi0/1 ↔ SW1 Gi0/1 with a crossover cable. Shut the unused test port on SW3. Only after the wrong connection is removed, reset SW1 Fa0/5.

```ios SW3
SW3# configure terminal
SW3(config)# interface fastethernet0/1
SW3(config-if)# shutdown
SW3(config-if)# end
```

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/5
SW1(config-if)# shutdown
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show interfaces status
SW1# show spanning-tree vlan 10
```

:::expected
Fa0/5 returns to connected/forwarding with PC-A attached. Repeat PC-A's pings to 10.0.10.12 and 10.0.10.3. SW2 is still root and SW3's root cost is 23. A repeating violation means a BPDU source is still reaching the protected port; a timer or repeated reset would not correct that source.
:::

steps.title: Guard the downstream boundary and introduce a superior root
steps.body:
SW1 Gi0/1 is a designated boundary toward SW3, so install root guard there. Then change SW3's VLAN 10 priority to zero. Keep all permanent cables exactly as in the topology.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# spanning-tree guard root
SW1(config-if)# end
```

```ios SW3
SW3# configure terminal
SW3(config)# spanning-tree vlan 10 priority 0
SW3(config)# end
SW3# show spanning-tree vlan 10
```

```ios SW1
SW1# show spanning-tree inconsistentports
SW1# show spanning-tree vlan 10
```

:::expected
SW1 Gi0/1 becomes root-inconsistent for VLAN 10, often displayed with `*ROOT_Inc`; it does not become BPDU-guard err-disabled. SW1 still identifies SW2 as root. PC-A can reach PC-B but cannot reach SW3's 10.0.10.3 address across the blocked VLAN. SW3 may identify itself as root in its isolated portion. The objective is to hold the upstream boundary, not change SW3's configuration automatically.
:::

steps.title: Correct the downstream priority
steps.body:
Restore SW3's explicit priority 28672 and allow STP to process the new information. Leave the protective root-guard command on SW1 while observing automatic recovery.

```ios SW3
SW3# configure terminal
SW3(config)# spanning-tree vlan 10 priority 28672
SW3(config)# end
SW3# show spanning-tree vlan 10
```

```ios SW1
SW1# show spanning-tree inconsistentports
SW1# show spanning-tree vlan 10
```

:::expected
The root-inconsistent condition clears without a manual port bounce. SW3 again learns SW2's root ID and uses Gi0/1 at cost 23; PC-A can again ping 10.0.10.3. Record the observed recovery rather than requiring exactly 20 seconds. If it persists, verify that the command changed VLAN 10 and that no other superior source exists.
:::

steps.title: Prepare loop guard and record received BPDUs
steps.body:
For the missing-BPDU exercise, remove root guard from SW1's sending port to keep this experiment focused on one feature. Configure loop guard on SW3's receiving root port. These commands require platform support; if your Packet Tracer image rejects loop guard, use the worksheet exercise in Step 8 and skip the suppression command entirely.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# no spanning-tree guard
SW1(config-if)# end
```

```ios SW3
SW3# configure terminal
SW3(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW3(config-if)# spanning-tree guard loop
SW3(config-if)# end
SW3# show spanning-tree interface gigabitethernet0/1 detail
SW3# show spanning-tree inconsistentports
```

:::expected
SW3 Gi0/1 is still root/forwarding for VLAN 10 and receives BPDUs before the fault. On an implementing image, detail identifies loop guard as enabled; repeated readings show received BPDU activity. The inconsistent-port list is empty. Do not infer enabled loop protection from command acceptance alone, and do not inject the fault if you cannot establish this baseline.
:::

steps.title: Observe a controlled BPDU-loss fault or interpret the exhibit
steps.body:
**CML/hardware only, isolated line topology:** confirm that SW3 has only its Gi0/1 cable and the temporary Fa0/1 test port is shut. On SW1 Gi0/1, temporarily enable interface BPDU filtering. This models lost BPDU delivery while the physical link remains up; it does not reproduce every property of a one-way fiber fault. There is no extra SW2–SW3 link.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# spanning-tree bpdufilter enable
SW1(config-if)# end
```

```ios SW3
SW3# show interfaces status
SW3# show spanning-tree inconsistentports
SW3# show spanning-tree interface gigabitethernet0/1 detail
```

**Packet Tracer/paper path:** do not enter the filter command. From the healthy baseline, predict the result if SW3 stopped receiving BPDUs but the link stayed up. Interpret the representative evidence below and compare it with root guard's trigger.

:::expected
On a supported implementation, expired expected BPDU information causes loop inconsistency on SW3 Gi0/1. Physical link status can remain connected while VLAN 10 cannot forward. A representative abbreviated entry is:

```output Representative loop-guard evidence
Name                 Interface                Inconsistency
-------------------- ------------------------ ------------------
VLAN0010             GigabitEthernet0/1        Loop Inconsistent
```

The reason is missing expected BPDUs, not a received superior BID. VLAN 999 may also be listed depending on its roles and received information. Do not require a fixed role label or six-second trigger from every software version. Root guard would not detect this same absence of control traffic.
:::

steps.title: Remove filtering and restore the boundary
steps.body:
On the CML/hardware path, remove the exact filter introduced in Step 8. On the Packet Tracer/paper path no filter was installed, so simply verify the running configuration and restore root guard. Root guard on SW1 and loop guard on SW3 are on different interfaces at opposite ends and are compatible with this intended design.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# no spanning-tree bpdufilter
SW1(config-if)# spanning-tree guard root
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show running-config
```

```ios SW3
SW3# show spanning-tree inconsistentports
SW3# show spanning-tree vlan 10
```

:::expected
If a fault was executed, BPDUs resume and loop inconsistency clears automatically; SW3 returns to root/forwarding on Gi0/1 with cost 23. PC-A's pings to SW3 and PC-B succeed. No interface BPDU filter remains in the running configuration. On a simulator that rejects the optional removal command, verify that no filter was configured and continue with supported commands.
:::

steps.title: Inspect optional timed recovery without repeating the fault
steps.body:
On an IOS image supporting these commands, enable automatic recovery for BPDU guard and set the interval to 60 seconds. This is a configuration-reading exercise: do not reconnect the prohibited switch. Packet Tracer users whose image rejects the commands should identify the two separate requirements from the lesson and retain manual recovery.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# errdisable recovery cause bpduguard
SW1(config)# errdisable recovery interval 60
SW1(config)# end
SW1# show errdisable recovery
```

:::expected
The output identifies BPDU-guard recovery as enabled and the interval as 60 seconds. No interface is waiting for recovery because the fault was already corrected. Changing only the timer would not enable recovery for the cause. The setting permits future recovery attempts; it does not prevent another violation.
:::

steps.title: Remove the optional timer policy and save the protected baseline
steps.body:
If Step 10 was supported, remove its cause and interval settings to return to manual BPDU-guard recovery. Keep PortFast/BPDU guard on the host ports, root guard on SW1's downstream boundary, and supported loop guard on SW3's uplink. Save each switch and then save the workspace as `stp-protected.pkt` or the equivalent CML lab.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# no errdisable recovery cause bpduguard
SW1(config)# no errdisable recovery interval
SW1(config)# end
SW1# show spanning-tree inconsistentports
SW1# show spanning-tree vlan 10
SW1# copy running-config startup-config
```

```ios SW2
SW2# show spanning-tree vlan 10
SW2# copy running-config startup-config
```

```ios SW3
SW3# show spanning-tree vlan 10
SW3# copy running-config startup-config
```

:::expected
No deliberate fault remains: SW3 priority is 28672, its temporary Fa0/1 is shut, filtering is absent, and SW2 remains root. All three management IPs and both PCs are reachable within VLAN 10. Record any simulator-only omissions in your notes so the saved project does not imply a feature was demonstrated when it was only studied.
:::

lab.troubleshooting:
- Fa0/5 stays err-disabled after restoring the PC: remove the BPDU source first, then issue both `shutdown` and `no shutdown`; a lone `no shutdown` is not the complete recovery sequence.
- Root guard does not trigger: confirm it is on SW1 Gi0/1, the SW3 priority change is for VLAN 10, and the correct trunk carries that VLAN.
- SW3 unexpectedly becomes root of the main network: the boundary guard was absent or the switch was attached through a different port. Disconnect the temporary source, correct placement, and restore priority before reconnecting.
- Loop inconsistency does not appear: first determine whether this is the paper/simulator path. On supported equipment verify prior BPDU reception, correct interface, point-to-point status, enabled loop guard, and the exact BPDU-suppression location.
- A management SVI cannot be pinged: check its address and operational line protocol as well as STP. A VLAN without an active forwarding member can make its SVI unavailable.
lab.challenge:
On paper, move root guard from SW1 Gi0/1 to SW1 Fa0/24 while keeping SW2 root at 24576. Predict the result, and explain why putting every guard on every trunk is not a sound template. Also predict what changing only `errdisable recovery interval 60` would do for a BPDU-guard-disabled port when its recovery cause remains disabled.

:::expected
SW1 Fa0/24 is the legitimate path toward SW2. Root guard there rejects the superior information that SW1 needs and creates root inconsistency, isolating the downstream side for VLAN 10. Restore root guard only on the boundary toward SW3; loop guard expresses the appropriate missing-BPDU expectation on a root/alternate path. Root and loop guard cannot coexist on one interface. Changing only the interval does not enable automatic BPDU-guard recovery, so the disabled port still needs the cause enabled or manual recovery after the fault is removed.
:::

questions.prompt: What caused the outage on Fa0/5, and which recovery sequence fits the evidence?
options: A better root was received; raise SW1's bridge priority to clear the state.
A BPDU arrived on the guarded port; remove its source, then shut/no-shut the port.
Expected BPDUs stopped arriving; lower the recovery interval to force learning.
The port is a normal alternate; remove the redundant uplink to make it designated.
questions.explanation: The log names BPDU guard, and interface status confirms errdisable. Remove the unexpected BPDU source, then perform manual recovery or use an explicitly enabled recovery policy.

whyWrong.0: Root guard produces root inconsistency rather than this BPDU-guard error.
whyWrong.2: Missing expected BPDUs describe loop guard, not the received-BPDU log.
whyWrong.3: Err-disabled is not the normal alternate/discarding state.

exhibit.title: SW1 representative evidence
exhibit.text:
Fa0/5   err-disabled   10
%PM-4-ERR_DISABLE: bpduguard error detected on Fa0/5, putting Fa0/5 in err-disable state

questions.prompt: What does PortFast change on a correctly designed end-device access port?
options: It filters all BPDUs so the host can never influence the bridge election.
It makes the port a root port so user traffic avoids the normal tree.
It permits immediate forwarding while spanning tree remains active.
It waits for a PC's agreement BPDU before skipping the learning state.
questions.explanation: PortFast permits a genuine edge port to enter forwarding immediately. It does not disable STP; a received BPDU changes operational edge behavior or triggers an enabled guard.

whyWrong.0: BPDU suppression is filtering, not PortFast itself.
whyWrong.1: PortFast does not elect the port as a root port.
whyWrong.3: End hosts do not have to participate in a bridge proposal/agreement handshake.

questions.prompt: On a 2960-style IOS switch, which global command enables PortFast for operationally nontrunking ports?
options: spanning-tree portfast trunk
spanning-tree bpduguard enable
spanning-tree guard root
spanning-tree portfast default
questions.explanation: The global default applies PortFast to nontrunking interfaces. A trunk to a legitimate end device needs the appropriate interface trunk form instead.

whyWrong.0: This is an interface command for a PortFast trunk, not the global nontrunking default.
whyWrong.1: This enables interface BPDU guard and does not enable global PortFast.
whyWrong.2: Root guard protects a designated boundary and does not create an edge port.

questions.prompt: VLAN 20 is blocked on Gi1/0/10 while another VLAN on the trunk still works. Which diagnosis best fits the representative evidence?
options: Root guard received superior information for VLAN 20 and blocked that instance.
BPDU guard disabled the entire physical interface after receiving a BPDU.
Loop guard detected missing expected BPDUs from the intended root neighbor.
PortFast suppressed the interface's BPDUs until a recovery timer expires.
questions.explanation: The inconsistency explicitly names root guard's condition. In Rapid PVST+, root inconsistency can affect one VLAN while another instance on the physical trunk remains operational.

whyWrong.1: Conventional BPDU-guard errdisable affects the interface and is identified by a different state/cause.
whyWrong.2: Loop inconsistency is a different indication with a missing-BPDU trigger.
whyWrong.3: PortFast does not suppress BPDUs or create this recovery state.

exhibit.title: DSW1# show spanning-tree inconsistentports — excerpt
exhibit.text: VLAN0020             GigabitEthernet1/0/10       Root Inconsistent

questions.prompt: Which two statements about recovery from a BPDU-guard violation are correct? (Choose two.)
options: The source should be corrected before the interface is re-enabled.
Changing the recovery interval alone enables recovery for BPDU guard.
Root-inconsistent recovery must be enabled before errdisable can clear.
An enabled recovery timer can retry the port but cannot remove the BPDU source.
A single received inferior BPDU cannot cause another violation after recovery.
questions.explanation: Recovery restores the interface's ability to operate; it does not correct a wrong connection. Automatic retries must be explicitly enabled for the cause and can fail again if BPDUs continue arriving.

whyWrong.1: The cause must be enabled separately from the interval setting.
whyWrong.2: Root inconsistency and BPDU-guard errdisable are different states with separate recovery behavior.
whyWrong.4: BPDU guard reacts to any received BPDU, including an inferior one.

questions.prompt: Which event is the intended trigger for loop guard on a point-to-point root port that has been receiving BPDUs?
options: The peer advertises a lower root BID while continuing normal BPDU exchange.
The port receives its first BPDU while operational PortFast is enabled.
Expected BPDU information expires while the physical link remains up.
The local switch learns a host MAC address on the root interface.
questions.explanation: Loop guard handles the loss of expected spanning-tree information on an applicable root or alternate port. It prevents expiry from making that port designated and forwarding on an unsafe assumption.

whyWrong.0: Superior received information is associated with root-guard policy, not loop guard's silence condition.
whyWrong.1: Unexpected BPDU reception on a protected edge is the BPDU-guard case.
whyWrong.3: MAC learning from user frames is not the loop-guard trigger.

questions.prompt: CORE must remain the allowed root. A training switch will attach only to ASW1 Gi0/2, currently a designated boundary port. Where should root guard enforce that boundary?
options: On CORE's console connection, where the intended priority was configured.
On ASW1's uplink toward CORE, where the best root information is received.
On the training switch's own uplink, where its lower-priority BID originates.
On ASW1 Gi0/2, where superior information could enter from the training switch.
questions.explanation: The controlled side of the boundary is ASW1 Gi0/2. Root guard there prevents the downstream attachment from supplying superior root information into the rest of the topology.

whyWrong.0: STP protection applies to Layer 2 interfaces, not the console session.
whyWrong.1: That would reject the legitimate root path needed by ASW1.
whyWrong.2: Placing policy only on the outside device does not enforce the managed boundary described.

questions.prompt: How do the two Cisco IOS BPDU-filter forms differ?
options: The global PortFast form withdraws filtering after a BPDU; the interface form suppresses BPDUs independently.
The global form err-disables after a BPDU; the interface form waits for a superior root advertisement.
The global form applies only to trunks; the interface form applies only to nontrunking access ports.
The global form filters user broadcasts; the interface form filters user multicast without affecting STP.
questions.explanation: The global PortFast default has conditional behavior: received BPDUs remove operational edge/filter status. Interface filtering independently suppresses BPDU participation and does not provide that same fallback.

whyWrong.1: These describe guard-like actions, not the two BPDU-filter behaviors.
whyWrong.2: The global form follows operational PortFast status, and the interface form is not limited as stated.
whyWrong.3: The feature concerns BPDUs, not general user broadcast or multicast filtering.

questions.prompt: Fa0/7 is operationally an access port with no interface overrides. What should happen when a BPDU-sending switch is attached under the shown global configuration?
options: The port remains unprotected because no interface-specific guard line exists.
The operational PortFast port is covered by BPDU guard and becomes err-disabled.
The port enters root inconsistency only if the attached bridge has a lower BID.
The port silently filters the received BPDU and remains an operational edge.
questions.explanation: The PortFast default covers this nontrunking port, and the BPDU-guard default covers its operational edge state. A received BPDU therefore triggers the guard even without an interface-specific enable line.

whyWrong.0: Applicable global defaults do not require duplicate per-interface commands.
whyWrong.2: Any received BPDU triggers BPDU guard, regardless of root superiority.
whyWrong.3: No BPDU-filter command is configured in this exhibit.

exhibit.title: SW1 running-config excerpt
exhibit.text:
spanning-tree portfast default
spanning-tree portfast bpduguard default
interface FastEthernet0/7
 switchport mode access
 switchport access vlan 10

questions.prompt: A non-PortFast trunk to a server must be err-disabled if it receives any BPDU. Which interface command directly configures that behavior?
options: spanning-tree portfast trunk
spanning-tree guard root
spanning-tree bpduguard enable
spanning-tree loopguard default
questions.explanation: Interface BPDU guard operates independently of PortFast state. Its trigger is any received BPDU, which matches the requirement without relying on a global edge default.

whyWrong.0: PortFast controls initial forwarding and does not itself configure errdisable on BPDU reception.
whyWrong.1: Root guard permits ordinary BPDUs and reacts to superior information instead.
whyWrong.3: This is a global loop-guard command for missing expected BPDUs, not interface BPDU guard.

questions.prompt: Which comparison correctly distinguishes root guard from BPDU guard?
options: Root guard rejects every BPDU; BPDU guard rejects only a lower-priority root.
Root guard detects BPDU silence; BPDU guard detects changes in interface speed.
Root guard uses errdisable; BPDU guard uses a per-VLAN root-inconsistent state.
Root guard rejects superior information; BPDU guard reacts to any received BPDU.
questions.explanation: Root guard enforces a designated boundary against superior spanning-tree information. BPDU guard enforces an expectation that no BPDU should arrive, so it does not need to compare the advertised root first.

whyWrong.0: The trigger comparison is reversed.
whyWrong.1: Missing BPDUs are the loop-guard case, and speed changes do not define BPDU guard.
whyWrong.2: The normal state distinction is root inconsistency versus BPDU-guard errdisable, not the reverse.

questions.prompt: With no configured errdisable recovery timer, which two states can clear automatically when their own triggering conditions end? (Choose two.)
options: BPDU-guard errdisable after the switch stops sending BPDUs.
Root inconsistency after superior information ceases.
Loop inconsistency after expected BPDUs resume.
Administrative shutdown after the peer link becomes healthy.
An administratively disabled SVI after the correct VLAN is created.
questions.explanation: Root and loop inconsistency include automatic return to normal STP processing after their conditions clear. BPDU-guard errdisable needs manual recovery or an enabled recovery policy; administrative shutdown also requires configuration action.

whyWrong.0: Without enabled automatic recovery, removing the source alone does not reset errdisable.
whyWrong.3: A configured shutdown is not cleared by peer health.
whyWrong.4: Creating a VLAN does not remove a configured SVI shutdown.

questions.prompt: SW3 Gi0/2 was a root port and had received BPDUs before this event. Which conclusion is supported by these observations?
options: Expected BPDUs stopped arriving; the output does not by itself prove the physical cause.
A newly received priority-zero BPDU forced SW3 to reject a superior root bridge.
The interface was disabled by BPDU guard, so every VLAN must be physically down.
The fiber receive strand is conclusively broken because the port is still connected.
questions.explanation: Loop inconsistency indicates the loss of expected STP information on the applicable port. A one-way fault is one possibility, but filtering or a neighbor control-plane problem can produce the same symptom.

whyWrong.1: Superior information would fit a root-guard event, which is not the displayed reason.
whyWrong.2: The state is loop inconsistency while the physical link remains connected, not BPDU-guard errdisable.
whyWrong.3: The observations identify the symptom but do not distinguish all possible underlying causes.

exhibit.title: SW3 representative observations
exhibit.text:
Gi0/2 physical status: connected
VLAN0010  GigabitEthernet0/2  Loop Inconsistent
VLAN0020  GigabitEthernet0/2  Loop Inconsistent
Received BPDU counter stopped increasing before the event.

questions.prompt: This host-port template is supposed to detect unexpected BPDUs. What is the design problem that should be corrected?
options: PortFast changes BPDU guard into root guard on an access interface.
Interface filtering suppresses the BPDU processing on which the protection design relies.
BPDU guard automatically selects a lower root priority when a host sends traffic.
The access VLAN prevents the switch from receiving any spanning-tree control traffic.
questions.explanation: Unconditional interface filtering suppresses BPDU participation and conflicts with the goal of using received BPDUs to expose a wrong connection. Remove the unwanted filter and verify a supported PortFast/BPDU-guard policy, rather than relying on mixed-feature precedence assumptions.

whyWrong.0: PortFast and BPDU guard retain their own functions; they do not turn into root guard.
whyWrong.2: BPDU guard does not configure bridge priority.
whyWrong.3: An access VLAN can carry the corresponding spanning-tree control exchange.

exhibit.title: SW1 host-port configuration
exhibit.text:
interface FastEthernet0/5
 switchport mode access
 switchport access vlan 10
 spanning-tree portfast
 spanning-tree bpduguard enable
 spanning-tree bpdufilter enable

questions.prompt: A port is already err-disabled because of BPDU guard. The BPDU source has been removed. What does the shown recovery configuration establish?
options: The port will be retried after 60 seconds because every cause inherits the interval.
The port is now root-inconsistent and will recover when a superior BPDU expires.
The interval is 60 seconds, but BPDU-guard automatic recovery remains disabled.
The port must stay disabled until the interval is restored to the default 300 seconds.
questions.explanation: The timer interval and the enabled recovery causes are separate settings. The displayed cause remains disabled, so manual recovery or explicitly enabling BPDU-guard recovery is still required.

whyWrong.0: The interval does not enable all causes automatically.
whyWrong.1: Changing a timer does not convert the port into a different protection state.
whyWrong.3: The default interval is not a prerequisite for manual or enabled timed recovery.

exhibit.text:
ErrDisable Reason             Timer Status
bpduguard                     Disabled
Timer interval: 60 seconds

questions.prompt: A root-facing point-to-point uplink should use loop guard, while a downstream boundary should use root guard. Which implementation principle is correct?
options: Install both guards on each uplink so either a received or missing BPDU is covered.
Use root guard on every root port because its name identifies where it belongs.
Use loop guard on PC access ports because their lack of BPDUs needs protection.
Choose the guard by the intended role; root and loop guard cannot coexist on one interface.
questions.explanation: Root guard preserves a designated boundary, whereas loop guard protects appropriate root/alternate paths from BPDU loss. Their role expectations differ, and IOS does not allow both to operate on the same interface.

whyWrong.0: The two guards are mutually exclusive on a single interface.
whyWrong.1: A root port needs the legitimate superior information that root guard would reject.
whyWrong.2: A genuine edge normally sends no BPDUs and is not the loop-guard monitoring case.

cards.front: What does PortFast change on a genuine edge port?
cards.back: It permits immediate forwarding and avoids topology-change generation from ordinary edge transitions; STP still runs.

cards.front: 2960-style interface command for PortFast on an access port?
cards.back: `spanning-tree portfast`. Use only where the port is a genuine end-device edge.

cards.front: PortFast command for a trunk to a genuine end device?
cards.back: `spanning-tree portfast trunk`; some IOS XE images use `spanning-tree portfast edge trunk`. Verify that the host cannot form a Layer 2 transit loop.

cards.front: Global PortFast command and its scope on 2960-style IOS?
cards.back: `spanning-tree portfast default` applies to operationally nontrunking ports; a trunk is not covered by that default.

cards.front: Does PortFast disable STP or permanently guarantee edge status?
cards.back: No. BPDUs are still processed; with PortFast alone a received BPDU removes operational edge status. The configured command can remain.

cards.front: BPDU guard: trigger and conventional Catalyst result?
cards.back: Any received BPDU, not just a superior one, causes interface errdisable and stops traffic on the port.

cards.front: Interface versus global BPDU-guard scope?
cards.back: `spanning-tree bpduguard enable`: the interface, independently of PortFast. `spanning-tree portfast bpduguard default`: operational PortFast ports.

cards.front: Safe recovery after BPDU-guard errdisable?
cards.back: Remove/correct the BPDU source, then `shutdown` / `no shutdown`, or use an explicitly enabled recovery policy. Verify traffic and roles afterward.

cards.front: Does the default 300-second errdisable interval enable recovery?
cards.back: No; the cause must be enabled separately. The discussed IOS range is 30–86400 seconds, but a configured interval alone does not enable retries.

cards.front: Which log evidence distinguishes BPDU guard from other errdisable causes?
cards.back: Look for the affected interface and the `bpduguard` cause, such as `BLOCK_BPDUGUARD` or an `ERR_DISABLE` line naming bpduguard.

cards.front: Root guard: trigger, state, and interface command?
cards.back: Superior BPDU information at the boundary → root inconsistency. Configure `spanning-tree guard root`.

cards.front: Where should root guard be placed?
cards.back: On a designated boundary toward a switch through which the root must not be learned; not on the legitimate root-facing uplink.

cards.front: How does root inconsistency recover?
cards.back: Automatically after superior information ceases and STP permits normal forwarding; correct the source rather than removing the guard to hide it.

cards.front: Loop guard: trigger, state, and configuration?
cards.back: Loss of expected BPDUs on an applicable root/alternate port → loop inconsistency. Interface `spanning-tree guard loop` or global `spanning-tree loopguard default`.

cards.front: What is the operational scope of loop guard?
cards.back: Applicable point-to-point root/alternate ports with received information to monitor; not ordinary host edges or shared segments.

cards.front: Root guard versus BPDU guard?
cards.back: Root guard reacts to superior information and blocks the affected instance; BPDU guard reacts to any BPDU and conventionally err-disables the port.

cards.front: Can root guard and loop guard operate on one interface together?
cards.back: No. Their designated versus root/alternate expectations differ, and IOS treats them as mutually exclusive.

cards.front: What does *ROOT_Inc in a Rapid PVST+ port row mean?
cards.back: Root inconsistency: a superior BPDU was rejected at a guarded boundary. It is not proof that the physical port is err-disabled.

cards.front: BPDU filter: interface form versus global PortFast form?
cards.back: Interface filtering suppresses BPDUs independently. Global PortFast filtering withdraws filtering/operational edge status on received BPDUs. Filter is explicit v1.1 context.

cards.front: Which commands inspect guards, defaults, and disabled-port causes?
cards.back: `show spanning-tree inconsistentports`, `show spanning-tree summary`, interface STP detail, `show interfaces status`, and `show logging`.

commands.task: On 2960-style IOS, make this genuine end-device access port a PortFast edge.
commands.note: STP remains active. IOS XE may use the explicit edge keyword.

commands.task: Enable PortFast on this trunk to a verified end device with no Layer 2 transit path.
commands.note: A trunk toward another transit switch must not be treated as an edge.

commands.task: Enable the global PortFast default for nontrunking ports.
commands.note: Check exceptions and actual operational trunk state.

commands.task: Configure this interface to err-disable when any BPDU is received, independently of PortFast.
commands.note: Interface scope differs from the global PortFast default.

commands.task: Enable BPDU guard by default on operational PortFast ports.
commands.note: The global default alone does not protect every non-PortFast trunk.

commands.task: Enable automatic errdisable recovery attempts for the BPDU-guard cause.
commands.note: Correct the BPDU source first; a recovery attempt can otherwise trigger another violation.

commands.task: Set the shared errdisable recovery interval to 60 seconds.
commands.note: Changing the interval does not enable a recovery cause.

commands.task: Protect this designated boundary against superior root information from downstream.
commands.note: Do not apply this to the legitimate root-facing uplink.

commands.task: Enable the global loop-guard default for applicable point-to-point interfaces.
commands.note: Protective action depends on an applicable root/alternate role and received information; it does not treat every quiet host port as failed.

commands.task: Enable loop guard on this point-to-point uplink expected to receive BPDUs.
commands.note: It cannot operate together with root guard on the same interface.

commands.task: Display STP inconsistent interfaces and their affected instances.
commands.note: Root/loop inconsistency belongs here; use interface status and logs for BPDU-guard errdisable.

commands.task: Display the STP mode and global PortFast and guard/filter defaults.
commands.note: Confirm individual operational ports separately; configured global defaults do not imply every port inherits them.

tickets.title: A conference-room port fails again after every reset
tickets.scenario: ASW3 Fa0/12 is a VLAN 30 host port covered by PortFast and BPDU-guard defaults. A desktop switch was recently added under the conference table. The help desk resets Fa0/12, but the room loses connectivity again shortly afterward. These are representative diagnosis exhibits.

exhibits.title: ASW3# show interfaces status — excerpt
exhibits.text: Fa0/12    Conference room     err-disabled 30           auto   auto 10/100BaseTX

exhibits.title: ASW3 log excerpt
exhibits.text:
%SPANTREE-2-BLOCK_BPDUGUARD: Received BPDU on port FastEthernet0/12 with BPDU Guard enabled. Disabling port.
%PM-4-ERR_DISABLE: bpduguard error detected on Fa0/12, putting Fa0/12 in err-disable state

exhibits.title: ASW3# show errdisable recovery — excerpt
exhibits.text:
bpduguard                     Disabled
Timer interval: 300 seconds

tickets.question: What explains the repeated failure after each manual reset?
options: The 300-second interval is too long for a normal Rapid PVST+ handshake.
The attached desktop switch continues supplying the BPDUs that trigger the guard.
The port is an alternate that should remain blocked until the root switch fails.
The absence of automatic recovery itself creates new BPDU-guard violations.
tickets.explanation: The log proves BPDU-guard reception on the same interface that becomes err-disabled. Resetting the interface while the BPDU source remains attached simply exposes it to another violation. Disabled automatic recovery explains why it stays down afterward, not why it repeatedly fails.
tickets.fix:
Remove the unexpected switch and reconnect the authorized end device before recovery.
```ios ASW3
ASW3# configure terminal
ASW3(config)# interface fastethernet0/12
ASW3(config-if)# shutdown
ASW3(config-if)# no shutdown
ASW3(config-if)# end
ASW3# show interfaces status
ASW3# show logging
```
Retest host connectivity and confirm no new bpduguard event. If more ports are required, design an approved interswitch connection with its intended VLAN and STP policy instead of leaving a transit bridge on a protected host edge.

tickets.title: Only one VLAN fails behind the new lab switch
tickets.scenario: LAB1 connects through DSW1 Gi1/0/10, a trunk for VLANs 10 and 20. CORE is the intended VLAN 10 root at configurable priority 24576. LAB1 copied a priority-zero setting for VLAN 10 but uses defaults in VLAN 20. VLAN 20 works; VLAN 10 behind LAB1 fails. These are representative excerpts.

exhibits.title: DSW1# show spanning-tree inconsistentports — excerpt
exhibits.text: VLAN0010             GigabitEthernet1/0/10       Root Inconsistent

exhibits.title: LAB1 running configuration excerpt
exhibits.text:
spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst
spanning-tree vlan 10 priority 0

exhibits.title: DSW1 interface configuration excerpt
exhibits.text:
interface GigabitEthernet1/0/10
 switchport mode trunk
 switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20
 spanning-tree guard root

tickets.question: What is the cause of the VLAN 10 outage?
options: The allowed-VLAN list excludes VLAN 10 and therefore disables only that instance.
BPDU guard err-disabled the trunk after LAB1 sent any spanning-tree control frame.
LAB1 supplies superior root information, triggering root guard for VLAN 10.
Loop guard detected that LAB1 has stopped transmitting expected BPDUs.
tickets.explanation: The displayed root inconsistency and interface root-guard configuration identify the mechanism. LAB1's priority zero is lower than CORE's stated 24576, so the boundary blocks VLAN 10 rather than accept its claim. The differing VLAN 20 result is consistent with separate Rapid PVST+ instances.
tickets.fix:
Restore the intended downstream priority on LAB1; preserve the boundary protection.
```ios LAB1
LAB1# configure terminal
LAB1(config)# spanning-tree vlan 10 priority 32768
LAB1(config)# end
LAB1# show spanning-tree vlan 10
```
Then inspect `show spanning-tree inconsistentports` on DSW1 and verify VLAN 10 traffic. Recovery is automatic after superior information ceases and STP permits forwarding; no exact twenty-second guarantee or manual bounce is required.

tickets.title: The uplink stays connected but STP reports loop inconsistency
tickets.scenario: SW3 Gi0/1 is its VLAN 10 root port toward SW1 in an isolated line topology. It had received BPDUs normally. After a configuration change on SW1, the physical link remains connected but SW3 reports loop inconsistency. Read the supplied configuration and state together; the exhibits are representative.

exhibits.title: SW3 observations
exhibits.text:
Gi0/1 physical status: connected
VLAN0010  GigabitEthernet0/1  Loop Inconsistent

exhibits.title: SW3 interface configuration excerpt
exhibits.text:
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 switchport mode trunk
 spanning-tree guard loop

exhibits.title: SW1 interface configuration excerpt
exhibits.text:
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 description To SW3
 switchport mode trunk
 spanning-tree bpdufilter enable

tickets.question: Which explanation is supported by both the observed state and the peer configuration?
options: A new superior root BID forced BPDU guard to disable the physical uplink.
SW3's host IP address duplicates the root bridge MAC address in the BID.
The physical receive strand is certainly broken despite the filter setting.
Peer interface filtering stopped expected BPDUs, and loop guard blocked the instance.
tickets.explanation: The peer explicitly suppresses BPDUs on the relevant interface. SW3's loop-guard configuration and loop-inconsistent condition fit loss of previously received information. The state alone would not prove a physical fault, and this exhibit supplies a configuration cause to correct first.
tickets.fix:
Remove the unintended filter at the source, then observe recovery without disabling loop guard.
```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# no spanning-tree bpdufilter
SW1(config-if)# end
```
On SW3, check `show spanning-tree inconsistentports` and `show spanning-tree interface gigabitethernet0/1 detail`. Expected BPDUs should resume, inconsistency should clear, and user traffic should recover. Save only the corrected policy.
