lab.title: Verify an access-port security policy
devices: RA guard extension: supported Catalyst switch, two IPv6 routers and test PC
lab.intro:
Build a working IPv4 LAN, apply one control at a time, and diagnose a controlled failure from its evidence. The final exercise covers IPv6 RA guard. Keep the exercises on an isolated lab network.

Record your Packet Tracer version and check the selected switch's command help. It implements a subset of IOS; DHCP snooping, DAI, ARP ACL and storm-control support vary by simulated device and version. If a required command is missing, use a supporting image or switch, or complete that step as an interpretation exercise and record it as **not executed**. For v2.0, return to any unexecuted configuration objective on a supporting platform.
lab.topology:
| Connection | SW1 port | Endpoint addressing |
|---|---|---|
| R1 Gi0/0 | Gi0/1 | `10.1.10.1/24`, gateway and DHCP server |
| PC-A FastEthernet0 | Fa0/1 | DHCP |
| PC-B FastEthernet0 | Fa0/2 initially | DHCP; temporarily substitutes for PC-A |
| PRINTER FastEthernet0 | Fa0/3 | `10.1.10.20/24`, gateway `10.1.10.1` |

Use copper straight-through cables. All four switch ports are access ports in VLAN 10. R1 excludes `.1` through `.49`, keeping the static printer outside the allocation range. Record your actual leases and MAC addresses.

```diagram
{"type":"topology","title":"One controlled server path","caption":"Only Gi0/1 receives legitimate DHCP server replies on SW1.","nodes":[{"id":"R1","kind":"router","label":"R1","sub":"10.1.10.1/24","x":6,"y":0.5},{"id":"SW1","kind":"switch","label":"SW1","sub":"VLAN 10","x":6,"y":3,"highlight":true},{"id":"A","kind":"pc","label":"PC-A","sub":"DHCP","x":2,"y":5.5},{"id":"B","kind":"pc","label":"PC-B","sub":"DHCP","x":6,"y":5.5},{"id":"P","kind":"printer","label":"PRINTER","sub":"10.1.10.20/24","x":10,"y":5.5}],"links":[{"from":"R1","to":"SW1","fromLabel":"Gi0/0","toLabel":"Gi0/1","accent":true},{"from":"A","to":"SW1","toLabel":"Fa0/1"},{"from":"B","to":"SW1","toLabel":"Fa0/2"},{"from":"P","to":"SW1","toLabel":"Fa0/3"}]}
```

steps.title: Establish a working LAN
steps.body:
Set the printer's address and gateway in its Config tab. Configure R1 and SW1:

```ios R1
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R1
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.1.10.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# ip dhcp excluded-address 10.1.10.1 10.1.10.49
R1(config)# ip dhcp pool USERS
R1(dhcp-config)# network 10.1.10.0 255.255.255.0
R1(dhcp-config)# default-router 10.1.10.1
R1(dhcp-config)# end
R1# show ip interface brief
```

```ios SW1
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname SW1
SW1(config)# vlan 10
SW1(config-vlan)# name USERS
SW1(config-vlan)# exit
SW1(config)# interface range fastethernet0/1 - 3
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport access vlan 10
SW1(config-if-range)# exit
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if)# switchport access vlan 10
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show vlan brief
```

On each PC select Desktop → IP Configuration → DHCP. Record `ipconfig /all`, then ping `10.1.10.1` and `10.1.10.20`. Wait for ports to forward and repeat initial pings if ARP resolution consumed an attempt. Record the printer's MAC from its interface information.

:::expected
R1 Gi0/0 is up/up and the switch ports belong to VLAN 10. The PCs have unique addresses in the pool and gateway `10.1.10.1`; both reach the gateway and printer. Correct this baseline before continuing.
:::

steps.title: Learn the authorized MAC
steps.body:
Leave only PC-A attached to Fa0/1. Enable sticky learning and send another PC-A ping.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# switchport port-security
SW1(config-if)# switchport port-security mac-address sticky
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show port-security interface fastethernet0/1
SW1# show port-security address
SW1# show running-config interface fastethernet0/1
```

If the image rejects the interface-specific running-config command, find the block in `show running-config`. Compare the learned address with PC-A's actual MAC before saving.

:::expected
Fa0/1 is secure-up with maximum 1, shutdown violation mode and PC-A's sticky entry in running configuration. Its presence there does not establish that startup configuration contains it.
:::

steps.title: Trigger a MAC-limit violation
steps.body:
Disconnect PC-B from Fa0/2 and PC-A from Fa0/1. Connect PC-B to Fa0/1 and generate traffic. Keep PC-A's sticky entry and the existing maximum. Inspect `show port-security interface fastethernet0/1` and `show interfaces status`.

:::expected
PC-B presents a different source MAC while the one permitted entry belongs to PC-A. Shutdown mode error-disables the port; the security display indicates secure-shutdown and a violation. The whole port stops forwarding. If it remains up, verify the actual MACs and that PC-B transmitted.
:::

steps.title: Correct the cause and recover
steps.body:
Restore PC-A to Fa0/1 and PC-B to Fa0/2, then reset the affected port:

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# shutdown
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show port-security interface fastethernet0/1
```

Ping the gateway from PC-A. Keep maximum 1 because that is the intended policy here. Automatic error recovery cannot correct an unauthorized device that remains attached.

:::expected
Fa0/1 returns to secure-up and PC-A regains service. Historical violation counters may remain; verify current state and a fresh traffic test.
:::

steps.title: Establish snooping and fresh bindings
steps.body:
This simple design does not use Option 82 for server policy. Disable its insertion explicitly and trust the interface receiving R1's replies. Client ports remain untrusted.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# ip dhcp snooping
SW1(config)# ip dhcp snooping vlan 10
SW1(config)# no ip dhcp snooping information option
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# ip dhcp snooping trust
SW1(config-if)# exit
SW1(config)# interface range fastethernet0/1 - 2
SW1(config-if-range)# ip dhcp snooping limit rate 15
SW1(config-if-range)# end
SW1# show ip dhcp snooping
```

Run `ipconfig /release` and `ipconfig /renew` on each PC. If unavailable, use its IP Configuration controls to request a fresh lease. Compare `show ip dhcp snooping binding` on SW1 with `show ip dhcp binding` on R1. The server lease table and switch binding table are separate records.

:::expected
Snooping covers VLAN 10, Gi0/1 is trusted, and each PC has a binding with its actual IP, MAC, VLAN and access port. No dynamic binding is expected for the static printer. A lease acquired before snooping was enabled does not establish a switch binding.
:::

steps.title: Observe a missing server-trust fault
steps.body:
```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# no ip dhcp snooping trust
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show ip dhcp snooping
```

Release PC-B's lease and request a new one. Where supported, inspect snooping statistics or use Simulation mode filtered to DHCP to follow R1's reply into SW1. Retaining an old lease does not test the new policy.

:::expected
A fresh DHCP exchange cannot complete through the now-untrusted server ingress, even though R1's interface and pool can be operational. The configuration and reply-path evidence identify the cause; a failed lease alone would not.
:::

steps.title: Restore the permitted reply path
steps.body:
```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# ip dhcp snooping trust
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show ip dhcp snooping
```

Renew PC-B's lease, inspect its binding and ping the gateway. Do not make every port trusted as a workaround.

:::expected
The fresh lease completes and PC-B's binding names Fa0/2 and VLAN 10. Only Gi0/1 has server trust.
:::

steps.title: Enable DAI and investigate the static host
steps.body:
Confirm both PC bindings first. Trust ARP from the controlled router connection separately, then enable inspection.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# ip arp inspection trust
SW1(config-if)# exit
SW1(config)# ip arp inspection vlan 10
SW1(config)# end
SW1# show ip arp inspection vlan 10
SW1# show ip arp inspection interfaces
SW1# show ip arp inspection statistics vlan 10
```

Ping the gateway from both DHCP clients. For a fresh printer ARP exchange, clear PC-B's printer entry with `arp -d 10.1.10.20` if supported, or restart only PC-B and renew its lease. Ping the printer and compare DAI counters before and after. Existing ARP caches can temporarily conceal the missing binding.

:::expected
The DHCP clients' valid ARP claims pass. The printer has no snooping binding, so its fresh ARP claim entering Fa0/3 is rejected by the binding check. A legitimate static host needs an explicit exception; this result does not establish malicious activity.
:::

steps.title: Permit the printer's verified pair
steps.body:
Substitute the printer's actual MAC recorded in Step 1. The following example assumes `000c.2911.7a3e`.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# arp access-list STATIC-HOSTS
SW1(config-arp-nacl)# permit ip host 10.1.10.20 mac host 000c.2911.7a3e
SW1(config-arp-nacl)# exit
SW1(config)# ip arp inspection filter STATIC-HOSTS vlan 10
SW1(config)# end
SW1# show arp access-list STATIC-HOSTS
SW1# show ip arp inspection vlan 10
SW1# show ip arp inspection statistics vlan 10
```

Repeat a fresh printer ping and the client gateway tests. Omitting `static` allows ACL nonmatches to continue to DHCP-binding validation. Adding it would make the ACL's implicit denial final, blocking unlisted DHCP clients.

:::expected
The verified printer pair passes and DHCP clients still work. Fa0/3 remains untrusted: the ACL authorizes a specific claim instead of bypassing inspection on the entire port.
:::

steps.title: Interpret storm-control thresholds
steps.body:
```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/2
SW1(config-if)# storm-control broadcast level 1.00 0.50
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show storm-control fastethernet0/2 broadcast
```

Record the thresholds. Interpret this authored observation: broadcast utilization reaches 3.2%, falls to 0.7%, then falls to 0.3%. Suppression begins at the rising threshold and forwarding resumes below the falling threshold. The intermediate 0.7% is still above recovery. Hardware measurement and reporting vary; these observations are a worksheet, not captured results. Do not create a switching loop.

:::expected
The policy shows rising 1.00% and falling 0.50%. Its default action filters the controlled traffic type; it does not automatically shut down the port. Normal low-volume client traffic still works.
:::

steps.title: Configure and verify IPv6 RA guard
steps.body:
Use a separate isolated LAN and a supporting switch; the command reference is Catalyst 9300 with IOS XE 17.12. Connect a test PC to SW-H Gi1/0/1, legitimate R1 Gi0/0 to Gi1/0/24, and test R2 Gi0/0 to Gi1/0/4. Use compatible copper media and substitute verified interface names for your hardware. All three switch ports use access VLAN 10.

Before configuring the feature, run `show version` and `show sdm prefer` on SW-H. Confirm a supported image and an active resource template that accommodates IPv6; the cited 9300 Access template supports IPv6 entries. If this isolated 9300 needs that template selected, enter `sdm prefer access` in global configuration, return to EXEC, save with `copy running-config startup-config`, and `reload` before starting the exercise. Verify the active template after restart. A pending template change is not yet active, and template names on other Catalyst families differ. Do not apply a 2960-specific SDM command to the 9300 by assumption.

The supplied router setup enables advertisements on this LAN. Explicit link-local addresses identify their sources. Chapter 19 explains IPv6 addressing and neighbor discovery in detail.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ipv6 unicast-routing
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ipv6 address fe80::1 link-local
R1(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001:db8:16:10::1/64
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
```

```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# ipv6 unicast-routing
R2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R2(config-if)# ipv6 address fe80::2 link-local
R2(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001:db8:16:99::1/64
R2(config-if)# shutdown
R2(config-if)# end
```

```ios SW-H
SW-H# configure terminal
SW-H(config)# vlan 10
SW-H(config-vlan)# exit
SW-H(config)# interface range gigabitethernet1/0/1, gigabitethernet1/0/4, gigabitethernet1/0/24
SW-H(config-if-range)# switchport mode access
SW-H(config-if-range)# switchport access vlan 10
SW-H(config-if-range)# exit
SW-H(config)# ipv6 nd raguard policy ENDPOINTS
SW-H(config-nd-raguard)# device-role host
SW-H(config-nd-raguard)# exit
SW-H(config)# ipv6 nd raguard policy ROUTERS
SW-H(config-nd-raguard)# device-role router
SW-H(config-nd-raguard)# exit
SW-H(config)# interface range gigabitethernet1/0/1, gigabitethernet1/0/4
SW-H(config-if-range)# ipv6 nd raguard attach-policy ENDPOINTS
SW-H(config-if-range)# exit
SW-H(config)# interface gigabitethernet1/0/24
SW-H(config-if)# ipv6 nd raguard attach-policy ROUTERS
SW-H(config-if)# end
SW-H# show ipv6 nd raguard policy ENDPOINTS
SW-H# show ipv6 nd raguard policy ROUTERS
SW-H# show running-config interface gigabitethernet1/0/4
```

Enable automatic IPv6 configuration on the PC. In Wireshark, choose the adapter cabled to this lab, start capture, and enter display filter `icmpv6.type == 134` for RAs. Confirm an RA from `fe80::1`; record the PC's IPv6 address and default router in its OS network settings or Windows `ipconfig /all`. Enable R2 Gi0/0 with `no shutdown`. Allow for the advertisement interval. Absence of R2's packets at the PC alone would not prove filtering, so establish the permitted comparison next.

On this isolated topology, enter interface Gi1/0/4 configuration on SW-H and remove the attachment with `no ipv6 nd raguard attach-policy ENDPOINTS`. Observe an RA sourced from `fe80::2` at the PC. That permitted capture proves R2 is transmitting across the intended path. Record its observed interval, restore `ipv6 nd raguard attach-policy ENDPOINTS` on Gi1/0/4, and compare a new capture over several of those intervals: fresh R2 RAs should no longer arrive while R1 RAs still do. Keep the cables and R2 configuration unchanged during the comparison. Previously learned addresses and default routes can remain until their lifetimes expire; immediate removal is not the pass criterion. Shut R2's interface when finished.

:::expected
Both policies exist and are attached correctly. The host policy blocks R2's RAs at ingress; the router policy permits the legitimate role. The comparison establishes transmission, a permitted baseline and a blocked result. If your platform cannot execute this exercise, record the interpretation separately and leave hands-on completion pending.
:::

steps.title: Save the verified result
steps.body:
Repeat fresh DHCP leases, gateway pings and printer communication in the IPv4 lab. Check port-security state, both trust settings, bindings, DAI counters and the storm threshold. Save SW1 and R1 with `copy running-config startup-config`; accept the destination filename prompt with Enter. Save the Packet Tracer project too. In the extension, restore RA guard, shut R2's test interface and save each participating device.

:::expected
Your notes include versions, actual addresses, evidence before and after each repair, and any unexecuted feature. Saving configuration preserves sticky entries present in it; it does not automatically preserve the operational DHCP snooping database after a restart. Database persistence needs a separately supported configuration.
:::

lab.troubleshooting:
| Symptom | Check |
|---|---|
| PC-A immediately violates again | Correct endpoint, actual MAC and sticky entry; a reset cannot correct a mismatch |
| No fresh lease | VLAN, server reply path, pool and Option 82 policy; a self-assigned address alone does not identify the fault |
| DAI blocks a DHCP client | Current IP/MAC/VLAN/port binding and the relevant counters |
| Printer still blocked | Actual MAC, ACL permit, VLAN application and unintended final implicit denial |
| All ARP on a busy port stops | Error-disable reason and rate policy; individual validation drops differ from a rate-limit shutdown |
| RA policy exists but RAs pass | Attachment on the actual ingress port, role, VLAN path and whether these are fresh advertisements |
| Legitimate IPv6 setup is delayed | Router-facing role, solicitation forwarding and observed advertisements |
lab.challenge:
Add a downstream SW2 to the paper topology, connecting its Gi0/1 to SW1 Fa0/4. Its clients use R1's server. Mark the ingress ports needing DHCP server trust on each switch and explain why SW1's downlink need not be trusted merely because it connects another switch. State where Option 82 is inserted or disabled and how the upstream policy handles it. Explain why these DHCP choices do not automatically establish a correct DAI or RA guard policy.

:::expected
Trust SW1 Gi0/1, where R1's replies enter, and SW2 Gi0/1, where replies from upstream enter SW2. Keep SW1 Fa0/4 and the client ports untrusted for DHCP server messages. In this simple design, enable snooping for VLAN 10 and disable Option 82 insertion on both switches. If the design instead inserts Option 82 at SW2, the upstream handling must explicitly permit the intended relay information without blindly granting server trust to the downlink. DAI needs its own trust and binding/ARP-ACL plan; SW1 can inspect downstream claims if it has the required bindings, while a controlled upstream bypass on SW2 is a separate design decision. IPv6 RA guard needs host/router roles and attachments independently of either IPv4 feature.
:::

exhibit.title: SW1: port-security status (excerpt)
exhibit.text:
Port Status             : Secure-shutdown
Violation Mode          : Shutdown
Maximum MAC Addresses   : 1
Total MAC Addresses     : 1
Sticky MAC Addresses    : 1
Security Violation Count: 1

questions.prompt: PC-A is the authorized sticky device. After a different PC is connected to Fa0/1, the exhibit is recorded. Which action restores the intended one-device policy?
options: Leave the new PC connected and clear all sticky entries
Keep the new PC connected and raise the maximum to two
Reconnect PC-A, then shut and re-enable Fa0/1
Reconnect PC-A and wait for the default automatic recovery
questions.explanation: Secure-shutdown identifies a shutdown-mode violation. Restore the authorized endpoint before resetting the interface; otherwise the same cause can immediately recur.

whyWrong.0: Clearing the approved entry would allow a different device to be learned and changes the intended policy.
whyWrong.1: Increasing the limit authorizes additional addresses instead of restoring the specified one-device policy.
whyWrong.3: Automatic recovery for this cause must be enabled; it is not established by the exhibit.

questions.prompt: Which mode discards violating frames and records violations while continuing to forward traffic from secure MAC addresses?
options: restrict
protect
shutdown
disabled
questions.explanation: Restrict preserves service for permitted addresses while dropping violating traffic and providing violation reporting.

whyWrong.1: Protect drops violating traffic without restrict's counter and notification behavior.
whyWrong.2: Shutdown error-disables the port, affecting permitted traffic too.
whyWrong.3: Disabling port security removes this enforcement.

questions.prompt: On the documented Catalyst default configuration, which two settings apply after port security is enabled? (Choose two.)
options: The maximum is one secure MAC
The violation mode is restrict
Sticky learning is enabled
The violation mode is shutdown
The aging interval is five minutes
questions.explanation: The documented defaults are maximum 1 and shutdown mode. Port security itself must be enabled; sticky learning and address aging are separate choices.

whyWrong.1: Restrict requires an explicit configuration.
whyWrong.2: Enabling port security does not enable sticky learning.
whyWrong.4: Default aging time is 0, meaning disabled.

exhibit.title: SW1 command result
exhibit.text:
SW1(config-if)# switchport port-security
Command rejected: FastEthernet0/1 is a dynamic port.

questions.prompt: Fa0/1 connects one untagged PC. What should be corrected before retrying port security?
options: Enable trunk negotiation on the PC
Set the port to static access mode
Configure a native VLAN on the PC
Enable port security globally
questions.explanation: The port is still in a dynamic switchport mode. For this endpoint, configure `switchport mode access`, verify its access VLAN, then enable port security.

whyWrong.0: A normal untagged PC does not negotiate a trunk.
whyWrong.2: Native-VLAN configuration does not repair the dynamic-mode restriction.
whyWrong.3: Port security is enabled per interface; a global enable command is not the solution.

questions.prompt: A sticky address was learned after the last configuration save. No later save occurred before power was lost. What should you expect after restart?
options: The unsaved address becomes a permanent static entry
The switch restores it from its ordinary MAC table
The address persists because sticky means nonvolatile
Startup configuration does not contain that new address
questions.explanation: Sticky learning adds a configuration entry to running configuration. Persistence depends on saving that entry to startup configuration before the restart.

whyWrong.0: Learning does not convert the address into an independently persistent static entry.
whyWrong.1: The ordinary forwarding table is not a backup for unsaved configuration.
whyWrong.2: Sticky describes the learning/configuration behavior, not automatic saving.

questions.prompt: R1 serves DHCP. SW1 Gi0/1 connects to R1; SW1 Gi0/2 connects to downstream SW2 Gi0/1. Clients are below SW2. Both switches have snooping enabled and Option 82 insertion disabled. Which server-trust placement fits this reply path?
options: Trust both ports on SW1 and every client port on SW2
Trust only SW1 Gi0/2 because it is the inter-switch link
Trust SW1 Gi0/1 and SW2 Gi0/1; leave SW1 Gi0/2 untrusted
Leave both uplinks untrusted and trust only client ports
questions.explanation: Trust is an ingress decision. R1's replies enter SW1 on Gi0/1 and enter SW2 on its Gi0/1. SW1's downlink receives client traffic and does not need server trust merely because it connects another switch.

whyWrong.0: Trusting client ports permits server messages from endpoints and expands the boundary unnecessarily.
whyWrong.1: The server reply actually enters SW1 on Gi0/1; downstream connectivity alone does not identify a trusted ingress.
whyWrong.3: This permits the wrong direction and leaves legitimate server replies blocked.

exhibit.title: Authored server diagnostic summary
exhibit.text:
Request received: giaddr 0.0.0.0, relay-agent information (Option 82) present
Request rejected by relay-information trust policy

questions.prompt: The server-facing switch port is trusted. The isolated lab does not use relay-agent information for policy, and the server records the exhibit. Which switch change removes the explicitly observed cause?
options: Disable DHCP snooping on every VLAN
Make all client-facing interfaces trusted
Configure a new DHCP default gateway
Disable Option 82 insertion on the switch
questions.explanation: The evidence specifically identifies Option 82 with a zero relay address on a path the server does not trust. In this stated design, `no ip dhcp snooping information option` removes the unused inserted information. Other designs may deliberately retain it and configure an appropriate server/relay trust policy.

whyWrong.0: Removing all snooping also removes the required access-layer protection.
whyWrong.1: Client trust does not establish a correct relay-information policy and would permit unauthorized server replies.
whyWrong.2: The gateway option does not repair rejection of the DHCP request.

exhibit.title: SW1 relevant configuration
exhibit.text:
ip dhcp snooping
ip dhcp snooping vlan 20
ip arp inspection vlan 10
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 ip dhcp snooping trust
 ip arp inspection trust
!
DHCP snooping binding table: 0 entries

questions.prompt: Clients in VLAN 10 have leases, but their fresh ARP requests are dropped after DAI is enabled. Which correction addresses the missing source of bindings shown here?
options: Enable snooping for VLAN 10, then obtain fresh client leases
Disable the clients' default gateways and renew their leases
Add VLAN 20 to every client access port without changing IPs
Enable sticky MAC learning on every client-facing port
questions.explanation: DAI is inspecting VLAN 10, while snooping is configured only for VLAN 20. Enable snooping on VLAN 10 and verify new bindings from fresh leases before retesting ARP.

whyWrong.1: A gateway option does not populate the switch binding table.
whyWrong.2: Moving clients changes the intended LAN and does not correct its missing protection policy.
whyWrong.3: Port-security entries do not replace DHCP snooping bindings for DAI.

questions.prompt: Which two statements correctly describe DAI? (Choose two.)
options: DHCP snooping trust automatically makes an interface ARP trusted
DHCP bindings can validate a client's sender IP/MAC claim
An explicit ARP ACL can permit a verified static host
DAI authenticates the user who owns a MAC address
Every inter-switch trunk must bypass ARP inspection
questions.explanation: DAI can use snooping bindings and configured ARP ACLs. Its interface trust is independent of DHCP snooping trust, and trust placement follows the actual design.

whyWrong.0: `ip arp inspection trust` is a separate interface setting.
whyWrong.3: Validating an address claim is not user authentication.
whyWrong.4: A trunk's existence does not establish that all ARP arriving on it should bypass inspection.

questions.prompt: Which optional DAI validation detects an Ethernet source MAC that differs from the ARP sender hardware address?
options: ip
dst-mac
src-mac
lease-time
questions.explanation: `src-mac` compares the Ethernet source with the sender MAC inside ARP. It supplements the underlying binding or ACL validation.

whyWrong.0: The `ip` option checks invalid IP-address values in ARP fields, not this MAC comparison.
whyWrong.1: The `dst-mac` check compares the Ethernet destination with the ARP target MAC in replies.
whyWrong.3: Lease time is binding information, not this validation keyword.

questions.prompt: A verified static printer has no snooping binding. Its ARP is rejected on an untrusted port. DHCP clients in the same VLAN must still use their bindings. Which change is appropriate?
options: Exclude the printer from the DHCP allocation pool only
Permit its exact IP/MAC in an applied ARP ACL without `static`
Add its MAC to the switch's ordinary forwarding table only
Apply an ARP ACL with `static` and list only the printer
questions.explanation: An exact ARP ACL permit can admit the static printer. Without the `static` application keyword, an ACL nonmatch can fall back to the snooping database, preserving validation for DHCP clients.

whyWrong.0: An exclusion prevents DHCP allocation; it does not create a DAI authorization.
whyWrong.2: A Layer 2 forwarding entry does not establish a valid ARP sender IP/MAC pair.
whyWrong.3: Here `static` makes the ACL's implicit denial final, so unlisted DHCP clients lose the fallback.

exhibit.title: SW1 interface configuration
exhibit.text: storm-control broadcast level 1.00 0.50

questions.prompt: The broadcast level crossed the rising threshold. It now measures 0.7%. Under the displayed policy, what is the threshold interpretation?
options: Suppression continues until it falls below 0.50%
The port is necessarily error-disabled at 0.7%
Forwarding resumes whenever the rate falls below 1.00%
All unicast traffic is discarded at the same threshold
questions.explanation: After suppression begins, the falling threshold governs recovery. 0.7% is above 0.50%. Exact sampling and counter presentation depend on the hardware.

whyWrong.1: A threshold alone does not specify a shutdown action; filtering is the documented default.
whyWrong.2: The separately configured falling threshold prevents immediate recovery at the rising threshold.
whyWrong.3: This policy selects broadcast traffic, not all unicast.

questions.prompt: No explicit storm-control action is configured. What is the documented default response when broadcast suppression is triggered?
options: Shut down the entire switch
Convert broadcasts to unicasts
Disable spanning tree on the port
Filter the controlled traffic type
questions.explanation: The default action filters the storm-controlled traffic. Treat this as suppression, not a guarantee that precisely the excess percentage is discarded; implementation and measurement depend on the platform.

whyWrong.0: The default does not power off or shut down the entire switch.
whyWrong.1: Storm control does not rewrite broadcasts into unicast traffic.
whyWrong.2: It does not disable spanning tree.

questions.prompt: An RA guard policy with `device-role host` has been defined, but unwanted router advertisements still enter through an endpoint port with no attached policy. What is missing?
options: A DHCP snooping binding for the IPv6 router
The policy attachment on the actual ingress interface
A larger port-security maximum for the IPv6 host
An IPv4 ARP ACL for the router's link-local address
questions.explanation: Defining the policy does not enforce it on an interface. Apply `ipv6 nd raguard attach-policy NAME` to the intended endpoint ingress and verify the policy and attachment.

whyWrong.0: IPv4 DHCP snooping bindings do not activate RA guard.
whyWrong.2: A MAC count does not decide whether IPv6 router advertisements are permitted.
whyWrong.3: IPv4 ARP inspection does not validate IPv6 RAs.

questions.prompt: Why can a large number of forged source MAC addresses create a Layer 2 security concern?
options: They make every VLAN share one routing table
They automatically replace every static ARP entry
They can pressure learning resources and increase unknown-unicast flooding
They require the switch to copy every frame to every physical port
questions.explanation: Excess source addresses can consume MAC-learning resources. If destinations are unknown, frames may be flooded to eligible forwarding ports in that VLAN. The scope and device response depend on the platform and configuration.

whyWrong.0: MAC learning does not merge VLAN routing tables.
whyWrong.1: Learning source MACs does not automatically replace every host's static ARP mapping.
whyWrong.3: Known unicast, VLAN boundaries and forwarding state still matter; universal flooding is an overstatement.

questions.prompt: In the documented RA guard design, which two actions support a valid verification? (Choose two.)
options: Attach the host policy to the endpoint ingress
Judge success from the policy name alone
Confirm the legitimate router-facing role and fresh permitted RAs
Assume DHCP snooping also validates IPv6 RAs
Require old SLAAC addresses to disappear immediately
questions.explanation: Verification needs the attachment on the real ingress and evidence that authorized advertisements still pass. Old host state can remain for its advertised lifetime, so fresh packet behavior is the stronger test.

whyWrong.1: A policy can exist without being applied anywhere.
whyWrong.3: These are separate features protecting different traffic.
whyWrong.4: Previously learned addresses and routes need not vanish immediately when future RAs are blocked.

cards.front: On the documented Catalyst platform, what are the initial port-security settings after enablement?
cards.back: Maximum 1 secure MAC, violation mode shutdown and aging time 0 (disabled). Sticky learning is separate.

cards.front: What switchport mode should precede port security for one untagged PC?
cards.back: Use static access mode and the intended access VLAN. A dynamically negotiated switchport mode can prevent port-security configuration. Supported trunk use is platform dependent.

cards.front: What does protect mode do?
cards.back: Drops violating traffic while leaving permitted traffic forwarding, without restrict-mode violation counting and notifications.

cards.front: What does restrict mode add to protect mode?
cards.back: Violation counting and reporting while the port remains available for permitted source MACs.

cards.front: What does shutdown mode do to a violating port?
cards.back: Error-disables the port, stopping its forwarding. Inspect secure-shutdown/error-disable state and the recorded cause; a fixed counter value is not a universal diagnostic requirement.

cards.front: How does a newly learned sticky MAC survive restart?
cards.back: It appears as a sticky entry in running configuration. Save that configuration to startup configuration after verifying the address.

cards.front: How do static, dynamic and sticky secure addresses differ?
cards.back: Static: explicitly configured. Dynamic: learned operationally without a configuration entry. Sticky: learned into running configuration and retained across restart only if saved.

cards.front: How should a shutdown-mode violation be recovered?
cards.back: Correct the cause, then shut and re-enable the interface. Timed recovery is an optional global policy for the specific cause, not an automatic repair of a persistent violation.

cards.front: How do absolute and inactivity aging differ?
cards.back: Absolute aging uses elapsed age; inactivity aging requires the configured interval without traffic from the address. Default aging is disabled. Sticky-address aging is unsupported on the cited Catalyst platform; check the actual image.

cards.front: Which two settings enable snooping for VLAN 10?
cards.back: Global `ip dhcp snooping` and `ip dhcp snooping vlan 10`. Then establish a correct server-reply trust path.

cards.front: Which interfaces should receive DHCP snooping trust?
cards.back: Interfaces where legitimate server replies enter that switch. Trust is an ingress decision; a trunk or switch-to-switch cable alone is not sufficient justification.

cards.front: What does a DHCP snooping binding associate?
cards.back: A client MAC and IPv4 address with lease information, VLAN and access interface. It is learned from observed DHCP operation, not from every host that happens to have an address.

cards.front: Does DHCP failure after enabling snooping prove an Option 82 problem?
cards.back: No. Check the VLAN, reply ingress, pool and observed exchange. If logs show rejected inserted Option 82 with zero giaddr, choose a supported relay-information policy or disable insertion when the design does not use it.

cards.front: What does `ip dhcp snooping limit rate 15` configure?
cards.back: An interface DHCP-message limit of 15 packets/s on the documented platform. Exceeding it can error-disable the interface. Choose limits for actual traffic; aggregate links can carry many clients.

cards.front: How does DAI validate ARP on an untrusted interface?
cards.back: It checks sender claims against snooping bindings or an applied ARP ACL, with optional additional validation. Its trust setting is independent of DHCP snooping trust.

cards.front: What DAI rate defaults apply on the cited Catalyst configuration?
cards.back: Untrusted ports: 15 ARP packets/s with a 1-second burst interval. Trusted ports: unlimited by default. An exceeded rate can error-disable the interface; verify the actual device policy.

cards.front: What do the optional DAI checks validate?
cards.back: `src-mac`: Ethernet source versus ARP sender MAC. `dst-mac`: Ethernet destination versus ARP target MAC in replies. `ip`: invalid ARP IP values. Enter the intended complete check set; a later command can replace it.

cards.front: What does `static` mean when applying a DAI ARP ACL?
cards.back: It makes the ACL's implicit denial final. Without it, an ACL nonmatch can fall back to DHCP bindings. It does not mean that the ACL is required to authorize a static-IP host.

cards.front: How should rising and falling storm thresholds be read?
cards.back: The rising threshold triggers suppression; the falling threshold controls recovery. The default action filters the controlled traffic type. Exact measurement behavior depends on hardware, so do not assume precise excess-only trimming.

cards.front: What is required beyond defining an RA guard host policy?
cards.back: Attach it to the intended endpoint ingress. Establish the legitimate router-facing role too, then verify fresh blocked and permitted advertisements; old host state can outlive the change.

commands.task: Enable port security on the interface, which is already a static access port.
commands.note: Verify the endpoint and the default one-address, shutdown policy.

commands.task: The approved design requires exactly two observed secure entries on this port. Set its total maximum.
commands.note: The number follows observed endpoint/VLAN behavior; phone-plus-PC is not a universal two-entry guarantee.

commands.task: Enable learning of secure MAC addresses into running configuration.
commands.note: Verify learned identities before saving to startup configuration.

commands.task: Drop and report violating frames while preserving forwarding for permitted addresses.
commands.note: Shutdown mode instead error-disables the port.

commands.task: Enable the approved automatic-recovery policy for port-security error-disable events.
commands.note: This enables a specific cause. The documented default interval is 300 seconds; the underlying violation still needs correction.

commands.task: Inspect Fa0/1 port-security state, configured maximum and violations.
commands.note: Use current port state and fresh traffic tests alongside historical counters.

commands.task: Snooping is globally enabled. Add VLAN 10 to its inspection list.
commands.note: Both global and VLAN enablement are required.

commands.task: Legitimate DHCP server replies enter on this interface. Configure snooping trust here.
commands.note: Server trust follows reply ingress, not every trunk.

commands.task: This lab does not use Option 82 for server policy. Disable the switch's insertion of it.
commands.answer: no ip dhcp snooping information option
commands.note: This is an explicit design choice, not a universal repair whenever DHCP fails.

commands.task: Bindings and the separate ARP trust policy are verified. Enable DAI for VLAN 10.
commands.note: Plan verified static-host exceptions before enforcing binding checks.

commands.task: Set broadcast storm thresholds to 1% rising and 0.5% falling.
commands.note: Rising controls entry into suppression; falling controls recovery.

commands.task: Attach the existing RA guard policy HOSTS to this endpoint interface.
commands.note: The policy must have the intended host role; inspect both definition and attachment.

commands.task: Display learned DHCP snooping client bindings.
commands.note: Compare IP, MAC, VLAN and interface with the actual client.

commands.task: Display the RA guard policy named HOSTS on a supporting Catalyst.
commands.answer: show ipv6 nd raguard policy HOSTS
commands.note: A correct policy definition alone does not prove attachment or packet enforcement.

tickets.title: DHCP fails after snooping is enabled
tickets.scenario: ASW3 has one uplink, Gi0/2, to a distribution switch that relays client requests to DHCP. VLAN 10 clients cannot complete fresh leases after snooping is enabled. The upstream capture confirms a valid server reply reaches ASW3 Gi0/2. Option 82 insertion is disabled in this lab.

exhibits.title: ASW3 relevant configuration
exhibits.text:
ip dhcp snooping
ip dhcp snooping vlan 10
no ip dhcp snooping information option
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/2
 switchport mode trunk
 switchport trunk allowed vlan 10
!
interface FastEthernet0/1
 switchport mode access
 switchport access vlan 10

exhibits.title: Authored verification observations
exhibits.text:
Gi0/2: up, VLAN 10 forwarding
DHCP snooping: Gi0/2 untrusted
Valid DHCP Offer reaches Gi0/2; snooping records a server-message drop
Client binding table: empty

tickets.question: Which fault is established by the combined evidence?
options: The client-facing port lacks a sticky MAC entry
The DHCP pool must be using the wrong subnet mask
The legitimate reply arrives on an untrusted ingress
Option 82 insertion must be enabled on every client
tickets.explanation: The evidence locates a valid Offer at Gi0/2 and a snooping drop on that untrusted ingress. The necessary repair is server trust on this verified reply path. The exhibit does not establish a pool, port-security or Option 82 requirement.
tickets.fix:
```ios ASW3
ASW3# configure terminal
ASW3(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/2
ASW3(config-if)# ip dhcp snooping trust
ASW3(config-if)# end
ASW3# show ip dhcp snooping
```
Request a fresh client lease, inspect `show ip dhcp snooping binding`, and test the gateway. Keep client ports untrusted. Save only after the intended path and successful lease are verified.

tickets.title: A phone and PC exceed the permitted MAC total
tickets.scenario: Fa0/7 serves an approved phone and attached PC. Both lose network service when the PC starts transmitting. Inventory and a previous permitted capture establish that this particular phone/PC combination uses exactly two secure entries: the phone in voice VLAN 20 and the PC in data VLAN 10. No additional device is present.

exhibits.title: ASW1 port-security state (excerpt)
exhibits.text:
Port Status             : Secure-shutdown
Violation Mode          : Shutdown
Maximum MAC Addresses   : 1
Total MAC Addresses     : 1
Sticky MAC Addresses    : 1
Last Source Address:Vlan : 0050.56b1.9c22:10

exhibits.title: ASW1 Fa0/7 configuration
exhibits.text:
interface FastEthernet0/7
 switchport mode access
 switchport access vlan 10
 switchport voice vlan 20
 switchport port-security
 switchport port-security mac-address sticky
 switchport port-security mac-address sticky 0011.bb27.4e10 vlan voice

exhibits.title: Verified endpoint inventory
exhibits.text:
Phone: 0011.bb27.4e10, VLAN 20
PC:    0050.56b1.9c22, VLAN 10
No other secure entries required on this tested combination

tickets.question: What explains the repeated error-disable event?
options: The approved PC exceeds the one-entry total already occupied by the phone
The phone's tagged voice traffic requires all data traffic to be trunked
Sticky learning has enabled a five-minute address-aging timer
The voice VLAN automatically disables port security on the data VLAN
tickets.explanation: The one-entry maximum is already occupied by the phone. The approved PC becomes a second source and triggers shutdown mode. Correct the limit to the verified endpoint requirement before resetting the port; merely bouncing it would leave the cause intact.
tickets.fix:
```ios ASW1
ASW1# configure terminal
ASW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/7
ASW1(config-if)# switchport port-security maximum 2
ASW1(config-if)# shutdown
ASW1(config-if)# no shutdown
ASW1(config-if)# end
ASW1# show port-security interface fastethernet0/7
ASW1# show port-security address
```
Generate phone and PC traffic, verify the two intended address/VLAN entries and restored service, then save. A different phone model or VLAN behavior may need a different total; derive it from the actual design.

sections.title: Separate route selection from packet forwarding
Read the fields in a route entry
Compare metrics and recognize equal-cost paths
Resolve next hops and use a default route
Verify the decision and its limits

lab.title: Read, predict and verify an IPv4 forwarding decision
lab.intro:
Use a small routed network to compare a predicted route with actual traffic. Static commands are supplied as a baseline; Chapter 18 teaches their construction and failure behavior. Dynamic-route and ECMP examples are worksheets, so you do not need to configure OSPF before its lesson.

Packet Tracer is suitable for the core topology. Record its version and each router image. CEF and filtered display commands vary by simulator; use the full routing table where a filter is unavailable and mark any CEF interpretation that was not executed.
lab.topology:
| Link or device | Address |
|---|---|
| R1 Gi0/0 ↔ R2 Gi0/0 | R1 `10.0.12.1/30`; R2 `10.0.12.2/30` |
| R1 Gi0/1 ↔ PC-A FastEthernet0 | R1 `192.0.2.1/24`; PC-A `192.0.2.10/24`, gateway `192.0.2.1` |
| R2 Gi0/1 ↔ PC-B FastEthernet0 | R2 `198.51.100.1/24`; PC-B `198.51.100.200/24`, gateway `198.51.100.1` |
| R2 Loopback0 | `203.0.113.9/32`, test destination |

Use Packet Tracer's automatic cable selection or copper crossover for these direct Ethernet connections. No switch, Internet service or previous chapter project is required. A loopback is a logical router interface; its address gives the default-route test a real destination.

```diagram
{"type":"topology","title":"A route in each direction","caption":"R1 and R2 need routes to the opposite PC's subnet. The R2 loopback is used later to test a default.","nodes":[{"id":"A","kind":"pc","label":"PC-A","sub":"192.0.2.10/24","x":1,"y":3},{"id":"R1","kind":"router","label":"R1","sub":"10.0.12.1/30","x":4,"y":3},{"id":"R2","kind":"router","label":"R2","sub":"10.0.12.2/30","x":8,"y":3},{"id":"B","kind":"pc","label":"PC-B","sub":"198.51.100.200/24","x":11,"y":3}],"links":[{"from":"A","to":"R1","toLabel":"Gi0/1"},{"from":"R1","to":"R2","fromLabel":"Gi0/0","toLabel":"Gi0/0","accent":true},{"from":"R2","to":"B","fromLabel":"Gi0/1"}]}
```

steps.title: Build and address the network
steps.body:
Create fresh devices and configure both routers. Leave routing protocols disabled.

```ios R1
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R1
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.0.12.1 255.255.255.252
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ip address 192.0.2.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip interface brief
```

```ios R2
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R2
R2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R2(config-if)# ip address 10.0.12.2 255.255.255.252
R2(config-if)# no shutdown
R2(config-if)# exit
R2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R2(config-if)# ip address 198.51.100.1 255.255.255.0
R2(config-if)# no shutdown
R2(config-if)# exit
R2(config)# interface loopback0
R2(config-if)# ip address 203.0.113.9 255.255.255.255
R2(config-if)# end
R2# show ip interface brief
```

Set each PC's static address, mask and gateway using Desktop → IP Configuration. Ping each PC's own gateway and ping `10.0.12.2` from R1. Repeat an initial attempt if needed for address resolution.

:::expected
The connected Ethernet interfaces are up/up. Each PC reaches its own gateway and R1 reaches R2's transit address. End-to-end PC traffic is not expected yet because the routers lack routes to the opposite LAN.
:::

steps.title: Identify connected and local entries
steps.body:
Run `show ip route` on both routers. On R1, find the connected `192.0.2.0/24` and local `192.0.2.1/32` entries. Record their codes and interfaces. Inspect `show ip route 192.0.2.1` and `show ip route 192.0.2.10` where supported.

:::expected
The router's own address matches its local /32; PC-A's address matches the connected /24. A display heading that groups prefixes is not another route. R2's /32 loopback may not use the same two-line C/L pattern as an ordinary /24 Ethernet interface.
:::

steps.title: Install the supplied bidirectional baseline
steps.body:
These commands name the remote destination network, its mask and the neighboring router. The return route on R2 is as necessary as the forward route on R1.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip route 198.51.100.0 255.255.255.0 10.0.12.2
R1(config)# end
R1# show ip route
```

```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# ip route 192.0.2.0 255.255.255.0 10.0.12.1
R2(config)# end
R2# show ip route
```

From PC-A, ping `198.51.100.200`. From PC-B, ping `192.0.2.10`. Record each router's selected prefix, next hop and outgoing interface for the opposite host.

:::expected
Each router installs an `S` route to the opposite LAN, normally showing `[1/0]`. Both PC tests succeed once adjacency resolution completes. A route on only R1 would not establish a working reply path.
:::

steps.title: Predict overlapping-prefix lookups
steps.body:
Use this authored worksheet without entering configuration:

| Installed route | Next hop |
|---|---|
| `S 172.16.32.0/19 [1/0]` | `10.0.0.2` |
| `O 172.16.40.0/21 [110/20]` | `10.0.0.3` |
| `O 172.16.44.0/23 [110/30]` | `10.0.0.4` |
| `S 172.16.44.128/25 [200/0]` | `10.0.0.5` |

All listed routes are installed and their next hops are resolvable. Determine the selected next hop for `172.16.44.9`, `172.16.44.200`, `172.16.45.200` and `172.16.60.7`. Show the ranges that establish each match.

:::expected
The next hops are `10.0.0.4`, `10.0.0.5`, `10.0.0.4` and `10.0.0.2`, respectively. The /25 wins for its matching destination despite AD 200 because forwarding compares installed prefix lengths.
:::

steps.title: Introduce a more-specific discard route
steps.body:
Add a controlled fault on R1:

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip route 198.51.100.128 255.255.255.128 Null0
R1(config)# end
R1# show ip route
R1# show ip route 198.51.100.200
```

From PC-A, ping `198.51.100.200` and `198.51.100.1`. Explain the different results before changing anything. Where supported, inspect `show ip cef 198.51.100.200`.

:::expected
PC-B's `.200` matches the /25 discard route and fails. R2's LAN address `.1` lies outside that /25 and still matches the working /24. The presence of a route does not necessarily mean its action is forwarding to a live neighbor.
:::

steps.title: Remove the exact fault and retest
steps.body:
```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# no ip route 198.51.100.128 255.255.255.128 Null0
R1(config)# end
R1# show ip route 198.51.100.200
```

Repeat both PC-A pings and the reverse PC-B-to-PC-A ping.

:::expected
PC-B's address again matches the /24 through `10.0.12.2`, and the end-to-end tests work. You repaired the more-specific discard without removing the legitimate /24 route.
:::

steps.title: Add and verify a default route
steps.body:
Before changing R1, ping R2's loopback `203.0.113.9` from PC-A and confirm that R1 has no matching route. Add the default:

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 10.0.12.2
R1(config)# end
R1# show ip route
R1# show ip route 0.0.0.0
```

Repeat the PC-A ping and inspect `show ip cef 203.0.113.9` if available. Also compare the destination-specific `show ip route 203.0.113.9` result with the full table. Its exact default-lookup display is image dependent; record what yours actually reports.

:::expected
The full table contains the `S*` default through R2, and PC-A can now reach R2's actual loopback. R2 already has the return route to PC-A's subnet. The default changes this lookup but does not replace the more-specific route to PC-B.
:::

steps.title: Distinguish AD from protocol metrics
steps.body:
For this paper exercise, three eligible candidates describe exactly `10.50.0.0/16`: OSPF AD 110/cost 20, RIP AD 120/hop count 2, and static AD 130. All next hops are reachable and no policy changes these preferences. Identify the installed source, then remove the OSPF candidate on paper and repeat.

:::expected
OSPF is preferred first by AD. Without OSPF, RIP is preferred over the static candidate. OSPF cost 20 is not compared numerically with RIP's two hops. The static route is selected only after the more-preferred sources disappear; actual failover also requires a working forwarding and return path.
:::

steps.title: Interpret two equal-cost next hops
steps.body:
Read this representative entry:

```output Authored ECMP worksheet
O    10.70.0.0/16 [110/20] via 10.0.12.2, 00:00:30, GigabitEthernet0/0
                [110/20] via 10.0.13.2, 00:00:30, GigabitEthernet0/2
```

List the available paths and decide whether the output proves that one file transfer will run twice as fast. This is a supplied example, not a claim that your two-router topology has a second link.

:::expected
Both next hops are installed for the same prefix at equal cost. The output does not establish a 50/50 byte split, packet-by-packet alternation or doubled throughput for one flow. Hashing behavior and path limits depend on the device and configuration.
:::

steps.title: Save the corrected lab and evidence
steps.body:
Confirm that R1's temporary Null0 route is absent, both remote LAN routes are present and the default points from R1 to R2. Repeat PC-to-PC traffic and the PC-A-to-loopback test. On each router run `copy running-config startup-config` and accept the filename with Enter. Save the Packet Tracer project.

:::expected
The saved network has working bidirectional LAN routing and a default on R1. Your worksheet separately records the overlapping-prefix, AD and ECMP exercises. Record unsupported CEF commands as unexecuted rather than treating written answers as device verification.
:::

lab.troubleshooting:
| Symptom | Evidence to inspect |
|---|---|
| Own gateway unreachable | PC mask/gateway, cable, router address and interface state |
| R1 reaches R2 but PC-to-PC fails | Routes to both LANs and the hosts' gateways; a transit ping exercises different addresses |
| Only `.200` fails after Step 5 | The /25 Null0 match, compared with the /24 used by `.1` |
| A configured static route is missing from the table | Destination/mask, next-hop resolution and a preferred route for the same prefix |
| Default exists but loopback ping fails | Selected forwarding entry, R2 loopback state and route back to PC-A |
| Route looks correct but neighbor traffic fails | ARP/adjacency, interface state and any unexpected filtering |
lab.challenge:
Without changing the lab, predict what would happen if R1 had both its /24 route to PC-B's LAN and a /32 Null0 route for `198.51.100.200`. Then explain why deleting R2's route to `192.0.2.0/24` can break PC-A's pings even when R1's forward lookup remains correct. Include the request and reply source/destination addresses in your explanation.

:::expected
The /32 would discard traffic addressed specifically to `198.51.100.200`; the /24 would still serve other matching addresses. For the separate return-route problem, PC-A's request has source `192.0.2.10` and destination `198.51.100.200`. PC-B's reply reverses those addresses. If R2 has no remaining route or default covering `192.0.2.10`, it cannot forward that reply toward PC-A even though R1 can send the request toward PC-B.
:::

questions.prompt: Which next hop is selected for 10.20.30.150 by ordinary destination-based routing?
options: 10.0.12.2, because its route has a smaller OSPF cost
10.0.13.2, because its /25 is the longest matching prefix
10.0.14.2, because static routes always beat OSPF
Both OSPF neighbors, because both routes start with O
questions.explanation: The address is in 10.20.30.128/25. That prefix is more specific than the matching /24 and /16, so it determines this lookup.

whyWrong.0: OSPF cost does not override longest prefix match between different installed prefixes.
whyWrong.2: The static /16 is less specific than the installed /25.
whyWrong.3: These are different prefixes, not equal-cost paths for one prefix.

questions.prompt: In `O 10.1.1.0/24 [110/35] via 10.0.0.2`, what do the bracketed numbers mean?
options: 110 is cost; 35 is the number of hops
110 is bandwidth; 35 is the interface delay
110 is administrative distance; 35 is the metric
110 is the process ID; 35 is the router ID
questions.explanation: Route brackets display administrative distance first, then metric. Here the metric is OSPF cost, not necessarily a hop count.

whyWrong.0: The order and units are incorrect; OSPF cost is not a fixed hop count.
whyWrong.1: The bracket does not directly report bandwidth and delay.
whyWrong.3: Process and router IDs are not these two fields.

options: An external EIGRP route using the default external distance
An external OSPF route whose metric is its hop count
A directly connected route with manually configured distance
An external BGP route using the default external distance
questions.explanation: `D EX` identifies EIGRP external routing information, whose Cisco default AD is 170. Recognizing the code does not require configuring redistribution.

whyWrong.1: OSPF external codes are O E1 or O E2, not D EX.
whyWrong.2: Connected routes use C; D is an EIGRP source code.
whyWrong.3: BGP uses B, and its external default AD is 20.

questions.prompt: OSPF offers 10.1.0.0/16 with cost 10; RIP offers the same /16 with two hops. Both are eligible and use default ADs. Which two statements are correct? (Choose two.)
options: RIP wins because 2 is less than 10
OSPF wins because 110 is less than 120
The router compares both metrics in the same units
Administrative distance compares these sources
Both sources must appear as equal-cost next hops
questions.explanation: The destination prefix and length are identical, so the eligible sources compete by AD. The metrics have different meanings and are not compared directly.

whyWrong.0: Two hops and OSPF cost 10 are unlike measurements.
whyWrong.2: Protocol metrics are not a common unit across RIP and OSPF.
whyWrong.4: Equal-cost multipath is not established merely by having two different route sources.

questions.prompt: The static next hop is operationally reachable. Why is the configured /24 static absent from the installed route table?
options: The static mask is less specific than the OSPF mask
The next hop must be an address on the destination subnet
Static routes cannot share a prefix with dynamic routes
OSPF is preferred over the static route's AD of 130
questions.explanation: Both candidates describe the same /24. OSPF's 110 is preferred over the explicitly configured static distance 130, so the static is a floating candidate.

whyWrong.0: Both masks are /24.
whyWrong.1: A next-hop router can be on a transit network separate from the destination subnet.
whyWrong.2: A static candidate can coexist in configuration with a preferred dynamic route.

questions.prompt: No installed route matches a packet's destination, and no default is present. With ordinary unicast routing and no alternative policy, what happens?
options: The router discards the packet
The router broadcasts it to all routed interfaces
The router chooses the lowest-AD unrelated prefix
The router learns a destination route from the packet
questions.explanation: There is no applicable forwarding route, so the packet is discarded. An ICMP unreachable may be generated subject to implementation, configuration and rate limits.

whyWrong.1: Routers do not flood unmatched unicast traffic across routed interfaces to discover a path.
whyWrong.2: A low distance does not make a nonmatching prefix applicable.
whyWrong.3: An arriving data packet does not automatically install a route to its destination.

questions.prompt: All listed routes are installed. Which next hop is selected for 172.16.44.9?
questions.explanation: The /19, /21 and /23 contain the address. The /25 begins at 172.16.44.128, so it does not. The /23 is the longest match.

whyWrong.0: The /19 matches but is less specific than the matching /23.
whyWrong.1: The /21 matches but is less specific than the matching /23.
whyWrong.3: The destination's last octet is 9, outside this /25's 128–255 range.

exhibit.title: Representative IOS observations
exhibit.text:
R1# show ip route 8.8.8.8
% Network not in table
R1# show ip route
Gateway of last resort is 10.0.12.2 to network 0.0.0.0
S* 0.0.0.0/0 [1/0] via 10.0.12.2

questions.prompt: This IOS image reports the two outputs shown. Assume ordinary routing and no more-specific route to 8.8.8.8. What is the justified interpretation?
options: The default can never forward traffic on this image
The installed default supplies a lookup match, but delivery still needs verification
The destination is unreachable solely because the first display says so
The static entry supplies a complete end-to-end reachability guarantee
questions.explanation: The full table establishes a default through 10.0.12.2. Cisco documents destination-specific lookup behavior of this kind on an IOS example; it is not a universal output guarantee. Check CEF where supported, adjacency and the actual traffic path.

whyWrong.0: The first display does not negate the installed default.
whyWrong.2: The full table contains a matching /0, so this conclusion ignores relevant evidence.
whyWrong.3: Installation alone does not prove next-hop forwarding, remote reachability or the reply path.

questions.prompt: An ordinary IOS IPv4 interface is up/up with address 192.168.1.1/24. Which pair describes its connected subnet and local address?
questions.explanation: The connected entry covers the subnet; the local /32 identifies the router's own interface address. This question concerns the ordinary /24 interface case, not every possible /32 or platform-specific display.

whyWrong.0: The connected and local meanings are reversed.
whyWrong.1: Interface-derived entries are not static and OSPF routes.
whyWrong.2: The local address is .1; .255 is the subnet's directed broadcast address.

questions.prompt: Which two Cisco administrative-distance defaults are correct? (Choose two.)
options: Connected: 0
OSPF: 90
Static: 1
RIP: 110
External EIGRP: 20
questions.explanation: Connected routes use AD 0 and ordinary static routes default to 1. Displayed configuration can change a configurable source preference.

whyWrong.1: OSPF defaults to 110; 90 is the common EIGRP internal default.
whyWrong.3: RIP defaults to 120.
whyWrong.4: EIGRP external defaults to 170; 20 is external BGP.

questions.prompt: What is established by this installed route?
options: Two different prefixes will be alternated for every packet
One flow is guaranteed twice the throughput of a single link
Two equal-cost next hops are available for the same prefix
Exactly half the bytes must leave each interface
questions.explanation: The two path lines belong to the same OSPF prefix and have equal cost. Actual sharing depends on the forwarding implementation and traffic; flow hashing does not guarantee an equal byte split.

whyWrong.0: Both paths serve one prefix; the exhibit does not specify per-packet alternation.
whyWrong.1: One flow can remain on one selected path.
whyWrong.3: Equal-cost eligibility does not establish a 50/50 byte distribution.

exhibit.title: R1 configuration and table
exhibit.text:
ip route 172.16.0.0 255.255.0.0 Null0

S 172.16.0.0/16 is directly connected, Null0

questions.prompt: What is this route's AD, and what happens to ordinary traffic for 172.16.9.9 when it is the longest match?
options: AD 0; forward through the connected LAN
AD 1; discard through Null0
AD 110; use an OSPF neighbor
AD 255; try the default route
questions.explanation: The configuration omits an AD override, so this static uses its default distance of 1. Its selected action is Null0 discard. The phrase 'directly connected' does not change the S source to C.

whyWrong.0: The source is static, and Null0 is not a live attached LAN.
whyWrong.2: There is no OSPF route in this exhibit.
whyWrong.3: The route is installed with its static default; a selected Null0 match does not trigger retry through a less-specific default.

questions.prompt: R1 has eligible candidates for exactly 10.5.0.0/16: OSPF costs 10 and 25, plus a static route with default AD and a resolvable next hop. What is installed as the preferred source?
options: OSPF cost 10 because metric selection overrides source preference
Both OSPF paths because their route codes match
OSPF cost 25 because it has a higher path value
The static source because AD 1 is preferred over 110
questions.explanation: The static source is preferred for this identical prefix because its default AD is 1. OSPF chooses among its own paths using its rules, but that does not give it precedence over the eligible static.

whyWrong.0: A lower OSPF cost does not override the better AD of an eligible source for the same prefix.
whyWrong.1: Different OSPF costs are not equal-cost paths, and the static source is preferred.
whyWrong.2: Higher OSPF cost is not better, and source AD still matters here.

questions.prompt: Which next hop receives traffic to 10.20.31.7?
options: No route matches
questions.explanation: The address matches 10.20.0.0/16, but not 10.20.30.0/24. The /16 is more specific than the default, so its OSPF next hop is selected.

whyWrong.1: The /24 contains 10.20.30.x, not 10.20.31.x.
whyWrong.2: The default loses to the matching /16 regardless of its lower AD.
whyWrong.3: Both the /16 and default match.

questions.prompt: An installed nondefault route covers 10.20.30.150. Which command requests matching route details, including the source, distance and metric?
options: show ip interface brief
show ip arp 10.20.30.150
show ip route 10.20.30.150
show running-config interface gigabitethernet0/0
questions.explanation: The destination-specific route command requests routing-entry detail. Read the returned prefix and source rather than assuming the destination itself must be a /32 route.

whyWrong.0: This reports interface addresses and states, not route-selection detail.
whyWrong.1: ARP reports neighbor resolution, not the route source and distance.
whyWrong.3: An interface configuration block does not identify the matching installed route.

questions.prompt: R1 has the expected route to a remote PC. Which two observations could still explain why a ping from the user's PC fails? (Choose two.)
options: The route's source code is S rather than O
ARP for the Ethernet next-hop router remains incomplete
The route's prefix is longer than the default
The remote router lacks a route back to the user's subnet
The installed route has an outgoing interface
questions.explanation: The forward RIB entry is only part of the path. Unresolved next-hop adjacency can prevent transmission, and a missing return route can prevent replies.

whyWrong.0: Static routing can forward correctly; the source code alone is not a failure.
whyWrong.2: A more-specific match is normal routing behavior.
whyWrong.4: An outgoing interface is expected forwarding information, not evidence of failure.

cards.front: What is the order of the two values in [110/20]?
cards.back: Administrative distance first, metric second. In an OSPF entry, 20 is a cost rather than necessarily a hop count.

cards.front: What are the default ADs for connected and static routes?
cards.back: Connected 0; ordinary static 1. A configured static distance can override its default.

cards.front: What are the common internal and external EIGRP ADs?
cards.back: Internal EIGRP 90; external EIGRP 170. Recognize them in route exhibits; EIGRP configuration is outside this chapter.

cards.front: What are the OSPF and RIP AD defaults?
cards.back: OSPF 110; RIP 120. If both offer the same eligible prefix, OSPF is preferred by distance, not by comparing cost to hops.

cards.front: What are the eBGP and iBGP AD defaults?
cards.back: External BGP 20; internal BGP 200. These are source preferences, not a complete BGP path-selection algorithm.

cards.front: What does administrative distance 255 mean?
cards.back: The route is not usable for installation. Do not treat it as a usable last-resort backup distance.

cards.front: What does L identify in an IPv4 routing table?
cards.back: A local router address, commonly a /32 for an ordinary IPv4 interface. It distinguishes delivery to the router from forwarding to another host on the connected subnet.

cards.front: What do O IA, O E1 and O E2 mean?
cards.back: OSPF inter-area, external type 1 and external type 2. Recognize the source/type; multi-area and redistribution configuration are outside the single-area CCNA labs.

cards.front: What does D EX identify?
cards.back: An EIGRP external route, normally using administrative distance 170 on Cisco IOS.

cards.front: How is an installed route chosen for a packet destination?
cards.back: Find every prefix containing the address, then select the longest matching prefix. Read its action: next hop, local delivery or discard.

cards.front: When does administrative distance compare route sources?
cards.back: When eligible sources offer the same destination prefix and length. It does not override longest prefix match between different installed prefixes.

cards.front: What selects paths within a routing protocol?
cards.back: That protocol's route-selection rules, including its metric. In a simple single-area OSPF comparison, lower cost is preferred; do not generalize this into every protocol's complete algorithm.

cards.front: How do common protocol metrics differ?
cards.back: RIP uses hop count, OSPF uses accumulated cost, and EIGRP's usual metric considers bandwidth and delay. Their numerical values are not interchangeable.

cards.front: What happens with no matching route and no default?
cards.back: Ordinary routed unicast is discarded. ICMP feedback may be generated subject to configuration and limits; silence does not prove the packet was not dropped.

cards.front: What does the asterisk mean alongside a route code?
cards.back: It marks a candidate default. In S*, S is still the static source; inspect the actual prefix and gateway-of-last-resort information.

cards.front: Does 'S ... is directly connected, Null0' mean a connected route?
cards.back: No. S identifies a static source and Null0 a discard action. Read detailed output or configuration for the distance; omitted brackets alone do not establish it.

cards.front: What is a floating static route?
cards.back: A static candidate with a higher AD than the intended primary source for the same prefix. It can be configured but inactive, and needs valid resolution before it can take over.

cards.front: A destination lookup says 'Network not in table' but a default is listed. What next?
cards.back: Inspect the full table, default entry and CEF lookup where available. Cisco documents this lookup behavior on an IOS example; it is not a universal command-output rule or proof that no default forwarding match exists.

cards.front: How should CEF receive, attached and drop be interpreted?
cards.back: Receive: local delivery. Attached: directly attached prefix/adjacency context. Drop: discard. An attached prefix does not prove that every host has a resolved adjacency.

cards.front: Do two ECMP paths guarantee twice the throughput for one transfer?
cards.back: No. Flow hashing can select one path for a flow. Equal-cost paths do not guarantee per-packet alternation or equal byte counts, and maximum path counts vary by platform and configuration.

commands.note: Begin with the full table so a filter does not hide a relevant prefix.

commands.task: Using the supplied static-route form, configure a default through 203.0.113.1.
commands.note: The neighbor must resolve; this command alone does not establish Internet or end-to-end access.

commands.task: Using ip route PREFIX MASK NEXT-HOP AD, configure the 10.20.30.0/24 backup via 10.0.99.2 with distance 130.
commands.note: This is less preferred than default-distance OSPF for the same prefix. Installation still requires an eligible resolved path.

commands.task: Request the matching route details for 10.20.30.150, which has a nondefault match.
commands.note: Read the returned prefix, source, distance and metric.

commands.task: On this CEF-capable image, inspect the forwarding lookup for 8.8.8.8.
commands.note: A forwarding entry does not prove successful remote delivery or a reply path.

commands.task: Show currently installed OSPF routes.
commands.note: This filter excludes routes selected from other sources.

commands.task: Show currently installed static routes.
commands.note: An inactive configured floating static will not appear as an installed route.

commands.task: Display global static-route configuration lines using an include filter anchored to ip route.
commands.note: Compare configuration with the installed table; presence in one does not guarantee presence in the other.

commands.note: A selected more-specific discard does not fall back to a working less-specific route.
