commands.note: Also inspect the full table; output forms differ by image.

commands.task: Display the complete IPv4 CEF table on this supporting router.
commands.note: Distinguish forwarding, attached, local-receive and discard actions.

commands.task: Display interface addresses and operational state before investigating missing connected routes.
commands.note: A configured address on a shut interface does not establish a live connected path.

tickets.title: Only part of the branch subnet is reachable
tickets.scenario: After a route change, a user can reach branch host 10.20.30.50 but not 10.20.30.200. Both hosts share the intended /24, have verified local connectivity, and previously worked from this source. R1's current output and the change record follow.

exhibits.title: R1 destination lookup
exhibits.text:
Routing entry for 10.20.30.128/25
Known via "static", distance 1, metric 0
Routing Descriptor Blocks:
* directly connected, via Null0

exhibits.title: Change record
exhibits.text:
Added: ip route 10.20.30.128 255.255.255.128 Null0
Intended policy: all of 10.20.30.0/24 remains reachable through the branch router

tickets.question: Which change explains the split result?
options: OSPF cost 20 exceeds the permitted number of hops
The new /25 discard overrides the /24 for the .200 destination
The /24 route cannot coexist with a /25 in one routing table
The /25 lowers OSPF's administrative distance to zero
tickets.explanation: The .200 address lies inside 10.20.30.128/25; .50 does not. The more-specific static sends .200 to Null0 while the /24 continues to serve .50. This is longest prefix match, not a comparison between static and OSPF distances.
tickets.fix:
```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# no ip route 10.20.30.128 255.255.255.128 Null0
R1(config)# end
R1# show ip route 10.20.30.200
```
Confirm that the /24 is now selected, then test both .50 and .200 from the affected source. Verify replies and save the corrected configuration after the intended policy is restored.

tickets.title: The intended backup link is preferred
tickets.scenario: Traffic for 10.60.0.0/16 uses the backup path through 10.0.99.2. The intended primary is OSPF. Both next hops are reachable. A protocol inspection confirms a currently eligible OSPF candidate for exactly 10.60.0.0/16 with distance 110 and cost 20; the selected table entry is shown below.

exhibits.title: Verified candidate and next-hop observations
exhibits.text:
OSPF candidate: 10.60.0.0/16, AD 110, cost 20, via 10.0.12.2
10.0.12.2: resolved and reachable
10.0.99.2: resolved and reachable
Required policy: OSPF primary, static backup

tickets.question: What makes the backup preferred?
options: The static route's next hop has the numerically larger address
The OSPF route is more specific than the static candidate
The static command uses default AD 1, which beats OSPF 110
The OSPF cost must be lower than the static metric of zero
tickets.explanation: The candidates describe the same /16, so source preference applies. The static command omits an AD override and uses 1. Its metric is not compared directly with the OSPF metric. The separate exact-prefix candidate evidence establishes that a usable OSPF alternative exists.
tickets.fix:
```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# no ip route 10.60.0.0 255.255.0.0 10.0.99.2
R1(config)# ip route 10.60.0.0 255.255.0.0 10.0.99.2 130
R1(config)# end
R1# show ip route 10.60.0.0
R1# show running-config | include ^ip route
```
With the stated OSPF candidate still eligible, its AD 110 is preferred over 130. Verify the selected source and traffic in both directions. A planned failure test must separately establish that the backup remains eligible and actually forwards when the primary is withdrawn.

lab.title: Verify primary, backup, host and default IPv4 routes
lab.intro: Build a new isolated Packet Tracer project. You will first observe a missing return route, then establish a working baseline, test a backup, and compare network, host and default routes. These are guided configuration and reasoning exercises, not a record of an executed simulator session. Output is representative; wording, interface displays and supported diagnostic options can vary by version. If a command is unavailable, use the stated alternative and record the limitation.
lab.topology:
Use two 2911 routers with `GigabitEthernet0/0`, `0/1` and `0/2`. Use two 2960 switches at their default VLAN 1 settings. No trunk, management address, DHCP service, DNS server or Internet connection is required. The switches make the PC-to-router cabling unambiguous.

| Connection | Cable |
|---|---|
| PC-A FastEthernet0 — SW1 FastEthernet0/1 | Copper straight-through |
| SW1 FastEthernet0/24 — R1 GigabitEthernet0/2 | Copper straight-through |
| R1 GigabitEthernet0/0 — R2 GigabitEthernet0/0 | Copper cross-over |
| R1 GigabitEthernet0/1 — R2 GigabitEthernet0/1 | Copper cross-over |
| R2 GigabitEthernet0/2 — SW2 FastEthernet0/24 | Copper straight-through |
| SW2 FastEthernet0/1 — PC-B FastEthernet0 | Copper straight-through |

If a model uses different interface names, record the substitutions before continuing. Do not connect the two switches to one another.

| Device/interface | IPv4 address | Mask | PC gateway |
|---|---|---|---|
| R1 Gi0/0 | `10.0.12.1` | `255.255.255.252` | — |
| R2 Gi0/0 | `10.0.12.2` | `255.255.255.252` | — |
| R1 Gi0/1 | `10.0.13.1` | `255.255.255.252` | — |
| R2 Gi0/1 | `10.0.13.2` | `255.255.255.252` | — |
| R1 Gi0/2 | `192.168.10.1` | `255.255.255.0` | — |
| PC-A | `192.168.10.11` | `255.255.255.0` | `192.168.10.1` |
| R2 Gi0/2 | `192.168.20.1` | `255.255.255.0` | — |
| PC-B | `192.168.20.12` | `255.255.255.0` | `192.168.20.1` |
| R2 Loopback0, added in Step 10 | `203.0.113.8` | `255.255.255.255` | — |

A loopback is a logical router interface used here as a stable test destination. The documentation address does not represent a public Internet service.

steps.title: Cable the project and configure R1
steps.body:
Place and label the devices. Set each PC's static address, mask and gateway under Desktop → IP Configuration. Leave DNS blank. On a new router, decline the initial configuration dialog if offered, then configure R1.

```ios R1
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R1
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.0.12.1 255.255.255.252
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.0.13.1 255.255.255.252
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# interface gigabitethernet0/2
R1(config-if)# ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip interface brief
```

:::expected
After switch ports finish transitioning, Gi0/2 should be up/up. The transit ports may remain down until R2 is enabled. From PC-A's Desktop → Command Prompt, run `ping 192.168.10.1`. Repeat after address resolution if the first attempt loses a reply. Resolve any local failure before adding routes.
:::

steps.title: Configure R2 and prove the local links
steps.body:
Use R2's console, not R1's.

```ios R2
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R2
R2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R2(config-if)# ip address 10.0.12.2 255.255.255.252
R2(config-if)# no shutdown
R2(config-if)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R2(config-if)# ip address 10.0.13.2 255.255.255.252
R2(config-if)# no shutdown
R2(config-if)# interface gigabitethernet0/2
R2(config-if)# ip address 192.168.20.1 255.255.255.0
R2(config-if)# no shutdown
R2(config-if)# end
R2# show ip interface brief
R2# show ip route
R2# ping 10.0.12.1
R2# ping 10.0.13.1
```

:::expected
Both transit pings should succeed, and PC-B should ping `192.168.20.1`. Each router has connected routes for its three /30 or /24 networks and local routes for its own addresses on images that display L entries. Neither router has a route to the other LAN. PC-A's ping to `192.168.20.12` should fail at this stage. This is a planned baseline, not a reason to change the PC mask.
:::

steps.title: Observe the missing return route
steps.body:
Add only R1's remote-LAN route.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip route 192.168.20.0 255.255.255.0 gigabitethernet0/0 10.0.12.2
R1(config)# end
R1# show ip route static
R1# ping 192.168.20.12
```

On PC-A, run:

```text
ping 192.168.20.12
```

:::expected
R1 should list the /24 static through Gi0/0 and `10.0.12.2` at distance 1. R1's ordinary ping normally succeeds because its source is `10.0.12.1`, reachable through R2's connected transit route. PC-A's ping fails because R2 has no route back to `192.168.10.11`. Confirm that absence with R2's `show ip route`. In Simulation mode, you can follow the request toward PC-B and the return failure at R2. Do not infer this diagnosis from a failed ping alone outside this controlled configuration.
:::

steps.title: Restore the return path
steps.body:
```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# ip route 192.168.10.0 255.255.255.0 gigabitethernet0/0 10.0.12.1
R2(config)# end
R2# show ip route static
```

:::expected
R2 now has the return /24 at distance 1. Repeat PC-A's ping to PC-B, then ping `192.168.10.11` from PC-B. Both should succeed. Optionally run `tracert 192.168.20.12` from PC-A; response addresses may vary, so use the selected routes and completed ping as the core evidence.
:::

steps.title: Add R1's floating route
steps.body:
```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip route 192.168.20.0 255.255.255.0 gigabitethernet0/1 10.0.13.2 5
R1(config)# end
R1# show running-config
R1# show ip route static
```

:::expected
The configuration has two routes to `192.168.20.0/24`. The installed table still selects the primary at distance 1. Distance 5 makes the other route a backup; it does not mean five hops. The named interfaces prevent the primary from being resolved through the alternate link.
:::

steps.title: Add R2's floating return route
steps.body:
```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# ip route 192.168.10.0 255.255.255.0 gigabitethernet0/1 10.0.13.1 5
R2(config)# end
R2# show running-config
R2# show ip route static
```

:::expected
R2 likewise keeps the distance-1 primary selected while retaining the distance-5 backup in its configuration. Ping between PCs once more before introducing the next fault.
:::

steps.title: Fail the primary and inspect both tables
steps.body:
Shut only R1 Gi0/0. Keep it shut until you have collected the evidence.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip interface brief
R1# show ip route static
```

Inspect `show ip interface brief` and `show ip route static` on R2 as well. The direct cable should make its primary link lose carrier. Repeat ordinary PC pings; a continuous-ping option is not required.

:::expected
After link and route updates, R1 should select the backup shown below, and R2 should select its return /24 through Gi0/1 and `10.0.13.1` at distance 5. Some probes may fail during the transition; no exact loss count or recovery time is promised.

```output R1# show ip route static
S    192.168.20.0/24 [5/0] via 10.0.13.2, GigabitEthernet0/1
```

PC-to-PC pings should recover over the backup. If they do not, inspect both directions and the backup interface state before restoring the primary.
:::

steps.title: Restore the primary link
steps.body:
```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip route static
```

:::expected
Allow the physical link to recover. Both routers should again select distance-1 routes through Gi0/0, while their backup lines remain configured. Recheck endpoint pings. Save a separate working project copy now if you want a checkpoint before the next experiment.
:::

steps.title: Make one host use the alternate path
steps.body:
```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip route 192.168.20.12 255.255.255.255 gigabitethernet0/1 10.0.13.2 200
R1(config)# end
R1# show ip route
R1# show ip route 192.168.20.12
```

:::expected
The /32 at distance 200 can coexist with the distance-1 /24. Traffic for PC-B selects /32 through Gi0/1; traffic for `192.168.20.1` selects /24 through Gi0/0. Ping both addresses from PC-A. Use Simulation mode or the installed entries to verify the destination decisions. Replies can return over the primary; an asymmetric path is not itself a failure in this unfiltered lab.
:::

steps.title: Create a real destination for the default route
steps.body:
On R2, add a loopback. It needs no cable.

```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# interface loopback0
R2(config-if)# ip address 203.0.113.8 255.255.255.255
R2(config-if)# end
R2# show ip route
```

:::expected
R2 has a connected/local entry covering `203.0.113.8/32`; exact C/L presentation for loopbacks varies. From PC-A, `ping 203.0.113.8` should fail because R1 has no matching route or default. Record R1's current table to establish that reason.
:::

steps.title: Add the default and verify its limits
steps.body:
```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 gigabitethernet0/0 10.0.12.2
R1(config)# end
R1# show ip route
```

:::expected
R1 lists an S* /0 route through R2. PC-A should now ping `203.0.113.8` successfully, using R2's existing return route to the PC LAN. No more specific route at R1 covers that loopback. The /32 for PC-B still takes precedence over the default. This proves a default to a known lab destination; it does not establish Internet connectivity.
:::

steps.title: Remove temporary routes and save the baseline
steps.body:
```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# no ip route 192.168.20.12 255.255.255.255 gigabitethernet0/1 10.0.13.2 200
R1(config)# no ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 gigabitethernet0/0 10.0.12.2
R1(config)# end
R1# show running-config
R1# copy running-config startup-config
```

At the destination-filename prompt, press Enter and wait for completion. Then use R2's console:

```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# no interface loopback0
R2(config)# end
R2# copy running-config startup-config
```

:::expected
Accept R2's filename prompt separately. Each router retains exactly its primary and floating remote-LAN route, and all physical interfaces are enabled. Confirm PC-to-PC ping. Save the project as `18-ipv4-static-baseline.pkt`. A project save and an IOS startup-configuration save are separate actions.
:::

lab.troubleshooting:
- **Local ping fails:** compare the address table, cable endpoints, switch port state and router `no shutdown`. A remote route cannot fix a local addressing problem.
- **A route is configured but absent:** inspect its distance, destination mask and required interface. Next-hop-only routes also need successful route resolution.
- **A route is installed but traffic fails:** confirm the actual peer address with its interface configuration, then inspect downstream and return routes.
- **Backup does not take over:** check that Gi0/0 really became unusable and Gi0/1 is still up. Compare both backup masks with their primary masks.
- **Two paths have distance 1:** the backup's distance may be omitted. Read the running configuration, remove the incorrect line, and re-enter it with distance 5.
- **A command or display differs:** use IOS `?` to check availability. Record the model/version and verify the same route decision using the full table; do not invent a matching screenshot.
lab.challenge:
Without looking at the earlier commands, change both backup distances from 5 to 200. Verify failure and restoration again, then restore distance 5. On paper, predict what a mistaken R1 backup for `192.168.20.0/25` at distance 200 would do while the /24 primary is working.

:::expected
Remove each current distance-5 line and re-add the same destination, interface and next hop with `200`. It still follows the static primary at distance 1 and becomes eligible after primary withdrawal. It would also follow an OSPF route to the same prefix at distance 110.

The mistaken /25 is a different prefix, covering `192.168.20.0` through `192.168.20.127`. It can install alongside /24 and wins forwarding for PC-B because /25 is longer, despite distance 200. Addresses .128 through .255 do not match that /25. Do this calculation on paper; do not leave the mistake in the saved baseline.
:::

whyWrong.1: A /32 identifies one address, not a default.
whyWrong.2: ip default-gateway serves host-mode management; it does not create this static route on an IP-routing router.
whyWrong.3: This names the transit subnet as the destination and does not create a default.

questions.explanation: The /32 host route matches only 10.20.30.40.

whyWrong.0: The /24 applies to the whole subnet.
whyWrong.2: The host bits are nonzero for that /24 network mask.
whyWrong.3: The default covers all destinations without a more specific match.

R1 automatically discovers the correct IP next hop using CDP.
R1 treats covered destinations as on-link and may ARP for each destination.

Distance 5 makes the route less preferred than OSPF.
The backup's next hop must still be usable when it is needed.
Distance 255 is the safest usable standby value.
questions.explanation: The backup must lose the distance comparison while the preferred route exists, and must have a usable path when that route disappears.

whyWrong.1: 5 is lower than 110 and would be preferred for the same prefix.

R2 learns the return route automatically from the received request.
The request can reach PC-B, but R2 lacks a route for its reply to PC-A.

whyWrong.0: The /24 already covers PC-B.
whyWrong.1: The reply destination is the PC-A LAN, not the transit subnet.
whyWrong.2: Receiving an ordinary packet does not install a reverse static route.

show ip route static
show ip arp
show interfaces

options: The remote network must use the transit link's /30 mask.
IOS cannot resolve the configured next hop.
Static routes require a routing-protocol neighbor.
A static route never installs until its destination answers a ping.
questions.explanation: A recursive route requires a valid route that resolves its next hop. The stated resolving route is gone.

whyWrong.0: The destination mask describes the remote LAN independently of the transit subnet.
whyWrong.2: Static routing does not require a dynamic-protocol adjacency.

questions.prompt: A usable fully specified route was entered as shown. Which description is correct?
options: It names R1's LAN address as its source.
It has distance 13 because the next hop contains .13.
It directs the remote /16 to 10.0.13.2 through Gi0/1.
It disables ARP on Gi0/1.
questions.explanation: The destination and mask define 10.9.0.0/16; the interface and next hop jointly define its exit.

whyWrong.0: This command does not select packet source addresses.

questions.prompt: R1 and R2 have usable defaults pointing at one another and no other route covering 203.0.113.77. With ordinary forwarding and no filtering, what happens to a packet for that address?
options: It is broadcast onto both routers' LANs.
R1 creates a host route from the first reply.
The default itself creates an Internet path.
It can loop between the routers until its TTL expires.
questions.explanation: Each lookup selects a default back to the other router. Each forwarding hop reduces TTL, limiting the loop.

whyWrong.0: Routing a unicast packet does not turn it into a LAN broadcast.
whyWrong.1: No destination or reply is supplied, and pings do not teach static routes.
whyWrong.2: A forwarding instruction cannot create downstream connectivity.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements about an Ethernet interface-only default route are correct?
options: It may cause ARP requests for many distinct destination IP addresses.
It guarantees a working path whenever the interface is up.
Specifying the peer's next-hop address avoids treating every remote destination as directly attached.
It uses IPv6 Neighbor Discovery to find IPv4 destinations.
questions.explanation: An explicit peer address identifies the local Layer 2 recipient for remote traffic, instead of making every destination appear on-link.

whyWrong.1: Link state does not prove destination resolution or downstream/return connectivity.
whyWrong.3: Ordinary IPv4 Ethernet address resolution uses ARP.

questions.prompt: Both displayed routes are installed. Which next hop handles 10.1.0.77?
options: 10.0.13.2, because /24 is the longer match
10.0.12.2, because distance 1 is lower
Both, because every overlapping route load-shares
Neither, because a /32 is required
questions.explanation: 10.1.0.77 matches both prefixes. Forwarding selects /24, independently of the distances of different prefixes.

whyWrong.1: Distance is not compared between different installed prefix lengths for forwarding.
whyWrong.2: Overlapping prefixes are not equal-cost paths to one identical prefix.
whyWrong.3: A network route covers all matching addresses.

questions.prompt: A completed traceroute from PC-A lists R1, R2 and PC-B. Which conclusion is justified?
options: Every application on PC-B is healthy.
The trace reached PC-B and received its responses.
No route in the network can change.
The reverse data path must use exactly the same interfaces.
questions.explanation: A successful trace provides evidence about its probes and replies at that time. It is not a general application or symmetric-routing guarantee.

whyWrong.0: Application services require their own tests.
whyWrong.2: Routes can change after the measurement.
whyWrong.3: Replies can take another valid route.

10.0.12.2, R2's transit address
192.168.20.12, PC-B's address

questions.prompt: A preferred route to 10.8.0.0/16 has distance 90. Which static route is a usable lower-preference backup through 10.0.13.2?
questions.explanation: 120 is greater than the supplied primary distance 90 and below 255. Its next hop must also be usable.

whyWrong.1: 5 would beat 90.
whyWrong.2: The ordinary default static distance 1 would beat 90.
whyWrong.3: 255 is not usable for installation.

questions.prompt: R1's primary interface remains up because it connects to a switch. A remote router beyond that switch fails. No tracking is configured. What should you conclude about the static backup?
options: The backup must install after exactly three lost pings.
The primary may remain installed despite the remote failure.
Static routes exchange updates and will learn the failure.
Setting backup distance 255 enables health checks.
questions.explanation: Ordinary static routing does not provide an end-to-end health check. A local active interface can keep a fully specified route installed even when downstream delivery fails.

whyWrong.0: No ping monitor or timer is configured.
whyWrong.2: Static routes do not exchange routing-protocol updates.
whyWrong.3: Distance changes preference; 255 is unusable and adds no tracking.

cards.front: IPv4 static-route core syntax?
cards.back: `ip route destination-network subnet-mask next-hop` in global configuration. Use the destination network and the actual next router's address.

cards.front: Ordinary IOS static and connected distances?
cards.back: Static: 1. Connected: 0. Compare candidate sources for the same prefix.

cards.front: Can distance 255 be a working floating static?
cards.back: No. Distance 255 is unusable. A backup must have a usable path and a distance greater than the primary but below 255.

cards.front: Mask for an IPv4 host route?
cards.back: `255.255.255.255`, or /32. It matches one destination address.

cards.front: How do you write an IPv4 default route?
cards.back: `ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 next-hop`. Substitute the real peer address. A fully specified form also names the exit interface.

cards.front: What does S* identify in an IPv4 route table?
cards.back: S means static; * marks a candidate default. Inspect the /0 entry and gateway-of-last-resort line.
A static route to /24 through 10.0.12.2. Brackets show administrative distance 1 and metric 0.

cards.front: Does 'S ... is directly connected' mean a C route?
cards.back: No. S still means static, commonly with an exit-interface-only form. C is derived from an interface's connected prefix.

cards.front: What makes a static route fully specified?
cards.back: It names both exit interface and next hop. On Ethernet ARP still resolves the next hop's MAC address.

cards.front: How is a recursive next hop resolved?
cards.back: Another usable routing-table entry determines the path to it. A connected transit prefix is the simplest case. Self-dependent resolution is invalid.

cards.front: Why avoid an Ethernet interface-only route to a remote LAN?
cards.back: It treats remote destinations as on-link and may ARP for each. Name the peer next hop; do not rely on proxy ARP hiding a mistake.

cards.front: What makes a route a floating static?
cards.back: A higher distance than the preferred route to the same prefix. It can install after primary withdrawal if the backup path is usable.

cards.front: Example backup distances behind static 1 and OSPF 110?
cards.back: 5 follows static 1; 120 follows OSPF 110. A distance-5 route would beat OSPF 110 for the same prefix.

cards.front: Where can you see an unselected floating static?
cards.back: `show running-config`. The static filter on the route table shows selected entries, not every candidate.

cards.front: Does a /32 at distance 200 lose to a /24 at distance 1?
cards.back: When both are installed, /32 wins forwarding for its one destination. Distance selects candidates for the same prefix.

cards.front: Why select a source address in extended ping?
cards.back: An ordinary router ping normally uses its outgoing interface address. A LAN source tests the return route covering that LAN.

cards.front: Router ping works but a LAN PC ping fails: what next?
cards.back: Compare test sources, reverse routes and PC addressing/gateway. The symptom alone does not uniquely identify a missing return route.

cards.front: Risk of two routers defaulting to one another?
cards.back: Unknown destinations can loop until TTL expires. The default is an instruction, not proof of delivery.

cards.front: How do you verify forwarding when only a default matches?
cards.back: Inspect the installed /0 with `show ip route`, calculate the longest match, and test a real destination. Destination-specific diagnostic behavior can vary.

cards.front: Can a configured static disappear from the routing table?
cards.back: Yes: its interface can fail, its next hop can stop resolving, or a better candidate can win. The configuration may remain unchanged.
