tickets.title: A backup takes half the LAN traffic
tickets.scenario: R1 should use 10.0.12.2 for branch 192.168.20.0/24 and reserve 10.0.13.2 as standby. Both transit links work. Traffic to .50 uses standby while .150 uses primary. Excerpts are representative.
tickets.question: Which error explains this?
options: Distance 5 means five failures.
The backup is a separate /25 prefix and wins for .0 through .127.
Every overlapping prefix load-shares.
The primary must be removed for the backup to float.
tickets.explanation: The /25 covers .50 and wins longest match. .150 does not match it. Distance does not count failures, overlapping prefixes are not equal-cost paths, and removing the primary defeats standby operation.
tickets.fix:
```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# no ip route 192.168.20.0 255.255.255.128 10.0.13.2 5
R1(config)# ip route 192.168.20.0 255.255.255.0 10.0.13.2 5
R1(config)# end
R1# show ip route static
```
Only the distance-1 /24 should remain selected while the primary works. Verify both destination decisions, then test backup failure/recovery in the isolated lab before saving.

tickets.title: Router ping works; PC ping fails
tickets.scenario: PC-A is 192.168.10.11/24, gateway 192.168.10.1 on R1. PC-B is 192.168.20.12/24, gateway 192.168.20.1 on R2. Local/transit pings work, with no filtering. R1's ping uses source 10.0.12.1 and succeeds; PC-A's fails.

exhibits.title: Complete relevant R2 routes; no default

tickets.question: Which repair addresses the evidence?
options: Add another outbound route to PC-B on R1.
Change PC-A to /16.
Add R2's route to 192.168.10.0/24 through 10.0.12.1.
Use R2's own 10.0.12.2 as the return next hop.
tickets.explanation: R2's connected /30 covers the router's ping source, but no route covers PC-A. The outbound route exists, /16 violates the plan, and R2's own address is not its next router.
tickets.fix:
```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# ip route 192.168.10.0 255.255.255.0 gigabitethernet0/0 10.0.12.1
R2(config)# end
R2# show ip route static
```
Repeat PC-A-to-PC-B and reverse pings. Both should succeed under the stated conditions. Verify before saving.

lab.title: Configure IPv6 addresses and observe local discovery
lab.intro:
Create a fresh isolated file. You will configure one LAN manually, use modified EUI-64 and SLAAC on another, inspect the actual addresses, and test the difference between a router answering for itself and forwarding traffic. No DHCPv6 server, DNS service or static route is required: R1 directly connects both LANs.

This lab has not been executed on your simulator. The examples are representative; Packet Tracer's supported commands, client address-generation method and event detail depend on its version. Compare concepts and actual configuration rather than expecting identical MAC addresses or timings.
lab.topology:
| Connection | Cable |
|---|---|
| PC-A FastEthernet0 — SW1 FastEthernet0/1 | Copper straight-through |
| SW1 FastEthernet0/24 — R1 GigabitEthernet0/0 | Copper straight-through |
| PC-B FastEthernet0 — SW2 FastEthernet0/1 | Copper straight-through |
| SW2 FastEthernet0/24 — R1 GigabitEthernet0/1 | Copper straight-through |

Use fresh 2960 switches with default VLAN 1 access ports. Do not connect the switches together. The two LANs are different links, so R1 can use `fe80::1` on each without a same-link duplicate. Gi0/2 is unused.

| Interface or host | Address/prefix | Gateway |
|---|---|---|
| R1 Gi0/0 | `2001:db8:acad:1::1/64`; link-local `fe80::1` | — |
| R1 Gi0/1 | `2001:db8:acad:2::/64` plus its EUI-64 identifier; link-local `fe80::1` | — |
| PC-A | `2001:db8:acad:1::10/64`, static | `fe80::1` |
| PC-B initially | Automatic IPv6 address from LAN 2's RA | Learned from R1 |
| PC-B later, for a stable fault test | `2001:db8:acad:2::20/64`, static | `fe80::1` |

All documentation addresses stay inside this project.

steps.title: Configure R1's first LAN
steps.body:
Place, label and cable the devices. Decline the router setup dialog if offered. Configure the first interface and enable forwarding.

```ios R1
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R1
R1(config)# ipv6 unicast-routing
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001:db8:acad:1::1/64
R1(config-if)# ipv6 address fe80::1 link-local
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ipv6 interface brief
```

:::expected
After the switch port becomes ready, Gi0/0 should show up/up with `fe80::1` and `2001:db8:acad:1::1`. The other interfaces may remain administratively down. A link-local plus another unicast address on one interface is normal.
:::

steps.title: Address PC-A manually and verify its local link
steps.body:
Under PC-A → Desktop → IP Configuration, select IPv6 Static. Enter address `2001:db8:acad:1::10`, prefix length `64` and gateway `fe80::1`. Leave IPv4 and DNS unused. Open Command Prompt:

```text
ipconfig /all
ping 2001:db8:acad:1::1
```

:::expected
Confirm the entered address and a link-local address in the client's display. The ping should succeed after discovery completes. If your version provides different display options, inspect IP Configuration directly. A successful local ping establishes this one link; it does not yet test routing between LANs.
:::

steps.title: Calculate R1's second interface identifier
steps.body:
Read Gi0/1's MAC before configuring its IPv6 address.

```ios R1
R1# show interfaces gigabitethernet0/1
```

Find the hardware-address line. Record the operational MAC shown as `address is`; a separate `bia` field is the burned-in address and can differ if manually overridden. With this fresh router they should normally match.

On paper, split the six MAC bytes after byte three, insert `ff:fe`, and XOR the first byte with hexadecimal `02`. Regroup the resulting eight bytes into four hexadecimal groups.

:::expected
Your calculation produces a 64-bit identifier. As a worked example only, MAC `00:1a:2b:3c:4d:5e` produces `021a:2bff:fe3c:4d5e`. A first byte of `02` would become `00`, not `04`. Keep your own MAC and result; the example is not a prediction of your router's hardware address.
:::

steps.title: Configure and verify modified EUI-64
steps.body:
```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001:db8:acad:2::/64 eui-64
R1(config-if)# ipv6 address fe80::1 link-local
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ipv6 interface gigabitethernet0/1
```

:::expected
Gi0/1 should have a global-form address beginning `2001:db8:acad:2:` followed by the identifier you calculated. Record the entire address as **R1-LAN2** in your notes. The manual link-local stays `fe80::1`; do not assume its suffix matches the EUI-64 global address.

The detailed output should identify the /64 prefix and ND/RA settings on supported images. If the generated suffix differs, recheck the operational MAC, inserted bytes and bit inversion before changing the configuration.
:::

steps.title: Let PC-B obtain an automatic address
steps.body:
Open PC-B → Desktop → IP Configuration and select Automatic in the IPv6 area. Allow router advertisements and duplicate-address checks to complete. Inspect the resulting address and gateway with the GUI and, where supported, `ipconfig /all`.

:::expected
PC-B should acquire an address in `2001:db8:acad:2::/64` and learn R1's link-local address `fe80::1` as a default gateway. Record its complete address as **PC-B-AUTO**. The client may use an EUI-64-derived or another supported identifier; the router's explicit `eui-64` command does not dictate how the PC builds its own identifier.

DNS may remain empty because this lab provides no DNS information. That does not prevent numeric-address pings. If automatic assignment is unavailable in your version, record that limit, use the static values in Step 8 and substitute `2001:db8:acad:2::20` wherever Step 6 refers to **PC-B-AUTO**. Study the representative RA sequence in the lesson rather than claiming a successful SLAAC observation.
:::

steps.title: Test both LANs and inspect neighbors
steps.body:
From PC-B, ping PC-A by its known address.

```text
ping 2001:db8:acad:1::10
```

From PC-A, ping **PC-B-AUTO**, substituting the exact address recorded in Step 5. Do not paste the label itself. Then inspect R1:

```ios R1
R1# show ipv6 route
R1# show ipv6 neighbors
```

:::expected
Both endpoint pings should succeed. R1 has connected /64 routes for both LANs; it needs no static route for either one. Its neighbor table should contain bindings learned while delivering traffic, with the correct interface for each LAN. It need not list every IPv6 address each PC owns.

An entry may be reachable or stale depending on timing. Stale alone is not a failure. An incomplete entry that persists while pings fail calls for checking the target address and local link.
:::

steps.title: Observe a new neighbor-resolution exchange
steps.body:
First configure a temporary, previously unused **secondary** address on R1 Gi0/0. Do not remove the original.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001:db8:acad:1::99/64
R1(config-if)# end
```

Switch Packet Tracer to Simulation mode. Enable ICMPv6/ND events in the event filter if available. From PC-A, ping `2001:db8:acad:1::99` for the first time. Step through the events and inspect the packet details. Because the destination is new to PC-A, this avoids pretending that clearing only R1's neighbor cache also clears the PC's cache.

:::expected
For normal address resolution, PC-A should send an NS for target `2001:db8:acad:1::99` to solicited-node group `ff02::1:ff00:99`. R1's NA supplies neighbor information; echo traffic can then complete. Earlier DAD or other discovery events may also appear. Identify each message by its actual source, destination and target rather than assuming the first envelope is the requested exchange.

If event detail is not modeled, record that limit and draw the expected sequence from the lesson. Return to Realtime mode before continuing.
:::

steps.title: Prepare stable host addresses for the forwarding test
steps.body:
Remove the temporary secondary address.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# no ipv6 address 2001:db8:acad:1::99/64
R1(config-if)# end
```

Set PC-B to IPv6 Static: `2001:db8:acad:2::20`, prefix `64`, gateway `fe80::1`. Keep PC-A unchanged. On PC-B, ping the recorded **R1-LAN2** address and `2001:db8:acad:1::10`. From PC-A, ping `2001:db8:acad:2::20`.

:::expected
Local and cross-LAN pings should succeed before the fault. Record both PC configurations. Static host values make the next observation independent of whether an old SLAAC address or RA-learned route remains cached.
:::

steps.title: Disable forwarding and observe the difference
steps.body:
Only in this isolated lab, remove the forwarding command.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# no ipv6 unicast-routing
R1(config)# end
R1# show ipv6 interface brief
```

Repeat PC-A's ping to its local router address `2001:db8:acad:1::1`, then to remote PC-B `2001:db8:acad:2::20`. On PC-B, separately ping **R1-LAN2**.

:::expected
Each PC can still reach the router address on its own LAN, but PC-to-PC forwarding should fail. Interface addresses remain configured. This distinguishes “the router answers for itself” from “the router forwards between interfaces.”

The router also ceases acting as an advertising IPv6 router in this basic configuration. Do not assume existing automatic host addresses vanish immediately; their lifetimes and simulator handling are separate. The test deliberately uses static PC addresses.
:::

steps.title: Restore forwarding and save
steps.body:
```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ipv6 unicast-routing
R1(config)# end
R1# show ipv6 route
```

Repeat pings in both directions. When they succeed, save R1:

```ios R1
R1# copy running-config startup-config
```

:::expected
Press Enter at the destination-filename prompt and wait for completion. Both LAN /64s are present and PC-to-PC communication works. Save the project as `19-ipv6-addressing-baseline.pkt`. Record R1-LAN2's exact value so that later work does not mistakenly use `2001:db8:acad:2::1` as though EUI-64 had created it.
:::

lab.troubleshooting:
- **A numeric local ping fails:** compare every group of the target and interface address, link state and /64 prefix. Do not diagnose DNS when the test uses a literal address.
- **PC-B has only link-local while Automatic:** inspect R1's global forwarding command, Gi0/1 state and RA/prefix information. A DHCPv6 server is not required for SLAAC.
- **The supposed `::1` gateway is absent:** read the complete configured router address. EUI-64 does not create `::1` merely because it is convenient.
- **Neighbor resolution stays incomplete:** verify the target actually exists on the stated link. Clear or refresh caches only as a deliberate isolated-lab action; a correct route cannot resolve a nonexistent target.
- **Local router pings work, cross-LAN fails:** confirm `ipv6 unicast-routing`, both PC gateways and the connected prefixes. Use the controlled Step 9 evidence to distinguish this fault from general routing problems.
- **A source field or output label differs:** record what your simulator actually shows. Do not replace a correct calculated address merely to imitate illustrative output.
lab.challenge:
On paper, derive the modified EUI-64 address for MAC `02:aa:bb:cc:dd:ee` under `2001:db8:44:7::/64`. Give its solicited-node multicast address. Then calculate the first and last /64 inside `2001:db8:44:ab30::/60`. Finally explain why the lab uses the same `fe80::1` on two R1 interfaces without a duplicate.

:::expected
The MAC first byte changes from `02` to `00`. The identifier is `00aa:bbff:fecc:ddee`, so the complete address is `2001:db8:44:7:aa:bbff:fecc:ddee`. Its low 24 bits are `cc:ddee`, giving `ff02::1:ffcc:ddee`.

A /60 leaves four bits to choose /64 subnets: 16 choices. They range from `2001:db8:44:ab30::/64` through `2001:db8:44:ab3f::/64`. The two `fe80::1` addresses in the lab are on separate links. Putting them on the same ordinary unicast LAN would instead create a conflict.
:::

questions.prompt: Which is the canonical representation of 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:0a00:0000:0001?
questions.explanation: Remove leading zeros and compress the longest run of three zero groups. The trailing zeros in a00 remain significant.

whyWrong.1: Changing a00 to a changes its numeric value.
whyWrong.2: Two double-colon sequences are invalid.
whyWrong.3: This is valid but does not use the canonical compression of the longest zero run.

questions.prompt: A fresh IOS interface has no configured IPv6 address. Which single interface command enables IPv6 processing and an automatic link-local address without adding a global prefix?
options: ipv6 unicast-routing
ipv6 enable
ipv6 address 2001:db8:1::1/64
questions.explanation: ipv6 enable provides the requested interface behavior without supplying a global prefix.

whyWrong.0: That is a global forwarding command, not this interface-addressing instruction.
whyWrong.2: This also configures a global-form address, contrary to the requested result.
whyWrong.3: This configures IPv4.

questions.prompt: MAC 00:1a:2b:3c:4d:5e uses modified EUI-64 on 2001:db8:10:1::/64. Which address results?
questions.explanation: Insert ff:fe after the first three MAC bytes and invert the first byte's U/L bit, changing 00 to 02. Regrouping yields 021a:2bff:fe3c:4d5e.

whyWrong.0: The first byte's U/L bit was not inverted.
whyWrong.1: The inserted bytes are in the wrong position.
whyWrong.3: EUI-64 does not assign the convenient suffix ::1.

questions.prompt: Which TWO groups identify all IPv6 nodes and all IPv6 routers, respectively, on the local link?
questions.explanation: ff02::1 is all-nodes and ff02::2 is all-routers, both with link-local multicast scope.

whyWrong.2: ff05::2 has site scope, not the requested link scope.
whyWrong.3: This is a solicited-node group, not the all-nodes group.

exhibit.title: Representative configuration or observation
exhibit.text:
RA source: fe80::1; Router Lifetime: 1800 seconds
Header: M=0, O=1
Prefix: 2001:db8:acad:1::/64; A=1, L=1
No RA DNS option. A working stateless DHCPv6 server supplies DNS.

questions.prompt: A client supports SLAAC and stateless DHCPv6, with no manual DNS settings. What behavior is supported by the shown RA and available server?
options: DHCPv6 must provide the default router.
A=1 forces the host to derive its identifier from its MAC.
The host cannot form an address without M=1.
SLAAC address, DHCPv6 DNS, and RA-learned default router.
questions.explanation: The A-enabled /64 permits SLAAC. O indicates other DHCPv6 information, supplied here by a server. The nonzero RA lifetime permits the advertised router as default.

whyWrong.0: Ordinary default-router discovery uses RA, not DHCPv6.
whyWrong.1: SLAAC does not require the EUI-64 identifier method.
whyWrong.2: M is not required for SLAAC.

exhibit.title: Representative configuration or observation
exhibit.text:
Complete relevant R1 settings:
no ipv6 unicast-routing
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ipv6 address 2001:db8:acad:1::1/64
 no shutdown
Interface up/up; no other advertising router exists.

questions.prompt: Automatic PCs receive only link-local addresses. The router answers a manually addressed PC on the local LAN. What missing prerequisite is directly shown?
options: IPv6 forwarding/router operation has not been enabled globally.
The router needs an IPv4 default route.
All clients must use DHCPv6 for an IPv6 address.
A /64 cannot be advertised on Ethernet.
questions.explanation: The displayed no ipv6 unicast-routing setting leaves the router acting as an IPv6 endpoint instead of the advertising/forwarding router needed here.

whyWrong.1: An IPv4 default does not enable IPv6 advertisements.
whyWrong.2: SLAAC can form addresses without a DHCPv6 address server.
whyWrong.3: An ordinary Ethernet /64 is suitable for SLAAC.

questions.prompt: What is true of fd12:3456:789a:1::a1/64?
options: It is multicast because it begins with f.
It is a unique local address for routed private connectivity.
It is link-local and can never cross a router.
It is a public documentation address from 2001:db8::/32.
questions.explanation: fd falls inside the locally generated half of ULA fc00::/7. ULA can be routed within suitable private networks but is not intended for global Internet routing.

whyWrong.0: Multicast begins ff, not fd.
whyWrong.2: Link-local belongs to fe80::/10.
whyWrong.3: Its prefix is fd12, not 2001:db8.

questions.prompt: An example allocation is 2001:db8:5c00::/56. How many /64s fit, and which is the last?
questions.explanation: 64−56 leaves 8 subnet bits: 256 choices. They occupy the low byte of the fourth group, from 00 through ff.

whyWrong.0: 16 choices correspond to four extra bits, as with /60 to /64.
whyWrong.1: This changes retained bits in the third group.
whyWrong.3: The /56 fixes the upper byte of the fourth group; all 16 bits are not available.

exhibit.title: Representative configuration or observation
exhibit.text:
PC-A: 2001:db8:acad:1::10/64
PC-A gateway: 2001:db8:acad:10::1
R1 Gi0/0 up/up:
 FE80::1
 2001:DB8:ACAD:1::1
No router owns 2001:db8:acad:10::1.

questions.prompt: PC-A's manually configured gateway does not answer. Which evidenced mismatch should be corrected?
options: The router needs a DHCPv6 server.
Uppercase letters on the router mean it is in another subnet.
The PC cannot use a manually configured global-form gateway.
The PC names acad:10::1, but the actual router address is acad:1::1.
questions.explanation: The displayed gateway has fourth group 10 rather than 1 and does not match the configured router address. Verify the intended gateway rather than assuming every failure is caused by routing.

whyWrong.0: Both addresses are manual; a DHCPv6 server is not required.
whyWrong.1: Hexadecimal letter case does not change the address.
whyWrong.2: A manually configured on-link global unicast gateway can be valid; the fault is the specific incorrect address.

questions.prompt: Which TWO Neighbor Discovery statements are correct?
options: Address-resolution NS messages can target a solicited-node multicast group.
Every NS is broadcast to ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff.
A unicast NS can be used to verify a known neighbor's reachability.
Every stale neighbor entry proves a failed device.
questions.explanation: ND distinguishes initial address resolution from reachability confirmation. NS can be multicast or unicast depending on the operation.

whyWrong.1: IPv6 has no IP broadcast; ordinary IPv6 multicast uses multicast delivery.
whyWrong.3: Stale means reachability is not recently confirmed, not that failure is proven.

questions.prompt: A host obtains an address and DNS information from stateful DHCPv6. It has no manual routes. What ordinarily supplies its default router?
options: A Router Advertisement with a usable nonzero router lifetime
The DHCPv6 address lease's last 64 bits
The solicited-node multicast address
The server's MAC-derived interface identifier
questions.explanation: The host learns a default router from RA, independently of how DHCPv6 supplied its address and DNS.

whyWrong.1: The identifier is part of the host address, not a router instruction.
whyWrong.2: A solicited-node group supports discovery; it is not a default router.
whyWrong.3: A DHCPv6 server's identifier does not become the host's gateway.

questions.prompt: Which interface command explicitly creates an EUI-64-derived address in 2001:db8:acad:2::/64?
options: ipv6 address 2001:db8:acad:2::1/64
ipv6 address 2001:db8:acad:2::/64 eui-64
ipv6 address fe80::1 link-local
ipv6 enable
questions.explanation: The eui-64 keyword instructs IOS to build the interface identifier from the interface MAC.

whyWrong.0: This manually sets ::1 rather than deriving an identifier.
whyWrong.2: This sets a link-local address.
whyWrong.3: This enables processing and link-local addressing without the requested global prefix.

questions.prompt: The same unicast-format service address is assigned to instances in several locations and routing sends each packet to one preferred instance. What is this?
options: Broadcast to all locations
Multicast, requiring the address to start ff
Anycast; selection follows the routing system's preferred path
A duplicate that is forbidden even across separate routed links
questions.explanation: Anycast uses one shared address at multiple locations with routing choosing an instance. Its text has no unique anycast prefix.

whyWrong.0: IPv6 has no broadcast addressing type.
whyWrong.1: Multicast is group delivery and uses multicast-format addresses; this scenario is anycast.
whyWrong.3: Deliberate anycast across locations is a defined use, not an ordinary same-link unicast conflict.

exhibit.title: Representative configuration or observation
exhibit.text:
Complete Gi0/1 address configuration:
 ipv6 address 2001:db8:acad:2::/64 eui-64
 ipv6 address fe80::1 link-local
Displayed addresses:
 FE80::1
 2001:DB8:ACAD:2:21A:2BFF:FE3C:4D5E

questions.prompt: Hosts use 2001:db8:acad:2::1 as a manual gateway. What does this excerpt establish?
options: The eui-64 keyword guarantees ::1 also exists.
A reload always changes the interface's MAC.
The link-local address is invalid because it is short.
The derived address exists, but the expected ::1 is absent.
questions.explanation: The listed global address is not ::1. Repair the addressing plan or gateway expectation; do not assume EUI-64 creates both addresses.

whyWrong.0: EUI-64 supplies the derived suffix, not an additional ::1.
whyWrong.1: No before/after MAC evidence establishes such a change.
whyWrong.2: fe80::1 is a valid short form for a manually configured link-local address.

questions.prompt: What is the prefix containing 2001:db8:5:c7f2::1/60?
questions.explanation: A /60 retains the first three groups and the first three hex digits of the fourth. Zero the last digit and all following bits.

whyWrong.1: c700 discards retained prefix bits.
whyWrong.2: The low fourth-group digit is outside /60 and must be zero in the network address.
whyWrong.3: This removes the entire retained c7f part.

questions.prompt: The same MAC is available, but an automatically addressed host does not contain ff:fe in its identifier. Which conclusion is justified?
options: IPv6 cannot operate without a modified EUI-64 identifier.
Another valid identifier method may be in use.
Its address must be multicast.
It must be using IPv4 instead.
questions.explanation: SLAAC can use stable opaque or other supported identifiers; not all IIDs embed the MAC. Address appearance alone does not establish a fault.

whyWrong.0: Modified EUI-64 is one method, not a universal requirement.
whyWrong.2: Multicast is identified by ff00::/8, not by absence of ff:fe inside an IID.
whyWrong.3: Identifier-generation choice does not turn a 128-bit address into IPv4.

cards.front: How long is an IPv6 address?
cards.back: 128 bits: eight 16-bit groups. Each full group has four hexadecimal digits.

cards.front: What are the IPv6 compression and canonical spelling rules?
cards.back: Drop leading zeros within groups; use :: only once. Canonical text uses lowercase, compresses the longest zero run, chooses the leftmost on ties, and does not compress a single zero group.

cards.front: Which space is commonly allocated for global unicast?
cards.back: 2000::/3. Having a global-form address does not itself prove Internet reachability; allocation, routes and policy also matter.

cards.front: What is the ULA block and locally generated half?
cards.back: fc00::/7 is ULA. Locally generated prefixes use fd00::/8, with a pseudorandom 40-bit Global ID. They are not intended for global Internet routing.

cards.front: What is link-local scope?
cards.back: The reserved block is fe80::/10; a normal link-local address has fe80 followed by zero prefix bits and its identifier. It is meaningful on one link and is not forwarded onto another.

cards.front: Which multicast groups mean all nodes and all routers on a link?
cards.back: ff02::1 is all IPv6 nodes; ff02::2 is all IPv6 routers. Multicast addresses are in ff00::/8.

cards.front: How do you form a solicited-node multicast address?
cards.back: Append the address's last 24 bits to ff02::1:ff00:0/104. For an address ending 12:3456, the group is ff02::1:ff12:3456.

cards.front: What do ::1 and :: mean?
cards.back: ::1/128 is loopback, the local node itself. ::/128 is the unspecified address, used when no source address is assigned in permitted initialization cases.

cards.front: How is modified EUI-64 derived from a MAC?
cards.back: Split the six MAC bytes after byte three, insert ff:fe, invert the first byte's U/L bit with XOR 02, and regroup into four 16-bit groups.

cards.front: EUI-64 first byte: 00 becomes what, and 02 becomes what?
cards.back: 00 becomes 02; 02 becomes 00. Invert the bit rather than always adding 2.

cards.front: ICMPv6 types for RS, RA, NS, NA and Redirect?
cards.back: RS 133; RA 134; NS 135; NA 136; Redirect 137. Know each message's purpose as well as its number.

cards.front: Where are the A, M and O flags, and what do they indicate?
cards.back: A is in a prefix-information option and permits autonomous addressing. M and O are RA-header flags for managed addressing and other DHCPv6 configuration. They are not mutually exclusive address modes.

cards.front: Where does an automatically learned IPv6 default router come from?
cards.back: A valid RA with a usable nonzero router lifetime. Its link-local source identifies the router; the host's address may separately come from SLAAC or DHCPv6.

cards.front: What does ipv6 unicast-routing enable on a basic IOS router?
cards.back: IPv6 forwarding. With enabled IPv6 interfaces and normal unsuppressed RA settings, it also lets the device operate as an advertising router. Addressing alone is not inter-interface forwarding.

cards.front: ipv6 enable versus ipv6 address prefix/64 eui-64?
cards.back: ipv6 enable supplies IPv6 processing and automatic link-local addressing without a global prefix. The eui-64 form also creates a global-form address using the supplied prefix and derived identifier.

cards.front: How many /64 subnets fit in /48, /56 and /60?
cards.back: 65,536; 256; 16. Compute 2^(64 minus the original prefix length). These are subnet counts, not IPv4-style usable-host counts.

cards.front: What do EUI-derived and duplicate address indications tell you?
cards.back: An EUI indication identifies the configured derivation method; a duplicate indication means a conflict was detected and must be investigated. Exact [EUI] or [DUP] display labels vary by image.

cards.front: Is 2001:db8::/32 public Internet address space for deployment?
cards.back: No. It is reserved for documentation. Use it in written examples and isolated labs, not as an assigned public production prefix.

cards.front: Does assigning an IPv6 address automatically prove its prefix is on-link?
cards.back: No. On-link information is separate from address assignment. RA prefix L flags and other explicit on-link configuration supply that information.

cards.front: What does Duplicate Address Detection test?
cards.back: Whether a tentative unicast address conflicts on its local link. A DAD NS can use the unspecified source ::. It does not check uniqueness across the entire Internet.

commands.task: Enable IPv6 forwarding globally on R1.
commands.note: RA behavior also depends on interface state and RA configuration.

commands.task: Assign 2001:db8:acad:1::1 with prefix length 64 to this interface.
commands.note: Use a prefix length, not an IPv4 dotted mask.

commands.task: Set this interface's link-local address to fe80::1.
commands.note: Ensure no other ordinary interface on the same link uses that unicast address.

commands.task: Derive this interface's global identifier from its MAC under 2001:db8:acad:2::/64.
commands.note: Calculate the result from the actual operational interface MAC.

commands.task: Enable IPv6 processing and automatic link-local addressing without adding a global prefix.
commands.note: This does not by itself enable global inter-interface IPv6 forwarding.

commands.task: List IPv6 interface addresses and basic status.
commands.note: Read both address values and link/protocol state.

commands.task: Inspect Gi0/0's detailed IPv6 addressing, prefix and ND settings.
commands.note: Look for the actual configured address and advertised prefix; wording varies.

commands.task: Display R1's IPv6 neighbor cache.
commands.note: Generate relevant traffic first; an empty cache is not an inventory of absent devices.

commands.task: Display the installed IPv6 route table.
commands.note: Both locally connected LANs need connected routes, not extra statics.

commands.task: Read Gi0/1's interface details, including its MAC for EUI-64 calculation.
commands.note: Use the actual operational address; a separately listed BIA may differ after a manual override.

commands.task: Remove only the temporary address 2001:db8:acad:1::99/64 from this interface.
commands.note: Keep the original interface address and verify the result.

commands.task: Temporarily disable IPv6 forwarding in the isolated lab for the controlled fault test.
commands.note: Observe local versus cross-LAN pings before restoring ipv6 unicast-routing.

tickets.title: Automatic clients have only link-local addresses
tickets.scenario: A fresh LAN has one R1 router and several SLAAC-capable PCs. All physical links are up. R1 answers a manually configured PC at its global-form interface address. Automatic PCs receive no usable global prefix or default router. There is no other router and no DHCPv6 server. Excerpts are representative.

exhibits.title: Complete relevant R1 configuration
exhibits.text:
no ipv6 unicast-routing
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ipv6 address 2001:db8:acad:1::1/64
 ipv6 address fe80::1 link-local
 no shutdown
No RA-suppression configuration.

exhibits.title: PC observations
exhibits.text:
Manual PC 2001:db8:acad:1::10/64 can ping 2001:db8:acad:1::1.
Automatic PCs show only link-local addresses; no RA is observed.

tickets.question: Which correction addresses the shown missing prerequisite?
options: Enable ipv6 unicast-routing globally on R1.
Add an IPv4 default route.
Require every PC to use a MAC-derived identifier.
Change the LAN to /128.
tickets.explanation: R1's IPv6 interface can answer for itself without globally forwarding/advertising as a router. Enabling ipv6 unicast-routing addresses the shown setting. IPv4 routes do not supply RAs, SLAAC does not require EUI-64, and /128 is unsuitable for this ordinary Ethernet SLAAC LAN.
tickets.fix:
```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ipv6 unicast-routing
R1(config)# end
R1# show ipv6 interface gigabitethernet0/0
```
Confirm the /64 and RA settings. Allow clients to receive a new RA, or refresh Automatic mode if supported. Verify their actual prefix and learned gateway, then test numeric-address connectivity. A DHCPv6 address server is not required for this SLAAC exercise.

tickets.title: The documented gateway was never assigned
tickets.scenario: On an isolated LAN, PCs use 2001:db8:acad:2::1 as their manual gateway. The router interface is up and its current configuration uses EUI-64. A PC can ping the actual derived address but cannot resolve the documented ::1 address. No other device owns ::1.

exhibits.title: Complete Gi0/1 address settings
exhibits.text:
ipv6 address 2001:db8:acad:2::/64 eui-64
ipv6 address fe80::1 link-local

exhibits.title: Representative address display
exhibits.text:
GigabitEthernet0/1 [up/up]
 FE80::1
 2001:DB8:ACAD:2:21A:2BFF:FE3C:4D5E

tickets.question: Which diagnosis matches the evidence?
options: EUI-64 always creates ::1, so the display must be wrong.
The PC's /64 must be shortened to /48.
The expected manual gateway is absent; the derived address has a different suffix.
The short link-local address proves a duplicate.
tickets.explanation: The configured EUI-64 address is not ::1. A working ping to the actual address supports basic local connectivity. EUI-64 makes no ::1 guarantee, /48 does not create the missing gateway, and no duplicate evidence is shown.
tickets.fix:
Choose and document a consistent addressing plan. To retain the intended ::1 gateway in this isolated lab, add it explicitly:
```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001:db8:acad:2::1/64
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ipv6 interface gigabitethernet0/1
```
This adds the manual address alongside the existing derived address; it does not remove it. Verify no duplicate is reported and test the configured gateway. Alternatively, update the manual PC gateway to the correctly scoped fe80::1, then verify that chosen design before saving.

sections.title: Apply the IPv4 routing method to IPv6
Network, default, host and floating routes

lab.title: Route IPv6 between two LANs and diagnose a scoped next-hop error
lab.intro:
Start a new isolated project. This lab reuses the physical layout from the IPv4 static-routing chapter but supplies the complete IPv6 setup here. You will verify a missing return route, fail and restore the primary link, and repair a link-local next hop attached to the wrong link.

No simulator execution is claimed. Output and prompts below are representative of documented IOS behavior. Packet Tracer may omit diagnostic options or detailed neighbor states. Record your version's differences and use the full tables and configuration as alternative evidence.
lab.topology:
Use two 2911 routers with three GigabitEthernet ports each. Use default 2960 switch access ports in VLAN 1, without a connection between SW1 and SW2.

| Connection | Cable |
|---|---|
| PC-A FastEthernet0 — SW1 FastEthernet0/1 | Copper straight-through |
| SW1 FastEthernet0/24 — R1 GigabitEthernet0/2 | Copper straight-through |
| R1 GigabitEthernet0/0 — R2 GigabitEthernet0/0 | Copper cross-over |
| R1 GigabitEthernet0/1 — R2 GigabitEthernet0/1 | Copper cross-over |
| R2 GigabitEthernet0/2 — SW2 FastEthernet0/24 | Copper straight-through |
| SW2 FastEthernet0/1 — PC-B FastEthernet0 | Copper straight-through |

| Interface | IPv6 address/prefix | Link-local |
|---|---|---|
| R1 Gi0/0, primary | `2001:db8:12::1/64` | `fe80::1` |
| R2 Gi0/0, primary | `2001:db8:12::2/64` | `fe80::2` |
| R1 Gi0/1, backup | `2001:db8:13::1/64` | `fe80::1` |
| R2 Gi0/1, backup | `2001:db8:13::2/64` | `fe80::3` |
| R1 Gi0/2, LAN A | `2001:db8:10::1/64` | `fe80::1` |
| R2 Gi0/2, LAN B | `2001:db8:20::1/64` | `fe80::2` |
| PC-A | `2001:db8:10::11/64` | Automatic local-link address |
| PC-B | `2001:db8:20::12/64` | Automatic local-link address |
| R2 Loopback0, added later | `2001:db8:99::8/128` | Not used as a next hop |

PC-A's static IPv6 gateway is `fe80::1`. PC-B's is `fe80::2`. These gateway values belong to the router on each PC's own LAN. R2 intentionally uses `fe80::3` on the backup transit link, so the scope exercise has distinct peers to verify.

steps.title: Configure R1
steps.body:
Place and cable the devices. Decline a new router's setup dialog if offered. Configure R1's three interfaces.

```ios R1
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R1
R1(config)# ipv6 unicast-routing
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001:db8:12::1/64
R1(config-if)# ipv6 address fe80::1 link-local
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001:db8:13::1/64
R1(config-if)# ipv6 address fe80::1 link-local
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# interface gigabitethernet0/2
R1(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001:db8:10::1/64
R1(config-if)# ipv6 address fe80::1 link-local
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ipv6 interface brief
```

:::expected
The assigned addresses appear. Gi0/2 should become up/up after its switch port is ready; the transit ports may remain down until R2 is configured. R1 can use `fe80::1` on separate links without a same-link duplicate.
:::

steps.title: Configure R2
steps.body:
Check that you are on R2's console.

```ios R2
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R2
R2(config)# ipv6 unicast-routing
R2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R2(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001:db8:12::2/64
R2(config-if)# ipv6 address fe80::2 link-local
R2(config-if)# no shutdown
R2(config-if)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R2(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001:db8:13::2/64
R2(config-if)# ipv6 address fe80::3 link-local
R2(config-if)# no shutdown
R2(config-if)# interface gigabitethernet0/2
R2(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001:db8:20::1/64
R2(config-if)# ipv6 address fe80::2 link-local
R2(config-if)# no shutdown
R2(config-if)# end
R2# show ipv6 interface brief
R2# ping 2001:db8:12::1
R2# ping 2001:db8:13::1
```

:::expected
Both transit links should become up/up and both pings should succeed after discovery. Read the actual interface names and peer addresses rather than relying only on green cable indicators. Correct a local-link failure before adding remote routes.
:::

steps.title: Address the PCs and verify link-local scope
steps.body:
Under Desktop → IP Configuration, choose IPv6 Static on each PC. Enter the addresses, prefix length `64` and gateways from the topology table. Leave DNS and IPv4 unused.

From PC-A:

```text
ping 2001:db8:10::1
```

From PC-B:

```text
ping 2001:db8:20::1
```

On R1, run the following command by itself, then answer its interactive prompt:

```ios R1
R1# ping fe80::2
```

:::expected
Both local PC pings should succeed. Documented IOS behavior asks `Output Interface:` for the link-local ping; enter `gigabitethernet0/0` and allow the test to finish. It should reach R2's primary address. Repeat `ping fe80::3` and select `gigabitethernet0/1` for the backup neighbor.

If this prompt is not modeled, use the successful global transit pings from Step 2 and the peer's interface display as evidence, and record the unsupported scoped-ping observation. Do not infer a link's identity from the address text alone.
:::

steps.title: Add only the outbound remote-LAN route
steps.body:
```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::/64 gigabitethernet0/0 fe80::2
R1(config)# end
R1# show ipv6 route static
R1# ping 2001:db8:20::12
```

Then ping `2001:db8:20::12` from PC-A. Inspect R2's full IPv6 table before fixing anything.

:::expected
R1 selects the remote /64 through `fe80::2` on Gi0/0. Its router-originated ping may succeed using a transit source that R2 knows as connected; inspect the source if your image displays it. PC-A's ping should fail because R2 has no route covering `2001:db8:10::11`. The missing return prefix in R2's table establishes the fault; router ping source selection alone is not assumed as universal evidence.
:::

steps.title: Add the return route and establish the baseline
steps.body:
```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# ipv6 route 2001:db8:10::/64 gigabitethernet0/0 fe80::1
R2(config)# end
R2# show ipv6 route static
```

:::expected
PC-A-to-PC-B ping and the reverse ping should now succeed. R2 has the return /64 through R1 on the primary link. Record both installed entries before adding standby routes. A successful test in only one direction can still conceal a source-dependent issue, so perform both endpoint tests.
:::

steps.title: Configure both floating routes
steps.body:
First add R1's standby path.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::/64 gigabitethernet0/1 fe80::3 5
R1(config)# end
R1# show running-config
R1# show ipv6 route static
```

Then add R2's standby return path in its separate console:

```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# ipv6 route 2001:db8:10::/64 gigabitethernet0/1 fe80::1 5
R2(config)# end
R2# show ipv6 route static
```

:::expected
Each router retains two configured candidates for its remote /64. With both primary links working, the installed route remains distance 1 through Gi0/0. The distance-5 candidate is not normally displayed by the installed-static filter.
:::

steps.title: Fail the primary and observe the backup
steps.body:
Shut R1 Gi0/0 and keep it shut until the checks are complete.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ipv6 interface brief
R1# show ipv6 route static
```

On R2, inspect the same two show commands. Repeat PC pings after allowing link and route updates; no continuous-ping extension is required.

:::expected
Because the primary routers are directly cabled, R2's Gi0/0 should lose carrier as well. The remote /64 on each router should move to Gi0/1 at distance 5. R1 uses `fe80::3`; R2 uses `fe80::1`.

```output R1# show ipv6 route static
S   2001:DB8:20::/64 [5/0]
     via FE80::3, GigabitEthernet0/1
```

Endpoint pings should recover on the backup. No exact loss count or convergence time is promised. If the path fails, inspect the backup neighbor and the reverse route before bringing the primary back.
:::

steps.title: Restore the primary
steps.body:
```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ipv6 route static
```

:::expected
After link recovery, both routers select their distance-1 primary routes again. Backup candidates remain in the running configuration. Verify both endpoint pings before the next controlled fault.
:::

steps.title: Introduce a host route with the wrong scoped neighbor
steps.body:
This deliberately incorrect /128 is syntactically complete. It identifies R2's **primary** link-local address on R1's **backup** interface, where that address does not exist.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::12/128 gigabitethernet0/1 fe80::2 200
R1(config)# end
R1# show ipv6 route
```

From PC-A, ping `2001:db8:20::12`, then separately ping `2001:db8:20::1`. On R1 inspect `show ipv6 neighbors`. On R2 confirm Gi0/1 actually uses `fe80::3`.

:::expected
The host route can install on the active interface and wins for PC-B's address despite distance 200. It cannot resolve the intended next hop on that link, so PC-B's test should fail. The LAN router address `2001:db8:20::1` is not covered by /128 and should still work through the /64 primary.

An unresolved neighbor may appear as incomplete or may disappear between attempts. Compare the interface/address pair rather than requiring one exact state label. If the simulator does not model the expected resolution failure, record that limitation; the peer-address mismatch is still clear in the configuration.
:::

steps.title: Repair the host next hop and verify longest match
steps.body:
```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# no ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::12/128 gigabitethernet0/1 fe80::2 200
R1(config)# ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::12/128 gigabitethernet0/1 fe80::3 200
R1(config)# end
R1# show ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::12
```

:::expected
PC-A should now reach PC-B through the /128's valid backup next hop. The /64 primary still serves the other LAN addresses. Use the full table if the address-specific query is unsupported. A reply can return over the primary; this asymmetry is valid in the stated lab with no filtering or translation.
:::

steps.title: Add a real destination for a default route
steps.body:
On R2 create the logical test interface:

```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# interface loopback0
R2(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001:db8:99::8/128
R2(config-if)# end
R2# show ipv6 route
```

From PC-A, ping `2001:db8:99::8` before adding a default to R1.

:::expected
R2 has the loopback destination locally, but R1 has no covering remote route or default. The PC ping should fail. Confirm the absent covering prefix in R1's table. No cable or external service is needed for the loopback.
:::

steps.title: Add and test the default route
steps.body:
```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ipv6 route ::/0 gigabitethernet0/0 fe80::2
R1(config)# end
R1# show ipv6 route static
```

:::expected
R1 lists the default `::/0` through R2. PC-A's ping to `2001:db8:99::8` should now succeed. R2 already has the return route to the PC-A LAN. PC-B still follows its more specific /128; a default does not override specific routes. This is an isolated routing test, not proof of public IPv6 connectivity.
:::

steps.title: Remove temporary routes and the test loopback
steps.body:
Clean up R1:

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# no ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::12/128 gigabitethernet0/1 fe80::3 200
R1(config)# no ipv6 route ::/0 gigabitethernet0/0 fe80::2
R1(config)# end
R1# show running-config
R1# show ipv6 route static
```

Then clean up R2:

```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# no interface loopback0
R2(config)# end
R2# show ipv6 route
```

:::expected
R1 retains only its primary and floating remote-LAN candidates; R2 retains its corresponding return candidates. No temporary host route, default or loopback remains. Both physical paths are enabled. Confirm PC-to-PC ping once more.
:::

steps.title: Save the verified baseline
steps.body:
```ios R1
R1# copy running-config startup-config
```

Accept the destination-filename prompt with Enter and wait for completion. Then save R2 separately:

```ios R2
R2# copy running-config startup-config
```

:::expected
Accept R2's prompt separately. Save the Packet Tracer project as `20-ipv6-static-baseline.pkt`. Keep your route and neighbor observations with the file. Project saving and startup-configuration saving are distinct actions.
:::

lab.troubleshooting:
- **No local transit connectivity:** check the cable endpoints, interface state and exact /64 addresses before adding a route.
- **A link-local route is rejected:** include the local exit interface. Valid syntax still needs the correct neighbor on that link.
- **An installed route does not deliver:** compare the scoped next hop against the peer's interface, generate traffic, and inspect neighbor resolution. Then check downstream and return routes.
- **Router pings work but PC pings fail:** confirm the source used by the router, the return prefix for the PC, both PC gateways and `ipv6 unicast-routing`.
- **The standby never appears:** inspect the preferred route's eligibility and the backup interface. The ordinary route is not an end-to-end health monitor.
- **Both paths have distance 1:** read the backup configuration and restore its intended distance 5. Equal-cost multipath is different from standby.
- **One address fails while the rest of the LAN works:** check for a more specific /128 overriding the working /64.
lab.challenge:
From the cleaned baseline, replace only R1's primary route with the next-hop-only form using `2001:db8:12::2`. Predict its resolving route, test primary failure and restoration again, and return to the fully specified baseline. Also state whether a link-local next hop could use that same interface-omitted syntax.

:::expected
Remove `ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::/64 gigabitethernet0/0 fe80::2` and add `ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::/64 2001:db8:12::2`. Its next hop resolves through connected `2001:db8:12::/64`. With no default or other resolving route left in this baseline, loss of Gi0/0 removes that resolver and allows the distance-5 backup.

After restoration, remove the recursive line and re-add the original fully specified primary. Verify the installed route and endpoint pings before saving. A next hop of `fe80::2` cannot omit the interface; its link must be supplied explicitly.
:::

exhibit.title: Representative IOS excerpt
exhibit.text:
S 2001:DB8:20::/64 [1/0]
  via FE80::2, GigabitEthernet0/0

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly reads the installed static entry?
options: The remote /64 uses fe80::2 on Gi0/0 with distance 1.
The /64 has a hop count of 1 and a loss count of 0.
The route describes R1's own local /128 address.
The route applies only to a host whose suffix is ::2.
questions.explanation: The destination prefix is 2001:db8:20::/64; the bracketed values are distance and metric. The interface scopes the link-local next hop.

whyWrong.1: The brackets are not hop count and loss count.
whyWrong.2: The S /64 is a remote static network route, not an L /128.
whyWrong.3: fe80::2 is the next hop, not the destination prefix's host identifier.

questions.prompt: Neighbor fe80::2 is reachable on R1 Gi0/0. Which command routes the remote 2001:db8:20::/64 through that neighbor?
options: ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::/64 gigabitethernet0/0 fe80::2
ip route 2001:db8:20::/64 gigabitethernet0/0 fe80::2
ipv6 route fe80::2/128 gigabitethernet0/0 2001:db8:20::
questions.explanation: The fully specified IPv6 command supplies the destination prefix, local interface and link-local next hop.

whyWrong.0: A link-local next hop needs an interface.
whyWrong.2: ip route is the IPv4 command family.
whyWrong.3: This changes the destination into the neighbor's own link-local address instead of the remote LAN.

exhibit.title: Representative IOS excerpt
exhibit.text:
R1(config)# ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::/64 fe80::2
The command is rejected; exact error text varies by image.

questions.prompt: Why does the shown command lack required information?
options: The remote LAN must use /128.
A link-local next hop can never carry routed traffic.
The link-local next hop needs its exit interface.
The static route must specify a metric of 110.
questions.explanation: A link-local address is meaningful on a particular link, so the IOS route must name that link's interface.

whyWrong.0: A /64 network route is valid and covers the remote LAN.
whyWrong.1: Link-local next hops are valid when scoped to the correct interface.
whyWrong.3: 110 is a common OSPF distance, not a required static metric.

exhibit.title: Representative IOS excerpt
exhibit.text:
ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::/64 GigabitEthernet0/0 FE80::2
ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::/64 GigabitEthernet0/1 FE80::3 5

questions.prompt: Both links and their neighbors are usable. Which TWO statements follow from the configured routes?
options: The primary is preferred because its ordinary distance is 1.
The distance-5 route forwards half the traffic while the primary is installed.
The backup can become selected if the preferred route is withdrawn.
Distance 5 means the backup traverses five routers.
questions.explanation: These are candidates for the same /64. Lower distance selects the primary; the backup can be selected after withdrawal if its path remains usable.

whyWrong.1: The unequal distances implement standby rather than equal-cost multipath.
whyWrong.3: The final 5 is administrative distance, not a hop count.

exhibit.title: Representative IOS excerpt
exhibit.text:
Primary: R1 Gi0/0 fe80::1 — R2 Gi0/0 fe80::2
Backup: R1 Gi0/1 fe80::1 — R2 Gi0/1 fe80::3
Remote LAN behind R2: 2001:db8:20::/64

questions.prompt: R1 must route the remote LAN through R2 on the primary link. Which choice uses the correct scoped link-local next hop?
options: ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::/64 gigabitethernet0/0 fe80::1
ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::/64 gigabitethernet0/1 fe80::2
ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::/64 gigabitethernet0/0 fe80::2
questions.explanation: R2's primary link-local address is fe80::2, reachable through R1 Gi0/0.

whyWrong.0: fe80::1 is R1's own local address in this plan.
whyWrong.1: fe80::2 is not the peer on the backup link.
whyWrong.2: The link-local next hop lacks an interface.

exhibit.title: Representative IOS excerpt
exhibit.text:
::/0 via Gi0/0, distance 1
2001:db8:20::/64 via Gi0/1, distance 1
2001:db8:20::12/128 via Gi0/2, distance 200

questions.prompt: All displayed routes are installed. Which interface handles destination 2001:db8:20::12?
options: Gi0/2, because the /128 is the longest match
Gi0/1, because its distance is less than 200
Gi0/0, because a default takes priority
All three, because the address matches all three
questions.explanation: The /128 matches the single destination more specifically than /64 or /0. Different installed prefix lengths are not ranked by distance during forwarding.

whyWrong.1: The lower distance of a different prefix does not override the /128.
whyWrong.2: A default is the least specific match.
whyWrong.3: Overlapping prefixes do not form equal-cost paths to the same prefix.

questions.prompt: Which global command enables inter-interface IPv6 forwarding on the basic IOS router?
options: ipv6 enable
ipv6 unicast-routing
ip routing
ipv6 address autoconfig
questions.explanation: ipv6 unicast-routing enables IPv6 router forwarding. Interfaces also need appropriate addressing and usable links.

whyWrong.0: ipv6 enable is an interface command for IPv6 processing/link-local operation.
whyWrong.2: ip routing controls IPv4 forwarding.
whyWrong.3: Autoconfig is an interface address-assignment instruction, not this global forwarding setting.

exhibit.title: Representative IOS excerpt
exhibit.text:
S 2001:DB8:20::/64 [5/0]
  via FE80::3, GigabitEthernet0/1

questions.prompt: R1 is configured with a distance-1 primary and distance-5 backup. What does this installed entry establish?
options: The primary cable is certainly unplugged.
The backup has exactly five intermediate hops.
The backup is selected; the cause needs more evidence.
The backup is only configured and cannot forward traffic.
questions.explanation: The table shows the selected backup. The absence of the primary alone does not distinguish physical failure from other eligibility or configuration causes.

whyWrong.0: A table entry does not uniquely prove a cable fault.
whyWrong.1: 5 is distance, not hops.
whyWrong.3: This is the installed table, so the route is selected; neighbor and end-to-end checks still matter.

questions.prompt: An IOS router has active IPv6-addressed interfaces but no ipv6 unicast-routing. In this basic unfiltered setup, which TWO behaviors are expected?
options: It can answer a directly attached host pinging its own interface address.
It forwards packets between its IPv6 interfaces normally.
It does not provide the required inter-interface IPv6 forwarding.
Its interface IPv6 addresses must immediately be erased.
questions.explanation: The router can function as an IPv6 endpoint without being enabled to forward IPv6 traffic between interfaces.

whyWrong.1: That forwarding requires the global IPv6 routing setting in this setup.
whyWrong.3: Disabling forwarding does not erase assigned interface addresses.

questions.prompt: Which command adds an IPv6 default using the resolvable non-link-local next hop 2001:db8:12::2?
questions.explanation: ::/0 matches all IPv6 addresses and provides the default when no longer installed prefix matches.

whyWrong.0: ::/128 identifies one special address, not all destinations.
whyWrong.1: An IPv4 dotted destination is not the IPv6 default syntax.
whyWrong.2: Use ipv6 route for this address family.

exhibit.title: Representative IOS excerpt
exhibit.text:
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ipv6 address 2001:db8:12::1/64
!
ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::/64 GigabitEthernet0/0
Remote PC 2001:db8:20::12 is behind R2, not on this transit link.

questions.prompt: R2 owns the remote LAN, but no proxy ND is configured. Why is this Ethernet interface-only route inappropriate for reaching a host behind R2?
options: It attempts discovery for the remote host on the transit link.
It causes R1 to ask ARP for the remote IPv6 host.
It changes the PC's IPv6 destination into an IPv4 address.
It proves that IPv6 routing cannot use Ethernet links.
questions.explanation: With no explicit next hop, the route makes remote destinations appear on-link. The remote PC does not hear neighbor discovery on the transit segment.

whyWrong.1: IPv6 uses Neighbor Discovery, not ARP.
whyWrong.2: The command performs no address-family translation.
whyWrong.3: Ethernet IPv6 routing works with a correct next hop.

questions.prompt: A working /64 route uses Gi0/0. Only 2001:db8:20::12 should use usable backup neighbor fe80::3 on Gi0/1. Which addition achieves that?
options: ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::/64 gigabitethernet0/1 fe80::3
ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::12/128 gigabitethernet0/1 fe80::3
ipv6 route ::/0 gigabitethernet0/1 fe80::3
ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::12/64 gigabitethernet0/1 fe80::3
questions.explanation: A /128 matches only that host, leaving other /64 addresses on their existing network route.

whyWrong.0: Another /64 affects the whole network candidate, not just one host.
whyWrong.2: A default cannot override the existing /64 for that host.
whyWrong.3: A host address with /64 does not describe the intended single-address route.

questions.prompt: Which syntax difference is correct?
options: IPv6 routes use dotted-decimal subnet masks.
IPv4 static routes must always use link-local next hops.
IPv6 uses prefix/length and scopes link-local next hops by interface.
IPv6 route commands select a source rather than a destination.
questions.explanation: IPv6 uses slash prefix notation. The link-local scope rule is an additional constraint on its next-hop form.

whyWrong.0: Dotted subnet masks are the IPv4 form here.
whyWrong.1: IPv4 statics do not have the IPv6 link-local scope rule.
whyWrong.3: The route identifies destination reachability; it does not generally choose the packet source.

exhibit.title: Representative IOS excerpt
exhibit.text:
PC-A: 2001:db8:10::11 behind R1
PC-B: 2001:db8:20::12 behind R2
Complete relevant R2 unicast routes; no default:
C 2001:DB8:12::/64, Gi0/0
L 2001:DB8:12::2/128, Gi0/0
C 2001:DB8:20::/64, Gi0/2
L 2001:DB8:20::1/128, Gi0/2

questions.prompt: Both hosts have correct local gateways and all links work. R1 has a route to PC-B's LAN. Which missing route explains why replies to PC-A cannot return through R2?
options: An R1 route to R2's already connected transit prefix
An R2 host route to its own LAN address
An IPv4 default on R2
An R2 route covering 2001:db8:10::/64 through R1
questions.explanation: The reply destination is PC-A in 2001:db8:10::/64. R2's supplied complete table lacks that prefix or a covering default.

whyWrong.0: R1's connected transit is not the missing reverse destination.
whyWrong.1: R2 already owns its local LAN address.
whyWrong.2: An IPv4 route cannot carry the IPv6 reply.

questions.prompt: In S 2001:DB8:20::/64 [1/0], what are the bracketed numbers?
options: Administrative distance 1 and metric 0
Metric 1 and administrative distance 0
One route advertisement and zero errors
One next-hop router and zero alternate paths
questions.explanation: IOS displays [administrative distance/metric]. These values do not count traffic events or alternate routes.

whyWrong.1: The order is reversed.
whyWrong.2: The fields are not packet or advertisement counters.
whyWrong.3: Next-hop and path counts are not encoded in this pair.

questions.prompt: A repeated test cannot resolve fe80::2 on Gi0/1. Another cache entry shows fe80::2 on Gi0/0. What should you check?
options: Use the Gi0/0 binding automatically for all interfaces.
Verify whether the intended peer actually owns fe80::2 on the Gi0/1 link.
Assume the repeated address proves global routing is disabled.
Delete all IPv6 routes because a neighbor state is not REACH.
questions.explanation: Link-local neighbor identity includes its link. A binding on Gi0/0 does not establish a valid next hop on Gi0/1.

whyWrong.0: Cross-link reuse ignores scope and cannot supply the required neighbor.
whyWrong.2: The evidence concerns one address/interface binding, not the global forwarding setting.
whyWrong.3: Non-REACH states have different meanings; inspect the targeted fault rather than deleting all routes.

cards.front: Which command enables IPv6 forwarding on a basic IOS router?
cards.back: Global `ipv6 unicast-routing`. Addressed interfaces alone can answer local traffic without providing inter-interface forwarding.

cards.front: Why does a link-local next hop need scope?
cards.back: The same address can exist on different links. Its useful neighbor identity includes the local exit interface.

cards.front: Required IPv6 static-route form for a link-local next hop?
cards.back: `ipv6 route destination/prefix-length exit-interface link-local-next-hop`. Substitute the actual prefix, interface and neighbor values.

cards.front: What is wrong with ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::/64 fe80::2?
cards.back: The next hop is link-local but no interface identifies its link. IOS requires the interface; the exact rejection text is platform dependent.

cards.front: IPv6 default-route prefix?
cards.back: ::/0. It matches all IPv6 addresses but is used only when no longer installed prefix matches.

cards.front: IPv6 host-route prefix length?
cards.back: /128. All address bits are specified, so the route matches one destination.

cards.front: Ordinary static route distance, and unusable distance?
cards.back: Default static distance 1; distance 255 is not usable for installation.

cards.front: How does an IPv6 floating static become selected?
cards.back: It has higher distance than the preferred candidate to the same prefix. It can install after primary withdrawal if the backup path remains usable.

cards.front: Read [5/0] in an IPv6 static route.
cards.back: Administrative distance 5, metric 0. The values do not mean five hops and zero packet loss.

cards.front: What does fully specified mean for an IPv6 static route?
cards.back: Both exit interface and next hop are supplied. Ethernet still needs Neighbor Discovery to resolve the next hop's MAC.

cards.front: Problem with an Ethernet interface-only route to a remote IPv6 LAN?
cards.back: It treats remote destinations as on-link and can attempt ND for them on the transit segment. Name the adjacent router rather than relying on unconfigured proxy behavior.

cards.front: What does a non-link-local next-hop-only route need?
cards.back: A usable resolving route to that next hop without self-dependency. A connected transit prefix provides this in the lab; do not assume default-based recursion is enabled.

cards.front: What do C, L and S mean in the IPv6 route table?
cards.back: C: connected prefix. L: local interface address, usually /128. S: static route. A remote static /128 is different from a local L /128.

cards.front: What address identifies a router learned through RA?
cards.back: The RA's link-local source, with a usable router lifetime. Manually configured gateways can follow a different valid on-link addressing plan.

cards.front: Which command shows IPv6 neighbor bindings?
cards.back: `show ipv6 neighbors`. Entries include interface scope; the cache is not an inventory of all peer addresses.

cards.front: Does a stale IPv6 neighbor entry prove failure?
cards.back: No. It lacks recent reachability confirmation. Incomplete means resolution has not completed and can be temporary; persistent failures justify further checks.

cards.front: Why can IOS ask for Output Interface during a link-local ping?
cards.back: The destination is meaningful only on one link. Supply the local exit interface. Prompt availability and wording can vary by simulator image.

cards.front: How do you assign a predictable interface link-local address?
cards.back: For example, `ipv6 address fe80::1 link-local` in interface configuration. Ensure uniqueness among ordinary unicast addresses on that link.

cards.front: How is an IPv6 route destination written?
cards.back: As prefix/length, such as 2001:db8:20::/64. Do not append an IPv4 dotted mask.

cards.front: Does lower distance make /64 beat an installed /128?
cards.back: No. A matching /128 wins forwarding because it is longer. Distance selects candidates for the same prefix before forwarding compares installed entries.

commands.note: Interfaces and routes must also be usable.

commands.note: Assigning an address is separate from global forwarding.

commands.task: Set this interface's link-local address to fe80::1.
commands.note: Do not duplicate another ordinary unicast address on the same link.

commands.task: Route 2001:db8:20::/64 through neighbor fe80::2 on GigabitEthernet0/0.
commands.note: Both link-local address and interface are required.

commands.task: Add a next-hop-only route to 2001:db8:20::/64 through 2001:db8:12::2.
commands.note: A usable resolving route to that non-link-local next hop is required.

commands.task: Add an IPv6 default through fe80::2 on GigabitEthernet0/0.

commands.task: Route only host 2001:db8:20::12 through fe80::3 on GigabitEthernet0/1.
commands.note: /128 covers just this address.

commands.task: Add a backup to 2001:db8:20::/64 through fe80::3 on GigabitEthernet0/1 at distance 5.
commands.note: This follows a working distance-1 route to the same /64.

commands.task: Display installed IPv6 static routes.
commands.note: Use running configuration to see unselected backup candidates.

commands.task: List IPv6 interface addresses and basic state.
