tickets.title: The selected backup has the wrong link-local neighbor
tickets.scenario: R1's directly cabled primary failed and its distance-5 backup was selected. Both backup ports remain up. R2's onward LAN and its return route to R1's LAN work. Repeated endpoint pings fail. No ND proxy is configured. Excerpts are representative.

exhibits.title: R1 route and neighbor observation
exhibits.text:
S 2001:DB8:20::/64 [5/0]
 via FE80::2, GigabitEthernet0/1
Repeated resolution for FE80::2 on Gi0/1 does not complete.

exhibits.title: R2 actual interface addresses
exhibits.text:
Gi0/0 primary: FE80::2; link down
Gi0/1 backup: FE80::3; up/up
Gi0/2 LAN: 2001:DB8:20::1/64; up/up

exhibits.title: R1 configured backup
exhibits.text: ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::/64 GigabitEthernet0/1 FE80::2 5

tickets.question: Which targeted repair matches the evidence?
options: Change the backup next hop to FE80::3 while retaining Gi0/1 and distance 5.
Change the backup distance to 255.
Use FE80::2 without any interface.
Delete the remote prefix because the route is installed.
tickets.explanation: The backup link's actual peer is FE80::3. The current route uses the primary link's address on the backup interface. Distance 255 is unusable, an unscoped link-local next hop is invalid, and deleting the destination would not repair connectivity.
tickets.fix:
```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# no ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::/64 gigabitethernet0/1 fe80::2 5
R1(config)# ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::/64 gigabitethernet0/1 fe80::3 5
R1(config)# end
R1# show ipv6 route static
R1# show ipv6 neighbors
```
Keep the primary down long enough to test the repaired backup with endpoint pings. The route should identify FE80::3 on Gi0/1 and neighbor resolution should work. Restore the primary separately, verify preferred-route recovery, then save.

tickets.title: The router answers its LANs but does not forward between them
tickets.scenario: A new R1 directly connects two correctly addressed IPv6 /64 LANs. Each PC has R1's link-local gateway on its own link. Both interfaces are up. Each PC can ping R1's local address, but PC-to-PC traffic fails. There is no filtering and no remote router is needed.

exhibits.title: Complete relevant global and interface configuration
exhibits.text:
no ipv6 unicast-routing
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ipv6 address 2001:db8:10::1/64
 ipv6 address fe80::1 link-local
 no shutdown
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 ipv6 address 2001:db8:20::1/64
 ipv6 address fe80::1 link-local
 no shutdown

exhibits.title: PC settings
exhibits.text:
PC-A 2001:db8:10::11/64, gateway fe80::1
PC-B 2001:db8:20::12/64, gateway fe80::1
The PCs are on separate links.

tickets.question: What should be corrected first?
options: Assign an IPv4 default route.
Enable global IPv6 unicast routing.
Remove one fe80::1 because reuse across separate links is forbidden.
Add a static route to each already connected LAN.
tickets.explanation: The missing global forwarding setting is explicit. R1 can answer as an endpoint without routing between interfaces. IPv4 routing cannot fix IPv6 forwarding, identical link-local values on separate links are valid, and extra statics do not replace the forwarding prerequisite.
tickets.fix:
```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ipv6 unicast-routing
R1(config)# end
R1# show ipv6 route
```
Verify connected routes for both /64s, then test PC-A-to-PC-B and reverse traffic. Confirm the successful result before saving; addressing and forwarding are separate checks.

sections.title: From neighbor discovery to a full adjacency

lab.title: Build and troubleshoot a single-area IPv4 network
lab.intro:
Build from blank devices. You will prove a broadcast election, a point-to-point adjacency, two client routes, and failover between known-cost paths. Keep a table of observations before and after each fault.

Use a new Packet Tracer file with **three 2911 routers**, **one 2960 switch**, and **two PCs**. The 2911 provides Gi0/0, Gi0/1, and Gi0/2. Use straight-through copper for router–switch links, and crossover or the auto-connect tool for router–router and direct PC–router links. On CML/other images, map the interfaces explicitly before typing. All output in this guide is representative, not a recorded run; simulator commands and timing can differ.
lab.topology:
```diagram
{"type": "topology", "title": "Lab 21 — Shared transit and a separate direct link", "caption": "R1 and R3 have client LANs, a shared transit through SW1, and an independent direct link.", "nodes": [{"id": "A", "kind": "pc", "label": "PC-A", "x": 0.5, "y": 1}, {"id": "R1", "kind": "router", "label": "R1", "x": 3.5, "y": 1}, {"id": "SW", "kind": "switch", "label": "SW1", "sub": "10.0.123.0/24", "x": 7, "y": 1}, {"id": "R2", "kind": "router", "label": "R2", "x": 11, "y": 1}, {"id": "R3", "kind": "router", "label": "R3", "x": 7, "y": 5}, {"id": "B", "kind": "pc", "label": "PC-B", "x": 11, "y": 5}], "links": [{"from": "A", "to": "R1", "toLabel": "Gi0/2"}, {"from": "R1", "to": "SW", "fromLabel": "Gi0/0", "toLabel": "Fa0/1"}, {"from": "R2", "to": "SW", "fromLabel": "Gi0/0", "toLabel": "Fa0/2"}, {"from": "R3", "to": "SW", "fromLabel": "Gi0/0", "toLabel": "Fa0/3"}, {"from": "R1", "to": "R3", "label": "Gi0/1 to Gi0/1"}, {"from": "R3", "to": "B", "fromLabel": "Gi0/2"}]}
```

| Device/interface | IPv4 address/prefix | Connection or gateway |
|---|---|---|
| R1 Gi0/0 | 10.0.123.1/24 | SW1 Fa0/1 |
| R2 Gi0/0 | 10.0.123.2/24 | SW1 Fa0/2 |
| R3 Gi0/0 | 10.0.123.3/24 | SW1 Fa0/3 |
| R1 Gi0/1 | 10.0.13.1/30 | R3 Gi0/1 |
| R3 Gi0/1 | 10.0.13.2/30 | R1 Gi0/1 |
| R1 Gi0/2 | 192.168.10.1/24 | PC-A FastEthernet0 |
| R3 Gi0/2 | 192.168.30.1/24 | PC-B FastEthernet0 |
| PC-A | 192.168.10.10/24 | Gateway 192.168.10.1 |
| PC-B | 192.168.30.10/24 | Gateway 192.168.30.1 |

The switch needs no management IP for this lab. There is no simulated Internet destination and no default route is needed: OSPF will carry both specific client prefixes. Shared-interface costs will be 10, direct-link costs 25, and client-LAN costs 1, in both directions.

steps.title: Cable and address the devices
steps.body:
Cable exactly as shown. Set each PC under Desktop > IP Configuration to the static address, mask 255.255.255.0, and gateway in the table; DNS is not needed. Decline the initial router setup dialog if it appears. Configure SW1 and all router addresses below. The shared interfaces deliberately remain shut until the election steps.

```ios SW1
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname SW1
SW1(config)# interface range fastethernet0/1 - 3
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport access vlan 1
SW1(config-if-range)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if-range)# end
```

```ios R1
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R1
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.0.123.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# shutdown
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.0.13.1 255.255.255.252
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/2
R1(config-if)# ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# end
R1# show ip interface brief
```

```ios R2
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R2
R2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R2(config-if)# ip address 10.0.123.2 255.255.255.0
R2(config-if)# shutdown
R2(config-if)# exit
R2(config)# end
R2# show ip interface brief
```

```ios R3
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R3
R3(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R3(config-if)# ip address 10.0.123.3 255.255.255.0
R3(config-if)# shutdown
R3(config-if)# exit
R3(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R3(config-if)# ip address 10.0.13.2 255.255.255.252
R3(config-if)# no shutdown
R3(config-if)# exit
R3(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/2
R3(config-if)# ip address 192.168.30.1 255.255.255.0
R3(config-if)# no shutdown
R3(config-if)# exit
R3(config)# end
R3# show ip interface brief
```


:::expected
Each PC can ping its own gateway. R1 and R3 can ping each other on 10.0.13.1/30 and 10.0.13.2/30. Gi0/0 is administratively down on all routers. A PC-to-remote-PC ping is not expected to work yet.
:::

steps.title: Start R1 first and establish its DR role
steps.body:
Configure only R1 now. Wait until its shared interface reports State DR, normally after the initial wait interval (40 seconds with these defaults), before starting R2 or R3. Verify rather than relying on wall-clock timing.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# router ospf 10
R1(config-router)# router-id 1.1.1.1
R1(config-router)# passive-interface default
R1(config-router)# no passive-interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-router)# no passive-interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-router)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ip ospf 10 area 0
R1(config-if)# ip ospf cost 10
R1(config-if)# ip ospf priority 100
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ip ospf 10 area 0
R1(config-if)# ip ospf network point-to-point
R1(config-if)# ip ospf cost 25
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/2
R1(config-if)# ip ospf 10 area 0
R1(config-if)# ip ospf cost 1
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# end
R1# show ip ospf interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1# show ip ospf neighbor
```


:::expected
R1 has RID 1.1.1.1 and process 10. Gi0/0 is broadcast, cost 10, priority 100, and DR after the wait. There is no neighbor yet. Gi0/1 is point-to-point; Gi0/2 is OSPF-enabled but passive.
:::

steps.title: Add R2 and R3
steps.body:
Run R2 first and wait until it is Full with R1 and its interface shows BDR. Then run R3. Different local process numbers are intentional.

```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# router ospf 20
R2(config-router)# router-id 2.2.2.2
R2(config-router)# passive-interface default
R2(config-router)# no passive-interface gigabitethernet0/0
R2(config-router)# exit
R2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R2(config-if)# ip ospf 20 area 0
R2(config-if)# ip ospf cost 10
R2(config-if)# ip ospf priority 50
R2(config-if)# no shutdown
R2(config-if)# exit
R2(config)# end
R2# show ip ospf interface gigabitethernet0/0
R2# show ip ospf neighbor
```

```ios R3
R3# configure terminal
R3(config)# router ospf 30
R3(config-router)# router-id 3.3.3.3
R3(config-router)# passive-interface default
R3(config-router)# no passive-interface gigabitethernet0/0
R3(config-router)# no passive-interface gigabitethernet0/1
R3(config-router)# exit
R3(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R3(config-if)# ip ospf 30 area 0
R3(config-if)# ip ospf cost 10
R3(config-if)# ip ospf priority 0
R3(config-if)# no shutdown
R3(config-if)# exit
R3(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R3(config-if)# ip ospf 30 area 0
R3(config-if)# ip ospf network point-to-point
R3(config-if)# ip ospf cost 25
R3(config-if)# exit
R3(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/2
R3(config-if)# ip ospf 30 area 0
R3(config-if)# ip ospf cost 1
R3(config-if)# exit
R3(config)# end
R3# show ip ospf interface gigabitethernet0/0
R3# show ip ospf neighbor
```


:::expected
R1 remains DR, R2 becomes BDR, and R3 is DROTHER on Gi0/0. R1 sees R2 as FULL/BDR and R3 as FULL/DROTHER on Gi0/0, plus R3 as FULL/ - on Gi0/1. R3 sees R1 as FULL/DR and R2 as FULL/BDR on the shared link. Process 10, 20, and 30 do not have to match.
:::

steps.title: Prove the client routes and their metrics
steps.body:
On R1 and R3, inspect routes and the database. Then open each PC Desktop > Command Prompt and ping the remote PC. Repeat once if initial ARP resolution causes a lost first echo.

```ios R1
R1# show ip route ospf
R1# show ip ospf database
R1# ping 192.168.30.1 source 192.168.10.1
```

```ios R3
R3# show ip route ospf
R3# ping 192.168.10.1 source 192.168.30.1
```

If the simulator rejects the one-line source option, use the corresponding PC ping below; those packets already have the client-LAN source.
```text
ping 192.168.30.10
```
Run that command on PC-A. On PC-B run:
```text
ping 192.168.10.10
```


:::expected
R1 learns 192.168.30.0/24 [110/11] via 10.0.123.3, Gi0/0. R3 learns 192.168.10.0/24 [110/11] via 10.0.123.1, Gi0/0. Each metric is outgoing shared cost 10 plus remote LAN cost 1. Both PC pings succeed after convergence; connected local LANs appear as C, not O.
:::

steps.title: Test a higher priority without restarting anything
steps.body:
Raise R3 shared-interface priority while R1 and R2 are healthy. Do not clear a process or bounce a link.

```ios R3
R3# configure terminal
R3(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R3(config-if)# ip ospf priority 200
R3(config-if)# end
R3# show ip ospf interface gigabitethernet0/0
```


:::expected
R3 now has configured priority 200 but remains DROTHER. R1 remains DR and R2 BDR. This proves non-preemption; changing priority alone does not reset existing roles.
:::

steps.title: Remove the preferred transit and observe failover
steps.body:
On R1 only, shut the shared transit. Keep the direct link and both PC LANs up. Observe before restoring it.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip ospf neighbor
R1# show ip route ospf
```

```ios R2
R2# show ip ospf interface gigabitethernet0/0
```

```ios R3
R3# show ip ospf interface gigabitethernet0/0
R3# show ip route ospf
```


:::expected
After loss is detected, R2 is promoted from BDR to DR and R3 becomes BDR. R1 still has a Full point-to-point adjacency to R3. R1 reaches LAN 30 via 10.0.13.2, Gi0/1, at cost 25 + 1 = 26; R3 reaches LAN 10 via 10.0.13.1 at cost 26. PC traffic may lose packets during convergence, then recover. Do not assume an exact duration.
:::

steps.title: Restore transit and inspect the surviving election
steps.body:
Restore R1 Gi0/0. Check both shared interface roles and client routes.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip ospf interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1# show ip route ospf
```

```ios R3
R3# show ip ospf interface gigabitethernet0/0
```


:::expected
R2 remains DR and R3 BDR. Returning R1 is DROTHER; a return does not erase existing roles. R1 and R3 resume the cost-11 shared path after convergence. Save these roles in your notes, not as a promise about roles after a future cold restart.
:::

steps.title: Introduce a timer mismatch on the direct link
steps.body:
Change both timer values on R1 Gi0/1 only, leaving R3 at its defaults. Wait for the adjacency to disappear and compare both ends. The shared link remains available.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ip ospf hello-interval 5
R1(config-if)# ip ospf dead-interval 20
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip ospf interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1# show ip ospf neighbor
```

```ios R3
R3# show ip ospf interface gigabitethernet0/1
R3# show ip ospf neighbor
```


:::expected
The direct adjacency cannot remain healthy with R1 at 5/20 and R3 at 10/40. R1 and R3 can still exchange routes over the shared segment, so client ping success alone can hide this failed backup adjacency. No process-ID or priority change would fix the timer mismatch.
:::

steps.title: Restore the timers and save the working network
steps.body:
Remove only the deliberate timer overrides. Verify the direct neighbor returns and both client pings work before saving each device.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# no ip ospf hello-interval
R1(config-if)# no ip ospf dead-interval
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip ospf interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1# show ip ospf neighbor
R1# copy running-config startup-config
```

```ios R2
R2# copy running-config startup-config
```

```ios R3
R3# copy running-config startup-config
```

```ios SW1
SW1# copy running-config startup-config
```

Accept the default destination filename when asked, then save the Packet Tracer project file.

:::expected
Both direct interfaces use 10/40 and the point-to-point adjacency is Full. R2/R3 may retain DR/BDR on the shared segment. The saved priorities are R1 100, R2 50, R3 200; those preferences do not retroactively alter the current election.
:::

lab.troubleshooting:
- No shared neighbor: check SW1 access VLAN 1, the three /24 addresses, shutdown state, area 0, and passive exceptions.
- Direct neighbor absent: compare /30 addresses, point-to-point settings, timers, and interface activation on both ends.
- Full neighbors but no remote LAN: verify Gi0/2 is up, has its correct /24 address, and is activated in the local OSPF process. Passive is intended there.
- A wrong metric: check explicit interface costs and calculate from the router issuing the command. Incoming interface cost is not added.
- A ping fails: inspect the source PC's mask/gateway and the return route. Initial ARP loss is different from repeated failure after convergence.
lab.challenge:
Without changing R3, set R1's shared outgoing cost to 40. Predict R1's route to LAN 30 and R3's route to LAN 10, then test. Restore cost 10 afterward. Rebuild the original lab in a fresh file using only the topology and requirements once you can explain the results.

:::expected
R1 chooses the direct path, cost 25 + 1 = 26, instead of shared cost 40 + 1 = 41. R3 still chooses its shared outgoing path at cost 10 + 1 = 11; changing R1's outgoing cost does not change R3's outgoing cost. On R1 use interface Gi0/0, `ip ospf cost 10` to restore, then verify and save. Asymmetric paths are possible and do not by themselves indicate a fault.
:::

questions.prompt: R4 is a DROTHER on a healthy four-router broadcast segment. Which conclusion follows from its neighbor table?
options: The 2WAY relationship with R3 is normal for two DROTHERs.
R3 must be changed to point-to-point on this shared segment.
R4 must have a Full adjacency with every router on the segment.
R3 must receive a different process number to complete synchronization.
questions.explanation: R4 is Full with the DR and BDR and 2-Way with the other DROTHER. That is the expected broadcast adjacency pattern, not evidence of failed database synchronization.

whyWrong.1: All routers should retain the intended common broadcast network type.
whyWrong.2: Two DROTHERs normally stop at 2-Way while each is Full with DR/BDR.
whyWrong.3: Process numbers are local and do not cause this normal state.

exhibit.title: Representative configuration or output
exhibit.text:
R4# show ip ospf neighbor
Neighbor ID     Pri State          Address       Interface
1.1.1.1         100 FULL/DR        10.0.123.1    Gi0/0
2.2.2.2          50 FULL/BDR       10.0.123.2    Gi0/0
3.3.3.3           1 2WAY/DROTHER   10.0.123.3    Gi0/0

questions.prompt: When a fresh IOS OSPF process starts, no explicit RID is configured. Loopback0 at 10.1.1.1 and Loopback1 at 10.9.9.9 are both up. Physical interfaces 172.16.1.1 and 192.168.1.1 are also up/up. Which RID is selected?
options: 10.1.1.1 from the lower-addressed loopback
10.9.9.9 from the higher-addressed loopback
192.168.1.1 from the highest physical address
172.16.1.1 from the first listed physical interface
questions.explanation: IOS prefers a loopback address over physical-interface addresses when no RID is explicit. With both loopbacks available, the higher loopback address 10.9.9.9 is selected.

whyWrong.0: Both loopbacks are available, and 10.9.9.9 is numerically higher.
whyWrong.2: Loopback preference is applied before comparing physical-interface addresses.
whyWrong.3: Listing order is not the selection rule.

questions.prompt: Two routers share an addressed broadcast Ethernet subnet. Which two values must match to form the intended OSPFv2 relationship? Choose two.
options: Local process ID
Area ID on the link
Router ID
Hello and dead intervals
Interface priority
questions.explanation: The area and effective Hello/dead intervals must agree. RIDs must be unique, while process IDs and election priorities may differ.

whyWrong.0: The process ID selects a local process and is not a neighbor matching field.
whyWrong.2: Using the same RID would introduce a duplicate identity.
whyWrong.4: Different priorities are normal when selecting preferred DR/BDR roles.

questions.prompt: A fresh broadcast election occurs after all four candidates are known, with no existing DR or BDR. Who becomes DR and BDR?
options: RB is DR; RD is BDR.
RA is DR; RC is BDR.
RD is DR; RC is BDR.
RD is DR; RA is BDR.
questions.explanation: RD wins by priority 50. Among the remaining eligible candidates, RA and RC tie at 1, so RA wins BDR by RID 4.4.4.4 over 3.3.3.3.

whyWrong.0: Priority 0 makes RB ineligible regardless of its high RID.
whyWrong.1: RD has a higher eligible interface priority than RA and RC.
whyWrong.2: RA and RC tie in priority, and RA has the higher RID.

exhibit.title: Representative configuration or output
exhibit.text:
Candidate  Interface priority  RID
RA         1                   4.4.4.4
RB         0                   9.9.9.9
RC         1                   3.3.3.3
RD         50                  1.1.1.1

questions.prompt: R1 reaches a remote LAN through R2 then R3. The outgoing costs along that direction are R1-to-R2 = 10, R2-to-R3 = 20, and R3-to-LAN = 1. What OSPF metric should R1 calculate?
questions.explanation: Add the outgoing costs from the router performing the calculation to the destination network: 10 + 20 + 1 = 31. The receiving interfaces are not added again.

whyWrong.1: This omits the final outgoing interface toward the destination LAN.
whyWrong.2: This omits R1's outgoing cost.
whyWrong.3: 110 is IOS OSPF administrative distance, not this path metric.

questions.prompt: R1 and R3 are the only two routers on an Ethernet link. They report Full, but remote LAN routes are missing. Which visible inconsistency should be corrected first?
options: Change R3 process 30 to process 10.
Configure the same intended OSPF network type at both ends.
Change both interfaces to Hello 30 and dead 120.
Replace the /30 addressing with a /24 subnet.
questions.explanation: A Full adjacency is not proof that both routers describe the link consistently. The displayed broadcast/point-to-point mismatch should be corrected on this two-router link, then neighbors and routes rechecked.

whyWrong.0: Different local process IDs do not explain the displayed topology mismatch.
whyWrong.2: The existing effective timer values already agree and are normal here.
whyWrong.3: The two /30 addresses are valid peers; this is not a shortage of host addresses.

exhibit.title: Representative configuration or output
exhibit.text:
R1: 10.0.13.1/30, Area 0, Process 10, Network Type BROADCAST
    Hello 10, Dead 40
R3: 10.0.13.2/30, Area 0, Process 30, Network Type POINT_TO_POINT
    Hello 10, Dead 40

questions.prompt: Which timers are effective on this IOS OSPF interface?
options: Hello 5 seconds and dead 20 seconds.
Hello 10 seconds and dead 40 seconds.
Hello 5 seconds and dead 40 seconds.
Hello 40 seconds and dead 5 seconds.
questions.explanation: Read the configured timer commands separately: Hello is 5 and dead is explicitly 40. A default relationship does not override an explicit dead timer.

whyWrong.0: An explicit dead interval of 40 is present; it is not forced to 4 times Hello.
whyWrong.1: The explicit Hello override replaces the ordinary 10-second value.
whyWrong.3: The commands identify the two intervals in the opposite order.

exhibit.title: Representative configuration or output
exhibit.text:
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip ospf hello-interval 5
 ip ospf dead-interval 40

questions.prompt: Gi0/0 is addressed 172.16.5.33/27. Which router-mode network statement activates only that exact interface address in area 0?
questions.explanation: An all-zero wildcard requires every address bit to match. OSPF then advertises the interface's actual prefix, 172.16.5.32/27; the selector does not turn it into a /32 destination.

whyWrong.0: This matches the entire /27 address range, not only the exact address.
whyWrong.1: This uses a subnet mask where the command expects a wildcard.
whyWrong.2: This exact match selects .32, not the configured .33 address.

questions.prompt: R2 has a correctly addressed, up/up transit interface but no neighbor there. Which configuration line explains the absence?
options: passive-interface default without a Gi0/0 exception
router-id 2.2.2.2 in the routing process
router ospf 20 rather than process 10
questions.explanation: The interface is selected into OSPF, but passive-interface default suppresses its Hellos. Add no passive-interface gigabitethernet0/0 under that process after confirming it is the intended transit.

whyWrong.1: A unique explicit RID is appropriate.
whyWrong.2: This statement correctly activates the interface at .2.
whyWrong.3: Neighbors may use different process numbers.

exhibit.title: Representative configuration or output
exhibit.text:
router ospf 20
 router-id 2.2.2.2
 passive-interface default
 network 10.0.123.2 0.0.0.0 area 0

questions.prompt: R1 is the established DR, R2 is BDR, and R3 joins later with priority 200. After R1 fails, what happens if R2 and R3 remain healthy?
options: R3 becomes DR immediately when it joins.
R2 becomes DR, and R3 can become BDR.
R1 stays DR in the remaining routers indefinitely.
R3 becomes DR after R1 fails, bypassing R2.
questions.explanation: The non-preemptive election preserves existing roles while healthy. On DR failure, the BDR R2 is promoted and a new BDR can be selected from eligible remaining routers.

whyWrong.0: A later higher priority does not preempt an existing DR.
whyWrong.2: The failed DR is removed after failure detection.
whyWrong.3: The existing BDR is promoted before a replacement BDR is chosen.

questions.prompt: This adjacency repeatedly stalls during database exchange. Which evidence best identifies the fault?
options: Point-to-point operation omits the required DR.
The two process numbers are different.
The interface MTU values differ.
The peer uses a unique router ID.
questions.explanation: ExStart/Exchange involves DBD negotiation, including an MTU check. The explicit 1500/1400 mismatch is actionable evidence; fix the intended MTU rather than assuming every ExStart case has the same cause.

whyWrong.0: A point-to-point adjacency does not require a DR.
whyWrong.1: Process IDs are local and can differ.
whyWrong.3: Unique RIDs are required, not a fault.

exhibit.title: Representative configuration or output
exhibit.text:
R1 Gi0/1: up/up, MTU 1500, area 0, point-to-point, Hello 10, Dead 40
R2 Gi0/1: up/up, MTU 1400, area 0, point-to-point, Hello 10, Dead 40
R1 neighbor 2.2.2.2: repeatedly EXSTART/ -

questions.prompt: A cloned router configuration produces the log below. What is the durable identity repair?
options: Give every router a different local process number.
Raise the new router interface election priority.
Put each shared-interface peer in a different area.
Assign unique explicit RIDs and apply any required controlled process restart.
questions.explanation: The log identifies duplicate router ID 10.255.255.1, not a duplicate process number. Configure a unique RID on the affected router, verify the active value, and use a controlled restart only if needed to apply it.

whyWrong.0: Different process numbers do not repair duplicate advertised RIDs.
whyWrong.1: Priority affects DR eligibility, not unique identity.
whyWrong.2: Different areas on the same intended link prevent the required adjacency.

exhibit.title: Representative configuration or output
exhibit.text: %OSPF-4-DUP_RTRID_NBR: OSPF detected duplicate router-id 10.255.255.1 from 10.0.123.3

questions.prompt: R1 uses router ospf 10 and R2 uses router ospf 20. Their shared /30 link is in area 0 with matching timers, compatible point-to-point types, and unique RIDs. What should happen?
options: They can form an adjacency despite the different process IDs.
They must change both process IDs to area number 0.
They discover each other but stop at 2-Way because of process IDs.
They require identical RIDs to join the same routing process.
questions.explanation: The process number is locally significant. Shared-link parameters and unique router IDs determine the intended relationship, not equality of the process labels.

whyWrong.1: Process numbers do not have to match area numbers, and IOS process 0 is not the intended valid process.
whyWrong.2: Different local process IDs do not prevent Full synchronization.
whyWrong.3: RIDs must be different.

questions.prompt: With no explicit interface cost overrides, which command on every OSPF router makes 100-Mbps, 1-Gbps, and 10-Gbps interfaces cost 100, 10, and 1?
options: auto-cost reference-bandwidth 1000
auto-cost reference-bandwidth 10000
ip ospf priority 100
auto-cost reference-bandwidth 100
questions.explanation: The command value is in Mbps: 10000 / 100 = 100, 10000 / 1000 = 10, and 10000 / 10000 = 1. Consistent reference bandwidth prevents inconsistent automatic cost scales.

whyWrong.0: A 1000-Mbps reference gives costs 10, 1, and 1.
whyWrong.2: Priority affects the DR/BDR election, not routing cost.
whyWrong.3: The default 100-Mbps reference gives these links minimum cost 1.

questions.prompt: What does [110/26] mean in this OSPF route?
options: OSPF metric 110 and administrative distance 26.
A /26 prefix learned from router ID 110.
Administrative distance 110 and OSPF metric 26.
A 110-second age and 26-second dead timer.
questions.explanation: The bracket is [administrative distance/metric]. The route uses an OSPF path of cost 26; the /24 prefix and next-hop address are displayed elsewhere.

whyWrong.0: IOS displays administrative distance before metric.
whyWrong.1: The destination prefix is /24, and neither bracket field is a RID.
whyWrong.3: Route age and neighbor timers are separate fields.

questions.prompt: R1's Gi0/2 is an up client LAN, activated in area 0 and configured passive. Which two results are expected? Choose two.
options: The LAN prefix can be advertised through other OSPF links.
PCs must establish OSPF neighbors before sending traffic.
The interface sends no OSPF Hellos to discover neighbors.
The LAN connected route disappears from R1.
The interface must be shut to keep it passive.
questions.explanation: Passive OSPF stops neighbor formation on the interface without removing its enabled connected prefix from advertisements. PCs use the router as their gateway and do not run OSPF in this design.

whyWrong.1: PCs do not participate in the routing protocol here.
whyWrong.3: The up addressed interface retains its connected route.
whyWrong.4: Passive is an OSPF setting, not an interface shutdown.

cards.front: Default Cisco IOS OSPF administrative distance?
cards.back: 110. It is separate from the OSPF cost.

cards.front: OSPFv2 protocol number and multicast groups?
cards.back: IP protocol 89; 224.0.0.5 AllSPFRouters, 224.0.0.6 AllDRouters. No TCP/UDP port.

cards.front: What jobs do the five OSPF packet types perform?
cards.back: Hello discovers; DBD summarizes; LSR requests; LSU carries LSAs; LSAck acknowledges. These are not a rigid one-time sequence.

cards.front: How does IOS choose a RID when a process starts?
cards.back: Explicit router-id; otherwise highest eligible up IPv4 loopback, then highest eligible active IPv4 interface. Verify the active RID.

cards.front: Normal IOS Hello/dead defaults for broadcast and point-to-point?
cards.back: 10/40 seconds. An explicitly configured dead interval can differ; compare effective values on both ends.

cards.front: What do 2-Way and Full establish?
cards.back: 2-Way confirms bidirectional Hello recognition. Full means database synchronization completed for that adjacency.

cards.front: What should you compare before forming an IPv4 Ethernet OSPF adjacency?
cards.back: Area, subnet/mask, timers, activation, passive state, network type, and filtering; RIDs must be unique. Authentication must agree if configured.

cards.front: Repeated ExStart/Exchange: which common fault should you check?
cards.back: Compare interface MTUs and exchange errors. MTU mismatch is common, not the only cause; correct the mismatch before considering a bypass.

cards.front: When is 2WAY/DROTHER normal?
cards.back: Between two DROTHERs on a broadcast segment, while each is Full with the DR and BDR.

cards.front: DR/BDR election preference and IOS priority default/range?
cards.back: Higher interface priority, then RID; default 1, range 0–255, 0 ineligible. Existing roles are non-preemptive; BDR succeeds failed DR.

cards.front: Broadcast versus point-to-point OSPF roles?
cards.back: Broadcast elects DR/BDR. Point-to-point has no DR/BDR and normally shows FULL/ -.

cards.front: Configure OSPF point-to-point on a two-router Ethernet link?
cards.back: ip ospf network point-to-point under both interfaces. Ethernet framing stays Ethernet.

cards.front: IOS automatic OSPF cost formula and default reference?
cards.back: Reference bandwidth / configured interface bandwidth, integer cost with minimum 1. Default reference 100 Mbps.

cards.front: With 100-Mbps reference, costs at 10, 100, and 1000 Mbps?
cards.back: 10, 1, and 1, unless an explicit interface cost overrides automatic calculation.

cards.front: Which interface costs make up a route metric?
cards.back: Outgoing costs from the calculating router to the destination, including the remote LAN interface; do not add receiving costs again.

cards.front: Set an OSPF reference of 1 Gbps?
cards.back: auto-cost reference-bandwidth 1000 in router mode, consistently across the routing domain. Units are Mbps.

cards.front: Two IOS ways to enable OSPFv2 on an interface?
cards.back: A matching network ADDRESS WILDCARD area statement, or ip ospf PROCESS area AREA directly on the interface.

cards.front: What does a passive OSPF interface still advertise?
cards.back: Its enabled, up connected prefix, through other OSPF links. It does not form neighbors on that interface.

cards.front: IOS OSPF process ID significance and range?
cards.back: Local configuration identifier, 1–65535. It may differ between neighbors and is distinct from the RID and area.

cards.front: What does [110/11] in an IOS OSPF route mean?
cards.back: Administrative distance 110, total OSPF cost 11. Neither number is the prefix length.

tickets.title: Database exchange stalls after an MTU change
tickets.scenario: R1 and B2 share a direct point-to-point Ethernet link. The link supports IPv4 MTU 1500, both interfaces are up/up, and small pings work. B2 alone received an accidental ip mtu 1400 command. These excerpts are representative evidence.

exhibits.title: R1 OSPF neighbor
exhibits.text:
2.2.2.2  EXSTART/ -  10.0.12.2  Gi0/1
State repeatedly returns to EXSTART.

exhibits.title: Interface comparison
exhibits.text:
R1: 10.0.12.1/30, area 0, point-to-point, Hello 10, Dead 40, IP MTU 1500
B2: 10.0.12.2/30, area 0, point-to-point, Hello 10, Dead 40, IP MTU 1400

tickets.question: Which fault is supported by the evidence?
options: No DR exists on the point-to-point link.
B2 has an inconsistent IP MTU during database exchange.
The /30 subnet cannot carry OSPF LSAs.
B2 must use R1's router ID for synchronization.
tickets.explanation: The displayed MTUs differ even though the link supports 1500 and the other intended parameters agree. OSPF database exchange checks MTU; small ping success does not prove a large packet or DBD can be accepted. Restore the intended value and verify Full and the remote LAN route.
tickets.fix:
```ios B2
B2# configure terminal
B2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
B2(config-if)# no ip mtu
B2(config-if)# end
B2# show ip interface gigabitethernet0/1
B2# show ip ospf neighbor
B2# show ip route ospf
```
This scenario explicitly states that 1500 is supported. If the underlying service requires a smaller MTU, agree a consistent supported value instead; do not bypass the check as a routine repair.

tickets.title: A copied timer template prevents shared-LAN neighbors
tickets.scenario: R2 and R3 are in the same Ethernet VLAN. Both /24 interfaces are up/up and bidirectional ping succeeds. R3 received an explicit 30/120 timer template; the intended shared-LAN design is 10/40. Output below is representative.

exhibits.title: R2 Gi0/2 interface
exhibits.text:
10.0.23.2/24, Area 0, Process 10, RID 2.2.2.2
Network Type BROADCAST; Hello 10, Dead 40

exhibits.title: R3 Gi0/2 interface
exhibits.text:
10.0.23.3/24, Area 0, Process 30, RID 3.3.3.3
Network Type BROADCAST; Hello 30, Dead 120

tickets.question: What must be repaired to establish the intended relationship?
options: Make both process IDs 10.
Change one router to a new area for the VLAN.
Restore matching effective Hello/dead intervals.
Replace the /24 with a /30 mask on R3's only.
tickets.explanation: The Hello and dead values differ. The process IDs may differ, the shared area already matches, and changing one mask would introduce another fault. Restore the intended timer defaults and verify rather than promising an exact time to Full.
tickets.fix:
```ios R3
R3# configure terminal
R3(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/2
R3(config-if)# no ip ospf hello-interval
R3(config-if)# no ip ospf dead-interval
R3(config-if)# end
R3# show ip ospf interface gigabitethernet0/2
R3# show ip ospf neighbor
```
Confirm the effective timer pair is 10/40 and the expected adjacency reaches Full before saving.

lab.title: Build IPv6 OSPF neighbors and trace a global prefix
lab.intro:
Build a separate IPv6-only file from blank devices. This lab uses the classic IPv6-specific IOS syntax; the final step translates the core into address-family syntax without changing the working lab.

Use a new Packet Tracer file with **three 2911 routers**, **one 2960 switch**, and **two PCs**. The 2911 provides Gi0/0, Gi0/1, and Gi0/2. Use straight-through copper for router–switch links, and crossover or the auto-connect tool for router–router and direct PC–router links. On CML/other images, map the interfaces explicitly before typing. All output in this guide is representative, not a recorded run; simulator commands and timing can differ.

| R3 Gi0/1 | 2001:db8:13::3/64 | fe80::13:3, to R1 Gi0/1 |
| R1 Gi0/2 | 2001:db8:10::1/64 | fe80::10:1, to PC-A |
| R3 Gi0/2 | 2001:db8:30::1/64 | fe80::30:1, to PC-B |
| PC-A FastEthernet0 | 2001:db8:10::10/64 | Gateway fe80::10:1 |
| PC-B FastEthernet0 | 2001:db8:30::10/64 | Gateway fe80::30:1 |

The PCs may generate their own unique link-local addresses. No DNS or IPv4 address is required. SW1 is an ordinary Layer 2 switch in VLAN 1, with no management address. Shared costs are 10, direct costs 25, and client-LAN costs 1.

steps.title: Cable and configure IPv6 addressing
steps.body:
Set the PCs under Desktop > IP Configuration: IPv6 static, /64, and the listed link-local gateway. Leave IPv4 unused. Decline the router setup dialog. Shared links remain administratively down until OSPF is ready.

```ios SW1
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname SW1
SW1(config)# interface range fastethernet0/1 - 3
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport access vlan 1
SW1(config-if-range)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if-range)# end
```

```ios R1
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R1
R1(config)# ipv6 unicast-routing
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001:db8:123::1/64
R1(config-if)# ipv6 address fe80::1 link-local
R1(config-if)# shutdown
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001:db8:13::1/64
R1(config-if)# ipv6 address fe80::13:1 link-local
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/2
R1(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001:db8:10::1/64
R1(config-if)# ipv6 address fe80::10:1 link-local
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# end
R1# show ipv6 interface brief
```

```ios R2
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R2
R2(config)# ipv6 unicast-routing
R2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R2(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001:db8:123::2/64
R2(config-if)# ipv6 address fe80::2 link-local
R2(config-if)# shutdown
R2(config-if)# exit
R2(config)# end
R2# show ipv6 interface brief
```

```ios R3
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R3
R3(config)# ipv6 unicast-routing
R3(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R3(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001:db8:123::3/64
R3(config-if)# ipv6 address fe80::3 link-local
R3(config-if)# shutdown
R3(config-if)# exit
R3(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R3(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001:db8:13::3/64
R3(config-if)# ipv6 address fe80::13:3 link-local
R3(config-if)# no shutdown
R3(config-if)# exit
R3(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/2
R3(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001:db8:30::1/64
R3(config-if)# ipv6 address fe80::30:1 link-local
R3(config-if)# no shutdown
R3(config-if)# exit
R3(config)# end
R3# show ipv6 interface brief
```


:::expected
Each PC can ping its own global gateway address. R1 can ping 2001:db8:13::3 and R3 can ping 2001:db8:13::1. Shared Gi0/0 interfaces are administratively down. The manual link-local addresses are unique on each link.
:::

steps.title: Enable the processes and establish known roles
steps.body:
Configure R1 first and wait until Gi0/0 becomes DR before configuring R2. Wait for R2 to become Full with R1 and BDR, then configure R3. The distinct process numbers demonstrate local significance. If a classic command is unavailable on your image, use a supported IOS image; do not silently substitute OSPFv2.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ipv6 router ospf 10
R1(config-rtr)# router-id 1.1.1.1
R1(config-rtr)# passive-interface default
R1(config-rtr)# no passive-interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-rtr)# no passive-interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-rtr)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ipv6 ospf 10 area 0
R1(config-if)# ipv6 ospf cost 10
R1(config-if)# ipv6 ospf priority 100
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ipv6 ospf 10 area 0
R1(config-if)# ipv6 ospf network point-to-point
R1(config-if)# ipv6 ospf cost 25
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/2
R1(config-if)# ipv6 ospf 10 area 0
R1(config-if)# ipv6 ospf cost 1
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# end
R1# show ipv6 ospf interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1# show ipv6 ospf neighbor
```

```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# ipv6 router ospf 20
R2(config-rtr)# router-id 2.2.2.2
R2(config-rtr)# passive-interface default
R2(config-rtr)# no passive-interface gigabitethernet0/0
R2(config-rtr)# exit
R2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R2(config-if)# ipv6 ospf 20 area 0
R2(config-if)# ipv6 ospf cost 10
R2(config-if)# ipv6 ospf priority 50
R2(config-if)# no shutdown
R2(config-if)# exit
R2(config)# end
R2# show ipv6 ospf interface gigabitethernet0/0
R2# show ipv6 ospf neighbor
```

```ios R3
R3# configure terminal
R3(config)# ipv6 router ospf 30
R3(config-rtr)# router-id 3.3.3.3
R3(config-rtr)# passive-interface default
R3(config-rtr)# no passive-interface gigabitethernet0/0
R3(config-rtr)# no passive-interface gigabitethernet0/1
R3(config-rtr)# exit
R3(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R3(config-if)# ipv6 ospf 30 area 0
R3(config-if)# ipv6 ospf cost 10
R3(config-if)# ipv6 ospf priority 0
R3(config-if)# no shutdown
R3(config-if)# exit
R3(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R3(config-if)# ipv6 ospf 30 area 0
R3(config-if)# ipv6 ospf network point-to-point
R3(config-if)# ipv6 ospf cost 25
R3(config-if)# exit
R3(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/2
R3(config-if)# ipv6 ospf 30 area 0
R3(config-if)# ipv6 ospf cost 1
R3(config-if)# exit
R3(config)# end
R3# show ipv6 ospf interface gigabitethernet0/0
R3# show ipv6 ospf neighbor
```


:::expected
All routers have explicit, unique RIDs without needing IPv4 interface addresses. Shared roles are R1 DR, R2 BDR, R3 DROTHER. The classic IPv6-unicast instance is 0 on each shared interface. R1/R3 Gi0/1 interfaces are point-to-point.
:::

steps.title: Read neighbors and next-hop identities
steps.body:
Inspect R1 and R3. Record the local interface, neighbor RID, neighbor interface ID, link-local next hop, network type, and timers.

```ios R1
R1# show ipv6 ospf neighbor
R1# show ipv6 ospf interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1# show ipv6 route ospf
```

```ios R3
R3# show ipv6 ospf neighbor
R3# show ipv6 route ospf
```


:::expected
R1 sees RID 3.3.3.3 twice: FULL/DROTHER on shared Gi0/0 and FULL/ - on direct Gi0/1. Interface ID is the neighbor interface identifier; it is neither an IPv4 next hop nor necessarily the local process ID. Interface ID values can vary by image.
:::

steps.title: Prove the advertised /64 routes
steps.body:
Use the client PCs so the test requires return routes to the actual client prefixes. On PC-A run:
```text
ping 2001:db8:30::10
```
On PC-B run:
```text
ping 2001:db8:10::10
```
Then inspect the two routers again.

```ios R1
R1# show ipv6 route ospf
```

```ios R3
R3# show ipv6 route ospf
```


:::expected
After Neighbor Discovery and convergence, both pings work. R1 learns 2001:DB8:30::/64 [110/11] via FE80::3, Gi0/0. R3 learns 2001:DB8:10::/64 [110/11] via FE80::1, Gi0/0. The IP destination remains global while the next-hop address is link-local.
:::

steps.title: Break only the direct adjacency
steps.body:
Set R1 direct-link timers to 5/20 while R3 remains at 10/40. Wait until the direct neighbor no longer remains Full and compare effective timer output.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ipv6 ospf hello-interval 5
R1(config-if)# ipv6 ospf dead-interval 20
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ipv6 ospf interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1# show ipv6 ospf neighbor
```

```ios R3
R3# show ipv6 ospf interface gigabitethernet0/1
```


:::expected
The direct relationship fails because both timer values disagree. The shared adjacency and cost-11 route remain healthy, so PC traffic can still work. This is an adjacency fault hidden by another usable path.
:::

steps.title: Restore the direct timers
steps.body:
Remove the deliberate overrides from R1 only.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# no ipv6 ospf hello-interval
R1(config-if)# no ipv6 ospf dead-interval
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ipv6 ospf interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1# show ipv6 ospf neighbor
```


:::expected
R1 reports 10/40 again and the direct neighbor reaches FULL/ -. A process clear, RID change, or new IPv4 address is unnecessary.
:::

steps.title: Remove a LAN advertisement while keeping neighbors
steps.body:
On R3, disable OSPF activation on Gi0/2 without shutting the interface or changing its address. Inspect R1 after convergence and test PC-A to PC-B.

```ios R3
R3# configure terminal
R3(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/2
R3(config-if)# no ipv6 ospf 30 area 0
R3(config-if)# end
R3# show ipv6 interface brief
R3# show ipv6 ospf neighbor
```

```ios R1
R1# show ipv6 route ospf
```


:::expected
R3 remains Full with its routers, and PC-B can still ping its local gateway. R1 loses the OSPF route to 2001:db8:30::/64 and PC-A cannot reach PC-B. A Full adjacency proves synchronization, not that every desired LAN participates.
:::

steps.title: Restore LAN participation
steps.body:
Re-enable the intended LAN in area 0. Its process-level passive setting remains correct.

```ios R3
R3# configure terminal
R3(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/2
R3(config-if)# ipv6 ospf 30 area 0
R3(config-if)# end
R3# show ipv6 ospf interface gigabitethernet0/2
```

```ios R1
R1# show ipv6 route ospf
```


:::expected
R1 relearns the /64 at cost 11 and PC-A/PC-B pings recover. Gi0/2 remains passive: it advertises the LAN through other interfaces while forming no PC-facing adjacency.
:::

steps.title: Translate the core syntax on paper and save
steps.body:
In notes, translate R1 process 10 and its three area-0 activations into address-family syntax. Do not paste a migration into this working file. Compare with the answer below, then save each router and switch.

```ios R1
R1# copy running-config startup-config
```

```ios R2
R2# copy running-config startup-config
```

```ios R3
R3# copy running-config startup-config
```

```ios SW1
SW1# copy running-config startup-config
```

Accept the default filename and save the Packet Tracer file. If you later use a clean CML IOS XE image for the alternative syntax, verify feature support and map the interfaces first.

:::expected
The process begins with global `router ospfv3 10`, `router-id 1.1.1.1`, then `address-family ipv6 unicast`. Put passive-interface default and the Gi0/0/Gi0/1 exceptions in that family. Each interface activation is `ospfv3 10 ipv6 area 0`. The configured IPv6 addresses and need for IPv6 forwarding do not disappear. Use show ospfv3 neighbor/interface to verify that syntax family.
:::

lab.troubleshooting:
- No process RID: configure it explicitly; IPv6-only addressing does not supply a dotted-decimal RID automatically on classic IOS.
- No neighbor: compare interface activation, area, instance, timers, passive exceptions, link-local addresses, and link status.
- Repeated ExStart/Exchange: compare MTUs and exchange evidence. Bypassing the MTU check is not the first repair.
- Neighbor Full but missing /64: check the remote physical LAN's state and OSPF activation.
- A link-local next hop looks repeated: include the exit interface when interpreting it. Link-local scope is per link.
- Client failure with routes present: check /64 and gateway on both PCs, then route back to the source.
lab.challenge:
Predict the result if R1's shared cost becomes 50 while its direct cost stays 25 and R3's LAN cost stays 1. Test only after the baseline works, then restore the shared cost to 10.

:::expected
R1 selects cost 26 through FE80::13:3 on Gi0/1 rather than cost 51 through FE80::3 on Gi0/0. The destination stays 2001:db8:30::/64. R3's reverse route stays at cost 11 unless its own outgoing settings also change. Restore with `ipv6 ospf cost 10` under R1 Gi0/0, verify, and save.
:::

questions.prompt: What does the value 3 in the Interface ID column identify?
options: The neighboring router's interface used for this relationship.
The local OSPF process number on R1.
The third configured IPv6 prefix in the routing table.
The number of Full neighbors on Gi0/0.
questions.explanation: OSPFv3 neighbor output includes the neighbor's interface ID. The final Interface column names the local interface, while the Neighbor ID column names the remote router RID.

whyWrong.1: Process number is not the neighbor's Interface ID field.
whyWrong.2: The column is an OSPF interface identifier, not a prefix index.
whyWrong.3: This row describes one neighbor; it is not a count.

exhibit.title: Representative configuration or output
exhibit.text:
R1# show ipv6 ospf neighbor
Neighbor ID     Pri State        Dead Time Interface ID Interface
2.2.2.2          50 FULL/BDR     00:00:35  3            GigabitEthernet0/0

questions.prompt: Which source address does an OSPFv3 Hello use on an ordinary IPv6 Ethernet link?
options: The interface global unicast address.
The interface link-local unicast address.
The multicast address ff02::5.
The 32-bit dotted-decimal router ID.
questions.explanation: On ordinary links, OSPFv3 uses the local link-local address as its packet source. The Hello destination is the link-local multicast group ff02::5.

whyWrong.0: OSPFv3 neighbor communication on this link uses link-local source addressing.
whyWrong.2: ff02::5 is a destination group, not the source address.
whyWrong.3: The RID is a protocol identifier rather than an IPv6 packet source.

questions.prompt: On a healthy IPv6 Ethernet link with unique RIDs and link-local addresses, which two values must agree for the intended classic OSPFv3 relationship? Choose two.
options: Local process ID
Area ID
Global unicast prefix
Classic IPv6 instance ID
Interface priority
questions.explanation: The area and instance identify the intended OSPFv3 relationship on the link. Local process labels and interface priorities may differ; matching global prefixes are not a Hello requirement.

whyWrong.0: The process number is local and is not compared between neighbors.
whyWrong.2: OSPFv3 neighbor exchange uses link-local addressing and does not require identical global prefixes.
whyWrong.4: Different priorities can intentionally select DR/BDR preferences.

questions.prompt: R2 is IPv6-only and the OSPFv3 process reports it cannot select a RID. What is the appropriate correction?
options: Replace the global IPv6 address with ff02::5.
Disable IPv6 unicast routing so automatic selection can run.
Use R1's existing RID so both routers join the same process.
Configure an explicit unique RID such as 2.2.2.2.
questions.explanation: Classic IOS needs a 32-bit RID even for IPv6-only operation. Configuring it explicitly supplies the identifier without adding an unnecessary IPv4 interface.

whyWrong.0: A multicast group is not a usable interface unicast address or RID.
whyWrong.1: This routed IPv6 lab requires IPv6 forwarding enabled.
whyWrong.2: The RIDs must be unique.

exhibit.title: Representative configuration or output
exhibit.text: %OSPFv3-4-NORTRID: OSPFv3 process 20 could not pick a router-id, please configure manually

questions.prompt: What are the normal IOS OSPFv3 Hello/dead defaults for the broadcast Ethernet and point-to-point types in this chapter?
options: 10 seconds and 40 seconds.
3 seconds and 10 seconds.
1 second and approximately 3.6 seconds.
30 seconds and 120 seconds.
questions.explanation: The IOS broadcast and point-to-point types studied here use 10/40 by default. Always inspect effective values because explicit timer configuration can override defaults.

whyWrong.1: Those are ordinary HSRP Hello/hold values, not these OSPF defaults.
whyWrong.2: Those resemble VRRP timing, not OSPFv3 defaults.
whyWrong.3: Those are associated with other OSPF network types, not the types named here.

questions.prompt: R1 is DROTHER while healthy R2 and R3 are the established DR and BDR. An engineer raises R1's interface priority from 1 to 200. What immediately follows?
options: R1 preempts R2 and becomes DR as soon as its next Hello arrives.
R1 keeps its current role while the existing DR/BDR remain healthy.
R1 must become BDR because the new priority is highest.
R1 stops forming adjacencies because 200 is outside the range.
questions.explanation: A priority change changes future election preference but does not erase current segment roles. It differs from a clean election where no DR or BDR already exists.

whyWrong.0: OSPF DR/BDR election is non-preemptive.
whyWrong.2: An existing healthy BDR is not displaced merely by a higher-priority arrival.
whyWrong.3: 200 is within the IOS range 0–255.

questions.prompt: On R1, a direct two-router adjacency to RID 3.3.3.3 is FULL/ -. What does the dash indicate?
options: The neighbor has no link-local address.
The neighbor has not completed database synchronization.
No DR or BDR role applies to that point-to-point adjacency.
The local process has no router ID.
questions.explanation: The role suffix is separate from the synchronization state. A dash is expected for point-to-point operation, which has no DR/BDR election.

whyWrong.0: A valid link-local relationship is still required on the ordinary link.
whyWrong.1: Full indicates synchronization completed.
whyWrong.3: An operating OSPFv3 adjacency already has router identity.

questions.prompt: R1 has addressed IPv6 interfaces and a configured classic process 10 with RID 1.1.1.1. IPv6 forwarding and Gi0/0 activation are not yet configured. Which two commands supply these missing parts? Choose two.
options: ipv6 unicast-routing in global mode
network 2001:db8:123::/64 area 0 in process mode
ip ospf 10 area 0 in interface mode
ipv6 ospf 10 area 0 in Gi0/0 mode
router-id 2001:db8::1 in process mode
questions.explanation: IPv6 unicast-routing enables IPv6 forwarding, and ipv6 ospf 10 area 0 activates the classic IPv6 OSPF process on the interface. The process RID and addressing are already supplied by the question.

whyWrong.1: Classic OSPFv3 does not use an IPv4-style network activation statement.
whyWrong.2: ip ospf activates OSPFv2 for IPv4 rather than this OSPFv3 interface.
whyWrong.4: A RID is 32-bit dotted decimal, not a 128-bit IPv6 address.

questions.prompt: R3's Loopback0 has 2001:db8:3::3/64 and OSPFv3 network state LOOPBACK. R1 learns 2001:db8:3::3/128. What explains the prefix length?
options: Normal loopback advertisement represents the interface address as a host route.
R1 translated the /64 into IPv4-compatible addressing.
The remote /64 has an invalid prefix length for IPv6.
A Full adjacency always converts every prefix into a /128.
questions.explanation: OSPFv3 represents addresses of an interface in Loopback state as /128 host prefixes. Do not assume that the address command prefix length always equals the advertised prefix length.

whyWrong.1: No address-family translation occurred.
whyWrong.2: A /64 is valid; the OSPF loopback representation explains the /128.
whyWrong.3: Physical LAN prefixes can be advertised as /64; this is loopback-specific.

questions.prompt: Two routers on the same Ethernet link have valid unique link-local addresses and matching OSPFv3 parameters. Their global addresses are 2001:db8:1::1/64 and 2001:db8:2::2/64. Which statement is correct?
options: They must fail Hellos because an IPv6 subnet mask field differs.
They can form an adjacency, but that does not validate the intended global addressing.
They must use the same RID to compensate for different prefixes.
They automatically renumber their global prefixes to match.
questions.explanation: The adjacency uses link-local communication and has no matching-global-prefix requirement. A network intended to share one global prefix should still be addressed consistently, and client reachability must be verified separately.

whyWrong.0: OSPFv3 Hellos do not carry the OSPFv2 subnet-mask field.
whyWrong.2: Duplicate RIDs would introduce another fault.
whyWrong.3: OSPF neighbor discovery does not renumber interfaces.

questions.prompt: A supported IOS XE router has router ospfv3 10 and address-family ipv6 unicast configured. Which interface command activates that process in area 0?
options: ip ospf 10 area 0
ospfv3 10 ipv4 area 0
ospfv3 10 ipv6 area 0
network 2001:db8:123::/64 area 0
questions.explanation: The address-family interface command names the process, IPv6 family, and area. Keep it distinct from classic ipv6 ospf syntax and from OSPFv2.

whyWrong.0: That activates OSPFv2 for IPv4.
whyWrong.1: That selects the IPv4 family, not the requested IPv6 family.
whyWrong.3: This is not the address-family interface activation command.

questions.prompt: The direct IPv6 adjacency repeatedly stalls in ExStart. Which issue is supported by the comparison?
options: An area mismatch during Hello acceptance.
A mismatch between local process labels.
An election failure because no DR exists.
An MTU mismatch during database exchange.
questions.explanation: The interfaces agree on the displayed adjacency parameters but have different MTUs. Inspect and correct the supported MTU value rather than treating ping success as proof that database exchange can complete.

whyWrong.0: Both areas are 0 in the evidence.
whyWrong.1: Different process labels are allowed.
whyWrong.2: Both sides intentionally use point-to-point, which does not elect DR/BDR.

exhibit.text:
R1: Area 0, Instance 0, RID 1.1.1.1, POINT_TO_POINT, Hello 10, Dead 40, MTU 1500
R3: Area 0, Instance 0, RID 3.3.3.3, POINT_TO_POINT, Hello 10, Dead 40, MTU 1400
Neighbor repeatedly EXSTART/ -

questions.prompt: All candidates are known before a fresh OSPFv3 broadcast election, with no existing DR/BDR. Who is DR and BDR?
options: RID 4.4.4.4 is DR; RID 3.3.3.3 is BDR.
RID 2.2.2.2 is DR; RID 4.4.4.4 is BDR.
RID 1.1.1.1 is DR; RID 3.3.3.3 is BDR.
The highest global IPv6 address is DR; the next highest is BDR.
questions.explanation: Exclude the priority-0 router, then compare the RIDs of the priority-1 candidates. The higher two eligible RIDs win in this clean-election scenario.

whyWrong.1: Priority 0 excludes 2.2.2.2 from either role.
whyWrong.2: Among equal eligible priorities, higher RIDs are preferred.
whyWrong.3: The election tiebreaker is RID, not global IPv6 address.

questions.prompt: R1 is a DROTHER and shows this stable entry for R4; its DR and BDR neighbors are Full. What does the entry mean?
options: The global /64 masks must differ.
Bidirectional Hellos work, and this DROTHER pair need not become Full.
The link-local addresses must be duplicated.
R1 should clear its process until every neighbor becomes Full.
questions.explanation: Two DROTHERs normally remain 2-Way on a broadcast segment. The Full relationships with DR/BDR provide the expected synchronization pattern.

whyWrong.0: This state does not prove a global-prefix mismatch.
whyWrong.2: The entry alone does not support duplicate-address diagnosis.
whyWrong.3: A reset is unnecessary for the expected DROTHER pattern.

exhibit.title: Representative configuration or output
exhibit.text:
Neighbor ID  Pri State          Dead Time Interface ID Interface
4.4.4.4       1 2WAY/DROTHER   00:00:34  4            Gi0/0

questions.prompt: R1 and R3 remain Full, but R1 loses the route to R3's LAN 2001:db8:30::/64. Which missing line explains the result?
options: no passive-interface gigabitethernet0/2 under process 30
An IPv4 address on R3's Gi0/2
ipv6 ospf 30 area 0 on R3's Gi0/2
ipv6 ospf priority 255 on R3's Gi0/2
questions.explanation: Gi0/2 remains addressed and up, but it is not activated in the OSPFv3 process. Passive-interface only controls neighbor formation; it does not activate a prefix by itself.

whyWrong.0: A client LAN can correctly remain passive; activation is what is missing.
whyWrong.1: An IPv4 address is not required for this IPv6 LAN advertisement.
whyWrong.3: Election priority is irrelevant on a passive client LAN.

questions.prompt: R1 can reach R3 directly at outgoing cost 25 or across a shared segment at outgoing cost 10. R3's LAN cost is 1. Which route matches the lower-cost choice?
options: [110/26] via FE80::13:3, GigabitEthernet0/1
[11/110] via FE80::3, GigabitEthernet0/0
[110/10] via 3.3.3.3, GigabitEthernet0/0
[110/11] via FE80::3, GigabitEthernet0/0
questions.explanation: The shared path costs 10 + 1 = 11. Its next hop is R3's link-local address on that link, combined with R1's exit interface.

whyWrong.0: That is the more expensive direct path while the shared path is healthy.
whyWrong.1: The bracket fields reverse administrative distance and metric.
whyWrong.2: This omits the remote LAN cost and substitutes a RID for an IPv6 next hop.

exhibit.title: Representative configuration or output
exhibit.text:
R1 Gi0/0: shared path, next hop FE80::3, cost 10
R1 Gi0/1: direct path, next hop FE80::13:3, cost 25
R3 LAN: 2001:db8:30::/64, outgoing cost 1

cards.front: OSPFv3 for IPv6 uses which Next Header number?
cards.back: 89, directly over IPv6 rather than TCP or UDP.

cards.front: OSPFv3 multicast groups on an ordinary IPv6 link?
cards.back: ff02::5 AllSPFRouters; ff02::6 AllDRouters. They have link-local scope.

cards.front: Source address of an OSPFv3 Hello on an ordinary link?
cards.back: The sending interface's link-local address. ff02::5 is the multicast destination.

cards.front: Must OSPFv3 neighbors have the same global IPv6 prefix?
cards.back: No. They communicate per link using link-local addressing; still verify the intended global addressing and client path.

cards.front: OSPFv3 router ID size and format?
cards.back: 32 bits, dotted decimal, such as 1.1.1.1. It is not a 128-bit IPv6 next-hop address.

cards.front: No IPv4 addresses and no explicit RID on classic IOS OSPFv3?
cards.back: The process can fail to obtain a RID. Configure a unique router-id explicitly.

cards.front: Normal IOS broadcast/point-to-point OSPFv3 Hello and dead defaults?
cards.back: 10 seconds and 40 seconds. Compare effective timers after any configuration changes.

cards.front: Which OSPFv3 identifier distinguishes instances on the same link?
cards.back: The instance ID; it must agree for the intended relationship. Classic IPv6-unicast syntax uses instance 0 by default.

cards.front: Does the local OSPFv3 process number have to match the neighbor?
cards.back: No. It is local configuration, unlike the area and compatible on-link instance ID.

cards.front: Classic command to activate OSPFv3 process 10 in area 0?
cards.back: ipv6 ospf 10 area 0 under the interface. It is not an IPv4-style network statement.

cards.front: Address-family process and interface activation for IPv6?
cards.back: router ospfv3 10, address-family ipv6 unicast; interface: ospfv3 10 ipv6 area 0.

cards.front: Global command that enables IPv6 forwarding on IOS?
cards.back: ipv6 unicast-routing. Include it in this routed IPv6 lab.

cards.front: Meaning of O and [110/11] in show ipv6 route?
cards.back: O is an intra-area OSPF route here; 110 is administrative distance, 11 is metric. Interpret the next hop with its exit interface.

cards.front: Normal OSPFv3 advertisement of an interface in Loopback state?
cards.back: A global address is represented as a /128 host prefix, even if its address command has /64. Verify the actual advertised route.

cards.front: OSPFv3 DR/BDR election rule?
cards.back: Highest eligible priority, then RID. IOS default 1; 0 is ineligible. Existing DR/BDR roles are non-preemptive.

cards.front: What does Interface ID mean in show ipv6 ospf neighbor?
cards.back: The neighbor's interface identifier. The final Interface column names the local interface.

cards.front: OSPFv3 repeatedly in ExStart/Exchange: what should you compare?
cards.back: MTUs and database-exchange evidence, along with the intended link parameters. Do not bypass MTU checking as the first repair.

cards.front: What does a controlled OSPFv3 process restart do to adjacencies?
cards.back: It drops the local process adjacencies and can apply a pending RID change. It does not guarantee a fresh segment-wide DR election.

cards.front: Does a passive OSPFv3 LAN still need interface activation?
cards.back: Yes. Passive suppresses neighbor formation; activation is needed to advertise its connected prefix.

cards.front: What is the route cost for outgoing transit 25 plus remote LAN 1?
cards.back: 26. Add outgoing costs only; the next hop remains tied to its particular IPv6 link.

tickets.title: OSPFv3 cannot select an identity after an IPv6-only rebuild
tickets.scenario: R2 was rebuilt without IPv4 addresses and reloaded. IPv6 forwarding and addressed transit Gi0/0 are configured, but the classic OSPFv3 process never establishes neighbors. The supplied excerpts are representative.

exhibits.title: R2 configuration
exhibits.text:
ipv6 unicast-routing
ipv6 router ospf 20
 passive-interface GigabitEthernet0/2
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ipv6 address 2001:db8:123::2/64
 ipv6 ospf 20 area 0
 no shutdown

exhibits.title: R2 log
exhibits.text: %OSPFv3-4-NORTRID: OSPFv3 process 20 could not pick a router-id, please configure manually

tickets.question: Which configuration gap is established by the evidence?
options: OSPFv3 requires an IPv4 address on every transit.
The IPv6-only process lacks an explicit usable router ID.
Passive Gi0/2 disables Hellos on Gi0/0 too.
The process number must equal the area number.
tickets.explanation: The log explicitly says the process cannot obtain a RID. Configure a unique 32-bit identifier; it does not have to be assigned to an IPv4 interface. The passive setting names only Gi0/2, not the transit.
tickets.fix:
```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# ipv6 router ospf 20
R2(config-rtr)# router-id 2.2.2.2
R2(config-rtr)# end
R2# show ipv6 ospf
R2# show ipv6 ospf neighbor
R2# show ipv6 route ospf
```
This process lacked an active RID. If a different scenario has an already running process with a pending RID change, schedule any required process restart separately and expect adjacency disruption.

tickets.title: A direct adjacency disappears after a one-sided timer change
tickets.scenario: R1 and R3 share an up/up two-router link on Gi0/1. Their alternate routed path through R2 still works, but the direct OSPFv3 neighbor is absent. R3 received explicit timer overrides. These are representative interface excerpts.

exhibits.title: R1 Gi0/1
exhibits.text:
Area 0, Instance 0, RID 1.1.1.1, POINT_TO_POINT
Hello 10, Dead 40
Neighbor Count 0

exhibits.title: R3 Gi0/1
exhibits.text:
Area 0, Instance 0, RID 3.3.3.3, POINT_TO_POINT
Hello 3, Dead 12
Neighbor Count 0

tickets.question: What prevents the intended direct neighbor relationship?
options: The two interfaces use different area IDs.
The interfaces disagree on network type.
The effective Hello/dead intervals disagree.
The RIDs are different from one another.
tickets.explanation: Area, instance, and intended network type agree. The effective timer pairs do not, so the Hellos do not meet the required parameters. The alternate path can mask this fault from an end-to-end ping.
tickets.fix:
```ios R3
R3# configure terminal
R3(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R3(config-if)# no ipv6 ospf hello-interval
R3(config-if)# no ipv6 ospf dead-interval
R3(config-if)# end
R3# show ipv6 ospf interface gigabitethernet0/1
R3# show ipv6 ospf neighbor
```
Verify 10/40 at both ends and a Full direct adjacency. If a new timer pair is intentional, configure and verify both values consistently on both peers instead.

sections.title: Why hosts need a redundant gateway

lab.title: Observe a redundant gateway and track its uplink
lab.intro:
The main build uses Packet Tracer and HSRP. VRRP status is a paper exercise because simulator support varies. Configuration is guided practice for understanding FHRP concepts and status; neither track asks you to memorize this entire optional build.

Use blank devices and a new file. The 2911 provides the three GigabitEthernet ports named below. Use straight-through copper between routers/PC and the switch; use crossover or auto-connect for router–router and direct server–router links. In CML or on hardware, map your image's interfaces before typing. All examples and expected outputs are authored, not captured from a manual device run.
lab.topology:
```diagram
{"type":"topology","title":"Lab 23 — Two gateways with separate routed uplinks","caption":"PC-A uses the virtual gateway; R3 learns a return path through whichever LAN advertisement remains reachable.","nodes":[{"id":"PC","kind":"pc","label":"PC-A","x":0.5,"y":3},{"id":"SW","kind":"switch","label":"SW1","sub":"VLAN 10","x":3,"y":3},{"id":"R1","kind":"router","label":"R1","sub":"LAN .2, priority 110","x":6,"y":1},{"id":"R2","kind":"router","label":"R2","sub":"LAN .3, priority 100","x":6,"y":5},{"id":"R3","kind":"router","label":"R3","x":9,"y":3},{"id":"S","kind":"server","label":"Server","sub":"203.0.113.10","x":12,"y":3}],"links":[{"from":"PC","to":"SW","toLabel":"Fa0/3"},{"from":"SW","to":"R1","fromLabel":"Fa0/1","toLabel":"Gi0/0"},{"from":"SW","to":"R2","fromLabel":"Fa0/2","toLabel":"Gi0/0"},{"from":"R1","to":"R3","fromLabel":"Gi0/1","toLabel":"Gi0/0","label":"10.0.13.0/30"},{"from":"R2","to":"R3","fromLabel":"Gi0/1","toLabel":"Gi0/1","label":"10.0.23.0/30"},{"from":"R3","to":"S","fromLabel":"Gi0/2"}]}
```

| Device/interface | IPv4 address/mask | Host gateway or peer |
|---|---|---|
| R1 Gi0/0 | 192.168.10.2 / 255.255.255.0 | SW1 Fa0/1 |
| R2 Gi0/0 | 192.168.10.3 / 255.255.255.0 | SW1 Fa0/2 |
| HSRP group 1 | Virtual 192.168.10.1 | PC-A's default gateway |
| PC-A FastEthernet0 | 192.168.10.10 / 255.255.255.0 | Gateway 192.168.10.1, SW1 Fa0/3 |
| R1 Gi0/1 | 10.0.13.1 / 255.255.255.252 | R3 Gi0/0 |
| R3 Gi0/0 | 10.0.13.2 / 255.255.255.252 | R1 Gi0/1 |
| R2 Gi0/1 | 10.0.23.1 / 255.255.255.252 | R3 Gi0/1 |
| R3 Gi0/1 | 10.0.23.2 / 255.255.255.252 | R2 Gi0/1 |
| R3 Gi0/2 | 203.0.113.1 / 255.255.255.0 | Server FastEthernet0 |
| Server | 203.0.113.10 / 255.255.255.0 | Gateway 203.0.113.1 |

203.0.113.0/24 is a documentation prefix used for simulated remote service, not actual Internet access. No NAT, DNS, HTTP service, or default route is needed for this ping lab. OSPF area 0 supplies specific remote and return routes. Both gateway LANs are passive in OSPF, so R1 and R2 do not form an OSPF adjacency through VLAN 10.

steps.title: Cable the LAN and prepare the hosts
steps.body:
Cable the ports in the table. Configure the PC and Server through Desktop > IP Configuration with the static address, mask, and gateway shown. Use a blank 2960 and put all three used switch ports in VLAN 10.

```ios SW1
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname SW1
SW1(config)# vlan 10
SW1(config-vlan)# name USERS
SW1(config-vlan)# exit
SW1(config)# interface range fastethernet0/1 - 3
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport access vlan 10
SW1(config-if-range)# spanning-tree portfast
SW1(config-if-range)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if-range)# end
SW1# show vlan brief
```


:::expected
Fa0/1–3 belong to VLAN 10. These ports connect to hosts or routed router interfaces, so PortFast is appropriate. The switch does not require a management IP. The gateway will not respond until the routers are configured.
:::

steps.title: Configure both HSRP gateways
steps.body:
Create R1 and R2 with the full configurations below. The two physical LAN addresses differ, but the group and virtual address agree. OSPF is included so that a later failover has a valid return path.

```ios R1
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R1
R1(config)# router ospf 10
R1(config-router)# router-id 1.1.1.1
R1(config-router)# passive-interface default
R1(config-router)# no passive-interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-router)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ip address 192.168.10.2 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# ip ospf 10 area 0
R1(config-if)# ip ospf cost 1
R1(config-if)# standby version 1
R1(config-if)# standby 1 ip 192.168.10.1
R1(config-if)# standby 1 priority 110
R1(config-if)# standby 1 preempt
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.0.13.1 255.255.255.252
R1(config-if)# ip ospf 10 area 0
R1(config-if)# ip ospf network point-to-point
R1(config-if)# ip ospf cost 10
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show standby brief
```

```ios R2
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R2
R2(config)# router ospf 10
R2(config-router)# router-id 2.2.2.2
R2(config-router)# passive-interface default
R2(config-router)# no passive-interface gigabitethernet0/1
R2(config-router)# exit
R2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R2(config-if)# ip address 192.168.10.3 255.255.255.0
R2(config-if)# ip ospf 10 area 0
R2(config-if)# ip ospf cost 1
R2(config-if)# standby version 1
R2(config-if)# standby 1 ip 192.168.10.1
R2(config-if)# standby 1 priority 100
R2(config-if)# standby 1 preempt
R2(config-if)# no shutdown
R2(config-if)# exit
R2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R2(config-if)# ip address 10.0.23.1 255.255.255.252
R2(config-if)# ip ospf 10 area 0
R2(config-if)# ip ospf network point-to-point
R2(config-if)# ip ospf cost 10
R2(config-if)# no shutdown
R2(config-if)# end
R2# show standby brief
```


:::expected
After election processing, R1 is Active at priority 110 and R2 Standby at 100. Both show the P flag and virtual IP 192.168.10.1. R2 can become active if R1 fails; preempt additionally allows either router to challenge a healthy lower-priority active router.
:::

steps.title: Complete the remote routing and save a baseline
steps.body:
Configure R3 and verify both OSPF adjacencies before testing the server. R3 uses cost 10 toward R1 and 20 toward R2, so its normal return path to the client LAN is unambiguous.

```ios R3
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R3
R3(config)# router ospf 10
R3(config-router)# router-id 3.3.3.3
R3(config-router)# passive-interface default
R3(config-router)# no passive-interface gigabitethernet0/0
R3(config-router)# no passive-interface gigabitethernet0/1
R3(config-router)# exit
R3(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R3(config-if)# ip address 10.0.13.2 255.255.255.252
R3(config-if)# ip ospf 10 area 0
R3(config-if)# ip ospf network point-to-point
R3(config-if)# ip ospf cost 10
R3(config-if)# no shutdown
R3(config-if)# exit
R3(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R3(config-if)# ip address 10.0.23.2 255.255.255.252
R3(config-if)# ip ospf 10 area 0
R3(config-if)# ip ospf network point-to-point
R3(config-if)# ip ospf cost 20
R3(config-if)# no shutdown
R3(config-if)# exit
R3(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/2
R3(config-if)# ip address 203.0.113.1 255.255.255.0
R3(config-if)# ip ospf 10 area 0
R3(config-if)# ip ospf cost 1
R3(config-if)# no shutdown
R3(config-if)# end
R3# show ip ospf neighbor
R3# show ip route ospf
```

```ios R1
R1# copy running-config startup-config
```

```ios R2
R2# copy running-config startup-config
```

```ios R3
R3# copy running-config startup-config
```

```ios SW1
SW1# copy running-config startup-config
```

Accept the default destination filename. On PC-A run:
```text
ping 203.0.113.10
```

:::expected
R3 is Full with R1 and R2 over the two point-to-point links. R3 learns 192.168.10.0/24 via 10.0.13.1 at cost 10 + 1 = 11. R1 and R2 learn 203.0.113.0/24 at cost 10 + 1 = 11. PC-A reaches the server after ARP and convergence.
:::

steps.title: Inspect the virtual identity and forwarding path
steps.body:
Record baseline roles on both routers and the virtual MAC learned on the switch. On PC-A, ping the server again, then display the ARP cache.

```ios R1
R1# show standby
R1# show ip route 203.0.113.0
```

```ios R2
R2# show standby brief
```

```ios SW1
SW1# show mac address-table
```

```text
arp -a
```
If the Packet Tracer switch accepts filtering, `show mac address-table address 0000.0c07.ac01` narrows the result. The unfiltered command is sufficient.


:::expected
The gateway is 192.168.10.1 and the ordinary HSRPv1 group-1 virtual MAC is 0000.0c07.ac01. SW1 should learn it toward Fa0/1, R1. Keep separate notes for the PC ARP mapping, switch port mapping, and remote route; they describe different layers.
:::

steps.title: Fail the active LAN interface and observe
steps.body:
On R1 shut only Gi0/0. This is an interface-failure demonstration, not a promise to reproduce the timer of an unannounced power failure. Repeat the server ping and inspect R2/R3 before restoring anything.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
```

```ios R2
R2# show standby brief
```

```ios R3
R3# show ip route 192.168.10.0
```

```ios SW1
SW1# show mac address-table
```


:::expected
R2 becomes Active after the failure is processed. R3 withdraws the unavailable R1 LAN path and uses R2 at cost 20 + 1 = 21. SW1 learns the virtual MAC toward Fa0/2. After convergence PC-A again reaches the server using the same configured virtual gateway; record any lost pings without claiming a fixed failover duration.
:::

steps.title: Restore R1 and observe preemption
steps.body:
Restore R1 Gi0/0 and wait for HSRP and OSPF to settle.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show standby brief
```

```ios R3
R3# show ip route 192.168.10.0
```


:::expected
R1 can reclaim Active because it has priority 110 and preempt. R3 returns to its lower-cost path through R1. Without preempt on R1, recovery alone would not require R2 to give up Active.
:::

steps.title: Add uplink tracking
steps.body:
