On the Packet Tracer image, first check interface-mode `standby 1 track ?`. If the legacy interface form is supported, use this R1 block:

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# standby 1 track gigabitethernet0/1 20
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show standby
```

On IOS XE images that support object tracking instead, use the following alternative, not both forms:

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# track 1 interface gigabitethernet0/1 line-protocol
R1(config-track)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# standby 1 track 1 decrement 20
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show standby
```

If neither form exists in your simulator image, leave configuration unchanged and do Steps 8–9 as a paper exercise using the expected results. The basic failover in Steps 5–6 remains executable.

:::expected
While the uplink is up, R1 shows current/configured priority 110 and the track condition Up. R2 already has preempt configured, which is necessary to take over when R1 remains alive on the LAN but its effective priority falls below 100.
:::

steps.title: Fail the uplink while the gateway stays on the LAN
steps.body:
If Step 7 tracking is configured, shut R1 Gi0/1 only. Leave Gi0/0 up. Inspect both HSRP peers and R3, and repeat the remote ping.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show standby
```

```ios R2
R2# show standby brief
```

```ios R3
R3# show ip route 192.168.10.0
```


:::expected
The tracked condition goes Down and R1 becomes priority 110 − 20 = 90. R2 at 100 preempts and becomes Active. R3 uses the R2 return path at cost 21 after OSPF converges. Without tracking, R1 could keep Active while lacking the remote route; without R2 preemption, the priority drop alone would not produce the intended takeover.
:::

steps.title: Restore the uplink and verify recovery
steps.body:
Restore the exact interface changed in Step 8. If you used the paper fallback, state the same expected transition without changing the working devices.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show standby
R1# show ip ospf neighbor
```

```ios R3
R3# show ip route 192.168.10.0
```


:::expected
Tracking returns Up, R1 effective priority returns to 110, and R1 can preempt again. Wait until OSPF is Full and the remote ping works. The configured tracking decrement stays 20; recovery restores the effective priority rather than deleting the tracking configuration.
:::

steps.title: Compare HSRP versions
steps.body:
In this isolated lab, change both interfaces to HSRPv2 and verify the group again. A temporary mismatch is expected while only one peer has changed; complete both before testing. If your simulator lacks `standby version 2`, compare the expected MAC on paper instead.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# standby version 2
R1(config-if)# end
```

```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R2(config-if)# standby version 2
R2(config-if)# end
R2# show standby
```

```ios R1
R1# show standby brief
```


:::expected
The virtual IP stays 192.168.10.1 but the IPv4 group-1 virtual MAC becomes 0000.0c9f.f001. Both peers must use the same version. Let announcements refresh the host mapping and retest. If a stale PC cache persists, use Desktop > Command Prompt `arp -d` as supported or wait for refresh; this version change differs from ordinary same-version failover.
:::

steps.title: Interpret VRRP status on paper
steps.body:
Read these authored summaries as status evidence from a hypothetical supported IOS XE pair; they are not commands to paste or recorded Packet Tracer output.
```output Representative VRRP status summaries
R1 — Group 1 — Address-Family IPv4
  State Master, Priority 110, Preemption enabled, Address owner No
  Virtual address 192.168.10.1, Master address 192.168.10.2
R2 — Group 1 — Address-Family IPv4
  State Backup, Priority 100, Preemption enabled, Address owner No
  Virtual MAC 0000.5e00.0101
R1 — Group 1 — Address-Family IPv6
  State Backup, Priority 90, Preemption enabled, Address owner No
  Virtual address FE80::1, Master address FE80::3
  Virtual MAC 0000.5e00.0201
```
Write who forwards for each family, whether the IPv4 Master result proves IPv6 leadership, and whether IPv6 uses ARP. Then predict what happens when an IPv4 non-owner with priority 120 and preemption enabled joins.

:::expected
R1 is the IPv4 forwarding router. R1 is IPv6 Backup; FE80::3 identifies the IPv6 Master on that link. IPv4 and IPv6 instances are independent. IPv6 uses Neighbor Discovery. A healthy IPv4 priority-120 non-owner can preempt the priority-110 non-owner, subject to election processing and any configured delay. An address-owner case would need separate priority-255 reasoning.
:::

steps.title: Save only the restored working configuration
steps.body:
Confirm R1 Gi0/0 and Gi0/1 are up, both HSRP peers agree on the supported version, routing is restored, and PC-A reaches the server. Then save all device configurations and the project file.

```ios R1
R1# copy running-config startup-config
```

```ios R2
R2# copy running-config startup-config
```

```ios R3
R3# copy running-config startup-config
```

```ios SW1
SW1# copy running-config startup-config
```


:::expected
Your saved lab has no intentional shutdown fault. Record whether you ran HSRPv1 or HSRPv2 and which tracking syntax was supported. A paper exercise does not count as a command executed on a device.
:::

lab.troubleshooting:
- Both peers Active with unknown Standby: compare VLAN 10 membership, version, group 1, VIP, and control-plane communication.
- Remote ping fails while the VIP responds: inspect the active router's route to 203.0.113.0/24 and R3's return route to 192.168.10.0/24.
- R1 uplink fails but role does not change: inspect effective priority, tracking support/status, decrement, and R2 preempt.
- R1 recovers but stays Standby: inspect R1 preempt and effective priority; do not assume highest configured priority always wins immediately.
- A PC loses service only when R1 fails: confirm its gateway is .1, not R1's real address .2.
- An unsupported command: use the documented alternative or paper fallback. Do not claim a feature was verified just because a configuration line was supplied.
lab.challenge:
Assume R1 priority 110 and R2 priority 100, both with preempt. Predict failover if tracking subtracts 5, 10, or 20 from R1 after an uplink failure. Explain why a successful HSRP transition is still insufficient evidence that the remote application works.

:::expected
The resulting priorities are 105, 100, and 90. Only decrement 20 creates the intended strict advantage for R2. Equal priority does not let R2 preempt R1 merely because R2 has a higher IP address. A working application additionally needs valid destination/return routes and usable links. Verify the remote server, not only the virtual gateway, and restore the original decrement 20 before saving any optional test changes.
:::

questions.prompt: Which interpretation of R2's HSRP status is correct?
options: R2 is Standby, preemption is configured, and hosts should use 192.168.10.1.
R2 is Active because the Standby column says local.
R2 is Standby, so hosts should use the active real address 192.168.10.2.
R2 is Active because the P flag means preemption has completed.
questions.explanation: State describes the local role and local identifies the device issuing the command. The Virtual IP is the host gateway; the P flag indicates configured preemption.

whyWrong.1: Local in the Standby column confirms R2 is the standby.
whyWrong.2: Hosts should use the virtual address to preserve gateway redundancy.
whyWrong.3: P means preemption is configured, not that it just occurred.

exhibit.title: Representative configuration or output
exhibit.text:
R2# show standby brief
Interface Grp Pri P State   Active        Standby Virtual IP
Gi0/0     1   100 P Standby 192.168.10.2  local   192.168.10.1

questions.prompt: R1's real address is 192.168.10.2, R2 is .3, and HSRP VIP is .1. A PC incorrectly uses .2 as its gateway. R1 fails and R2 becomes Active. What is expected?
options: R2 automatically adopts R1's real address .2 as well as the VIP.
The PC still targets the failed real gateway and may lose off-subnet access.
OSPF on R2 automatically rewrites the PC gateway to .1.
The PC immediately uses .3 because it is the next address in the subnet.
questions.explanation: The PC must use the VIP .1 for the intended redundancy. R2 taking over that virtual identity does not repair a host still configured to send to R1's real address.

whyWrong.0: Ordinary HSRP takeover moves the virtual identity, not all peer real addresses.
whyWrong.2: The host gateway is not rewritten by the routers' routing protocol.
whyWrong.3: A statically configured gateway is not selected by incrementing the address.

questions.prompt: An IPv4 HSRPv1 group has group number 10 and default virtual MAC behavior. Which virtual MAC corresponds to it?
questions.explanation: HSRPv1 uses 0000.0c07.acXX with the group number encoded in hexadecimal. Decimal 10 is hex 0a; the address does not identify the current physical active router.

whyWrong.0: The suffix uses hexadecimal; decimal group 10 is 0a, not 10.
whyWrong.1: That is the HSRPv2 pattern for group 10.
whyWrong.3: That is the IPv4 VRRP pattern for VRID 10.

questions.prompt: An IOS interface is currently using HSRPv1. Group 300 is rejected. Which required version change supports that IPv4 group number?
options: Change the virtual IP to another address in the same subnet.
Set standby 300 priority 255 before creating the virtual address.
Change the LAN VLAN number to 300 on the access switch.
Configure standby version 2 on each participating interface.
questions.explanation: HSRPv1 supports groups 0–255; HSRPv2 supports 0–4095. Both peers need compatible version configuration, and a version change also changes the ordinary IPv4 virtual MAC format.

whyWrong.0: The error concerns the version group-number range, not the virtual IP.
whyWrong.1: Priority does not expand the HSRPv1 group range.
whyWrong.2: HSRP group support is independent of the chosen VLAN number.

questions.prompt: For an ordinary VRRP group with non-owner routers and default settings, which two statements are true? Choose two.
options: VRRP is carried in UDP port 1985.
A higher-priority returning router can preempt the current lower-priority router.
The default non-owner priority is 100.
The lower numeric priority is preferred.
VRRPv2 supports IPv6 as well as IPv4.
questions.explanation: Default non-owner priority is 100 and preemption is normally enabled. VRRP uses protocol number 112; VRRPv3, not v2, provides IPv6 support.

whyWrong.0: UDP 1985 is IPv4 HSRP transport, not VRRP.
whyWrong.3: Higher priority is preferred.
whyWrong.4: VRRPv2 is IPv4; v3 supports IPv4 and IPv6.

questions.prompt: R1 loses its tracked uplink. R2 is priority 100 with preempt enabled. Why does the shown tracking configuration fail to make R2 preferred?
options: R1's effective priority becomes 5, so R2 needs a lower priority.
R1's effective priority falls only to 105, which still exceeds 100.
R2 cannot preempt while R1 still has any up interface.
Tracking changes the virtual IP instead of changing priority.
questions.explanation: The configured 110 minus decrement 5 equals 105. A decrement must give R2 the intended strict priority advantage; in this pair, decrement 20 gives R1 90.

whyWrong.0: The decrement is subtracted from the configured priority; it does not replace it.
whyWrong.2: Preemption can take over from a live router when priority conditions are met.
whyWrong.3: This tracking action reduces effective priority.

exhibit.title: Representative configuration or output
exhibit.text:
R1 Gi0/0:
 standby 1 priority 110
 standby 1 preempt
 standby 1 track GigabitEthernet0/1 5
R1 Gi0/1: down/down

questions.prompt: R1 rebooted and R2 took over. R1 has recovered with effective priority 110, but preemption is disabled. R2 remains healthy at 100. Which role result is expected?
options: R1 must become Active immediately because 110 exceeds 100.
Both routers must become Active because priorities differ.
R2 can remain Active while recovered R1 is Standby.
R2 must disable its LAN interface to release the virtual IP.
questions.explanation: HSRP preemption is disabled by default. A higher-priority recovered router does not necessarily displace a healthy active router unless preemption is enabled.

whyWrong.0: Taking over from a healthy active router requires preemption in this scenario.
whyWrong.1: Different priorities are normal and do not cause isolation.
whyWrong.3: A physical shutdown is not required for ordinary protocol role selection.

exhibit.title: Representative R1 show standby excerpt
exhibit.text:
State is Standby
Preemption disabled
Active router is 192.168.10.3, priority 100
Priority 110 (configured 110)

questions.prompt: During ordinary same-version HSRP failover, what helps the switch send frames for the virtual MAC toward the new Active router?
options: Changing every PC gateway to the new router real IP.
Increasing the OSPF router ID on the new Active router.
Giving the same virtual IP a randomly selected new MAC.
Frames sourced from the virtual MAC, including gratuitous ARP announcements.
questions.explanation: Switches learn source MAC addresses on incoming ports. The new active router announcements and traffic using the virtual MAC update that location while the host can retain the same IP-to-MAC mapping.

whyWrong.0: The virtual gateway lets hosts retain their configured gateway.
whyWrong.1: OSPF identity does not update a switch MAC-to-port entry.
whyWrong.2: Ordinary same-version group failover retains the virtual identity.

questions.prompt: An HSRP standby uses a 10-second active hold timer. It accepted its last active Hello 3 seconds ago, and no further Hello or Resign arrives. How much hold time remains before expiry?
options: Approximately 7 seconds.
Approximately 3 seconds.
Approximately 10 seconds from now.
Exactly three additional Hello transmissions.
questions.explanation: The remaining interval is 10 − 3 = 7 seconds before timer expiry. Actual forwarding recovery also includes state processing and the rest of the network, so this is not an exact application-recovery promise.

whyWrong.1: Three seconds is elapsed time in the question, not the remaining hold time.
whyWrong.2: The timer was already started by the last accepted Hello.
whyWrong.3: The receiver uses a timer; it does not require counting a fixed number of future sends.

questions.prompt: Two intended IPv4 HSRP peers share a VLAN and VIP but each remains Active with unknown Standby. Which two configuration mismatches can create separate groups that do not recognize each other? Choose two.
options: Different HSRP versions on the interfaces
Different configured HSRP priorities
Different real interface IPs in the same subnet
Different HSRP group numbers
Preemption enabled on both peers
questions.explanation: Version and group identity must agree for the intended HSRP relationship. Different real addresses and priorities are normal in a redundant gateway pair.

whyWrong.1: Different priorities intentionally establish preference and do not isolate peers.
whyWrong.2: The routers need different real interface addresses.
whyWrong.4: Preemption on both peers does not by itself create two active routers.

questions.prompt: VRRP R2 is currently Master at priority 100. R1 returns at 110, both are non-owners, and R1's preemption is at its default. What is expected?
options: R1 must remain Backup because VRRP preemption defaults off.
R2 becomes the address owner because it was Master first.
R1 can preempt R2 and take the forwarding role.
R1 must first change its virtual address to a new subnet.
questions.explanation: For ordinary non-owner VRRP routers, preemption is enabled by default and higher priority is preferred. R1 can reclaim the forwarding role after protocol processing and any configured delay.

whyWrong.0: VRRP normally enables preemption by default.
whyWrong.1: Ownership depends on real/virtual address identity, not startup order.
whyWrong.3: Peers should retain the intended virtual gateway identity.

questions.prompt: R1 recovered at effective HSRP priority 110 while healthy R2 remains Active at 100. R1's preemption is disabled. Which interface command enables the intended takeover?
options: standby 1 priority 100
standby version 2
standby 1 ip 192.168.10.2
standby 1 preempt
questions.explanation: The preempt command allows the higher-priority R1 to take over from a healthy lower-priority Active router. It changes the normal HSRP default of preemption being disabled.

whyWrong.0: That reduces R1 preference rather than enabling preemption.
whyWrong.1: A version change is unrelated and must be coordinated with peers.
whyWrong.2: Changing the intended VIP would change the gateway identity.

questions.prompt: Both routers have preemption enabled. R1 uses priority 110 for VLAN 10 and 90 for VLAN 20; R2 uses 90 for VLAN 10 and 110 for VLAN 20. Each VLAN has its own agreed group/VIP. What is the intended steady-state arrangement?
options: R1 forwards for VLAN 10 while R2 forwards for VLAN 20.
R1 and R2 both forward concurrently for each single HSRP group.
R1 becomes Active for both VLANs because it has a 110 somewhere.
R2 becomes Standby for both VLANs because its VLAN 10 priority is lower.
questions.explanation: Different groups can prefer different routers, distributing gateway duties across VLANs. This is per-group sharing, not two routers simultaneously Active for the same group.

whyWrong.1: Ordinary HSRP has one Active per group in steady state.
whyWrong.2: Priority is evaluated within each group rather than router-wide.
whyWrong.3: Its higher VLAN 20 priority makes it preferred in that separate group.

exhibit.title: Representative per-group priority plan
exhibit.text:
VLAN 10 / HSRP group 10: R1 priority 110, R2 priority 90
VLAN 20 / HSRP group 20: R1 priority 90, R2 priority 110
Both routers have preempt enabled in both groups.

questions.prompt: A VRRP router owns real IPv4 address 192.168.10.1, which is also the group virtual address. Which priority identifies this owner case?
questions.explanation: VRRP reserves priority 255 for the address owner. Identify ownership before applying ordinary non-owner priority and preemption assumptions.

whyWrong.0: 100 is the normal non-owner default.
whyWrong.2: 254 is the highest ordinary non-owner configurable priority.
whyWrong.3: Priority 0 signals relinquishing the role in protocol advertisements.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion follows from these VRRPv3 summaries on R1?
options: R1 forwards for both because both use group number 1.
The IPv6 summary is invalid because VRRP supports only IPv4.
R1 forwards for IPv4 but is Backup for the separate IPv6 instance.
The IPv6 virtual MAC should be changed to the IPv4 virtual MAC.
questions.explanation: Address family is essential context. R1 is IPv4 Master and IPv6 Backup, while the IPv6 instance uses a virtual link-local address and IPv6 virtual MAC.

whyWrong.0: The IPv4 and IPv6 instances are independent.
whyWrong.1: VRRPv3 supports IPv6 as well as IPv4.
whyWrong.3: The IPv6 MAC block differs intentionally from the IPv4 block.

exhibit.title: Representative configuration or output
exhibit.text:
R1 Group 1, Address-Family IPv4: State Master, VIP 192.168.10.1
R1 Group 1, Address-Family IPv6: State Backup, VIP FE80::1
IPv6 virtual MAC: 0000.5e00.0201

questions.prompt: R1 is healthy HSRP Active at priority 100 and real address .2. R2 joins at priority 100 with real address .3 and preempt enabled. Does the higher real address require R2 to preempt R1?
options: Yes; the IP tiebreaker always preempts an existing Active router.
Yes; preempt forces takeover regardless of priority.
No; R2 must use the same real interface IP as R1.
No; an equal-priority router does not preempt solely because its IP is higher.
questions.explanation: Cisco distinguishes election tiebreaking from equal-priority preemption. A higher interface IP can break an election tie, but an equal-priority arriving router does not preempt a healthy Active router merely for that reason.

whyWrong.0: The initial-election tiebreaker is not an equal-priority preemption guarantee.
whyWrong.1: Preemption still depends on the required priority relationship.
whyWrong.2: Duplicate real interface addresses would be a fault.

cards.front: Default IPv4 HSRPv1 virtual MAC for group 10?
cards.back: 0000.0c07.ac0a. The acXX suffix encodes the group in hexadecimal.

cards.front: Default IPv4 HSRPv2 virtual MAC for group 1?
cards.back: 0000.0c9f.f001; the final three hexadecimal digits encode the group.

cards.front: IPv4 HSRP multicast and UDP port, v1 versus v2?
HSRP default Hello/hold and what starts the active hold timer?
cards.back: 3/10 seconds. Accepted active Hellos refresh the timer; silent failure is detected at expiry, not by counting exactly three missed packets.

cards.front: HSRP priority range/default and election tie?
cards.back: 0–255, default 100; higher preferred. Higher real interface IP breaks an election tie, but does not cause equal-priority preemption.

cards.front: HSRP preemption default and purpose?
cards.back: Disabled. Enabling it lets a higher-priority router take over from a healthy lower-priority Active router.

cards.front: What HSRP states should you recognize?
cards.back: Initial, Learn, Listen, Speak, Standby, Active. They are conditions, not a mandatory linear sequence for every router.

cards.front: IPv4 HSRP group ranges for versions 1 and 2?
cards.back: v1 0–255; v2 0–4095. Peers must use a compatible version and group.

cards.front: VRRP virtual MAC forms for IPv4 and IPv6?
cards.back: IPv4 0000.5e00.01XX; IPv6 0000.5e00.02XX. XX is VRID 1–255 in hexadecimal.

cards.front: VRRP multicast addresses and transport?
cards.back: IPv4 224.0.0.18; IPv6 ff02::12. IP protocol/IPv6 Next Header 112, not UDP.

cards.front: VRRP ordinary advertisement and default-priority down interval?
cards.back: Advertisements normally 1 second; a non-owner priority-100 backup has about a 3.6-second down interval, including skew.

cards.front: VRRP non-owner priority, owner priority, and preemption default?
cards.back: Non-owner 1–254, default 100; owner 255. Preemption normally enabled; priority 0 signals relinquishment.

cards.front: VRRP forwarding role in Cisco output versus the current RFC?
cards.back: Cisco often says Master; RFC 9568 says Active. Backup is the non-forwarding role for that virtual instance.

cards.front: What changes in the switch during ordinary HSRP failover?
cards.back: The learned port for the virtual MAC changes. The virtual IP/MAC identity remains, so hosts need not change their configured gateway.

cards.front: HSRP Hello, Coup, and Resign purposes?
cards.back: Hello maintains status; Coup requests takeover during preemption; Resign relinquishes the active role.

cards.front: R1's priority 110 minus tracking decrement 20: what else allows R2 takeover?
cards.back: R1 becomes 90; R2 at 100 needs preempt to take over while R1 remains alive on the LAN.

cards.front: Command selecting HSRPv2 on an IOS interface?
cards.back: standby version 2. Coordinate peers; ordinary IPv4 virtual MACs change with the version.

cards.front: What does unknown in an HSRP peer-role field mean?
cards.back: No peer in that role is currently known. In an intended pair, compare VLAN, version, group, and control traffic.

cards.front: Which HSRP states send periodic Hellos?
cards.back: Speak, Standby, and Active. Listen does not.

cards.front: Which VRRP version supports IPv6, and does IPv4 Master prove IPv6 Master?
cards.back: VRRPv3 supports IPv4 and IPv6. Their instances are independent; inspect the address family and virtual address.

commands.task: Guided HSRP practice: set group 1 virtual IPv4 address to 192.168.10.1.
commands.note: Use the same VIP on peers, with different real interface addresses.

commands.task: Guided HSRP practice: set group 1 configured priority to 110.
commands.note: Verify effective priority separately if tracking is configured.

commands.task: Guided HSRP practice: allow group 1 takeover from a healthy lower-priority Active.
commands.note: This does not promise equal-priority preemption based only on IP.

commands.task: On an image supporting legacy interface tracking, subtract 20 if Gi0/1 fails.
commands.note: Alternative to object tracking; inspect support and use only one form.

commands.task: Optional HSRP timer practice: use Hello 1 second, hold 3 seconds for group 1.
commands.note: Coordinate peers; the main lab keeps normal 3/10 timers.

commands.task: Select HSRPv2 for the groups on this interface.
commands.note: Apply the same intended version on all group peers.

commands.task: Optional practice: delay group 1 preemption at least 60 seconds after recovery.
commands.note: A delay can give routing time to recover before taking the gateway role.

commands.task: Display compact HSRP roles, priorities, preemption flags, and virtual IPs.
commands.note: P means configured to preempt. Read local role and peer addresses separately.

commands.task: Display HSRP detail including virtual MAC, effective priority, and tracking.
commands.note: Use detail to distinguish configured priority from a tracking-reduced value.

commands.task: Optional classic IOS VRRPv2 practice: set group 1 virtual IPv4 address .1.
commands.note: For the 192.168.10.0/24 LAN on a supporting image; current VRRPv3 uses an address-family configuration form.

commands.task: Create object 1 to track the line protocol of Gi0/1 on a supporting IOS image.
commands.note: HSRP can reference it with standby 1 track 1 decrement 20.

commands.task: Display the classic IOS VRRP per-group summary.
commands.note: Output varies by release; read ownership/preemption and the local Master/Backup role.

tickets.title: A responsive virtual gateway has lost its only upstream path
tickets.scenario: R1 and R2 are a healthy IPv4 HSRP pair for 192.168.10.1. R1's priority is 110 and R2 is 100; both have preempt. R1's only upstream link Gi0/1 failed. R2 still has a working path and a verified return route. R1 configuration has no HSRP track command. Representative evidence follows.

exhibits.title: R1 HSRP detail
exhibits.text:
State Active
Active router local; Standby router 192.168.10.3
Preemption enabled
Priority 110 (configured 110)

tickets.question: Which configuration gap explains why the upstream failure has not changed gateway preference?
options: R2 has no preemption configured.
R1's uplink health is not linked to its HSRP priority.
R1 and R2 use the same virtual IP.
R1's configured priority is already below R2.
tickets.explanation: The group still hears a healthy Active router on the LAN, and R1 remains priority 110. Its failed uplink is not tracked, so that failure does not lower its preference. A tracking decrement of 20 makes R1 90 and permits preempt-enabled R2 at 100 to take over.
tickets.fix:
```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# track 1 interface gigabitethernet0/1 line-protocol
R1(config-track)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# standby 1 track 1 decrement 20
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show standby
```
Use this object form on a supporting IOS image; the legacy interface form is an alternative as explained in the lab. Verify R2 Active and a real remote destination. Restore the physical fault separately, then verify R1 priority returns to 110 and routing works.

tickets.title: Two active routers use different HSRP versions
tickets.scenario: R1 and R2 should share group 1 and VIP 192.168.10.1. Their switch ports are confirmed in VLAN 10, both real addresses can ping, and the condition persists after convergence time. Each device reports Active with unknown Standby. These are representative excerpts.

exhibits.title: R1 show standby excerpt
exhibits.text:
GigabitEthernet0/0 - Group 1 (version 2)
State Active; Priority 110; Preemption enabled
Virtual IP 192.168.10.1
Active virtual MAC 0000.0c9f.f001
Standby router unknown

exhibits.title: R2 show standby excerpt
exhibits.text:
GigabitEthernet0/0 - Group 1 (version 1)
State Active; Priority 100; Preemption enabled
Virtual IP 192.168.10.1
Active virtual MAC 0000.0c07.ac01
Standby router unknown

tickets.question: Which fault is directly established?
options: Both routers must have identical real interface addresses.
Both priorities must be equal before any election can occur.
The peers run incompatible HSRP versions for the intended group.
Preemption must be disabled on both routers to avoid duplicate Active.
tickets.explanation: The version lines and virtual MAC patterns identify v2 on R1 and v1 on R2. They do not exchange compatible group Hellos, so each can consider itself Active. Raising priority will not repair the version mismatch.
tickets.fix:
```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R2(config-if)# standby version 2
R2(config-if)# end
R2# show standby
R2# show standby brief
```
This scenario assumes version 2 is the intended supported design. Verify one Active, one Standby, peer addresses known, and successful client traffic before saving.

lab.title: Trace DHCP clients through a relay, then diagnose two allocation failures
devices: 3 × Cisco 2911 routers (R1 relay, R2 server, R3 client)
lab.intro: Build a remote DHCP service, obtain leases on a PC and an IOS router, and test a misplaced helper separately from an exhausted pool. Start with new devices and use console CLI tabs throughout. Answer `no` if the initial configuration dialog appears. These configurations were reviewed against Cisco documentation; they have not been executed in Packet Tracer during this audit. Output formatting, supported show commands, and retry timing can differ.
lab.topology:
```diagram
{"type":"topology","title":"Client subnet and remote server subnet","caption":"R1 relays from VLAN 10 toward R2 in VLAN 20; R2 needs a return route to the client subnet.","nodes":[{"id":"PC","kind":"pc","label":"PC-A","sub":"DHCP","x":1,"y":2},{"id":"SW1","kind":"switch","label":"SW1","sub":"VLAN 10","x":3,"y":3},{"id":"R1","kind":"router","label":"R1","sub":"Relay","x":6,"y":3},{"id":"SW2","kind":"switch","label":"SW2","sub":"VLAN 20","x":9,"y":3},{"id":"R2","kind":"router","label":"R2","sub":"10.10.20.2","x":11,"y":1},{"id":"DNS","kind":"server","label":"DNS1","sub":"10.10.20.53","x":11,"y":5}],"links":[{"from":"PC","to":"SW1","toLabel":"Fa0/1"},{"from":"SW1","to":"R1","fromLabel":"Gi0/1","toLabel":"Gi0/0"},{"from":"R1","to":"SW2","fromLabel":"Gi0/1","toLabel":"Gi0/1"},{"from":"SW2","to":"R2","fromLabel":"Gi0/2","toLabel":"Gi0/0"},{"from":"SW2","to":"DNS","fromLabel":"Fa0/1"}]}
```

| Local device/port | Peer device/port | Role |
|---|---|---|
| PC-A FastEthernet0 | SW1 Fa0/1 | First DHCP client |
| R3 Gi0/0 | SW1 Fa0/2 | IOS DHCP client, enabled in step 5 |
| PC-B FastEthernet0 | SW1 Fa0/3 | Fresh client for helper fault; connect in step 6 |
| PC-C FastEthernet0 | SW1 Fa0/4 | Fresh fourth client for exhaustion; connect in step 8 |
| SW1 Gi0/1 | R1 Gi0/0 | Client gateway, VLAN 10 |
| R1 Gi0/1 | SW2 Gi0/1 | Server subnet, VLAN 20 |
| R2 Gi0/0 | SW2 Gi0/2 | DHCP server |
| DNS1 FastEthernet0 | SW2 Fa0/1 | Actual DNS service address advertised to clients |

All listed cables are copper straight-through because each connects an end device/router to a switch. These are access links, not trunks. Leave PC-B and PC-C uncabled initially. Do not enable DHCP on R3 before step 5.

| Interface/device | Address and mask | Gateway/DNS |
|---|---|---|
| R1 Gi0/0 | 10.10.10.1 / 255.255.255.0 | Client gateway |
| R1 Gi0/1 | 10.10.20.1 / 255.255.255.0 | Server-subnet router |
| R2 Gi0/0 | 10.10.20.2 / 255.255.255.0 | Static return route via 10.10.20.1 |
| DNS1 FastEthernet0 | 10.10.20.53 / 255.255.255.0 | Gateway 10.10.20.1; DNS 10.10.20.53 |
| DHCP clients | Initially only 10.10.10.50–10.10.10.52 available | Gateway 10.10.10.1; DNS 10.10.20.53 |

The three-address initial range is deliberate, so a fourth new client exposes exhaustion without generating hundreds of clients. The precise address assigned to each client is not predetermined.

steps.title: Build the two subnets
steps.body:
Cable the initially listed devices and explicitly prepare the access VLANs.

```ios SW1
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname SW1
SW1(config)# vlan 10
SW1(config-vlan)# name CLIENTS
SW1(config-vlan)# exit
SW1(config)# interface range fastethernet0/1 - 4
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport access vlan 10
SW1(config-if-range)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if-range)# exit
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if)# switchport access vlan 10
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if)# end
```

```ios SW2
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname SW2
SW2(config)# vlan 20
SW2(config-vlan)# name SERVICES
SW2(config-vlan)# exit
SW2(config)# interface range gigabitethernet0/1 - 2
SW2(config-if-range)# switchport mode access
SW2(config-if-range)# switchport access vlan 20
SW2(config-if-range)# no shutdown
SW2(config-if-range)# exit
SW2(config)# interface fastethernet0/1
SW2(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW2(config-if)# switchport access vlan 20
SW2(config-if)# no shutdown
SW2(config-if)# end
```

```ios R1
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R1
R1(config)# service dhcp
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.10.10.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.10.20.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
```

```ios R2
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R2
R2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R2(config-if)# ip address 10.10.20.2 255.255.255.0
R2(config-if)# no shutdown
R2(config-if)# end
```

On DNS1, use Desktop → IP Configuration to enter the address, mask, gateway, and DNS value in the table. Under Services → DNS, turn the service On and add an A record named `portal.dhcp.example` with address `10.10.20.53`. Under Services → HTTP, turn HTTP On. This single record supplies a controlled optional name test; chapter 25 teaches DNS diagnosis in depth.

:::expected
R1's two interfaces and R2 Gi0/0 become operational. SW1's connected client ports belong to VLAN 10; SW2's service ports belong to VLAN 20. DNS1 has the stated static configuration. No helper is configured yet, and no client lease is expected.
:::

steps.title: Configure the server, small pool, and return route
steps.body:
```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# service dhcp
R2(config)# ip dhcp excluded-address 10.10.10.1 10.10.10.49
R2(config)# ip dhcp excluded-address 10.10.10.53 10.10.10.254
R2(config)# ip dhcp pool USERS
R2(dhcp-config)# network 10.10.10.0 255.255.255.0
R2(dhcp-config)# default-router 10.10.10.1
R2(dhcp-config)# dns-server 10.10.20.53
R2(dhcp-config)# domain-name dhcp.example
R2(dhcp-config)# lease 0 8 0
R2(dhcp-config)# exit
R2(config)# ip route 10.10.10.0 255.255.255.0 10.10.20.1
R2(config)# end
R2# show ip dhcp pool
R2# show ip dhcp binding
R2# show ip route
R2# ping 10.10.10.1
```

On R1 verify server reachability:

```ios R1
R1# ping 10.10.20.2
R1# ping 10.10.20.53
```

:::expected
Both subnets and the return path are correct. A /24 has 254 ordinary host addresses. The exclusions cover 49 plus 202 addresses, leaving three candidates: .50, .51, .52. Bindings should be empty on these fresh devices. Pool counters and their headings vary; derive eligibility from the actual network and exclusions rather than demanding one exact display.
:::

steps.title: Observe acquisition before the relay exists
steps.body:
On PC-A, open Desktop → IP Configuration and select DHCP. In Simulation mode, filter for DHCP (some versions group this under DHCP/BOOTP), advance the events, and inspect the client's initial request. Use Realtime afterward. Do not configure a static client address to conceal the missing service.

```ios R1
R1# show ip interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1# show running-config
```

```ios R2
R2# show ip dhcp binding
R2# show ip dhcp server statistics
```

:::expected
PC-A cannot complete remote allocation because its local broadcast has no relay on R1 Gi0/0. The server receives no corresponding relayed attempt. The PC may report DHCP failure or assign a link-local address; record what this image actually does. The expected fact is no valid pool lease, not a particular message or timeout length.
:::

steps.title: Enable the client-facing helper and obtain the first lease
steps.body:
```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ip helper-address 10.10.20.2
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip interface gigabitethernet0/0
```

Retry DHCP on PC-A. If necessary, select Static and then DHCP in its IP Configuration to start another acquisition attempt. Inspect its address, mask, gateway, and DNS fields. In its Command Prompt, ping `10.10.10.1` and `10.10.20.53`. Optionally browse to `http://portal.dhcp.example` once the received DNS setting is correct.

```ios R2
R2# show ip dhcp binding
R2# show ip dhcp pool
R2# show ip dhcp server statistics
```

:::expected
PC-A receives one address in .50–.52, mask /24, gateway 10.10.10.1, and DNS 10.10.20.53. The server binding matches its actual client identity. In a supported packet-detail view, the relayed request carries giaddr 10.10.10.1; reply delivery on the client link may be broadcast or unicast according to the flag/state. A packet on the server subnet is not expected to look identical to the client's original broadcast. If the simulator omits a field, use the lesson's protocol explanation as a paper observation, not a captured result.
:::

steps.title: Obtain the second lease on an IOS client
steps.body:
R3 Gi0/0 is already cabled to SW1 Fa0/2. Configure it now.

```ios R3
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R3
R3(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R3(config-if)# ip address dhcp
R3(config-if)# no shutdown
R3(config-if)# end
R3# show ip interface brief
R3# show ip route
R3# show dhcp lease
R3# ping 10.10.10.1
```

```ios R2
R2# show ip dhcp binding
R2# show ip dhcp pool
```

:::expected
R3 receives a second distinct address in the range and reaches R1's local gateway. The Method field commonly identifies DHCP. If the image implements `show dhcp lease`, inspect the actual state and timers; if it does not, use the interface, server binding, and traffic evidence. Inspect any default route instead of assuming it exists with a fixed distance on every image. The documented eight-hour default timer calculation is T1 4 hours, T2 7 hours; waiting eight hours is not required. Save a working Packet Tracer checkpoint.
:::

steps.title: Move the helper to the wrong interface and observe a fresh client
steps.body:
Use Save As to create an experiment copy. Move the helper from the client interface to the server-facing interface on R1. Keep existing clients' leases; they are useful evidence that old connectivity can conceal a new-allocation failure.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# no ip helper-address 10.10.20.2
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ip helper-address 10.10.20.2
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1# show ip interface gigabitethernet0/1
```

Connect fresh PC-B to SW1 Fa0/3 with a straight-through cable, select DHCP, and let it attempt acquisition. Leave the fault installed until you record the result.

:::expected
PC-B gets no valid pool lease even though one candidate remains. Its broadcasts arrive on Gi0/0, which no longer has the helper. Previously configured PC-A and R3 may still use their unexpired addresses; this does not prove the relay works. Record the incorrect helper placement and the fresh-client failure before recovery.
:::

steps.title: Restore the helper and obtain the third lease
steps.body:
```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# no ip helper-address 10.10.20.2
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ip helper-address 10.10.20.2
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip interface gigabitethernet0/0
```

Retry PC-B's DHCP acquisition and test its gateway and DNS1 address. Then inspect R2:

```ios R2
R2# show ip dhcp binding
R2# show ip dhcp pool
```

:::expected
There are now three distinct active allocations in the only three eligible addresses. Do not continue to the exhaustion test until PC-A, R3, and PC-B all have valid leases and the server records them. If a prior lease expired during a long interruption, reacquire and verify this baseline first.
:::

steps.title: Observe genuine pool exhaustion
steps.body:
Connect fresh PC-C to SW1 Fa0/4 and select DHCP. Do not clear any existing client's binding or change exclusions yet.

```ios R2
R2# show ip dhcp pool
R2# show ip dhcp binding
R2# show ip dhcp conflict
R2# show ip dhcp server statistics
```

:::expected
The fourth client cannot obtain a new address because the three eligible candidates are already allocated. The working relay alone cannot solve that capacity problem. Existing leases need not lose immediate connectivity. Confirm the three bindings and the exclusion arithmetic; do not diagnose exhaustion solely from a link-local client address or a Discover counter.
:::

steps.title: Expand the lab range and recover PC-C
steps.body:
Remove only the upper exclusion range. The gateway and infrastructure exclusion .1–.49 stays in place.

```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# no ip dhcp excluded-address 10.10.10.53 10.10.10.254
R2(config)# end
R2# show ip dhcp pool
R2# show running-config
```

Retry DHCP on PC-C and verify its parameters and pings to 10.10.10.1 and 10.10.20.53. Recheck server bindings.

:::expected
The potential dynamic range is now .50–.254, or 205 addresses before existing bindings/conflicts. PC-C receives a distinct available address. The existing clients keep their current valid addresses. No broad binding clear or address duplication was needed to demonstrate recovery.
:::

steps.title: Save and document the recovered configuration
steps.body:
On R1, R2, R3, SW1, and SW2, individually enter `copy running-config startup-config` from privileged EXEC. Complete each `Destination filename [startup-config]?` prompt with Enter before moving to the next device. Save the Packet Tracer project as `24-dhcp-complete.pkt`.

Record each client's actual leased address, R1's client-facing helper, R2's network/exclusions/options, and R2's return route. Record any unavailable simulator commands separately from successful observations.

:::expected
The final state has the helper only on R1 Gi0/0, the wider intended dynamic range, four valid client allocations, and reachable DNS1. The project contains the server GUI configuration as well as the device configurations. Your record can explain why the two fault tests failed for different reasons.
:::

lab.troubleshooting:
- No local link: inspect cable, port, power, and administrative state before DHCP settings.
- Wrong or absent lease: check access VLAN, fresh versus renewing state, client-facing helper, and service dhcp.
- Server sees the attempt but offers nothing: inspect pool selection, exclusions, bindings, conflicts, and security policy.
- Server offers but client does not complete: verify the route to giaddr, reply delivery, snooping trust, and client state; counters alone do not select one cause.
- Correct address but wrong gateway/DNS: inspect the corresponding pool option and the client's actual refreshed settings.
- A snooping-enabled topology differs from this lab: inspect Option 82/giaddr and the deliberate trust policy taught in chapter 16. This fresh topology adds neither snooping nor Option 82 policy.
lab.challenge:
In a copy, add a new 2960 and PC-D behind unused R1 Gi0/2. Use gateway 10.10.30.1/24. Allow only .50–.59 for this new subnet, with the same actual DNS1 service. Keep the original USERS pool working. Use straight-through links from R1 Gi0/2 to the new switch Gi0/1 and PC-D FastEthernet0 to its Fa0/1; configure both switch ports as access VLAN 30 after creating VLAN 30.

:::expected Answer key
On R1, configure Gi0/2 with `ip address 10.10.30.1 255.255.255.0`, `ip helper-address 10.10.20.2`, and `no shutdown` in interface configuration. On R2, globally exclude 10.10.30.1–10.10.30.49 and 10.10.30.60–10.10.30.254. Create pool GREEN with network 10.10.30.0/24, default-router 10.10.30.1, dns-server 10.10.20.53, and the intended lease. Add `ip route 10.10.30.0 255.255.255.0 10.10.20.1` in global configuration. The new exclusions total 244 of 254 host addresses, leaving ten candidates. PC-D should obtain one of .50–.59 with the correct gateway and DNS. Verify its binding, gateway/DNS1 pings, and the original clients. The expected giaddr for the new subnet is 10.10.30.1; no existing pool needs renaming or replacement.
:::

exhibit.title: Representative client settings
exhibit.text:
Autoconfiguration IPv4 Address : 169.254.87.14
Subnet Mask                  : 255.255.0.0
Default Gateway              :

questions.prompt: A Windows client was set to obtain IPv4 settings automatically. What conclusion is supported by this output?
options: IPv4 link-local is in use; the intended DHCP configuration is absent.
The relay certainly discarded the first DHCPDISCOVER.
The DNS server supplied an incorrect IPv4 address to the PC.
The DHCP server is definitely out of addresses.
questions.explanation: The 169.254/16 address is link-local, and no gateway is shown. This is evidence that the intended DHCP configuration was not obtained or retained. It does not identify where the exchange failed; check link/VLAN, client settings, relay, server, and return delivery.

whyWrong.1: There is no packet or relay evidence locating the failure at the Discover stage.
whyWrong.2: DNS resolves names; it does not assign the client interface address.
whyWrong.3: Pool exhaustion is one possible cause, but no pool or binding evidence is given.

questions.prompt: A DHCPv4 client has no usable address and starts its initial allocation on Ethernet. Which IPv4 source and destination normally carry its DHCPDISCOVER?
options: Its previous address to the DNS server
The proposed address to the selected DHCP server
questions.explanation: The initial client cannot use an assigned source address or assume that it knows a DHCP server. It sends an IPv4 broadcast from 0.0.0.0, normally UDP source 68 to destination 67.

whyWrong.0: This client has no usable address and is discovering a DHCP service, not querying DNS.
whyWrong.2: A proposed address is not yet an acknowledged lease; discovery precedes server selection.
whyWrong.3: 127/8 is loopback and 224.0.0.5 is an OSPF multicast address, not this DHCP exchange.

questions.prompt: In the initial Discover–Offer–Request–ACK exchange, which two messages are sent by the client? Select two.
options: DHCPDISCOVER
DHCPOFFER
DHCPREQUEST
DHCPACK
questions.explanation: The client discovers available service and then requests the selected offer. The server offers configuration and acknowledges the accepted allocation.

whyWrong.1: An Offer is a server response proposing configuration.
whyWrong.3: An ACK is a server response confirming configuration.

questions.prompt: R1 receives client broadcasts on Gi0/0. Its DHCP server is reachable at 10.10.20.2 through Gi0/1. Where should the ordinary relay helper be configured?
options: Under the DHCP pool on the remote server
On the server-facing Gi0/1 interface only
On the client-facing Gi0/0 interface
On every interface, including unused interfaces
questions.explanation: The helper belongs on the Layer 3 interface that receives the client subnet broadcast. R1 then sends a relayed request toward the configured server using normal IP forwarding.

whyWrong.0: Pool settings select the configuration to offer; they do not receive and relay R1’s local broadcast.
whyWrong.1: The initial client broadcast arrives on Gi0/0, not Gi0/1.
whyWrong.3: Configure the required client subnet interface deliberately; unused or server-facing helpers do not replace it.

exhibit.title: Representative R1 configuration
exhibit.text:
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 10.10.10.1 255.255.255.0
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 ip address 10.10.20.1 255.255.255.0
 ip helper-address 10.10.20.2

questions.prompt: A fresh client on 10.10.10.0/24 cannot obtain a lease. R2 has an available matching pool; both R1 interfaces are up and routing between them works. Which correction addresses the shown relay mistake?
options: Change the pool network to 10.10.20.0/24.
Configure the server’s 10.10.20.2 address as the PC’s gateway.
Remove DHCP and assign every PC a 169.254 address.
Move the helper from Gi0/1 to Gi0/0.
questions.explanation: The helper is on the server-facing interface. The fresh client’s broadcast reaches Gi0/0, where no helper is configured. Place it there and test a new request.

whyWrong.0: The clients belong to 10.10.10.0/24; changing the pool to the server subnet would give the wrong network.
whyWrong.1: The client’s gateway must be its reachable local router address, 10.10.10.1.
whyWrong.2: Link-local addressing does not provide the planned routed network service.

questions.prompt: An ordinary relayed request arrives at an IOS server with giaddr 10.10.30.1. The server has matching /24 pools for 10.10.20.0 and 10.10.30.0 and no special class/link-selection policy. Which pool should supply the client?
options: The 10.10.30.0/24 pool, because giaddr identifies the client subnet.
The 10.10.20.0/24 pool, because that is the server’s connected subnet.
Whichever pool has the alphabetically first name.
Neither pool, because relayed requests must have giaddr zero.
questions.explanation: The relay gateway field identifies the subnet on whose behalf the relay is requesting service. In this ordinary case, 10.10.30.1 matches the 10.10.30.0/24 pool.

whyWrong.1: Selecting solely from the receiving server interface would assign addresses for the wrong subnet.
whyWrong.2: Pool names are administrative labels, not this subnet selection rule.
whyWrong.3: The ordinary relay sets a nonzero giaddr; zero is typical of a directly received initial client message.

questions.prompt: This is the only installed default route. What does its bracketed value establish?
options: Every Cisco platform always gives every DHCP-learned route a distance of 254.
This installed default route has administrative distance 254 and metric 0.
The client lease lasts 254 seconds.
The route is more specific than an installed /24 route to the same destination.
questions.explanation: In IOS route output, the bracketed pair is administrative distance/metric. This record establishes the values of this installed route. The documented IOS DHCP default-route distance can be 254 when not overridden; verify the actual route instead of extending one display to every platform.

whyWrong.0: The exhibit is evidence for this route, not a universal platform/default assertion.
whyWrong.2: Routing brackets do not display DHCP lease duration.
whyWrong.3: A /24 is more specific than /0 and wins longest-prefix forwarding for a matching destination.

questions.prompt: A client has a 12-hour lease. The server supplies no alternate renewal or rebinding timers. What does the standard default T1 behavior call for?
options: Broadcast a Discover immediately after three hours.
Stop using the address after six hours even if renewal succeeds.
Attempt renewal with the leasing server by unicast after six hours.
Wait until all twelve hours have elapsed before contacting a server.
questions.explanation: Default T1 is half the lease: 12 × 0.5 = 6 hours. A renewing client still has a valid address and attempts a DHCPREQUEST to its leasing server. Failure at T1 does not immediately invalidate the lease.

whyWrong.0: T1 is not one quarter of the lease, and renewal is not a new initial Discover.
whyWrong.1: The address remains leased while the client seeks renewal before expiry.
whyWrong.3: Waiting until expiry would omit the renewal and rebinding opportunities.

questions.prompt: The server has no conflicts or reservations beyond those shown. A fourth fresh client’s Discover reaches it. Why can the server not supply another address from this pool?
options: A /24 contains only three host addresses.
The excluded addresses remain available when the pool becomes busy.
The client must use TCP instead of UDP to obtain the fourth address.
All three available candidates are leased: 254 − 251 − 3 = 0 free.
questions.explanation: A /24 has 254 ordinary host addresses. Excluding 10.10.10.1–49 and 53–254 excludes 49 + 202 = 251. The remaining .50, .51, and .52 are already leased, leaving none for a fourth client.

whyWrong.0: The pool is deliberately restricted by exclusions; /24 itself has 254 ordinary host addresses.
whyWrong.1: Excluded addresses are withheld, not an emergency allocation reserve.
whyWrong.2: DHCPv4 uses UDP; changing transport does not create pool capacity.

questions.prompt: A packet capture shows the server receiving a Discover and sending an Offer to relay giaddr 10.10.10.1. The client capture contains repeated Discovers and no received Offer. Which two faults are consistent with that evidence? Select two.
options: The path from server to relay drops the reply.
The server has no matching pool and therefore never sent an Offer.
The relay-to-client delivery path drops the Offer.
The client successfully received and accepted this Offer.
questions.explanation: The server demonstrably sent a reply, but the client did not observe it. Investigate the return path to the relay and delivery from the relay to the client. These captures narrow the failure stage without proving which of those paths failed.

whyWrong.1: The captured outgoing Offer contradicts the claim that none was sent.
whyWrong.3: The supplied client capture has no received Offer and no accepted allocation.

questions.prompt: Which explicit global configuration disables the documented IOS DHCP server and relay service?
options: no ip domain-lookup
no service dhcp
no ip dhcp excluded-address 10.10.10.1
no ip host server
questions.explanation: The global no service dhcp command disables the documented IOS server and relay functions. service dhcp enables them; do not diagnose disabled DHCP merely because a default command is absent from an abbreviated configuration.

whyWrong.0: This controls the router’s DNS client lookups.
whyWrong.2: This removes an exclusion for one address; it does not disable the DHCP service.
whyWrong.3: This removes a local hostname mapping, not DHCP service.

questions.prompt: An IOS DHCP server records 10.10.10.60 as a Ping-detected conflict. What should you do before clearing the conflict entry?
options: Immediately lease .60 to another host to prove it is free.
Delete every binding and every exclusion in the server.
Investigate the existing use of .60 and resolve the duplicate or stale condition.
Change the client DNS suffix to make the conflict disappear.
questions.explanation: A conflict entry means the server is withholding an address because it detected evidence of a collision. Identify the responding device or stale condition, correct the address plan, and clear only an appropriately resolved entry. The display alone does not identify the owner.

whyWrong.0: Allocating an address that may already be in use can create an actual duplicate.
whyWrong.1: Broad clearing can disrupt healthy clients and remove planned protection for infrastructure.
whyWrong.3: A DNS suffix does not resolve duplicate IPv4 use.

exhibit.title: Representative request and configuration
exhibit.text:
Relayed DHCPDISCOVER: giaddr = 10.10.30.1
Configured dynamic pool networks:
 USERS  10.10.10.0 255.255.255.0
 SERVER 10.10.20.0 255.255.255.0

questions.prompt: The relay and server paths work. No special subnet-selection policy is configured. Why does the request fail to find a suitable dynamic pool?
options: The giaddr must be an address assigned to the DHCP server itself.
The pool name must match the relay router’s hostname.
DHCP cannot relay to a server in another /24.
The server has no pool matching client subnet 10.10.30.0/24.
questions.explanation: The ordinary pool selection uses the nonzero giaddr to identify the client subnet. A request relayed for 10.10.30.1 needs a matching 10.10.30.0/24 pool; the two shown networks do not match.

whyWrong.0: The gateway address is supplied by the relay for the client-facing subnet.
whyWrong.1: Pool names do not have to match device hostnames.
whyWrong.2: Reaching an off-subnet DHCP server is a normal purpose of relay.

questions.prompt: A client moves to another subnet and requests reuse of its previous address. A DHCP server determines from authoritative subnet information that the requested address is invalid on the new subnet. Which response tells the client to abandon that configuration?
options: DHCPNAK
DHCPDECLINE
DHCPRELEASE
DHCPINFORM
questions.explanation: A server uses DHCPNAK to reject a configuration it determines is invalid. The client must stop using the rejected address and restart appropriate acquisition. This does not mean every server must NAK every request it cannot satisfy; a server without the necessary knowledge can remain silent.

whyWrong.1: DECLINE is sent by a client reporting that the offered address appears to be in use.
whyWrong.2: RELEASE is a client message relinquishing a lease.
whyWrong.3: INFORM is a client request for additional configuration when it already has an address.

questions.prompt: A client receives the intended address, mask, and gateway, and reaches a lab web server by its IPv4 address. Its current DNS setting is 10.10.20.99; the design specifies 10.10.20.53. Which repair directly addresses the demonstrated DHCP option mistake?
options: Replace the correct gateway option with 10.10.20.53.
Correct the pool’s dns-server value and refresh and verify the client’s configuration.
Change the client mask from /24 to /16 without changing the design.
Move the helper to the DHCP-server-facing interface.
questions.explanation: DHCP option 6 supplies resolver addresses. Correct dns-server to 10.10.20.53, then renew or reacquire settings as appropriate and verify the actual client configuration. An edited pool does not instantly rewrite an existing client’s settings.

whyWrong.0: The DNS resolver is not thereby the client’s local default gateway.
whyWrong.2: The evidence identifies an incorrect resolver setting, not an incorrect subnet design.
whyWrong.3: The helper must remain on the client-facing Layer 3 interface.

questions.prompt: A server answers an initial client directly on the same subnet: giaddr and ciaddr are zero, and the client sets the BROADCAST flag. How should the server deliver its Offer or ACK under the RFC 2131 rule for this case?
options: Always to a multicast group selected by the subnet mask.
Only by unicast to the DNS server.
Broadcast the Offer or ACK.
By TCP to the offered address.
questions.explanation: With no relay gateway or current client address and the broadcast flag set, the server broadcasts the Offer/ACK. Other cases can use unicast to a current address, to the relay, or to the offered address/client hardware address. “Offer and ACK are always broadcast” is therefore inaccurate.

whyWrong.0: The specified rule uses broadcast, not a DHCP multicast group.
whyWrong.1: The DNS server is not the recipient of the DHCP allocation reply.
whyWrong.3: The server reply uses UDP, not TCP.

cards.front: What is the purpose of each message in initial DORA?
cards.back: Discover: client seeks service. Offer: server proposes configuration. Request: client selects an offer. ACK: server confirms allocation. This initial sequence does not describe every later renewal exchange.

cards.front: What IP addresses do an initial Discover and a selecting client’s Request normally use?
cards.back: Source 0.0.0.0 to destination 255.255.255.255. Scope this to initial acquisition before the client has a usable lease; a renewing Request can instead use the current address and unicast to the server.

cards.front: Which UDP ports belong to DHCPv4 clients and servers?
cards.back: Client port 68; server port 67. Initial client messages normally travel 68→67. A server replies to a relay’s giaddr on server port 67, and the relay then delivers toward client port 68.

cards.front: Why is the selecting DHCPREQUEST broadcast?
cards.back: It identifies the chosen server and requested address while allowing other offering servers to learn that their proposals were not selected. Do not extend that broadcast rule to renewal Requests.

cards.front: What are default T1 and T2, and what happens at lease expiry?
cards.back: If the server does not specify other values, T1 is 50% and T2 is 87.5% of the lease. T1 starts unicast renewal with the leasing server; T2 starts broadcast rebinding. At expiry the client must stop using an unrenewed address.

cards.front: What lease duration does the referenced IOS DHCP server use if no lease command overrides its default?
cards.back: One day in Cisco’s documented IOS server behavior. Check the configured pool and actual client lease rather than assuming this duration for every DHCP product. lease 0 8 0 specifies eight hours on the documented IOS syntax.

cards.front: What does a Windows 169.254/16 address tell you after an attempted DHCP setup?
cards.back: The client is using IPv4 link-local configuration rather than the planned DHCP assignment. It does not identify a unique cause such as a bad helper or exhausted pool. Check actual settings and trace the acquisition path.

cards.front: How do you exclude 10.10.10.1 through 10.10.10.49 on IOS?
cards.back: In global configuration: ip dhcp excluded-address 10.10.10.1 10.10.10.49. Exclusions protect addresses from dynamic allocation; both endpoints are included.

cards.front: What do network, default-router, and dns-server supply inside an IOS DHCP pool?
cards.back: network identifies the pool subnet and mask; default-router supplies the client’s local gateway; dns-server supplies resolver addresses. A DNS resolver is not automatically the gateway. Required options depend on the intended service.

cards.front: How do you make an IOS routed Ethernet interface a DHCPv4 client?
cards.back: Enter interface configuration and use ip address dhcp, then no shutdown. Verify the learned interface address, lease where supported, and actual routing table. Do not assume a default route’s presence or distance without checking it.

cards.front: Where is ip helper-address placed for ordinary DHCP relay?
cards.back: On the Layer 3 interface receiving the client subnet’s broadcasts, such as its gateway SVI or routed interface. Its value is the reachable DHCP server address. A helper only on the server-facing interface misses that initial broadcast.

cards.front: What does nonzero giaddr do in an ordinary relayed DHCP request?
cards.back: It identifies the relay gateway for the client subnet, allowing normal server pool selection and return delivery to the relay. The server also needs a route to that address. Specialized policies can add selection rules.

cards.front: What does no service dhcp disable on the documented IOS implementation?
cards.back: The IOS DHCP server and relay agent. service dhcp enables them. Absence of a displayed service dhcp line does not prove disabled service because an enabled default can be omitted from running configuration.

cards.front: Which four IOS server displays help separate allocation, capacity, conflicts, and messages?
cards.back: show ip dhcp binding: allocations; show ip dhcp pool: pool capacity; show ip dhcp conflict: withheld conflict addresses; show ip dhcp server statistics: message counters. Inspect a fresh attempt because historical counters alone can mislead.

cards.front: How do you verify which interface carries a helper?
cards.back: Inspect the relevant interface in show running-config and show ip interface interface-name. Confirm the helper’s address, the client-facing interface, and its operational state; exact display text varies by image.

cards.front: What should happen before clearing a DHCP conflict entry?
cards.back: Identify and correct the underlying duplicate address or stale evidence. Clearing an entry does not evict the host that might already use the address. Preserve infrastructure exclusions and healthy active bindings.

cards.front: Do increasing Discover counters with no successful allocation identify one exact DHCP fault?
cards.back: No. Check matching pools, capacity, server policy, outgoing replies, relay return routing, and delivery to the client. Counters establish stages only when correlated with the current attempt and other evidence.

cards.front: How do NAK, DECLINE, RELEASE, and INFORM differ?
cards.back: NAK: server rejects invalid configuration. DECLINE: client reports a proposed address appears in use. RELEASE: client gives up its lease. INFORM: an already-addressed client requests other configuration information.

cards.front: Are initial DHCP Offers and ACKs always broadcasts?
cards.back: No. Delivery depends on giaddr, ciaddr, and the BROADCAST flag. A relay receives a server reply at nonzero giaddr; an already-addressed client can receive unicast. A directly attached initial client that requests broadcast gets broadcast delivery under RFC 2131.

cards.front: How do giaddr, Option 82, and DHCP trust settings differ?
cards.back: giaddr identifies the relay gateway/subnet. Option 82 carries relay-agent information such as circuit/remote identity. DHCP snooping port trust and IOS relay-information trust control different checks. A server may reject Option 82 with giaddr zero unless the intended trust policy permits it.

commands.task: Exclude 10.10.10.1 through 10.10.10.49 from dynamic allocation.
commands.note: Both endpoints are excluded: 49 addresses, preserving the client gateway and planned static infrastructure.

commands.task: Create or enter the DHCP pool named USERS.
commands.note: The prompt becomes R2(dhcp-config)#. A pool name alone does not define an address range.

commands.task: Set the USERS pool network to 10.10.10.0/24, using dotted-decimal mask syntax.
commands.note: The network identifies the client subnet, even when the server is on 10.10.20.0/24.

commands.task: Supply 10.10.10.1 as the clients’ default gateway.
commands.note: The gateway belongs to the clients’ local subnet, not necessarily to the DHCP server subnet.

commands.task: Supply 10.10.20.53 as the resolver for this pool.
commands.note: This supplies DHCP option 6; it does not configure the router’s own DNS client.

commands.task: Set a lease of zero days, eight hours, zero minutes.
commands.note: This is an eight-hour lease. Without alternate T1/T2 values, default renewal starts at four hours and rebinding at seven hours.

commands.task: Relay DHCP for clients arriving on this client-facing interface to 10.10.20.2.
commands.note: First confirm this is the interface with the client subnet gateway. The server must be reachable and have a route back to giaddr.

commands.task: Make this routed Ethernet interface obtain its IPv4 configuration with DHCP.
commands.note: Enable the interface with no shutdown if needed; then inspect its actual learned address and routes.

commands.task: Display the server’s current DHCP address bindings.
commands.note: Correlate an address and client identifier with the current test client. A displayed binding does not alone prove the client received the ACK.

commands.task: Display DHCP pools and their address usage.
commands.note: Compare the network, exclusions, active allocations, and available capacity; do not infer exhaustion from a client timeout alone.

commands.task: Display addresses withheld because of detected DHCP conflicts.
commands.note: Investigate a conflict before clearing it. An empty table does not by itself prove every address on the LAN is unused.

commands.task: On an IOS image supporting DHCP server event debugging, enable that specific event debug for a short controlled observation.
commands.note: Use only in an isolated lab or approved troubleshooting window. Output and support vary. Finish with undebug all; do not leave event debugging enabled or assume it exposes every packet field.

tickets.title: Fresh branch clients cannot obtain a lease
tickets.scenario: R1 connects clients on Gi0/0, 10.10.10.1/24, to R2 through Gi0/1, 10.10.20.1/24. R2 is the server at 10.10.20.2/24. DHCP service is enabled on both routers. A new PC has no prior lease; an older PC still has a valid lease and can reach a server. Links and VLAN membership are verified. The following abbreviated records are representative teaching evidence.

exhibits.title: R1 relevant interface configuration
exhibits.text:
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 10.10.10.1 255.255.255.0
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 ip address 10.10.20.1 255.255.255.0
 ip helper-address 10.10.20.2

exhibits.title: R2 pool and return-path checks
exhibits.text:
Pool USERS network: 10.10.10.0/24
Ordinary host addresses: 254
Excluded: 10.10.10.1–10.10.10.49 (49)
Active bindings: 2
Conflicts: none
Route: 10.10.10.0/24 via 10.10.20.1
Ping to 10.10.10.1: successful

exhibits.title: Current attempt capture
exhibits.text:
Client-side capture: DHCPDISCOVER arrives at R1 Gi0/0.
Server-side capture: no matching forwarded Discover reaches R2.

tickets.question: Which demonstrated configuration mistake should be corrected first?
options: The DHCP server has no free addresses.
The existing lease proves the helper is correct.
The helper is on the server-facing interface instead of the client-facing interface.
The DHCP server needs a default-router option equal to its own address.
tickets.explanation: The client broadcast arrives on Gi0/0, but only Gi0/1 has the helper. Move it to the receiving client interface. Capacity is not exhausted: 254 − 49 − 2 = 203 addresses are available under the stated conditions. The return route is supplied. An old client can keep working with a valid lease; its later unicast renewal might also work without this helper, so it does not validate initial relay acquisition.
tickets.fix:
Move the helper, then repeat the fresh client request.

```ios
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# no ip helper-address 10.10.20.2
R1(config-if)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ip helper-address 10.10.20.2
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip interface gigabitethernet0/0
```

Verify a new R2 binding and the client’s actual address, mask, gateway, and DNS setting. Test the gateway and intended remote service. Save the corrected configuration after verification.

tickets.title: The fourth training-room client receives no lease
tickets.scenario: An isolated training room uses R1 as a verified relay and R2 as an IOS DHCP server. The first three clients still have valid leases and are powered on. A fourth fresh client receives no allocation. Its Discover reaches R2. The reserved infrastructure range is .1–.49; the upper exclusion was temporary for this exercise. These are representative records, not simulator captures.

exhibits.title: R2 pool configuration
exhibits.text:
ip dhcp excluded-address 10.10.10.1 10.10.10.49
ip dhcp excluded-address 10.10.10.53 10.10.10.254
ip dhcp pool USERS
 network 10.10.10.0 255.255.255.0
 default-router 10.10.10.1
 dns-server 10.10.20.53
 lease 0 8 0

exhibits.title: Current allocation and conflict checks
exhibits.text:
Active leases: 10.10.10.50, 10.10.10.51, 10.10.10.52
Conflict entries: none
Fourth client’s Discover received; no candidate address remains.

tickets.question: Which repair restores capacity while preserving the intended static-address range and healthy leases?
options: Clear every existing binding even though those clients are still using their addresses.
Remove only the temporary .53–.254 exclusion and retry the fourth client.
Move the helper from the client-facing interface to the server-facing interface.
Remove the .1–.49 infrastructure exclusion and allocate the gateway address.
tickets.explanation: The two exclusions leave only .50–.52, all of which are occupied. Removing the temporary upper exclusion expands the candidate range to .50–.254, 205 addresses, while preserving static infrastructure. Broadly deleting bindings risks allocating an address still in use. Changing a working helper does not add capacity; removing gateway protection is unsafe. Existing eight-hour leases can expire or be released; they are not permanent.
tickets.fix:
Remove only the temporary exclusion.

```ios
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# no ip dhcp excluded-address 10.10.10.53 10.10.10.254
R2(config)# end
R2# show ip dhcp pool
R2# show ip dhcp binding
```

Retry DHCP on the fourth client, confirm its new address is outside .1–.49 and distinct from active clients, and test the gateway. Verify all original clients retain service. Save after the check.

sections.title: What names and DNS records provide
Follow a lookup and its cached answer
Choose and verify the correct record type
Configure the router as a DNS client

lab.title: Build DNS records, compare lookup failures, and diagnose all six record types
devices: Optional: another Server-PT for the challenge
lab.intro:
Use Packet Tracer for the address/name comparison and IOS client configuration. Use the supplied paper records for types and response details that the simulator may not implement. The paper cases are required practice for record diagnosis, not claims of a working recursive or authoritative DNS deployment in Packet Tracer.

Start with new devices. Use their console CLI tabs, answer `no` to any initial configuration dialog, and inspect the named ports before cabling. This exact lab has not been executed in Packet Tracer during this review. Its GUI labels, cache behavior, and supported record/query types may vary; where a feature is absent, use the explicit paper alternative.
lab.topology:
```diagram
{"type":"topology","title":"Separate DNS and web services on one lab LAN","caption":"PC-A and R1 ask DNS1 for names, then reach WEB1 at the returned address.","nodes":[{"id":"PC","kind":"pc","label":"PC-A","sub":"10.1.1.10/24","x":1,"y":3},{"id":"SW","kind":"switch","label":"SW1","x":5,"y":3},{"id":"R","kind":"router","label":"R1","sub":"10.1.1.1/24","x":9,"y":1},{"id":"DNS","kind":"server","label":"DNS1","sub":"10.1.1.53/24","x":9,"y":3},{"id":"WEB","kind":"server","label":"WEB1","sub":"10.1.1.80/24","x":9,"y":5}],"links":[{"from":"PC","to":"SW","toLabel":"Fa0/1"},{"from":"SW","to":"R","fromLabel":"Gi0/1","toLabel":"Gi0/0"},{"from":"SW","to":"DNS","fromLabel":"Fa0/2"},{"from":"SW","to":"WEB","fromLabel":"Fa0/3"}]}
```

| Device/port | Peer | Address / mask | Gateway; DNS |
|---|---|---|---|
| PC-A FastEthernet0 | SW1 Fa0/1 | 10.1.1.10 / 255.255.255.0 | 10.1.1.1; 10.1.1.53 |
| DNS1 FastEthernet0 | SW1 Fa0/2 | 10.1.1.53 / 255.255.255.0 | 10.1.1.1; 10.1.1.53 |
| WEB1 FastEthernet0 | SW1 Fa0/3 | 10.1.1.80 / 255.255.255.0 | 10.1.1.1; 10.1.1.53 |
| R1 Gi0/0 | SW1 Gi0/1 | 10.1.1.1 / 255.255.255.0 | No upstream route needed; DNS 10.1.1.53 |

Use straight-through copper cables for all four links. Every switch port used here is access VLAN 1. This is a simple isolated addressing exercise, not a recommendation to use VLAN 1 for production management. No real Internet connection or public DNS change is required. Reserve unused 10.1.1.54 and 10.1.1.81 for the stated fault tests; do not add devices at those addresses until the optional challenge.

steps.title: Configure and prove the IP path
steps.body:
Set PC-A, DNS1, and WEB1 in Desktop → IP Configuration using the complete table. Configure the router and switch explicitly.

```ios R1
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R1
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.1.1.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip interface brief
```

```ios SW1
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname SW1
SW1(config)# interface range fastethernet0/1 - 3
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport access vlan 1
SW1(config-if-range)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if-range)# exit
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if)# switchport access vlan 1
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show vlan brief
```

From PC-A's Command Prompt, ping 10.1.1.1, 10.1.1.53, and 10.1.1.80. Repeat after link startup and ARP resolution if necessary.

:::expected
All three addresses respond once the links forward. This is local-subnet connectivity, so no route to another network is involved. An IP ping is not yet a DNS or HTTP test. Correct any addressing/cabling fault before proceeding.
:::

steps.title: Add controlled DNS records and a web service
steps.body:
On DNS1, open Services → DNS, turn it On, and add the following records with the Name, Type, and Address/target fields. Use Add or the equivalent save action for each entry.

| Name | Type | Data |
|---|---|---|
| app.lab.example | A | 10.1.1.80 |
| fresh.lab.example | A | 10.1.1.80 |
| ns1.lab.example | A | 10.1.1.53 |
| www.lab.example | CNAME | app.lab.example |

If the selected simulator does not offer CNAME or does not follow it in a query, retain the A-record exercises and use this explicit paper result for the alias: `www.lab.example CNAME app.lab.example`, followed by `app.lab.example A 10.1.1.80`. Do not silently replace the alias with an A record and call that a CNAME test. Record the available type list; no fixed list of unsupported simulator types is assumed.

On WEB1, enable Services → HTTP. Keep its default simple page or replace its title with `CCNA DNS lab`. From PC-A, open Web Browser and request `http://10.1.1.80`.

:::expected
The stored records match the table, and WEB1 serves the controlled HTTP page by address. This page is intentionally suitable for both IP-literal and hostname access. These local records do not simulate the public root/TLD delegation process.
:::

steps.title: Configure and verify R1's DNS client
steps.body:
```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip domain-lookup
R1(config)# ip name-server 10.1.1.53
R1(config)# ip domain name lab.example
R1(config)# end
R1# ping app.lab.example
R1# ping app
R1# show hosts
```

The hyphenated lookup command and two-word form `ip domain lookup` are accepted/displayed differently by IOS releases. Use the image's supported spelling. If short-name completion is absent in the simulator, retain the successful full-name test and inspect the configured domain as a paper explanation of the documented IOS behavior.

:::expected
The full name resolves to 10.1.1.80 and reaches WEB1. On the documented IOS behavior, `app` is completed with the default domain. `show hosts` identifies DNS1 and the configured suffix and may show a temporary cached mapping. Record what is actually present; no exact cache lifetime or formatting is required. Do not query `fresh.lab.example` yet.
:::

steps.title: Distinguish static mapping from disabled DNS lookup
steps.body:
Create a local static name and disable the router's DNS client. Test the static name, then the deliberately unused fresh name so an earlier successful cache entry cannot hide the difference.
