tickets.title: A source-selector typo prevents new translations
tickets.scenario: An isolated branch exercise uses EDGE with the displayed interface-overload rule and no other NAT rules or interface filters. Fresh LAN traffic from 10.20.30.0/24 can reach gateway 10.20.30.1 but cannot complete outside requests. The provider has a return path to EDGE’s outside address, but no route to the untranslated LAN. The excerpts below are representative.

exhibits.title: EDGE# show ip interface brief | exclude unassigned
exhibits.text:
Interface                  IP-Address      OK? Method Status                Protocol
GigabitEthernet0/0         10.20.30.1      YES manual up                    up
GigabitEthernet0/1         198.51.100.1    YES manual up                    up

exhibits.title: EDGE# show running-config | include ip nat|access-list|ip route
exhibits.text:
ip nat inside
 ip nat outside
ip nat inside source list 1 interface GigabitEthernet0/1 overload
ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 198.51.100.2
access-list 1 permit 10.20.3.0 0.0.0.255

exhibits.title: EDGE# show ip nat statistics
exhibits.text:
Total active translations: 0 (0 static, 0 dynamic; 0 extended)
Outside interfaces:
  GigabitEthernet0/1
Inside interfaces:
  GigabitEthernet0/0
Hits: 0  Misses: 0
Expired translations: 0
Dynamic mappings:
-- Inside Source
[Id: 1] access-list 1 interface GigabitEthernet0/1 refcount 0

tickets.question: What is the root cause?
options: The inside and outside marks are on the wrong interfaces, so no packet enters an inside interface
Access list 1 permits 10.20.3.0/24 instead of 10.20.30.0/24, so no LAN host is selected for translation
The overload keyword is present but the interface form of PAT needs a pool as well
The default route points to the ISP, so translated packets are sent before the table entry is created
tickets.explanation: The NAT interface lists match the intended LAN and outside paths. ACL 1 instead selects 10.20.3.0/24, so fresh 10.20.30.x sources do not match it. The explicit mismatch establishes the error; zero counters alone would not. Untranslated traffic lacks the stated return route.
tickets.fix:
Because this lab confirms ACL 1 is used only by NAT, replace its incorrect selector.

```ios
EDGE# configure terminal
EDGE(config)# no access-list 1
EDGE(config)# access-list 1 permit 10.20.30.0 0.0.0.255
EDGE(config)# end
EDGE# show access-lists 1
```

Generate a fresh request from a LAN client, then run `show ip nat translations`. Verify that its global address is 198.51.100.1 and that the actual application receives its expected response before saving.

tickets.title: Replies follow the wrong route after a pool change
tickets.scenario: EDGE now uses pool overload with global addresses 198.51.100.20–198.51.100.23 in an isolated routed exercise. Its neighbor CORE receives replies from test server 203.0.113.10 for those global addresses. A packet capture confirms the replies arrive on CORE’s upstream interface. CORE has no policy routing or filtering; the representative excerpts show the relevant destination routes. The CORE–EDGE link is 198.51.100.0/30, with EDGE at .1.

exhibits.title: CORE# show ip route | begin Gateway
exhibits.text:
Gateway of last resort is 192.0.2.1 to network 0.0.0.0

S*    0.0.0.0/0 [1/0] via 192.0.2.1
      192.0.2.0/30 is subnetted, 1 subnets
C        192.0.2.0 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/1
      198.51.100.0/30 is subnetted, 1 subnets
C        198.51.100.0 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0

tickets.question: What is the root cause?
options: The shown TCP ports exceed the permitted NAT port range
The selector excludes the fresh requests represented by the shown translations
CORE selects its upstream default for pool replies instead of a route toward EDGE
Pool overload requires a separate global address for every inside host
tickets.explanation: The pool addresses are outside the connected .0/30. Without a more specific route, CORE selects its upstream default for the confirmed arriving replies, sending them away from EDGE. The capture and routing evidence establish that forwarding error; one-sided NAT debug alone would not prove it.
tickets.fix:
Install the route to the pool block through the directly connected EDGE address.

```ios
CORE# configure terminal
CORE(config)# ip route 198.51.100.16 255.255.255.240 198.51.100.1
CORE(config)# end
CORE# show ip route 198.51.100.20
```

Repeat the same client request. Verify CORE now selects the /28 toward EDGE, the reply is reverse-translated, and the application succeeds. Save after verification. No counter or debug line by itself substitutes for these observations.

lab.title: Synchronize two routers and investigate their management records
devices: 2 × Cisco 2911 routers (R1 time source, R2 client)
lab.intro: Use a new isolated Packet Tracer project. R1 provides an explicitly configured local lab clock; R2 synchronizes to it and sends events to LOG1. PC1 reads R2's management information. This avoids assuming a particular Server-PT NTP stratum or switch NTP implementation. These are authored procedures and expected observations, not a recorded simulator run. If your image lacks a required operation, use a supporting IOS/CML lab with equivalent interfaces, or complete the accompanying evidence worksheet and record that it was a worksheet.
lab.topology:
All five devices share VLAN 10 and `10.60.0.0/24`. Connect each listed Ethernet port with a copper straight-through cable. R2's Loopback99 is a disposable local test interface; it does not carry management traffic.

```diagram
{"type":"topology","title":"Management services on a single isolated LAN","caption":"The test interface is local to R2, so changing it does not interrupt the path to the time source or collector.","nodes":[{"id":"R1","kind":"router","label":"R1","sub":"10.60.0.1 · NTP","x":2,"y":1},{"id":"R2","kind":"router","label":"R2","sub":"10.60.0.2 · agent","x":2,"y":5},{"id":"SW","kind":"switch","label":"SW1","sub":"VLAN 10","x":6,"y":3},{"id":"LOG","kind":"server","label":"LOG1","sub":"10.60.0.50","x":10,"y":1},{"id":"PC","kind":"pc","label":"PC1","sub":"10.60.0.60","x":10,"y":5}],"links":[{"from":"R1","to":"SW","fromLabel":"Gi0/0","toLabel":"Fa0/1"},{"from":"R2","to":"SW","fromLabel":"Gi0/0","toLabel":"Fa0/2","accent":true},{"from":"SW","to":"LOG","fromLabel":"Fa0/3","toLabel":"Fa0"},{"from":"SW","to":"PC","fromLabel":"Fa0/4","toLabel":"Fa0"}]}
```

| Device | Interface/address | Gateway or purpose |
|---|---|---|
| R1 | Gi0/0 `10.60.0.1/24` | Isolated stratum-8 source |
| R2 | Gi0/0 `10.60.0.2/24` | NTP client, syslog sender, SNMP agent |
| R2 | Loopback99 `192.0.2.99/32` | Test interface only |
| LOG1 | FastEthernet0 `10.60.0.50/24` | Gateway `.1`; syslog service |
| PC1 | FastEthernet0 `10.60.0.60/24` | Gateway `.1`; MIB Browser |

No router default route or switch management SVI is needed for these same-subnet tests. The gateway fields prepare the endpoints consistently but do not explain successful same-subnet communication.

steps.title: Establish the management LAN
steps.body:
Set LOG1 and PC1 under Desktop → IP Configuration. Configure the switch and both routers from their console/CLI tabs:

```ios SW1
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname SW1
SW1(config)# vlan 10
SW1(config-vlan)# name MANAGEMENT-LAB
SW1(config-vlan)# exit
SW1(config)# interface range fastethernet0/1 - 4
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport access vlan 10
SW1(config-if-range)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if-range)# end
```

```ios R1
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R1
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.60.0.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
```

```ios R2
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R2
R2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R2(config-if)# ip address 10.60.0.2 255.255.255.0
R2(config-if)# no shutdown
R2(config-if)# exit
R2(config)# interface loopback99
R2(config-if)# ip address 192.0.2.99 255.255.255.255
R2(config-if)# end
R2# show ip interface brief
R2# ping 10.60.0.1
R2# ping 10.60.0.50
```

:::expected
After the links settle, R2 reaches R1 and LOG1. PC1 can ping `10.60.0.2` and `.50`. Gi0/0 and Loopback99 on R2 are up/up. Resolve persistent failures using addresses, VLAN membership and interface state before testing application protocols. Record `show clock detail` and `show ntp status` on both routers as the initial state without assuming a particular default date.
:::

steps.title: Prepare an isolated time source
steps.body:
Set a suitable current lab date/time; the literal example below uses 20 September 2026. R1 has no other NTP sources in this project.

```ios R1
R1# clock set 12:00:00 20 Sep 2026
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ntp master 8
R1(config)# end
R1# show ntp status
R1# show clock detail
```

:::expected
On a supporting image, R1 advertises its local clock at stratum 8. Its NTP status identifies the local reference; an IOS-style reference may be `127.127.1.1`. Record the actual display. This deliberately supplied lab time is not an independently verified UTC source and is not an appropriate automatic repair for a production NTP outage.
:::

steps.title: Synchronize R2 and read the association
steps.body:
```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# ntp server 10.60.0.1
R2(config)# end
R2# show ntp associations
R2# show ntp status
R2# show clock detail
```

Observe repeated samples over the displayed poll intervals. Compare R1's and R2's time and status. Synchronization may require several exchanges; do not repeatedly reconfigure the association during convergence.

:::expected
When R2 actually selects the stratum-8 source, its status reports synchronized at stratum 9. The association identifies `.1`, its stratum and recent reach history. `377` means eight recent successful poll results, not 377 replies. Worksheet fallback: for a source at stratum 8 with `*~` and reach `377`, identify remote stratum 8, local synchronized stratum 9, a configured selected association and eight retained successes; confirm local state separately with `show ntp status`.
:::

steps.title: Observe an incorrect server address
steps.body:
There is no host at `10.60.0.254` in this isolated project. Replace R2's server address and inspect the new association:

```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# no ntp server 10.60.0.1
R2(config)# ntp server 10.60.0.254
R2(config)# end
R2# show ntp associations
R2# show ntp status
```

:::expected
The configured target is now wrong. The new association cannot receive a response from the nonexistent host; its reach remains zero. R2's clock may continue displaying plausible time or retain previous synchronization status temporarily. This does not validate the new source. Worksheet: a recent good clock and a new association with reach zero are compatible observations, because clock state and new exchange success are different evidence.
:::

steps.title: Restore the intended association
steps.body:
```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# no ntp server 10.60.0.254
R2(config)# ntp server 10.60.0.1
R2(config)# end
R2# show ntp associations
R2# show ntp status
```

:::expected
R2 resumes successful exchanges with `.1` and, after source selection, reports synchronized stratum 9. Record actual recovery time and reach progression. If it does not recover, check R1's source state and the actual NTP exchanges rather than assuming that successful ICMP proves the NTP service.
:::

steps.title: Prepare local and remote logging
steps.body:
On LOG1, open Services → SYSLOG and turn the service On. Configure R2's timestamp format, buffer and collector:

```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# service timestamps log datetime msec
R2(config)# logging buffered 16384
R2(config)# logging host 10.60.0.50
R2(config)# logging trap debugging
R2(config)# end
R2# show logging
```

:::expected
The actual logging output identifies `.50` as the destination and debugging as the remote threshold. Record the local buffer's enabled state and level instead of assuming a default. The timestamp command changes format, not time accuracy. A configured host does not yet prove LOG1 received an event. If the buffer command is unavailable, use console output for the local observation; if remote logging is unsupported, use the next step's supplied records as a worksheet.
:::

steps.title: Record an administrative interface event
steps.body:
Change only the disposable loopback:

```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# interface loopback99
R2(config-if)# shutdown
R2(config-if)# end
R2# show ip interface brief
R2# show logging
```

Open LOG1's SYSLOG view and compare newly received records with R2's local output. Identify the interface, description, severity and timestamp from what was actually produced.

:::expected
Loopback99 becomes administratively down; Gi0/0 stays up and the collector path remains intact. Supporting images generate administrative and/or line-protocol messages with platform-dependent wording. A representative record is `%LINK-5-CHANGED: Interface Loopback99, changed state to administratively down`: component LINK, severity 5, mnemonic CHANGED, administrative-state description. Do not require every platform to produce an identical pair of messages. If the simulator omits the event, interpret this supplied record as the worksheet rather than treating its absence as a proven transport fault.
:::

steps.title: Restore the test interface
steps.body:
```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# interface loopback99
R2(config-if)# no shutdown
R2(config-if)# end
R2# show ip interface brief
R2# show logging
```

:::expected
Loopback99 returns up/up. Compare its new event with Step 7 in the local buffer and collector, using the actual severity encoded in each record. Do not assume that every `no shutdown` produces a level-3 message. Confirm the management interface, NTP association and collector path remain intact.
:::

steps.title: Apply severity thresholds to supplied evidence
steps.body:
This worksheet is required even if the simulator cannot configure every threshold. Consider these representative records and a remote threshold of `logging trap warnings`:

```output Event worksheet
%SYS-2-MALLOCFAIL: Memory allocation failed
%LINK-3-UPDOWN: Interface GigabitEthernet0/1, changed state to down
%SEC_LOGIN-4-LOGIN_FAILED: Login failed
%LINEPROTO-5-UPDOWN: Line protocol on Interface Loopback99, changed state to up
%SYS-6-LOGGINGHOST_STARTSTOP: Logging to host started
```

List the records eligible for the remote destination. On an image supporting `logging trap warnings`, optionally configure it and inspect `show logging`, then restore `logging trap debugging`. Do not generate memory failures or login attacks to reproduce the worksheet.

:::expected
Levels 2, 3 and 4 pass that threshold; levels 5 and 6 do not. Eligibility is not proof of successful delivery. In an existing SSH session with monitor logging enabled, `terminal monitor` would subscribe that session to eligible live messages; it would not change the collector threshold. `logging synchronous` would affect input presentation, not collection. Restore the lab's debugging threshold after any optional configuration test.
:::

steps.title: Read an SNMP object with limited access
steps.body:
The selector below permits PC1's source address only. It is attached to a read-only community used exclusively in this isolated lab.

```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# access-list 10 permit host 10.60.0.60
R2(config)# snmp-server community LABREAD ro 10
R2(config)# snmp-server location Training rack
R2(config)# end
R2# show snmp
```

On PC1, open Desktop → MIB Browser. Set the agent address to `10.60.0.2`, destination port `161`, read community `LABREAD`, and version v2c (some interfaces label this version 2). Leave write credentials unused. Use Get for scalar instance `1.3.6.1.2.1.1.5.0` (`sysName.0`), then `1.3.6.1.2.1.1.6.0` (`sysLocation.0`). If the tree interface supplies the instance automatically, select the corresponding system object. If only v1 Get is exposed, that read can demonstrate basic request/response; record the selected version and do not claim it demonstrates GetBulk or v3.

:::expected
The name query identifies R2; the location query returns `Training rack`. Compare `show snmp` before and after to see relevant request/response counter changes. Exact counters vary. If the MIB Browser or agent operation is unsupported, worksheet responses `sysName.0 = R2` and `sysLocation.0 = Training rack` demonstrate the object/instance relationship; mark this as interpretation practice. Read-only access does not authorize Set and the lab performs no write request.
:::

steps.title: Observe a community mismatch
steps.body:
Change only PC1's read community to `WRONG-LAB` and repeat the same Get. Keep the target, object, port and version unchanged. Inspect R2's counters again where supported.

:::expected
The agent rejects or does not provide the requested value under the mismatched community; a browser may display a timeout. A bad-community counter may rise. Because this controlled test changed one known parameter, the mismatch is supported here. An unexplained timeout in another network would require checking the service, version, object, policy and path as well; it would not alone prove the community is wrong.
:::

steps.title: Restore the read query and interpret a rate
steps.body:
Set PC1's read community back to `LABREAD` and repeat the same object query. Then calculate the average rate from these supplied values for the same interface counter, assuming no reset or wrap:

```output Counter worksheet
At 12:00:00: ifInOctets for interface index 4 = 1,000,000,000
At 12:00:30: ifInOctets for interface index 4 = 1,037,500,000
Known interface speed = 100,000,000 bit/s
```

:::expected
The restored query returns the expected value. The counter difference is 37,500,000 octets, or 300,000,000 bits over 30 seconds: 10 Mbit/s and 10% of the stated line rate in that direction. It is an interval average, not a measured peak. A restart or counter wrap would invalidate simple subtraction without additional handling.
:::

steps.title: Verify the final state and save
steps.body:
```ios R2
R2# show ntp status
R2# show ip interface brief
R2# show logging
R2# show snmp
R2# copy running-config startup-config
```

On R1 and SW1, save with `copy running-config startup-config` at the privileged EXEC prompt. Save the project as `management-services-lab.pkt`. If any operation was completed as a worksheet, note that separately in your study notes.

:::expected
R2 uses `.1` as its NTP server, Loopback99 is restored, LOG1 is the collector, and PC1 can make the limited read query on supported images. The wrong NTP address and mismatched manager community are absent from the final procedure. No read-write SNMP community or Telnet service was required.
:::

lab.troubleshooting:
- Reach zero plus a working ping narrows the checks to NTP-specific service, source, authentication, path and convergence; it does not identify one cause.
- A stratum-16 upstream is not a usable synchronized source. Verify the intended reference rather than masking the problem with a local master.
- Missing remote logs require checking new event generation, thresholds, destination, transport and collector processing.
- A memory-buffer counter or configured logging host does not establish remote delivery.
- SNMP queries need matching address, version, community/security, authorization and object instance. Packet counters must be read with that context.
lab.challenge:
Using the given topology, explain what changes if R1 advertises stratum 6 instead of 8, R2's remote logging threshold becomes errors (3), and PC1 remains read-only. Which worksheet log levels pass, what stratum should a successfully synchronized R2 report, and can PC1 legitimately issue Set? Then restore the baseline if you choose to configure the variation on a supporting image.

:::expected
A successfully synchronized client of R1 at stratum 6 reports stratum 7. Remote levels 0–3 are eligible; the supplied level-2 and level-3 records pass, while 4–6 do not. Read-only access does not authorize Set. For the optional configuration variation, use `ntp master 6` on R1 and `logging trap errors` on R2, then inspect the resulting state. Restore `ntp master 8` and `logging trap debugging` and wait for R2's selected synchronization to return to stratum 9. A displayed old stratum immediately after a change is not evidence that the new source was already selected.
:::

exhibit.title: R2# show ntp associations
exhibit.text:
address         ref clock       st   when   poll reach  delay  offset   disp
*~10.0.12.1       127.127.1.1      8     28     64   377  1.000   0.000   0.230
 * sys.peer, # selected, + candidate, - outlyer, x falseticker, ~ configured

questions.prompt: R2 uses the shown IOS-style association to a configured local-clock lab source. Which interpretation matches the representative output?
options: The st column gives R2’s own stratum, while ref clock is R2’s destination
The configured source is unselected because 127.127.1.1 must be remotely routed
The remote source advertises stratum 8, is selected, and has eight recent successful poll results
The reach value records 377 replies since the current router was powered on
questions.explanation: The st column describes the remote source; * marks the selected peer in the supplied legend. Octal reach 377 represents eight retained successful poll results. Confirm R2’s own synchronization and expected stratum 9 with show ntp status; the local-clock reference is not an address R2 should ping.

whyWrong.0: The association columns describe the peer and its reference, not R2’s local stratum.
whyWrong.1: The reference field is descriptive and the * marker identifies selection.
whyWrong.3: 377 is an octal bit register, not a lifetime response counter.

questions.prompt: A switch synchronises its clock to a router that reports stratum 4. What stratum does the switch report once it is synchronised?
questions.explanation: A device synchronized to a stratum-4 source reports stratum 5. These are NTP hierarchy levels, not IP router hops along the path.

whyWrong.0: A downstream client of this source adds one rather than subtracting one.
whyWrong.1: A synchronized client of this specific source does not retain the source’s stratum.
whyWrong.2: The question states successful synchronization; stratum 16 is the unsynchronized condition.

questions.prompt: An isolated router has ntp master 8, no other time source, and selects its own local reference. Which two statements follow? Choose two.
options: The router obtains time from a stratum 8 public server automatically
Clients that synchronise to the router report stratum 9
The command is required before the router will forward NTP packets between its subnets
The router advertises its own software clock as a stratum 8 reference
It enables NTP authentication using key number 8
questions.explanation: The selected local master advertises its clock at the configured stratum 8, and a successfully synchronized client reports stratum 9. This makes the isolated clock distributable; it does not independently establish its accuracy.

whyWrong.0: The command does not locate or authenticate an external server.
whyWrong.2: Transit NTP packets are IP traffic; routing them does not require a local NTP master.
whyWrong.4: The number configures stratum, not an authentication key.

exhibit.title: R2# show ntp status / show ntp associations
exhibit.text:
R2# show ntp status
Clock is unsynchronized, stratum 16, no reference clock
...
R2# show ntp associations

  address         ref clock       st   when   poll reach  delay  offset   disp
 ~10.0.12.1       .INIT.          16      -     64     0  0.000   0.000 15937.
 * sys.peer, # selected, + candidate, - outlyer, x falseticker, ~ configured

questions.prompt: R2 can ping 10.0.12.1, and other clients use that server successfully. After observing the shown NTP state, which next action is justified?
options: Check the NTP service path, source policy, authentication and convergence for R2
Conclude that successful ICMP also verifies R2’s UDP 123 request and reply path
Add ntp master to R2 because an NTP client must first become a local master
Wait for exactly 377 polls because the tilde marks an unfinished negotiation
questions.explanation: A working ICMP exchange does not verify R2’s NTP exchange. Reach zero shows no successful results retained by this association, not a unique failure cause or lifetime history. Inspect actual NTP requests/replies and service policy while allowing initial source selection.

whyWrong.1: Different protocols and source policies can have different outcomes.
whyWrong.2: A client association does not require a local-master configuration.
whyWrong.3: The tilde means configured; 377 is octal reach history, not a required poll count.

questions.prompt: A router logs `%LINEPROTO-5-UPDOWN: Line protocol on Interface GigabitEthernet0/1, changed state to down`. Which severity keyword does the 5 in the message represent?
options: warnings
notifications
informational
errors
questions.explanation: In the displayed message, severity 5 means notifications: a normal but significant condition. The number alone does not measure the business impact of this interface transition.

whyWrong.0: Warnings is severity 4.
whyWrong.2: Informational is severity 6.
whyWrong.3: Errors is severity 3.

questions.prompt: A router has logging host 10.60.0.50 and a basic logging trap warnings threshold with no additional message filters. Which severity levels are eligible for that destination?
options: Only level 4 messages
Levels 4 through 7
Levels 0 through 3
Levels 0 through 4
questions.explanation: Warnings is severity 4, and the basic threshold includes levels 0–4. Eligibility for forwarding does not prove network delivery or collector retention.

whyWrong.0: This threshold includes lower, more severe levels as well.
whyWrong.1: Levels 5–7 are less severe and excluded by the stated threshold.
whyWrong.2: The boundary value 4 is included.

exhibit.title: R1# show logging | include CONFIG_I
exhibit.text: *Mar  1 00:04:12.987: %SYS-5-CONFIG_I: Configured from console by admin on vty0 (10.0.0.55)

questions.prompt: Which statement about this logged message is correct?
options: The timestamp is marked nonauthoritative; verify the clock source before correlating it
SYS is the numeric transport facility selected by the logging facility command
Severity 5 is numerically higher and therefore more severe than severity 3
The recorded session is a physical console login because the text includes console
questions.explanation: The IOS timestamp marker indicates the clock is not considered authoritative. It does not establish that the device has never synchronized or uniquely explain the date. The explicit VTY and source-address details identify the recorded remote session.

whyWrong.1: SYS is the IOS component; the transport facility is a separate field.
whyWrong.2: Lower severity numbers are more severe.
whyWrong.3: The specific vty0 and source address identify remote access despite the traditional message wording.

exhibit.title: show logging (representative excerpt)
exhibit.text:
Console logging: level debugging
Monitor logging: level informational
Buffer logging: level warnings
Trap logging: level informational
 Logging to 10.60.0.50 (udp port 514)

questions.prompt: The representative output gives the current logging settings. No additional filters apply. Which two statements are correct? Choose two.
options: The console threshold includes severity 7 messages
The remote collector receives a TCP connection by the displayed configuration
The remote threshold makes severity 0–6 eligible for forwarding
The memory buffer threshold includes severity 5 notifications
The monitor threshold overrides the remote collector’s own configuration
questions.explanation: The displayed console level is debugging (7), while the remote threshold is informational (6). Each destination has its own settings. Read these values from the device rather than assuming universal defaults.

whyWrong.1: The displayed destination explicitly uses UDP 514.
whyWrong.3: Warnings (4) excludes the less severe level 5.
whyWrong.4: Monitor and remote collector controls are separate.

questions.prompt: New eligible events are being generated, monitor logging is enabled at debugging, and a current SSH session has not subscribed to monitor output. Which EXEC command subscribes this session?
options: logging monitor debugging
terminal monitor
logging synchronous
logging console debugging
questions.explanation: terminal monitor subscribes the current remote terminal session to eligible live messages. The global monitor threshold and event generation must also be suitable; the command does not replay every historical event.

whyWrong.0: The global monitor state is already supplied; the missing setting is in this session.
whyWrong.2: Logging synchronous changes how messages interact with typed input.
whyWrong.3: Console logging controls a different destination.

questions.prompt: Which SNMP notification expects a Response and can be retransmitted according to configured retry limits?
options: Trap
GetBulk
Set
Inform
questions.explanation: An InformRequest expects a Response. Retries are bounded by the sender’s policy; an inform is not guaranteed delivery and does not prove a human processed the event.

whyWrong.0: An SNMP Trap has no protocol acknowledgment.
whyWrong.1: GetBulk is a read request rather than an unsolicited notification.
whyWrong.2: Set requests a change to managed objects, not an event notification.

questions.prompt: Which community-based SNMP version supports GetBulk and Inform, unlike v1?
options: SNMPv1
SNMPv2c
SNMPv3 authNoPriv
SNMPv3 noAuthNoPriv
questions.explanation: SNMPv2c uses community-based access while supporting the v2 operations and data types, including GetBulk and Counter64. It does not encrypt community strings.

whyWrong.0: SNMPv1 does not implement GetBulk or the v2 InformRequest operation.
whyWrong.2: This is a v3 security level, not a community-based version.
whyWrong.3: This is also a v3 level, despite lacking cryptographic authentication and privacy.

exhibit.title: R1# show running-config | include access-list 10|snmp
exhibit.text:
access-list 10 permit host 10.60.0.50
snmp-server community MONITOR ro 10
snmp-server community CHANGE rw
snmp-server host 10.60.0.50 version 2c MONITOR

questions.prompt: This excerpt shows the communities and their attached source restrictions. Which weakness is visible without assuming that every MIB object is writable?
options: ACL 10 restricts all SNMP communities regardless of where it is attached
The notification host command makes both communities read-only
MONITOR permits Set because the manager is listed in ACL 10
CHANGE has read-write access without a source ACL attached to that community
questions.explanation: The source ACL is attached to MONITOR only. CHANGE has no displayed community-specific source restriction and grants read-write scope, subject to reachability, other controls, views and writable-object definitions. Knowing a community does not make every object writable.

whyWrong.0: The ACL attachment is per community in this configuration.
whyWrong.1: Notification destination settings do not change incoming community access rights.
whyWrong.2: MONITOR is read-only even for an allowed manager.

questions.prompt: Using the conventional SNMP-over-UDP mapping with no custom receiver port, which destination receives a linkDown trap?
questions.explanation: The notification receiver normally listens on UDP 162. Agent request service normally uses UDP 161; a response returns to the requester’s source endpoint.

whyWrong.1: 161 is normally the agent request-service destination.
whyWrong.2: 514 is the conventional UDP syslog destination.
whyWrong.3: 123 is the NTP service destination.

questions.prompt: The public server is stratum 1, R1 has `ntp server 203.0.113.10`, and SW1 has `ntp server 10.0.12.1`. Both associations show `synchronized`. What stratum does SW1 report in `show ntp status`?
questions.explanation: The stated selected hierarchy has source 1, R1 at 2 and SW1 at 3. This depends on the associations actually being synchronized and usable; the mere presence of server configuration lines would not establish those states.

whyWrong.0: The stated reference server is at stratum 1.
whyWrong.1: Stratum 2 belongs to R1 in this hierarchy.
whyWrong.3: The premise explicitly states successful synchronization.

questions.prompt: A supplied syslog record uses transport facility local7, numeric value 23, and PRI <189>. Which severity does it encode?
options: 3, errors
4, warnings
5, notifications
6, informational
questions.explanation: The supplied facility contributes 23 × 8 = 184. Subtracting it from PRI 189 gives severity 5, notifications. The IOS component mnemonic inside the message is a separate field.

whyWrong.0: Severity 3 from local7 would be encoded as <187>.
whyWrong.1: Severity 4 from local7 would be <188>.
whyWrong.3: Severity 6 from local7 would be <190>.

exhibit.title: Manager samples of one input-octet counter
exhibit.text:
12:00:00 counter = 1,000,000,000 octets
12:00:30 counter = 1,037,500,000 octets
Same interface instance; no reset or wrap during the interval

questions.prompt: What average input bit rate do these samples indicate?
options: 1.25 Mbit/s
10 Mbit/s
37.5 Mbit/s
300 Mbit/s
questions.explanation: The difference is 37,500,000 octets. Multiplying by 8 and dividing by 30 seconds gives 10,000,000 bit/s, or 10 Mbit/s. This is an average over the interval, not a peak measurement.

whyWrong.0: 1.25 million is the octets-per-second value before conversion to bits.
whyWrong.2: 37.5 million is the total octet increase, not a bit rate.
whyWrong.3: 300 million is the total bit increase before division by the time interval.

cards.front: NTP transport protocol and port?
cards.back: UDP destination 123 for NTP service. Cisco associations commonly use 123 at both ends; other clients can randomize their source port.

cards.front: NTP stratum 0 versus stratum 1?
cards.back: In a hierarchy diagram, stratum 0 denotes the reference clock and stratum 1 its directly referenced network server. A packet’s stratum-0 value is not an ordinary preferred server.

cards.front: What does NTP stratum 16 mean?
cards.back: Unsynchronized state; it is not a usable synchronized source for an ordinary client. Network synchronization strata are 1–15.

cards.front: A client syncs to a stratum N server. Its stratum?
cards.back: A successfully synchronized downstream device adds one to its selected source’s stratum, within the usable hierarchy. This is not an IP hop count.

cards.front: Default stratum set by `ntp master` with no number?
cards.back: The cited IOS default is 8. With the local reference selected, a successfully synchronized client reports 9. The command does not certify time accuracy.

cards.front: Command to make a router an NTP client of 10.0.12.1?
cards.back: `ntp server 10.0.12.1` in global configuration. Confirm actual selection with show ntp status and associations.

cards.front: Meaning of reach 377 in `show ntp associations`?
cards.back: Octal 377 is eight retained successful poll results. Zero can mean an initial association or no successful results left in that window, not never in the device’s lifetime.

cards.front: `*` and `~` in front of a line in `show ntp associations`?
cards.back: In the shown IOS legend, * identifies the selected peer and ~ a configured association. Other symbols vary; read the actual legend and confirm show ntp status.

cards.front: What does ref clock 127.127.1.1 mean?
cards.back: In the local-master example it identifies the server’s local-clock reference. It is not the network destination the client should ping.

cards.front: How do you determine an NTP association’s poll interval?
cards.back: Read the poll column for the current interval in seconds. Many IOS examples use 64–1024 seconds, but platform, configuration and convergence affect the actual interval.

cards.front: The 8 syslog severities, 0 to 7?
cards.back: 0 emergencies; 1 alerts; 2 critical; 3 errors; 4 warnings; 5 notifications; 6 informational; 7 debugging. Lower is more severe.

cards.front: `logging trap warnings` sends which levels?
cards.back: Levels 0–4 are eligible under the basic threshold. Other filters, transport and collector processing still affect reception.

cards.front: How do you verify logging defaults and active destination thresholds?
cards.back: Read show logging and the actual platform documentation. Console, monitor, memory buffer and remote collector have independent controls; there is no universal buffer setting.

cards.front: Syslog server transport and port?
cards.back: Conventional syslog uses UDP destination 514 without transport acknowledgment. Other transports require compatible endpoints and explicit configuration.

cards.front: How do you read an IOS SYS-5-CONFIG_I message and timestamp marker?
cards.back: Sequence, timestamp, IOS component SYS, severity 5, mnemonic CONFIG_I and description. A relevant IOS * timestamp marker means nonauthoritative time, not proof of never using NTP.

cards.front: Command to see syslog messages in your SSH/Telnet session?
cards.back: `terminal monitor` subscribes this remote session to eligible live messages. The global monitor threshold and event generation must also permit them.

cards.front: `%LINK-3-UPDOWN` versus `%LINK-5-CHANGED`?
cards.back: Read the full event text and encoded severity. Administrative-down text establishes that state, but a mnemonic alone does not identify a cable failure or the responsible user; platform messages vary.

cards.front: Default IOS syslog facility and how PRI is built?
cards.back: The cited Cisco logging guide uses local7 (23). PRI = facility × 8 + severity; local7 with severity 5 gives 189. IOS component SYS is a separate meaning of facility.

cards.front: SNMP ports?
cards.back: Common UDP destinations: 161 for agent requests, 162 for notification receivers. Responses return to the request source endpoint.

cards.front: SNMP Trap versus Inform?
cards.back: Trap has no SNMP acknowledgment. Inform expects a Response and can retry according to configured limits; neither guarantees a human acted on the event.

cards.front: SNMPv1 / v2c / v3 security?
cards.back: v1/v2c use unencrypted communities. v2c adds operations such as GetBulk and Counter64. Common v3 user-based security supports selectable authentication and privacy levels.

cards.front: The three SNMPv3 security levels?
cards.back: noAuthNoPriv: neither cryptographic authentication nor encryption. authNoPriv: authentication. authPriv: authentication and encryption. v3 alone does not imply privacy.

cards.front: MIB versus OID?
cards.back: A MIB defines managed objects and types; an OID identifies an object or instance. The agent supplies its value; correlate table indexes with actual interface names.

tickets.question: Which displayed setting explains why these level-5 events are ineligible for the remote destination?
options: An access list between R1 and the collector permits ICMP but drops UDP 514, so most datagrams are lost
R1's clock is not synchronised, so the collector discards messages whose timestamps it cannot order
`logging trap errors` sets the syslog-server threshold to severity 3, so the severity 5 OSPF and configuration messages are never sent
`logging host` was entered without `transport udp`, so only messages generated by hardware interfaces are forwarded
tickets.explanation: The errors threshold permits levels 0–3, excluding the displayed level-5 records before remote forwarding. Console and buffer settings are independent. The received level-3 records establish those particular deliveries, not that every datagram or future event must arrive.
tickets.fix:
Change the remote threshold to match the stated requirement.

```ios
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# logging trap informational
R1(config)# end
R1# show logging
```

Generate a harmless new configuration event in the isolated lab and verify the corresponding record on the collector. The new threshold makes levels 0–6 eligible; it does not replay the old buffer or guarantee transport/retention. Save after verification.

tickets.question: What is the root cause of R2's failure to synchronise?
options: R2 must become a local master before accepting time from R1
R1 is currently unsynchronized and cannot provide a usable synchronized source to R2
R2 must use a symmetric peer association solely because R1 is a router
The failed ICMP test proves every NTP datagram is blocked by a WAN ACL

sections.title: Why a busy link needs a policy
Marking: CoS, IP precedence and DSCP
Congestion avoidance: act before the queue fills
Policing and shaping: enforce a rate
Verify the behavior, not just the configuration

lab.title: Trace a QoS policy and verify a marking
lab.topology:
The core worksheet in Steps 1–4 requires only the lesson and a notebook. Steps 5–12 are **optional implementation practice** on an isolated Packet Tracer project or a supporting IOS/IOS XE lab image. They do not measure real voice quality. The commands and outputs have been reviewed against Cisco documentation, but this lab has not been executed in Packet Tracer. Unsupported commands or absent counters are a simulator limitation; complete the worksheet and record the limitation rather than inventing results.

For the optional experiment, create one ISR 2911 named R1, two 2960 switches named SW-A and SW-B, and two PC-PT endpoints. Use copper straight-through cables for every listed link. Default switch VLAN 1 is sufficient; neither switch needs an IP address or QoS commands.

| Connection | Address |
|---|---|
| PC-A Fa0 — SW-A Fa0/1 | PC-A 10.28.1.10/24, gateway 10.28.1.1 |
| SW-A Fa0/2 — R1 Gi0/0 | R1 10.28.1.1/24 |
| R1 Gi0/1 — SW-B Fa0/2 | R1 10.28.2.1/24 |
| SW-B Fa0/1 — PC-B Fa0 | PC-B 10.28.2.10/24, gateway 10.28.2.1 |

No DNS, Internet connection, server, static route or traffic generator is needed. In CML, use an authorized IOS image, an unmanaged switch node on each side and Linux endpoints with these addresses; translate interface names from `show ip interface brief`.

steps.title: — Calculate the offered voice rate
steps.body:
Use the lesson's assumptions: 160 payload bytes, 40 header bytes, one packet every 20 ms, in one direction. Calculate packets per second, bytes per second and bits per second. Then calculate the Layer 3 rate for two calls.

:::expected
One call sends 50 packets/s, 10,000 bytes/s and 80,000 bits/s. Two calls require 160 kb/s before Layer 2 overhead. A 128 kb/s priority allowance is smaller than their sustained Layer 3 rate. This calculation predicts pressure on a congestion-time priority policer; it does not predict an exact drop count because burst allowances and actual packet sizes matter.
:::

steps.title: — Follow the classifier and marking
steps.body:
For this worksheet, a boundary policy classifies managed phone traffic as VOICE and writes EF. Other client traffic receives DSCP 0. A later router selects its priority class using DSCP EF. Trace these two packets: a managed phone initially marked 0, and an ordinary PC initially marked EF.

:::expected
After the boundary, the phone packet is EF and the PC packet is 0. At the later router, only the phone packet matches the EF class. Classification chose a category; marking changed the header; the later classification used that resulting header. Neither marking alone nor the category name creates a queue reservation.
:::

steps.title: — Distinguish the two rate actions
steps.body:
On paper, compare these policies for a 20 Mb/s service: A transmits conforming packets and drops excess packets; B queues packets until allowed to transmit. A burst arrives after each rate meter's token allowance has been used. State what happens immediately and what happens if the offered rate stays above 20 Mb/s indefinitely.

:::expected
A is policing and drops the excess described by its action. B is shaping and initially buffers traffic. Persistent overload eventually fills a finite shaping queue unless the sender slows; shaping can also drop. Neither policy lowers the Ethernet physical link speed.
:::

steps.title: — Read evidence before changing a policy
steps.body:
Study this representative worksheet excerpt. It is an authored example, not captured output.

```output R1# show policy-map interface GigabitEthernet0/1
Service-policy output: WAN-OUT
  Class-map: VOICE
    Match: dscp ef (46)
    Priority: 128 (kbps), burst bytes 3200
    b/w exceed drops: 400
  Class-map: DATA
    bandwidth 512 (kbps)
```

A second sample after a busy minute shows `b/w exceed drops: 900`. Explain the difference and whether DATA is capped at 512 kb/s.

:::expected
There were 500 additional priority bandwidth-exceed drops during the interval. In this classic IOS LLQ example, the configured priority allowance is limiting traffic under congestion. DATA's bandwidth command is a minimum share during congestion, not a 512 kb/s ceiling. Investigate actual classification and demand before increasing the priority rate. The displayed 3,200-byte burst allowance belongs to this example, not every platform.
:::

steps.title: — Build and verify the optional IP baseline
steps.body:
Configure both PC addresses in Desktop → IP Configuration → Static using the topology table. Leave DNS blank. On a new R1, decline the initial setup dialog if presented, then enter:

```ios R1
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R1
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# description SW-A_PC-A
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.28.1.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# description SW-B_PC-B
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.28.2.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip interface brief
```

Wait for the switch ports to forward. From PC-A's command prompt, run:

```text
ping 10.28.1.1
ping 10.28.2.10
```

:::expected
Both router interfaces should be up/up. After initial ARP resolution, PC-A should receive replies from its gateway and PC-B. If not, repair addressing or cabling before adding QoS. Save the project as `qos-baseline.pkt`, then use Save As `qos-marking.pkt` for the experiment.
:::

steps.title: — Create a simple marking policy
steps.body:
This isolated demonstration changes default-marked IP packets to AF21; it is not a production classification design. Check `class-map ?` and `match dscp ?` if the image rejects a command. Do not enable global `mls qos` on the switches.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# class-map match-all DEFAULT-IP
R1(config-cmap)# match dscp default
R1(config-cmap)# exit
R1(config)# policy-map MARK-IN
R1(config-pmap)# class DEFAULT-IP
R1(config-pmap-c)# set dscp af21
R1(config-pmap-c)# end
R1# show class-map
R1# show policy-map
```

:::expected
DEFAULT-IP matches DSCP 0. MARK-IN contains the AF21 marking action. The policy is defined but not attached, so this configuration alone does not change traffic. If MQC or packet marking is unsupported, use the worksheet interpretation for the remaining steps and record which function was unavailable.
:::

steps.title: — Attach the policy where requests enter
steps.body:
PC-A's requests enter R1 on Gi0/0. Attach MARK-IN there in the input direction.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# service-policy input MARK-IN
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show policy-map interface gigabitethernet0/0
```

:::expected
The output identifies MARK-IN as an input policy on Gi0/0. Record current DEFAULT-IP counters before generating test traffic. A definition in `show policy-map` without an interface attachment is not enough.
:::

steps.title: — Generate and inspect a known packet
steps.body:
From PC-A, ping `10.28.2.10` again. Read R1's interface policy counters after the test. In Packet Tracer Simulation mode, filter for ICMP, create a simple PDU from PC-A to PC-B, and step through R1. Open the packet details and compare the incoming and outgoing IPv4 service fields if your version exposes them. On CML, capture the two lab links and inspect the same echo request in Wireshark; start capture before sending it and stop afterward.

:::expected
On an implementation that models the policy, default-marked requests should match the input class and leave toward PC-B with DSCP AF21, decimal 18. If ECN is 0, the entire eight-bit service field is `18 × 4 = 72`, hexadecimal `0x48`. Do not confuse that byte with DSCP 72. Counter increments support matching; packet fields support marking. Absent packet fields or counters mean that observation is unavailable, not that you measured success. Echo replies enter the opposite interface and are not covered by this input policy.
:::

steps.title: — Introduce a direction fault
steps.body:
Remove the correct attachment and attach the same policy to Gi0/1 in the input direction.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# no service-policy input MARK-IN
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# service-policy input MARK-IN
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show policy-map interface
```

Repeat the same PC-A-to-PC-B echo test and inspect the request, not just a total policy counter.

:::expected
The request enters Gi0/0, so it no longer encounters MARK-IN and should retain its original DSCP. Replies may now match on Gi0/1. Nonzero counters on the wrong interface therefore do not prove the intended direction works. Connectivity itself should remain available because this policy marks rather than drops.
:::

steps.title: — Restore the intended direction
steps.body:
Only after recording Step 9's observation, restore the attachments:

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# no service-policy input MARK-IN
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# service-policy input MARK-IN
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show policy-map interface
```

Repeat the request inspection.

:::expected
MARK-IN is input on Gi0/0 only. Requests again receive AF21 where the platform supports the function. The repair addresses attachment and direction, not the rate or DSCP value.
:::

steps.title: — Predict a congestion-avoidance result
steps.body:
Given two traffic aggregates in the **same AF class**, one marked AF11 and one AF13, the downstream router is explicitly configured to give AF13 a higher WRED drop probability at the current average queue depth. Predict the relative treatment over many packets. Then state whether that determines which particular packet is dropped next.

:::expected
AF13 has greater discard probability under the stated policy. It does not mean every AF13 packet must disappear before any AF11 packet is dropped, and it says nothing about the scheduler's next packet without a scheduling policy. Probability and transmission priority answer different questions.
:::

steps.title: — Save the evidence and finish cleanly
steps.body:
Record whether you used the worksheet, Packet Tracer or a specific IOS image, plus the actual supported observations. Save the project as `qos-complete.pkt`. In an actual isolated router lab, save the intended configuration separately:

```ios R1
R1# copy running-config startup-config
```

Accept the displayed destination filename with Enter before issuing another command.

:::expected
Your notes distinguish predicted behavior, representative examples and observations you actually made. The final experiment has only the Gi0/0 input attachment; the original baseline project remains available.
:::

lab.troubleshooting:
- No ping baseline: check each PC's mask and gateway, both router interface states and switch forwarding. QoS cannot repair an incorrect IP path.
- No matches: inspect the actual ingress interface, direction and incoming DSCP. ICMP requests and replies are different packets.
- Matches but no visible marking: confirm the action and inspect the egress header; document simulator limitations if it does not expose or implement the field.
- Low average interface utilization with drops: identify whether the counter belongs to a policer or a queue, and consider bursts or a slower downstream service.
- A command rejected by a simulator: use context help and the referenced platform guide. Do not substitute an unrelated hardware command merely to produce accepted syntax.
lab.challenge:
Without using the earlier answers, explain this case: a 100 Mb/s physical interface connects to a 10 Mb/s provider service. The provider reports policer drops during 15 Mb/s bursts. The local interface averages only 6 Mb/s. A voice packet is marked EF locally but DSCP 0 after a boundary switch. Identify two separate investigations and propose a treatment for each. Explain why increasing a queue size alone cannot solve both.

:::expected
First inspect the boundary's trust, classification and remarking rules using matched packets on both sides. Correct the intended trusted marking policy only for authorized traffic; increasing priority bandwidth cannot restore a mark that was removed.

Second investigate burst duration, provider accounting and contracted rate. An appropriately designed outbound shaper can smooth traffic to the provider's allowance, with local queue service protecting delay-sensitive traffic. Its rate/burst policy must be compatible with the provider, and sustained overload still needs demand reduction or more capacity. Larger queues merely store more traffic, can increase delay, and do not change either DSCP or the service rate.
:::

exhibit.title: Representative classic IOS excerpt
exhibit.text:
Class-map: VOICE
  Match: dscp ef (46)
  Priority: 128 (kbps), burst bytes 3200
  b/w exceed drops: 400

questions.prompt: During congestion, this classic IOS LLQ counter increases by 400. What does it identify?
options: The physical interface has dropped to a speed of 128 kb/s
The voice classifier failed to match the arriving packets
The priority class exceeded its permitted rate/burst allowance
The DATA class was capped at its minimum bandwidth
questions.explanation: The bandwidth-exceed counter belongs to the priority class's congestion-time policer. It identifies that action, not a link-speed change.

whyWrong.0: Priority policy changes service, not the Ethernet physical speed.
whyWrong.1: A class-specific policer drop occurs after traffic has been assigned to the class.
whyWrong.3: A bandwidth minimum for another class does not explain this counter.

questions.prompt: Which interpretation of AF32 is correct?
options: DSCP 32; AF class 3 with drop precedence 2
DSCP 28; AF class 3 with drop precedence 2
DSCP 26; AF class 2 with drop precedence 3
DSCP 46; the recommended Expedited Forwarding code
questions.explanation: AFxy uses 8x + 2y: 8×3 + 2×2 = 28. The digits identify the AF class and drop precedence, not a decimal DSCP written without conversion.

whyWrong.0: The letters and two digits are a symbolic name, not decimal 32.
whyWrong.2: AF32 uses x=3, y=2. DSCP 26 is AF31.
whyWrong.3: EF is 46; AF32 is a different codepoint.

questions.prompt: Where is the three-bit Ethernet CoS/PCP marking carried?
options: In the priority field of an IEEE 802.1Q tag
In the final three bits of an IPv4 source address
In the complete eight-bit IPv6 Traffic Class field
In the destination port of a UDP transport header
questions.explanation: The 802.1Q priority code point has three bits. Untagged Ethernet has no PCP field, but an enclosed IP packet can still carry DSCP.

whyWrong.1: Source addresses identify endpoints; their final bits are not a QoS field.
whyWrong.2: IPv6 Traffic Class contains DSCP and ECN, not an Ethernet PCP tag.
whyWrong.3: A UDP port may be a classification criterion, but it is not a CoS marking.

questions.prompt: Which two statements accurately compare policing and shaping? Choose two.
options: A shaper guarantees delivery by allowing an unlimited queue
A policer can remark excess traffic instead of discarding it
A policer lowers the interface's negotiated physical speed
A shaper can buffer excess traffic and add waiting time
A shaper cannot transmit a short burst above its average rate
questions.explanation: Policing applies the configured action after metering; shaping controls departure timing with a buffer. Both can allow bursts, and a finite shaping queue can overflow.

whyWrong.0: Real buffers are finite; sustained excess demand can cause loss.
whyWrong.2: A policy rate is independent of the negotiated physical rate.
whyWrong.4: Burst allowances and measurement intervals matter; the configured average is not a limit on every instantaneous interval.

exhibit.title: Representative policer excerpt
exhibit.text:
police cir 1000000
  conform-action transmit
  exceed-action set-dscp-transmit af13
exceeded 1750 packets; actions: set-dscp-transmit

questions.prompt: What happens to the 1,750 packets counted as exceeding this policer?
options: They wait until the policer's dedicated shaping queue drains
They are discarded because all exceed actions mean drop
They receive EF so they can bypass downstream congestion
They are transmitted with AF13 instead of their earlier mark
questions.explanation: The explicit exceed action remarks and transmits. Downstream discard behavior depends on the downstream policy; AF13 does not force immediate loss.

whyWrong.0: This action does not create a shaping queue.
whyWrong.1: The configured action is set-dscp-transmit, not drop.
whyWrong.2: The action names AF13, which is DSCP 14, not EF.

questions.prompt: A capture confirms that many TCP flows reduce sending together after a full FIFO queue drops a burst. Which mechanism is intended to spread earlier congestion signals across flows?
options: Strict priority for every class on the output interface
Changing all packets to the same AF drop precedence
Random early detection before the queue is completely full
Increasing each endpoint's advertised Ethernet link speed
questions.explanation: RED/WRED can act probabilistically before a queue fills, reducing the chance that many responsive flows react to one large loss event. It does not guarantee steady utilization.

whyWrong.0: Giving everything strict priority does not distinguish traffic or provide early congestion signals.
whyWrong.1: A shared marking alone does not create early queue management.
whyWrong.3: Endpoint link speed does not remove this bottleneck's finite capacity.

questions.prompt: Ordinary users can set DSCP on their PCs. The policy reserves preferred treatment for verified managed-phone traffic. Where should the network first validate those markings?
options: Only at the destination, after traffic has crossed every queue
At the ingress boundary where the endpoint traffic enters the policy domain
On every endpoint, while trusting all received marks without checking them
Only at an Internet router outside the organization's control
questions.explanation: Validation belongs at a boundary with reliable traffic information before untrusted markings influence preferred service. A managed phone can be part of that design, but its presence alone is not authentication.

whyWrong.0: Validation after all congested hops cannot protect resources already consumed.
whyWrong.2: Users control the premise's endpoint marks; blindly accepting them defeats the policy.
whyWrong.3: An external provider cannot substitute for the organization's own ingress policy.

questions.prompt: EF has decimal DSCP 46. Which six-bit binary value represents it?
questions.explanation: 32 + 8 + 4 + 2 = 46, so EF is 101110. These are the DSCP bits; the two ECN bits are separate.

whyWrong.1: 101000 is decimal 40, CS5.
whyWrong.2: 100110 is decimal 38, AF43.
whyWrong.3: 110010 is decimal 50.

questions.prompt: A voice design worksheet uses limits of 150 ms one-way delay, 30 ms jitter and 1% loss. Which two measurements exceed that worksheet's limits? Choose two.
options: One-way delay of 175 ms
Jitter of 22 ms
Packet loss of 0.4%
Packet loss of 1.8%
One-way delay of 110 ms
questions.explanation: 175 exceeds 150, and 1.8% exceeds 1%. These are the stated design limits, not a claim that every voice implementation fails at the same threshold.

whyWrong.1: 22 ms is below the worksheet's 30 ms limit.
whyWrong.2: 0.4% is below 1%.
whyWrong.4: 110 ms is below 150 ms.

questions.prompt: A classifier requires both: source belongs to the managed-phone subnet AND DSCP is EF. A PC outside that subnet sends an EF-marked packet. How is it evaluated?
options: It matches because DSCP has a higher numeric value than the subnet
It matches because any one criterion is enough for an AND rule
It fails because one required criterion is false
It fails because EF packets cannot originate at a PC
questions.explanation: An AND rule requires both criteria. The source criterion fails even though the DSCP criterion succeeds. A PC is capable of marking EF.

whyWrong.0: Address membership and DSCP are separate tests, not comparable numeric priorities.
whyWrong.1: That describes OR/match-any, not AND/match-all.
whyWrong.3: The packet is possible; the configured rule excludes it.

questions.prompt: An application uses changing ports. The router has a supported application signature and sufficient visibility into this traffic. Which classifier may identify it beyond a simple port test?
options: A fixed output queue size
An Ethernet speed negotiation policy
NBAR application recognition
A shaping rate without match criteria
questions.explanation: NBAR can use supported application recognition. Encrypted content, image support and signatures constrain its capabilities; it is not guaranteed to identify every application.

whyWrong.0: Queue size controls storage, not application recognition.
whyWrong.1: Link negotiation does not inspect an application's identity.
whyWrong.3: A rate action does not identify traffic by itself.

questions.prompt: On classic IOS LLQ, why is a rate allowance associated with a priority class during congestion?
options: To reserve unused priority capacity so other classes cannot use it
To limit priority consumption so other classes can receive service
To reduce every other class to the priority class's configured rate
To convert the class's DSCP into an Ethernet duplex setting
questions.explanation: The congestion-time policer constrains the priority class's use of a busy link. Unused capacity remains available; the policy does not change link duplex.

whyWrong.0: Unused allowance is not held idle for a silent application.
whyWrong.2: Each class has its own scheduling treatment; other classes are not all set to that rate.
whyWrong.3: DSCP and duplex describe unrelated functions.

exhibit.title: Policy fragment
exhibit.text:
policy-map WAN-OUT
 class DATA
  bandwidth 512

questions.prompt: In a supporting IOS CBWFQ policy, what does `bandwidth 512` mean for DATA?
options: A minimum 512 kb/s share during congestion, with excess capacity usable
A permanent 512 kb/s ceiling, with all additional packets discarded
A 512-byte queue limit, with later arriving packets tail-dropped
A 512 kb/s physical link speed, negotiated with the neighboring device
questions.explanation: The bandwidth command provides a minimum class share during congestion. It is not a policer or a physical interface speed command.

whyWrong.1: A ceiling requires a rate-limiting action such as policing or shaping.
whyWrong.2: The argument here is kilobits per second, not queue bytes.
whyWrong.3: Physical speed is separate from class scheduling.

questions.prompt: A legacy Catalyst 2960 initially had QoS disabled. An engineer enables `mls qos`, leaves all other QoS defaults unchanged, and voice packets now leave with DSCP 0. Which documented behavior explains this?
options: Enabling QoS rewrites the IP destination address to the gateway
The priority queue changes EF into DSCP 0 when it becomes empty
The switch removes the whole IP header when forwarding a frame
Default untrusted classification assigns best-effort treatment
questions.explanation: This specific legacy platform defaults to untrusted classification when standard QoS is enabled, with default marking behavior that can set DSCP to 0. Check trust and mappings for the authorized ingress port.

whyWrong.0: QoS classification does not replace IP destinations.
whyWrong.1: An empty priority queue does not explain this ingress trust behavior.
whyWrong.2: Normal Layer 2 forwarding does not discard the IP header.

questions.prompt: A 1,500-byte packet is serialized onto a 1 Mb/s link. Ignoring all additional framing overhead, how long does serialization take?
options: 1.5 ms
8 ms
150 ms
12 ms
questions.explanation: 1,500 bytes × 8 = 12,000 bits; divided by 1,000,000 bits/s gives 0.012 s, or 12 ms.

whyWrong.0: This treats bytes as though they were bits.
whyWrong.1: Eight is the bits-per-byte conversion, not the resulting time.
whyWrong.2: 150 ms is a voice design guideline, not this size/rate calculation.

exhibit.title: Observed attachment
exhibit.text:
GigabitEthernet0/1
 Service-policy input: MARK-IN
  Class-map: DEFAULT-IP
   Match: dscp default (0)

questions.prompt: PC-A requests enter Gi0/0 and leave Gi0/1. MARK-IN is applied input on Gi0/1. Its counters increase while a ping succeeds. What should be checked before declaring requests correctly marked?
options: Whether the request packet encounters the policy in its actual direction
Whether a larger shaping rate changes the classifier's interface
Whether successful ICMP automatically reserves priority bandwidth
Whether the policy name includes the destination PC's hostname
questions.explanation: Replies can enter Gi0/1 and increment counters even though requests enter Gi0/0. Inspect request headers and the relevant attachment; connectivity alone does not prove marking.

whyWrong.1: A rate change does not move the policy attachment.
whyWrong.2: ICMP success does not establish a QoS reservation.
whyWrong.3: Policy names do not determine classification or direction.

cards.front: Voice planning limits used in the lesson?
cards.back: About 150 ms one-way delay, 30 ms jitter and 1% loss in the cited Cisco branch guidance. Treat them as design guidelines, not universal application failure thresholds.

cards.front: How does interactive video differ from a buffered download?
cards.back: Interactive media needs timely delivery; buffering and retransmission may make file transfer more tolerant of delay. Neither application has unlimited tolerance for loss or poor throughput.

cards.front: G.711: 160 payload bytes every 20 ms plus 40 header bytes — Layer 3 rate?
cards.back: 50 packets/s × 200 bytes × 8 = 80,000 bits/s per direction. This excludes Layer 2 and additional tunnel overhead.

cards.front: Where is the three-bit CoS/PCP field?
cards.back: In an IEEE 802.1Q tag, with values 0–7. An untagged Ethernet frame has no PCP field, but its IP packet may carry DSCP.

cards.front: How are the IP service field's eight bits divided?
cards.back: Six bits carry DSCP (0–63); two carry ECN. This applies to the IPv4 DS field and IPv6 Traffic Class interpretation.

cards.front: How many bits does legacy IP precedence use?
cards.back: Three high-order service bits, values 0–7. DSCP uses six bits and provides more codepoints.

cards.front: EF: decimal and six-bit binary DSCP?
cards.back: 46 = 101110. EF commonly marks voice media; CoS 5 is a separate field and needs a mapping policy.

cards.front: Calculate AFxy and interpret its two digits.
cards.back: DSCP = 8x + 2y. x is AF class 1–4; y is drop precedence 1–3. Higher y means greater discard eligibility within that AF class.

cards.front: Must AF41 receive more bandwidth than AF21?
cards.back: No. AF class labels are not a universal bandwidth ranking. Resources and mappings depend on the configured policy.

cards.front: Calculate CS3 and CS6.
cards.back: CSn = 8n: CS3 is DSCP 24 and CS6 is 48. An application's use of either codepoint depends on the stated design.

cards.front: Given CoS→DSCP map 0 8 16 24 32 40 48 56, where does CoS 5 map?
cards.back: DSCP 40, the sixth entry because indexing starts at CoS 0. It does not map to EF 46 in this table.

cards.front: What is a QoS trust boundary?
cards.back: Where the network decides whether incoming markings may be used as policy input. Validate untrusted endpoint markings before granting preferred service.

cards.front: Why can enabling legacy Catalyst 2960 QoS erase received DSCP?
cards.back: With other QoS settings at defaults, untrusted classification assigns best effort and can remark DSCP to 0. Check the exact platform, port trust and mapping policy.

cards.front: What does NBAR add to classification?
cards.back: Supported application recognition beyond simple port matching. Image, signature and traffic visibility limits matter; encrypted traffic is not universally identifiable.

cards.front: MQC match-all versus match-any?
cards.back: match-all requires every configured criterion (AND); match-any requires at least one (OR). Classification is separate from a policy action.

cards.front: What can unconstrained strict priority do to other queues?
cards.back: Sustained priority traffic can starve lower-priority traffic. Suitable rate control and capacity planning protect other service classes.

cards.front: CBWFQ bandwidth versus classic IOS LLQ priority?
cards.back: bandwidth supplies a minimum share during congestion. priority also gives priority scheduling, with a congestion-time rate/burst limit in the classic IOS example.

cards.front: Tail drop versus WRED?
cards.back: Tail drop acts when a queue is full. WRED can act probabilistically earlier and differentiate drop behavior by marking; it is queue management, not scheduling.

cards.front: Policing versus shaping?
cards.back: A policer meters then applies transmit/drop/remark actions without queuing excess traffic to wait. A shaper delays traffic in a finite buffer; overflow can still drop.

cards.front: Does shaping change physical Ethernet speed?
cards.back: No. Frames still transmit at the physical rate; the shaper regulates departure timing. Its rate and burst accounting determine the resulting traffic profile.

commands.note: Legacy platform syntax; use only where the design permits trusting this traffic. Trusting CoS instead has different mapping behavior.

commands.note: Marking changes a header field; a downstream scheduling policy must provide treatment.

commands.task: Optional classic IOS LLQ practice: give this class priority service with a 128 kb/s allowance.

commands.task: Optional CBWFQ practice: give this class a 256 kb/s minimum share during congestion.
commands.note: This is a minimum, not a 256 kb/s ceiling.

accept: police cir 128000 conform-action transmit exceed-action drop

commands.note: Shaping buffers traffic; it does not change the physical interface speed.

tickets.title: Voice marking changes at a boundary switch
tickets.scenario: On a legacy Catalyst 2960 running the cited IOS QoS model, standard QoS was enabled with other settings left at defaults. A managed phone connects directly to Fa0/1; no PC is connected through it. The approved design says to preserve this phone's received IP DSCP. R1's downstream priority class matches EF. The following observations concern the same voice stream during a busy period; they are representative exhibits.

exhibits.title: Packet observations on either side of SW1
exhibits.text:
Phone → SW1 Fa0/1: IPv4 DSCP 46
SW1 uplink → R1: same stream, IPv4 DSCP 0

exhibits.title: SW1 configuration excerpt
exhibits.text:
mls qos
interface FastEthernet0/1
 switchport mode access
! No explicit QoS trust or marking policy on this port.

exhibits.title: R1 class definition
exhibits.text:
class-map match-all VOICE
 match dscp ef

tickets.question: Which change addresses the demonstrated marking fault?
options: Increase R1's priority rate while leaving the zero marking unchanged
Trust the approved phone's received IP DSCP on the specific ingress port
Enable trust on every endpoint port regardless of device ownership
Replace the phone's IP gateway with the switch's management address
tickets.explanation: The same stream changes from EF to 0 at SW1, consistent with default untrusted classification on this legacy platform. A DSCP-preserving policy on the authorized ingress port addresses that evidence. Raising a rate cannot make DSCP 0 match EF, indiscriminate trust expands access to preferred treatment, and a management address is not a substitute gateway.
tickets.fix:
On this isolated, approved legacy port only:

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# mls qos trust dscp
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show mls qos interface fastethernet0/1
```
Repeat matched packet observations across the switch and inspect the downstream EF counter during the test. Then assess voice delay/loss under real load; preserving the mark alone does not prove end-to-end quality. Different switch families use different trust mechanisms.

tickets.title: Average utilization is low but a WAN policer drops bursts
tickets.scenario: A branch has a 1 Gb/s physical handoff and a 20 Mb/s provider service. An engineer placed a local outbound policer on all traffic. Average demand is 14 Mb/s, but measured short bursts exceed the configured token allowance. The local policer's drop counter grows during those bursts. The requirement is to smooth bursts before the provider while allowing short waits for file traffic.

exhibits.title: Local policy excerpt
exhibits.text:
policy-map WAN-OUT
 class class-default
  police 20000000 conform-action transmit exceed-action drop

exhibits.title: Two observations of the same local counter
exhibits.text:
10:00:00 — exceeded packets dropped: 200
10:01:00 — exceeded packets dropped: 920
Physical interface speed: 1000 Mb/s

tickets.question: Which treatment best addresses the stated burst-smoothing requirement?
options: Increase physical speed to make the provider service become 1 Gb/s
Change file traffic to EF so the configured policer stops metering it
Use a suitable outbound shaper and verify its rate/burst agreement with the provider
Increase the displayed interface bandwidth without changing the rate policy
tickets.explanation: A shaper can queue short excess bursts and regulate their departure. The 720-counter increase demonstrates local policer drops, not merely a guessed provider failure. Physical speed and interface bandwidth metadata do not alter the 20 Mb/s service; EF does not bypass a class-default policer.
tickets.fix: Plan an outbound shaper compatible with the provider's rate, burst and overhead accounting, with suitable class scheduling for voice and data. On a supporting IOS lab image the shaping action is `shape average 20000000`, normally under a policy's class. Do not attach an incomplete hierarchy copied from another platform. Verify the full policy, counters, queue depth and downstream loss in a controlled test. Sustained demand above 20 Mb/s still requires application backoff, less demand or more service capacity; an unlimited buffer is not a solution.

sections.title: Find the file and its storage
Read a copy operation from left to right
Stage and verify software before activation

lab.title: Back up configurations and stage files safely
lab.topology:
Steps 1–8 use **Packet Tracer**, one ISR 2911 R1, one 2960 SW1 and Server-PT SRV1. Connect R1 Gi0/0 to SW1 Fa0/1 and SRV1 Fa0 to SW1 Fa0/2 with copper straight-through cables. Use default VLAN 1. R1 is `10.29.0.1/24`; SRV1 is `10.29.0.100/24`, gateway `10.29.0.1`. No Internet or default route is required.

Steps 9–15 use a **separate isolated secure-transfer lab**, not Packet Tracer: a Catalyst 9300 with a supporting IOS XE 17.x image, or an authorized virtual IOS XE image that supports the demonstrated features, plus an Ubuntu 24.04 lab VM. The explicit switch example uses S1 Gi1/0/1 as a routed port, `10.29.0.1/24`. Linux uses `10.29.0.100/24` on its dedicated lab NIC. Connect that NIC directly to the isolated switch port using copper Ethernet; in a virtual lab, connect both nodes to one isolated virtual segment. Do not connect this segment to a workplace or home LAN. Interface names and storage prefixes must be adapted from the actual inventory.

The exercise uses newly created lab accounts and uniquely named files. It does not erase startup configuration, reload a device, delete software or activate an image. Console access must remain available throughout SSH setup. These procedures have not been executed in Packet Tracer or IOS XE during authoring. If a feature is absent, record the exact limitation and complete the interpretation exercise; do not claim a successful secure transfer without a supporting environment.

steps.title: — Establish the Packet Tracer baseline
steps.body:
On SRV1 Desktop → IP Configuration, set the static address, mask `255.255.255.0` and gateway from the table. Leave DNS blank. On R1, decline the initial setup dialog if presented:

```ios R1
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R1
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# description ISOLATED_FILE_LAB
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.29.0.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip interface brief
R1# ping 10.29.0.100
```

Wait for SW1's ports to forward. Save the project as `files-baseline.pkt` and continue in `files-working.pkt`.

:::expected
Gi0/0 is up/up and ping replies arrive after address resolution. No router default route is needed for a server on the same subnet. Repair connectivity before starting file operations.
:::

steps.title: — Save and inspect the correct stores
steps.body:
Run the save command alone:

```ios R1
R1# copy running-config startup-config
```

Accept the destination filename with Enter. After the copy completes, inspect:

```ios R1
R1# show startup-config
R1# show file systems
R1# dir flash:
R1# show version
```

:::expected
The startup configuration includes hostname R1 and the lab interface address. Record actual local prefixes, available bytes and the running image filename. Do not expect an exact capacity or image version from a screenshot. If `flash:` is not listed, use the actual persistent-storage prefix in subsequent local-file commands.
:::

steps.title: — Send a named TFTP backup
steps.body:
In SRV1 → Services → TFTP, enable the service. On R1:

```ios R1
R1# copy running-config tftp:
```

At the prompts, provide server `10.29.0.100` and destination `R1-before.cfg`. Wait until the copy completes; do not paste the prompt answers as IOS commands.

:::expected
The router reports completion and SRV1's TFTP file list contains `R1-before.cfg`. Record the actual file size if shown. This operation did not also save startup-config. TFTP offers no encrypted transport; use only this isolated, nonsensitive lab.
:::

steps.title: — Retrieve to a staged file
steps.body:
Download the same backup into a new local filename, not into running-config:

```ios R1
R1# copy tftp: flash:R1-received.cfg
```

Enter `10.29.0.100` for the remote host and `R1-before.cfg` for the source. Accept the specified destination. Once complete:

```ios R1
R1# dir flash:
R1# more flash:R1-received.cfg
```

:::expected
The staged file contains the R1 baseline. Its presence does not mean a configuration has been applied. If the simulator omits `more`, inspect the file through the server/GUI where supported and mark local content inspection unavailable.
