Do not substitute `copy ... running-config` merely to read a file.
:::

steps.title: — Observe a merge without reloading
steps.body:
Make two harmless isolated changes. Loopback29 has no address and is not used by the topology.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# hostname R1-TEMP
R1-TEMP(config)# interface loopback29
R1-TEMP(config-if)# description TEMPORARY_MERGE_TEST
R1-TEMP(config-if)# end
R1-TEMP# copy flash:R1-received.cfg running-config
```

Accept the destination prompt, wait for completion, then inspect:

```ios R1
R1# show running-config
R1# show ip interface brief
```

:::expected
The hostname returns to R1 because the file contains `hostname R1`. Loopback29 remains because the earlier backup did not contain a command to remove it. Transfer completion and hostname restoration do not prove exact replacement.
:::

steps.title: — Recover the baseline explicitly
steps.body:
After recording the merge result, remove the temporary interface:

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# no interface loopback29
R1(config)# end
R1# show ip interface brief
R1# ping 10.29.0.100
```

Then save separately:

```ios R1
R1# copy running-config startup-config
```

Accept Enter when asked for the destination.

:::expected
Loopback29 is absent, the server remains reachable, and startup-config again represents the intended lab state. A carefully reviewed explicit removal repaired this one known change; no reload or complete replacement was necessary.
:::

steps.title: — Compare FTP and introduce an authentication fault
steps.body:
In SRV1 → Services → FTP, enable FTP and create account `filelab` with fictional lab password `FileLab2026!`. Grant that account Read, Write and List permissions in the simulator; additional Delete/Rename permissions are unnecessary. Save/add the account before testing.

Configure an intentionally wrong router FTP client password:

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip ftp username filelab
R1(config)# ip ftp password WrongLabPassword
R1(config)# end
R1# copy running-config ftp:
```

Supply server `10.29.0.100` and destination `R1-ftp.cfg` when prompted.

:::expected
The server should reject authentication; exact error text depends on the simulator. No successful backup should appear under that name. The IP baseline can still work. These `ip ftp` commands configure the router's client credentials, not an FTP server on R1.
:::

steps.title: — Repair FTP and verify the destination
steps.body:
Set the matching fictional password:

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip ftp password FileLab2026!
R1(config)# end
R1# copy running-config ftp:
```

Use the same server and filename. After completion, inspect SRV1's FTP file list and retrieve `R1-ftp.cfg` with `copy ftp: flash:R1-ftp-received.cfg` if supported, answering its prompts individually. Inspect the staged text.

:::expected
The repaired credentials permit the authorized transfer. FTP control and data use separate TCP connections; a login alone would not prove the data transfer succeeded. The backup may include the stored lab FTP password, demonstrating why configuration files need access protection. Save `files-complete.pkt`. Do not use this cleartext method for real secrets.
:::

steps.title: — Prepare the independent Linux transfer server
steps.body:
Create an Ubuntu 24.04 VM with a console and a dedicated isolated lab NIC. Before isolating it, install OpenSSH using the official Ubuntu procedure:

```bash
sudo apt update
sudo apt install openssh-server
sudo systemctl enable --now ssh
sudo adduser ccnafile
```

Choose a unique password for the new `ccnafile` account; it need not have sudo rights. Record it privately. At the VM console, identify the lab NIC:

```bash
ip -br link
```

The following example assumes its name is `ens3`. Replace that name with the actual dedicated lab NIC. Do not run these commands on the host computer's working network adapter.

```bash
sudo ip link set ens3 up
sudo ip address add 10.29.0.100/24 dev ens3
ip -br address
sudo sshd -t
sudo ss -lntp
sudo -iu ccnafile
```

The address command is temporary and does not require a gateway. As `ccnafile`, create the working directory and test file:

```bash
mkdir -p ~/ccna-files
chmod 700 ~/ccna-files
printf 'CCNA secure transfer practice\n' > ~/ccna-files/probe.txt
chmod 600 ~/ccna-files/probe.txt
sha512sum ~/ccna-files/probe.txt
exit
```

:::expected
The dedicated NIC has `10.29.0.100/24`. SSH configuration validation produces no error, and a TCP 22 listener exists. The file is 30 bytes including its final newline. If a firewall is active, permit TCP 22 only from `10.29.0.1` on the lab NIC using your distribution's firewall controls; do not disable the firewall globally. Keep the VM console open and verify the account can log in locally.
:::

steps.title: — Configure a fresh IOS XE lab device for SSH and SCP
steps.body:
This block is for a fresh, isolated Catalyst 9300 S1. A virtual router uses its actual Layer 3 port name and omits `no switchport`. Do not apply it over an existing production AAA policy.

```ios S1
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname S1
S1(config)# interface gigabitethernet1/0/1
S1(config-if)# no switchport
S1(config-if)# ip address 10.29.0.1 255.255.255.0
S1(config-if)# no shutdown
S1(config-if)# exit
S1(config)# username labbackup privilege 15 secret RouterLab2026!
S1(config)# ip domain name ccna.example
S1(config)# aaa new-model
S1(config)# aaa authentication login default local
S1(config)# aaa authorization exec default local
S1(config)# line console 0
S1(config-line)# login authentication default
S1(config-line)# exit
S1(config)# line vty 0 15
S1(config-line)# login authentication default
S1(config-line)# transport input ssh
S1(config-line)# exit
S1(config)# crypto key generate rsa modulus 2048
S1(config)# ip ssh version 2
S1(config)# ip ssh source-interface gigabitethernet1/0/1
S1(config)# ip scp server enable
S1(config)# end
S1# show ip interface brief
S1# show ip ssh
S1# ping 10.29.0.100
```

Generate keys only on this new device; if it already has keys, inspect and retain the intended key rather than replacing it. Keep the current console session open. Before the first Linux login, read `show ip ssh` **through that trusted console**. In its SECSH public-key section, locate the actual `ssh-rsa` key used by this SSH server. Copy the key into `~/S1-console-key.pub` on Linux using a text editor: one line containing `ssh-rsa`, one space, and the complete base64 key. Join wrapped key lines without inserting spaces into the base64 data. Do not copy the label, modulus line, terminal prompt or an example key.

Calculate its fingerprint on Linux:

```bash
ssh-keygen -lf ~/S1-console-key.pub -E sha256
```

The result identifies an RSA public key and a SHA256 fingerprint. `show crypto key mypubkey rsa` alone may display ASN.1 hexadecimal data; that is not directly comparable with OpenSSH's fingerprint. If this release cannot display/export the active SSH public key in a supported comparable format, stop this checkpoint and use its documented trusted key-export procedure.

Now test a separate login:

```bash
ssh labbackup@10.29.0.1
```

Compare the offered **RSA** fingerprint with the locally calculated value before accepting it. An unexpected key type, mismatch or changed-key warning requires investigation through the console; do not bypass the check. Enter the fictional router password only after identity verification.

:::expected
The second session reaches S1 and has the intended privilege. Run `show privilege` there, then `exit`. The verified login records the server key in Linux's known-hosts file for the later SCP connection. If algorithms are incompatible, use a supported current image and inspect both ends' SSH logs; do not globally enable obsolete algorithms or disable host-key checks. If SFTP/SCP commands are unavailable, this environment cannot complete the secure-transfer part.
:::

steps.title: — Pull a configuration backup with classic SCP
steps.body:
On S1, inventory local storage and create a snapshot:

```ios S1
S1# show file systems
S1# copy running-config flash:S1-before.cfg
```

Accept the destination prompt and wait. If this device uses `bootflash:` instead of `flash:`, consistently substitute it. On Linux, create a protected local destination and pull the staged file:

```bash
mkdir -p ~/ccna-received
chmod 700 ~/ccna-received
scp -O labbackup@10.29.0.1:flash:S1-before.cfg ~/ccna-received/S1-before.cfg
chmod 600 ~/ccna-received/S1-before.cfg
ls -l ~/ccna-received/S1-before.cfg
```

Inspect the received file privately; do not paste secrets into a shared transcript.

:::expected
The workstation initiates SCP and the Cisco device acts as server. `-O` is deliberate because the cited Cisco server supports classic SCP and OpenSSH 9+ defaults to SFTP. A successful file transfer and readable configuration confirm more than a successful SSH login. The local snapshot and remote backup do not automatically update startup-config.
:::

steps.title: — Pin the SFTP server identity, then stage a harmless file
steps.body:
S1 is now the client; Ubuntu's SSH/SFTP service is the server. Client authentication by password and verification of the **server's identity** are different checks. The documented IOS XE procedure uses a trusted server public key and `ip ssh stricthostkeycheck`; do not assume it offers OpenSSH's interactive acceptance prompt.

On the trusted Ubuntu console, inspect its existing **server** RSA public key, not a user's login key:

```bash
ssh-keygen -lf /etc/ssh/ssh_host_rsa_key.pub -E sha256
awk '{print $1" "$2}' /etc/ssh/ssh_host_rsa_key.pub | fold -w 70
```

Record the fingerprint and retain the complete wrapped public-key text. These are public-key data; never copy the file without the `.pub` suffix.

First verify enforcement on this fresh S1, which has no server public-key entry yet:

```ios S1
S1# configure terminal
S1(config)# ip ssh stricthostkeycheck
S1(config)# end
S1# copy sftp://ccnafile@10.29.0.100//home/ccnafile/ccna-files/probe.txt flash:probe-sftp.txt
```

An initial destination-filename prompt may appear. The SSH connection must then fail server authentication before requesting the account password or transferring a file. If it instead reaches a password prompt, cancel with Ctrl+C: do not enter credentials or count this image as demonstrating authenticated SFTP. Check the exact release's supported client/server-authentication procedure or use a compatible image.

After observing that expected rejection, enter the trusted key on S1:

```ios S1
S1# configure terminal
S1(config)# ip ssh pubkey-chain
S1(conf-ssh-pubkey)# server 10.29.0.100
S1(conf-ssh-pubkey-server)# key-string
```

At the `conf-ssh-pubkey-data` prompt, paste **all** of Ubuntu's wrapped `ssh-rsa` public-key text from above, with no shell prompts. Wait for the key text to be entered before continuing:

```ios S1
S1(conf-ssh-pubkey-data)# exit
S1(conf-ssh-pubkey-server)# end
S1# show running-config | section ip ssh
```

Confirm the server-address entry and strict checking. IOS may store the entered key as a hash. Repeat the file operation:

```ios S1
S1# copy sftp://ccnafile@10.29.0.100//home/ccnafile/ccna-files/probe.txt flash:probe-sftp.txt
```

Answer the account-password and destination prompts individually. If server authentication still fails, inspect the trusted key, exact server address and negotiated key type; keep strict checking enabled. Use the matching server public key and documented support for that release, rather than substituting an unverified key.

After completion:

```ios S1
S1# dir flash:probe-sftp.txt
S1# more flash:probe-sftp.txt
S1# verify /sha512 flash:probe-sftp.txt
```

:::expected
The missing-key attempt was rejected before account authentication; the trusted-key attempt succeeds. Record both outcomes. This checks the actual SFTP implementation's enforcement instead of inferring it from a configured command alone.

The file contains `CCNA secure transfer practice` and its SHA-512 matches the server's Step 9 value. On an image without SHA-512 verification, compare MD5 at both ends (`md5sum` on Linux and `verify /md5` on IOS) for this benign transfer exercise and record the limitation. Do not treat MD5 as proof of software authenticity. If the specific release requires interactive `copy sftp: flash:`, supply the same host, user, absolute source path and destination when prompted. An unsupported identity check is a documented lab limitation, not a successful secure-transfer result.
:::

steps.title: — Demonstrate a path failure, then recover separately
steps.body:
Attempt a source filename that does not exist:

```ios S1
S1# copy sftp://ccnafile@10.29.0.100//home/ccnafile/ccna-files/missing.txt flash:missing-test.txt
```

Record the error. Check the source directory from Linux's console with `sudo -u ccnafile ls -l /home/ccnafile/ccna-files` before changing any network settings.

:::expected
Authentication may succeed while the file operation fails. The directory contains `probe.txt`, not `missing.txt`, so the source path is the demonstrated fault. After recording it, recover by using the existing source and a new destination:

```ios S1
S1# copy sftp://ccnafile@10.29.0.100//home/ccnafile/ccna-files/probe.txt flash:probe-recovered.txt
```

Wait for completion, then inspect `dir flash:probe-recovered.txt` and its hash. Connectivity and credentials did not need changing.
:::

steps.title: — Apply the same checks to an approved software file
steps.body:
If you have an authorized Cisco software download for this exact lab platform, place it in `/home/ccnafile/ccna-files` with owner `ccnafile` and read permission for that account. Record its exact filename, size, release compatibility and Cisco-published SHA-512. Check available Cisco storage and keep the working image and package files intact.

Use the Step 12 SFTP operation with the **actual approved filename** as source and destination, or push it from Linux with `scp -O` to the named local Cisco file. Replace only the filename and path, not the protocol's security checks. Compute the stored file's hash and compare with Cisco's published value.

:::expected
A file with the expected size and matching trusted hash is staged, not activated. `show version` still reports the original running software. If no licensed suitable image is available, use the benign file from Step 12 to demonstrate the mechanics and produce the software preflight worksheet; explicitly mark actual software staging as unperformed. Never rename the text file to `.bin` or attempt to boot it.
:::

steps.title: — Preserve a usable completion record
steps.body:
Record source/destination roles, filenames, actual hashes, image/version, successful operations, errors and any unsupported features. Preserve the secure backup in a restricted directory. Keep the original lab checkpoint and working software. If the lab will be retained, save only the verified intended device configuration:

```ios S1
S1# copy running-config startup-config
```

Accept the destination prompt before doing anything else. Stop the isolated lab when finished.

:::expected
The record distinguishes a transferred file, a verified file, an applied configuration and active software. No boot setting or image activation was changed by this exercise.
:::

lab.troubleshooting:
- Timeout with successful ping: inspect the particular transfer service, transport ports, source interface, return path and server logs. ICMP success does not uniquely identify a firewall or service fault.
- FTP login works but file transfer stalls: investigate the separate active/passive data connection and permissions.
- SCP subsystem error with OpenSSH 9+: confirm the Cisco server supports classic SCP, then use `-O`. Authentication and authorization must still work.
- SSH authentication succeeds but file access is denied: check EXEC authorization, device privilege and file/directory permissions.
- SFTP file not found: compare case and absolute path at the server; a working login does not prove the named path exists.
- Hash mismatch: stop before applying or activating anything. Recheck the source identity, expected hash, filename and actual destination bytes.
lab.challenge:
You have a verified `S1-before.cfg` copied to flash. Since the backup, someone added an unused Loopback29 and changed the hostname. A colleague copies the file into running-config, sees the old hostname return, and declares complete restoration. Another colleague transfers a new software image successfully and declares the device upgraded.

Explain what each colleague has and has not demonstrated. Describe a safe verification and recovery plan without issuing reload, erase or image-activation commands.

:::expected
The configuration copy merged commands. The hostname can be restored while Loopback29 remains because the file lacks an explicit removal. Compare the result against the desired configuration; for this known harmless temporary interface, an approved `no interface loopback29` removes it. Broader exact replacement needs a complete validated file, supported replacement procedure and console recovery.

The software transfer only staged bytes. Verify platform/release compatibility, local size, trusted hash and relevant authenticity checks, then inspect current software and boot mode. Plan activation separately under the platform's documented procedure and a recovery window. Neither transfer completion nor a matching filename proves that new software is running.
:::

exhibit.title: Representative show file systems excerpt
exhibit.text:
Size(b)      Free(b)     Type  Flags  Prefixes
*   256000000     180000000     disk     rw  flash0: flash:
       262144        240000    nvram     rw  nvram:
            -             -  network    rw  tftp:

questions.prompt: Which statement is supported by this file-system inventory?
options: The TFTP prefix is a local disk containing 180 MB of free space
The startup configuration occupies the complete flash file system
The two flash prefixes refer to the same listed local storage
The 256,000,000-byte value is the free capacity available now
questions.explanation: The prefixes flash0: and flash: share one row, identifying aliases in this example. The Free column, not Size, reports available bytes.

whyWrong.0: Type network describes remote transfer access, not local storage capacity.
whyWrong.1: The inventory distinguishes flash storage from nvram; it does not show configuration contents.
whyWrong.3: Size reports total capacity; Free is 180,000,000 bytes.

questions.prompt: How does base TFTP start a file transfer?
options: A UDP request goes to server port 69; selected transfer ports carry the exchange
A TCP control session goes to port 69; TCP 70 carries all file contents
A UDP request goes to port 21; the client supplies an FTP login password
A TCP session goes to port 22; an SSH subsystem negotiates the transfer
questions.explanation: The initial TFTP request targets UDP 69. The server then selects a transfer identifier/UDP port for the exchange. Retries can resend a request to 69.

whyWrong.1: Base TFTP uses UDP and does not define TCP 70 as a data connection.
whyWrong.2: FTP control normally uses TCP 21; TFTP has no FTP username/password login.
whyWrong.3: SSH-based SFTP/SCP uses this different transport model.

questions.prompt: Which two statements describe classic FTP? Choose two.
options: Passive mode sends file contents inside the control connection
The server initiates the active-mode data connection toward the client
A username/password login encrypts the subsequent file contents
The normal control connection uses server TCP port 21
Passive mode requires every data connection to use server port 20
questions.explanation: FTP has a control connection and a separate data connection. Active/passive describes who initiates the data connection. Classic FTP does not provide encryption.

whyWrong.0: Directory listings and files use the separate data connection in passive mode too.
whyWrong.2: Authentication and encryption are different; classic FTP sends credentials/data in cleartext.
whyWrong.4: In passive mode the server advertises a data endpoint; it is not fixed to port 20.

exhibit.title: Representative console extract
exhibit.text:
R1-TEMP# copy flash:R1-before.cfg running-config
Destination filename [running-config]?
[OK]
R1# show ip interface brief
Loopback29       unassigned      YES unset  up  up

questions.prompt: R1-before.cfg contains `hostname R1` but no reference to Loopback29. The shown copy restored the hostname but left that interface. Why?
options: The TFTP protocol refused to transmit the interface-related lines
The file was merged, and no command removed the extra interface
The loopback exists only in startup-config and cannot be removed live
The hostname proves the device reloaded into its earlier configuration
questions.explanation: Applying a file to running-config merges its commands. It can change the hostname while leaving an unrelated extra interface. Explicit no commands in a merged file could remove configuration; absence alone generally does not.

whyWrong.0: The result is explained by configuration application, not a TFTP line filter.
whyWrong.2: The interface appears in active configuration and can be removed explicitly.
whyWrong.3: A hostname change does not imply a reload.

questions.prompt: A verified backup is copied into startup-config. No other operation is performed. What changes immediately?
options: The device erases all extra interfaces from running-config
The booted IOS image changes to the one named in the backup
The active configuration becomes identical to the backup
The saved startup file changes; the active configuration does not
questions.explanation: The destination is the saved startup configuration. Applying it to the running system is a separate decision. A later normal startup may load it, subject to platform boot settings.

whyWrong.0: This destination is not running-config.
whyWrong.1: Copying a configuration file does not load a new running image.
whyWrong.2: The active configuration is not applied by this copy alone.

exhibit.title: Classic ISR: show version excerpt
exhibit.text: Configuration register is 0x2102 (will be 0x2142 at next reload)

questions.prompt: On this classic ISR platform, 0x2142 is documented to ignore startup-config. What should the engineer recognize from this output before planning a restart?
options: The next startup is set to skip the saved configuration
The current saved configuration has already been erased
The device will immediately exit IOS into ROMMON
The current console speed must change after this display
questions.explanation: The output distinguishes the current register from the next-startup value. On the explicitly stated classic platform, the pending 0x2142 value skips startup-config; it does not erase the file.

whyWrong.1: Ignoring a file at startup is not deletion.
whyWrong.2: A pending startup setting does not immediately stop IOS.
whyWrong.3: The exhibited difference is the ignore-configuration behavior, not proof of a console speed change.

exhibit.title: Saved configuration extract
exhibit.text:
boot system flash:old.bin
boot system flash:new.bin

questions.prompt: For this classic platform, assume valid saved boot commands are tried in order. Both image files are compatible and valid. Which image is configured as the first boot candidate?
options: new.bin because its filename suggests a later release
Neither file because two candidates are not permitted
old.bin because it is the first saved boot entry
The larger file regardless of the displayed boot order
questions.explanation: The premise defines this platform's selection behavior and the saved entries put old.bin first. File age and size do not reorder the explicit list.

whyWrong.0: A suggestive filename does not override the configured order.
whyWrong.1: The premise allows an ordered fallback list.
whyWrong.3: Size is relevant to storage checks, not the stated candidate order.

questions.prompt: SSH already works on the cited IOS XE device. Which two additional conditions belong to its classic SCP server setup? Choose two.
options: SCP server functionality is enabled with `ip scp server enable`
FTP client credentials are stored with `ip ftp username`
AAA EXEC authorization permits the user's required access
The SFTP server subsystem must be enabled on this device
The VTY transport must accept Telnet instead of SSH
questions.explanation: The Cisco SCP server requires its server feature and appropriate authentication/authorization. The lab uses local AAA and an authorized privilege-15 account; successful SSH authentication alone does not prove all file access is permitted.

whyWrong.1: These credentials apply to the router acting as an FTP client.
whyWrong.3: Classic SCP does not require an SFTP server; the cited implementation is SFTP-client-only.
whyWrong.4: SCP relies on SSH, not Telnet.

questions.prompt: An OpenSSH 9 client authenticates successfully to a verified classic-SCP-only IOS server, but its default `scp` command fails at SFTP subsystem negotiation. Which client option addresses that known mismatch?
options: `-r`, to recursively copy the configuration directory
`-O`, to select classic SCP instead of the SFTP default
`-P 21`, to move the secure operation to FTP's control port
`-p`, to preserve timestamps while changing the protocol
questions.explanation: OpenSSH 9 changed scp's default transfer protocol to SFTP. Uppercase -O selects classic SCP, still over SSH. The premise establishes a protocol mismatch rather than an unknown login fault.

whyWrong.0: Recursive copying does not change the transfer protocol.
whyWrong.2: The server is an SSH/SCP service, not an FTP control service.
whyWrong.3: Preserving file times does not select the SCP protocol.

exhibit.title: Verification worksheet
exhibit.text:
Cisco download metadata: SHA-512 value A
Local staged candidate: SHA-512 value B
A and B differ
Current running image remains unchanged

questions.prompt: The computed SHA-512 for a staged image differs from the value recorded from Cisco's trusted download page. What is the appropriate next action?
options: Activate it because a completed transfer overrides the hash result
Change the expected value to the computed value and declare success
Delete the working image to make more space for this new candidate
Stop activation and investigate the filename, expected hash and stored bytes
questions.explanation: A mismatch prevents accepting the file as the intended verified candidate. Recheck the exact image and trusted metadata, then transfer again if needed while preserving the working software.

whyWrong.0: Transfer completion does not establish that the intended bytes arrived.
whyWrong.1: Replacing the trusted comparison defeats the integrity check.
whyWrong.2: Removing working recovery software does not repair a hash mismatch.

questions.prompt: What do `ip ftp username filelab` and `ip ftp password ...` configure on the IOS device?
options: An encrypted login service for incoming FTP users
A local authorization list for access to every stored file
Credentials used by the device's FTP client operations
The username and password needed by a TFTP transfer
questions.explanation: The device uses these settings when acting as an FTP client. Stored credentials may appear in configuration backups; keeping them out of a URL does not make those backups nonsensitive.

whyWrong.0: These commands do not create an encrypted FTP server.
whyWrong.1: Remote client credentials are not a local file authorization policy.
whyWrong.3: Base TFTP has no username/password exchange.

exhibit.title: Two tests
exhibit.text:
R1# ping 10.29.0.100
Success rate is 100 percent (5/5)

R1# copy running-config tftp:
%Error opening tftp://10.29.0.100/R1-before.cfg (Timed out)

questions.prompt: R1 can ping its TFTP server, but a write request times out. What is the best next investigation supported by those results?
options: Check the TFTP service, transfer traffic, permissions and server logs
Replace the subnet mask because any TFTP timeout proves it is wrong
Disable the router's SSH service because it occupies UDP port 69
Assume success because ICMP replies prove that the file was written
questions.explanation: ICMP reachability narrows the investigation but does not prove that TFTP requests and replies complete or that a write is permitted. Inspect the actual transfer and server evidence.

whyWrong.1: A timeout alone does not establish a mask error.
whyWrong.2: SSH normally uses TCP 22 and does not occupy TFTP's UDP service.
whyWrong.3: ICMP responses do not establish file creation.

questions.prompt: Which comparison is correct for the cited Catalyst 9300 IOS XE implementation?
options: SFTP is FTP over TLS, while SCP uses unencrypted TCP
Both protocols need FTP's separate active data connection
SFTP server support is required before the router can use SCP
SCP can be served by the device; its documented SFTP role is client
questions.explanation: The cited platform can act as an SCP server when prerequisites are met and documents SFTP client support rather than an SFTP server. Both protocols use SSH; the restriction should not be generalized to every Cisco OS.

whyWrong.0: FTPS is FTP over TLS; SFTP and SCP are SSH-based protocols.
whyWrong.1: They do not use FTP's separate control/data connection model.
whyWrong.2: An SCP server does not require the SFTP subsystem.

questions.prompt: An approved software image has just been transferred to local storage. Which check belongs before any planned activation?
options: Erase the saved configuration so old settings cannot be loaded
Compare the staged file's hash with trusted metadata for that exact image
Rename the existing working image so the bootloader cannot locate it
Set the legacy ignore-startup register value on every IOS XE platform
questions.explanation: Verify the intended image's integrity and compatibility before activation. The exact upgrade path and recovery plan remain platform-specific.

whyWrong.0: Routine staging does not require deleting the saved configuration.
whyWrong.2: Preserve working software and its recovery role while validating a candidate.
whyWrong.3: Legacy register values are not universal IOS XE activation steps.

questions.prompt: After `copy running-config tftp:` completes, what does it establish about startup-config?
options: It now equals the remote server's complete directory contents
It was automatically merged with the remote backup copy
The operation did not use startup-config as a destination
It must be empty until the remote backup is downloaded again
questions.explanation: The named source is running-config and the named destination is a remote TFTP file. Saving startup-config is a separate operation.

whyWrong.0: A remote directory is not copied into startup-config.
whyWrong.1: This operation does not target the saved startup file.
whyWrong.3: The backup operation does not clear it.

questions.prompt: A device reports 180,000,000 free bytes. The approved file is 70,000,000 bytes. What conclusion is justified from these two numbers alone?
options: The file fits in reported free space, but installation requirements still need checking
The image is compatible because free capacity exceeds twice its file size
The device has 110,000,000 bytes of RAM available for the new software
The transfer protocol will automatically activate the file after it is written
questions.explanation: 180,000,000 − 70,000,000 = 110,000,000 bytes of arithmetic storage headroom. RAM, expansion workspace, platform compatibility and activation are separate checks.

whyWrong.1: Storage size does not establish software/platform compatibility.
whyWrong.2: The numbers describe storage, not available RAM.
whyWrong.3: Writing the file does not activate it.

cards.front: How does a TFTP transfer use UDP ports?
cards.back: Requests target server UDP 69. The server selects a transfer ID/port for the exchange with the client's selected port; retransmitted requests can still use 69.

cards.front: Base TFTP block size and security?
cards.back: Base data blocks hold up to 512 bytes; extensions can negotiate block size. Base TFTP supplies neither user login authentication nor encryption.

cards.front: FTP control port and classic active data direction?
cards.back: The control connection normally targets server TCP 21. In classic active mode the server initiates data toward the client's advertised endpoint; the standard default server data port is 20.

cards.front: Active versus passive FTP data connections?
cards.back: Active: server initiates toward client. Passive: client initiates toward the server's advertised data endpoint. Both use a separate control connection; defaults depend on implementation.

cards.front: Common transport for SCP and SFTP?
cards.back: SSH, normally TCP 22. Both protect data in transit; permissions and protection of files at rest remain separate responsibilities.

cards.front: IOS FTP client credential commands?
cards.back: `ip ftp username` and `ip ftp password` supply client credentials. They do not create a server, and saved configuration may contain sensitive credential information.

cards.front: What does a Cisco SCP server require?
cards.back: Working SSH, suitable authentication and EXEC authorization, adequate user privilege and `ip scp server enable`. Successful login alone does not prove permission for a file operation.

cards.front: SFTP role in the cited Catalyst 9300 IOS XE guide?
cards.back: Client support, with SSH and `ip ssh source-interface` configured. The cited implementation does not support an SFTP server or SFTP boot; check other platforms separately.

cards.front: Why might OpenSSH 9+ scp need `-O` for an IOS server?
cards.back: Its default transfer protocol is SFTP. Uppercase `-O` selects classic SCP for a verified SCP-only server; it does not repair passwords or file permissions.

cards.front: Copying a saved file into running-config: merge or replace?
cards.back: Merge. The file's commands are applied to current configuration. Extra settings absent from the file can remain; explicit commands, including `no`, can change or remove settings.

cards.front: What changes when a file is copied into startup-config?
cards.back: The saved startup file is replaced; the active configuration does not change immediately. A later configuration application/startup is separate, and saving running-config over it would overwrite it.

cards.front: What does `configure replace` require?
cards.back: A complete compatible replacement configuration and a supporting platform. It applies differences, including removals; use validated recovery access and inspect errors/results.

cards.front: What does the configuration archive feature provide?
cards.back: Configured snapshots, optionally triggered by saves or intervals. Local archives aid comparison/recovery but share the device's storage-failure risk; keep protected off-device copies.

cards.front: How should a staged image hash be verified?
cards.back: Compute a supported strong hash, such as `verify /sha512 flash:filename`, and compare with trusted Cisco metadata for that exact image. MD5 can detect transfer errors but is not modern proof of authenticity.

cards.front: Does the first filename in a directory prove the next boot image?
cards.back: No. Inspect the platform's actual boot settings, mode and release documentation. In an explicitly ordered classic boot list, entries are tried in the configured order.

cards.front: Classic ISR: what distinguishes 0x2142 from normal 0x2102?
cards.back: On that legacy platform, 0x2142 ignores startup-config during startup. It does not erase the saved file. Do not generalize legacy register procedures to every IOS XE device.

cards.front: Does copying a software image activate it?
cards.back: No. Transfer, integrity/compatibility verification and activation are separate stages. Confirm active software with the platform's operational displays.

cards.front: What does an asterisk in `show file systems` identify?
cards.back: The default file system. Prefer explicit storage prefixes, and inspect `show version`/boot information separately to identify running or planned software.

cards.front: What makes a backup filename useful?
cards.back: It identifies the device and a known checkpoint, with a date/change label when appropriate. Verify the destination file and restrict access to its sensitive contents.

cards.front: IOS XE install mode: why is packages.conf alone insufficient as a software backup?
cards.back: It is a provisioning manifest that references package files. Preserve the files and follow the exact platform's documented install/backup workflow; bundle mode differs.

cards.front: `copy run start` versus `copy start run`?
cards.back: Running to startup saves the active configuration. Startup to running applies the saved commands as a merge, so unrelated active additions can remain.

commands.task: Back up running-config to TFTP, prompting for the remote host and filename.
commands.note: Complete each interactive prompt before entering another IOS command. This does not save startup-config.

commands.task: Stage a file from TFTP into the device's verified flash: storage, prompting for filenames.
commands.note: Check free space and choose a new destination filename. A software transfer does not activate it.

commands.task: In the isolated FTP lab, set the router's FTP client username to filelab.
commands.note: This configures the client. FTP credentials and data are not encrypted.

commands.task: Enable the Cisco SCP server after SSH and appropriate AAA authorization have been verified.
commands.note: Server access still depends on user authentication, privilege and file permissions.

commands.task: On a legacy supporting image, compute the MD5 of flash:probe-sftp.txt for a benign transfer comparison.
commands.note: Compare it with the source's MD5. Prefer a supported strong published hash for real software verification.

commands.task: Read the running software identity and platform details before planning any image change.
commands.note: A directory listing alone does not identify the active software.

commands.task: List file-system types and prefixes, including the default file system.
commands.note: Network protocol prefixes refer to remote access, not local disk capacity.

commands.task: List the files and capacity in the explicitly verified flash: file system.
commands.note: Use the actual prefix reported on the device; an unqualified dir may target a different default.

commands.task: On the classic router used by this worksheet, display the BOOT variable and register using its supported command.
commands.note: This command is platform-specific. Compare active/saved settings before interpreting a planned startup.

commands.task: On a supporting IOS XE image with server identity and credentials verified, stage /home/ccnafile/ccna-files/probe.txt from SFTP user ccnafile at 10.29.0.100 as flash:probe-sftp.txt. Do not put the password in the URL.
commands.note: Complete the password/destination prompts individually; verify the server identity and resulting file.

commands.task: Paper recognition only: name the command to replace the active configuration from a complete validated flash:R1-good.cfg on a supporting device.
commands.note: Unlike a merge, this applies differences including removals. Do not execute without verified compatibility and console recovery; no force option is required by this task.

commands.task: Replace only the saved startup file from a TFTP server, prompting for the source details.
commands.note: This does not immediately apply the configuration. Do not append reload; first inspect and validate the intended result.

tickets.title: The old hostname returned but a temporary interface remains
tickets.scenario: In an isolated lab, R1-before.cfg was saved before an unused, unnumbered Loopback29 was created. The file contains hostname R1 and no reference to Loopback29. A learner changed the hostname and added the loopback, then applied the backup. No other changes are intended.

exhibits.title: Console history
exhibits.text:
R1-TEMP# copy flash:R1-before.cfg running-config
Destination filename [running-config]?
[OK]
R1#

exhibits.title: Active configuration excerpt
exhibits.text:
hostname R1
interface Loopback29
 description TEMPORARY_MERGE_TEST

tickets.question: What explains the remaining interface?
options: The transfer protocol excludes loopback configuration from every backup
The file merged into running-config without a command removing the interface
The backup automatically replaced startup-config instead of running-config
The configuration register moved the new loopback into immutable storage
tickets.explanation: The explicit destination was running-config. The hostname command took effect, while the unrelated interface remained because the older file did not remove it. Nothing indicates a protocol filter, a changed destination or immutable interface state.
tickets.fix:
Compare the active result with the intended lab baseline, then remove only the known unused interface:

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# no interface loopback29
R1(config)# end
R1# show ip interface brief
```
Retest the actual lab connectivity. Save the verified result with a separate `copy running-config startup-config` operation, completing its prompt. A full configuration replacement would require a complete validated file and an appropriate recovery procedure; it is unnecessary for this demonstrated harmless change.

tickets.title: The software file was copied but the planned boot entry was not saved
tickets.scenario: A classic ISR lab uses the documented saved boot-entry order. Its previously saved configuration explicitly selected old.bin. An engineer verified a compatible new.bin, changed only the running boot entry to new.bin, then performed a restart without saving. The device still runs old.bin. The exhibits are representative; this ticket asks for diagnosis, not another reload.

exhibits.title: Saved configuration before and after the restart
exhibits.text: boot system flash:old.bin

exhibits.title: Engineer’s pre-restart console log
exhibits.text:
R1(config)# no boot system flash:old.bin
R1(config)# boot system flash:new.bin
R1(config)# end
System configuration has been modified. Save? [yes/no]: no

exhibits.title: Current software and storage worksheet
exhibits.text:
Running image: flash:old.bin
Stored files: old.bin and new.bin
new.bin: verified against trusted metadata before the earlier restart

tickets.question: Which demonstrated mistake explains why the intended boot selection was lost?
options: The new image's presence forces the old image to be selected as a backup
Two compatible files cannot coexist on the same flash file system
The changed boot entry was never written to the saved configuration
The SCP transfer should have modified the configuration register itself
tickets.explanation: The known saved entry still selects old.bin. The running-only change was discarded at restart, so the persisted selection remained. No directory-order assumption is needed; copying through SCP does not change boot configuration.
tickets.fix: Preserve both files and investigate the change record. Compare `show running-config`, `show startup-config`, the supported boot display and `show version`. Before any later approved activation, validate the exact platform procedure, intended entry order, saved state and recovery plan. Do not delete old.bin or repeat an unscheduled reload to test a guess. A completed transfer and trusted hash establish staging, not active software or saved boot intent.

sections.title: Start with the active adapter and its parameters
Ask the same questions on three operating systems
Recognize fault patterns and their limits
Verify wireless connection and security settings
Test a path and verify the repair

lab.title: Isolate client address, gateway, DNS and wireless faults
lab.topology:
Build a new isolated Packet Tracer project. Use an ISR 2911 R1, a 2960 SW1, two PC-PT endpoints and Server-PT. The optional wireless extension uses WRT300N and a Laptop-PT with a compatible wireless adapter.

| Connection | Cable | Address / gateway |
|---|---|---|
| PC-A Fa0 — SW1 Fa0/1 | Copper straight-through | DHCP |
| Server-A Fa0 — SW1 Fa0/2 | Copper straight-through | 192.168.40.20/24, GW 192.168.40.1 |
| R1 Gi0/0 — SW1 Fa0/3 | Copper straight-through | R1 192.168.40.1/24 |
| R1 Gi0/1 — PC-B Fa0 | Copper crossover | R1 192.168.50.1/24; PC-B 192.168.50.10/24, GW 192.168.50.1 |
| Optional WRT1 Ethernet 1 — SW1 Fa0/4 | Copper straight-through | WRT1 LAN 192.168.40.2/24; its DHCP service disabled |

Server-A provides DHCP, DNS and HTTP. Its DHCP range is **192.168.40.100–149**, safely excluding the router, wireless device and static server. There is no Internet connection. R1 needs only its connected routes.

These are documented, reviewed procedures with expected results, not a record of an executed Packet Tracer run. Packet Tracer's PC shell and wireless controls differ by version. Use its IP Configuration GUI if a PC command is absent, and record unsupported observations honestly. The final OS inspection is read-only on a real Windows, Mac or Linux machine; all deliberate faults stay in the isolated simulator.

steps.title: — Configure router and static endpoints
steps.body:
Set Server-A and PC-B in Desktop → IP Configuration → Static from the topology table, mask `255.255.255.0`. Server-A's DNS field is `192.168.40.20`; PC-B's is also `192.168.40.20`.

On a new router, decline the setup dialog if presented:

```ios R1
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R1
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ip address 192.168.40.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# no ip proxy-arp
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ip address 192.168.50.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip interface brief
R1# show ip route connected
```

:::expected
Both router interfaces become up/up and both /24 networks are connected. Proxy ARP is explicitly disabled on Gi0/0 so the later mask error will not be concealed by the router answering for a remote host. If the filtered route command is unavailable, use `show ip route` and identify the connected routes. If `no ip proxy-arp` is rejected or its state cannot be verified, complete the wrong-mask steps as an address-decision worksheet: predict the on-link ARP request and explain why proxy ARP could conceal the fault. Do not record the predicted timeout as an observed result. The DNS, gateway and wireless exercises can still proceed.
:::

steps.title: — Configure DHCP, DNS and HTTP explicitly
steps.body:
On Server-A → Services:

1. **DHCP:** turn the service On. Create a pool named `CLIENTS` with default gateway `192.168.40.1`, DNS `192.168.40.20`, starting address `192.168.40.100`, mask `255.255.255.0` and maximum users `50`. Add/save the pool. Remove or correct any default pool that could serve this same interface with conflicting values.
2. **DNS:** turn the service On. Add A records `lab.example` and `fresh.example`, each resolving to `192.168.40.20`.
3. **HTTP:** explicitly turn HTTP On. The default page is adequate; its content is not part of the diagnosis.

On PC-A → Desktop → IP Configuration, select DHCP.

:::expected
PC-A receives an address in .100–.149, /24 mask, gateway .40.1 and DNS .40.20. Do not assume which exact address it receives. If the fields are wrong, fix the server pool before continuing; the static server at .20 is outside the lease range.
:::

steps.title: — Record a known working baseline
steps.body:
On PC-A inspect its actual address with `ipconfig` or the GUI. Then use its command prompt:

```text
ping 192.168.40.20
ping 192.168.40.1
ping 192.168.50.10
nslookup lab.example
```

Open Desktop → Web Browser and visit `http://192.168.40.20`, then `http://lab.example`. If `nslookup` is absent, record that limitation and use the DNS request/response in Simulation mode as the query observation.

:::expected
After any initial ARP delay, local server, gateway and remote PC respond. The query resolves lab.example to .40.20 and both browser tests show the server page. The remote PC ping exercises routing; browsing the local server alone does not. Save `clients-baseline.pkt` and continue in `clients-faults.pkt`.
:::

steps.title: — Introduce only a DNS-selection fault
steps.body:
Write down PC-A's leased address. Change PC-A to Static, retaining that exact address, /24 mask and gateway .40.1, but change DNS to unused `192.168.40.99`. No other device uses .99 in this topology.

Repeat numeric pings and try `nslookup fresh.example`. Read which DNS server the query uses; do not rely solely on a previously cached browser result.

:::expected
Numeric local and routed tests should still work. The DNS request to .99 has no configured server to answer it. Cached lab.example data might still work in an application, so it is not a reliable test of the new resolver setting. The demonstration identifies the wrong configured resolver by comparison with the known server address.
:::

steps.title: — Restore DNS and verify its response
steps.body:
Keep the same static address, mask and gateway, and restore DNS to `192.168.40.20`. Repeat `nslookup fresh.example` or inspect the DNS exchange in Simulation mode, then open `http://fresh.example`.

:::expected
The configured resolver is .40.20 and returns .40.20 for the name. The page opens. Record this recovery before creating the next fault.
:::

steps.title: — Introduce only a gateway fault
steps.body:
In PC-A's static IP settings, change gateway to unused `192.168.40.254`. Keep its address, /24 mask and correct local DNS. Test:

```text
ping 192.168.40.20
ping 192.168.50.10
arp -a
```

If the neighbor command is absent, watch ARP in Simulation mode.

:::expected
The local server remains reachable; the intended remote PC should fail because the configured next hop is unused. Observe the attempted resolution for .40.254 where the simulator exposes it. A local DNS server can still answer, so this fault need not make every name lookup fail. Exact ping error wording is platform-dependent.
:::

steps.title: — Restore the gateway
steps.body:
Return PC-A's gateway to `192.168.40.1` without changing its other values. Repeat the local and remote pings.

:::expected
Both tests work after necessary address resolution. Successful recovery agrees with the demonstrated wrong next hop. Keep the known configuration rather than making unrelated DNS or router changes.
:::

steps.title: — Introduce only a subnet-mask fault
steps.body:
Change PC-A's mask to `255.255.0.0`. Retain its address, gateway and DNS. Test the local server and remote `192.168.50.10`. In Simulation mode, filter ARP/ICMP, clear the event list, send a new PC-A-to-PC-B simple PDU and inspect PC-A's decision. Do not interpret an old event as a new test.

:::expected
The local .40.20 server remains within the client's perceived /16. The client incorrectly treats .50.10 as on-link and tries to resolve it directly. With proxy ARP disabled on R1 Gi0/0, that remote endpoint is not resolved on this LAN. The failure concerns the mask's local/remote decision, even though the displayed gateway value is correct.
:::

steps.title: — Restore the mask and repeat the same destination test
steps.body:
Return PC-A's mask to `255.255.255.0`. Repeat the remote ping and inspect a new simulation event if available.

:::expected
PC-A now recognizes .50.10 as outside its /24 and sends toward .40.1. The remote ping succeeds. Save a separate checkpoint `clients-recovered.pkt`.
:::

steps.title: — Observe a DHCP acquisition failure
steps.body:
First return PC-A to DHCP and verify it again receives the correct settings. Turn **Server-A's DHCP service Off**, leaving DNS and HTTP On. On this isolated PC-A only, discard the existing lease and request another:

```text
ipconfig /release
ipconfig /renew
```

If those commands are unsupported, toggle PC-A's IP Configuration to Static, then back to DHCP after the server is Off. In Simulation mode, observe the client's DHCP attempts.

:::expected
PC-A cannot acquire a new lease from the disabled server. Depending on simulator timing, it may report a failed request, show no usable IPv4 configuration or display an autoconfiguration address. Record the actual result; do not require an invented exact APIPA address. The absence of a lease alone would not prove which DHCP message failed, but this controlled service-off change supplies the known cause.
:::

steps.title: — Restore DHCP without changing unrelated services
steps.body:
Turn Server-A's DHCP service On. Confirm the CLIENTS pool still contains .100–.149, gateway .40.1 and DNS .40.20. Renew on PC-A or click DHCP in its GUI. Repeat the baseline tests after a valid lease appears.

:::expected
The client again obtains intended settings, resolves lab.example and reaches PC-B. The numeric address may differ from its earlier lease. Server-A's static .20 address has not entered the pool, and DNS/HTTP did not need restarting.
:::

steps.title: — Build the optional wireless client path
steps.body:
Add a WRT300N named WRT1. Connect **Ethernet 1, a LAN port**, to SW1 Fa0/4; leave its Internet/WAN port disconnected. Through WRT1's GUI:

- Set Local IP Address to `192.168.40.2` with mask `255.255.255.0`.
- Disable its DHCP server; Server-A remains the only intended DHCP server.
- Set the SSID to `CCNA-LAB`.
- Set wireless security to **WPA2-Personal**, encryption **AES**, and fictional lab passphrase `StudyNet2026!`.
- Save each relevant page. If changing the LAN address interrupts a management page, reopen the GUI at the new address.

For Laptop-PT, use an available compatible wireless module. If the model lacks one, open Physical, power it off, replace its removable Ethernet module with the listed WPC300N wireless module where supported, then power it on. In Desktop → PC Wireless, select/connect to CCNA-LAB with matching WPA2-Personal/AES settings and the lab passphrase. In IP Configuration, select DHCP for the wireless interface.

:::expected
The laptop joins the intended WLAN and obtains a .100–.149 address from Server-A, gateway .40.1 and DNS .40.20. Test its local server and PC-B, then browse lab.example. An address in the WRT's former default subnet means its DHCP service or cabling is wrong. If the installed version lacks the named model/security controls, use an available equivalent documented WPA2-Personal AP or complete the real-OS inspection in Step 15; record the missing simulated wireless exercise.
:::

steps.title: — Observe a wireless credential fault
steps.body:
On the simulated laptop, disconnect from CCNA-LAB and change only its saved profile passphrase to `WrongStudyKey!`. Reconnect with that profile. Do not change the AP, DHCP pool or router.

:::expected
The client should fail to establish usable protected access with the mismatched key. UI wording and whether an old IP address remains displayed vary. An old lease is not proof of a currently functioning wireless data path. Compare the failed new connection attempt and intended security settings instead of asserting a particular DHCP packet sequence without observing it.
:::

steps.title: — Repair wireless access and save the complete lab
steps.body:
Correct the laptop's profile to `StudyNet2026!`, reconnect and request DHCP if needed. Retest the server, remote PC and name-based page. Confirm PC-A is also using correct DHCP settings. Save `clients-complete.pkt`. Save R1 separately:

```ios R1
R1# copy running-config startup-config
```

Complete the destination prompt with Enter.

:::expected
Both clients have intended addresses and can use the lab services. WRT1's DHCP service remains disabled, its LAN port provides the bridge to SW1, and every introduced fault is repaired.
:::

steps.title: — Inspect the operating systems without creating real faults
steps.body:
Use whichever actual OS environments you have. These are **read-only inspections**: do not release a working lease, alter DNS, disconnect Wi-Fi or disable security on a personal/work machine. Its addresses will not match the simulator unless it is intentionally part of that isolated network. For an unavailable OS, interpret the chapter's representative output and mark direct practice pending.

**Windows:** open Command Prompt and run:

```text
ipconfig /all
route print -4
route print -6
arp -a
netsh wlan show interfaces
netsh wlan show profiles
```

Record the intended adapter, IPv4/IPv6 addresses, prefixes, gateway/route and resolver choices. If a wireless adapter is active, record its displayed SSID, authentication and cipher. To inspect a chosen saved profile without displaying its cleartext password, use `netsh wlan show profile name="PROFILE-NAME"` after replacing the name with one from the list. If location/privacy permission restricts radio fields, note the restriction; an absent field is not proof of a network fault.

**macOS:** in System Settings → Network, inspect the active service → Details → TCP/IP and DNS. In Terminal:

```text
networksetup -listallhardwareports
ifconfig
route -n get default
netstat -rn
scutil --dns
```

Map the active service to its actual interface. For Wi-Fi, Option-click its menu-bar icon and open Wireless Diagnostics. Read current connection/security details available in that release; the analysis does not change settings. Keep generated diagnostic archives private because they contain network details.

**Linux:** use:

```bash
ip -br address
ip route
ip -6 route
ip neigh
```

On NetworkManager systems, add:

```bash
nmcli device status
nmcli device show
nmcli connection show --active
nmcli -f IN-USE,SSID,SECURITY,SIGNAL device wifi list
```

For an active wireless profile, use `nmcli -f 802-11-wireless-security.key-mgmt connection show "PROFILE-NAME"` with its actual profile name. On systemd-resolved systems, inspect `resolvectl status`. Missing NetworkManager or resolved tools can simply mean a different network manager is in use.

:::expected
For every available OS, produce a small private worksheet mapping the active adapter to its address/prefix, usable routes, DNS configuration and wireless security evidence. Identify which observations came from saved configuration and which describe the current connection. A VPN-specific resolver or route may explain a path different from the default. Do not record passwords or claim direct practice on operating systems you did not access.
:::

lab.troubleshooting:
- Initial link failure: check the exact ports, crossover for the direct router-to-PC link, interface shutdown state and switch forwarding.
- DHCP serves .20 or the wrong subnet: repair/remove conflicting simulator pools; reserve .1, .2 and .20 outside .100–.149.
- Local web access works but remote PC fails: that local application test did not exercise routing; inspect the client mask and selected next hop.
- DNS change appears ineffective: query a fresh name and inspect the actual resolver; caches or another adapter may hide the change.
- Wrong mask still reaches a remote endpoint: confirm proxy ARP is disabled in this controlled exercise and inspect actual packet decisions.
- Wireless laptop receives a different subnet: check WRT DHCP is disabled and the switch cable is in a LAN port, not the WAN port.
- Wi-Fi says connected but no lease: inspect current authentication/data-path evidence, WLAN-to-LAN mapping and DHCP exchange; the icon does not identify one unique cause.
lab.challenge:
A client on the .40.0/24 LAN has `192.168.40.120/16`, gateway `192.168.40.1` and DNS `192.168.40.99`. Proxy ARP remains disabled. It can reach Server-A by numeric address but cannot reach PC-B or resolve a fresh lab name.

Without randomly changing several fields, identify two independent faults, predict the failed next-hop decision for PC-B, and specify a repair/test sequence. Then explain why a wireless client's retained .40.120 address would not by itself prove that a new Wi-Fi connection succeeded.

:::expected
The /16 mask makes .50.10 appear on-link, so the client tries to resolve PC-B directly instead of using .40.1. Restore /24 first and verify numeric reachability to .50.10 while leaving DNS unchanged. Then correct DNS from unused .99 to Server-A .20 and verify a direct fresh-name query and the web application. The address and gateway were already appropriate.

A retained address may belong to an earlier lease and can remain visible after a failed association/key exchange. Verify current SSID/security/data-path evidence and a new connectivity test before relying on the address.
:::

exhibit.title: Representative ipconfig /all excerpt
exhibit.text:
DHCP Enabled. . . . . . . . . . . : Yes
Autoconfiguration IPv4 Address. . : 169.254.83.117
Subnet Mask . . . . . . . . . . . : 255.255.0.0
Default Gateway . . . . . . . . . :

questions.prompt: What does this Windows adapter output most directly indicate?
options: The adapter successfully obtained the intended office DHCP lease
The DHCP client has fallen back to an IPv4 link-local address
The server explicitly assigned the laptop a globally routed address
The Wi-Fi passphrase is definitely the sole cause of the failure
questions.explanation: The DHCP-enabled autoconfiguration context identifies link-local fallback rather than an intended LAN lease. It does not say which DHCP message, server condition or underlying path failed.

whyWrong.0: The shown address is link-local fallback, not the intended routed office configuration.
whyWrong.2: 169.254.0.0/16 is link-local and is not globally routed.
whyWrong.3: No wireless security evidence is shown.

questions.prompt: A single-homed host has 10.1.20.57/24 and gateway 10.1.20.254. The actual router is 10.1.20.1; .254 is unused. With no alternate routes, what pattern is expected from this gateway error?
options: Local peers fail because every local packet must use the gateway
Numeric remote tests work while only local DNS queries fail
Local peers can work while destinations requiring the default route fail
All clients on the switch lose their addresses at the same time
questions.explanation: A correct connected-subnet decision permits direct local delivery. Traffic requiring the default route cannot reach the configured unused next hop. Other faults may exist, but this is the stated gateway error's effect.

whyWrong.0: On-link delivery does not normally require the default gateway.
whyWrong.1: The wrong next hop affects routed numeric traffic, not only name queries.
whyWrong.3: One host's gateway setting does not erase other hosts' addresses.

questions.prompt: PC-A is 192.168.40.100/16 on a real /24 LAN. Its gateway is .40.1, proxy ARP is disabled, and remote 192.168.50.10 sits behind another router interface. Which destination does this mask error incorrectly classify as on-link?
questions.explanation: The configured /16 is 192.168.0.0/16, so .50.10 is mistakenly treated as a direct neighbor. The other remote examples remain outside the /16; this says how they are forwarded, not that their entire paths work.

whyWrong.1: The gateway is correctly on-link under both the intended /24 and wrong /16.
whyWrong.2: 172.16.5.5 is outside the wrong /16 too.

questions.prompt: On a Linux machine using NetworkManager, which two commands can display IPv4 default-gateway information? Choose two.
options: ip route
ip link
nmcli device show
resolvectl status
ip -br address
questions.explanation: The routing table can contain a default via entry, and NetworkManager's device details can include IP4.GATEWAY. These reports serve different views of the active configuration.

whyWrong.1: ip link reports link attributes, not the IP routing table.
whyWrong.3: resolvectl reports resolver information, not default forwarding routes.
whyWrong.4: The brief address view lists addresses/prefixes rather than gateways.

exhibit.title: Representative ifconfig en0 extract
exhibit.text:
inet 10.1.20.58 netmask 0xffffff00 broadcast 10.1.20.255
status: active

questions.prompt: What mask and prefix correspond to this macOS netmask?
questions.explanation: 0xffffff00 has six f digits, each contributing four one-bits: 24 one-bits followed by eight zeros. The displayed address and broadcast are consistent with that /24.

whyWrong.0: A /16 mask would be 0xffff0000.
whyWrong.1: A /32 mask would be 0xffffffff.
whyWrong.3: A /20 mask would be 0xfffff000.

exhibit.title: ip route excerpt
exhibit.text: default via 10.1.20.1 dev enp0s3 proto dhcp src 10.1.20.59 metric 100

questions.prompt: Which interpretation of this Linux default route is supported?
options: The default next hop is 10.1.20.1, reached through enp0s3
The default next hop is 10.1.20.59 because it follows src
The route proves every interface address was assigned by DHCP
The route applies only to destinations inside 10.1.20.0/24
questions.explanation: The next hop follows via; dev identifies the interface. proto dhcp labels this route's origin, while src identifies the preferred source. Other routes must also be considered for a particular destination.

whyWrong.1: src names a preferred local source address, not the next hop.
whyWrong.2: A route-origin label does not prove the origin of every address.
whyWrong.3: default is the fallback route, not a connected /24 route.

questions.prompt: A client can ping its gateway and one remote IPv4 address, but a fresh nslookup query times out. Which client setting is the most relevant next check?
options: The configured subnet mask
The configured DNS server
The configured default gateway
The configured DHCP server identity
questions.explanation: Inspect the DNS server actually queried, then test its service/path and the name. The successful numeric test does not certify all masks, routes or applications; it simply makes DNS-specific evidence the useful next step.

whyWrong.0: One remote ping does not prove the mask universally correct, but the fresh query failure makes the resolver choice the direct next check.
whyWrong.2: The tested numeric route worked; inspect the resolver selected for the failing query before changing that working path.
whyWrong.3: The DHCP server identity can explain where settings originated, but it is not the server that must answer this DNS query.

questions.prompt: On an isolated Windows lab PC, which sequence deliberately discards the current DHCP lease and requests configuration again?
options: ipconfig /displaydns then ipconfig /flushdns
route print -4 then arp -a
netsh wlan show profiles then ipconfig /all
ipconfig /release then ipconfig /renew
questions.explanation: Release discards DHCP configuration and renew requests configuration. This can interrupt connectivity, so it belongs in the isolated exercise or an approved change; the command alone is not proof of a captured four-message exchange.

whyWrong.0: These commands inspect/clear DNS cache rather than releasing an address lease.
whyWrong.1: These are read-only route and neighbor displays.
whyWrong.2: These inspect profiles and configuration rather than discarding a lease.

questions.prompt: The security mode is already correctly set to WPA2-Personal. Which two values must match the intended WLAN for the normal shared-passphrase connection? Choose two.
options: The AP's management IPv4 address
The case-sensitive SSID
The client's static Ethernet speed
The configured shared passphrase
The DHCP server's Ethernet port number
questions.explanation: The client must select the intended SSID and use the matching WPA2-Personal credential. Security mode is stipulated correct; these two values address network selection and key agreement.

whyWrong.0: The AP's management address is not the client's wireless network name or shared key.
whyWrong.2: Ethernet speed is not a WPA2-Personal credential.
whyWrong.4: The DHCP server's physical port is not a wireless profile setting.

exhibit.title: Representative client details
exhibit.text:
Wireless state: connected
SSID: CCNA-LAB
Authentication: WPA2-Personal
IPv4: 169.254.201.44/16 (Autoconfiguration)
Default gateway: none

questions.prompt: The laptop reports a connection to the intended SSID but has no usable DHCP lease. Which next investigation is justified?
options: Declare the passphrase correct and exclude all WLAN/VLAN issues
Change the client mask to /8 to reach more DHCP servers
Inspect DHCP acquisition together with the intended WLAN data path
Replace DNS immediately because it assigns the IPv4 lease
questions.explanation: The output warrants checking the DHCP exchange and how the current wireless connection reaches the intended LAN. It does not prove that every mapping, security state or data-path condition is correct.

whyWrong.0: A connection indicator is useful evidence but does not validate every WLAN/VLAN detail.
whyWrong.1: A wider static mask does not repair DHCP delivery.
whyWrong.3: DNS resolves names; it does not assign the DHCP lease.

questions.prompt: Which observation most directly supports investigating a WPA2-Personal key mismatch rather than starting with DNS?
options: The new connection attempt fails key exchange after a profile password change
A valid lease is present while a direct DNS query returns NXDOMAIN
A file server responds by IP but a browser rejects its certificate
The client has two usable default routes with different metrics
questions.explanation: A failed key-exchange event after a credential change focuses the next check on the shared key and security settings. Confirm the event and intended configuration rather than depending on one generic UI message.

whyWrong.1: NXDOMAIN is a name-resolution response, not a wireless key-exchange failure.
whyWrong.2: Certificate validation is a later application/security issue.
whyWrong.3: Multiple routes are forwarding configuration evidence, not a key mismatch.

questions.prompt: These are the complete relevant IPv4 routes. Which gateway is selected for 8.8.8.8?
options: 192.168.1.1 because its row appears first
10.1.20.1 because both matches are /0 and its metric is lower
Both gateways alternately because all default routes are equal
No gateway because 8.8.8.8 is inside one of the on-link /24s
questions.explanation: Both matching routes are default routes with equal prefix length. Under the stated usable-route conditions, metric 25 is preferred to 50. Neither connected /24 matches 8.8.8.8.

whyWrong.0: Printed order does not override the different metrics.
whyWrong.2: The metrics differ; this is not an equal-cost selection.
whyWrong.3: 8.8.8.8 is outside both connected networks.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes IPv4 link-local addressing?
options: It supplies a routable fallback gateway for Internet access
It can appear only on Windows, never on Linux or macOS
It proves no DHCP reply of any kind reached the client
It uses 169.254.0.0/16 and is intended for local-link communication
questions.explanation: IPv4 link-local addresses are link-scoped. Operating-system and profile behavior varies; a displayed fallback address alone does not reconstruct every DHCP packet or exclude other usable adapters/address families.

whyWrong.0: Link-local addressing is not an Internet routing fallback.
whyWrong.1: Other operating systems can implement IPv4 link-local addressing.
whyWrong.2: A failed lease may involve several DHCP stages; an address display is not a packet trace.

questions.prompt: Only the DNS server selection differs from the intended client plan. Server-A has a verified A record for intranet.example → 192.168.50.20. Numeric HTTP works, but a fresh query is sent to unused 192.168.40.99 and times out. Which correction addresses the shown fault?
options: Set the client's DNS server to Server-A at 192.168.40.20
Set the client's default gateway to the unused .40.99 address
Change the client's mask from /24 to /16 for wider local reach
Replace the verified A record with the router's gateway address
questions.explanation: The intended resolver is .40.20, while the failed query targets unused .40.99. Correcting that selection addresses the demonstrated fault; the numeric HTTP result only establishes that tested IP/application path.

whyWrong.1: The unused address is not the intended next hop.
whyWrong.2: A broader mask does not select the proper DNS service and can introduce an on-link error.
whyWrong.3: The record is stipulated correct and should remain pointed at the web server.

questions.prompt: Which macOS command reports current DNS resolver configuration, including supplemental domain-specific resolvers?
options: networksetup -listallhardwareports
route -n get default
scutil --dns
ifconfig -a
questions.explanation: scutil --dns reports resolver configuration. Supplemental domain-specific resolvers can affect VPN queries, so do not assume a single displayed nameserver handles every name.

whyWrong.0: This maps hardware ports/services to interface names.
whyWrong.1: This reports a default route, not resolver selection.
whyWrong.3: The interface-address display does not provide the complete resolver configuration.

questions.prompt: On Windows, `Test-NetConnection 192.168.50.20 -Port 443` reports TCP success. Which conclusion stays within that evidence?
options: The tested TCP connection succeeded; TLS and the application still need verification
The web certificate must be trusted because TCP used the HTTPS port
The client's DNS configuration is correct because the destination was numeric
The IPv6 route must work because the same server supports both address families
questions.explanation: A successful TCP connection tests transport reachability to that address/port. A numeric IPv4 test does not validate DNS, IPv6, TLS certificates or application authorization.

whyWrong.1: Certificate verification occurs in TLS, after the underlying TCP connection.
whyWrong.2: A numeric target does not require name resolution for that target.
whyWrong.3: IPv4 success is not proof of IPv6 reachability.

cards.front: IPv4 link-local prefix and dynamic selection range?
cards.back: The prefix is 169.254.0.0/16, mask 255.255.0.0. RFC 3927 selects from 169.254.1.0–169.254.254.255, excluding the first/last /24. It is not routed Internet fallback.

cards.front: What does DHCP-enabled Windows autoconfiguration suggest?
cards.back: An Autoconfiguration IPv4 Address in 169.254/16 indicates link-local fallback rather than a usable intended lease. It does not identify the exact failed DHCP stage or device.

cards.front: Must Linux DHCP failure look the same on every distribution?
cards.back: No. Manager/profile settings can leave no usable IPv4 address, retain other configuration, or provide link-local fallback. Inspect actual configuration and manager evidence.

cards.front: Windows command for detailed adapter IP, DHCP and DNS settings?
cards.back: `ipconfig /all`. Identify the intended adapter; DHCP-enabled addressing does not prove every DNS value came from DHCP.

cards.front: Windows DHCP release/renew versus DNS cache clearing?
cards.back: `ipconfig /release` then `/renew` changes DHCP lease state and interrupts connectivity. `ipconfig /flushdns` clears the resolver cache, not the address lease.

cards.front: How are competing Windows routes selected?
cards.back: Inspect `route print -4` or `-6`. Longest matching prefix comes first; for matching routes of equal prefix length, the lower effective metric is preferred.

cards.front: Does a gateway entry in the ARP cache prove the current path works?
cards.back: No. `arp -a` shows a stored mapping that may be stale/static/incorrect. Combine it with fresh traffic and link/route evidence.

cards.front: macOS masks: 0xffffff00 and 0xffffff80?
cards.back: 255.255.255.0 (/24) and 255.255.255.128 (/25). Each f gives four one-bits, and 0x80 adds one further one-bit.

cards.front: macOS command for the default IPv4 route?
cards.back: `route -n get default`; `netstat -rn` gives broader route information. Check the actual interface and any more specific route for the destination.

cards.front: macOS service details versus complete DNS resolver configuration?
cards.back: `networksetup -getinfo "Wi-Fi"` reads that named service's IP details; `scutil --dns` reports current resolvers, including supplemental domain-specific configuration.

cards.front: Linux command for compact addresses and prefixes?
cards.back: `ip -br address`. Use full address output and network-manager/lease information when investigating acquisition; one route label does not prove every address came from DHCP.

cards.front: In `default via 10.1.20.1 ... src 10.1.20.59`, which is the gateway?
cards.back: The next hop is 10.1.20.1 after `via`. `src` is the preferred local source address. Inspect other routes before applying the default to a destination.

cards.front: Linux: why might resolv.conf show only 127.0.0.53?
cards.back: It can point to systemd-resolved's local DNS stub. Inspect `resolvectl status` for per-link upstream information, or the actual manager's tools such as `nmcli device show`.

cards.front: Expected effect of an unused default gateway on a simple single-homed LAN?
cards.back: Local peers can remain reachable while traffic needing the default route fails. This assumes no alternate routes; verify the configured next hop and neighbor resolution.

cards.front: Numeric access works but a fresh name lookup times out: next check?
cards.back: Read the actual resolver choice and query result, then test its service/path and the record. Numeric success does not prove that every mask, route or application is correct.

cards.front: How can a mask that is too wide break selected destinations?
cards.back: The client may consider a remote destination on-link and try direct ARP instead of its gateway. Proxy ARP can conceal this under some conditions; compute the actual prefix decision.

cards.front: Wireless profile fields to compare with the intended WLAN?
cards.back: SSID, security/authentication mode and required credentials. SSIDs are case-sensitive, up to 32 octets. WPA2-Personal passphrase rules are not universal rules for WPA3/Enterprise.

cards.front: Why can WPA2 association exist before a wrong-key failure?
cards.back: Initial 802.11 association can precede the four-way key handshake. Failed key agreement prevents usable protected data; OS connection/error displays vary.

cards.front: Connected Wi-Fi plus no usable DHCP lease: what should be checked?
cards.back: The current wireless/security state, intended WLAN-to-LAN/VLAN path, and DHCP request/reply evidence. A connection icon alone does not isolate a unique cause.

cards.front: A disciplined client troubleshooting sequence?
cards.back: Identify the adapter/address family; compare address/prefix/routes/DNS/security; test local, routed, DNS and application paths; repair one demonstrated fault and repeat its test.

commands.task: Display Windows adapter IP settings, DHCP details and DNS configuration.
commands.note: Read the intended adapter; disconnected unused adapters need not be the active fault.

commands.task: On an isolated Windows DHCP lab PC, request renewal on the adapter named Ethernet.
commands.note: Renewal may change configuration. Do not release a working remote-session adapter without an intended maintenance action.

commands.task: Display the Windows IPv4 routing table explicitly.
commands.note: Compare longest matching prefixes before metrics; use -6 separately for IPv6.

commands.task: Display current Windows wireless interface connection details.
commands.note: SSID/security fields may be restricted by permissions or OS release. A connected indication does not validate the whole data path.
