commands.task: In an approved Windows lab, clear the DNS resolver cache.
commands.note: This does not renew a DHCP lease or repair a server record.

commands.task: On macOS, display the default IPv4 route and its interface.
commands.note: Use netstat -rn separately for the broader route table.

commands.task: On macOS, report current DNS resolvers including supplemental domain-specific configuration.
commands.note: A single service's manually configured DNS list is not an equivalent complete resolver view.

commands.task: On Linux, show each interface and its addresses in the brief form.
commands.note: Full ip address output is useful too, but it is not the brief format requested.

commands.task: On Linux, show the IPv4 routing table.
commands.note: The default via entry is a fallback; more specific destination routes take precedence.

commands.task: On a Linux machine using systemd-resolved, display resolver status.
commands.note: The local stub address alone is not the upstream server configuration.

commands.task: On an IOS DHCP server, list current address bindings for comparison with the client's identifier.
commands.note: A missing binding does not prove a DISCOVER never arrived; investigate server pool state and the actual exchange.

commands.task: On NetworkManager Linux, show detailed current device configuration including IP gateway and DNS information.
commands.note: This reads device information; device reapply is not a universal DHCP renewal operation.

tickets.title: A static client reaches local peers but selects an unused gateway
tickets.scenario: A single-homed sales PC has no VPN or alternate routes. The verified network plan assigns 10.1.20.57/24 to this PC and 10.1.20.1 to its router. Address 10.1.20.254 is unused. A local file server at .20 responds. Other clients can reach the approved remote test server at 10.1.50.20. These are representative diagnostic observations.

exhibits.title: PC configuration
exhibits.text:
DHCP Enabled: No
IPv4 Address: 10.1.20.57
Subnet Mask: 255.255.255.0
Default Gateway: 10.1.20.254
DNS Server: 10.1.10.5

exhibits.title: Packet/route worksheet
exhibits.text:
Only default route: 0.0.0.0/0 via 10.1.20.254
Remote numeric test: 10.1.50.20
Observed ARP: Who has 10.1.20.254? Tell 10.1.20.57
No reply to these ARP requests is observed.

tickets.question: Which configuration fault is directly supported?
options: The DNS record for the remote server is missing
The default route names the unused address .254 instead of router .1
The /24 mask places 10.1.20.1 outside the local subnet
The DHCP server silently replaced every static field
tickets.explanation: The actual plan, route and ARP observations agree: the host is trying to resolve an unused next hop. The test is numeric, the /24 includes .1, and the address is statically configured; none of the alternatives explains the shown route.
tickets.fix:
On this approved isolated/static client, open its adapter's IPv4 settings and retain 10.1.20.57 with mask 255.255.255.0 and DNS 10.1.10.5; correct only the default gateway to 10.1.20.1. Then test:

```text
ping 10.1.20.1
arp -a
ping 10.1.50.20
```
Inspect the fresh neighbor/route evidence and then test the intended DNS/application operation. A ping timeout alone would not have proven this cause; the configuration plan and ARP evidence support it.

tickets.title: The new WLAN's DHCP requests stop at the routing boundary
tickets.scenario: STAFF-WLAN is intended to bridge clients into VLAN 30, 10.1.30.0/24. Current AP/controller records confirm the affected client is authorized for protected data on that VLAN. The only DHCP server is 10.1.10.5 on another routed subnet. Its VLAN 30 pool has free addresses, correct options and a verified return route. No local DHCP service exists in VLAN 30. Wired VLAN 20 leases work.

exhibits.title: Client details
exhibits.text:
Current SSID: STAFF-WLAN
DHCP Enabled: Yes
IPv4: 169.254.77.201/16 (Autoconfiguration)
Default gateway: none

exhibits.title: R1 subinterface configuration
exhibits.text:
interface GigabitEthernet0/0.20
 encapsulation dot1Q 20
 ip address 10.1.20.1 255.255.255.0
 ip helper-address 10.1.10.5
interface GigabitEthernet0/0.30
 encapsulation dot1Q 30
 ip address 10.1.30.1 255.255.255.0

exhibits.title: Observed DHCP request path
exhibits.text:
Client DHCP broadcast is observed entering R1 in VLAN 30.
No relayed request from R1 for that transaction is observed at 10.1.10.5.

tickets.question: Which missing configuration explains the demonstrated DHCP delivery fault?
options: A different WPA2 passphrase on every client
A DNS suffix appended to the existing client hostname
A DHCP relay destination on the VLAN 30 router interface
An additional default route pointing every host at the DHCP server
tickets.explanation: The verified protected data path carries the broadcast to R1, but the server is across a router and VLAN 30 has no relay configuration. The evidence and stated healthy pool distinguish this from a guessed key or exhaustion problem. A Wi-Fi icon and APIPA alone would not have established this diagnosis.
tickets.fix:
Configure the relay destination on the client-facing subinterface:

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0.30
R1(config-subif)# ip helper-address 10.1.10.5
R1(config-subif)# end
R1# show ip interface gigabitethernet0/0.30
```
Verify the helper address, then request a lease on one isolated client using its supported OS procedure. Inspect the request/reply path and confirm a 10.1.30.0/24 lease, gateway 10.1.30.1, intended DNS and actual application access. Save only the verified configuration as a separate prompted operation.

sections.title: Define the problem and preserve evidence
Interfaces, counters, MAC and ARP tables

lab.title: Diagnose four faults on a two-router path
lab.intro: Build a working network, collect its baseline, and break one feature at a time. For each fault, record the symptom, evidence, proposed cause, repair, and client retest. All outputs described below are expected or representative teaching evidence; this lab has not been manually executed in Packet Tracer or CML. Simulator support and response wording vary.
lab.topology:
```diagram
{"type":"topology","title":"Two LANs with a routed transit","caption":"The server and client each need their local gateway; R2 also needs a route back to the client LAN.","nodes":[{"id":"PC","kind":"pc","label":"PC-A","sub":"10.0.10.50/24","x":1,"y":1},{"id":"S1","kind":"switch","label":"SW1","sub":"VLAN 10","x":4,"y":1},{"id":"R1","kind":"router","label":"R1","x":8,"y":1},{"id":"R2","kind":"router","label":"R2","x":8,"y":5},{"id":"S2","kind":"switch","label":"SW2","sub":"VLAN 20","x":4,"y":5},{"id":"SRV","kind":"server","label":"SRV","sub":"10.0.20.10/24","x":1,"y":5}],"links":[{"from":"PC","to":"S1","toLabel":"Fa0/1"},{"from":"S1","to":"R1","fromLabel":"Fa0/24","toLabel":"Gi0/0"},{"from":"R1","to":"R2","fromLabel":"Gi0/1","toLabel":"Gi0/1","label":"10.0.99.0/30","accent":true},{"from":"R2","to":"S2","fromLabel":"Gi0/0","toLabel":"Fa0/24"},{"from":"S2","to":"SRV","fromLabel":"Fa0/1"}]}
```

| Device/interface | Address and mask | Connection/cable |
|---|---|---|
| PC-A FastEthernet0 | 10.0.10.50, 255.255.255.0; gateway 10.0.10.1; DNS 10.0.20.10 | SW1 Fa0/1, straight-through |
| R1 Gi0/0 | 10.0.10.1, 255.255.255.0 | SW1 Fa0/24, straight-through |
| R1 Gi0/1 | 10.0.99.1, 255.255.255.252 | R2 Gi0/1, crossover or Auto-Connect |
| R2 Gi0/1 | 10.0.99.2, 255.255.255.252 | R1 Gi0/1, same transit cable |
| R2 Gi0/0 | 10.0.20.1, 255.255.255.0 | SW2 Fa0/24, straight-through |
| SRV FastEthernet0 | 10.0.20.10, 255.255.255.0; gateway 10.0.20.1; DNS 10.0.20.10 | SW2 Fa0/1, straight-through |

All devices are fresh lab devices. Switch ports are access ports, with no trunks required. Leave 10.0.20.99 unused for a later DNS fault. This is an isolated simulated network; no Internet connection or NAT is required.

steps.title: Build the complete baseline
steps.body:
Cable the listed ports. Set PC-A and SRV under Desktop → IP Configuration. Open each Cisco CLI, decline the initial setup dialog if offered, and configure the following. If a logging command is unsupported, record that limitation and use current interface state plus Simulation observations for the log portion.

```ios R1
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R1
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.0.10.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.0.99.1 255.255.255.252
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# ip route 10.0.20.0 255.255.255.0 10.0.99.2
R1(config)# service timestamps log datetime msec
R1(config)# logging buffered 16384 informational
R1(config)# end
```

```ios R2
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R2
R2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R2(config-if)# ip address 10.0.99.2 255.255.255.252
R2(config-if)# no shutdown
R2(config-if)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R2(config-if)# ip address 10.0.20.1 255.255.255.0
R2(config-if)# no shutdown
R2(config-if)# exit
R2(config)# ip route 10.0.10.0 255.255.255.0 10.0.99.1
R2(config)# service timestamps log datetime msec
R2(config)# logging buffered 16384 informational
R2(config)# end
```

```ios SW1
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname SW1
SW1(config)# vlan 10
SW1(config-vlan)# name USERS
SW1(config-vlan)# vlan 20
SW1(config-vlan)# name FAULT-TEST
SW1(config-vlan)# exit
SW1(config)# interface range fastethernet0/1, fastethernet0/24
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport access vlan 10
SW1(config-if-range)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if-range)# end
```

```ios SW2
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname SW2
SW2(config)# vlan 20
SW2(config-vlan)# name SERVERS
SW2(config-vlan)# exit
SW2(config)# interface range fastethernet0/1, fastethernet0/24
SW2(config-if-range)# switchport mode access
SW2(config-if-range)# switchport access vlan 20
SW2(config-if-range)# no shutdown
SW2(config-if-range)# end
```

On SRV → Services, turn HTTP and DNS On. Add A record `app.lab.example` with address `10.0.20.10`, and a second A record `fresh.lab.example` with the same address. Leave DHCP Off on SRV; R2 will supply an optional DHCP demonstration later. Wait for switch ports to reach forwarding before testing.

:::expected
The router interfaces become up/up with the table's addresses. SW1 VLAN 10 contains Fa0/1 and Fa0/24; SW2 VLAN 20 contains its two used ports. Both static routes are installed. Server records use the intended address; neither .99 nor a public resolver is involved.
:::

steps.title: Record a healthy path and a sourced test
steps.body:
On PC-A run these commands, then open Web Browser to `http://10.0.20.10` and `http://app.lab.example`.

```text
ipconfig /all
ping 10.0.10.1
ping 10.0.20.10
nslookup app.lab.example
tracert 10.0.20.10
```

If PC `nslookup` is absent, use a fresh name-based ping and inspect the DNS PDU in Simulation. On R1, compare two source addresses. If one-line `source` syntax is unavailable, enter `ping`, supply the target, choose extended commands `y`, and enter the required source; accept unrelated defaults. Use that same alternative throughout the lab.

```ios R1
R1# show ip interface brief
R1# show ip route
R1# show arp
R1# show cdp neighbors
R1# ping 10.0.20.10 source 10.0.99.1
R1# ping 10.0.20.10 source 10.0.10.1
R1# copy running-config startup-config
```

```ios R2
R2# show ip route
R2# show logging
R2# copy running-config startup-config
```

```ios SW1
SW1# show interfaces status
SW1# show mac address-table
SW1# copy running-config startup-config
```

```ios SW2
SW2# copy running-config startup-config
```

Accept the destination filename prompt with Enter. Save the project as `toolkit-baseline.pkt`, then use Save As `toolkit-work.pkt` before injecting faults. Record PC-A's actual MAC address from its configuration/PC output.

:::expected
Both source tests and the client tests succeed after any transient startup delays. The name resolves to .20.10 and HTTP works. A conventional PC trace can show R1, R2, and SRV; exact interface addresses and response timing may differ. Do not require an initial ping loss. The next-hop ARP entries and PC MAC appear after relevant traffic; a successful test is stronger evidence than assuming an entry must already exist.
:::

steps.title: Remove and diagnose the return route
steps.body:
Keep all client settings unchanged. Remove only R2's return route:

```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# no ip route 10.0.10.0 255.255.255.0 10.0.99.1
R2(config)# end
R2# show ip route
```

```ios R1
R1# ping 10.0.20.10 source 10.0.99.1
R1# ping 10.0.20.10 source 10.0.10.1
```

Repeat PC-A's server-address ping and trace. In Simulation mode, clear old events, filter ICMP and ARP, generate one test, and inspect the forward request and return attempt. If the simulator does not expose a particular drop reason, record the available route and PDU evidence instead.

:::expected
The transit-source ping works because R2 knows 10.0.99.0/30. The LAN-source and PC tests fail because R2 now lacks a route to 10.0.10.0/24 and has no default. A trace may lose later responses even while forward probes progress. The route table establishes the cause here; source-test failure alone would also be compatible with source-based filtering.
:::

steps.title: Restore the return route and verify the client
steps.body:
```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# ip route 10.0.10.0 255.255.255.0 10.0.99.1
R2(config)# end
R2# show ip route 10.0.10.50
```

```ios R1
R1# ping 10.0.20.10 source 10.0.10.1
```

Return Simulation to Realtime after observation. Repeat PC-A's ping and HTTP-by-name test. Write the cause and recovery evidence before continuing.

:::expected
R2 selects the static return route through 10.0.99.1; the LAN-source ping and client HTTP work. The earlier failure is resolved before another fault is introduced.
:::

steps.title: Diagnose a shutdown at the far endpoint
steps.body:
Shut only R2's transit interface, then inspect both ends.

```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R2(config-if)# shutdown
R2(config-if)# end
R2# show ip interface brief
R2# show logging
```

```ios R1
R1# show ip interface brief
R1# show ip route
R1# show cdp neighbors
R1# show logging
```

Repeat PC-A's gateway and server pings. Keep current evidence; do not clear logs.

:::expected
R2 reports Gi0/1 administratively down. R1's peer link normally reports down/down, and its static route loses usable next-hop resolution. PC-A can still reach R1's LAN address but not SRV. A cached CDP entry may persist until it ages; its presence does not override current link state. Log messages and timing vary, but R2's administrative state directly identifies the deliberate shutdown.
:::

steps.title: Restore the transit interface
steps.body:
```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R2(config-if)# no shutdown
R2(config-if)# end
R2# show ip interface brief
```

```ios R1
R1# show ip route
R1# ping 10.0.20.10 source 10.0.10.1
```

Repeat the client's server ping and HTTP test after convergence.

:::expected
The transit becomes up/up, the intended routes are installed, and both sourced and client tests work. Record restoration separately from the earlier fault evidence.
:::

steps.title: Move the client into the wrong access VLAN
steps.body:
```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# switchport access vlan 20
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show interfaces status
SW1# show vlan brief
```

Keep PC-A's 10.0.10.50/24 settings unchanged. Ping its gateway, then inspect the MAC table. On R1, ping 10.0.10.50 and inspect ARP. Existing cached entries can persist; use the current VLAN configuration and newly generated frames rather than demanding instantaneous table erasure.

```ios SW1
SW1# show mac address-table
```

```ios R1
R1# ping 10.0.10.50
R1# show arp
```

:::expected
The physical PC link remains connected, but its port is now in VLAN 20 while R1's port remains in VLAN 10. New source frames from PC-A are learned in VLAN 20. Gateway communication fails despite link-up status. ARP may be incomplete, absent, or temporarily stale depending on timing; the mismatched VLAN membership supplies the decisive evidence.
:::

steps.title: Restore the client VLAN
steps.body:
```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# switchport access vlan 10
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show vlan brief
```

Repeat gateway and server pings from PC-A, then inspect the MAC table again.

:::expected
PC-A's new source frames appear in VLAN 10 on Fa0/1, and the intended service works. Old entries in another VLAN may age independently; judge current forwarding from the test and intended configuration.
:::

steps.title: Introduce a valid but wrong DNS answer
steps.body:
On SRV → Services → DNS, edit only `app.lab.example` to `10.0.20.99`, the unused address. Keep `fresh.lab.example` unchanged. From PC-A, explicitly query `app.lab.example` with `nslookup` if supported and compare the answer with a ping to `10.0.20.10`. Inspect the DNS response in Simulation. If the client uses cached data or lacks the direct-query tool, add a new fault-test name `wrong.lab.example` → .20.99 and query that new name.

:::expected
The controlled IP-address service remains reachable. The fresh/direct DNS result points to unused .20.99, so a name-based connection cannot reach the intended server. This is a received positive answer containing wrong design data, distinct from NXDOMAIN or silence. Record what was actually queried and returned.
:::

steps.title: Restore DNS and verify the complete service
steps.body:
Restore `app.lab.example` → `10.0.20.10` and delete optional `wrong.lab.example`. Repeat a direct query and browser test. If an application retains stale data, close and reopen it or use a new correctly configured test name, recording the cache limitation instead of changing unrelated routing.

:::expected
The responsible DNS service returns .20.10 and the client's intended HTTP test works. Verify the returned address as well as the page. All four injected faults have now been restored.
:::

steps.title: Trace a fresh DHCP transaction through the same path
steps.body:
This additional integration exercise uses R2 as the DHCP server and R1 as relay. Keep SRV DHCP Off. Configure a pool beginning at .100, distinct from PC-A's old static .50 address.

```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# service dhcp
R2(config)# ip dhcp excluded-address 10.0.10.1 10.0.10.99
R2(config)# ip dhcp pool USERS
R2(dhcp-config)# network 10.0.10.0 255.255.255.0
R2(dhcp-config)# default-router 10.0.10.1
R2(dhcp-config)# dns-server 10.0.20.10
R2(dhcp-config)# end
```

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# service dhcp
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ip helper-address 10.0.99.2
R1(config-if)# end
```

In Simulation, filter DHCP and ARP and clear previous events. Change PC-A → Desktop → IP Configuration to DHCP, then use Capture/Forward until allocation completes. Inspect the original request on the LAN, the relayed request toward R2, and delivery back to PC-A. Return to Realtime before subsequent pings. Inspect `show ip dhcp binding` on R2 and actual client settings.

:::expected
PC-A receives an available .100–.254 address, /24 mask, gateway .10.1, and DNS .20.10; do not assume allocation of the numerically first address. The relay's giaddr identifies 10.0.10.1. Offer/ACK delivery can be broadcast or unicast depending on client state and flags. A simulated event may appear at several devices, so the event count is not a protocol message count. Client HTTP still works with the new source.
:::

steps.title: Save the verified final state
steps.body:
Keep the verified DHCP client/relay/server configuration as the final extension. Record PC-A's assigned address and the differences from the initial static baseline. Verify both router interfaces, routes, switch membership, DNS response, and HTTP. Save each Cisco device from privileged EXEC with `copy running-config startup-config`, then save the project as `toolkit-complete.pkt`. Preserve `toolkit-baseline.pkt` separately.

:::expected
The final network has no outstanding injected fault. Four device startup configurations and the Packet Tracer project are saved; notes contain the original symptoms and the evidence supporting each repair. No debug or experimental capture is left running.
:::

lab.troubleshooting:
- If the first baseline fails, inspect exact masks, both host gateways, switch membership, and both static routes before injecting any fault.
- A failed ping with stars or periods does not identify a unique failure; compare source, route lookup, current link state, and capture point.
- If pipe filters or `show running-config interface` are unsupported, use the complete `show running-config` and locate the intended interface manually.
- Empty logs can reflect destination configuration, buffer history, or simulator limits. Use current configuration/state and record the missing evidence.
- A missing DNS event can mean cached resolution, a different test name, an incorrect resolver, or capture filtering; inspect these before blaming the server.
lab.challenge:
Starting from the saved static baseline, change only SRV's default gateway to unused `10.0.20.254`. Before repairing it, predict these results: R2 pinging SRV from .20.1; R1 pinging SRV from .99.1; PC-A pinging its own gateway; and PC-A reaching SRV. Identify a direct observation that distinguishes this from a missing route on R2. Restore the exact original gateway and verify the client.

:::expected
R2's server-LAN-source ping can succeed locally; SRV needs no gateway to reply to .20.1. R1's .99.1-source ping and PC-A's remote test fail because SRV tries to return off-subnet traffic through nonexistent .20.254. PC-A's local gateway ping still works. R2's route to the client remains installed, while SRV's configuration and ARP attempts identify the wrong next hop. Restore SRV's gateway to 10.0.20.1, then verify both router-source tests, client DNS, and HTTP. Exact timeout text is not required evidence.
:::

exhibit.title: Representative teaching evidence
exhibit.text:
Sending 5, 100-byte ICMP Echos; timeout 2 seconds:
.!!!!
Success rate: 80 percent (4/5)

questions.prompt: What does this ping result establish?
options: One request did not receive a reply within its wait; the cause needs more evidence.
The first request was definitely discarded during ARP resolution.
A routing update installed the route immediately after the first request.
The destination enforced a four-reply ICMP limit for this source.
questions.explanation: The period reports a timeout and the four exclamation marks report replies. ARP startup delay is one possible explanation; repeat the test and correlate a current ARP/capture observation before assigning that cause.

whyWrong.1: The output contains no ARP observation.
whyWrong.2: No routing change is shown.
whyWrong.3: Four replies do not establish a configured response limit.

exhibit.title: Representative teaching evidence
exhibit.text:
R1# ping 10.0.50.1
U.U.U
Success rate: 0 percent

questions.prompt: What conclusion follows from the U characters?
options: The source router had no usable interface for every probe.
Destination-unreachable responses were reported for some probes.
The destination application accepted and then closed its connections.
Each period proves a fixed 500-ms ICMP response limiter on R2.
questions.explanation: U indicates unreachable evidence, unlike a period indicating a wait expired. Inspect the ICMP source and code, then routing/policy, rather than infer one device or a fixed rate limiter from the pattern.

whyWrong.0: The display does not establish all interfaces were unusable.
whyWrong.2: Echo testing does not create an application connection.
whyWrong.3: The pattern alone supplies neither the timer nor its location.

questions.prompt: Which two statements correctly compare conventional IOS traceroute and Windows tracert? Select two.
options: IOS normally requires an HTTP response from the destination.
Windows tracert normally probes by establishing TCP port 49.
IOS normally uses UDP probes toward high destination ports.
Windows tracert normally uses ICMP echo requests.
questions.explanation: Both use increasing TTL to obtain transit time-exceeded responses. Their probe protocols differ, which matters when comparing source and policy paths.

whyWrong.0: A conventional UDP trace normally ends with destination port-unreachable evidence, not HTTP.
whyWrong.1: TCP 49 belongs to TACACS+, not the normal Windows trace method.

questions.prompt: A web application is slow. Which interpretation of this trace is justified?
options: The third router dropped every packet and caused the slow application.
The three stars establish three seconds of forwarding delay for each user packet.
The destination replies certify that HTTP performance is normal.
Later probes received replies, so the middle stars alone do not prove a forwarding break.
questions.explanation: A star is a missing probe response within the wait. Later replies weaken the claim of a complete path break, but load sharing, response policy, and application behavior still require investigation.

whyWrong.0: Later responses contradict an assertion that all traffic necessarily stops there.
whyWrong.1: A response timeout is not a measurement of per-packet forwarding delay.
whyWrong.2: Traceroute does not test the HTTP transaction.

exhibit.title: Representative teaching evidence
exhibit.text: Gi0/1 10.0.99.1 YES manual down down

questions.prompt: On this routed Ethernet interface, what should be investigated first?
options: Local media and peer link availability, including the far-end administrative state.
The local shutdown command, which is directly shown by this status.
The DHCP lease duration, which controls Ethernet carrier detection.
The DNS suffix, which determines whether line protocol can start.
questions.explanation: Down/down directs attention to physical/link availability and the peer. It does not uniquely identify a cable defect; a local shutdown normally has the distinct administratively-down status.

whyWrong.1: This is not the displayed administrative-shutdown state.
whyWrong.2: A DHCP timer does not establish Ethernet carrier.
whyWrong.3: DNS suffix selection is unrelated to link detection.

exhibit.title: Representative teaching evidence
exhibit.text:
SW1 Fa0/24: 100 Mb/s, half duplex; late collisions rose 40→65
R1 Gi0/0: speed 100; duplex full

questions.prompt: Which demonstrated problem should be corrected before further performance testing?
options: The late-collision count measures the number of full output queues.
The two endpoints operate at different duplex settings.
The link operates at different speeds at its endpoints.
The zero input CRC count proves every cable pair is undamaged.
questions.explanation: Half duplex at SW1 and full duplex at R1 establishes a mismatch. Coordinate matching supported settings at both ends, then compare new error increments; clean CRC alone does not certify media.

whyWrong.0: Late collisions and output-queue drops are different events.
whyWrong.2: Both displayed speeds are 100 Mb/s.
whyWrong.3: One clean counter is not a cable certification.

exhibit.title: Representative teaching evidence
exhibit.text:
R1 source 10.0.99.1 → 10.0.20.10: success
R1 source 10.0.10.1 → 10.0.20.10: failure
PC-A 10.0.10.50/24: local gateway ping succeeds

questions.prompt: R1 can ping the server from its transit source, but not from its LAN source. What should the engineer check next?
options: Rebuild the forward route, because the two source tests prove it is absent.
Remove the server gateway, because the server can reply locally.
Return routes and source-dependent policy for the LAN-source address.
Replace the PC cable, because the router test passed through it.
questions.explanation: Changing the source changes the return destination and may change policy handling. The failed sourced test supports investigating those differences; it does not alone prove a missing route.

whyWrong.0: One successful server test contradicts a blanket claim that no forward path exists.
whyWrong.1: Off-subnet replies generally require the intended gateway.
whyWrong.3: A router-originated test did not traverse the PC cable.

exhibit.title: Representative teaching evidence
exhibit.text:
logging trap warnings
%LINK-3-UPDOWN: Gi0/1 changed state to down
%LINEPROTO-5-UPDOWN: Gi0/1 line protocol changed state to down

questions.prompt: Which shown message is eligible for remote syslog at the configured threshold?
options: Only the severity-5 LINEPROTO message is selected by this threshold.
Both messages are selected because both concern the same interface.
Neither message is selected because warnings means exactly severity 4.
Only the severity-3 LINK message is selected by this threshold.
questions.explanation: Warnings admits severity 4 and lower-numbered, more severe messages. This selects the severity-3 message; actual receipt still requires a working logging path.

whyWrong.0: Severity 5 is less severe than the configured level 4 threshold.
whyWrong.1: Each message is filtered by its own severity.
whyWrong.2: The threshold includes more severe levels, not just exact level 4.

questions.prompt: What does this client-side TCP observation support?
options: A matching reset was received; identify the generating endpoint or intermediary before attributing the refusal.
The SYN was silently discarded and no response reached the client.
The capture alone proves the application server itself generated the reset.
The reset proves the client cannot receive any packet from that direction.
questions.explanation: The reset is an active response, unlike silence. A firewall or intermediary can generate resets using the endpoint address, so correlate server-side capture and service status before declaring the server process at fault.

whyWrong.1: The matching RST is an observed response.
whyWrong.2: The observed source address alone does not exclude an intermediary.
whyWrong.3: The reset itself arrived from that direction.

exhibit.title: Representative teaching evidence
exhibit.text:
Query: app.lab.example A
Response: NXDOMAIN; no alias chain is present

questions.prompt: Which failure stage is directly demonstrated for this exact-name lookup?
options: The resolver reported SERVFAIL while following a delegation.
A DNS response reported the queried name absent.
The client timed out without receiving a DNS response.
The resolver returned an address that the application rejected.
questions.explanation: NXDOMAIN is a received negative name result. Investigate spelling, intended data, and relevant caching; it does not certify every network path or establish that an application connection was attempted.

whyWrong.0: SERVFAIL is a different DNS status.
whyWrong.2: The exhibit contains a response.
whyWrong.3: No address answer or application exchange is shown.

questions.prompt: Which two statements about these tables are accurate? Select two.
options: A learned MAC establishes the host has the correct mask and gateway.
An absent ARP entry proves the host has never received a neighbor reply.
A dynamic MAC entry identifies a VLAN/port that learned that source MAC.
An incomplete ARP entry shows resolution is incomplete at this observation.
questions.explanation: The tables describe different current mappings. Aging, clearing, and recent traffic affect their contents; neither alone certifies host addressing or all historical communication.

whyWrong.0: MAC learning does not inspect the host mask/gateway as proof of correctness.
whyWrong.1: Entries can age or be cleared after earlier successful communication.

exhibit.title: Representative teaching evidence
exhibit.text:
10.0.99.2 → 10.0.10.50
ICMP Destination Unreachable: communication administratively prohibited (type 3, code 13)

questions.prompt: Which next check is supported by the received ICMP error?
options: Replace the missing default route that this code uniquely identifies.
Correct the expired TTL that is explicitly reported in this message.
Repair ARP for the destination because this is a host-unreachable code.
Inspect administrative forwarding policy at the reporting device and the matching flow.
questions.explanation: Type 3 code 13 reports administrative prohibition. It supports investigating policy, but does not identify one exact ACL line without further configuration/counter evidence.

whyWrong.0: No-route evidence would be a different unreachable reason.
whyWrong.1: TTL expiry uses time-exceeded rather than this administrative prohibition.
whyWrong.2: Host unreachable is a different code.

questions.prompt: On supporting IOS, which bounded command compares a 1500-byte IPv4 datagram with the path MTU?
options: ping 10.0.20.10 source 10.0.10.1 repeat 5 size 1500 df-bit
ping 10.0.20.10 source 10.0.10.1 repeat 5 size 1500
ping 10.0.20.10 source 10.0.10.1 repeat 5 size 1472
ping 10.0.20.10 source 10.0.10.1 repeat 5 size 100 df-bit
questions.explanation: IOS size specifies the datagram size in this command and df-bit prevents fragmentation. A received fragmentation-needed error is informative; a timeout alone does not prove the MTU value.

whyWrong.1: Without DF, IPv4 fragmentation can occur.
whyWrong.2: That requests a different IOS datagram size, not 1500.
whyWrong.3: A 100-byte datagram does not perform the requested large-size comparison.

questions.prompt: An engineer begins with an IP-address ping to choose useful next tests above or below Layer 3. Which approach is being used?
options: Follow-the-path checking each router individually.
Divide-and-conquer.
Bottom-up starting at the cable.
Top-down starting at the application transaction.
questions.explanation: A middle-layer test is characteristic of divide-and-conquer. Its result narrows the investigation; a working ping does not clear all lower-layer performance or policy issues.

whyWrong.0: One end-to-end ping does not inspect each router.
whyWrong.2: No initial physical inspection is described.
whyWrong.3: The initial test is not the application transaction.

exhibit.title: Representative teaching evidence
exhibit.text:
Fa0/3: err-disabled
Fa0/4: inactive, configured access VLAN 30
show vlan brief: VLAN 30 absent

questions.prompt: The design requires VLAN 30 on Fa0/4. Which action pair follows the supplied evidence?
options: Disable spanning tree on both ports to restore the missing VLAN.
Move both ports to VLAN 1 without checking the endpoint addressing plan.
Investigate Fa0/3’s recorded protection cause; create the missing intended VLAN 30 for Fa0/4.
Replace both cables; these statuses establish damaged copper at both ports.
questions.explanation: Err-disabled requires its recorded cause and corrective action before controlled recovery. The explicit VLAN inventory identifies the missing intended VLAN for Fa0/4; do not move clients into an unrelated network.

whyWrong.0: Spanning-tree removal does not create the missing VLAN and weakens the design.
whyWrong.1: An arbitrary VLAN move can introduce a separate addressing failure.
whyWrong.3: Neither status proves a damaged cable.

exhibit.title: Representative teaching evidence
exhibit.text:
Server-side: relayed Discover received; Offer sent to giaddr 10.0.10.1
Client-side: Discover transmitted; no Offer observed in the same interval

questions.prompt: Which conclusion is justified by these captures from the same fresh DHCP attempt?
options: The server certainly had no matching pool and never constructed an Offer.
The client certainly received the ACK but lost its default gateway setting.
The helper must be absent because no server reply can exist without it.
Investigate delivery of the Offer from the server through the relay to the client.
questions.explanation: The server-side observation shows an outgoing Offer while the client-side view does not show receipt. Narrow the investigation to return and relay delivery, including capture coverage; do not assert a unique fault yet.

whyWrong.0: An outgoing Offer contradicts the claim that none was constructed.
whyWrong.1: No ACK receipt is shown.
whyWrong.2: A forwarded Discover and outgoing reply have already been observed.

cards.front: What are the referenced IOS basic ping defaults?
cards.back: Five 100-byte datagrams with a two-second wait. Read actual output; tool defaults and payload/datagram size conventions differ.

cards.front: What do IOS !, ., U, and fragmentation-needed evidence mean?
cards.back: ! reports an echo reply; . a wait expiry; U unreachable evidence. A fragmentation-needed error supports an IPv4 DF/MTU constraint; silence alone does not.

cards.front: Does an initial .!!!! prove an ARP delay?
cards.back: No. ARP delay is possible, but the timeout itself does not identify a cause. Repeat and correlate current ARP/capture evidence.

cards.front: How is a period different from an unreachable result?
cards.back: A period reports no timely usable reply. An unreachable result reports an error; inspect its source/code rather than assume one missing route.

cards.front: How can supporting IOS send five 1500-byte DF probes?
cards.back: ping 10.0.20.10 repeat 5 size 1500 df-bit. IOS datagram size is not the same as a host tool’s payload argument.

cards.front: What changes when you select a router ping source?
cards.back: The reply destination and possibly policy handling change. It helps test return reachability but does not reproduce the PC’s full ingress path.

cards.front: What probes does conventional IOS traceroute use?
cards.back: UDP toward high destination ports beginning at 33434, with increasing TTL. A closed destination port normally returns ICMP port unreachable.

cards.front: How do Windows tracert and Linux traceroute methods differ?
cards.back: Windows normally uses ICMP echo. Common Linux implementations offer UDP, ICMP, and TCP methods; inspect the selected options.

cards.front: Which IPv4 ICMP messages help a conventional trace?
cards.back: Time exceeded type 11/code 0 at transit TTL expiry; destination unreachable type 3/code 3 for a UDP probe to a closed target port.

cards.front: What does a traceroute star report?
cards.back: No usable response for that probe within its wait. It does not prove the probe stopped at the last responding router.

cards.front: How should middle stars and later replies be interpreted?
cards.back: Later probes got replies, so middle stars alone do not prove a complete path break. They also do not certify application performance or one fixed path.

cards.front: What do routed Ethernet administrative down and down/down suggest?
cards.back: Administrative down identifies local shutdown state. Down/down directs investigation toward link/media/peer availability; it is not a unique cable diagnosis.

cards.front: How do err-disabled and inactive guide switch diagnosis?
cards.back: Find the recorded error/protection cause for err-disabled. Inspect intended VLAN availability for inactive; recover only after correcting the demonstrated cause.

cards.front: What directly establishes a duplex mismatch?
cards.back: Different operational duplex settings at the two ends. Late collisions can support the diagnosis; compare both ends and fresh increments.

cards.front: What do CRC, runt/giant, and output-drop counters describe?
cards.back: Received corruption, frames outside accepted size limits, and outgoing drops respectively. Exact counting/size thresholds vary; none alone identifies one physical cause.

cards.front: What are syslog severity levels 0 through 7?
cards.back: Emergency, alert, critical, error, warning, notification, informational, debugging. Lower numbers are more severe.

cards.front: What does logging trap warnings select?
cards.back: Severity 0–4 for the remote logging destination. Selection does not prove collector receipt; check the logging path.

cards.front: How do you request remote terminal logs and stop debugging?
cards.back: terminal monitor requests eligible output for the current remote terminal. undebug all stops enabled debug functions; destination settings and feature support still matter.

cards.front: Does a matching TCP reset prove the server application sent it?
cards.back: No. It is an active response, potentially from an endpoint or intermediary. Correlate server-side evidence; unanswered SYNs leave both directions uncertain.

cards.front: What should a useful troubleshooting note preserve?
cards.back: Affected flow/source, time and clock confidence, original evidence, hypothesis, focused change, and the final client/application retest.

commands.note: Use supported one-line syntax or the interactive extended-ping source prompt. Check return routing and policy.

commands.task: On supporting IOS, send five 1500-byte IPv4 datagrams to 10.0.20.10 with fragmentation prohibited.
commands.note: A received fragmentation-needed message supports an MTU constraint; a timeout alone does not.

commands.task: Trace the route toward 10.0.20.10 using this IOS router’s conventional command.
commands.note: Compare the actual source and probe protocol with the affected client traffic.

commands.task: Display IPv4 addresses and interface status/protocol pairs.
commands.note: Up/up does not certify VLAN, route, or application policy correctness.

commands.task: Display Gi0/1 speed, duplex, and interface counters.
commands.note: Compare counters across a known observation interval and inspect the other endpoint.

commands.task: After preserving the original snapshot, clear this isolated lab’s Gi0/1 counters.
commands.note: Accept the confirmation only for this intended interface. A before/after snapshot can also reveal increments without clearing.

commands.task: Filter buffered log output to lines containing the literal text LINK.
commands.note: The literal LINK filter selects matching LINK events; inspect LINEPROTO separately or use a supported combined expression. Read timestamps with current state.

commands.note: Verify the buffer and severity with show logging; a finite buffer overwrites older records.

commands.note: Monitor destination settings also determine what can appear.

commands.note: A current learned MAC does not establish the host’s IP mask or gateway.

commands.task: Display this router’s IPv4 ARP mappings.
commands.note: Incomplete or absent entries are current observations, not proof the neighbor never replied.
