tickets.title: The transit link is down at both ends
tickets.scenario: R1 Gi0/1 at 10.0.99.1/30 connects directly to R2 Gi0/1 at .2/30. Users behind R1 cannot reach R2’s server LAN. Both routers are available through independent console access. These are representative current records.

exhibits.title: R1 state
exhibits.text: Gi0/1 down/down

exhibits.title: R2 current configuration/state
exhibits.text:
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 ip address 10.0.99.2 255.255.255.252
 shutdown
State: administratively down/down

exhibits.title: R2 relevant event
exhibits.text: %LINK-5-CHANGED: Gi0/1 changed state to administratively down

tickets.question: Which correction addresses the demonstrated configuration fault?
options: Replace R1’s client gateway address.
Remove the unused DNS name from R1.
Restore the intended no-shutdown state on R2 Gi0/1.
Clear R1’s MAC table to create carrier.
tickets.explanation: R2’s current shutdown configuration and administrative state identify the deliberate disabling of the transit. They do not identify who made the change. Restore the approved interface state, then verify both ends, routes, and the client service.
tickets.fix:
```ios
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R2(config-if)# no shutdown
R2(config-if)# end
R2# show ip interface brief
```

Check R1’s state and routes separately, test from the affected PC, and save after verification.

tickets.title: The transit-source test works while client traffic fails
tickets.scenario: PC-A is 10.0.10.50/24, gateway R1 10.0.10.1. R1/R2 transit is 10.0.99.1/.2 on /30. SRV is 10.0.20.10/24 with gateway R2 .20.1. R1 has the intended route to the server; no policy routing is configured.

exhibits.title: R1 paired tests
exhibits.text:
Source 10.0.99.1 to SRV succeeds
Source 10.0.10.1 to SRV fails

exhibits.title: R2 complete installed forwarding prefixes
exhibits.text:
10.0.99.0/30 connected Gi0/1
10.0.20.0/24 connected Gi0/0
Local /32 interface routes only; no other route or default

tickets.question: Which demonstrated missing dependency explains the source difference?
options: R1 has no route toward the server network.
R2 has no route to the client-source subnet.
SRV has no local gateway configured.
PC-A’s access cable is disconnected.
tickets.explanation: R2 can return toward the transit-source .99.1 over a connected route, but no listed prefix matches .10.1 or .10.50. Unlike the source-test result alone, the complete route evidence establishes this missing return route.
tickets.fix:
```ios
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# ip route 10.0.10.0 255.255.255.0 10.0.99.1
R2(config)# end
R2# show ip route 10.0.10.50
```

On R1 separately:
```ios
R1# ping 10.0.20.10 source 10.0.10.1
```
Then verify PC-A by address, name, and actual service before saving.

tickets.title: A 100-Mb/s link has conflicting duplex settings
tickets.scenario: SW1 Fa0/24 connects to R1 Gi0/0. The approved lab design pins both endpoints to 100 Mb/s full duplex. Transfer performance declined after a change. Counters below cover the same current observation interval.

exhibits.title: SW1
exhibits.text:
Fa0/24: 100 Mb/s, half duplex
Late collisions: 100→135

exhibits.title: R1
exhibits.text: Gi0/0: speed 100; duplex full

exhibits.title: Neighbor evidence
exhibits.text: CDP reports local not-full duplex and peer full duplex

tickets.question: Which correction follows the stated design and evidence?
options: Set SW1 Fa0/24 to the intended matching 100/full settings.
Change R1 to 1000/full while retaining SW1 at 100/half.
Clear counters without changing either operational duplex.
Change both endpoint IP masks to /16.
tickets.explanation: The displayed settings directly establish a duplex mismatch. Correct the one deviating endpoint in this explicitly fixed-speed design, then compare fresh increments under a controlled transfer. This does not establish that every other aspect of the link is fault-free.
tickets.fix:
```ios
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/24
SW1(config-if)# speed 100
SW1(config-if)# duplex full
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show interfaces fastethernet0/24
```
Preserve previous counters, verify both endpoints, repeat a bounded transfer, and compare new errors before saving.

sections.title: Reconnaissance, spoofing and denial of service
The security program: awareness, training, physical access

lab.title: Review policy and verify local management controls
lab.intro: Build a small isolated management LAN, verify local SSH, and observe a controlled remote-login block. You will also evaluate controls that a basic simulator cannot implement. Public example passwords are for this disposable lab only. This procedure was reviewed against documentation, not manually executed in Packet Tracer/CML; use the named fallback when a feature is unavailable.
lab.topology:
```diagram
{"type":"topology","title":"Management LAN with a separate console path","caption":"Keep the console available while testing remote access; both PCs are controlled lab clients.","nodes":[{"id":"A","kind":"pc","label":"Admin-PC","sub":"10.0.0.10/24","x":1,"y":1},{"id":"T","kind":"pc","label":"Test-PC","sub":"10.0.0.66/24","x":1,"y":5},{"id":"S","kind":"switch","label":"SW1","x":5,"y":3},{"id":"R","kind":"router","label":"R1","sub":"10.0.0.1/24","x":10,"y":3}],"links":[{"from":"A","to":"S","toLabel":"Fa0/1"},{"from":"T","to":"S","toLabel":"Fa0/2"},{"from":"S","to":"R","fromLabel":"Fa0/24","toLabel":"Gi0/0"},{"from":"A","to":"R","label":"RS-232 to Console","style":"dashed"}]}
```

| Device/interface | IPv4 settings | Cable/port |
|---|---|---|
| R1 Gi0/0 | 10.0.0.1 / 255.255.255.0 | Straight-through to SW1 Fa0/24 |
| Admin-PC FastEthernet0 | 10.0.0.10 / 255.255.255.0; gateway .1 | Straight-through to SW1 Fa0/1 |
| Test-PC FastEthernet0 | 10.0.0.66 / 255.255.255.0; gateway .1 | Straight-through to SW1 Fa0/2 |
| Admin-PC RS-232 | Terminal defaults: 9600 baud, 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit, no flow control | Console cable to R1 Console |

No DNS service, Internet connection, or AAA server is required. All Ethernet ports use VLAN 1. Both PCs and all login attempts belong to this isolated exercise.

steps.title: Define the intended policy on paper
steps.body:
Write a five-row worksheet: named administrator access; protected management transport; restricted handling of configuration backups; bounded idle sessions; recovery during remote-login failure. For each row, record the desired outcome and the evidence you will collect. Add three program actions: a reminder describing how to report suspicious requests, role-specific practice for account recovery, and restricted physical access to the console.

Review this proposed general password policy: “Eight characters, three character classes, shared admin account, change every 60 days.” Identify its weaknesses using current NIST guidance from the lesson and the need for individual accountability. Do not claim that a router length command implements the whole replacement policy.

:::expected
The worksheet separates transport, stored credentials, access, and recovery. For NIST's covered single-factor password use, the revised minimum is 15 characters, with common/compromised-value screening and no mandatory composition or routine expiry rule. A named account, unique secret, managed recovery, and protected backups address additional needs. The simulator cannot certify compliance with that complete policy.
:::

steps.title: Cable and configure the LAN
steps.body:
Use fresh devices and the table's exact cables. Set the two PCs under Desktop → IP Configuration. Open Admin-PC → Desktop → Terminal for R1; decline the initial configuration dialog if offered.

```ios R1
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R1
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.0.0.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip interface brief
```

```ios SW1
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname SW1
SW1(config)# interface range fastethernet0/1 - 2, fastethernet0/24
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport access vlan 1
SW1(config-if-range)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if-range)# end
```

If this image rejects the combined interface range, apply the same three interface commands separately to Fa0/1, Fa0/2, and Fa0/24. Wait for forwarding, then ping 10.0.0.1 from both PCs.

:::expected
R1 Gi0/0 is up/up at .1/24 and both PC pings work. A successful ping tests addressing and ICMP reachability; it does not yet prove that remote management is configured.
:::

steps.title: Create local secrets and SSH
steps.body:
Keep the console open. Configure length, local secrets, and SSH. If `security passwords min-length 15` is unsupported, record the missing enforcement and continue with the supplied longer lab secrets. This fallback does not claim enforcement. Use the basic `secret` form for simulator compatibility; inspect the actual resulting storage type and record if the image provides only a legacy hash.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# security passwords min-length 15
R1(config)# enable secret Lab-Enable-Only-2026!
R1(config)# username admin privilege 15 secret Lab-Admin-Only-2026!
R1(config)# ip domain-name lab.example
R1(config)# crypto key generate rsa general-keys modulus 2048
R1(config)# ip ssh version 2
R1(config)# line console 0
R1(config-line)# login local
R1(config-line)# exec-timeout 10 0
R1(config-line)# exit
R1(config)# line vty 0 4
R1(config-line)# login local
R1(config-line)# transport input ssh
R1(config-line)# exec-timeout 5 0
R1(config-line)# end
R1# show running-config
R1# show ip ssh
```

If the RSA one-line form is rejected, enter `crypto key generate rsa` from global configuration and supply 2048 at the modulus prompt. Inspect the full running configuration. If a `line vty 5 15` block exists, apply its controls too:

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# line vty 5 15
R1(config-line)# login local
R1(config-line)# transport input ssh
R1(config-line)# exec-timeout 5 0
R1(config-line)# end
```

Use this second block only when those lines exist on the selected image. Do not create a different range based on guesswork.

:::expected
A named privilege-15 account and enable secret exist, SSH version 2 is enabled, and every available VTY uses local login, SSH-only transport, and the five-minute timeout. The shown console timeout is ten minutes so you can complete the exercise without accidentally leaving an unattended session indefinitely. Record any unsupported feature instead of treating it as configured.
:::

steps.title: Verify a fresh login and inspect stored credentials
steps.body:
From Admin-PC Command Prompt:

```text
ssh -l admin 10.0.0.1
```

Enter `Lab-Admin-Only-2026!`. Verify the privilege with `show privilege`. Keep this tested SSH session open while you exit and reopen the console Terminal, authenticate as admin, and return to privileged EXEC. Then close the SSH session with `exit`; the console remains your control path.

On the console inspect `show running-config`, without posting the full secrets elsewhere. Interpret this separate paper excerpt:

```output Representative storage labels, values deliberately omitted
username olduser password 7 [omitted]  ← reversible credential exposure
username neweruser secret 9 [omitted]  ← scrypt verifier; still sensitive
```

The bracketed omissions are not valid configurations to paste. Try Telnet from a PC only as a transport check using `telnet 10.0.0.1`; do not supply a credential if any unexpected Telnet prompt appears. Inspect all VTY ranges if Telnet remains available.

:::expected
A fresh SSH login succeeds and reports privilege 15. Console reauthentication also works. Telnet is unavailable through the configured VTY transport. The paper type-7 entry is reversible; type 9 is a slow verifier but still warrants backup access control and a strong secret. Your simulator's actual type is recorded rather than assumed.
:::

steps.title: Configure remote-login observation
steps.body:
Enable the documented IOS login block and logging features from the console. If `login block-for` or `show login` is absent, perform Steps 5–7 as a paper state exercise using the stated configuration and outcomes; do not repeatedly attempt to trigger an unsupported feature. If only login event logging is absent, use `show login` plus the controlled session results and record the logging limitation.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# login block-for 120 attempts 3 within 60
R1(config)# login on-failure log
R1(config)# login on-success log
R1(config)# logging buffered 16384 informational
R1(config)# banner motd #Authorized lab access only. Activity may be logged.#
R1(config)# end
R1# show login
```

Record the configured threshold, watch window, block interval, and whether a quiet-mode exception is shown. Save the working state to a separate project file `security-before-test.pkt` before inducing failures.

:::expected
On a supporting image, login monitoring is enabled with the intended values and starts in normal mode. The banner communicates policy but does not enforce authentication. Existing console access remains available during the later remote block on the documented IOS feature.
:::

steps.title: Observe the controlled remote block
steps.body:
From Test-PC, make a small bounded set of new SSH attempts to `admin` using an intentionally wrong lab password. Use at most four failed attempts within the 60-second window and inspect `show login` on the console after each. Stop as soon as Quiet-Mode appears. If the image does not reproduce the documented behavior, stop testing and record its output; use the paper expectation rather than launching a guessing loop.

While Quiet-Mode is displayed, try one fresh SSH login from Admin-PC with the correct password. Keep using the established console to collect `show login` and `show logging`. Do not claim a precise message sequence if the simulator prints different text.

:::expected
With no quiet-mode exception, documented IOS restricts new remote Telnet/SSH logins during the quiet interval, including the correct Admin-PC attempt. The existing console is usable. This demonstrates a remote block, not a per-user lockout, and not permanent failure of the password. A paper result can state “87 seconds remain,” but no actual remaining value is guaranteed.
:::

steps.title: Recover and verify normal operation separately
steps.body:
Allow the remaining block interval shown by `show login` to expire while retaining console access. Then run `show login` again and open a fresh successful Admin-PC SSH session. If an unexpectedly persistent experimental block requires rollback, use the console to remove the experimental policy:

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# no login block-for
R1(config)# end
R1# show login
```

Reapply the Step 5 `login block-for 120 attempts 3 within 60` command only after normal access is verified and the selected image supports the exercise. Do not change an otherwise correct password to repair quiet mode.

:::expected
Normal mode permits the valid SSH login again. Your notes distinguish waiting for the defined interval from removal of the experimental feature. No wrong credential was promoted to a valid one. Record whether the final configuration retains the supported block or uses the documented paper fallback.
:::

steps.title: Finish the policy review and save
steps.body:
Inspect all VTY ranges, actual secret types, SSH status, and login state. Verify a new admin session, then close unused remote sessions. On R1 and SW1 save from privileged EXEC with `copy running-config startup-config`; save the project as `security-controls-complete.pkt`.

Finish the worksheet with two gaps this exercise does not implement, such as enterprise MFA, breached-password screening, protected centralized backup storage, or central command accounting. Assign each a suitable control or later chapter rather than declaring the router “fully secure.”

:::expected
The configuration matches the intended local lab design and no induced lockout remains. SSH and console have been tested with fresh sessions. The report distinguishes implemented controls from policy goals and simulator limits; no broad security guarantee is made.
:::

lab.troubleshooting:
- If SSH fails before a password prompt, inspect reachability, keys, SSH status, and every VTY transport setting; that symptom alone is not an authentication diagnosis.
- If credentials are rejected, confirm the account spelling, secret, and selected login method. Check current quiet-mode state separately.
- If the console was not retested, an old open session is not proof of future recovery access. Use the tested SSH session while checking it.
- A type-5 result on an old simulator is a legacy feature limit. Do not claim that `service password-encryption` upgrades it to type 8 or 9.
lab.challenge:
On paper, add a narrowly scoped quiet-mode exception permitting only Admin-PC at 10.0.0.10. The requirement is to let that source attempt normal authentication during quiet mode; it must not permit Test-PC or bypass a password check. Predict what happens if an independent VTY access restriction also denies Admin-PC. ACL configuration is developed in Chapter 34, so this is a complete reference answer and policy exercise, not a prerequisite for this lab.

:::expected
On supporting IOS, from privileged EXEC:

```ios
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip access-list standard QUIET-ADMIN
R1(config-std-nacl)# permit host 10.0.0.10
R1(config-std-nacl)# exit
R1(config)# login quiet-mode access-class QUIET-ADMIN
R1(config)# end
R1# show login
```

The exception permits .10 through this quiet-mode control, while normal authentication and other restrictions still apply. Test-PC remains outside the exception. A separate denying VTY access control can still prevent Admin-PC from connecting. This is not an all-purpose access guarantee. If applied only for the challenge, remove it with `no login quiet-mode access-class` and remove the temporary named ACL with `no ip access-list standard QUIET-ADMIN`, then verify and save the intended final state.
:::

questions.prompt: An unnecessary management service still accepts its publicly known default credential. Which term best describes that condition?
options: A vulnerability that can be used for unauthorized access.
An exploit already executed against the service.
An accounting record proving who used the service.
A mitigation that restricts the default account.
questions.explanation: The condition is a weakness, not evidence that an attack already occurred. Unauthorized use is a potential threat; using the credential would be a way to exploit the weakness.

whyWrong.1: A weakness can exist before any exploitation.
whyWrong.2: The statement contains no activity or attribution record.
whyWrong.3: Retaining an exposed default is not the described protective action.

exhibit.title: Representative teaching evidence
exhibit.text:
Configured: login block-for 120 attempts 3 within 60
Times shown as HH:MM:SS
02:00:00 admin failed
02:15:00 operator failed
02:30:00 support failed

questions.prompt: The investigation also confirms that the same candidate password was tried against each listed account. Which attack pattern and threshold result fit?
options: An account lockout; every different username shares one expired password.
Password spraying; the shown attempts do not meet three failures within 60 seconds.
Credential stuffing; the successful pairs must therefore have bypassed failure logging.
Single-account brute force; all shown failures belong to one identity.
questions.explanation: Trying one candidate across many accounts is spraying. The stated times keep the failures outside the configured watch window. Usernames alone would not reveal the candidate passwords; the investigation supplies that missing evidence.

whyWrong.0: No account expiry is demonstrated.
whyWrong.2: The records are failures, and the scenario identifies one shared candidate rather than exposed pairs.
whyWrong.3: Several distinct usernames are listed.

exhibit.title: Representative teaching evidence
exhibit.text:
Controlled worksheet: attacker sends an 80-byte UDP request using victim source IP.
A third-party service sends an 800-byte response to the victim.

questions.prompt: Using byte counts measured at the same layer, what mechanism and ratio does the exhibit demonstrate?
options: A DNS cache repair followed by an 800× amplification.
A direct client download with no source impersonation.
Reflection to the forged victim and 10× response amplification.
A TCP SYN backlog flood with a 10-second timeout.
questions.explanation: The response follows the forged victim address, which is reflection. The supplied ratio is 800/80 = 10; it is a measured example, not a universal DNS value.

whyWrong.0: No cache repair is shown, and the ratio is not 800.
whyWrong.1: The stated source forgery contradicts an ordinary direct download.
whyWrong.3: No TCP handshake or timer is shown.

questions.prompt: Which two controls address the stated access-LAN abuses when configured with valid trust/binding policy? Select two.
options: Dynamic ARP Inspection against invalid ARP bindings.
An SSH idle timeout against forged ARP mappings.
A login banner against unauthorized DHCP replies.
DHCP snooping against unauthorized server replies.
questions.explanation: Snooping and DAI inspect the relevant LAN traffic using their configured trust and validation rules. Correct placement and support for static endpoints matter; neither is automatically complete merely because enabled.

whyWrong.1: A terminal idle timeout does not validate ARP.
whyWrong.2: A banner communicates policy but does not filter DHCP.

questions.prompt: Which server behavior is targeted by a conventional TCP SYN-flood mechanism?
options: Resources retained while incomplete handshakes await their final ACK.
The authoritative DNS cache lifetime of each application name.
A switch’s source-MAC aging timer for established TCP sessions.
The password-history list used after successful authentication.
questions.explanation: A SYN flood can pressure resources associated with incomplete handshakes. Source spoofing is common but not mandatory, and the first exhausted resource depends on implementation and load.

whyWrong.1: DNS TTL is not the targeted handshake state.
whyWrong.2: MAC aging does not store TCP half-open connections.
whyWrong.3: Password history is unrelated to TCP handshake completion.

questions.prompt: Malware spreads automatically from one file server to twelve others through an unpatched service, without anyone opening an infected file. Which propagation category best fits?
options: Social engineering.
Worm.
File-infecting virus.
Password spraying.
questions.explanation: A worm can replicate and spread between systems without a user running a host file. The scenario identifies automated propagation through a service; this example does not mean every worm uses the same vulnerability.

whyWrong.0: No user is being persuaded to act in this scenario.
whyWrong.2: A file-infecting virus attaches to a host file; that mechanism is not the stated evidence.
whyWrong.3: Spraying tries a candidate password across accounts rather than describing malware replication.

questions.prompt: A caller impersonates the helpdesk and asks a user to read out an authentication code. Which channel-based label applies?
options: DNS pharming.
MAC flooding.
Vishing.
Smishing.
questions.explanation: Vishing is phishing over voice. A targeted call can also have other social-engineering labels; the requested distinction here is the voice channel.

whyWrong.0: Pharming concerns redirection, not this voice request.
whyWrong.1: MAC flooding is a network-table abuse.
whyWrong.3: Smishing uses text messages.

exhibit.title: Representative teaching evidence
exhibit.text:
Approved gateway: 10.0.10.1 at 0011.2233.4455
Unauthorized laptop claim: 10.0.10.1 at aaaa.bbbb.cccc

questions.prompt: An unauthorized laptop sends the shown gateway claim. Which intended control validates the ARP binding?
options: Port security allowing that laptop’s one observed source MAC.
Root guard selecting the spanning-tree root.
An SSH banner stating authorized use.
DAI using approved dynamic bindings or static ARP policy.
questions.explanation: DAI addresses ARP validation on its inspected ports. The legitimate gateway binding must be covered by the approved trust/static policy; a one-MAC allowance alone does not establish the claimed IP ownership.

whyWrong.0: One MAC can make a false IP claim without exceeding its allowed count.
whyWrong.1: Root guard handles BPDUs, not ARP bindings.
whyWrong.2: A banner does not inspect ARP.

exhibit.title: Representative teaching evidence
exhibit.text:
Representative labels; values omitted:
enable password 7 [value]
username admin password 7 [value]
line password 7 [value]

questions.prompt: What exposure is established if the following configuration is broadly readable?
options: The type-7 credentials are recoverable from their reversible representation.
The type-7 values are strong one-way password verifiers.
Only the line credential is recoverable; the username uses a different type.
Readers must obtain a separate per-device decryption key for type 7.
questions.explanation: Type 7 is reversible obfuscation. Restrict the exposed file and rotate affected secrets under the incident process; conversion to a hash alone does not undo disclosure.

whyWrong.1: Type 7 is not a one-way verifier.
whyWrong.2: All shown credentials have the same type label.
whyWrong.3: Type-7 recovery does not require a unique device-held key.

questions.prompt: Which combination uses two distinct authentication-factor categories?
options: A password and a memorized answer to a personal question.
A password and a code generated by a separate possessed authenticator.
A password and a memorized PIN entered into the same login.
A username and a longer memorized passphrase.
questions.explanation: The password is knowledge and the authenticator provides possession evidence. Distinct categories matter; a username identifies an account and is not itself an authenticator.

whyWrong.0: Both are knowledge-based evidence.
whyWrong.2: Both are knowledge factors.
whyWrong.3: The username is an identifier; only the passphrase is an authentication factor.

questions.prompt: Which two definitions of traditional password-policy terms are correct? Select two.
options: Complexity sets the number of seconds in a login failure window.
Lockout sets the minimum password character count.
History restricts reuse of a configured set of previous passwords.
Expiry sets a maximum age after which change is required.
questions.explanation: These are definitions of history and expiry, not a recommendation to impose routine expiry. Current NIST guidance in its scope rejects periodic forced changes without compromise evidence.

whyWrong.0: Complexity concerns composition rules, not the watch window.
whyWrong.1: Lockout concerns failed attempts/access restriction, not length.

exhibit.title: Representative teaching evidence
exhibit.text:
show login:
Router presently in Quiet-Mode.
Will remain in Quiet-Mode for 87 seconds.
No Quiet-Mode access list has been configured.

questions.prompt: On the documented IOS login-block feature, why can a correct new SSH attempt be refused in this state?
options: The displayed state proves a permanent per-user AAA lockout.
The console must also be unavailable for the same interval.
The SSH RSA key pair must be expired.
The remote quiet-mode control is active and no source exception is configured.
questions.explanation: Quiet mode restricts new remote login attempts under this feature. The console remains a separate recovery path; the output does not identify account lockout or a cryptographic key problem.

whyWrong.0: Remote quiet mode is distinct from per-user AAA lockout.
whyWrong.1: The documented feature retains console access.
whyWrong.2: No key expiry is shown.

questions.prompt: A short monthly reminder tells staff how to recognize unexpected credential requests and where to report them. Which program element is its primary purpose?
options: User awareness.
Physical access enforcement.
Per-command authorization.
Credential storage migration.
questions.explanation: The reminder maintains attention and a reporting route. Formal practice can add training; program activities can overlap, so classify the stated primary purpose rather than a rigid delivery format.

whyWrong.1: No room or equipment access is enforced.
whyWrong.2: The reminder does not evaluate administrator commands.
whyWrong.3: No stored credential format is changed.

questions.prompt: An office wants to reduce visitors following staff through a controlled door. Which control most directly addresses that entry behavior?
options: A daily router-configuration backup.
Controlled entry with individual admission and visitor checks.
A camera recording the room without changing entry control.
A longer administrator SSH idle timeout.
questions.explanation: Individual admission and visitor procedures address tailgating prevention. Detection and recovery controls remain useful but do not replace the entry control itself.

whyWrong.0: A backup helps recovery rather than preventing the entry behavior.
whyWrong.2: A camera primarily records/detects rather than enforces individual entry.
whyWrong.3: An SSH timer does not control a doorway.

questions.prompt: A client authenticates with a certificate and the server validates the expected trust and identity. What additional proof must the client supply?
options: A secret password embedded in the public certificate.
Possession of any copy of the certificate without its private key.
Control of the private key matching the certified public key.
Knowledge of the issuing certificate authority’s private key.
questions.explanation: The public certificate supplies a signed binding; authentication also requires proof of its matching private key. Private-key protection and certificate validation are both necessary.

whyWrong.0: A public certificate is not a container for the user password.
whyWrong.1: A public certificate copy alone does not prove private-key possession.
whyWrong.3: The client must not possess the CA’s signing key.

questions.prompt: Which proposed policy change matches NIST SP 800-63B-4 for its covered single-factor password use?
options: Require eight characters and four character classes, then force a change every month.
Permit any six-character value when the account is limited to administrator use.
Keep shared passwords but increase the login banner length.
Require at least 15 characters, screen blocked values, and change on compromise evidence rather than a fixed schedule.
questions.explanation: The specified NIST guidance sets a 15-character minimum for single-factor passwords, with different scoped minimums when used as part of MFA. It rejects mandatory composition and routine periodic changes; a router length command alone is not a complete implementation.

whyWrong.0: This retains superseded composition/periodic-change assumptions and the wrong single-factor minimum.
whyWrong.1: Administrative scope does not justify that minimum in the stated policy.
whyWrong.2: A banner does not remedy shared credentials or password requirements.

cards.front: What is a vulnerability?
cards.back: A weakness that can contribute to harm, such as an exposed default credential or excessive permissions. A required, protected open service is not automatically a vulnerability.

cards.front: What is an exploit?
cards.back: A method or action that takes advantage of a weakness. Distinguish the method from the weakness and from evidence of actual successful use.

cards.front: How do threat and threat actor differ?
cards.back: A threat is a potential adverse event/circumstance; a threat actor is a person or organization associated with intentional harm. Threats can also be accidental or environmental.

cards.front: What is mitigation?
cards.back: A measure that reduces likelihood or impact. It may prevent, detect, correct, or support recovery; no single control removes every risk.

cards.front: What does the CIA triad protect?
cards.back: Confidentiality protects against unauthorized disclosure; integrity against improper modification. Availability supports timely, reliable use. One incident can affect all three.

cards.front: What does a conventional SYN flood target?
cards.back: Resources associated with incomplete TCP handshakes. Spoofing is common but not required; actual exhaustion and effective mitigation depend on the implementation.

cards.front: How do reflection and amplification differ?
cards.back: Reflection sends replies toward a forged victim source. Amplification is a larger response/request ratio measured at the same layer; neither implies one fixed DNS multiplier.

cards.front: Distinguish a virus, worm, and Trojan.
cards.back: A virus attaches to executing content; a worm propagates without manual installation of each copy; a Trojan presents itself as legitimate/useful while doing something else. Categories can overlap.

cards.front: What distinguishes spear phishing, whaling, vishing, and smishing?
cards.back: Targeted phishing, senior-personnel targeting, voice, and text-message channels respectively. A targeted voice call can fit more than one label.

cards.front: How do spraying and credential stuffing differ?
cards.back: Spraying tries few candidate passwords across many accounts. Stuffing reuses exposed account/password pairs, which can succeed or fail. Logs of usernames alone do not reveal the candidates.

cards.front: Match DHCP spoofing, ARP poisoning, and unwanted BPDUs to controls.
cards.back: DHCP snooping, DAI with valid binding/static policy, and appropriately placed BPDU/root guard respectively. Each control addresses a specific trust decision.

cards.front: How does ARP poisoning support an on-path attack?
cards.back: A false IP-to-MAC association can redirect frames. Validated ARP policy and authenticated end-to-end protocols address different parts of the risk.

cards.front: What belongs in a password policy beyond complexity?
cards.back: Ownership, length, blocked choices, uniqueness, storage, recovery, compromise response, and account removal. Traditional history/expiry terms describe controls, not universal recommended values.

cards.front: What are the three authentication-factor categories?
cards.back: Knowledge, possession, and inherence. A certificate file alone is public; proof of a protected private key is the relevant possession mechanism.

cards.front: Is password plus PIN multifactor authentication?
cards.back: Not when both are simply knowledge secrets. A possessed cryptographic authenticator activated by a PIN can combine possession and knowledge.

cards.front: What does certificate authentication require?
cards.back: Proof of the matching private key plus appropriate chain, identity, usage, validity, and revocation checks. Copying a public certificate alone proves no private-key control.

cards.front: Why are biometrics not treated like replaceable passwords?
cards.back: They involve probabilistic comparison and sensitive characteristics that cannot simply be changed. NIST uses them with a physical authenticator as part of MFA and requires an alternative.

cards.front: How do awareness, training, and physical control differ?
cards.back: Awareness supports recognition/reporting; training develops skills; physical controls manage access to equipment and spaces. One program activity can serve more than one learning purpose.

cards.front: What are Cisco credential types 0, 5, 7, 8, and 9?
cards.back: 0 cleartext; 5 legacy salted MD5; 7 reversible obfuscation; 8 PBKDF2-SHA256; 9 scrypt. Inspect supported behavior and protect backups containing any of them.

cards.front: What does login block-for 120 attempts 3 within 60 configure?
cards.back: A remote-login failure threshold/watch window and 120-second quiet interval. Documented IOS retains console access; a quiet-mode source exception does not bypass normal authentication.

commands.task: On a supporting IOS image, set a 15-character minimum for newly configured passwords governed by this feature.
commands.note: This is one device control, not a full NIST implementation or a retroactive proof that old secrets comply.

commands.task: Set the isolated lab’s privileged EXEC secret to Lab-Enable-Only-2026! using basic simulator-compatible syntax.
commands.note: Inspect the stored type; older images may produce a legacy hash. Use stronger supported formats in an approved real deployment.

commands.task: Create local admin at privilege 15 with the public lab secret Lab-Admin-Only-2026!.
commands.note: Privilege 15 is broad administration; it is not appropriate for every user role.

commands.task: Enable classic IOS obfuscation for applicable remaining cleartext password configuration.
commands.note: This typically produces reversible type 7 for applicable fields; it does not provide SSH transport or upgrade secrets to type 8/9.

commands.task: Configure a 120-second remote quiet interval with threshold 3 failures in 60 seconds.
commands.note: This documented remote-login control leaves console access available and is distinct from per-user AAA lockout.

commands.task: Request logging of failed login events on supporting IOS.
commands.note: Verify logging support and destinations; the command does not guarantee delivery to an external collector.

commands.task: Use existing ACL QUIET-ADMIN as the source exception during remote quiet mode.
commands.note: Permitted sources still must pass authentication and other access controls; define the narrow intended ACL first.

commands.task: Before AAA new-model, select the local username database for this line.
commands.note: Create and test a valid account and recovery path before altering line authentication.

commands.task: Set a five-minute idle timeout for this line.
commands.note: This controls idle EXEC sessions; it is not a maximum password age or a failed-login threshold.

commands.task: Inspect login-block configuration and current quiet/normal state.
commands.note: A current state and timer are evidence; a login delay by itself does not identify this control.

commands.task: Show running-configuration lines containing secret.
commands.note: Inspect the actual stored type and protect the output; this filter does not display every credential elsewhere.

tickets.title: Valid remote logins fail during a quiet interval
tickets.scenario: In this isolated representative case, authorized administrators use 10.0.99.0/24. The console remains accessible. Remote SSH tests with the correct password fail intermittently after unrelated failed login attempts.

exhibits.title: Configuration
exhibits.text:
login block-for 120 attempts 3 within 60
No quiet-mode exception configured

exhibits.title: Current state
exhibits.text:
Router presently in Quiet-Mode
Will remain in Quiet-Mode for 64 seconds

exhibits.title: Events
exhibits.text: Remote failed-login threshold reached, followed by QUIET_MODE_ON

tickets.question: Which explanation follows from the current evidence?
options: An expired RSA key has permanently disabled SSH.
The active remote quiet interval is restricting new remote login attempts.
The console account must be locked by the same timer.
An idle EXEC timeout changed every stored password.
tickets.explanation: The active quiet state explains why a correct new remote login can be refused. It does not imply a permanent account lockout or console failure. Use console access, verify normal mode after the interval, and plan a narrow approved management exception/restriction rather than remove authentication.
tickets.fix: First use the existing console, observe the remaining interval, and retest a fresh valid SSH login after Normal-Mode returns. If the approved policy calls for a management exception, create its narrowly scoped ACL before applying login quiet-mode access-class. ACL design/configuration is developed in Chapter 34. An exception still requires authentication and does not override other restrictions; preserve evidence and save only the verified policy.

tickets.title: A broadly readable backup contains reversible credentials
tickets.scenario: An audit finds an old R2 backup readable by unauthorized users. A separate alert shows one unexpected successful admin login. Investigation has not established which person logged in or how the credential was obtained.

exhibits.title: Backup excerpt
exhibits.text:
enable password 7 [value omitted]
username admin privilege 15 password 7 [value omitted]

exhibits.title: Authentication evidence
exhibits.text: One unexpected successful admin login; no attributable credential-acquisition evidence

tickets.question: Which conclusion and response are justified now?
options: The successful login proves the backup was the only possible credential source.
The backup exposes reversible credentials; treat them as compromised and investigate the login separately.
The type-7 label proves the backup is protected by a one-way hash.
The absence of earlier failures proves the login was authorized.
tickets.explanation: Type 7 establishes recoverable-secret exposure regardless of whether it caused this particular login. Restrict the backup and rotate affected credentials through the approved process while preserving evidence and examining active sessions/configuration changes. Do not claim attribution from an account name alone.
tickets.fix: From an authorized working recovery session, protect the exposed backup, replace all affected credentials with new unique values and supported stronger storage, and verify intended access before retiring old access. Review the unexpected session and changes using the incident process. Do not paste public training passwords into a real repair or assume changing one enable secret covers every leaked shared key.

sections.title: Local accounts versus a central server
Enable AAA with a tested recovery path

lab.title: Configure and test TACACS+ and RADIUS management clients
lab.intro: Build local SSH and a tested console recovery path, then configure TACACS+ and RADIUS in separate saved copies of the same lab. Test success, rejection, and service unavailability. The main simulator configurations use classic server syntax; the final worksheet translates them to named server objects and groups. No Packet Tracer, CML, or hardware execution is claimed. Feature and server-policy support vary, so record unsupported behavior and use the specified paper fallback.
lab.topology:


|---|---|---|
| R1 Gi0/0 | 10.0.0.1, 255.255.255.0 | Straight-through to SW1 Gi0/1 |
| Admin-PC FastEthernet0 | 10.0.0.50, 255.255.255.0; gateway .1 | Straight-through to SW1 Fa0/1 |
