steps.title: Address the devices and establish a working baseline
steps.body:
Set every PC/server address under Desktop → IP Configuration → Static. On WEB, choose Services → HTTP and explicitly turn HTTP On. FILES is an addressable test host; no file-transfer or SSH server is required.

```ios R1
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R1
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.100.10.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.100.20.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip interface brief
R1# show ip route
```

From both PCs, ping `10.100.20.20` and `10.100.20.30`. From PC-A only, open Desktop → Web Browser and load `http://10.100.20.20`. Leave PC-B's browser unused until the deliberate fault in Step 7. Wait for links and initial ARP resolution before repeating an initially unsuccessful ping.

:::expected
Both routed interfaces are up/up. R1 has connected routes for both /24 LANs; no static route is needed. Both PCs reach both servers, and PC-A loads WEB over HTTP. Correct any baseline failure now. An ACL cannot fix a wrong host gateway or a stopped HTTP service.
:::

steps.title: Permit one source with a standard ACL
steps.body:
Allow only PC-A toward the entire server LAN. This is deliberately a source-only policy applied outbound on the destination-facing interface.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# access-list 10 permit host 10.100.10.10
R1(config)# access-list 10 deny any
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ip access-group 10 out
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show access-lists 10
R1# show ip interface gigabitethernet0/1
```

Record the displayed permit and deny counters. Repeat pings to both servers from both PCs, then read the counters again.

:::expected
PC-A still reaches both servers. PC-B reaches neither. The explicit deny gives a visible entry for rejected requests on images that report counters. A timeout or unreachable response is possible; neither exact wording nor exactly four matches is required. The outgoing list on G0/1 is 10. This placement restricts the whole server LAN, not an individual server.
:::

steps.title: Apply a service-specific extended policy
steps.body:
The new requirement allows both clients to use HTTP on WEB, denies their other traffic to WEB, and permits other destinations. Build CLIENTS-IN completely, remove the standard attachment, and attach the new list inbound on the client interface.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip access-list extended CLIENTS-IN
R1(config-ext-nacl)# 10 permit tcp 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.100.20.20 eq 80
R1(config-ext-nacl)# 20 deny ip 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.100.20.20
R1(config-ext-nacl)# 30 permit ip any any
R1(config-ext-nacl)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# no ip access-group 10 out
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ip access-group CLIENTS-IN in
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show access-lists CLIENTS-IN
R1# show ip interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1# show ip interface gigabitethernet0/1
```

If the image rejects explicit entry numbers, enter the three ACEs without them in the displayed order, then inspect their assigned numbers. For the following exercise use the complete replacement fallback if insertion is also unavailable.

From PC-A, reload HTTP on WEB, ping WEB, and ping FILES. From PC-B, ping FILES. Predict the first matching entry before each test.

:::expected
HTTP to WEB and pings to FILES succeed. Ping to WEB fails because it matches deny 20. R1 shows CLIENTS-IN inbound on G0/0 and no outbound ACL on G0/1. No server reply crosses CLIENTS-IN in its applied direction.
:::

steps.title: Add an exception and inspect the order
steps.body:
PC-A must be allowed to ping WEB; PC-B must still be denied. Insert a more specific ICMP permit before the general deny.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip access-list extended CLIENTS-IN
R1(config-ext-nacl)# 15 permit icmp host 10.100.10.10 host 10.100.20.20 echo
R1(config-ext-nacl)# end
R1# show access-lists CLIENTS-IN
```

If insertion is unsupported, build CLIENTS-V2 without sequence numbers, in order: the HTTP permit, the PC-A echo permit, the deny to WEB, and the final permit. The following is the complete fallback; use it only instead of insertion, and use CLIENTS-V2 wherever later instructions refer to the active client list.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip access-list extended CLIENTS-V2
R1(config-ext-nacl)# permit tcp 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.100.20.20 eq 80
R1(config-ext-nacl)# permit icmp host 10.100.10.10 host 10.100.20.20 echo
R1(config-ext-nacl)# deny ip 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.100.20.20
R1(config-ext-nacl)# permit ip any any
R1(config-ext-nacl)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ip access-group CLIENTS-V2 in
R1(config-if)# end
```

Ping WEB from each PC. On supported IOS, optionally run `ip access-list resequence CLIENTS-IN 100 10` in global configuration and inspect the resulting sequence order. It changes numbering, not the intended policy. If rejected, keep the existing numbers; subsequent steps do not depend on them. Do not assume resequencing preserves counter values on every image.

:::expected
PC-A's echo matches its exception before the deny and succeeds. PC-B's echo still reaches the deny. The HTTP policy is unchanged. An exception below the deny would have no effect.
:::

steps.title: Filter return traffic and recognize the limit of established
steps.body:
Apply this limited inbound filter on G0/1. It allows TCP segments with ACK or RST set and ICMP echo replies from the server LAN to the client LAN. It blocks other server-to-client packets. It does not verify whether clients really initiated those packets.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip access-list extended SERVERS-IN
R1(config-ext-nacl)# 10 permit tcp 10.100.20.0 0.0.0.255 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 established
R1(config-ext-nacl)# 20 permit icmp 10.100.20.0 0.0.0.255 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 echo-reply
R1(config-ext-nacl)# 30 deny ip any any
R1(config-ext-nacl)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ip access-group SERVERS-IN in
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show access-lists SERVERS-IN
```

If explicit sequence syntax was unavailable earlier, omit the numbers here and inspect the assigned numbers. From PC-A, test HTTP and ping to WEB again. From WEB's Desktop → Command Prompt, ping `10.100.10.10`. Then explain the result for an invented TCP packet from WEB to PC-A with ACK set, even though no matching client connection exists.

:::expected
PC-A's HTTP responses and echo replies are permitted. WEB's own echo requests are denied. The invented ACK packet would match the TCP permit: that is the important limitation. The observed application behavior is consistent with normal replies, but the ACL has no connection table.
:::

steps.title: Restrict incoming SSH management to PC-A
steps.body:
Create the SSH service first. These credentials are for this isolated exercise. Use the local CLI tab throughout. When the RSA command asks for a modulus, enter `2048`, then continue with the next block. If your image cannot create that key, complete the VTY policy as a configuration review and use a supported IOS image for live SSH; do not silently substitute an insecure production setting.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip domain-name ccna.test
R1(config)# username labadmin secret LabAdmin34!
R1(config)# crypto key generate rsa
```

```ios R1
R1(config)# ip ssh version 2
R1(config)# ip access-list standard VTY-ADMINS
R1(config-std-nacl)# permit host 10.100.10.10
R1(config-std-nacl)# exit
R1(config)# line vty 0 4
R1(config-line)# login local
R1(config-line)# transport input ssh
R1(config-line)# access-class VTY-ADMINS in
R1(config-line)# end
R1# show line
R1# show running-config
R1# show ip ssh
```

The 0–4 range is the baseline used here. If the running configuration also has `line vty 5 15`, enter that range and apply the same three line commands; every available VTY must have the restriction. Without the output filter, inspect the full configuration directly.

From PC-A, run `ssh -l labadmin 10.100.10.1`, enter `LabAdmin34!`, then `exit`. Repeat from PC-B. Also repeat PC-B's ping to FILES to distinguish management control from transit filtering.

:::expected
PC-A can authenticate to R1. PC-B cannot open an allowed SSH management session, but its ping to FILES still works. The client interface ACL permits traffic addressed to R1 through its final permit; the VTY access class supplies the source restriction. Exact refusal wording and VTY ACL counter totals are not required evidence.
:::

steps.title: Introduce a missing return rule and observe the failure
steps.body:
Remove only the TCP permit from SERVERS-IN. Use the sequence displayed for that permit; it is 10 in the explicit configuration above.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip access-list extended SERVERS-IN
R1(config-ext-nacl)# no 10
R1(config-ext-nacl)# end
R1# show access-lists SERVERS-IN
```

If sequence deletion is unsupported, remove the exact permit with `no permit tcp 10.100.20.0 0.0.0.255 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 established` inside the named ACL and verify the result. Now open PC-B's browser for the first time and request `http://10.100.20.20`. From PC-A, ping WEB. Read both ACLs before making a repair. In Simulation mode, include TCP/HTTP if needed to confirm that a fresh HTTP connection was attempted rather than relying on a cached page.

:::expected
The HTTP request is allowed into R1 by the client list, but WEB's TCP response reaches the explicit deny in SERVERS-IN. The connection fails. PC-A's ICMP ping still succeeds because echo-reply remains permitted. A working ping therefore does not prove the web application's return traffic is allowed. Stop and record this fault state before Step 8.
:::

steps.title: Restore the rule, retest and save
steps.body:
On an image supporting sequence insertion, restore the missing permit before the deny:

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip access-list extended SERVERS-IN
R1(config-ext-nacl)# 10 permit tcp 10.100.20.0 0.0.0.255 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 established
R1(config-ext-nacl)# end
```

If insertion is unsupported, create SERVERS-V2 with the TCP permit, echo-reply permit and deny in that order, then replace the G0/1 inbound attachment. Do not append the restored permit below the existing deny.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip access-list extended SERVERS-V2
R1(config-ext-nacl)# permit tcp 10.100.20.0 0.0.0.255 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 established
R1(config-ext-nacl)# permit icmp 10.100.20.0 0.0.0.255 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 echo-reply
R1(config-ext-nacl)# deny ip any any
R1(config-ext-nacl)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ip access-group SERVERS-V2 in
R1(config-if)# end
```

Use only the recovery appropriate to your image. Retry PC-B's HTTP request, both PCs' pings to FILES, PC-A's ping to WEB, and PC-B's ping to WEB. Confirm both interface attachments and every VTY range, then save:

```ios R1
R1# show ip interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1# show ip interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1# show access-lists
R1# copy running-config startup-config
```

:::expected
HTTP works again. Both clients reach FILES. PC-A can ping WEB; PC-B cannot. The SSH restriction remains in place. Press Enter to accept the startup-config filename, then save the Packet Tracer file as `acl-baseline.pkt`. Unattached demonstration ACLs do not filter traffic; document which names are active rather than assuming all displayed lists are applied.
:::

lab.troubleshooting:
- If both PCs fail before filtering, verify full addresses, /24 masks, gateways, cabling and R1's up/up interfaces. Repeat after ARP resolution.
- If PC-B loses FILES after Step 3, check whether ACL 10 is still attached outbound on G0/1. A second filter can deny a packet the first one permitted.
- If HTTP never matches its permit, inspect whether port 80 follows the destination and whether the server HTTP service is On.
- If an exception has no effect, locate the first matching entry. An earlier deny can prevent a later permit from being considered.
- If an ACL counter does not change, check its attachment, direction, the actual packet fields, and earlier rules. Counters alone do not prove the route or application is healthy.
- If SSH fails for PC-A, confirm SSH is enabled, local authentication is configured, the username is correct, the VTY source matches, and the interface list permits traffic to R1.
- If a command is unsupported, use the stated replacement-list or paper fallback. Do not erase the live ACL in an attempt to reproduce a screenshot.
lab.challenge:
Starting from the recovered state, write complete replacement lists with this policy: PC-A alone may send TCP destination port 22 to FILES; both clients may use HTTP on WEB; both clients may query a new DNS server `10.100.20.53` on TCP or UDP 53; all other traffic from clients to the server LAN is denied; other client destinations remain permitted. Include the reverse rules required by the existing server-side filter.

For an optional DNS test, add Server-PT DNS to SW2 Fa0/3 with straight-through cable, address `10.100.20.53/24`, gateway `10.100.20.1`; turn Services → DNS On and add A record `web.acl.test` → `10.100.20.20`. Set both PCs' DNS server to `.53`. Test a fresh lookup by name. SSH to FILES is a **packet-policy exercise only**: this Server-PT baseline has no SSH service, so an ACL permit does not guarantee an SSH login.

:::expected
Build the new lists before replacing either attachment. This answer permits UDP DNS replies with source port 53 and TCP replies with ACK/RST set; neither rule validates a remembered request.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip access-list extended CLIENTS-FINAL
R1(config-ext-nacl)# permit tcp host 10.100.10.10 host 10.100.20.30 eq 22
R1(config-ext-nacl)# permit tcp 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.100.20.20 eq 80
R1(config-ext-nacl)# permit tcp 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.100.20.53 eq 53
R1(config-ext-nacl)# permit udp 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.100.20.53 eq 53
R1(config-ext-nacl)# deny ip 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 10.100.20.0 0.0.0.255
R1(config-ext-nacl)# permit ip any any
R1(config-ext-nacl)# exit
R1(config)# ip access-list extended SERVERS-FINAL
R1(config-ext-nacl)# permit tcp 10.100.20.0 0.0.0.255 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 established
R1(config-ext-nacl)# permit udp host 10.100.20.53 eq 53 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255
R1(config-ext-nacl)# deny ip any any
R1(config-ext-nacl)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ip access-group CLIENTS-FINAL in
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ip access-group SERVERS-FINAL in
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show access-lists
```

Predictions: PC-A TCP/22 to FILES passes; PC-B TCP/22 to FILES is denied. HTTP to WEB and UDP/TCP DNS requests are permitted, along with the listed reply forms. Client pings to either server are now denied because the new policy contains no ICMP exception. PC-A still reaches R1's SSH service through the client list's final permit and VTY-ADMINS. Save this challenge under a new filename if you want to keep the earlier baseline.
:::

questions.prompt: CLIENTS-IN is applied inbound on R1 G0/0, facing 10.100.10.0/24. Which entry first matches an ICMP echo request from 10.100.10.11 to 10.100.20.20?
options: 10: the destination is the web server
15: this entry matches the ICMP protocol
20: neither earlier entry matches every field
30: the final permit overrides earlier denies
questions.explanation: Entry 10 requires TCP. Entry 15 requires source .10, not .11. The request therefore first matches deny 20; evaluation ends there.

whyWrong.0: A destination match is insufficient when the protocol differs.
whyWrong.1: All conditions must match, including the source address.
whyWrong.3: Later permits cannot override an earlier match.

questions.prompt: With base address 172.16.32.0, which wildcard matches exactly the /20 subnet?
questions.explanation: The /20 subnet mask is 255.255.240.0. Subtracting each octet from 255 produces 0.0.15.255, covering third octets 32 through 47.

whyWrong.1: 16 is the block size, not its wildcard. Binary 00010000 ignores only one third-octet bit.
whyWrong.2: This ignores five third-octet bits and matches a /19, twice the intended set.
whyWrong.3: This ignores all of the last two octets and matches the whole /16.

exhibit.title: Numbered standard ACL
exhibit.text: access-list 20 permit 192.168.16.0 0.0.7.255

questions.prompt: Which source range matches the displayed entry?
questions.explanation: Wildcard 7 is binary 00000111. It permits the third octet to vary from 16 to 23 while wildcard 255 ignores the last octet. ACL matching includes every address in that set.

whyWrong.0: That would use wildcard 0.0.0.255.
whyWrong.1: That /20-sized set would use wildcard 0.0.15.255.
whyWrong.2: The compared high bits require the third octet to remain in the 16–23 block.

questions.prompt: Which two numbers identify standard IPv4 ACLs on IOS? Choose two.
questions.explanation: Standard IPv4 ranges are 1–99 and 1300–1999. Thus 99 and 1400 are standard; the other values belong to extended ranges.

whyWrong.1: 150 belongs to 100–199, an extended range.
whyWrong.3: 2300 belongs to 2000–2699, an extended range.
whyWrong.4: 199 is an extended ACL number.

exhibit.title: Representative effective ACL order
exhibit.text:
access-list 101 permit ip any any
access-list 101 deny tcp any host 10.100.20.30 eq 22

questions.prompt: ACL 101 is applied inbound where client requests arrive. The goal is to block SSH to 10.100.20.30 and permit other IPv4 traffic. Why does SSH remain permitted?
options: The deny needs established to match initial SSH packets
The first permit matches SSH before the deny is considered
An extended ACL cannot filter incoming traffic
IOS cannot match SSH when port 22 is written numerically
questions.explanation: The first entry matches all IPv4 packets, including TCP destination port 22. Place the specific deny above the general permit.

whyWrong.0: An initial TCP SYN normally has neither ACK nor RST, so established would exclude it.
whyWrong.2: Extended lists can be applied inbound or outbound.
whyWrong.3: TCP destination port 22 is a valid numeric SSH match.

questions.prompt: On the classic IOS interface ACL behavior used in this chapter, CLIENTS-IN has not been created. What filtering is provided by referencing that absent list with ip access-group CLIENTS-IN in?
options: All IPv4 traffic is denied by the empty list
Only traffic addressed to the router is denied
Only TCP traffic is permitted through the interface
The absent list provides no restriction on IPv4 traffic
questions.explanation: The documented classic IOS behavior permits traffic through an absent or empty referenced list. A misspelled name can therefore leave the intended filtering absent. Create and review the complete ACL before applying it.

whyWrong.0: Implicit deny does not turn the absent list into a deny-all filter in the behavior specified.
whyWrong.1: There are no entries implementing a router-destination exception.
whyWrong.2: There are no entries selecting TCP.

exhibit.title: Topology and port roles
exhibit.text:
PC1 10.1.1.10/24 -> R1 G0/0
R1 G0/1 -> R2 -> R3 G0/0
R3 G0/1 -> LAN C 10.3.3.0/24
R3 G0/2 -> LAN D 10.4.4.0/24
All routes and baseline connectivity are working.

questions.prompt: A standard ACL denies source 10.1.1.10 and permits other sources. It must restrict PC1 only when reaching LAN C, leaving its traffic to R3 itself and LAN D available. Where should it be applied?
options: R1 G0/0 inbound
R1 G0/1 outbound
R3 G0/1 outbound
R3 G0/0 inbound
questions.explanation: G0/1 outbound on R3 is the path specifically into LAN C. A standard ACL cannot select a destination, so its attachment supplies the destination boundary.

whyWrong.0: This would reject PC1 traffic to every routed destination reached through R1.
whyWrong.1: This would also reject PC1 traffic continuing toward R3 and LAN D.
whyWrong.3: This would reject PC1 traffic arriving for R3 itself and for LAN D.

questions.prompt: An extended ACL must block only TCP destination port 23 from PC1 to SRV. Following the usual placement guideline, where should it first filter those requests?
options: R1 G0/0 inbound
R3 G0/1 outbound
R2 inbound on the transit link
R1 G0/1 inbound
questions.explanation: An extended list can identify this exact source, destination and service. R1 G0/0 inbound rejects the unwanted requests nearest their source, before they cross the transit network.

whyWrong.1: This could filter the requests, but carries them across the network before rejection and is not the requested placement guideline.
whyWrong.2: This is farther from the source and does not automatically filter the reverse direction.
whyWrong.3: Requests leave R1 G0/1; they do not enter it.

exhibit.title: Representative interface and ACL excerpts
exhibit.text:
R1# show ip interface gigabitethernet0/0
  Outgoing access list is not set
  Inbound access list is not set
R1# show access-lists CLIENTS-IN
  10 permit tcp 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.100.20.20 eq 80
  20 deny ip 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.100.20.20
  30 permit ip any any

questions.prompt: The list was intended to filter traffic arriving from clients on G0/0. Which fault is directly established by this output?
options: A broad permit is ahead of the specific deny
No IPv4 interface ACL is attached to G0/0
The ACL is attached outbound on G0/0
Counters must be cleared before the list can filter
questions.explanation: The interface reports no list in either direction. Defining the list does not attach it to this interface. Its use elsewhere is not established by this excerpt.

whyWrong.0: The displayed list places specific entries before the broad permit.
whyWrong.2: Outgoing also says not set.
whyWrong.3: Clearing counters is optional measurement housekeeping; it does not activate filtering.

questions.prompt: Which two statements describe the TCP established keyword accurately? Choose two.
options: It also tracks UDP replies and ICMP echo replies
It matches a TCP packet with ACK or RST set
It creates a state table for every TCP connection
It can admit a forged ACK without a prior connection
It requires log before matching is enabled
questions.explanation: Established is a per-packet TCP flag test. It allows typical SYN-ACK and later reply segments, but does not remember or validate that an inside host opened the connection.

whyWrong.0: UDP and ICMP do not have these TCP flags and require separate rules.
whyWrong.2: Ordinary ACL evaluation does not create a connection table.
whyWrong.4: Log requests logging for matches; it is not required to enable the match.

exhibit.title: Representative named ACL
exhibit.text:
10 permit tcp any host 10.100.20.20 eq 80
20 deny ip any host 10.100.20.20
30 permit ip any any

questions.prompt: On IOS supporting sequence editing, which action removes only sequence 20 from named extended ACL CLIENTS-IN?
options: Use no access-list CLIENTS-IN 20 in global mode
Enter CLIENTS-IN configuration mode and use delete 20
Enter CLIENTS-IN configuration mode and use no 20
Use ip access-list resequence CLIENTS-IN 20 10
questions.explanation: Enter ip access-list extended CLIENTS-IN, then no 20. Verify the resulting entries; the operation removes the selected ACE rather than deleting the whole list.

whyWrong.0: That is not the named-ACL sequence deletion syntax.
whyWrong.1: Sequence deletion uses no, not delete.
whyWrong.3: Resequencing renumbers remaining entries; it does not delete an entry.

questions.prompt: In the legacy IOS global ACL syntax documented by Cisco, an administrator tries to remove one ACE using no access-list 101 deny tcp any host 10.100.20.30 eq 22. What is the documented risk?
options: The entire numbered ACL is deleted
Only the matching entry is deleted safely
The command converts ACL 101 to a standard list
The list is detached but all its entries remain
questions.explanation: Cisco documents that this global no access-list form removes the entire numbered ACL. On an image supporting sequence editing, enter ip access-list extended 101 and remove the specific sequence instead.

whyWrong.1: That is the intended outcome of sequence deletion in ACL submode, not this legacy global command.
whyWrong.2: The operation deletes rather than changes the ACL type.
whyWrong.3: Deletion of the list and removal of an interface reference are different operations.

questions.prompt: R1 has only VTY lines 0–4. Which command, entered under those lines, restricts incoming management connections to sources permitted by standard ACL 10?
options: ip access-group 10 in
transport input 10
access-class 10 out
access-class 10 in
questions.explanation: Access-class 10 in restricts incoming VTY connections by the list. Configure SSH and authentication as well; the access class neither enables SSH nor verifies a password.

whyWrong.0: Ip access-group is an interface attachment command, not a VTY line command.
whyWrong.1: Transport input selects protocols such as ssh, not an ACL number.
whyWrong.2: Out applies to outgoing connections from the line, not the incoming sessions in the requirement.

questions.prompt: Which two statements are correct for ordinary routed IPv4 interface ACLs? Choose two.
options: One inbound and one outbound IPv4 list can be attached to an interface
A second inbound list is automatically evaluated after the first
A packet must match every permit entry before it can pass
Testing from a transit host avoids assuming a router-originated probe follows the same ACL path
An inbound list automatically filters packets leaving that interface
questions.explanation: The ordinary IPv4 attachment provides one list per interface direction. Router-originated traffic can follow different processing and source-address choices, so test from the affected host when checking a transit policy.

whyWrong.1: A second ip access-group for that direction replaces the reference.
whyWrong.2: The first matching entry decides; matching every permit is not required.
whyWrong.4: In and out refer to separate directions.

exhibit.title: Representative WEB-ONLY ACL
exhibit.text:
10 permit tcp 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 eq www host 10.100.20.20
20 deny ip any any

questions.prompt: The displayed ACL is inbound on the client-facing interface. A client uses source TCP port 51000 to request WEB port 80. Why is the request denied?
options: The explicit deny must be the first entry
Port 80 is tested as the source rather than destination
The www keyword is valid only for UDP
Host cannot identify an extended ACL destination
questions.explanation: Eq www follows the source address pair. The packet has source port 51000, so it misses the permit and reaches deny 20. Place eq 80 after host 10.100.20.20. The shown rule does not automatically match replies either: the source and destination address conditions would still need to match.

whyWrong.0: Moving deny ip any any first would deny every packet immediately.
whyWrong.2: Www is the familiar TCP port 80 alias.
whyWrong.3: Host is valid for source or destination.

questions.prompt: What sources match access-list 1 permit 10.100.10.0 255.255.255.0?
options: Exactly the addresses in 10.100.10.0/24
Only source address 10.100.10.0
Any IPv4 source whose fourth octet is zero
No sources because noncontiguous wildcards are invalid
questions.explanation: The wildcard ignores the first three octets and compares the fourth to zero. For example, 192.0.2.0 matches, whereas 10.100.10.25 does not.

whyWrong.0: IOS interprets the supplied value as a wildcard; it does not infer the intended subnet mask.
whyWrong.1: Matching a single host requires wildcard 0.0.0.0 or host.
whyWrong.3: The wildcard bit pattern need not be contiguous.

questions.prompt: Which single ACE matches a UDP DNS query from a client using source port 51000 to server 10.1.1.53 on destination port 53?
options: permit tcp any host 10.1.1.53 eq 53
permit udp any host 10.1.1.53 eq 67
permit udp any host 10.1.1.53 eq 53
permit udp any eq 53 host 10.1.1.53
questions.explanation: This packet is UDP and its service port is the destination port. The correct ACE puts eq 53 after the destination host. A complete DNS policy may also need TCP 53 and separate reverse-path permissions.

whyWrong.0: DNS can use TCP, but a TCP entry does not match the UDP packet specified.
whyWrong.1: UDP 67 is a DHCP server port, not this DNS destination.
whyWrong.3: This tests source port 53; the query source port is 51000.

cards.front: Which numbered ranges identify standard IPv4 ACLs?
cards.back: 1–99 and 1300–1999. These lists match source IPv4 addresses.

cards.front: Which numbered ranges identify extended IPv4 ACLs?
cards.back: 100–199 and 2000–2699. Extended lists can match protocol, source, destination and relevant transport fields.

cards.front: How does an ordinary nonempty IPv4 interface ACL decide a packet?
cards.back: Compare entries in effective order, stop at the first match, and implicitly deny a packet that matches no entry. A later permit does not override an earlier deny.

cards.front: How do you calculate the wildcard for a CIDR subnet?
cards.back: Subtract each subnet-mask octet from 255. A /20 mask of 255.255.240.0 gives wildcard 0.0.15.255. Not every valid wildcard represents a CIDR subnet.

cards.front: What do wildcard bits 0 and 1 mean?
cards.back: 0: compare the corresponding address bit. 1: ignore it. This is independent of whether the base address is a usable host.

cards.front: What are the wildcards for /27, /28 and /30?
cards.back: /27: 0.0.0.31. /28: 0.0.0.15. /30: 0.0.0.3. Use an appropriately aligned network base when describing those subnets.

cards.front: When is wildcard + 1 a useful block-size shortcut?
cards.back: For the changing octet of a contiguous subnet pattern. It does not describe arbitrary noncontiguous wildcards; use the individual bit comparisons for those.

cards.front: What do host and any replace in an IPv4 ACL?
cards.back: host A replaces A 0.0.0.0. any replaces 0.0.0.0 255.255.255.255.

cards.front: Which packet address does a standard IPv4 ACL match?
cards.back: The source. It cannot distinguish destination hosts, TCP from UDP, or one destination service from another.

cards.front: What additional fields can an extended IPv4 ACL use?
cards.back: Destination address and IP protocol, plus applicable fields such as TCP/UDP ports, ICMP type or TCP ACK/RST flag tests. All specified conditions must match.

cards.front: What are the usual placement guidelines for standard and extended ACLs?
cards.back: Standard: near the destination, to limit a source-only rule’s effect. Extended: near the source, when it can precisely identify unwanted traffic. Trace the actual path before choosing a direction.

cards.front: How is named ACL CLIENTS-IN attached inbound on an interface?
cards.back: Enter the interface configuration mode and use ip access-group CLIENTS-IN in. Verify the attachment with show ip interface for that interface.

cards.front: How does a standard ACL restrict incoming VTY management access?
cards.back: Apply access-class NAME in under every VTY range present. This restricts permitted source addresses; SSH transport and authentication are separate settings.

cards.front: How many ordinary IPv4 interface ACL references are available per interface?
cards.back: One inbound and one outbound. Applying another IPv4 ip access-group in the same direction replaces that reference. Other platform-specific ACL features are separate.

cards.front: What does TCP established actually check?
cards.back: ACK or RST set on the current segment. It does not validate a remembered connection and can match a forged ACK without a preceding client session.

cards.front: What sequence numbers does IOS commonly assign when you omit them?
cards.back: Usually 10, 20, 30 and so on. Inspect the actual entries before editing, because explicit numbers, remarks and platform behavior can affect what is displayed.

cards.front: How do you remove only sequence 20 from a named ACL on supported IOS?
cards.back: Enter ip access-list extended NAME (or standard as appropriate), then no 20. Verify the resulting list rather than deleting the whole ACL.

cards.front: What does ip access-list resequence CLIENTS-IN 100 10 do?
cards.back: Renumbers entries starting at 100 with an increment of 10. It preserves relative rule order and is not intended to change the policy. Verify syntax support and resulting entries.

cards.front: Why avoid legacy global no access-list N ACE-text when deleting one entry?
cards.back: Cisco documents that this form can delete the entire numbered ACL. Use sequence deletion within the correct ACL submode on supported IOS.

cards.front: Which two checks establish ACL contents and interface attachment?
cards.back: show access-lists NAME for entries and supported counters; show ip interface INTERFACE for inbound and outbound references. An ACL can exist without filtering that interface.

cards.front: Why is a successful router-originated ping insufficient to validate a transit ACL?
cards.back: Its source and processing path can differ from the host’s packet. Classic IOS outbound ACL behavior commonly bypasses locally generated traffic. Test the affected host’s actual path.

cards.front: What is the classic IOS behavior for an absent or empty referenced interface ACL?
cards.back: It provides no restriction in the documented classic behavior. Build and review the complete list before attachment; do not assume a misspelled or empty list supplies implicit deny.

commands.task: Permit sources in 10.100.10.0/24 using numbered standard ACL 10.
commands.note: This defines an entry, not its attachment. A standard list cannot select destination services.

commands.task: In numbered extended ACL 101, permit TCP from 10.100.10.0/24 to host 10.100.20.20 destination port 443.
commands.note: The service-port condition follows the destination. Other requirements, including return traffic, need separate evaluation.

commands.task: Attach IPv4 ACL 101 to packets entering the current interface.
commands.note: In is relative to this interface. A second inbound IPv4 attachment replaces the current one.

commands.task: Enter configuration mode for the named extended ACL CLIENTS-IN.
commands.note: The extended keyword chooses the matching capabilities. The name does not determine standard versus extended.

commands.task: Add sequence 15 permitting ICMP echo requests from 10.100.10.10 to 10.100.20.20 in the current extended ACL.
commands.note: Use an image supporting sequence insertion. The exception must appear before a broader matching deny.

commands.task: Delete only sequence 20 from the current named ACL on IOS supporting sequence editing.
commands.note: This removes one entry in ACL submode. Global no access-list N can remove the whole numbered list.

commands.task: Resequence CLIENTS-IN starting at 100 with increments of 10.
commands.note: Relative entry order is preserved. If unsupported, keep the numbering or build a complete replacement list.

commands.task: Permit TCP from any source to 10.100.10.0/24 when ACK or RST is set.
commands.note: This checks flags only; it does not prove the packet belongs to an established session.

commands.task: Restrict incoming sessions on the current VTY range using standard ACL VTY-ADMINS.
commands.note: Apply to every available VTY range. This does not filter unrelated transit packets.

commands.task: Display configured access lists and the match counters supported by this IOS image.
commands.note: Counter changes are evidence of matches, not proof of end-to-end application success.

commands.task: Display detailed IPv4 information, including ACL attachments, for GigabitEthernet0/0.
commands.note: Read both incoming and outgoing list names. show ip interface brief does not provide these ACL references.

commands.task: On IOS supporting this command, clear match counters for CLIENTS-IN before a controlled test.
commands.note: This resets counters, not ACEs. If unavailable in the simulator, record the before and after values instead.

tickets.title: A client policy also blocks router management
tickets.scenario: PC-A is 10.100.10.10/24 and connects through R1 G0/0 at 10.100.10.1. WEB is 10.100.20.20 behind G0/1. Before the change, PC-A could SSH to R1 and browse WEB. SSH, credentials and VTY-ADMINS remain unchanged; VTY-ADMINS permits PC-A. After CLIENTS-IN is attached inbound on G0/0, WEB still loads but a fresh SSH connection to R1 fails.

exhibits.title: Representative interface and ACL excerpts
exhibits.text:
GigabitEthernet0/0: Inbound access list is CLIENTS-IN
10 permit tcp 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.100.20.20 eq 80
20 deny ip any any

exhibits.title: Controlled test observations
exhibits.text:
PC-A -> 10.100.20.20 TCP destination 80: succeeds
PC-A -> 10.100.10.1 TCP destination 22: fails
Entry 20 increments during fresh SSH attempts.

tickets.question: Which missing permission explains the management failure?
options: An outbound VTY access class permitting WEB
An interface permission for PC-A TCP/22 to R1 before deny 20
A default route pointing from R1 toward WEB
An established keyword on the HTTP request permit
tickets.explanation: The interface list checks the incoming SSH packet even though its destination is R1 itself. It misses the WEB-only permit and reaches deny 20 before VTY access is considered. The working web test and explicit deny matches fit this policy error. An outgoing VTY restriction does not admit incoming SSH; the connected server network does not need a default route; established on HTTP would not match SSH and would reject ordinary initial SYNs.
tickets.fix:
Use the local console and a supported sequence-editing image.

```ios
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip access-list extended CLIENTS-IN
R1(config-ext-nacl)# 15 permit tcp host 10.100.10.10 host 10.100.10.1 eq 22
R1(config-ext-nacl)# end
R1# show access-lists CLIENTS-IN
```
Retry a new SSH session from PC-A, confirm WEB still loads, and confirm an unapproved client remains blocked. If insertion is unsupported, build an equivalent complete replacement ACL under a new name and replace the interface reference.

tickets.title: The deny rule is below a matching permit
tickets.scenario: A branch policy must deny TCP destination port 22 from 10.100.10.0/24 to FILES at 10.100.20.30, while permitting other IPv4 traffic. The list is correctly attached inbound on the branch LAN interface. There is no other filter in the path. Fresh SSH connections still succeed.

exhibits.title: Representative show access-lists BRANCH-IN
exhibits.text:
10 permit ip any any (64 matches)
20 deny tcp 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.100.20.30 eq 22 (0 matches)

exhibits.title: Interface attachment
exhibits.text: GigabitEthernet0/0: Inbound access list is BRANCH-IN

tickets.question: What change enforces the stated policy?
options: Move the list outbound on the same client interface
Add a second permit after sequence 20
Put the SSH deny before the general permit
Replace destination port 22 with UDP port 22
tickets.explanation: Every IPv4 packet matches sequence 10, so the router never reaches deny 20. Placing the specific deny first implements the intended exception. Reversing direction on the client interface would miss requests; another permit does not repair order; SSH uses TCP.
tickets.fix:
Build a complete replacement before changing the reference.

```ios
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip access-list extended BRANCH-FIXED
R1(config-ext-nacl)# deny tcp 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.100.20.30 eq 22
R1(config-ext-nacl)# permit ip any any
R1(config-ext-nacl)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ip access-group BRANCH-FIXED in
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show access-lists BRANCH-FIXED
```
Start a new SSH connection and verify denial. Test a separately permitted service and compare counter changes. Existing application sessions and cached displays are not sufficient fresh tests.

tickets.title: A source-only rule blocks more destinations than intended
tickets.scenario: PC-B is 10.100.10.11 on R1 G0/0. R1 G0/1 faces the protected server LAN 10.100.20.0/24. R1 G0/2 faces another reachable network 10.100.30.0/24. PC-B should be blocked only from the server LAN. The new standard ACL instead prevents PC-B from reaching either network; other clients still work.

exhibits.title: Representative relevant configuration
exhibits.text:
access-list 10 deny host 10.100.10.11
access-list 10 permit any
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip access-group 10 in
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 no shutdown
interface GigabitEthernet0/2
 no shutdown

exhibits.title: Baseline
exhibits.text:
Both /24 destination networks were reachable before applying ACL 10.
There are no other ACL attachments on these interfaces.

tickets.question: How can the same standard ACL enforce the intended destination boundary?
options: Move ACL 10 to G0/1 outbound
Move ACL 10 to G0/0 outbound
Delete the permit any entry
Apply ACL 10 inbound on all three interfaces
tickets.explanation: ACL 10 matches only the source. Inbound on G0/0 it rejects PC-B before any destination is selected. Outbound on G0/1 confines that rejection to traffic entering the server LAN. Outbound on G0/0 tests replies with different sources; deleting permit any would deny everyone evaluated by the list; applying it everywhere would broaden the error.
tickets.fix:
Configure through the console.

```ios
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# no ip access-group 10 in
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ip access-group 10 out
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1# show ip interface gigabitethernet0/1
```
Verify that PC-B is denied toward 10.100.20.0/24 and allowed toward 10.100.30.0/24, while another client retains its permitted access. If the policy later distinguishes two servers in the same LAN, use an extended ACL.

sections.title: Verify the path, negotiation and data

lab.title: Trace an IPsec VPN and distinguish transport, negotiation and application faults
devices: Optional encryption: 2 × ISR 4351 with supported IOS XE and IPsec capability, replacing the two edge routers
lab.intro:
The required exercise combines a reproducible Packet Tracer IP baseline with an IPsec evidence worksheet. Both exam versions ask you to **describe** these VPNs. You can complete the packet-path, protection, fault and recovery reasoning without an emulator that supports modern IPsec.

Step 4 is an optional complete IKEv2 configuration reference for two supported IOS XE routers. It is **not a Packet Tracer instruction**. Cisco documents this crypto-map/IKEv2 configuration family on ISR 4351 with IOS XE 16.12; use a suitable supported image with the necessary IPsec capability and confirm its command support. The explicit optional hardware target is two physical ISR 4351 routers with that configuration family available; virtual-platform names and interface numbering require their own image documentation. An arbitrary CML node or Packet Tracer router is not assumed to emulate these features. Do not substitute an obsolete IKEv1 or weak-algorithm configuration merely to make a simulator accept the commands.

No lab was executed in Packet Tracer or on IOS XE during this content review. All VPN status, counter and capture examples are representative teaching evidence. Keep the required baseline and worksheet separate from any claim that Packet Tracer encrypted a packet.
lab.topology:
Use new/default devices. All host-to-switch and switch-to-router links use copper straight-through. The two router-to-ISP links use copper crossover or Packet Tracer's automatic cable choice. SW-BR and SW-HQ use default VLAN 1 access ports; no switch management address is needed.

```diagram
{ "type": "topology", "title": "A branch and headquarters through a transit router", "caption": "ISP has only the two WAN /30 networks. An encrypted tunnel-mode packet is routed using the edge routers' WAN addresses.", "nodes": [ { "id": "P1", "kind": "pc", "label": "PC-BR", "sub": "10.1.1.10/24", "x": 0.5, "y": 3 }, { "id": "S1", "kind": "switch", "label": "SW-BR", "x": 2, "y": 3 }, { "id": "B", "kind": "router", "label": "R-BR", "sub": "198.51.100.1", "x": 4, "y": 3 }, { "id": "I", "kind": "router", "label": "ISP", "sub": "WAN routes only", "x": 6.5, "y": 3 }, { "id": "H", "kind": "router", "label": "R-HQ", "sub": "203.0.113.1", "x": 9, "y": 3 }, { "id": "S2", "kind": "switch", "label": "SW-HQ", "x": 11, "y": 3 }, { "id": "P2", "kind": "pc", "label": "PC-HQ", "sub": "10.2.2.20/24", "x": 12.5, "y": 3 } ], "links": [ { "from": "P1", "to": "S1" }, { "from": "S1", "to": "B" }, { "from": "B", "to": "I", "label": "198.51.100.0/30", "accent": true }, { "from": "I", "to": "H", "label": "203.0.113.0/30", "accent": true }, { "from": "H", "to": "S2" }, { "from": "S2", "to": "P2" } ] }
```

| Device / baseline port | Connected port | Address / mask | Gateway or next hop |
|---|---|---|---|
| R-BR G0/0 | ISP G0/0 | `198.51.100.1 / 255.255.255.252` | Default route via `198.51.100.2` |

For optional ISR 4351 edge routers, map baseline G0/0 to **GigabitEthernet0/0/0** and G0/1 to **GigabitEthernet0/0/1**. Use those substituted names when entering Step 1 on the edge devices. The optional Step 4 already uses the ISR 4351 names. For physical practice, use physical 2960 access switches, a 2911 transit router, and two Ethernet-connected host computers instead of PC-PT. On Windows, open the connected Ethernet adapter’s IPv4 properties, choose manual addressing, and enter the same address, mask and gateway from the table; DNS may remain blank. Use `ping` from the hosts’ command prompts. ISP uses G0/0 and G0/1. Do not configure NAT, GRE, OSPF or extra private routes on ISP.

steps.title: Build the routed baseline
steps.body:
Cable the devices and set both PC addresses and gateways under Desktop → IP Configuration → Static. Use the routers' local CLI tabs. No DNS is needed because every baseline test uses an address.

```ios R-BR
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R-BR
R-BR(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R-BR(config-if)# ip address 198.51.100.1 255.255.255.252
R-BR(config-if)# no shutdown
R-BR(config-if)# exit
R-BR(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R-BR(config-if)# ip address 10.1.1.1 255.255.255.0
R-BR(config-if)# no shutdown
R-BR(config-if)# exit
R-BR(config)# ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 198.51.100.2
R-BR(config)# end
```

```ios ISP
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname ISP
ISP(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
ISP(config-if)# ip address 198.51.100.2 255.255.255.252
ISP(config-if)# no shutdown
ISP(config-if)# exit
ISP(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
ISP(config-if)# ip address 203.0.113.2 255.255.255.252
ISP(config-if)# no shutdown
ISP(config-if)# end
```

```ios R-HQ
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R-HQ
R-HQ(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R-HQ(config-if)# ip address 203.0.113.1 255.255.255.252
R-HQ(config-if)# no shutdown
R-HQ(config-if)# exit
R-HQ(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R-HQ(config-if)# ip address 10.2.2.1 255.255.255.0
R-HQ(config-if)# no shutdown
R-HQ(config-if)# exit
R-HQ(config)# ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 203.0.113.2
R-HQ(config)# end
```

:::expected
Each PC and its local router share a /24. Each WAN link has the two usable addresses of its /30. ISP needs only its connected WAN routes to reach either edge's public address. These documentation WAN addresses model a transit network; this lab is not connected to the public Internet.
:::

steps.title: Verify what works before IPsec
steps.body:
On each router, inspect `show ip interface brief` and `show ip route`. From PC-BR ping `10.1.1.1`; from PC-HQ ping `10.2.2.1`. From the edge routers test the opposite public address:

```ios R-BR
R-BR# ping 203.0.113.1
R-BR# show ip route 203.0.113.1
```

```ios R-HQ
R-HQ# ping 198.51.100.1
R-HQ# show ip route 198.51.100.1
```

Then, from PC-BR, ping `10.2.2.20`. Record the result without adding a private route to ISP.

:::expected
Local gateway pings and edge-to-edge public-address pings should succeed after links and ARP settle. The private host-to-host ping fails: ISP has no route for the inner LAN destinations. A timeout or an unreachable may be displayed. This establishes underlay IP/ICMP reachability, not working IPsec. Save this required Packet Tracer baseline as `vpn-underlay.pkt`.
:::

steps.title: Draw the protected packet on paper
steps.body:
For an ESP tunnel-mode VPN with encryption between R-BR and R-HQ, write the source and destination at three points: PC-BR to R-BR, R-BR to ISP, and R-HQ to PC-HQ. Identify where the original IP header is encrypted and which destination ISP uses. Then describe what plain GRE would change.

:::expected
Before R-BR: original IP `10.1.1.10 -> 10.2.2.20`. Across ISP: outer IP `198.51.100.1 -> 203.0.113.1`, followed by ESP and protected inner content. After R-HQ decrypts: original IP `10.1.1.10 -> 10.2.2.20` again. ISP forwards using `203.0.113.1`, not the encrypted inner destination. Plain GRE would provide encapsulation but no encryption; its inner content would remain readable to a suitable observer.
:::

steps.title: Optional supported IOS XE IKEv2 configuration
steps.body:
Worksheet-only learners should read the purpose of each block and continue to Step 5. **Do not paste this into the Packet Tracer baseline.** For live optional practice, use the supported edge devices and interface mapping specified in Topology; complete Steps 1–2 on that environment first. Confirm `show version`, feature availability and the `crypto ikev2` command family. Use a fresh isolated configuration with no other crypto policy, NAT or ACL attachment.

The proposal specifies IKE algorithms; the policy references that proposal. The profile matches the peer's identity and configures authentication. The transform set specifies ESP data protection. The selector identifies the two LANs; the crypto map combines the peer, profile, transform and selector, then attaches to the WAN interface. The demonstration pre-shared key is the same at both ends and is intended only for this isolated exercise.

```ios R-BR — optional IOS XE
R-BR# configure terminal
R-BR(config)# crypto ikev2 proposal CCNA-PROPOSAL
R-BR(config-ikev2-proposal)# encryption aes-cbc-256
R-BR(config-ikev2-proposal)# integrity sha256
R-BR(config-ikev2-proposal)# prf sha256
R-BR(config-ikev2-proposal)# group 14
R-BR(config-ikev2-proposal)# exit
R-BR(config)# crypto ikev2 policy CCNA-POLICY
R-BR(config-ikev2-policy)# proposal CCNA-PROPOSAL
R-BR(config-ikev2-policy)# exit
R-BR(config)# crypto ikev2 profile CCNA-PROFILE
R-BR(config-ikev2-profile)# match identity remote address 203.0.113.1 255.255.255.255
R-BR(config-ikev2-profile)# identity local address 198.51.100.1
R-BR(config-ikev2-profile)# authentication remote pre-share key 0 CCNA-Only-35-Lab!
R-BR(config-ikev2-profile)# authentication local pre-share key 0 CCNA-Only-35-Lab!
R-BR(config-ikev2-profile)# exit
R-BR(config)# crypto ipsec transform-set CCNA-ESP esp-aes 256 esp-sha256-hmac
R-BR(cfg-crypto-trans)# mode tunnel
R-BR(cfg-crypto-trans)# exit
R-BR(config)# ip access-list extended VPN-SELECT
R-BR(config-ext-nacl)# permit ip 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255 10.2.2.0 0.0.0.255
R-BR(config-ext-nacl)# exit
R-BR(config)# crypto map CCNA-MAP 10 ipsec-isakmp
R-BR(config-crypto-map)# set peer 203.0.113.1
R-BR(config-crypto-map)# set transform-set CCNA-ESP
R-BR(config-crypto-map)# set ikev2-profile CCNA-PROFILE
R-BR(config-crypto-map)# match address VPN-SELECT
R-BR(config-crypto-map)# exit
R-BR(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0/0
R-BR(config-if)# crypto map CCNA-MAP
R-BR(config-if)# end
```

```ios R-HQ — optional IOS XE
R-HQ# configure terminal
R-HQ(config)# crypto ikev2 proposal CCNA-PROPOSAL
R-HQ(config-ikev2-proposal)# encryption aes-cbc-256
R-HQ(config-ikev2-proposal)# integrity sha256
R-HQ(config-ikev2-proposal)# prf sha256
R-HQ(config-ikev2-proposal)# group 14
R-HQ(config-ikev2-proposal)# exit
R-HQ(config)# crypto ikev2 policy CCNA-POLICY
R-HQ(config-ikev2-policy)# proposal CCNA-PROPOSAL
R-HQ(config-ikev2-policy)# exit
R-HQ(config)# crypto ikev2 profile CCNA-PROFILE
R-HQ(config-ikev2-profile)# match identity remote address 198.51.100.1 255.255.255.255
R-HQ(config-ikev2-profile)# identity local address 203.0.113.1
R-HQ(config-ikev2-profile)# authentication remote pre-share key 0 CCNA-Only-35-Lab!
R-HQ(config-ikev2-profile)# authentication local pre-share key 0 CCNA-Only-35-Lab!
R-HQ(config-ikev2-profile)# exit
R-HQ(config)# crypto ipsec transform-set CCNA-ESP esp-aes 256 esp-sha256-hmac
R-HQ(cfg-crypto-trans)# mode tunnel
R-HQ(cfg-crypto-trans)# exit
R-HQ(config)# ip access-list extended VPN-SELECT
R-HQ(config-ext-nacl)# permit ip 10.2.2.0 0.0.0.255 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255
R-HQ(config-ext-nacl)# exit
R-HQ(config)# crypto map CCNA-MAP 10 ipsec-isakmp
R-HQ(config-crypto-map)# set peer 198.51.100.1
R-HQ(config-crypto-map)# set transform-set CCNA-ESP
R-HQ(config-crypto-map)# set ikev2-profile CCNA-PROFILE
R-HQ(config-crypto-map)# match address VPN-SELECT
R-HQ(config-crypto-map)# exit
R-HQ(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0/0
R-HQ(config-if)# crypto map CCNA-MAP
R-HQ(config-if)# end
```

:::expected
The selector on each router is the reverse of the other's. The default routes send packets toward the WAN; the crypto map protects matching packets before they cross ISP. `ipsec-isakmp` in the crypto-map command is not evidence of IKEv1 here: the `set ikev2-profile` reference selects this IKEv2 implementation. No private route is added to ISP, and no GRE tunnel is required for these unicast host tests. If the required feature or algorithm is unavailable, use the evidence worksheet rather than assuming an equivalent command exists.
:::

steps.title: Read negotiation and data evidence separately
steps.body:
In the optional environment, send a fresh ping from PC-BR to PC-HQ. Initial requests may be lost while negotiation occurs; repeat after inspecting the status. Use the protected host as the source, not a router's public interface. The following commands are for supported IOS XE:

```ios R-BR
R-BR# show crypto ikev2 sa
R-BR# show crypto ipsec sa
R-BR# show crypto map
R-BR# show access-lists VPN-SELECT
```

Run the IKEv2 and IPsec checks on R-HQ as well. Worksheet learners should interpret this supplied evidence instead. It assumes no NAT, native ESP and the selector pair from Step 4; fields are simplified and totals illustrative.

```output Representative evidence for one controlled test interval
R-BR IKEv2: local 198.51.100.1/500, remote 203.0.113.1/500, READY
R-BR IPsec selectors: local 10.1.1.0/24, remote 10.2.2.0/24
R-HQ IPsec selectors: local 10.2.2.0/24, remote 10.1.1.0/24
Negotiated data protection: ESP AES-256 with SHA-256 integrity, tunnel mode
WAN packet type for protected data: native ESP, IP protocol 50

Counter deltas during fresh PC-BR -> PC-HQ echo tests:
R-BR: encaps +4, decaps +4
R-HQ: encaps +4, decaps +4
Host observation: echo replies received
```

:::expected
The IKE state shows a completed negotiation relationship. The selected IPsec SAs carried traffic in both directions during the interval, and the host test received replies. These conclusions rely on the combination of evidence, not on READY alone. Four is an illustrative test count, not an invariant command result. ISP can still have no route to either private LAN because it forwards the protected outer packets.
:::

steps.title: Introduce a native-ESP filter fault and observe
steps.body:
For the worksheet, assume the displayed native-ESP transport from Step 5. In the live optional lab, first verify that protected traffic actually uses native ESP; if it uses UDP encapsulation, this particular fault will not block that transport, so use the worksheet for this case.

On ISP, apply an outbound ACL toward R-HQ that denies native ESP from R-BR but leaves IKE and other IPv4 packets permitted. This configuration is a real interface filter, unlike the VPN-SELECT crypto selector.

```ios ISP — optional live VPN environment
ISP# configure terminal
ISP(config)# ip access-list extended VPN-FAULT
ISP(config-ext-nacl)# deny esp host 198.51.100.1 host 203.0.113.1
ISP(config-ext-nacl)# permit ip any any
ISP(config-ext-nacl)# exit
ISP(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
ISP(config-if)# ip access-group VPN-FAULT out
ISP(config-if)# end
ISP# show access-lists VPN-FAULT
ISP# show ip interface gigabitethernet0/1
```

Send new host-to-host pings and compare both peers' counters. Also test a public-address ping from R-BR. Do not remove the fault until you have explained the following representative observations.

```output Representative fault evidence
Public-address ping R-BR -> 203.0.113.1: succeeds
Fresh PC-BR -> PC-HQ ping: fails
R-BR IKEv2 relationship: still present
During the fresh host test:
  R-BR encaps increases; R-BR decaps does not increase
  ISP VPN-FAULT ESP deny counter increases
  R-HQ decaps does not increase
```

:::expected
The public ping uses ICMP, and IKE uses UDP; both can pass the final permit. The selected data packets use native ESP and hit the specific deny. This is why an underlay ping and an established IKE SA can coexist with failed user traffic. The ACL and controlled counter changes supply the fault evidence; the one-sided IPsec counters alone would not uniquely identify the cause. In the required Packet Tracer baseline no ESP is generated, so applying this ACL there would not reproduce an IPsec failure.
:::

steps.title: Remove the fault and verify recovery
steps.body:
In the live optional environment, remove the attachment through ISP's local console. Worksheet learners should predict the next observations before reading the expected result.

```ios ISP
ISP# configure terminal
ISP(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
ISP(config-if)# no ip access-group VPN-FAULT out
ISP(config-if)# end
ISP# show ip interface gigabitethernet0/1
```

Retry host-to-host traffic and recheck both IPsec counters. Existing SAs can carry the restored traffic; if negotiation expired, fresh matching traffic can establish it again. No broad clear-crypto reset is required merely to remove this filter fault.

:::expected
ISP reports no outbound ACL on G0/1. With the rest of the baseline unchanged, host replies resume and the appropriate encapsulation/decapsulation counters increase at both ends. Record new deltas instead of comparing cumulative counters with an earlier screenshot. Leave the now-unattached VPN-FAULT list as documentation or remove it only after confirming it has no other references.
:::

steps.title: Compare a remote-access user and NAT-T
steps.body:
This is a paper exercise; the topology does not include a configured remote-access headend. A laptop on hotel Wi-Fi authenticates to the corporate gateway using an IKEv2/IPsec client. The hotel translates the laptop's private source address with PAT. The gateway assigns VPN address `10.250.0.10` and a split-tunnel route for `10.2.2.0/24`.

Explain: which device is the remote IPsec endpoint; how the translated path can carry ESP; whether a public website outside the split route is protected by this tunnel; and whether a successful VPN login guarantees access to PC-HQ. Then contrast the arrangement with the site-to-site branch.

:::expected
The laptop, not the hotel's router, is the remote VPN endpoint. UDP NAT-T can carry ESP through PAT using UDP 4500. Traffic outside the split route follows the local connection in this stated policy and is not protected by this VPN. The client still needs an appropriate route, gateway policy, return route and working application service. In the site-to-site branch, R-BR protects traffic on behalf of its LAN hosts. DNS settings and DNS query routing require their own policy review.
:::

steps.title: Save the environment and write the evidence summary
steps.body:
Keep the required Packet Tracer file labeled as an underlay exercise. If you completed the optional live VPN, save the recovered configurations on all three routers and retain the actual show output separately from this worksheet.

```ios R-BR
R-BR# copy running-config startup-config
```

```ios R-HQ
R-HQ# copy running-config startup-config
```

```ios ISP
ISP# copy running-config startup-config
```

:::expected
Accept each default startup-config filename. Your written summary identifies the two protected LANs, both public peer addresses, IKE version, ESP mode and algorithms, whether data is native ESP or UDP-encapsulated, the successful application test, and the separate fault/recovery observations. If you used the worksheet only, label those observations as supplied representative evidence rather than live measurements.
:::

lab.troubleshooting:
- **Public-address ping fails:** check interfaces, /30 masks, connected routes and both edge default routes. Restore underlay reachability before investigating IKE.
- **Public ping works but IKE does not:** inspect the configured IKE version, UDP transport policy, peer identity, matching proposals and authentication. A ping does not test those requirements.
- **No data counters change:** confirm the actual source and destination match the selector and the correct map is attached. A public-interface-sourced ping is not the LAN-to-LAN test.
- **Only outbound protection increases:** check the far peer's received traffic, access policy, host reply generation, return route and return protection. Do not infer a unique wrong key or selector from that counter pattern alone.
- **Counter totals exist but current traffic fails:** they may be historical. Measure new deltas for the relevant SA while running a fresh test.
- **Both data directions work but an application fails:** test the service, host firewall, DNS if names are used, user authorization and packet-size behavior.
- **A crypto command is rejected:** confirm the exact model, release and supported features. Packet Tracer and a generic CML node are not substitutes for the optional IOS XE platform.
lab.challenge:
Use only the original topology and selector pair. Independently answer these cases before looking at the key:

1. PC-BR sends TCP destination port 8443 to PC-HQ. Does the crypto selector include it even though no application is configured on that port?
2. R-BR pings `203.0.113.1` with source `198.51.100.1`. Does that test select the same protected LAN traffic?
3. In the native-ESP fault, an engineer adds `permit udp host 198.51.100.1 host 203.0.113.1 eq 50`. Does it permit ESP?
4. A revised path uses UDP NAT-T. What transport must the relevant perimeter rule allow for the encapsulated data, and what remains encrypted?
5. A single screenshot shows encaps 800 and decaps 800. Is the application working now?

:::expected
1. Yes. The selector uses `permit ip` between the two LANs and is not limited to ICMP or a particular TCP port. Encryption does not create a listening application, so the service test can still fail.
2. No. Both addresses are outside the private LAN pair. This checks underlay reachability, not the same selection or protection.
3. No. Native ESP is IP protocol 50, not UDP destination port 50. The specific native-ESP deny must be removed or replaced with an appropriate earlier permit. Step 7 provides the complete recovery for this isolated fault.
4. The stated UDP-encapsulated data uses UDP 4500; initial IKE reachability commonly also requires UDP 500. ESP's protected content remains protected inside the UDP wrapper. Native-ESP permission is not a substitute for UDP-4500 permission.
5. No. Those are cumulative totals with no test interval or application observation. Record before/after counters and perform a fresh application test using the intended endpoints.
:::

questions.prompt: A branch needs protected access to headquarters for its LAN hosts, without installing VPN software on each host. Which arrangement fits?
options: An HTTPS application portal used separately by each person
A remote-access VPN client installed on every computer
A site-to-site IPsec VPN between the two gateways
A plain GRE tunnel with no cryptographic protection
questions.explanation: A site-to-site VPN lets the gateways protect selected traffic on behalf of their LANs. Hosts send ordinary traffic to their default gateways; they need no client for this gateway-to-gateway protection.

whyWrong.0: An application portal is not the requested LAN-to-LAN IPsec arrangement.
whyWrong.1: This makes each user device a VPN endpoint and violates the stated setup requirement.
whyWrong.3: Plain GRE encapsulates but does not encrypt.

exhibit.title: Representative counter comparison
exhibit.text:
Before: #pkts encaps 1180, #pkts decaps 100
After:  #pkts encaps 1184, #pkts decaps 100
Fresh client test: no reply received

questions.prompt: These deltas were measured for the same IPsec SA during a fresh host test. Which conclusion is supported?
options: Outbound protection increased; successful inbound decapsulation did not
No packet matched the local selector during the interval
The pre-shared keys are definitely different at the peers
The remote LAN default gateway is definitely missing
questions.explanation: The outgoing counter increased while incoming decapsulation did not. Check the far peer, WAN path, receive errors, remote host delivery and return path. The counters do not uniquely distinguish those possible causes.

whyWrong.1: An increase in encapsulation shows additional traffic was selected and protected locally.
whyWrong.2: The counter pattern does not prove an authentication mismatch; existing data SAs can also outlive a separate IKE event.
whyWrong.3: A missing return gateway is one possible fault, but no host configuration evidence identifies it here.

questions.prompt: Which two protocol identifiers are correct for the ordinary IPsec arrangements in this chapter? Choose two.
options: AH is UDP destination port 51
Native ESP is IP protocol 50
IKE commonly starts on UDP destination port 500
UDP NAT-T encapsulates ESP using TCP port 4500
Plain GRE is IP protocol 50
questions.explanation: Native ESP is identified in the IP Protocol field by 50. IKE commonly begins over UDP 500. AH is protocol 51; standard UDP NAT-T uses UDP 4500.

whyWrong.0: 51 is an IP protocol number for AH, not a UDP port.
whyWrong.3: The UDP encapsulation specified here uses UDP 4500, not TCP.
whyWrong.4: GRE is IP protocol 47 and does not itself provide encryption.

questions.prompt: An IKEv2/IPsec client connects through a hotel PAT device using UDP encapsulation. What carries the protected ESP data through PAT?
options: The gateway converts the connection into a browser portal
The client switches to IKEv1 aggressive mode
AH replaces ESP because it tolerates address translation
NAT-T wraps ESP in UDP using port 4500
questions.explanation: UDP NAT traversal supplies a UDP flow that the NAT/PAT device can handle while the ESP protection remains inside. IKEv2 includes NAT detection and supports this encapsulation.

whyWrong.0: Changing VPN type is not the mechanism described.
whyWrong.1: IKEv1 mode selection does not provide the UDP wrapper and is not part of this IKEv2 connection.
whyWrong.2: AH protects selected IP-header fields; ordinary address translation conflicts with that protection.

exhibit.title: Simplified layout, not readable captured ciphertext
exhibit.text:
Outer IP: 198.51.100.1 -> 203.0.113.1
ESP header: SPI and sequence
Encrypted: original IP 10.1.1.10 -> 10.2.2.20, TCP header, data, ESP trailer
Authentication data

questions.prompt: The packet layout is a teaching diagram of an ESP VPN with confidentiality enabled. Which mode is shown?
options: Transport mode, because ESP follows an IP header
Tunnel mode: the gateways use a newly added outer IP header
Transport mode, because the inner packet uses TCP
Tunnel mode, because the SPI specifies a GRE tunnel
questions.explanation: IPsec has added an outer header for the gateways and protected the original host-to-host packet inside it. That is ESP tunnel mode. A normal WAN capture cannot read the inner plaintext without decryption material.

whyWrong.0: ESP can follow an IP header in either mode; the new outer header is decisive here.
whyWrong.2: TCP versus UDP does not choose IPsec tunnel or transport mode.
whyWrong.3: An SPI identifies an SA, not a GRE tunnel, and no GRE header is shown.

questions.prompt: Which service is absent from AH even when AH uses tunnel mode?
options: Confidentiality through payload encryption
Integrity checking of protected content
Data-origin authentication using the agreed key
Anti-replay support through sequence processing
questions.explanation: AH authenticates protected information and supports replay checking, but it does not encrypt. Adding a tunnel-mode outer header does not turn AH into an encryption protocol.

whyWrong.1: Integrity is an AH service.
whyWrong.2: AH supports data-origin authentication.
whyWrong.3: AH includes sequence-number mechanisms for anti-replay processing.

questions.prompt: Which two statements describe remote-access IPsec correctly? Choose two.
options: The user device can be an IPsec endpoint
The whole remote LAN must use a permanent public address
Successful authentication authorizes every internal application
An IKEv2 client may authenticate the user, device, or both under the configured policy
The Secure Client name proves that TLS is the VPN transport
questions.explanation: Remote access protects a connection involving the remote device and a gateway. Authentication and authorization are policy-dependent; the client product name alone does not determine whether it uses IPsec or TLS.

whyWrong.1: A client can initiate from a changing address and operate through NAT-T; an entire remote LAN is not the required endpoint.
whyWrong.2: Network access and application permissions remain separate from successful authentication.
whyWrong.4: Cisco Secure Client supports more than one VPN transport.

exhibit.title: Representative legacy show crypto isakmp sa excerpt
exhibit.text:
dst             src             state        status
203.0.113.1     198.51.100.1    MM_NO_STATE  ACTIVE (deleted)

questions.prompt: What can be concluded from this single legacy IKEv1 excerpt?
options: Authentication completed and all user applications are working
This deleted negotiation entry is not evidence of a completed authenticated SA
The IPsec selectors are definitely reversed incorrectly
A wrong pre-shared key is uniquely proved by this state
questions.explanation: MM_NO_STATE with a deleted entry does not establish a completed authenticated IKEv1 relationship. Additional transport, proposal and authentication evidence is required. Do not map one transitional or failed state to one guaranteed cause.

whyWrong.0: The displayed entry does not establish completed authentication or application success.
whyWrong.2: No selectors or phase-2 evidence are shown.
whyWrong.3: A key mismatch is not uniquely determined by this state.

questions.prompt: Which example directly fits ESP transport mode without another encapsulating tunnel?
options: Two gateways adding a new outer header for hosts behind them
A gateway hiding an entire original host-to-host IP header inside ESP
A VPN whose packet uses two IP headers because IPsec added an outer one
Two IPsec-capable hosts protecting their own payload while retaining the original IP header
questions.explanation: In the straightforward host-to-host transport-mode case, the original IP header remains the routing header and ESP protects the carried upper-layer content. Tunnel mode supplies an additional outer header.

whyWrong.0: Adding an outer header for other hosts describes tunnel mode.
whyWrong.1: Putting the complete original packet inside ESP describes tunnel mode.
whyWrong.2: The added IPsec outer header identifies tunnel mode.

questions.prompt: In legacy IKEv1 terminology, what is phase 1 responsible for?
options: Encrypting every application packet directly in IKE messages
Replacing all IPsec data SAs with a permanent shared SPI
Establishing the authenticated IKE/ISAKMP SA for protected negotiation
Creating a route to the remote private subnet on the ISP
questions.explanation: Legacy phase 1 establishes the authenticated IKE/ISAKMP negotiation relationship; phase 2 negotiates IPsec data protection. Recognize this terminology in older output without treating IKEv1 as the recommended choice for a new implementation.

whyWrong.0: User data is normally carried in ESP, not IKE negotiation messages.
whyWrong.1: Data SAs remain distinct and directional; an SPI is an identifier, not a permanent universal key.
whyWrong.3: IKE negotiation does not install the inner LAN route on an intermediate ISP router.

questions.prompt: Which comparison of certificates and pre-shared keys is accurate for gateway authentication?
options: One shared key reused everywhere isolates each gateway compromise
Certificates support identity management at scale but require trust, validity and revocation checks
A certificate authority distributes the IPsec session keys instead of IKE
Certificates eliminate the need to authenticate the peer identity
questions.explanation: Certificates can make identities easier to manage across many peers, but the peers must validate those identities and their trust and validity conditions. Revocation also requires an effective checking policy. IKE still negotiates and derives traffic keying material.

whyWrong.0: Reusing one secret widens the impact of disclosure rather than isolating it.
whyWrong.2: The CA vouches for an identity/public-key association; IKE still handles session key establishment.
whyWrong.3: Authenticating the peer identity remains essential.

exhibit.title: Relevant crypto-map reference
exhibit.text:
ip access-list extended VPN-SELECT
 permit ip 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255 10.2.2.0 0.0.0.255
crypto map CCNA-MAP 10 ipsec-isakmp
 match address VPN-SELECT
 set peer 203.0.113.1

questions.prompt: VPN-SELECT is referenced only by a crypto map, not by ip access-group. What does its implicit deny mean for a packet outside the selected LAN pair?
options: The router must discard it as an interface ACL drop
It is encrypted with a default peer not shown here
It is not selected for protection by this crypto rule
It cannot be routed unless ESP is explicitly denied
questions.explanation: A crypto selector identifies traffic for protection. Exclusion from that selector does not itself impose an interface drop. If another route and policy permit it, unselected traffic can leave unprotected.

whyWrong.0: That confuses a crypto selection ACL with an attached packet filter.
whyWrong.1: An unmatched packet does not inherit an invented default encryption peer.
whyWrong.3: An ESP deny is not required for ordinary routing.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly separates IKEv2 from IPsec user-data protection?
options: IKEv2 negotiates and authenticates; its CHILD_SA supplies the directional IPsec SAs used for data
IKEv2 replaces ESP and carries all user data on UDP 500
IKEv2 is the same wire protocol as IKEv1 with renamed phases
A READY IKEv2 status proves the destination application accepted the user
questions.explanation: IKEv2 establishes an authenticated negotiation relationship and negotiates CHILD_SAs for IPsec data protection. That control-plane result must be checked separately from data forwarding and application access.

whyWrong.1: ESP remains a data protection protocol; UDP 500 negotiation is not a general user-data tunnel.
whyWrong.2: IKEv2 and IKEv1 are different protocols and are not backward compatible.
whyWrong.3: Negotiation status alone does not test the application.

questions.prompt: ISP has routes to both public gateway addresses but no route to either private LAN. Why can it still forward the encrypted tunnel-mode packet?
options: The ESP SPI tells ISP the private subnet route
IKE distributes every protected subnet to ISP
ISP decrypts the inner destination and uses a default private route
ISP forwards on the unencrypted outer destination 203.0.113.1
questions.explanation: The intermediate router forwards the outer packet toward the receiving VPN gateway. Only that gateway needs to recover the inner packet and route it onward to the local LAN.

whyWrong.0: ISP does not use the ESP SPI as a route to the private destination.
whyWrong.1: IKE between the gateways does not distribute those routes to ISP.
whyWrong.2: ISP has no IPsec keying role in this topology and does not decrypt the payload.

questions.prompt: A laptop has an IPsec split-tunnel policy for only 10.2.2.0/24. A public website is reached through the local Internet route. Which conclusion is correct?
options: Every laptop packet is protected because the VPN icon is connected
The local website traffic uses this VPN even without a matching route
The public website traffic is outside this VPN protection; it may have separate HTTPS protection
The laptop has become a site-to-site gateway for all hotel devices
questions.explanation: Only traffic selected by the stated split policy follows this VPN. A website using HTTPS can have independent application-layer encryption, but the VPN connection does not automatically protect the local Internet path.

whyWrong.0: Connection status does not change the stated split selection.
whyWrong.1: The scenario explicitly routes that destination outside the VPN.
whyWrong.3: A remote-access client does not automatically provide a gateway-to-gateway service for other hotel devices.

questions.prompt: Which two pairings correctly describe IPsec protection services? Choose two.
options: Confidentiality: prevent unauthorized reading of protected content
Integrity: guarantee delivery of every packet
Anti-replay: reject duplicate protected packets using receive sequence processing
Data-origin authentication: grant every authenticated peer unlimited application rights
Encryption: hide all outer addresses and traffic timing
questions.explanation: Confidentiality protects the content from unauthorized reading. Anti-replay processing helps reject duplicates and packets outside the acceptable receive window. These services do not imply availability, authorization or the concealment of all metadata.

whyWrong.1: Integrity detects unauthorized modification; it does not guarantee delivery.
whyWrong.3: Origin authentication and application authorization are different functions.
whyWrong.4: Outer routing information and timing remain observable.

cards.front: What identifies native ESP, and what protection can it provide?
cards.back: ESP is IP protocol 50. Its negotiated services can include confidentiality, integrity, data-origin authentication and anti-replay. Inspect the algorithms before assuming encryption is enabled.

cards.front: What identifies AH, and what does it not provide?
cards.back: AH is IP protocol 51. It provides integrity/authentication and anti-replay support, but no confidentiality. Tunnel mode does not add encryption to AH.

cards.front: Which port commonly carries the initial IKE exchange?
cards.back: UDP 500. IKE negotiates and authenticates; it is separate from ESP user-data protection.

cards.front: What is the purpose of standard UDP NAT-T?
cards.back: Encapsulate ESP in UDP, normally using port 4500, so NAT/PAT can handle a UDP flow. The protected ESP content remains inside the wrapper.

cards.front: Does permit udp any any eq 50 permit native ESP?
