cards.back: No. Native ESP is IP protocol 50, not UDP port 50. Standard UDP-encapsulated ESP uses UDP 4500 in the NAT-T arrangement described here.

cards.front: Distinguish confidentiality, integrity, origin authentication and anti-replay.
cards.back: Confidentiality protects content from reading; integrity detects modification; origin authentication establishes possession of the appropriate key; anti-replay helps reject duplicated protected packets. None grants unlimited application access.

cards.front: How do ESP tunnel and transport mode differ when encryption is enabled?
cards.back: Tunnel mode adds an outer IP header and protects the entire original packet. Transport mode retains the original routing header and protects the carried upper-layer content.

cards.front: Give a straightforward ESP transport-mode use case.
cards.back: Two IPsec-capable hosts protecting their own communication. The original host IP header remains outside ESP encryption. ESP transport mode can also protect an already encapsulated router-to-router GRE packet.

cards.front: What is legacy IKEv1 phase 1 for?
cards.back: Establish the authenticated IKE/ISAKMP negotiation SA. This is legacy terminology; IKEv1 is deprecated and IKEv2 uses different exchanges.

cards.front: What is legacy IKEv1 phase 2 for?
cards.back: Negotiate the IPsec data SAs under the protected IKE relationship. Data SAs are directional, distinct from the negotiation SA. This describes older material, not a new-design recommendation.

cards.front: What does IKEv2 establish for IPsec traffic?
cards.back: An authenticated IKE negotiation relationship and CHILD_SAs supplying the directional IPsec SAs. Initial setup normally includes IKE_SA_INIT and IKE_AUTH; later exchanges can create or rekey SAs.

cards.front: What does Diffie-Hellman provide, and what is still needed?
cards.back: It helps peers derive shared secret material without sending the secret directly. Authentication is still required to establish the peer identity. DH alone does not authenticate a person or encrypt application data.

cards.front: Why distinguish a negotiated algorithm from the label IPsec?
cards.back: IPsec permits different transforms. Modern implementations should follow current cryptographic guidance, commonly using AES with suitable integrity or authenticated encryption. Old simulator defaults are not proof of current suitability.

cards.front: How do pre-shared keys and certificates differ for peer authentication?
cards.back: A PSK is a configured shared secret. A certificate links an identity and public key through a trust system. Certificate use still requires identity, trust, time-validity and revocation-policy checks; IKE still derives session keying material.

cards.front: Where do site-to-site and remote-access IPsec terminate?
cards.back: Site-to-site normally terminates at two gateways acting for their networks. Remote access terminates at a user device and a VPN gateway.

cards.front: Does a Cisco Secure Client connection prove that the VPN uses TLS?
cards.back: No. Secure Client can use TLS-based VPNs or IKEv2/IPsec depending on configuration. A browser application portal is also not equivalent to assuming every device application has an IPsec tunnel.

cards.front: What does split tunneling change about VPN protection?
cards.back: Only selected traffic follows the VPN. Other traffic uses the local connection and is outside that VPN’s protection, though it may use separate HTTPS or other application security. DNS path policy must also be checked.

cards.front: What do READY and QM_IDLE indicate, and what do they not prove?
cards.back: They are familiar completed-negotiation indicators in appropriate IKEv2 and legacy IKEv1 output. They do not prove working data SAs, host return routes or application access. A failed or intermediate state also does not uniquely identify one cause.

cards.front: Encapsulation rises during a test but decapsulation does not. What is established?
cards.back: The observed SA protected more outbound packets but recorded no additional successful inbound decapsulation. Check both peers and the forward/return paths; the pattern alone does not prove a specific key, route or selector fault.

cards.front: Does a plain GRE tunnel protect its contents from reading?
cards.back: No. GRE supplies encapsulation, including support for carrying multicast between routers, but not encryption. IPsec can protect GRE; a tunnel interface being up does not prove that protection.

commands.task: Optional IOS XE: define CCNA-ESP using ESP AES-256 and SHA-256 HMAC.
commands.answer: crypto ipsec transform-set CCNA-ESP esp-aes 256 esp-sha256-hmac
commands.note: This sets data-protection transforms. It is not a complete VPN and differs from IKE proposal settings.

commands.task: Optional IOS XE: enter static crypto-map entry 10 named CCNA-MAP for negotiated IPsec.
commands.note: This syntax can be used by the IKEv2 example when set ikev2-profile references its profile; the keyword alone does not prove IKEv1.

commands.task: Optional IOS XE: attach the completed crypto map CCNA-MAP to the current WAN interface.
commands.note: The map references the peer, transforms, IKE profile and traffic selector. Check the actual interface and route used.

commands.task: Legacy output recognition: display IKEv1 ISAKMP security associations.
commands.note: Use this for a configured IKEv1 environment. It is not the IKEv2 status command, and negotiation state alone does not prove data delivery.

commands.task: On supported IOS XE, display IPsec SAs and encapsulation/decapsulation counters.
commands.note: Compare before/after counters for the relevant SA during a controlled test. Historical totals do not prove current application success.

commands.task: Optional route-based VPN inspection: display the detailed state and encapsulation of Tunnel0.
commands.note: Read the configured tunnel type rather than assuming GRE or a universal MTU. An up/up tunnel does not prove encryption or application reachability.

commands.task: On supported IOS XE, display IKEv2 security associations.
commands.note: Inspect the expected peer and negotiated relationship. Continue with data-SA and application checks.

commands.task: Check the selected IPv4 route to remote public peer 203.0.113.1.
commands.note: This inspects underlay routing. A route alone does not establish IKE reachability or IPsec protection.

commands.task: Display the configured IPv4 selection ACL VPN-SELECT.
commands.note: Read the source/destination pair and determine how the list is referenced. A crypto selector is not automatically an interface filter.

commands.task: On supported IOS XE, display configured crypto maps and their references.
commands.note: Check the peer, selector, transform and IKEv2 profile against the intended design. Definition alone does not prove a successful application test.

tickets.title: IKE works while a transit filter drops native ESP
tickets.scenario: R-BR 198.51.100.1 and R-HQ 203.0.113.1 protect LANs 10.1.1.0/24 and 10.2.2.0/24. ISP G0/0 faces R-BR and G0/1 faces R-HQ. The VPN previously worked. There is no NAT and a capture confirms native ESP, not UDP-encapsulated ESP. After a filter change on ISP G0/1 outbound, fresh branch-to-HQ pings fail although public-address ping and IKEv2 negotiation still work.

exhibits.title: Representative current IKE and controlled-test evidence
exhibits.text:
R-BR: IKEv2 peer 203.0.113.1 READY
Fresh host test counter deltas:
R-BR encaps +4, decaps +0
R-HQ decaps +0
ISP general deny +4; other traffic quiet during the test.

exhibits.title: ISP attachment and effective OUTSIDE-OUT list
exhibits.text:
GigabitEthernet0/1: Outgoing access list is OUTSIDE-OUT
10 permit udp host 198.51.100.1 host 203.0.113.1 eq 500
20 permit udp host 198.51.100.1 host 203.0.113.1 eq 4500
30 permit icmp any any
40 deny ip any any

exhibits.title: Representative capture immediately before ISP filtering
exhibits.text:
Source 198.51.100.1, destination 203.0.113.1
IPv4 Protocol: 50 (ESP)
No UDP encapsulation

tickets.question: Which policy omission explains this controlled test?
options: Missing TCP port 50 permission for the ESP payload
Missing native ESP permission before the final deny
A different pre-shared key uniquely proved by the counters
A requirement to place the private HQ route on ISP
tickets.explanation: The packet is explicitly native ESP. It misses both UDP permits and the ICMP permit, then reaches deny 40. IKE can remain healthy because its UDP traffic is permitted. Native ESP uses IP protocol 50, not TCP port 50. The evidence does not identify a PSK mismatch, and ISP routes on the outer public address rather than needing the encrypted inner LAN route.
tickets.fix:
On the isolated ISP device, add a specific native-ESP permit before deny 40.

```ios
ISP# configure terminal
ISP(config)# ip access-list extended OUTSIDE-OUT
ISP(config-ext-nacl)# 25 permit esp host 198.51.100.1 host 203.0.113.1
ISP(config-ext-nacl)# end
ISP# show access-lists OUTSIDE-OUT
```
Generate fresh host traffic and compare both peers’ counter deltas and application results. The filter is only on ISP G0/1 outbound in this scenario; it does not filter the reverse direction. A different deployment using UDP NAT-T needs permission for its actual UDP transport rather than assuming native ESP is always required.

tickets.title: The gateways have no compatible IKE proposal
tickets.scenario: A new IKEv2 VPN uses R-BR 198.51.100.1 and R-HQ 203.0.113.1. Public routing is working and a capture confirms IKE request and response traffic. A support log reports NO_PROPOSAL_CHOSEN. The listed policies are the only matching IKEv2 policies; there are no other proposals offered. Peer identities and configured authentication are correct. No data SA is installed.

exhibits.title: R-BR active proposal and policy
exhibits.text:
crypto ikev2 proposal BR-PROP
 encryption aes-cbc-256
 integrity sha256
 prf sha256
 group 14
crypto ikev2 policy BR-POLICY
 proposal BR-PROP

exhibits.title: R-HQ active proposal and policy
exhibits.text:
crypto ikev2 proposal HQ-PROP
 encryption aes-cbc-128
 integrity sha256
 prf sha256
 group 14
crypto ikev2 policy HQ-POLICY
 proposal HQ-PROP

exhibits.title: Deployment requirement
exhibits.text:
Both peers are approved to use IKE AES-CBC-256, SHA-256 integrity/PRF and DH group 14.
The HQ configuration should match that requirement.

tickets.question: Which mismatch is established by the shown configuration?
options: The policy names must be identical on both peers
The encryption algorithms offered by the only matching proposals have no common choice
The pre-shared key must be changed because every failed SA means bad authentication
The DHCP pools differ and therefore prevent IKE negotiation
tickets.explanation: One matching proposal offers only AES-CBC-256 and the other only AES-CBC-128. The stated single-offer policies have no common encryption transform. Names are local references and need not match across peers. The supplied evidence establishes proposal incompatibility, not a PSK or DHCP fault.
tickets.fix:
Correct the HQ proposal to the agreed deployment requirement on supported IOS XE. Clear the old encryption choice before setting the single agreed choice.

```ios
R-HQ# configure terminal
R-HQ(config)# crypto ikev2 proposal HQ-PROP
R-HQ(config-ikev2-proposal)# no encryption
R-HQ(config-ikev2-proposal)# encryption aes-cbc-256
R-HQ(config-ikev2-proposal)# end
R-HQ# show crypto ikev2 proposal HQ-PROP
```
Allow the failed negotiation to retry and generate fresh matching host traffic. Verify the negotiated IKEv2 relationship, IPsec SAs and actual host result. Proposal compatibility is necessary but does not by itself prove correct selectors, return routes or application permissions.

sections.title: How stations share a radio channel
Identify the WLAN and its cells

lab.title: Build a small WLAN and distinguish a key fault from an IP fault
lab.intro: Build a fresh, isolated project. You will configure a network name, radio channel, WPA2 security and DHCP, then test one deliberate fault at a time. The channel and interference exercises are worksheets: simulator graphics are not RF measurements.
lab.topology:
```diagram
{"type":"topology","title":"Lab 36 — One wireless cell and a wired destination","caption":"The Internet port is unused; the laptop and server share the wireless router's LAN.","nodes":[{"id":"W","kind":"router","label":"WRT300N","sub":"192.168.80.1/24","x":6,"y":1},{"id":"L","kind":"laptop","label":"Laptop-PT","sub":"DHCP · CCNA-LAB","x":2,"y":5},{"id":"S","kind":"server","label":"Server-PT","sub":"192.168.80.20/24","x":10,"y":5}],"links":[{"from":"W","to":"L","style":"wireless"},{"from":"W","to":"S","fromLabel":"Ethernet 1","toLabel":"Fa0","label":"straight-through"}]}
```

| Device/connection | Setting |
|---|---|
| WRT300N LAN | 192.168.80.1, mask 255.255.255.0 |
| Server-PT Fa0 to WRT Ethernet 1 | Copper straight-through; 192.168.80.20/24, gateway 192.168.80.1 |
| Laptop wireless interface | DHCP; SSID CCNA-LAB |
| DHCP | Start .100; 50 users, ending .149 |
| WLAN | 2.4 GHz, 20 MHz, channel 1, WPA2-Personal/AES |
| Fictional lab passphrase | Cedar-Lab-2026! |

Packet Tracer controls vary by version. Check the actual device dialog. Do not substitute WEP or an open network if the selected model lacks the required WPA2/AES option. Use a compatible model/activity or complete the affected fields as a worksheet and record the limitation. No simulator run was executed during authoring.

steps.title: — Place, power and cable the equipment
steps.body:
Place WRT300N, Laptop-PT and Server-PT. If the laptop lacks a wireless interface, power it off in Physical, remove its Ethernet module, insert the compatible WPC300N module when offered, and power it on. If that module name differs, use the device's compatible wireless option rather than forcing an incompatible module.

Cable Server-PT Fa0 to WRT Ethernet 1 with copper straight-through. Leave the WRT Internet/WAN port disconnected. Set the server's static address, mask and gateway from the table.

:::expected
The laptop exposes a wireless interface; the server's Ethernet link becomes active. Record actual interface labels. A default wireless association, if one appears, is not the configured secure baseline.
:::

steps.title: — Configure the LAN and DHCP
steps.body:
Open WRT300N → GUI → Setup → Basic Setup. Set Router IP to 192.168.80.1 and mask to 255.255.255.0. Enable the LAN DHCP service, set the starting host to 100 and maximum users to 50, then Save Settings. A field that accepts a full address uses 192.168.80.100.

From the server's command prompt:

```text
ping 192.168.80.1
```

:::expected
The saved page shows the intended LAN subnet and DHCP settings. After link/ARP convergence, the server can reach .1. The server's .20 address is outside .100–.149, so it cannot collide with this pool. This is a local LAN test; Internet service is not part of the topology.
:::

steps.title: — Set the WLAN name and channel
steps.body:
Under Wireless → Basic Wireless Settings, set SSID to CCNA-LAB, select a compatible mixed radio mode, choose Standard/20 MHz when exposed, channel 1 and SSID Broadcast Enabled. Save Settings. Record which width options your model actually exposes.

:::expected
A fresh client scan should list CCNA-LAB when the radio is enabled and the client is within simulated range. The configured channel is 1. If the model does not report width or signal numerically, do not invent those measurements.
:::

steps.title: — Apply WPA2-Personal security
steps.body:
Under Wireless → Wireless Security, select WPA2 Personal, AES, and Cedar-Lab-2026!, then save. Leave unrelated timing controls at their existing defaults.

:::expected
The saved security page shows WPA2-Personal and AES. This exercise does not require WPA3 support on the WRT model and makes no claim that a different Packet Tracer controller provides it. An existing client profile may need updating before data works.
:::

steps.title: — Join the laptop and request an address
steps.body:
On the laptop, open Desktop → PC Wireless. Refresh the network list and select CCNA-LAB; if the version uses profile creation, create a profile with that exact name, WPA2-Personal/AES and the lab passphrase. Connect. Set Desktop → IP Configuration to DHCP.

Inspect the status and run:

```text
ipconfig /all
ping 192.168.80.1
ping 192.168.80.20
```

:::expected
The client reports the intended WLAN/security and an address somewhere in .100–.149, mask /24 and gateway .1. Do not assume .100 specifically. Both local targets respond after any initial ARP delay. If ipconfig /all is absent, use the IP Configuration GUI. The dotted line alone is insufficient evidence: record the address and successful data tests too.
:::

steps.title: — Save the verified starting point
steps.body:
Save as wireless-principles-baseline.pkt, then Save As wireless-principles-faults.pkt for the experiments. Record the laptop's actual lease, SSID, security and observed status.

:::expected
Two separate files exist, and the recorded baseline includes successful pings. Continue only when the initial secure WLAN works; otherwise troubleshoot that state before adding a fault.
:::

steps.title: — Introduce a client passphrase fault
steps.body:
Change only the laptop's saved passphrase to Cedar-Lab-2025!. Disconnect/reconnect using its wireless utility so a new security exchange is required. Keep the router and DHCP settings unchanged.

Try reaching 192.168.80.20 and inspect client security status.

:::expected
The wrong shared secret prevents successful WPA2 key establishment and normal protected data access. The SSID may remain visible, and the laptop may retain its previous IP lease. A stale address does not prove security succeeded; an association indicator does not necessarily mean the four-way handshake completed.
:::

steps.title: — Restore the passphrase and retest
steps.body:
Restore Cedar-Lab-2026! in the laptop profile, reconnect, and request DHCP again if needed. Repeat both baseline pings.

:::expected
The known settings restore access. Record recovery separately from the fault observation. If failure remains, compare SSID, mode and AES selection before changing addressing or channels.
:::

steps.title: — Change the channel without changing the WLAN identity
steps.body:
On WRT300N, change only the standard channel from 1 to 6 and save. Refresh/reconnect the client when necessary. Record the SSID, reported channel and IP address, then ping the server.

:::expected
The WLAN name and passphrase remain the same while the channel changes. A brief reconnection may occur. Successful recovery demonstrates configuration compatibility; it does not measure improved throughput or reduced interference. Restore channel 1 and confirm it before continuing.
:::

steps.title: — Compare a second cell if the AP model supports the required settings
steps.body:
Optional: add AccessPoint-PT and cable its wired Port 0 to WRT Ethernet 2 with copper straight-through. In its radio/Port 1 settings, use CCNA-LAB, channel 6, WPA2-PSK, AES and the same passphrase. If this model lacks that security combination, leave it disconnected and use the lesson's ESS diagram as the worksheet instead.

Use available client status/scan information to distinguish the cells. You may move the laptop in the Physical workspace to encourage a change, but do not assume the simulator performs a particular roaming algorithm.

:::expected
Both cells bridge toward the same LAN/DHCP server. If the client changes serving BSSID, record that evidence and retest .20. Its lease may remain valid; do not claim guaranteed seamless roaming from an unchanged SSID. A real AP can have a management IP while still forwarding as a Layer 2 bridge.
:::

steps.title: — Complete the RF worksheet
steps.body:
For three mutually neighboring 2.4 GHz APs, propose a 20 MHz North American channel plan. Explain why 1/2/3 is different from 1/6/11. Calculate SNR for a client reporting −68 dBm signal and −94 dBm noise at the same receiver. Then compare a second measurement: −58 dBm signal, −64 dBm noise.

:::expected
Use 1/6/11 for the stated plan. Nearby channel numbers 1/2/3 overlap. The first SNR is 26 dB; the stronger second signal has only 6 dB SNR. These are arithmetic/policy conclusions, not simulator RF observations.
:::

steps.title: — Inspect a real connection without changing it
steps.body:
Optional, on an authorized Windows computer already connected to Wi-Fi, run the following read-only commands. They are Windows commands, not a guarantee of Packet Tracer PC support.

```text
netsh wlan show interfaces
netsh wlan show networks mode=bssid
netsh wlan show drivers
```

Windows may require location permission or an elevated context for particular wireless details. Use the permitted OS settings display if a field is unavailable; do not change networks or expose saved passwords. macOS/Linux inspection is covered in chapter 30.

:::expected
Record only needed fields: SSID/BSSID, band/channel, authentication/cipher and reported rate. A scan is a partial observation, not a complete site survey. Finish by saving the restored simulator file and noting every unsupported step.
:::

lab.troubleshooting:
- SSID not listed: check model/radio support, power, SSID broadcast, scan refresh and simulated range. The absence of a scan entry does not identify one unique cause.
- SSID visible but data fails: compare security mode, cipher and exact passphrase; then inspect IP configuration and DHCP. Existing leases can outlast a failed reconnection.
- .1 reachable but .20 fails: inspect the server address, link, port and host settings. A gateway mistake on a same-subnet server is not automatically the cause of a same-subnet ping failure.
- Optional second AP fails: verify its LAN cable and matching security. It must not introduce a second conflicting DHCP service.
lab.challenge:
A client reports SSID STAFF, BSSID 02:10:20:30:40:50, channel 6 and 80% signal. It has a retained 192.168.80.110/24 lease but cannot reach the local server after its saved WPA2 passphrase was changed. A nearby AP advertises STAFF on channel 11 with another BSSID.

Explain what the evidence establishes, what to check first, and why neither the strong signal nor the second AP proves working access. Then propose a safe channel-reuse decision for a fourth AP beyond a 1/6/11 row.

:::expected
The client can report a WLAN/cell and retain old IP configuration while the new security exchange fails. Compare the altered passphrase with the known authorized configuration and restore it; verify protected data and pings afterward. A second BSSID with the same SSID may be another legitimate cell, but physical ownership/security need inventory evidence. Signal percentage does not prove usable airtime or IP service. The fourth AP may reuse a channel after a survey confirms acceptable separation and interference; its position alone does not make channel 1 correct.
:::

exhibit.title: Windows-style scan — representative
exhibit.text:
SSID: STAFF
BSSID: 02:11:22:33:44:50   Band: 2.4 GHz   Channel: 6
BSSID: 02:11:22:33:44:51   Band: 5 GHz     Channel: 44

questions.prompt: What can be concluded from this representative scan without consulting an AP inventory?
options: The two identifiers establish that both radios belong to one physical AP
The different bands require the clients to use two different network names
Two BSSIDs advertise STAFF; the scan does not establish physical ownership
The similar addresses establish that the second entry is a spoofed radio
questions.explanation: One SSID can appear on multiple radios and APs. BSSID identifies the service set; similar MAC-style values do not establish which physical chassis owns them.

whyWrong.0: Address similarity is not a verified physical inventory mapping.
whyWrong.1: Different bands can advertise the same SSID.
whyWrong.3: A different or similar BSSID alone does not prove impersonation.

questions.prompt: An AP changes from 20 dBm transmit power to 23 dBm. What is its approximate new power?
options: 50 mW
200 mW
400 mW
questions.explanation: 20 dBm represents 100 mW. A 3 dB increase is approximately a doubling, giving about 200 mW; the exact value is about 199.5 mW.

whyWrong.0: About 50 mW corresponds to 17 dBm, a decrease.
whyWrong.2: About 400 mW corresponds to 26 dBm.
whyWrong.3: 1,000 mW corresponds to 30 dBm.

questions.prompt: At one receiver, signal is −65 dBm and noise is −92 dBm over the same observation period. What is SNR?
options: 27 dB
−157 dBm
27 dBm
−27 dB
questions.explanation: Subtract noise from signal: −65 − (−92) = 27. SNR is a power ratio expressed in dB, not an absolute dBm level.

whyWrong.1: Adding the levels does not calculate SNR.
whyWrong.2: The numeric result is correct but the unit is not.
whyWrong.3: This reverses the subtraction.

questions.prompt: For neighboring APs using the ordinary North American 2.4 GHz 20 MHz plan, which two statements are correct? Choose two.
options: A 40 MHz channel creates more independent frequency choices
Adjacent channel numbers have centers only 5 MHz apart
Channels 1, 2 and 3 provide three separate occupied ranges
Channels 1, 6 and 11 are the usual nonoverlapping reuse set
A different SSID lets nearby APs ignore shared airtime
questions.explanation: Channel spacing is narrower than the occupied width. The usual 1/6/11 plan separates neighboring cells; increasing width consumes more spectrum.

whyWrong.0: Wider operation consumes spectrum rather than creating additional independent channels.
whyWrong.2: These closely spaced channels overlap.
whyWrong.4: Different network names do not separate RF frequencies.

exhibit.title: Survey worksheet
exhibit.text:
AP-A: channel 1
AP-B: channel 6
AP-C: channel 6
AP-B and AP-C: strong mutual reception; high shared airtime utilization

questions.prompt: All APs use 20 MHz. The site survey shows AP-B and AP-C strongly hear each other and contend on channel 6. Which change addresses the displayed channel reuse?
options: Move AP-C to channel 8 to create a separate center frequency
Move AP-A to channel 6 so all APs can coordinate one channel
Move AP-B to channel 3 to separate it from AP-C numerically
Move AP-C to channel 11 and verify the resulting RF behavior
questions.explanation: The demonstrated problem is AP-B/AP-C sharing channel 6. Channel 11 is a suitable candidate in this stated plan; measurements after the change verify the result.

whyWrong.0: Channel 8 overlaps the neighboring channel-6 occupied spectrum.
whyWrong.1: Adding another co-channel AP does not remove the existing contention.
whyWrong.2: Channel 3 introduces overlap rather than using the planned nonoverlapping set.

questions.prompt: Why can an AP using a DFS-required 5 GHz channel leave that channel even when its clients have strong signals?
options: Radar protection requires it to vacate after a radar detection
SSID uniqueness requires each AP to change its channel periodically
A strong client signal causes a mandatory radio power shutdown
A WPA2 key renewal requires a different center frequency
questions.explanation: DFS protects radar users of shared spectrum. Signal strength does not override the regulatory requirement; exact channels and timing depend on the deployment.

whyWrong.1: SSID uniqueness is not a DFS mechanism.
whyWrong.2: Strong signal alone does not cause the stated radar-driven behavior.
whyWrong.3: Security key renewal is separate from channel selection.

questions.prompt: Which technology is Wi-Fi 5, using 5 GHz and supporting 80 MHz channels?
questions.explanation: 802.11ac is Wi-Fi 5. A dual-band AP marketed as Wi-Fi 5 uses another supported radio technology on its 2.4 GHz band.

whyWrong.0: 802.11n is Wi-Fi 4 and supports up to 40 MHz channels.
whyWrong.2: 802.11ax is Wi-Fi 6/6E rather than Wi-Fi 5.
whyWrong.3: 802.11g is an older 2.4 GHz technology.

questions.prompt: Wi-Fi 6E extends which radio technology into compatible 6 GHz equipment?
questions.explanation: Wi-Fi 6E identifies the 6 GHz extension of 802.11ax. Both AP and client need compatible hardware and local regulatory support.

whyWrong.0: 802.11ac is a 5 GHz technology.
whyWrong.1: 802.11n operates in 2.4 and 5 GHz.
whyWrong.2: 802.11a is an older 5 GHz technology.

questions.prompt: Which two statements describe a WPA3-Personal-only WLAN? Choose two.
options: It uses SAE for password-based authentication
It requires TKIP for compatibility with original WPA
It requires protected management frame support
It requires individual RADIUS accounts for every client
It removes the need to protect endpoints and credentials
questions.explanation: WPA3-Personal uses SAE and requires PMF. These improve wireless protection but do not eliminate endpoint risks or all forms of radio disruption.

whyWrong.1: TKIP is obsolete and is not the WPA3-Personal cipher requirement.
whyWrong.3: Per-user 802.1X/RADIUS is an Enterprise design, not a Personal requirement.
whyWrong.4: Wireless security does not replace endpoint and credential protection.

exhibit.title: netsh wlan show interfaces — representative
exhibit.text:
State: connected
SSID: STAFF
Authentication: WPA2-Personal
Cipher: CCMP
Channel: 44
Receive rate (Mbps): 866.7

questions.prompt: Which security interpretation is supported by the representative report?
options: The client is using an Enterprise EAP method against RADIUS
The client has completed a successful application throughput test
The connection uses WPA2-Personal with the reported CCMP cipher
The connection uses TKIP because Personal mode requires RC4
questions.explanation: The Authentication and Cipher fields establish the reported WLAN security combination. They do not show an application performance test or prove end-to-end service access.

whyWrong.0: The report says Personal, not Enterprise.
whyWrong.1: A link-rate field is not a throughput measurement.
whyWrong.3: The reported cipher is CCMP, not TKIP.

questions.prompt: Which pairing is appropriate for the WPA2-PSK configuration taught in the CCNA GUI objective?
options: WPA2-Personal with AES-CCMP
WEP with AES-CCMP
Original WPA with GCMP-256
WPA3-Personal with RC4
questions.explanation: The required WPA2-PSK exercise uses WPA2-Personal and AES-CCMP. WEP and TKIP are legacy choices, while WPA3 has its own authentication/security requirements.

whyWrong.1: WEP does not use AES-CCMP.
whyWrong.2: GCMP-256 is not the original WPA/TKIP combination.
whyWrong.3: RC4 is not the protection used by WPA3-Personal.

exhibit.title: Verified deployment
exhibit.text:
AP1: SSID STAFF, BSSID 02:00:00:00:01:10
AP2: SSID STAFF, BSSID 02:00:00:00:02:10
Both bridge to VLAN 20 through the wired LAN.
The roaming client's address remains 10.20.0.57/24.

questions.prompt: The managed deployment uses the same SSID and security on both APs with a common distribution system. What describes the combined service?
options: An independent basic service set
An extended service set
A single basic service set
A wireless mesh backhaul
questions.explanation: The cooperating infrastructure BSSs form an ESS. The given shared VLAN supports this example's unchanged IP addressing, but identical SSIDs alone would not prove the same result.

whyWrong.0: An IBSS is an ad hoc arrangement without these infrastructure APs.
whyWrong.2: Each shown BSSID identifies a separate BSS.
whyWrong.3: The exhibit specifies wired distribution, not wireless mesh backhaul.

exhibit.title: Authorized diagnostic observations — authored worksheet
exhibit.text:
2.4 GHz client: strong received level, heavy retries while nearby microwave runs
Spectrum observation: non-Wi-Fi energy increases during operation
Controlled appliance off/on trials: impairment repeatedly disappears/returns
5 GHz comparison client: unaffected

questions.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the controlled observations?
options: The noon timing proves a neighboring AP changes channel
A DFS event on 2.4 GHz causes the recorded loss
The laptop's strong signal rules out RF interference
The operating appliance is a demonstrated interference source
questions.explanation: The controlled repeated correlation and non-Wi-Fi energy measurement support the appliance as the source in this scenario. A lunchtime symptom alone would only suggest investigation.

whyWrong.0: No neighboring-AP channel change is shown.
whyWrong.1: The ordinary 2.4 GHz WLAN in this scenario does not use 5 GHz DFS.
whyWrong.2: Strong desired signal can coexist with interfering energy.

questions.prompt: A WLAN design must support revoking one employee's individual credential. Which design directly meets that requirement?
options: Enterprise 802.1X/EAP using individually managed credentials
Personal mode using one long passphrase shared by all staff
Personal mode using a hidden SSID shared by all staff
Personal mode using one shared passphrase with a new channel
questions.explanation: Individually managed Enterprise credentials allow targeted revocation. Enforcement can also require terminating existing sessions according to policy; disabling an account is not a promise that every active session ends instantly.

whyWrong.1: A shared passphrase does not identify one person's credential separately.
whyWrong.2: Hiding the name does not supply individual authentication.
whyWrong.3: Changing channels does not revoke a person who retains the shared credential.

questions.prompt: A surveyed point-to-point link needs a narrow beam aimed at a second building. Which listed pattern best matches that requirement?
options: An omnidirectional antenna covering the room horizontally
A broad wall-panel pattern covering a 120-degree sector
A directional dish with an 8-degree specified beamwidth
An omnidirectional ceiling pattern covering nearby desks
questions.explanation: The stated narrow-beam dish fits the specified point-to-point coverage pattern. Actual suitability still depends on link budget, alignment, clearance and permitted power; antenna names or distance alone are insufficient.

whyWrong.0: Room-wide horizontal coverage does not match the requested narrow beam.
whyWrong.1: The supplied 120-degree sector is much broader than the stated link needs.
whyWrong.3: The supplied pattern is for local area coverage rather than the specified beam.

exhibit.title: Client status
exhibit.text:
Receive PHY rate: 600 Mb/s
Client count on shared channel: 24
Application file-transfer rate: not measured

questions.prompt: Why does the reported PHY rate not establish a 600 Mb/s file-transfer rate?
options: The PHY figure is the client's DHCP lease capacity
The PHY figure is the rate of the wired Internet subscription
Shared airtime and protocol overhead reduce useful data capacity
The PHY figure measures only the length of the wireless frame
questions.explanation: The link rate describes radio transmission capability for that connection. Useful application throughput depends on airtime, overhead, retries and the rest of the path; no fixed percentage applies universally.

whyWrong.0: DHCP assigns addressing information, not a throughput rate.
whyWrong.1: The radio link does not determine an Internet service contract.
whyWrong.3: Rate is bits per second rather than frame length.

cards.front: Nonoverlapping 2.4 GHz channels in the usual North American 20 MHz plan?
cards.back: 1, 6 and 11. This is a reuse plan; the actual permitted channel list depends on the regulatory domain.

cards.front: Why do neighboring 2.4 GHz channel numbers overlap?
cards.back: Centers are generally 5 MHz apart while the occupied channel is much wider, commonly 20 MHz (legacy DSSS about 22 MHz).

cards.front: How many 2.4 GHz channels should you assume are legal everywhere?
cards.back: Do not use one universal count. Channels 1–11 are the usual US example; check the actual country, model and allowed-channel list.

cards.front: What happens when 5 GHz 20 MHz channels are bonded to 80 MHz?
cards.back: The wider transmission uses the component spectrum; it overlaps those narrower channels and leaves fewer independent choices.

cards.front: What is DFS for?
cards.back: Protecting radar users on designated shared channels. Detection can force a channel change; exact channels and timing are location/platform dependent.

cards.front: What must support a 6 GHz WLAN?
cards.back: The AP and client need suitable radio capability and local authorization; use the applicable WPA3 or Enhanced Open security design.

cards.front: Is a wider channel always a better choice?
cards.back: No. It can raise the PHY rate but consumes spectrum and may encounter more interference. Keep the ordinary crowded 2.4 GHz design at 20 MHz.

cards.front: 0 dBm, +3 dB and +10 dB mean what?
cards.back: 0 dBm = 1 mW. +3 dB is approximately twice the power; +10 dB is ten times. 20 dBm = 100 mW.

cards.front: dB versus dBm versus dBi?
cards.back: dB is a ratio; dBm is power relative to 1 mW; dBi is antenna gain relative to an isotropic reference.

cards.front: EIRP calculation?
cards.back: Transmit dBm + antenna dBi − cable/connector loss dB. Check local limits rather than assuming one worldwide maximum.

cards.front: How is SNR calculated from dBm readings?
cards.back: Signal minus noise at the same receiver and observation period, expressed in dB. −65 − (−92) = 27 dB.

cards.front: How does wavelength change with frequency?
cards.back: It decreases. Free-space examples: about 12.5 cm at 2.4 GHz, 6 cm at 5 GHz and 5 cm at 6 GHz; range also depends on many other factors.

cards.front: 802.11a, b and g: bands and headline PHY rates?
cards.back: a: 5 GHz / 54 Mb/s. b: 2.4 GHz / 11 Mb/s. g: 2.4 GHz / 54 Mb/s. These are PHY maxima, not application guarantees.

cards.front: How do n, ac, ax and be map to Wi-Fi generations?
cards.back: n → 4; ac → 5; ax → 6 (6E adds 6 GHz); be → 7. ac itself is 5 GHz-only; actual product capabilities still matter.

cards.front: SSID versus BSSID?
cards.back: SSID is the WLAN name, up to 32 octets. BSSID is a 48-bit service-set identifier, not proof of a particular physical AP.

cards.front: BSS, ESS and IBSS?
cards.back: Infrastructure BSS: an AP service and associated stations. ESS: connected infrastructure BSSs. IBSS: ad hoc stations without an infrastructure AP.

cards.front: Co-channel versus adjacent-channel effects?
cards.back: Co-channel cells share airtime; overlapping occupied channels can interfere. Either situation can involve retries; there is no fixed throughput-halving rule.

cards.front: What evidence identifies a non-Wi-Fi interferer?
cards.back: Correlate band, time, spectrum information and a controlled change. A nearby microwave or Bluetooth device is a candidate, not proof by itself.

cards.front: WEP, original WPA and WPA2/AES: key distinctions?
cards.back: WEP uses insecure RC4-based protection; original WPA uses TKIP/RC4; the WPA2-PSK lab uses AES-CCMP. WPA3 cipher suites vary by mode.

cards.front: What changes with WPA3-Personal?
cards.back: SAE password authentication and required PMF. These do not prevent all disruption, protect every management frame or secure a compromised endpoint.

cards.front: Shared Personal credentials versus Enterprise credentials?
cards.back: Ordinary shared-passphrase Personal access differs from individually managed 802.1X/EAP Enterprise authentication. Session enforcement remains a separate policy issue.

cards.front: Omnidirectional and directional antenna patterns?
cards.back: Omni provides coverage around an axis; patch, Yagi and dish designs focus energy in chosen directions. Use actual beamwidth/gain specifications, not a universal ranking.

commands.task: Show the current wireless interface status on Windows.
commands.note: Fields and permissions depend on the OS and adapter. Signal percentage has no universal conversion to dBm.

commands.task: Scan and display visible BSSID details on Windows.
commands.note: This is what the adapter currently reports, not every AP in the area. The same SSID can appear on several BSSIDs.

commands.task: Inspect the Windows wireless adapter driver's reported radio and authentication capabilities.
commands.note: Compare current driver/OS capabilities with the WLAN requirements; check documented upgrades before assuming hardware replacement.

commands.task: Display detailed IP configuration on the Packet Tracer laptop, including available DHCP details.
commands.note: If unsupported, use the GUI. A retained lease does not prove a new wireless security exchange succeeded.

commands.task: Test the local wireless router's LAN address 192.168.80.1 from the laptop.
commands.note: This tests one ICMP path. A successful result does not establish DNS or Internet access.

commands.task: Optional controller preview: list WLAN profiles on a Catalyst 9800.
commands.note: Read profile name, SSID, ID and state separately. Detailed controller configuration is taught in chapter 38.

commands.task: Optional controller preview: list joined APs on a Catalyst 9800.
commands.note: Use inventory to map physical APs; a neighboring BSSID alone does not establish the chassis.

commands.task: Optional controller preview: list wireless clients on a Catalyst 9800.
commands.note: Read the actual state and WLAN/AP mapping. A client list alone does not prove application connectivity.

tickets.title: An overlapping channel is confirmed by a controlled test
tickets.scenario: The office AP and a separately authorized test AP use 2.4 GHz, 20 MHz channels. A survey first identifies overlap, then the operator repeats an approved on/off test of the test AP while other conditions remain stable. The excerpts below are an authored diagnostic scenario, not a captured simulator run.

exhibits.title: Radio inventory
exhibits.text:
OFFICE-AP: channel 1, SSID OFFICE
TEST-AP: channel 3, SSID TEST
Client near OFFICE-AP: strong desired signal throughout the test

exhibits.title: Repeated controlled observation
exhibits.text:
TEST-AP transmitting: OFFICE client retries rise sharply; transfer rate falls
TEST-AP radio disabled: retries return near baseline; transfer rate recovers
Repeat trials reproduce the same result; the OFFICE channel remains 1

tickets.question: What cause is supported by the combined evidence?
options: A weak desired signal caused by increasing client distance
Interference from overlapping occupied channels 1 and 3
Co-channel contention because the SSIDs have different names
A DFS radar response on the office's 2.4 GHz channel
tickets.explanation: The inventory establishes overlap, and the controlled repeatable test supports its effect here. Strong desired signal does not exclude interference; a scan alone would not establish the causal conclusion.
tickets.fix: Restore the authorized baseline, then choose an allowed nonoverlapping channel using the complete survey. For a small North American 20 MHz plan, evaluate 1/6/11 across both APs. Change one radio at a time, reconnect clients and repeat the same measurements. Record actual retries and application results; do not infer an optimal channel solely from a neighbor's signal percentage.

tickets.title: The required authentication method is missing from the client
tickets.scenario: STAFF is changed to WPA3-Personal-only. A failing client's OS/driver report and vendor compatibility check confirm that this installed combination supports WPA2-Personal but not SAE. The passphrase is verified unchanged. Other compatible clients connect. The excerpts are representative.

exhibits.title: WLAN settings
exhibits.text:
SSID: STAFF
Band: 5 GHz
Security: WPA3-Personal only
Authentication: SAE
PMF: Required

exhibits.title: Client capability evidence
exhibits.text:
Radio support: 802.11a/n/ac
WPA2-Personal + CCMP: Supported
PMF: Supported
WPA3-Personal / SAE: Not supported by installed OS/driver

tickets.question: Which mismatch prevents this client's access?
options: The shared passphrase differs even though it was verified unchanged
The presence of an 802.11ax AP necessarily excludes 802.11ac clients
The client lacks the SAE authentication capability required by this WLAN
The client lacks CCMP even though the capability report lists support
tickets.explanation: The security capability evidence establishes the missing SAE support. PMF and CCMP support alone do not make a client WPA3-capable; radio generation names alone do not establish the security method.
tickets.fix: Check whether a supported OS/driver update provides the required capability for this hardware. Otherwise replace the client or use a separately approved migration design. On 2.4/5 GHz, a compatible WPA2/WPA3 transition design can allow older WPA2 clients, but they still use WPA2 and do not acquire SAE's properties. Confirm the exact controller security/PMF settings and client compatibility, document the exception, and retest. Do not apply a WPA2 fallback to a 6 GHz-only WLAN.

sections.title: Configure the AP and controller links
Verify the design one layer at a time

lab.title: Build the wired foundation for a controller WLAN
lab.intro:
Build a management VLAN, a separate client VLAN and the links required for centrally switched wireless service. This lab proves the wired foundation and, where the selected Packet Tracer model supports it, AP registration. The next chapter builds and tests the client WLAN.

:::note Simulator boundary
Start with a new file and record your Packet Tracer version. Use a WLC-3504 and LAP-PT if your palette offers them. Their setup pages and exposed features vary. The switch/router work below is independent of those pages. If the controller lacks a required control or the AP cannot register with the available models, complete the explicitly identified controller worksheet using the given values and record “not simulated”; do not record a successful join. No real RF, PoE negotiation, Meraki dashboard or Catalyst 9800 is simulated by this lab.
:::
lab.topology:
