| R1 Gi0/0.10 | `192.168.10.1/24` | Native VLAN 10 |
| R1 Gi0/0.20 | `192.168.20.1/24` | Tagged VLAN 20 |
| WLC management, Port 1 | `192.168.10.5/24` | `192.168.10.1`; untagged |
| ADMIN FastEthernet0 | `192.168.10.10/24` | `192.168.10.1`; VLAN 10 |
| TEST20 FastEthernet0 | `192.168.20.20/24` | `192.168.20.1`; VLAN 20 |
| AP1 wired management | DHCP `192.168.10.100–149/24` | `192.168.10.1`; VLAN 10 |
| Optional WLC dynamic interface `users` | `192.168.20.5/24` | `192.168.20.1`; tagged VLAN 20 |

No DNS or Internet service is required; all tests use addresses.

steps.title: Place, power and cable the devices
steps.body:
Place the named models, cable the listed interfaces and name the PCs ADMIN and TEST20. Open AP1's Physical tab. If it requires an external power adapter, fit the model's supplied adapter. A non-PoE 2960 model does not supply power simply because Ethernet is connected.

On both PCs, use Desktop → IP Configuration to enter their static address, `255.255.255.0` mask and gateway from the table. Leave DNS blank. Keep the controller disconnected from any real network.

:::expected
Both PCs show the intended values. AP1 has power if supported by the chosen model. The router's Ethernet link may remain down until Step 3. A powered device or green cable is not yet proof of IP reachability.
:::

steps.title: Configure VLANs and switchports
steps.body:
Start in the SW1 console. The native VLAN is deliberately 10 on both trunks; VLAN 20 remains tagged.

```ios SW1
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname SW1
SW1(config)# vlan 10
SW1(config-vlan)# name MANAGEMENT
SW1(config-vlan)# exit
SW1(config)# vlan 20
SW1(config-vlan)# name USERS
SW1(config-vlan)# exit
SW1(config)# interface range fastethernet0/1 - 2
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport access vlan 10
SW1(config-if-range)# spanning-tree portfast
SW1(config-if-range)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if-range)# exit
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/3
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if)# switchport access vlan 20
SW1(config-if)# spanning-tree portfast
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if)# exit
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk native vlan 10
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if)# exit
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/24
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk native vlan 10
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show vlan brief
SW1# show interfaces trunk
```

:::expected
Fa0/1–2 are access members of VLAN 10; Fa0/3 is in VLAN 20. Operational trunks show native VLAN 10 and allowed VLANs 10,20. A trunk whose far end is not yet up can be absent from `show interfaces trunk`; verify its configuration with `show interfaces gigabitethernet0/1 switchport`.
:::

steps.title: Configure routing and the AP DHCP pool
steps.body:
The exclusions leave 50 potential AP leases, `.100–.149`. VLAN 20 uses a static test PC, so it does not yet require a DHCP pool.

```ios R1
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R1
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0.10
R1(config-subif)# encapsulation dot1Q 10 native
R1(config-subif)# ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-subif)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0.20
R1(config-subif)# encapsulation dot1Q 20
R1(config-subif)# ip address 192.168.20.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-subif)# exit
R1(config)# ip dhcp excluded-address 192.168.10.1 192.168.10.99
R1(config)# ip dhcp excluded-address 192.168.10.150 192.168.10.254
R1(config)# ip dhcp pool AP-MGMT
R1(dhcp-config)# network 192.168.10.0 255.255.255.0
R1(dhcp-config)# default-router 192.168.10.1
R1(dhcp-config)# end
R1# show ip interface brief
R1# show ip dhcp pool AP-MGMT
```

:::expected
Gi0/0 and both subinterfaces are up/up once the switch link is active. The pool covers `192.168.10.0/24` with the stated exclusions. No DNS service has been falsely advertised at the router address.
:::

steps.title: Prove the wired paths first
steps.body:
From ADMIN's command prompt run:

```text
ping 192.168.10.1
ping 192.168.20.20
```

From TEST20 run:

```text
ping 192.168.20.1
ping 192.168.10.10
```

Retry after initial ARP resolution if necessary. Check the return gateway on the destination PC before changing routing.

:::expected
Both local gateways and the opposite PC respond in this isolated topology. This proves the two VLANs, R1's subinterfaces and both PCs' return paths. It does not prove the controller trunk or a wireless WLAN.
:::

steps.title: Address the controller and open its setup page
steps.body:
On WLC1 look for Config → Management. Where exposed, set `192.168.10.5`, mask `255.255.255.0` and gateway `192.168.10.1`. Choose Port 1. A management VLAN value `0` on this AireOS-style interface means untagged; the switch assigns those frames to native VLAN 10.

From ADMIN open Desktop → Web Browser. Try the controller's HTTPS management URL, `https://192.168.10.5`. A fresh Packet Tracer controller may instead expose its initial setup at `http://192.168.10.5`. Use that HTTP path only for this isolated simulator's day-zero page. Follow the displayed setup fields with these values:

| Field, if requested | Value |
|---|---|
| System name | `WLC1` |
| Administrator | `labadmin` |
| Lab-only administrator password | `Admin-Lab-2026!` |
| Management IP/mask/gateway | `192.168.10.5` / `255.255.255.0` / `192.168.10.1` |
| Management VLAN/port | Untagged (`0`) / Port 1 |
| Management primary DHCP server, if requested | `192.168.10.1` |
| Required initial employee SSID | `ARCH-SETUP` |
| Initial WLAN security/key | WPA2-Personal, AES / `Cedar-Lab-2026!` |

Apply only after checking the address and VLAN treatment. Reconnect with HTTPS if the model restarts. If the model has no applicable management control or wizard, record the limitation and use this table as the controller worksheet for the remaining architecture observations. Do not guess a different factory address or credentials.

:::expected
Where implemented, ADMIN reaches the management page and can log in. The controller's displayed management configuration matches the worksheet. If not implemented, wired Steps 1–4 remain valid and controller observations are explicitly worksheet answers. No particular setup-page order or restart duration is assumed.
:::

steps.title: Check AP addressing and registration separately
steps.body:
On AP1 select DHCP for its wired management interface if the model exposes the choice. Check the IP in its Config/status page. On R1 inspect:

```ios R1
R1# show ip dhcp binding
```

On the controller inspect Wireless → Access Points → All APs, or the model's AP summary. The AP and controller share VLAN 10 in this lab, allowing local discovery without requiring option 43. Wait for the simulator to process registration; do not repeatedly reboot the AP while it is joining.

:::expected
The AP's actual lease is within `192.168.10.100–149`; the first allocation is not guaranteed to be `.100`. A controller AP record in a registered/operational state is separate evidence that CAPWAP join succeeded. A lease alone is insufficient. If the available models do not implement registration, write the expected sequence: lease → discovery → protected join/configuration → operational AP, and mark it unexecuted.
:::

steps.title: Inspect the client VLAN mapping
steps.body:
If the controller offers Controller → Interfaces → New, create `users` with VLAN ID `20`, Port `1`, IP `192.168.20.5`, mask `255.255.255.0` and gateway `192.168.20.1`. Leave an optional DHCP-server field unset because this step uses static addresses and creates no client WLAN; if the GUI requires a DHCP server to save, stop this optional step and use the worksheet instead of inventing a service.

From TEST20 ping `192.168.20.5` if the model answers that interface. Then inspect SW1:

```ios SW1
SW1# show interfaces trunk
SW1# show mac address-table dynamic vlan 20
```

:::expected
The intended mapping is untagged management in VLAN 10 and tagged `users` in VLAN 20 on the same cable. A successful interface ping supports that mapping. A learned controller MAC or GUI interface entry still does not prove wireless client forwarding; Chapter 38 verifies an actual client. Missing dynamic-interface controls or ICMP support are worksheet limitations, not evidence that trunks are unnecessary.
:::

steps.title: Record and save the working baseline
steps.body:
Record the AP address/MAC, controller management values, switchport modes and whether AP registration was observed or only described. Save both IOS devices independently:

```ios R1
R1# copy running-config startup-config
```

Press Enter at the destination-filename prompt. On SW1:

```ios SW1
SW1# copy running-config startup-config
```

Press Enter there as well. On the controller use its Save Configuration action if available. Save `architecture-baseline.pkt`, then a second copy, `architecture-fault.pkt`.

:::expected
Your record distinguishes working wired tests from optional controller observations. The fault copy is open, and the baseline remains available for comparison.
:::

steps.title: Remove the AP's Ethernet path and observe
steps.body:
On SW1 administratively shut only the AP port:

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# shutdown
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show interfaces fastethernet0/1
```

Observe AP1's wired link, its controller record after the controller detects loss, and ADMIN's management access. Do not repair yet.

:::expected
Fa0/1 is administratively down. AP–controller communication is interrupted, while ADMIN can still reach R1 and normally WLC1. A stale DHCP binding or temporarily retained AP record can remain; neither proves the disconnected AP is working. If AP registration was not simulated, record this controller effect as a prediction.
:::

steps.title: Restore the AP path
steps.body:
```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show interfaces fastethernet0/1
```

Wait for link and, where supported, AP re-registration. Repeat the addressing and controller checks from Step 6. Save the recovered file separately from the original baseline.

:::expected
The link returns up and the AP regains its management path. A working controller implementation again lists the AP operational. The lease can be retained or renewed; do not require a new address to call the recovery successful.
:::

steps.title: Work through a local-switching change
steps.body:
This is a worksheet, because Packet Tracer's generic AP is not a verified FlexConnect implementation. AP2 is configured to send management untagged in VLAN 10 and a locally switched staff WLAN tagged in VLAN 20. Its only cable goes to SW1 Fa0/5. Write the switch configuration, then compare with the answer.

:::expected
```ios SW1 — worksheet answer; Fa0/5 reserved for the described AP2
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/5
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk native vlan 10
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20
SW1(config-if)# spanning-tree portfast trunk
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
```

If VLAN 20 is removed from this trunk's allowed list, AP management can remain healthy while locally switched clients lose their VLAN 20 path. Repair by restoring VLAN 20 to the allowed list and verifying client DHCP/reachability. Creating the VLAN and providing its DHCP/gateway services are additional prerequisites, not effects of changing the port mode.
:::

steps.title: Check power and supported aggregation
steps.body:
Complete this hardware worksheet without applying it to the non-PoE simulation. A documented MR53 deployment uses its PoE uplink and second Ethernet port in LACP, management untagged in VLAN 10, clients tagged in VLAN 20. The selected PoE switch has sufficient documented AP power and two compatible ports, Gi1/0/1–2. The AP's dashboard aggregation setting is enabled and its LACP mode is passive.

Write the required switch settings and the evidence you would collect. Configure an actual device only in an authorized isolated lab using its installation guide.

:::expected
The switch must initiate LACP with `active`; `passive` on both ends would not initiate negotiation. Both members and Port-channel1 need matching trunk/native/allowed VLAN configuration. A representative IOS XE template is:

```ios SW1 — supported hardware worksheet only
SW1(config)# interface range gigabitethernet1/0/1 - 2
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport mode trunk
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport trunk native vlan 10
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20
SW1(config-if-range)# power inline auto
SW1(config-if-range)# channel-group 1 mode active
SW1(config-if-range)# exit
SW1(config)# interface port-channel1
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk native vlan 10
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show power inline
SW1# show etherchannel summary
SW1# show interfaces trunk
```

Check the AP's actual power requirement, available switch budget and negotiated allocation; an “on” power status alone does not guarantee full radio capability. Expect a working Layer 2 port-channel with both members bundled, plus matching AP status. On documented legacy AireOS LAG, the switch's static `mode on` would be a different requirement.
:::

lab.troubleshooting:
- **PC cannot reach its gateway:** check access VLAN, mask, trunk allowed list, router encapsulation/native setting and interface state before controller settings.
- **AP lacks an address:** check power/link, access VLAN, DHCP mode and available pool. An old lease entry does not prove current connectivity.
- **AP has an address but is absent from the controller:** check discovery, IP reachability, permitted CAPWAP traffic, model/software compatibility and certificate/time errors where the platform exposes them.
- **Management works but a client VLAN fails:** compare the actual tagging and local/central forwarding design. Do not put client VLANs on an AP trunk merely because they exist somewhere in the WLAN.
- **GUI features are missing:** use the documented worksheet boundary. Do not silently substitute an autonomous AP and call it a registered lightweight AP.
lab.challenge:
A branch AP has management address `192.168.10.110/24`, gateway `192.168.10.1`. It locally switches staff traffic tagged in VLAN 20 and guest traffic tagged in VLAN 30; its management traffic is untagged. The controller is remote. The AP port currently allows only VLANs 10 and 20, and only guest clients fail. State the necessary port/VLAN/service changes and the proof of repair. Then explain whether losing the controller necessarily stops existing and new branch clients.

:::expected
Use a trunk with native VLAN 10 and allowed VLANs `10,20,30`; create VLAN 30 and provide the required gateway/DHCP path through all relevant uplinks. Verify the AP management connection, each client's intended address/gateway and actual destination access separately. The working staff WLAN and AP join do not prove the guest VLAN path.

Controller loss does not alone determine every outcome. Supported FlexConnect locally switched WLANs may keep existing traffic local; new authentication still depends on the configured authentication method, standalone support and available local/remote services. If guest DHCP or required RADIUS is across the failed WAN, that service remains unavailable even when local switching is correct.
:::

questions.prompt: Which work remains in a Cisco lightweight AP in the split-MAC architecture?
options: Defining the corporate RADIUS policy
Selecting all campus client VLAN mappings
Keeping the complete controller configuration
Sending time-sensitive radio acknowledgements
questions.explanation: Radio acknowledgements must meet local timing requirements, so the AP handles them. The controller coordinates functions such as WLAN policy and client state.

whyWrong.0: RADIUS policy belongs to the authentication design and controller/server configuration.
whyWrong.1: Client VLAN mapping is a WLAN policy function, although local switching applies it at the AP.
whyWrong.2: A lightweight AP obtains configuration from its controller; this is not the defining local function.

questions.prompt: Which controller UDP ports does CAPWAP use for control and data respectively?
options: 67 and 68
questions.explanation: CAPWAP control uses UDP 5246 and data uses UDP 5247. Discovery occurs before the established protected control session.

whyWrong.1: 1812/1813 are common RADIUS authentication/accounting ports.
whyWrong.2: This reverses the CAPWAP functions.
whyWrong.3: 67/68 are DHCP server/client ports.

exhibit.title: Representative AireOS interface summary
exhibit.text:
Interface    VLAN  IP Address       Type     Ap Mgr
management   10    192.168.10.5     Static   Yes
users        20    192.168.20.5     Dynamic  No
virtual      N/A   192.0.2.1        Static   No

questions.prompt: Which interface is shown providing the AP-manager function on this AireOS controller?
options: The users interface in VLAN 20
The virtual interface at 192.0.2.1
The management interface in VLAN 10
The service port outside this table
questions.explanation: The `Ap Mgr Yes` field identifies management as the AP-manager interface in this exhibit. Do not infer the role from an interface's IP address alone.

whyWrong.0: The users interface is a dynamic client VLAN interface and its Ap Mgr field is No.
whyWrong.1: The virtual interface is not the AP CAPWAP endpoint.
whyWrong.3: The table provides no service-port AP-manager function.

questions.prompt: Which two AP modes dedicate the device/radio to observation rather than ordinary client service? (Choose two.)
options: Local serving a central WLAN
Monitor performing RF observation
FlexConnect serving a branch WLAN
Sniffer forwarding selected-channel captures
Bridge with client access enabled
questions.explanation: Monitor mode dedicates resources to monitoring; a sniffer radio forwards frames it can receive on the selected channel to a capture system. Actual mode availability depends on model and release.

whyWrong.0: Local mode serves ordinary clients.
whyWrong.2: FlexConnect can serve ordinary clients.
whyWrong.4: A bridge/mesh design can include client access, as explicitly stated here.

questions.prompt: AP1 sends management untagged in VLAN 10 and locally switched clients tagged in VLANs 20 and 30. What port configuration matches?
options: Access VLAN 10 with all client traffic untagged
Trunk with native 10 and allowed 10,20,30
Trunk with native 20 and allowed 20,30
Access VLAN 20 with a voice VLAN of 30
questions.explanation: The untagged management traffic belongs to native VLAN 10, while client VLANs 20 and 30 must remain tagged. The allowed list must carry all three required VLANs.

whyWrong.0: An access port cannot carry the specified tagged client VLANs.
whyWrong.2: This misclassifies untagged management and omits VLAN 10.
whyWrong.3: A phone-style access/voice arrangement does not match the AP's required trunk.

questions.prompt: An AP family uses Cisco option-43 suboption 241. What does `f104.c0a8.0a05` supply?
options: A client lease of 192.168.10.5
A DNS server at 192.168.10.5
A default route through 192.168.10.5
A controller candidate at 192.168.10.5
questions.explanation: The value encodes suboption f1, length 04 and one four-byte controller address. It supplies a discovery candidate, not proof of successful IP reachability or registration.

whyWrong.0: The lease address is conveyed by DHCP's address allocation, not this vendor option.
whyWrong.1: DNS-server addresses normally use DHCP option 6.
whyWrong.2: A default gateway is normally conveyed by option 3.

questions.prompt: An inventory says that AP-A runs Embedded Wireless Controller software and manages the other APs. How should this existing deployment be classified?
options: An autonomous AP with no controller function
An AP hosting an embedded controller
A Meraki bridge-mode dashboard deployment
A controller VM running in a hypervisor
questions.explanation: The controller function is hosted in an AP, as the inventory explicitly states. EWC-on-AP is a legacy deployment to recognize; its end-of-sale status must be considered for new designs.

whyWrong.0: The device is explicitly running a controller for other APs.
whyWrong.2: The inventory does not describe Meraki management.
whyWrong.3: No hypervisor-hosted controller is described.

exhibit.title: AireOS design record — representative
exhibit.text:
Virtual interface: 192.0.2.1 (unused by routed hosts)
DHCP proxy: enabled
Guest web authentication: enabled
Client VLAN 20 default gateway: R1 192.168.20.1

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes the virtual interface in this documented AireOS design?
options: It supports internal functions and is not the clients' routed gateway
It is the dynamic interface carrying client VLAN 20 to the switch
It is the physical service port connected to the management network
It supplies the AP's default route before CAPWAP registration
questions.explanation: The virtual interface supports functions such as web authentication and DHCP proxy. The exhibit separately identifies R1 as the clients' default gateway.

whyWrong.1: The dynamic users interface, not virtual, maps VLAN 20.
whyWrong.2: A logical virtual interface is not a physical service port.
whyWrong.3: The AP receives its own gateway through static configuration or DHCP.

questions.prompt: The switch faces a legacy AireOS controller with static LAG enabled. VLAN and speed settings match, but LACP is configured on the switch. What change matches the controller?
options: Use PAgP channel-group mode desirable
Leave LACP and change the native VLAN
Use a static channel-group in mode on
Move both links into separate access VLANs
questions.explanation: Documented legacy AireOS LAG does not negotiate LACP or PAgP. A matching static bundle uses `channel-group ... mode on`, with compatible member and VLAN settings.

whyWrong.0: PAgP desirable would negotiate aggregation, which this legacy AireOS peer does not use.
whyWrong.1: The scenario already confirms VLAN compatibility; changing it would not supply static aggregation.
whyWrong.3: Separate access VLANs do not implement the required bundle.

questions.prompt: Which two statements correctly distinguish CAPWAP protection from wireless-link protection? (Choose two.)
options: CAPWAP discovery occurs before the protected control session
WPA2 encrypts client payloads across every wired CAPWAP path
Established Cisco AP control traffic normally uses DTLS
Data and control always share one mandatory DTLS policy
A controller needs TCP 5247 for centrally switched data
questions.explanation: Discovery precedes the established DTLS-protected control session. Wireless encryption terminates at the AP; protection of the CAPWAP data path is a separate capability/configuration.

whyWrong.1: WPA2 protects the radio link, not automatically the wired tunnel.
whyWrong.3: Data DTLS is separate from control protection.
whyWrong.4: CAPWAP uses UDP, not TCP, for this data path.

questions.prompt: An AireOS model has a dedicated service port. What is its intended purpose?
options: Carry every client VLAN through an 802.1Q trunk
Provide the virtual address used by a guest portal
Negotiate a dynamic LACP bundle with every AP
Provide separate out-of-band management access
questions.explanation: The service port provides a separate management path on platforms that include it. Its routing and addressing restrictions must be checked in that model's guide.

whyWrong.0: Client VLAN distribution normally uses distribution-system interfaces/ports.
whyWrong.1: The virtual interface is a separate logical construct.
whyWrong.2: The service port is not an AP link-aggregation mechanism.

questions.prompt: A centrally switched AP sends only untagged management traffic into VLAN 10. Which is the simplest matching switchport configuration?
options: Access VLAN 20, matching the users' subnet
Access VLAN 10, carrying the AP's outer traffic
Trunk native VLAN 20 with VLAN 10 excluded
Routed port addressed from the client subnet
questions.explanation: An access port in VLAN 10 carries the AP's untagged IP/CAPWAP traffic. Client VLANs emerge at the controller in this central-switching design.

whyWrong.0: The AP's management traffic is assigned to VLAN 10, not its clients' VLAN.
whyWrong.2: This fails to carry the specified AP management network.
whyWrong.3: The AP expects a Layer 2 attachment to VLAN 10, not this unrelated routed-port design.

exhibit.title: Controlled diagnostic record — representative
exhibit.text:
AP management lease/gateway: valid
AP has no remembered or configured WLC address
DHCP option 43: absent; controller DNS lookup: no record
Router does not relay local CAPWAP discovery broadcasts
Authorized probe to WLC UDP 5246: controller responds
AP capture: local discovery only; no remote WLC destination

questions.prompt: A new, unprimed AP is on a different subnet from its WLC. Which missing item is directly supported by this diagnostic record?
options: A method for discovering a controller address
A lease pool for the wireless staff clients
A trunk carrying the remote client VLAN to the AP
A change from central switching to local switching
questions.explanation: The AP has working management IP connectivity but no discovery candidate: local broadcast does not cross this router, and neither stored addresses, option 43 nor the DNS record supplies one. Configure a supported discovery method and then verify registration.

whyWrong.1: The failure is AP discovery before staff client service is relevant.
whyWrong.2: Central switching does not require that client VLAN at the AP.
whyWrong.3: Local switching is not needed to discover a reachable controller.

questions.prompt: A Meraki SSID is explicitly configured in bridge mode. A client prints to a server in the same local client VLAN. Where does that user traffic normally go?
options: Through a 9800-CL VM before reaching the printer
Through the cloud dashboard for each print packet
Through the AP into the local wired client VLAN
Through an AireOS virtual interface as its gateway
questions.explanation: Bridge mode forwards this client traffic into the local wired VLAN. Cloud management does not make the dashboard a mandatory transit point; other Meraki SSID modes must be considered separately.

whyWrong.0: No 9800-CL is part of this bridge-mode design.
whyWrong.1: The dashboard manages the AP rather than forwarding every bridge-mode print packet.
whyWrong.3: The design does not use an AireOS virtual interface.

questions.prompt: A technician needs an authorized wireless capture on one known channel rather than ordinary client access from that radio. Which mode fits?
options: Local mode forwarding all data centrally
FlexConnect with local VLAN switching
Rogue detector examining the wired side
Sniffer mode forwarding heard radio frames
questions.explanation: Sniffer mode is intended to send received frames on a selected channel to a capture system. It cannot guarantee reception of every frame, and the selected radio is not providing ordinary client access.

whyWrong.0: Ordinary local service is not a dedicated sniffer capture mode.
whyWrong.1: Local switching describes forwarding location, not capture collection.
whyWrong.2: A wired rogue-detector role is not a selected-channel radio capture.

exhibit.title: Power worksheet — representative, model requirements supplied
exhibit.text:
AP model guide: full radio operation requires 802.3at power
Switch: AP powered, 802.3af allocation only
Controller: AP joined; radio capability restricted by low power

questions.prompt: A powered AP has reduced radio capability. What is the best next check from this evidence?
options: Compare the AP power requirement with the allocated PoE and budget
Replace the WLAN passphrase and leave the power allocation unchanged
Convert the AP port to a trunk without checking its forwarding mode
Change CAPWAP control from UDP to TCP to improve registration
questions.explanation: The controller specifically reports a low-power restriction and the allocation is below the documented requirement for full operation. Check supported power sources, negotiation and the switch's total available budget before changing wireless security.

whyWrong.1: A passphrase change does not resolve a measured power restriction.
whyWrong.2: Trunking does not supply the missing power and depends on a different requirement.
whyWrong.3: CAPWAP control uses UDP; changing its transport is not a repair.

cards.front: CAPWAP control port and protection?
cards.back: UDP 5246. Discovery precedes DTLS; established Cisco AP control traffic uses DTLS.

cards.front: CAPWAP data port and protection?
cards.back: UDP 5247. Data DTLS is a separate policy; WPA2/WPA3 radio protection does not automatically encrypt this wired path.

cards.front: Which split-MAC operations stay in the AP?
cards.back: Time-sensitive radio work: beacons, acknowledgements, retransmissions, power-save handling and per-frame wireless encryption/decryption.

cards.front: Which work does a WLC coordinate?
cards.back: WLAN configuration, client state, authentication policy, mobility and radio management; details depend on mode and deployment.

cards.front: What does Cisco option-43 value f104.c0a8.0a05 encode?
cards.back: For APs using suboption 241: f1 type, 04-byte length, controller candidate 192.168.10.5. The encoding is vendor/model-specific.

cards.front: What DNS name can a Cisco AP use for controller discovery?
cards.back: `CISCO-CAPWAP-CONTROLLER` in the relevant DNS domain, with working DNS and IP connectivity.

cards.front: How do configured controller preferences affect AP selection?
cards.back: Primary/secondary/tertiary preferences guide selection among usable candidates; discovery information alone does not prove a join.

cards.front: Where can a controller function run?
cards.back: In an appliance, supported VM, or documented embedded deployment. EWC-on-AP is a legacy product, not a universal new-design recommendation.

cards.front: Cloud-based controller versus cloud-managed AP?
cards.back: A cloud-based WLC runs controller software remotely; cloud-managed identifies the manager's location. Determine client forwarding from the configured SSID mode.

cards.front: Port for a centrally switched AP with only untagged management in VLAN 10?
cards.back: An access port in VLAN 10 is sufficient; client traffic reaches its VLAN at the controller.

cards.front: Port for untagged management 10 and tagged local client VLANs 20/30?
cards.back: Trunk with native VLAN 10 and allowed VLANs 10,20,30, matching the AP's actual tagging configuration.

cards.front: Which physical controller connections might a model provide?
cards.back: Distribution, console, service-management and redundancy connections; presence and purpose vary by model.

cards.front: What are AireOS dynamic and management interfaces for?
cards.back: Dynamic interfaces map client VLANs; management provides controller access and, on common platforms, AP-manager functions.

cards.front: Is an AireOS virtual interface the clients' routed gateway?
cards.back: No. It supports internal functions such as WebAuth/DHCP proxy. Use a suitable unused address that does not conflict with routed hosts.

cards.front: Switch aggregation mode for documented legacy AireOS LAG?
cards.back: Static `channel-group N mode on`. Check platform docs for current 9800 or AP LACP support.

cards.front: Sniffer mode versus monitor mode?
cards.back: Sniffer exports heard frames on a selected channel; monitor dedicates radio resources to monitoring rather than ordinary client service.

cards.front: What is the legacy AireOS rogue-detector role?
cards.back: Correlate wired observations with suspected rogue wireless devices; it is not an ordinary client-serving AP role.

cards.front: What determines FlexConnect service during controller loss?
cards.back: Local switching, authentication/standalone support and service reachability. Existing clients and new joins can have different outcomes.

cards.front: A powered AP has reduced radio capability: what power evidence matters?
cards.back: Compare the model's requirements with negotiated PoE, power-source capability and the switch's remaining budget.

cards.front: Where does a 9800 map a WLAN profile to client policy?
cards.back: The policy tag maps the WLAN profile to a policy profile and is assigned to the intended APs.

commands.task: Select access mode for an AP that sends only untagged management traffic; its VLAN is configured separately.
commands.note: The actual traffic contract determines port mode; not every controller-based AP uses this design.

commands.task: The AP explicitly sends management untagged in VLAN 10. Set native VLAN 10 on its already configured trunk.
commands.note: The native VLAN must match this AP's untagged management design.

commands.task: The AP family uses Cisco suboption 241. Supply controller candidate 192.168.10.5 in the DHCP pool.
commands.note: f1 is type 241, 04 is length, c0a80a05 is 192.168.10.5.

commands.task: The documented legacy AireOS WLC uses static LAG. Put this compatible interface range in static group 1.
commands.note: LACP/PAgP negotiation would not match this peer; member VLAN and link settings must also match.

commands.task: Inspect the controller port-channel's protocol and bundled member status.
commands.note: For a working static Layer 2 bundle, look for SU on the channel and P on its members; protocol is normally '-'.

commands.task: Display detailed CDP neighbor identity and advertised address on the switch.
commands.note: An advertised address is not proof of a DHCP lease or CAPWAP registration. CDP may be disabled.

commands.task: On a PoE-capable Cisco switch, inspect inline power for FastEthernet0/1.
commands.note: Support and interface names depend on the platform. Compare allocation with the AP's required operating power.

commands.task: On an AireOS controller, display the registered AP summary.
commands.note: Use the GUI AP summary when the Packet Tracer controller has no supported CLI.

commands.task: On AireOS, display logical interface names, addresses and VLAN mappings.
commands.note: Management/AP-manager and dynamic client interfaces serve different purposes.

commands.task: On a supported AireOS controller in an isolated lab, select FlexConnect mode for AP1.
commands.note: Expect possible service disruption. Configure local switching/authentication and the AP port separately; mode alone supplies neither.

commands.task: Enable automatic power allocation on a supported Cisco PoE interface.
commands.note: The port and switch budget must still support the AP's power requirements.

commands.task: A supported AP is an LACP passive peer. Make this compatible port range initiate LACP group 1.
commands.note: Use only a model documented for AP aggregation; configure matching member and port-channel VLAN settings.

tickets.title: New APs discover the retired controller
tickets.scenario: A site replaced controller 10.10.0.5 with 10.10.50.5. Existing APs were manually pointed to the replacement, but newly installed, unprimed APs fail to join. Routing, AP/controller software compatibility and permitted CAPWAP connectivity to 10.10.50.5 have been independently verified. The following records are representative.

exhibits.title: R1 DHCP pool excerpt
exhibits.text:
ip dhcp pool AP-MGMT
 network 10.10.60.0 255.255.255.0
 default-router 10.10.60.1
 option 43 hex f104.0a0a.0005

exhibits.title: New AP discovery observation
exhibits.text:
Lease: 10.10.60.101/24; gateway 10.10.60.1
Received option 43 controller candidate: 10.10.0.5
No stored controller and no controller DNS record
Requests sent to 10.10.0.5; no response
Retired controller 10.10.0.5 is powered off

tickets.question: Which fault is directly supported by the records?
options: The AP must carry every client VLAN on its Ethernet link
The DHCP controller-discovery option still points to the retired WLC
The new controller requires a TCP 5247 access rule
The AP lease belongs to a subnet too distant for CAPWAP
tickets.explanation: The option-43 address decodes to the retired 10.10.0.5, and the AP observation confirms that it used that candidate. CAPWAP can cross routed subnets; the independently verified new-controller path should be used after discovery is corrected.
tickets.fix:
In the isolated lab, change only this pool's option, then have one test AP reacquire its DHCP discovery information using that platform's supported renewal/restart procedure. Do not clear every network lease.

```ios
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip dhcp pool AP-MGMT
R1(dhcp-config)# no option 43
R1(dhcp-config)# option 43 hex f104.0a0a.3205
R1(dhcp-config)# end
```

Confirm the next DHCP information names 10.10.50.5, then confirm discovery responses and actual AP registration. A successful ping alone does not prove the join.

tickets.title: The branch AP is joined, but local guests cannot get a lease
tickets.scenario: A FlexConnect AP sends management untagged in VLAN 10. CORP is centrally switched and works. GUEST is explicitly configured for local switching with tagged VLAN 30. VLAN 30, its gateway, DHCP pool and upstream trunk have been verified using a wired test client. Records below are representative.

exhibits.title: SW1 AP-facing port
exhibits.text:
interface GigabitEthernet1/0/7
 switchport mode access
 switchport access vlan 10
 spanning-tree portfast

exhibits.title: AP/WLAN and wired test
exhibits.text:
AP management: 10.10.0.51/24; controller state joined
GUEST: local switching, VLAN 30, security completed
Wireless GUEST client: no lease
Wired test in VLAN 30: 10.30.0.101/24, gateway 10.30.0.1; reachable

tickets.question: Which mismatch explains the guest failure?
options: The controller needs GUEST traffic to be centrally switched
The guest DHCP scope lacks a reachable default gateway
The AP link cannot carry its required tagged VLAN 30
The AP must share the guest subnet to remain registered
tickets.explanation: The access port carries untagged VLAN 10 but does not match the AP's required tagged local guest VLAN. Management and the centrally switched CORP WLAN can work while this separate local forwarding path fails.
tickets.fix:
In the authorized lab, change the AP port to the documented trunk contract:

```ios
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet1/0/7
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk native vlan 10
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,30
SW1(config-if)# spanning-tree portfast trunk
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show interfaces trunk
```

Allow any link/control reconvergence, confirm AP registration, and request a fresh guest lease. Verify a 10.30.0.x/24 address, gateway 10.30.0.1 and actual guest access; then retest CORP.

sections.title: Compare WEP, WPA, WPA2 and WPA3
Configure the WLAN through the GUI

lab.title: Configure and test a WPA2-Personal WLAN
lab.intro:
Build an isolated controller WLAN from a new file, configure its security through the GUI and prove that a wireless client reaches a known server. Then introduce a wrong passphrase and unavailable DHCP as separate faults, preserving evidence before each repair.

:::note Controller and simulator limits
Use the WLC-3504 and LAP-PT when your Packet Tracer version offers them. Record the version and the actual labels in its port picker. This is a legacy AireOS-style exercise, not a Catalyst 9800 emulator. If a required GUI control or AP/client function is unavailable, keep the working wired setup and complete the supplied configuration/status worksheet for that portion, labeled “not simulated.” Do not substitute an autonomous AP and call that completion of a controller GUI lab. WPA3, Enterprise authentication, realistic RF behavior and exact controller states are not assumed to be simulated.
:::
lab.topology:
```diagram
{"type":"topology","title":"Lab topology — isolated 10.0.10.0/24 WLAN","caption":"The controller uses a trunk with native VLAN 10; the other wired attachments use access VLAN 10 in this isolated single-subnet lab.","nodes":[{"id":"R","kind":"router","label":"R1","sub":"10.0.10.1; DHCP","x":2,"y":1},{"id":"S","kind":"switch","label":"SW1","sub":"VLAN 10","x":6,"y":3},{"id":"W","kind":"wlc","label":"WLC1","sub":"10.0.10.2","x":10,"y":1},{"id":"A","kind":"ap","label":"AP1","sub":"DHCP; CAPWAP","x":10,"y":5},{"id":"L","kind":"laptop","label":"LT1","sub":"SSID CCNA-Lab","x":12,"y":3},{"id":"P","kind":"pc","label":"ADMIN","sub":"10.0.10.10","x":2,"y":5},{"id":"V","kind":"server","label":"WEB1","sub":"10.0.10.20","x":6,"y":6}],"links":[{"from":"R","to":"S","fromLabel":"Gi0/0","toLabel":"Fa0/1"},{"from":"W","to":"S","fromLabel":"Port 1","toLabel":"Fa0/2","label":"trunk; native 10"},{"from":"P","to":"S","toLabel":"Fa0/3"},{"from":"A","to":"S","fromLabel":"Gi0","toLabel":"Fa0/4"},{"from":"V","to":"S","toLabel":"Fa0/5"},{"from":"L","to":"A","style":"wireless","label":"WPA2-PSK/AES"}]}
```

Use copper straight-through for all five wired device-to-switch links. WLC Port 1 is commonly displayed as `GigabitEthernet1` and LAP-PT's wired port as `GigabitEthernet0`; use the selected model's actual connector names.

| Device | IPv4 address/mask | Gateway | Assignment |
|---|---|---|---|
| R1 Gi0/0 | `10.0.10.1/24` | None required in this isolated lab | Static |
| WLC1 management, Port 1 | `10.0.10.2/24` | `10.0.10.1` | Static, untagged (`0`) |
| ADMIN FastEthernet0 | `10.0.10.10/24` | `10.0.10.1` | Static |
| WEB1 FastEthernet0 | `10.0.10.20/24` | `10.0.10.1` | Static |
| AP1 and LT1 | `10.0.10.21–254/24` | `10.0.10.1` | DHCP |

There is no DNS server or Internet connection. Leave DNS unset and test the supplied IP addresses.

steps.title: Cable, power and prepare the endpoints
steps.body:
Place all seven devices and connect the five wired links. Supply AP1 with its supported external power adapter if the selected model requires one; do not assume the 2960 model provides PoE. On LT1, check for an installed wireless interface. If absent and the model offers WPC300N, power the laptop off, replace its copper module with WPC300N, then power it on. Do not remove or insert modules while powered.

Use Desktop → IP Configuration on ADMIN and WEB1 to enter their static address, `255.255.255.0` mask and gateway. On WEB1 open Services → HTTP and turn HTTP On. This is a disposable local test page with no credentials.

:::expected
ADMIN and WEB1 display the static values in the table. LT1 has a wireless interface/control. AP1 is powered. No successful AP join or wireless client connection is claimed at this stage.
:::

steps.title: Configure the switch, router and DHCP pool
steps.body:
On the switch, configure endpoint access ports first, then override only Fa0/2 for the controller distribution-system trunk. Cisco documents trunk mode for that controller connection even though this lab carries only one native VLAN.

```ios SW1
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname SW1
SW1(config)# vlan 10
SW1(config-vlan)# name WLAN-LAB
SW1(config-vlan)# exit
SW1(config)# interface range fastethernet0/1 - 5
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport access vlan 10
SW1(config-if-range)# spanning-tree portfast
SW1(config-if-range)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if-range)# exit
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/2
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk native vlan 10
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan 10
SW1(config-if)# spanning-tree portfast trunk
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show vlan brief
SW1# show interfaces trunk
```

On the router:

```ios R1
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R1
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.0.10.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# ip dhcp excluded-address 10.0.10.1 10.0.10.20
R1(config)# ip dhcp pool WLAN-LAB
R1(dhcp-config)# network 10.0.10.0 255.255.255.0
R1(dhcp-config)# default-router 10.0.10.1
R1(dhcp-config)# end
R1# show ip interface brief
```

From ADMIN run `ping 10.0.10.1` and `ping 10.0.10.20` in Desktop → Command Prompt. Open `http://10.0.10.20` in ADMIN's browser.

:::expected
Fa0/1 and Fa0/3–5 are access members of VLAN 10. Fa0/2 is a trunk with native VLAN 10 and allowed VLAN 10; it appears operational once the controller link is up. R1 Gi0/0 becomes up/up. ADMIN reaches R1 and WEB1; the local test page loads. Retry an initial ping after ARP resolution if necessary. Do not start the wireless diagnosis while this wired baseline is broken.
:::

steps.title: Initialize controller management
steps.body:
In WLC1's Config → Management page, where provided, enter `10.0.10.2`, mask `255.255.255.0`, gateway `10.0.10.1` and Port 1. Keep management untagged; an AireOS VLAN value of `0` represents this. The controller trunk assigns the untagged traffic to its native VLAN 10.

From ADMIN's browser try `https://10.0.10.2`. A fresh model may expose its day-zero wizard at `http://10.0.10.2` instead; use HTTP only for this isolated simulator bootstrap. Enter the following fields if requested:

| Setup field | Value |
|---|---|
| Controller name | `WLC1` |
| Administrator username/password | `labadmin` / `Admin-Lab-2026!` |
| Management IP/mask/gateway | `10.0.10.2` / `255.255.255.0` / `10.0.10.1` |
| Management VLAN / physical port | Untagged (`0`) / `1` |
| DHCP server for management/WLAN use, if exposed | `10.0.10.1` |
| Required initial employee SSID, if any | `SETUP-LAB` |
| Initial security/passphrase | WPA2-Personal, AES / `Setup-Lab-2026!` |

Apply after checking the fields. If the model restarts, wait for management reachability and reconnect with HTTPS. Record the created WLAN IDs; the exercise below reserves ID 2. If ID 2 is already in use, choose another unused ID and use it consistently in your worksheet.

:::expected
The controller displays the intended management settings and accepts the newly configured administrator account. If the selected model lacks the required setup mechanism, record that limitation and use the supplied fields as a worksheet; do not guess a factory address or claim an operational WLC.
:::

steps.title: Verify the AP and DHCP path
steps.body:
Set AP1's wired management interface to DHCP where that control is exposed. Inspect R1:

```ios R1
R1# show ip dhcp binding
```

Record AP1's actual address and MAC from its interface/status view. On the controller inspect Wireless → Access Points → All APs, or its equivalent AP summary. AP and controller share the same VLAN here, so local discovery is possible without option 43. This does not imply that all real AP/controller combinations are compatible.

In Controller → Interfaces → management, if the model exposes a Primary DHCP Server field, set it to `10.0.10.1`. This is needed for the documented AireOS DHCP-proxy arrangement. Do not set an internal DHCP pool and R1's pool simultaneously for this exercise.

:::expected
AP1 receives an address in `10.0.10.21–254`, but no particular first lease is guaranteed. A separate controller record shows registration where implemented. The selected interface points to the actual DHCP server. Missing simulator controls are recorded as such; a DHCP lease alone is not proof of a completed AP join.
:::

steps.title: Create the WLAN and configure security while disabled
steps.body:
On the controller open WLANs → Create New → Go. Create profile `CCNA-USERS`, SSID `CCNA-Lab`, WLAN ID `2` (or your recorded unused ID). Leave the WLAN disabled while editing. Configure the following; click Apply where the model requires it to retain a tab's changes.

| Page/field | Required setting |
|---|---|
| General → Interface/Interface Group | `management` for this flat lab |
| General → Radio Policy | A band supported by AP1 and LT1; All if offered |
| General → Broadcast SSID | Enabled |
| Security → Layer 2 → security family | `WPA+WPA2` on AireOS-style pages |
| WPA Policy / WPA2 Policy | Off / On |
| TKIP / AES | Off / On |
| AKM 802.1X / PSK | Off / On |
| PSK Format / key | ASCII / `StudyLab-2026!` |
| Security → Layer 3 | None; no WebAuth for this test |

These settings deliberately match WPA2-Personal. They are not obtained simply by selecting a dropdown labeled WPA+WPA2.

:::expected
The stored WLAN is still disabled and its security summary indicates WPA2, PSK and AES/CCMP. It is mapped to the management network only because this is an isolated flat lab. There is no RADIUS requirement, captive portal or MAC filter in this design.
:::

steps.title: Inspect policy, enable and save
steps.body:
Read the QoS tab and record the profile and WMM setting that actually appear. For this best-effort data exercise, choose Silver if that AireOS-style option is available; leave WMM Allowed or its compatible enabled policy. Read the Advanced tab and record any session timeout, client exclusion, DHCP-required and P2P settings shown. Mark unavailable controls “not modeled.”

Return to General, enable the WLAN and Apply. Use Save Configuration if available. If a setup WLAN was automatically created, disable that unused WLAN so LT1 cannot accidentally connect to it.

:::expected
The lab WLAN is enabled with WPA2/PSK/AES and the intended interface. An Advanced value is a policy to interpret, not proof of a fault. For example, a displayed `1800`-second timer is 30 minutes, while a displayed 60-second exclusion value does not establish that any client is currently excluded.
:::

steps.title: Join LT1 and prove actual data access
steps.body:
On LT1 open Desktop → PC Wireless, refresh the network list, select `CCNA-Lab` and connect with WPA2-Personal/AES and `StudyLab-2026!`. If the model uses Config → Wireless0 instead, set the same SSID, security and key there. Select DHCP in Desktop → IP Configuration.

Run these commands separately in the PC command prompt:

```text
ipconfig
ping 10.0.10.1
ping 10.0.10.20
```

Open `http://10.0.10.20` in LT1's browser. Compare its wireless MAC/IP with the controller's Monitor → Clients entry and R1's DHCP bindings. Record whether the GUI exposes security completion/admitted state, rather than relying only on “Associated.”

:::expected
LT1 has a current `10.0.10.21–254/24` address and gateway `10.0.10.1`. The gateway and WEB1 respond, and the local page loads. Together these observations support a working WLAN data path. They do not prove Internet connectivity, DNS service, RF performance or any destination absent from this topology.
:::

steps.title: Save the baseline and introduce a wrong key
steps.body:
Save `wlan-security-baseline.pkt`, then save a working copy as `wlan-security-fault.pkt`. Disconnect LT1, edit its saved profile or remove and recreate that profile, and reconnect with `StudyLab-2026` (omit the final exclamation mark). Do not change the controller key.

Observe the client message and current controller state, then attempt the WEB1 test. Do not restore the key yet.

:::expected
With the new incorrect key actually in use, the secure data connection fails. The SSID can still be visible, and an old IP address can remain displayed. Neither proves the new key exchange succeeded. A popup alone does not prove which handshake message failed; record only the evidence your simulator exposes.
:::

steps.title: Restore the key and verify recovery
steps.body:
Disconnect again and replace the saved key with `StudyLab-2026!`. Reconnect. If the controller explicitly shows this client excluded, wait for its displayed remaining interval or clear only the lab client's exclusion using the supported GUI action. Do not assume a universal timeout.

Repeat the current IP, ping and WEB1 page checks.

:::expected
The client again passes the same baseline tests. If not, verify that its saved profile actually changed and that it chose `CCNA-Lab` rather than a different SSID. A repaired field alone is not the final proof.
:::

steps.title: Remove the DHCP service after clearing the client's lease
steps.body:
Keep AP1 and WLC1 powered and connected. This short fault is for a fresh client address request; do not reboot the AP while its DHCP server is temporarily absent.

On LT1, try:

```text
ipconfig /release
```

Confirm LT1 no longer has its usable DHCP address. If that operation is unsupported or the simulator retains a usable lease that you cannot release through its IP Configuration controls, stop the live DHCP fault and use the worksheet in Step 11. A reconnect by itself does not guarantee a fresh lease.

Only after confirming the release, remove the lab pool on R1:

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# no ip dhcp pool WLAN-LAB
R1(config)# end
R1# show ip dhcp pool
```

:::expected
The WLAN-LAB pool is absent, while the wireless security settings and AP's existing management connection have not been deliberately changed. A prior AP lease can remain valid during this brief fault. Record whether the prerequisites for the live test were actually met.
:::

steps.title: Observe a fresh address request
steps.body:
If Step 10's live prerequisites were met, request a new client lease:

```text
ipconfig /renew
ipconfig
```

Alternatively use the supported DHCP request control in LT1's IP Configuration page. Check the controller's security/admission/addressing information and R1's pool state before drawing a conclusion.

:::expected
With no available DHCP server in this isolated topology, a fresh DHCP attempt cannot obtain the intended lease. The client may show no address or a link-local address, depending on the model. Security may still be complete even though the client cannot reach WEB1.

Worksheet fallback: a controller diagnostic explicitly reports successful WPA2 key establishment; a fresh client capture shows repeated DHCP requests with no offer; R1 has no WLAN-LAB pool. The next repair is the missing DHCP service, not a passphrase change. This worksheet is supplied evidence, not a claimed simulator capture.
:::

steps.title: Restore DHCP and retest
steps.body:
If you removed the pool, recreate it. The excluded range from Step 2 remains configured.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip dhcp pool WLAN-LAB
R1(dhcp-config)# network 10.0.10.0 255.255.255.0
R1(dhcp-config)# default-router 10.0.10.1
R1(dhcp-config)# end
R1# show ip dhcp pool WLAN-LAB
```

Request DHCP again on LT1, inspect its current configuration and repeat the gateway/WEB1 tests. If AP1's management lease was affected during a long pause, restore its DHCP connectivity and registration before judging the client result.

:::expected
A valid client lease returns and the local page loads. The pool does not advertise an unconfigured DNS server. If the fault was worksheet-only, describe this repair and its required verification without claiming to have observed it.
:::

steps.title: Translate the configuration to a 9800 worksheet
steps.body:
Do not paste IOS XE commands into the Packet Tracer controller. For an already commissioned Catalyst 9800, write the equivalent GUI object plan:

- WLAN profile `CCNA-USERS`, SSID `CCNA-Lab`, ID `2`, WPA2/AES/PSK.
- Enabled policy profile `PP-LAB`, client VLAN `10`, central switching.
- Policy tag `PT-LAB` mapping `CCNA-USERS` to `PP-LAB`.
- The intended AP assigned `PT-LAB`, with appropriate existing site/RF tags and an operational radio.

Identify the current GUI pages that hold these objects and explain the symptom if the AP retains a different policy tag.

:::expected
Use Configuration → Tags & Profiles → WLANs; Policy; Tags → Policy; then Configuration → Wireless → Access Points for assignment. A correct WLAN and policy profile do not reach an AP unless its effective policy tag maps them. Verify the mapping and WLAN/radio states before changing the client password. This is a documented translation, not a 9800 deployment executed in Packet Tracer.
:::

steps.title: Save and document the recovered lab
steps.body:
Use Save Configuration on WLC1. Save the IOS devices separately:

```ios R1
R1# copy running-config startup-config
```

Accept the destination filename with Enter. On SW1:

```ios SW1
SW1# copy running-config startup-config
```

Accept the prompt there, then save `wlan-security-recovered.pkt`. Record the model/version, any unavailable GUI fields, final SSID/security/interface, client IP evidence, both fault observations and both recovery checks. Do not publish the administrative password or PSK in a real support record.

:::expected
The working baseline remains intact, and the recovered project is separately saved. Your notes clearly distinguish completed simulator actions from worksheet-only procedures. No controller reload is required for this verification.
:::

lab.troubleshooting:
- **Controller page unavailable:** first test the wired management path, address and controller-untagged/switch-native VLAN agreement; then check the displayed setup/HTTPS state. A failed ping alone does not establish that its web server is down.
- **AP absent from controller:** check power, Ethernet, AP addressing, discovery, software compatibility and exposed join errors. Same-subnet placement simplifies discovery; it does not guarantee compatibility.
- **SSID absent:** inspect AP/radio operation, enabled WLAN, compatible band and assignment. Do not start by changing the PSK.
- **Security fails:** compare exact saved profile, cipher, AKM, PMF support and controller diagnostics. Do not infer “RF is fine” from SSID visibility alone.
- **Security complete, fresh DHCP fails:** inspect interface mapping, actual server availability and any trunk/relay path. A stale displayed address is not a new lease.
- **Address works but application fails:** test the actual destination/service. Here WEB1's HTTP service must be On; DNS and Internet were never part of the topology.
lab.challenge:
In a separate copy, create WLAN ID 3 with profile `CCNA-SECOND`, SSID `CCNA-Second` and WPA2-Personal/AES key `Maple-Lab-2026!`. Keep the same flat client network. Disable the original test WLAN and join LT1 to the new one. Explain why copying the old client profile unchanged fails.

Then complete a design worksheet for separating management into VLAN 99 (`10.0.99.0/24`) while keeping clients in VLAN 10 (`10.0.10.0/24`). Specify controller mapping, switch tagging, router interfaces and DHCP settings.

:::expected
For the live variation, create the new disabled WLAN, map it to `management` in this flat file, configure WPA2/AES with PSK and no 802.1X, enable and save it. Disable the old WLAN. On LT1 use the new SSID and new key, request DHCP and retest R1 and WEB1. The old profile has the wrong SSID/key; neither a previous lease nor a saved connection name supplies the new credentials.

For the separation worksheet: WLC management becomes `10.0.99.2/24`, gateway `10.0.99.1`, untagged on its uplink. Its dynamic `users` interface uses VLAN 10, `10.0.10.2/24`, gateway/DHCP server `10.0.10.1`. Map the WLAN to `users`. Expand the existing WLC trunk to allowed VLANs `10,99` and change its native VLAN to 99; make the router port a trunk with the same native and allowed VLANs; ADMIN/AP ports become access VLAN 99, WEB1 stays access VLAN 10.

R1 removes the old IP from physical Gi0/0, keeps it enabled, and uses Gi0/0.99 with `encapsulation dot1Q 99 native` and `10.0.99.1/24`, plus Gi0/0.10 with `encapsulation dot1Q 10` and `10.0.10.1/24`. Retain the client DHCP pool and exclusions; add a management pool for `10.0.99.0/24` with gateway `10.0.99.1` and exclude its statically assigned addresses. ADMIN moves to `10.0.99.10/24` with gateway `10.0.99.1`. The AP receives a management lease while wireless clients receive client leases. Verify each VLAN's path independently; implement this extension only if the selected controller exposes dynamic-interface tagging.
:::

exhibit.title: Representative AireOS WLAN 2 security
exhibit.text:
WPA policy: disabled
WPA2 policy: enabled
AES: enabled; TKIP: disabled
AKM 802.1X: enabled
AKM PSK: disabled

questions.prompt: Clients are configured for WPA2-Personal with a shared passphrase. There is no RADIUS or local EAP service. Which change matches the intended design?
options: Enable legacy WPA policy and replace AES with TKIP
Select WEP shared-key authentication on the WLAN
Disable 802.1X AKM, enable PSK and set the matching key
Enable a MAC filter and retain the current AKM settings
questions.explanation: The cipher and WPA2 selection already match, but the configured key-management method is Enterprise 802.1X rather than Personal PSK. Configure the intended PSK method and key, then verify a fresh client connection.

whyWrong.0: Legacy WPA/TKIP does not correct the key-management mismatch.
whyWrong.1: WEP shared-key authentication is a different obsolete mechanism.
whyWrong.3: A MAC filter does not supply the missing PSK authentication/key establishment.

questions.prompt: Which description matches AES-CCMP, the cipher suite selected for the chapter's WPA2 WLAN?
options: AES-based encryption combined with CBC-MAC integrity
RC4 key mixing combined with Michael integrity
AES-GCM encryption combined with Galois integrity
Static RC4 keys combined with a CRC integrity check
questions.explanation: CCMP combines AES-based encryption and integrity protection using CBC-MAC. This is distinct from the authentication method, which can be Personal or Enterprise.

whyWrong.1: That describes TKIP-era protection associated with WPA.
whyWrong.2: That describes GCMP, not the specifically requested CCMP.
whyWrong.3: That describes WEP-era protection.

questions.prompt: Which two statements describe a WPA3-Personal connection? (Choose two.)
options: It removes the need for the four-way handshake
It uses SAE for password-based key establishment
It requires TKIP to support older Wi-Fi clients
It requires Protected Management Frames
It requires each client to authenticate through RADIUS
questions.explanation: WPA3-Personal uses SAE and requires PMF for its connections. The four-way handshake still follows key establishment; SAE is not simply a replacement name for the WPA2 PSK handshake.

whyWrong.0: The four-way handshake is retained after SAE.
whyWrong.2: TKIP is obsolete and does not provide WPA3 protection.
whyWrong.4: RADIUS is associated with Enterprise authentication rather than ordinary WPA3-Personal.

exhibit.title: Representative controlled WPA2-PSK diagnostic
exhibit.text:
802.11 association: completed
Message 1: sent
Message 2: received; integrity check invalid
No successful four-way handshake recorded
Client profile key differs from the configured WLAN key

questions.prompt: This diagnostic comes from a WPA2-PSK client that used the wrong passphrase. Which explanation fits the observed failure?
options: The AP rejected the SSID before sending any security frame
The peers derived different keys, so message 2's MIC failed
The client successfully obtained the GTK and then failed DHCP
The PMF policy required the client to use a RADIUS password
questions.explanation: The wrong passphrase leads to different master/transient key material, so the infrastructure cannot validate the client's message-2 integrity check. This specific conclusion is supported by the diagnostic, not just a generic connection popup.

whyWrong.0: The record shows association and handshake message 1 already occurred.
whyWrong.2: The diagnostic stops at message 2 before successful key establishment and addressing.
whyWrong.3: Nothing in the evidence indicates a PMF/RADIUS requirement.

questions.prompt: Which key entry violates Cisco's documented WPA2 PSK field length rules?
options: A 63-character entry in ASCII format
A 64-hexadecimal-digit entry in HEX format
A 20-character random entry in ASCII format
A 7-character entry in ASCII format
questions.explanation: The documented ASCII PSK passphrase range is 8–63 characters; HEX requires exactly 64 hexadecimal digits. Seven ASCII characters is too short.

whyWrong.0: 63 is within the documented ASCII length range.
whyWrong.1: 64 valid hex digits meet the raw-key format requirement.
whyWrong.2: 20 is within the documented ASCII length range.

questions.prompt: In this centrally authenticated WLAN, clients exchange EAP through a WLC with an external RADIUS server. Which device is the 802.1X authenticator?
options: The WLC that controls admission and relays EAP
The RADIUS server that evaluates the EAP method
The client software that supplies its credential
The DHCP server that allocates the client address
questions.explanation: The WLC is the authenticator in the stated central-authentication design. The client is the supplicant, and RADIUS is the authentication server.

whyWrong.1: That is the authentication-server role.
whyWrong.2: That is the supplicant role.
whyWrong.3: Address allocation is separate from the stated 802.1X roles.

questions.prompt: The required EAP method uses both client and server certificates for authentication, rather than a client password. Which choice fits?
options: PEAP with MS-CHAPv2 client authentication
Open-system authentication with a shared SSID
EAP-TLS with client and server certificates
WPA2-Personal with a common passphrase
questions.explanation: EAP-TLS provides certificate-based authentication for both endpoints. Certificates must be issued, trusted and validated correctly; simply selecting the method is not a complete deployment.

whyWrong.0: This common PEAP method uses password-based client authentication inside a protected tunnel.
whyWrong.1: Open-system association does not provide the required certificate authentication.
whyWrong.3: A shared PSK does not provide the required per-client EAP-TLS certificates.

exhibit.title: Representative AireOS client evidence
exhibit.text:
WLAN: CCNA-Lab; interface users; VLAN 20
Current diagnostic: WPA2 key establishment completed
Policy Manager State: DHCP_REQD
Current IP address: Unknown
Client: repeated fresh DHCP requests; no lease

questions.prompt: What should be investigated next from these current client diagnostics?
options: The passphrase, because association proves the handshake failed
The VLAN 20 DHCP path, because security completed but addressing did not
The captive portal, because every admitted client requires WebAuth
The exclusion timer, because RUN and DHCP_REQD are the same state
questions.explanation: The explicit security-complete event and current DHCP_REQD state place the next investigation at addressing. Check the mapped VLAN, DHCP service and transport path without assuming which one is faulty.

whyWrong.0: Association alone would not prove security either way; here the separate event explicitly confirms completion.
whyWrong.2: No portal requirement is shown, and WebAuth is a separate stage.
whyWrong.3: DHCP_REQD is an addressing wait state, not RUN or proof of exclusion.

questions.prompt: An AireOS data WLAN currently uses Silver. A design calls for the voice QoS profile for its compatible handsets. Which profile change matches the requirement?
options: Select Gold, the background traffic profile
Select Bronze, the voice traffic profile
Keep Silver, the video traffic profile
Select Platinum, the voice traffic profile
questions.explanation: Platinum is the AireOS voice QoS level; Silver is best effort. The profile must fit a consistent classification/WMM/wired QoS design and does not guarantee bandwidth.

whyWrong.0: Gold corresponds to video, not background or the requested voice level.
whyWrong.1: Bronze corresponds to background traffic.
whyWrong.2: Silver is best effort, not video.

questions.prompt: Which two protocols provide encrypted controller administration when configured with proper identity validation? (Choose two.)
options: HTTPS web access on TCP 443
Telnet CLI access on TCP 23
SSH CLI access on TCP 22
HTTP web access on TCP 80
SNMPv2c access with a community string
questions.explanation: HTTPS and SSH provide protected administration when the server/host identity and configuration are properly validated. This question does not assume a particular controller's factory enabled/disabled defaults.

whyWrong.1: Telnet does not encrypt the administration session.
whyWrong.3: HTTP does not supply TLS protection.
whyWrong.4: A community string does not give SNMPv2c confidentiality.

exhibit.title: Representative Catalyst 9800 configuration review
exhibit.text:
WLAN profile GUEST: enabled, SSID Guest, ID 20
Policy profile PP-GUEST: enabled, VLAN 30
AP1: joined; compatible radio enabled
AP1 effective policy tag: PT-BRANCH
PT-BRANCH entries: CORP → PP-CORP only

questions.prompt: Which configuration change addresses the missing SSID on AP1?
options: Renumber GUEST to ID 1 without checking AP assignments
Create an AireOS dynamic interface on the 9800
Map GUEST to PP-GUEST in AP1's effective policy tag
Move the guest VLAN number into AP1's RF tag
questions.explanation: A 9800 policy tag maps a WLAN profile to its policy profile, and AP1 must receive a tag containing that mapping. The provided radio and enabled-state checks rule out those alternatives.

whyWrong.0: A lower ID does not correct an explicitly missing mapping in this custom tag.
whyWrong.1: AireOS dynamic interfaces are not the 9800 policy-profile model.
whyWrong.3: An RF tag supplies radio policy, not the WLAN-to-client-policy mapping.

exhibit.title: Representative 9800 review
exhibit.text:
ID  Profile  SSID      Status  Security
1   CORP     Corp      UP      [WPA2][802.1X][AES]
2   IOT      IoT-Sens  DOWN    [WPA2][PSK][AES]
AP policy tag includes IOT; compatible radio is operational.
Sensors use WPA2-Personal/AES.

questions.prompt: Which first configuration correction is directly supported for IoT-Sens?
options: Enable the IOT WLAN, then verify its AP advertisement
Change IOT from PSK to Enterprise key management
Replace the IOT cipher with WEP for compatibility
Add every sensor to the controller's administrator list
questions.explanation: The IOT WLAN is administratively down while its intended security is already configured. Enable it, then verify the radio/AP assignment and a client rather than assuming one status change proves end-to-end access.

whyWrong.1: The sensors are configured for a PSK, so Enterprise would not match.
whyWrong.2: The evidence shows a disabled WLAN, not a cipher limitation; WEP is obsolete.
whyWrong.3: Administrator accounts are unrelated to advertising the client WLAN.

questions.prompt: A public hotspot wants radio encryption without asking users for a shared password. Which method fits, while not authenticating the hotspot's identity?
options: WPA2-Personal using a publicly printed shared key
OWE using unauthenticated key establishment
WebAuth terms over an otherwise unencrypted WLAN
A hidden SSID with MAC-address filtering
questions.explanation: OWE supplies encryption without authenticated peer identity or a shared user password. It helps against passive observation but does not replace validation of the destination application's identity.

whyWrong.0: This still requires a shared password and does not match the requirement.
whyWrong.2: A portal alone does not add radio encryption.
whyWrong.3: Neither hiding the name nor filtering a MAC address supplies encryption.

questions.prompt: No AAA override is configured. Which AireOS WLAN field selects the base client interface/VLAN mapping?
options: Security → Layer 2: the PSK checkbox
Advanced: the session-timeout field
QoS: the per-user rate contract
General: the Interface/Interface Group field
questions.explanation: The General interface selection supplies the base mapping to an AireOS logical interface and its VLAN. That VLAN still needs a valid wired path and addressing service.

whyWrong.0: The PSK setting chooses key management, not a client VLAN.
whyWrong.1: A session timer controls client lifetime behavior rather than VLAN selection.
whyWrong.2: A rate contract affects traffic treatment rather than the interface mapping.

questions.prompt: A departing employee knows the single shared key for the staff WPA2-Personal WLAN. Which response addresses future authentication and improves individual revocation?
options: Keep the key because a prior session's PTK has expired
Rotate the shared key and consider per-user Enterprise credentials
Enable SSID hiding while keeping the existing shared key
Enter the same raw PSK in HEX instead of ASCII format
questions.explanation: A person who retains the shared secret can attempt another Personal-mode join. Rotating the key changes that secret; Enterprise supports individual credential lifecycle management, with separate handling needed for active sessions/caches.

whyWrong.0: Fresh session keys do not invalidate knowledge of the shared secret.
whyWrong.2: Hiding the name does not revoke knowledge of the key.
whyWrong.3: Representing the same underlying key differently does not revoke it.

exhibit.title: Controlled test description — representative
exhibit.text:
WPA3 client has completed SAE/key establishment and negotiated PMF.
Forged unprotected deauthentication does not terminate its protected session.
Strong RF interference later prevents successful data reception.

questions.prompt: What does this evidence show about PMF?
options: It protects selected management exchanges but cannot prevent RF jamming
It must encrypt every beacon before a WPA3 client can discover the SSID
It replaces SAE when the radio environment contains interference
It guarantees data forwarding whenever the client retains an IP lease
questions.explanation: PMF protects specified robust management frames after the security relationship is established. Deliberate or accidental RF disruption can still prevent reception; PMF is not an anti-jamming guarantee.

whyWrong.1: PMF does not conceal every beacon or the SSID.
whyWrong.2: PMF and SAE provide different security functions.
whyWrong.3: A retained lease does not guarantee any current radio or data connection.

cards.front: Why is WEP unsuitable for a new WLAN?
cards.back: Its RC4/key/IV design and inadequate integrity protection are obsolete and vulnerable.

cards.front: Which legacy mechanisms identify WPA/TKIP?
cards.back: TKIP uses RC4-based per-packet key mixing and Michael integrity protection; do not choose it for a new WLAN.

cards.front: What is AES-CCMP?
cards.back: AES-based encryption combined with CBC-MAC integrity protection; the normal CCNA WPA2 configuration choice.

cards.front: Does every WPA3 WLAN use SAE and GCMP-256?
cards.back: No. Personal uses SAE; Enterprise uses Enterprise authentication. Personal can use CCMP-128; 192-bit Enterprise has stricter cipher requirements.

cards.front: Cisco WPA2 PSK field lengths: ASCII and HEX?
cards.back: ASCII passphrase: 8–63 characters. Raw HEX PSK: exactly 64 hexadecimal digits. Do not generalize this field rule to every SAE representation.

cards.front: In WPA2-Personal, what contributes to the passphrase-derived PMK?
cards.back: The configured passphrase and SSID. The four-way handshake does not transmit the passphrase as clear text.

cards.front: What does a bad message-2 MIC indicate in a controlled wrong-PSK test?
cards.back: Different derived key material prevents validation. A generic connection popup alone does not identify the exact failed message.

cards.front: Central 802.1X WLAN: supplicant, authenticator, authentication server?
cards.back: Client, WLC and external RADIUS server in the stated central design; other deployment modes can place functions differently.

cards.front: Common RADIUS authentication and accounting ports?
cards.back: UDP 1812 and 1813 respectively; the RADIUS shared secret is separate from client credentials and a WLAN PSK.

cards.front: EAP-TLS versus typical PEAP/MS-CHAPv2?
cards.back: EAP-TLS uses client/server certificates; PEAP/MS-CHAPv2 uses password-based client authentication inside a server-validated tunnel.

cards.front: What does SAE improve over WPA2-PSK key establishment?
cards.back: It is designed to resist passive offline dictionary verification and provide forward secrecy. The four-way handshake still follows.

cards.front: What does PMF protect, and what does it not prevent?
cards.back: Specified robust management frames such as deauthentication/disassociation; not every beacon, RF jamming or all service disruption.

cards.front: What assurance does OWE provide?
cards.back: Radio encryption without a shared user password or authenticated AP identity; application identity checks still matter.

cards.front: A new AireOS WLAN shows 802.1X AKM; how do you make the basic lab PSK-only?
cards.back: Select WPA2/AES, disable 802.1X AKM, enable PSK, set the key and verify. Inspect actual settings rather than assuming defaults.

cards.front: AireOS QoS levels, from voice to background?
cards.back: Platinum: voice; Gold: video; Silver: best effort (documented default); Bronze: background. A profile is not a bandwidth guarantee.

cards.front: A record shows session timeout 1800 and exclusion remaining 45. Meaning?
cards.back: 1800 seconds is 30 minutes of configured session policy; this client has 45 seconds of exclusion remaining. Correlate actual events before blaming either.

cards.front: Which controller administration protocols should you select?
cards.back: HTTPS on TCP 443 and SSH on TCP 22, with proper identity validation and access restrictions. Check actual enabled settings.

cards.front: What links a 9800 WLAN to a client VLAN policy on an AP?
cards.back: The policy tag maps the WLAN profile to a policy profile and must be assigned to the AP. Site/RF tags serve other purposes.

cards.front: What do DHCP_REQD, WEBAUTH_REQD and RUN indicate on AireOS?
cards.back: Addressing wait, portal-authentication wait and admitted forwarding state. RUN does not prove every remote application is reachable.

cards.front: Profile name, SSID and WLAN ID: how do they differ?
cards.back: Controller object name, client-visible network name and internal WLAN identifier. Verify the AP's actual assignment rather than assuming ID alone advertises it.

cards.front: Does Associated alone prove successful WPA2 security?
cards.back: No. Check current key-establishment/admission evidence and then IP/data access; a stale lease can survive a failed new join.
