tickets.title: A Personal WLAN is configured for Enterprise key management
tickets.scenario: Staff clients are configured for WPA2-Personal/AES on CCNA-Lab, with the issued lab passphrase StudyLab-2026!. They can see the SSID but cannot establish a working connection. The site has no external RADIUS server or local EAP configuration. The following are representative records.

exhibits.title: AireOS WLAN 2 security
exhibits.text:
Profile: CCNA-USERS; SSID: CCNA-Lab; enabled
WPA: disabled; WPA2: enabled
AES: enabled; TKIP: disabled
AKM 802.1X: enabled; PSK: disabled

exhibits.title: Authentication services
exhibits.text:
External RADIUS authentication servers: none
Local EAP: disabled

exhibits.title: Client profile
exhibits.text:
SSID: CCNA-Lab
Authentication: WPA2-Personal
Encryption: AES
Shared-key profile configured

tickets.question: Which configuration mismatch is established by these records?
options: The WLAN selected legacy WPA/TKIP instead of WPA2/AES
The WLAN expects 802.1X while clients expect PSK
The client VLAN is missing from an unspecified upstream trunk
The session timeout is expiring before any SSID is visible
tickets.explanation: The WLAN explicitly has 802.1X enabled and PSK disabled while the clients expect Personal key management. WPA2/AES is already correct. The record supports this mismatch without needing to infer an unshown exclusion event or exact handshake failure.
tickets.fix:
In the authorized lab's AireOS-style GUI, disable WLAN 2 while editing. Open Security → Layer 2, disable 802.1X AKM, enable PSK, set ASCII key StudyLab-2026!, retain WPA2/AES with WPA/TKIP off, Apply, then enable the WLAN and Save Configuration. If a client is actually shown excluded, handle only that client's remaining exclusion using the platform's supported procedure.

Start a fresh connection. Verify security/admitted state, intended VLAN/address/gateway and traffic to a known server. Do not conclude that a saved PSK field alone proves recovery.

tickets.title: The wireless client VLAN is absent from the WLC trunk
tickets.scenario: A centrally switched AireOS WLAN moved users to dynamic interface users in VLAN 10. Controller management uses tagged VLAN 99. DHCP proxy is explicitly disabled in this scenario, so client DHCP is bridged into VLAN 10. R1's 10.0.10.0/24 scope and gateway 10.0.10.1 work for a wired test client. The following are representative diagnostics.

exhibits.text:
Current client security event: WPA2 key establishment completed
Client state: DHCP_REQD; current IP: Unknown
WLAN interface users: VLAN 10, 10.0.10.2/24
DHCP proxy: disabled; bridging DHCP to client VLAN
Fresh wireless client requests observed; no lease

exhibits.title: SW1 controller-facing trunk
exhibits.text:
Port: Fa0/24; status trunking; native VLAN 1
VLANs allowed: 99
VLANs allowed and active: 99
VLANs forwarding: 99

exhibits.title: Wired validation
exhibits.text:
VLAN 10 exists and forwards on the R1 uplink
Wired VLAN 10 test client receives 10.0.10.101/24

tickets.question: Which failure is directly supported?
options: The unchanged PSK prevented key establishment for this client
The controller's management VLAN must be changed to VLAN 10
The WLC uplink omits required client VLAN 10
The client needs WebAuth before a DHCP request can be sent
tickets.explanation: Security has completed, but the central client VLAN is absent from the controller uplink's allowed list. In the explicitly stated DHCP-bridging design, VLAN 10's requests and replies cannot cross that link. The successful wired test establishes that the separate VLAN 10 service path exists.
tickets.fix:
On the lab switch add the client VLAN without removing management:

```ios
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/24
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan add 10
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show interfaces trunk
```

Confirm 10,99 are allowed/active/forwarding. Have the wireless client request a fresh lease, then verify its 10.0.10.x/24 address, gateway and server access. Retest controller management. A different DHCP-proxy design requires following that design's server/interface path instead of assuming every request remains an unchanged broadcast.

lab.title: Trace a host uplink and compare routing contexts

steps.title: Build and label the model
steps.body:
Create a new Packet Tracer file, cable the listed ports and enter the four static addresses through Desktop → IP Configuration. Identify the modeled VMs, virtual switch and physical uplink.

:::expected
VM-A/VM-B represent guest vNIC attachments. VSW represents the virtual switch and Gi0/1 its physical uplink. All actual PCs still run Packet Tracer's simulated client, not separate guest operating systems.
:::

steps.title: Configure both ends of the trunk
steps.body:
Start from each new switch's console. These blocks omit PortFast on the interswitch trunk: the model uses a simulated switch that runs STP.

```ios VSW
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname VSW
VSW(config)# vlan 10
VSW(config-vlan)# exit
VSW(config)# vlan 20
VSW(config-vlan)# exit
VSW(config)# vlan 999
VSW(config-vlan)# exit
VSW(config)# interface fastethernet0/1
VSW(config-if)# switchport mode access
VSW(config-if)# switchport access vlan 10
VSW(config-if)# spanning-tree portfast
VSW(config-if)# exit
VSW(config)# interface fastethernet0/2
VSW(config-if)# switchport mode access
VSW(config-if)# switchport access vlan 20
VSW(config-if)# spanning-tree portfast
VSW(config-if)# exit
VSW(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
VSW(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
VSW(config-if)# switchport trunk native vlan 999
VSW(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,999
VSW(config-if)# no shutdown
VSW(config-if)# end
```

```ios SW1
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname SW1
SW1(config)# vlan 10
SW1(config-vlan)# exit
SW1(config)# vlan 20
SW1(config-vlan)# exit
SW1(config)# vlan 999
SW1(config-vlan)# exit
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if)# switchport access vlan 10
SW1(config-if)# spanning-tree portfast
SW1(config-if)# exit
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/2
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if)# switchport access vlan 20
SW1(config-if)# spanning-tree portfast
SW1(config-if)# exit
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk native vlan 999
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,999
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if)# end
```

On both consoles run `show vlan brief` and `show interfaces trunk`.

:::expected
Fa0/1 belongs to VLAN 10 and Fa0/2 to VLAN 20. Gi0/1 is trunking, native VLAN 999, with 10/20/999 allowed at both ends. Wait for STP to forward. VLAN 999 has no endpoint here.
:::

steps.title: Observe successful forwarding
steps.body:
From VM-A run `ping 10.39.10.20`; from VM-B run `ping 10.39.20.20`. Repeat after initial ARP learning.

```ios SW1
SW1# show mac address-table
SW1# show interfaces trunk
```

Use Simulation mode filtered to ARP and ICMP if available. Follow an ARP exchange and the later ICMP exchange.

:::expected
Each same-VLAN pair communicates. SW1 learns VM-A's MAC on Gi0/1 in VLAN 10 and VM-B's in VLAN 20. MAC values differ by simulator file. A ping from VM-A to 10.39.20.20 has no routed path; a shared uplink does not provide inter-VLAN routing.
:::

steps.title: Remove one allowed VLAN and observe
steps.body:
On SW1 only:

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,999
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show interfaces trunk
```

Repeat both same-VLAN pings. Record the difference before repairing.

:::expected
VLAN 10 remains permitted; VLAN 20 cannot traverse this trunk end. Existing MAC entries may remain until aged out, so a stored entry does not establish current reachability.
:::

steps.title: Restore and save
steps.body:
```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,999
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show interfaces trunk
SW1# copy running-config startup-config
```

```ios VSW
VSW# copy running-config startup-config
```

Accept save prompts, repeat both pings and save `host-uplink-baseline.pkt`.

:::expected
Both VLANs pass again. Your record includes baseline, failure and recovery evidence.
:::

steps.title: Optional VRF setup on a supported image
steps.body:
Use a new isolated Cisco CML lab with **one IOSv router** and its console. No external connector, cables or PCs are required. Use your available CML/IOSv entitlement; no public sandbox is required. Start the node and inspect `show version`. Cisco lists VRF-lite among IOSv features; command forms depend on the image.

If `vrf definition` or verification commands are absent, use the supplied outputs as a paper exercise and label it unexecuted. Do not assume a similarly named Packet Tracer router supports VRFs.

```ios R1
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R1
R1(config)# vrf definition BLUE
R1(config-vrf)# address-family ipv4
R1(config-vrf-af)# exit-address-family
R1(config-vrf)# exit
R1(config)# vrf definition RED
R1(config-vrf)# address-family ipv4
R1(config-vrf-af)# exit-address-family
R1(config-vrf)# exit
R1(config)# interface loopback10
R1(config-if)# vrf forwarding BLUE
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.39.0.1 255.255.255.255
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# interface loopback20
R1(config-if)# vrf forwarding RED
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.39.0.1 255.255.255.255
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# interface loopback0
R1(config-if)# ip address 192.0.2.39 255.255.255.255
R1(config-if)# end
```

:::expected
Loopback10 and Loopback20 have the same /32 in different contexts. Loopback0 belongs to the global table. This exercise does not establish remote-host or inter-VRF forwarding.
:::

steps.title: Compare three contexts
steps.body:
```ios R1
R1# show vrf
R1# show ip route
R1# show ip route vrf BLUE
R1# show ip route vrf RED
R1# ping vrf BLUE 10.39.0.1
R1# ping vrf RED 10.39.0.1
```

:::expected
The global table contains 192.0.2.39/32. BLUE and RED each contain 10.39.0.1/32 through different loopbacks. Local pings in each VRF can answer. Representative abbreviated entries:

```output Context comparison
Routing Table: BLUE
C 10.39.0.1/32 is directly connected, Loopback10  ← BLUE's interface
Routing Table: RED
C 10.39.0.1/32 is directly connected, Loopback20   ← RED's interface
```

Exact local/connected presentation varies by release. Ordinary `ping 10.39.0.1` uses the global table, which has no route in this isolated configuration.
:::

steps.title: Observe address removal on reassignment
steps.body:
Move only Loopback10 to RED. Do not restore its address yet:

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface loopback10
R1(config-if)# vrf forwarding RED
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show running-config interface loopback10
R1# show ip route vrf BLUE
```

:::expected
The former IP address is removed on reassignment. BLUE loses its connected /32. RED's existing Loopback20 retains its own address. Changed membership and the missing address identify the injected change.
:::

steps.title: Restore membership and address
steps.body:
```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface loopback10
R1(config-if)# vrf forwarding BLUE
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.39.0.1 255.255.255.255
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show vrf
R1# show ip route vrf BLUE
R1# copy running-config startup-config
```

:::expected
Loopback10 again belongs to BLUE with its /32. Accept the save prompt and retain your CML lab separately.
:::

lab.troubleshooting:
- A peer ping fails: verify addresses, access VLANs, trunk operation and allowed list.
- One VM VLAN works: compare every trunk segment carrying the failed VLAN.
- A global ping fails while a VRF ping succeeds: compare routing contexts before changing routes.
- A command is unsupported: record platform/version and use the interpretation fallback.
lab.challenge:
A real host tags application traffic with VLAN 30 and has a separate untagged management uplink. Which physical port needs VLAN 30, and must the management port be a trunk? Separately, BLUE has no route to 192.0.2.39/32 but the global table does. Can BLUE automatically use that route?

:::expected
Permit tagged VLAN 30 on the application uplink and its downstream path. The separate management uplink can be an access port in its one VLAN. BLUE cannot automatically fall back to the global table; inter-context connectivity requires deliberate configuration.
:::

questions.prompt: Which description identifies a Type 1 hypervisor?
options: Virtualization runs directly over the physical hardware.
Virtualization runs as an application through a host OS.
Application processes share one operating-system kernel.
Routing lookups use separate tables within one router.
questions.explanation: A Type 1 hypervisor supplies virtual hardware directly over the physical platform. Its management tools may still run in an operating-system environment, as with Hyper-V's root partition.

whyWrong.1: A hosted Type 2 hypervisor uses a general-purpose host OS.
whyWrong.2: This describes ordinary process-isolated containers.
whyWrong.3: This describes VRF separation, not server virtualization.

questions.prompt: Which two are examples of hosted Type 2 hypervisors? Choose two.
options: VMware Workstation
VMware ESXi
Microsoft Hyper-V
Kubernetes
Oracle VirtualBox
questions.explanation: VirtualBox and Workstation are familiar hosted hypervisors. Product names are useful examples, but the defining distinction is the role of the host operating system.

whyWrong.1: ESXi is a Type 1 hypervisor.
whyWrong.2: Hyper-V uses a Type 1 architecture despite its Windows management environment.
whyWrong.3: Kubernetes orchestrates containers; it is not a hosted hypervisor.

questions.prompt: Why can ordinary process-isolated containers start with less overhead than full VMs?
options: They obtain a dedicated physical processor for each instance.
They bypass IP and Ethernet when communicating externally.
They start processes using the existing host-environment kernel.
They boot a separate guest kernel with fewer network drivers.
questions.explanation: Containers do not need to boot a complete guest OS for each instance. Actual startup time depends on the image, workload and platform; there is no universal seconds-per-container limit.

whyWrong.0: Dedicated physical processors are not a defining container feature.
whyWrong.1: Container traffic still uses the selected network stack and connectivity.
whyWrong.3: An independent guest-kernel boot is characteristic of a VM.

questions.prompt: A documented hypervisor uplink carries tagged VLANs 10 and 20. What is consistent with these stable entries?
options: The same source is repeatedly moving between switch ports.
SW1 has proved both guests use the correct default gateway.
The port is necessarily an access port with a voice VLAN.
Two guest vNIC sources reach SW1 through the host uplink.
questions.explanation: A virtual switch can forward different guest sources through one physical NIC. Learning their MACs in separate VLANs is expected, but it does not prove application connectivity.

whyWrong.0: The exhibit has distinct MACs on one port, not a source moving between ports.
whyWrong.1: A MAC table does not validate guest IP settings or gateway reachability.
whyWrong.2: The scenario specifies tagged VLANs on a trunked host uplink.

exhibit.title: Representative SW1 MAC table
exhibit.text:
Vlan  Mac Address       Type     Ports
10    0200.0000.0010    DYNAMIC  Gi0/1
20    0200.0000.0020    DYNAMIC  Gi0/1

questions.prompt: A host tags guest VLANs 10, 20 and 30; untagged traffic is deliberately assigned to unused VLAN 999. Which physical-port design matches?
options: A trunk allowing 10,20,30,999 with native VLAN 999.
An access port in VLAN 10 with native VLAN 999.
A routed port with one secondary address per guest.
A trunk allowing 10,20,999 with native VLAN 30.
questions.explanation: A trunk must permit the guest VLANs and agree with the host's treatment of untagged traffic. The physical port configuration follows the supplied host design, rather than a rule that every server requires a trunk.

whyWrong.1: An access port does not implement the stated multi-VLAN trunk design.
whyWrong.2: A routed interface does not terminate those VLANs without an appropriate subinterface design.
whyWrong.3: This excludes tagged VLAN 30 and changes the untagged VLAN mapping.

questions.prompt: Which two statements describe VRFs? Choose two.
options: Each VRF provides a separate routing/forwarding context.
Identical prefixes can exist in different VRF tables.
Each VRF encrypts packets using its routing-table key.
One routed interface belongs to every VRF by default.
A failed lookup automatically searches the global table.
questions.explanation: VRFs distinguish traffic and routes by context, allowing overlapping address space. They do not provide automatic inter-context routing or confidentiality.

whyWrong.2: VRF separation does not provide encryption.
whyWrong.3: A routed interface has one routing context; separate subinterfaces can use separate VRFs.
whyWrong.4: The lookup stays in its context unless deliberate connectivity is configured.

questions.prompt: R1's ordinary console ping to 10.10.10.20 fails. Which exhibit fact explains the local route-lookup problem?
options: The RED interface must be down because its address is duplicated.
The BLUE route has a lower metric and overrides RED's route.
ICMP requires a separate routing process inside the RED VRF.
The destination exists in RED, while the ping uses the global table.
questions.explanation: The ordinary ping consults the global routing table, which has no matching route. A VRF-aware ping tests RED's path; its eventual success still depends on the host and return path.

whyWrong.0: The stated interface is up/up and separate contexts permit overlap.
whyWrong.1: Routes in separate VRFs do not compete in a single lookup.
whyWrong.2: Connected reachability inside a VRF does not require a special ICMP routing process.

exhibit.title: Complete relevant state
exhibit.text:
Gi0/2: up/up, VRF RED, 10.10.10.1/24
Global routing table: no routes
RED: C 10.10.10.0/24 via Gi0/2
Host 10.10.10.20/24 is attached behind Gi0/2.

questions.prompt: After this supported IOS interface reassignment, what restores its intended IPv4 address?
options: Add a global default route toward the interface.
Remove BLUE's IPv4 address-family configuration.
Reload so the old interface address is recovered.
questions.explanation: IOS removes an interface's existing IP address when its VRF association changes. Configure the intended VRF first and then the address.

whyWrong.0: A route cannot substitute for the missing interface address.
whyWrong.2: Removing the address family does not restore the address.
whyWrong.3: The address was removed from running configuration; a reload is not the required repair.

exhibit.title: Representative IOS observation
exhibit.text:
Gi0/1 was up/up with 10.10.10.1/24.
Command: vrf forwarding BLUE
IOS reports that IPv4 addressing was removed.
Current Gi0/1 configuration: vrf forwarding BLUE; no ip address

questions.prompt: On an image using multiprotocol vrf definition BLUE, which interface command assigns its routing context?
options: vrf forwarding BLUE
vrf definition BLUE
address-family ipv4
ip route vrf BLUE
questions.explanation: The documented multiprotocol interface form is vrf forwarding BLUE. The legacy ip vrf form is separate optional reference, not a reason to guess syntax across platforms.

whyWrong.1: This creates/enters a VRF definition in global mode.
whyWrong.2: This enters the VRF address-family submode.
whyWrong.3: This begins a static-route command, not interface membership.

questions.prompt: Which comparison between VLANs and VRFs is correct?
options: VLANs separate routing tables; VRFs separate Ethernet broadcasts.
VLANs encrypt tagged frames; VRFs encrypt routed packets.
VLANs require a guest OS; VRFs require a separate hypervisor.
VLANs separate Layer 2 domains; VRFs separate Layer 3 contexts.
questions.explanation: A VLAN defines an Ethernet broadcast domain. A VRF selects a separate routing/forwarding table, and an SVI for a VLAN can belong to a VRF.

whyWrong.0: The two functions are reversed.
whyWrong.1: Neither construct by itself provides encryption.
whyWrong.2: Neither requires server virtualization.

questions.prompt: A packet enters RED for 172.16.1.10. No leaking or policy routing is configured. What does R1 do?
options: Uses the global default after RED's lookup fails.
Changes the packet's source to BLUE's gateway address.
Drops it because RED has no matching route.
Uses BLUE's connected route because it is more specific.
questions.explanation: The ingress context is RED, and its table has no route to the destination. The existence of matching routes in other tables does not make them usable.

whyWrong.0: There is no automatic global-table fallback.
whyWrong.1: VRF membership does not invoke NAT.
whyWrong.3: BLUE's route is not a candidate in RED's lookup.

exhibit.title: Complete routing-context summary
exhibit.text:
RED: 10.10.10.0/24 connected; no other routes
BLUE: 172.16.1.0/24 connected
Global: 0.0.0.0/0 via 192.0.2.1

questions.prompt: A customer rents VMs and manages their guest operating systems and applications. Which service model fits?
options: Community cloud deployment
Infrastructure as a service
Platform as a service
Software as a service
questions.explanation: IaaS supplies infrastructure resources while the customer manages the guest OS and application stack. Service model and deployment model describe different dimensions.

whyWrong.0: Community identifies a deployment arrangement, not the supplied service layer.
whyWrong.2: PaaS provides a managed application platform rather than requiring the customer to manage ordinary guest OSs.
whyWrong.3: SaaS provides a finished application.

questions.prompt: Policy requires a campus-to-cloud path that avoids the public internet. Which option meets that path requirement?
options: A private provider connection with the appropriate service agreement.
A site-to-site IPsec VPN over the existing public internet circuit.
A remote-access VPN from each server over public broadband.
An HTTPS session to the cloud application's public address.
questions.explanation: A private connection can satisfy the transport requirement. Encryption, latency and availability still need separate design and contractual verification.

whyWrong.1: IPsec protects traffic but does not change the public-internet transport.
whyWrong.2: A remote-access VPN still uses the stated public transport.
whyWrong.3: HTTPS protects an application exchange but does not supply a private network path.

questions.prompt: Which two commands on the documented IOS image directly list VRF interface membership? Choose two.
options: show ip interface brief
show ip ospf neighbor
show vrf
show ip vrf interfaces
show ip route
questions.explanation: The VRF summary and VRF-interface view identify the context of each member interface. Use the command forms supported by the selected image.

whyWrong.0: The ordinary brief IP view does not directly name the VRF.
whyWrong.1: OSPF neighbor output does not list every VRF interface.
whyWrong.4: The global routing table is not the VRF membership inventory.

questions.prompt: A private cloud and a public cloud are connected so one application can use capacity in both. Which deployment model fits?
options: Private cloud only
Software as a service
Hybrid cloud
Community cloud
questions.explanation: A hybrid deployment combines distinct cloud infrastructures with integration between them. Merely using unrelated services in two places would not demonstrate that integration.

whyWrong.0: The arrangement explicitly integrates private and public environments.
whyWrong.1: SaaS is a service model, not this deployment classification.
whyWrong.3: Community serves organizations with shared requirements; it does not describe this combination.

questions.prompt: Two redundant application VMs run on one host and use its only physical NIC. Which failure remains shared?
options: Removal of a file held only on one guest's disk.
Loss of that host or its physical uplink.
A restart confined to one guest's application.
A guest-only change to one VM's desktop settings.
questions.explanation: Both VMs depend on the same host and uplink. Redundancy must account for shared hardware, power, storage and network paths.

whyWrong.0: A file confined to one guest is not the host-wide failure identified here.
whyWrong.2: An isolated application restart need not affect the other VM.
whyWrong.3: A guest-only setting is not the common physical dependency.

cards.front: What distinguishes a Type 1 hypervisor?
cards.back: It supplies virtualization directly over hardware; ESXi and Hyper-V are examples.

cards.front: What distinguishes a Type 2 hypervisor?
cards.back: It operates through a general-purpose host OS; VirtualBox and Workstation are examples.

cards.front: How do a VM and an ordinary process-isolated container differ?
cards.back: The VM has its own guest kernel; the container shares its host environment's kernel.

cards.front: Container image versus running container?
cards.back: The image packages files/dependencies; a container is an instance with processes and a writable layer.

cards.front: Docker versus Kubernetes?
cards.back: Docker supplies container tooling; Kubernetes orchestrates workloads across a cluster.

cards.front: What do Linux namespaces and resource controls provide?
cards.back: Separate views of resources and limits on consumption; they do not create a guest kernel.

cards.front: Why do containers often have less startup overhead than VMs?
cards.back: Ordinary containers start processes without booting a separate guest OS; actual timing varies.

cards.front: What does a virtual switch connect?
cards.back: VM vNICs to other virtual ports and configured physical uplinks.

cards.front: When does a physical host uplink need a trunk?
cards.back: When its design carries multiple tagged VLANs; match allowed VLANs and untagged/native handling.

cards.front: Do several stable MACs on a host port prove virtualization?
cards.back: No. They are consistent with a virtual switch but also with other bridged arrangements.

cards.front: What does a VRF separate?
cards.back: Layer 3 routing/forwarding contexts and their interface membership; not encryption keys.

cards.front: VLAN versus VRF?
cards.back: VLAN: Layer 2 broadcast domain. VRF: Layer 3 routing context. An SVI can belong to a VRF.

cards.front: Multiprotocol IOS VRF definition and interface membership?
cards.back: vrf definition BLUE, address-family ipv4; then vrf forwarding BLUE on the interface.

cards.front: Legacy IPv4 IOS VRF command forms?
cards.back: ip vrf BLUE and interface ip vrf forwarding BLUE; optional reference, image-dependent.

cards.front: What happens when an addressed IOS interface changes VRF?
cards.back: Its IP address is removed; configure the VRF first and then restore the intended address.

cards.front: View BLUE's IPv4 routing table?
cards.back: show ip route vrf BLUE; plain show ip route examines the global table.

cards.front: List VRF interface membership on a supporting IOS image?
cards.back: show vrf or show ip vrf interfaces.

cards.front: How do an IOS ping and static route select BLUE?
cards.back: ping vrf BLUE 10.10.10.10; ip route vrf BLUE followed by the destination and next hop.

cards.front: What does VRF-lite mean?
cards.back: VRF separation without requiring MPLS transport; an isolated lab needs no MPLS VPN design.

cards.front: IaaS, PaaS and SaaS distinguish what?
cards.back: Customer/provider responsibility: infrastructure resources, application platform or finished application.

tickets.title: BLUE has no route beyond its connected networks
tickets.scenario: R1's BLUE interfaces are Gi0/1 10.10.10.1/24 and Gi0/3 198.51.100.2/30. The isolated global table has no connected networks. BLUE can ping its next hop 198.51.100.1. An approved default route was recently added, but BLUE still has no route to a remote service.

exhibits.title: Representative route/context evidence
exhibits.text:
BLUE: C 10.10.10.0/24 via Gi0/1
BLUE: C 198.51.100.0/30 via Gi0/3
BLUE: Gateway of last resort is not set
Running config: ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 198.51.100.1

tickets.question: Which local configuration error does this evidence establish?
options: The BLUE WAN interface needs a route distinguisher.
The static route was configured for the global context.
The router must encrypt the default route before using it.
The BLUE connected subnet has the wrong /30 prefix.
tickets.explanation: The route lacks vrf BLUE, while BLUE's table has only connected routes. The successful BLUE next-hop test also contradicts a simple loss of that adjacency. Correct the context and then verify the remote service and return path; a new route alone does not prove end-to-end recovery.
tickets.fix:
```ios
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# no ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 198.51.100.1
R1(config)# ip route vrf BLUE 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 198.51.100.1
R1(config)# end
R1# show ip route vrf BLUE
```
Repeat a BLUE-sourced service test and verify the far-end return route.

tickets.title: Only one guest VLAN crosses the host uplink
tickets.scenario: A host sends VLANs 10 and 20 tagged through its sole uplink to SW1 Gi0/1. Both VLANs exist on SW1 and their remote gateways respond from other access ports. No port-security policy is configured. VLAN 10 guests work; VLAN 20 guests do not.

exhibits.title: Representative SW1 trunk configuration
exhibits.text:
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 switchport mode trunk
 switchport trunk native vlan 999
 switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,999
Operational status: trunking

tickets.question: Which change addresses the demonstrated mismatch?
options: Enable guest tagging with the reserved VLAN ID 4095.
Move the working VLAN 10 guests to untagged traffic.
Add VLAN 20 to the physical trunk's allowed list.
Replace the physical trunk with an access port in VLAN 20.
tickets.explanation: The host transmits VLAN 20 tags, but the physical trunk explicitly excludes VLAN 20. The provided evidence rules out missing VLAN creation and configured port security. Reintroduce the VLAN and verify the host-to-gateway path in both VLANs.
tickets.fix:
```ios
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan add 20
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show interfaces trunk
SW1# show mac address-table
```
Generate fresh traffic from a VLAN 20 guest and check gateway reachability.

lab.title: Separate management access from forwarding
lab.intro: Build routed connectivity, observe OSPF and forwarding, then deliberately block one management session while leaving transit traffic working. Finish by classifying controller and overlay scenarios on paper. This lab does not emulate an SDN controller, VXLAN, NETCONF or RESTCONF. All displayed sample outputs are representative, not recorded device results.

steps.title: Configure addresses and baseline routing
steps.body:
Create a new file and configure the PCs through Desktop → IP Configuration. Enter these blocks on the fresh routers:

```ios R1
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R1
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.1.1.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.0.12.1 255.255.255.252
R1(config-if)# ip ospf network point-to-point
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# router ospf 1
R1(config-router)# router-id 1.1.1.1
R1(config-router)# passive-interface default
R1(config-router)# no passive-interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-router)# network 10.0.12.1 0.0.0.0 area 0
R1(config-router)# network 10.1.1.1 0.0.0.0 area 0
R1(config-router)# end
```

```ios R2
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R2
R2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R2(config-if)# ip address 10.2.2.1 255.255.255.0
R2(config-if)# no shutdown
R2(config-if)# exit
R2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R2(config-if)# ip address 10.0.12.2 255.255.255.252
R2(config-if)# ip ospf network point-to-point
R2(config-if)# no shutdown
R2(config-if)# exit
R2(config)# router ospf 1
R2(config-router)# router-id 2.2.2.2
R2(config-router)# passive-interface default
R2(config-router)# no passive-interface gigabitethernet0/0
R2(config-router)# network 10.0.12.2 0.0.0.0 area 0
R2(config-router)# network 10.2.2.1 0.0.0.0 area 0
R2(config-router)# end
```

:::expected
Both used physical interfaces are up/up. OSPF becomes FULL over the point-to-point link; no DR/BDR election is required on that link. The LANs are advertised but do not send OSPF hellos. If the point-to-point command is unavailable, use broadcast at both ends and interpret its DR/BDR role instead; record the variation.
:::

steps.title: Read control and forwarding evidence
steps.body:
```ios R1
R1# show ip ospf neighbor
R1# show ip route ospf
R1# show ip cef 10.2.2.10
```

```ios R2
R2# show ip ospf neighbor
R2# show ip route ospf
```

:::expected
R1 has a route to 10.2.2.0/24 via 10.0.12.2; R2 has the return route to 10.1.1.0/24 via 10.0.12.1. With the default reference bandwidth and these Gigabit interfaces, the expected OSPF path cost to the remote LAN is 2. The FULL adjacency concerns database synchronization, not proof of every application path. If PT lacks the CEF view, read the route and record that direct FIB inspection is unavailable.
:::

steps.title: Observe transit traffic
steps.body:
From PC-A's command window:

```text
ping 10.2.2.10
```

Repeat after ARP learning. Record router interface counters before and after several attempts using `show interfaces gigabitethernet0/0`. In Simulation mode, filter ICMP and follow the packets through both routers.

:::expected
The PCs can communicate in both directions. Routers forward transit ICMP using installed information; they do not invoke a new OSPF calculation per echo. Counters include other traffic as well, so their total increase is not necessarily the exact number of your pings.
:::

steps.title: Establish an SSH management checkpoint
steps.body:
On R2's console, generate keys only on this new isolated device. If prompted for a modulus, choose 2048:

```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# ip domain name ccna.example
R2(config)# username observer privilege 15 secret Lab-Observer-2026!
R2(config)# crypto key generate rsa modulus 2048
R2(config)# ip ssh version 2
R2(config)# line vty 0 4
R2(config-line)# login local
R2(config-line)# transport input ssh
R2(config-line)# end
R2# show ip ssh
```

If the model exposes VTY 5–15, apply the same `login local` and `transport input ssh` settings to that range too. Inspect `show running-config` to determine the available ranges. If the one-line RSA command is rejected, enter `crypto key generate rsa` and answer its modulus prompt.

From PC-A:

```text
ssh -l observer 10.2.2.1
```

Enter the fictional password at its prompt. On R2's console use `show users`; then type `exit` in the PC's SSH session.

:::expected
The VTY session identifies observer and source 10.1.1.10. R2 is the management endpoint; R1 forwards the same packets as transit traffic. This is a simulator exercise, not a claim to have verified production SSH host identity.
:::

steps.title: Block the management source and observe
steps.body:
Apply this deliberately restrictive VTY ACL from R2's still-open console. Include VTY 5–15 only if that range exists.

```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# ip access-list standard LAB-MGMT
R2(config-std-nacl)# 10 permit host 10.2.2.10
R2(config-std-nacl)# 20 deny any
R2(config-std-nacl)# exit
R2(config)# line vty 0 4
R2(config-line)# access-class LAB-MGMT in
R2(config-line)# end
```

Repeat the same ACL attachment on any existing VTY 5–15 range. Attempt a **new** PC-A SSH session. Separately ping PC-B and inspect OSPF neighbors.

:::expected
PC-A's source 10.1.1.10 is denied by the VTY ACL. Transit pings still work and OSPF remains FULL. This ACL applies to management access, not the routers' transit interfaces. If SSH still works, confirm that you opened a new session and covered every usable VTY range.
:::

steps.title: Restore authorized management access
steps.body:
Add PC-A before the explicit deny:

```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# ip access-list standard LAB-MGMT
R2(config-std-nacl)# 15 permit host 10.1.1.10
R2(config-std-nacl)# end
R2# show access-lists LAB-MGMT
```

Open a fresh SSH session and repeat the transit ping. Close the SSH session afterwards.

:::expected
PC-A now matches the permit at sequence 15. Management access and transit forwarding both work. Counter changes can support the test, but cumulative counters alone do not identify the source of every packet.
:::

steps.title: Identify drift before changing anything
steps.body:
On paper, the approved description for R2 Gi0/1 is exactly `Branch-B LAN`. Read:

```ios R2
R2# show running-config interface gigabitethernet0/1
```

If PT rejects that form, read the full running configuration and locate the interface stanza. Identify the smallest change needed. This is a harmless metadata example, not a claim to have run an automation engine.

:::expected
The fresh interface has no description, so it differs from approved intent. Existing addresses, OSPF and interface state already match the required network; changing them would be unnecessary.
:::

steps.title: Apply and verify the intended metadata
steps.body:
```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R2(config-if)# description Branch-B LAN
R2(config-if)# end
R2# show interfaces description
```

Use the full running configuration if the description summary is unavailable. Explain what a second comparison should report.

:::expected
The description matches and no further description change is needed. Reapplying the identical desired description has the same intended result; this illustrates idempotence. It does not establish that every arbitrary script is idempotent.
:::

steps.title: Map the architecture on paper
steps.body:
Draw an inventory application, controller and two managed switches. Label application/controller communication northbound and controller/device communication southbound. Then draw an inner 1500-byte IPv4 packet carried in an untagged inner Ethernet frame through VXLAN over outer IPv4.

Calculate the outer IP packet size using inner Ethernet 14, VXLAN 8, UDP 8 and outer IPv4 20 bytes. Identify which addresses an intermediate router uses. Finally explain what you can conclude when a management controller becomes unavailable but one existing user flow still works.

:::expected
Outer IP length is 1500 + 14 + 8 + 8 + 20 = 1550 bytes. The intermediate router uses the outer destination. The working flow proves that particular forwarding path still works at that moment; it does not prove new endpoint discovery, authentication or later convergence. No VXLAN packets were generated by this Packet Tracer lab.
:::

steps.title: Save the verified configuration
steps.body:
```ios R1
R1# copy running-config startup-config
```

```ios R2
R2# copy running-config startup-config
```

Accept the filename prompts. Save `management-planes-baseline.pkt` with a short record of each successful and failed test.

:::expected
The saved design includes both authorized management sources, correct routing and the intended description. Neither router exposes a NETCONF or RESTCONF server as part of this lab.
:::

lab.troubleshooting:
- OSPF fails: check the exact transit addresses, interface status, matching network type and area.
- Pings fail: check both PC gateways and both route tables before assuming an ACL fault.
- SSH fails after the ACL repair: inspect VTY ranges, sequence order, actual source address, keys and local login.
- A controller is unreachable in a real network: inspect its documented management protocols; a user ping tests a different service.
lab.challenge:
A cloud-hosted controller receives a reviewed policy from an automation pipeline. Describe which management approaches overlap. The device configuration then matches the policy, but a required application test fails. What additional evidence is needed before the change can be considered complete?

:::expected
The workflow is cloud-based, controller-based and automation-based; it also exemplifies IaC if the reviewed versioned definitions represent managed infrastructure intent. Configuration agreement alone does not prove service health. Check the relevant route/return path, policy decisions, application endpoints and current operational observations, then compare against the acceptance criteria.
:::

questions.prompt: Which functions learned this route and forward a transit packet using it?
options: OSPF supplies control information; the data plane forwards the packet.
The data plane computes OSPF routes; SSH forwards each packet.
The management plane learns the route; OSPF forwards each packet.
OSPF selects a new path separately for each transit packet.
questions.explanation: OSPF exchanges routing information and computes reachability. The forwarding function uses installed entries; whether that function runs in hardware or software depends on the platform.

whyWrong.1: OSPF is a control-plane protocol, while SSH provides management access.
whyWrong.2: SSH is not the source of this OSPF route.
whyWrong.3: Forwarding uses installed information rather than a new OSPF calculation for every packet.

questions.prompt: Which switch activity is a management-plane function?
options: Calculating the STP role for a redundant link.
Forwarding a received frame toward its destination.
Dropping transit traffic against an installed ACL.
Answering an SNMP request for interface counters.
questions.explanation: The SNMP exchange lets a management system inspect device state. A function is classified by its purpose, not merely by whether a CPU is involved.

whyWrong.0: STP role calculation is a control-plane function.
whyWrong.1: Frame forwarding is a data-plane function.
whyWrong.2: Applying an ACL to transit traffic is a data-plane function.

questions.prompt: Which two are data-plane functions? Choose two.
options: Exchanging OSPF link-state advertisements.
Retrieving interface statistics through an API.
Accepting a network administrator's SSH login.
Adding a VLAN tag while forwarding a frame.
Applying a configured ACL to a transit packet.
questions.explanation: The forwarding path processes transit frames and packets using existing forwarding and policy information. Tag insertion and ACL matching are per-traffic operations.

whyWrong.0: OSPF exchanges establish control information.
whyWrong.1: An API statistics query performs monitoring.
whyWrong.2: SSH administration terminates a management session.

questions.prompt: An application reads inventory from a controller over HTTPS. The controller manages switches using NETCONF. Which mapping is correct?
options: Both are southbound because each crosses physical network links.
Application/controller is northbound; controller/switch is southbound.
Application/controller is southbound; controller/switch is northbound.
Both are northbound because each retrieves structured information.
questions.explanation: Direction is relative to the controller's role in the architecture. HTTPS can also appear in a device-facing interface; protocol name alone is insufficient.

whyWrong.0: Physical location and transport do not define northbound/southbound.
whyWrong.2: The application-facing and infrastructure-facing roles are reversed.
whyWrong.3: Data format does not determine interface direction.

questions.prompt: Which labels complete the two interfaces?
options: A northbound; B southbound.
A southbound; B northbound.
A data plane; B underlay.
A overlay; B management plane.
questions.explanation: Applications consume the controller's northbound services. The controller communicates with managed devices through southbound interfaces.

whyWrong.1: This reverses the roles in the supplied sequence.
whyWrong.2: Planes and transport layers do not label these application interfaces.
whyWrong.3: An overlay is logical connectivity, not the application/controller interface.

exhibit.title: Architecture order
exhibit.text:
Inventory application
  interface A
Controller
  interface B
Managed routers and switches

questions.prompt: Which comparison is accurate?
options: Traditional control requires hand typing; controllers provide software automation.
Traditional devices hold no topology state; controllers store every forwarding table.
Traditional forwarding uses CPUs; controller-based forwarding always uses ASICs.
Traditional device control can be automated; controllers coordinate network-wide functions.
questions.explanation: A controller can centralize policy or coordination without eliminating every device protocol. Automation is possible with or without a controller.

whyWrong.0: Scripts can automate traditional devices through their management interfaces.
whyWrong.1: Distributed routing protocols maintain topology/reachability state on devices.
whyWrong.2: Implementation hardware does not define the management architecture.

questions.prompt: What does this application response establish?
options: The current endpoint data path is healthy because reachability says Reachable.
The controller forwarded a user packet to determine the software version.
The controller API returned a stored inventory observation in JSON.
The switch has just completed a direct NETCONF query from the application.
questions.explanation: The application received structured inventory data from the controller. The collection timestamp limits conclusions about current device state.

whyWrong.0: The supplied timestamp makes freshness relevant, and management status is not an application test.
whyWrong.1: An inventory representation does not imply user packets traverse the controller.
whyWrong.3: The participants and endpoint are an application and controller; no direct device NETCONF exchange is shown.

exhibit.title: Representative controller response
exhibit.text:
GET /inventory
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
{"device":"SW1","reachability":"Reachable","collectedAt":"2026-09-20T08:00:00Z"}
Current time: 2026-09-20T09:00:00Z

questions.prompt: In the SD-Access example, which technology encapsulates user traffic for overlay forwarding?
options: NETCONF
VXLAN
LISP
SNMP
questions.explanation: VXLAN carries the inner traffic across the underlay. The example distinguishes the data-plane encapsulation from endpoint-location control and management protocols.

whyWrong.0: NETCONF is a configuration/management protocol.
whyWrong.2: LISP provides endpoint/location control information in this design.
whyWrong.3: SNMP supplies management observations.

questions.prompt: Which two SD-Access role descriptions are correct? Choose two.
options: Catalyst Center acts as the transit router for every fabric flow.
Edge nodes are the workstations running controller applications.
Border nodes connect the fabric to external networks.
Control-plane nodes maintain endpoint/location information.
Intermediate nodes must terminate every endpoint's VXLAN tunnel.
questions.explanation: These role names identify separate responsibilities. The management controller and a fabric control-plane node are not interchangeable names for the same function.

whyWrong.0: Catalyst Center manages the system; it is not an ordinary user-traffic transit hop.
whyWrong.1: Edge nodes are infrastructure that attaches endpoints.
whyWrong.4: Intermediate nodes provide underlay transport rather than terminating each overlay flow.

questions.prompt: All overlays between A and B fail, while paths to C still work. Which is the best first shared-dependency check?
options: Replace every affected endpoint's IP address with a different subnet.
Refresh the application's northbound inventory token before testing traffic.
Delete all virtual networks and recreate their segmentation identifiers.
Check underlay routes, bidirectional reachability and usable MTU between A and B.
questions.explanation: A shared underlay path is a reasonable first investigation because multiple overlays depend on it. The symptom does not prove the underlay is the cause; tests must establish which dependency failed.

whyWrong.0: Changing every endpoint is broad and unsupported by the shared-path symptom.
whyWrong.1: An inventory token is a management credential, not evidence of a forwarding fault.
whyWrong.2: Rebuilding logical networks is disruptive and precedes basic evidence gathering.

exhibit.title: Observed reachability matrix
exhibit.text:
A ↔ B: all tested virtual networks fail
A ↔ C: tested virtual networks work
B ↔ C: tested virtual networks work
No route, MTU or policy checks have yet been performed.

questions.prompt: The vendor hosts the management service in its cloud. Devices use that service for configuration, while the described user traffic is locally forwarded. Which label directly describes the hosting arrangement?
options: An on-premises management service
Infrastructure as code by definition
Cloud-based management
Device-only management
questions.explanation: Cloud-based identifies the management service's hosting arrangement. The service can also be controller-based or used by automation; the approaches overlap.

whyWrong.0: The service location is explicitly off premises in the vendor cloud.
whyWrong.1: No versioned infrastructure definitions or reviewed code workflow are specified.
whyWrong.3: The service is hosted centrally in the vendor cloud, not only on each device.

questions.prompt: Which workflow best illustrates infrastructure as code?
options: Accept discovered device settings as approved intent automatically.
Review versioned infrastructure definitions and apply them with a tool.
Keep nightly device backups without defining an approved target.
Manually paste a template without recording its intended scope.
questions.explanation: IaC applies software-style practices to infrastructure definitions and changes. A plan and post-change tests are still needed; a repository does not guarantee safe behavior.

whyWrong.0: Discovery does not automatically approve whatever configuration it finds.
whyWrong.2: A backup records observed state but does not by itself define desired state.
whyWrong.3: Manual repetition alone does not establish a versioned code workflow.

questions.prompt: Approved intent requires exactly NTP servers 10.200.0.10 and .11. What is the smallest configuration correction?
options: Remove both current servers, then add 10.200.0.11.
Keep both servers and add 10.200.0.11 as a third.
Change the approved record to match the device.
questions.explanation: Preserve the matching .10 entry, replace the unintended .19 with .11 and compare again. Separately verify NTP operation; configuration agreement alone does not prove synchronization.

whyWrong.1: The correct .10 server need not be removed.
whyWrong.2: The intended set is exact, so leaving .19 preserves drift.
whyWrong.3: Observed state does not automatically override approved intent.

exhibit.title: Representative current configuration
exhibit.text:
ntp server 10.200.0.10
ntp server 10.200.0.19

questions.prompt: Which Catalyst SD-WAN component supplies the onboarding/orchestration role formerly named vBond?
options: SD-WAN Manager
SD-WAN Controller
WAN Edge router
SD-WAN Validator
questions.explanation: The Validator helps orchestrate onboarding and discovery of the other services. Recognize this as a product example of separated responsibilities rather than a configuration objective.

whyWrong.0: Manager supplies management workflows.
whyWrong.1: Controller supplies control-plane services.
whyWrong.2: The edge forwards traffic and joins the system.

questions.prompt: Which statement accurately describes Cisco ACI at this chapter's scope?
options: An APIC outage proves all future endpoint changes remain unaffected.
OpFlex is the mandatory protocol for every APIC-to-physical-switch message.
APIC manages fabric policy while switches forward application traffic.
APIC forwards each application packet before it reaches a leaf switch.
questions.explanation: ACI separates policy management from forwarding. The generic architectural distinction is more useful here than unsupported universal protocol or failure claims.

whyWrong.0: Outage impact must be assessed against the affected services and retained state.
whyWrong.1: OpFlex has specific integration uses; the blanket claim is not correct.
whyWrong.3: APIC is not the ordinary transit path for application traffic.

questions.prompt: A cloud-hosted controller is updated by a script using versioned, reviewed desired-state files. Which conclusion follows?
options: Automation removes the need to verify operational results.
Cloud, controller, automation and IaC approaches can overlap.
Cloud management excludes infrastructure-as-code workflows.
Controller-based management must move to an on-premises appliance.
questions.explanation: These labels describe different dimensions of the workflow. Hosting, coordination, execution and change discipline can all apply to the same system.

whyWrong.0: Operational verification remains necessary after automation.
whyWrong.2: IaC can use cloud APIs and controllers.
whyWrong.3: Controller describes coordination, not a required physical location.

cards.front: Control plane, data plane and management plane?
cards.back: Establish forwarding information; forward traffic; configure and monitor the system.

cards.front: Name two clear control-plane operations.
cards.back: Forming an OSPF adjacency and selecting an STP port role.

cards.front: Name three data-plane operations.
cards.back: Destination lookup, VLAN tag processing and applying an ACL to transit traffic.

cards.front: Name management protocols and their common transports.
cards.back: SSH TCP 22; SNMP UDP 161/162; NETCONF over SSH TCP 830; HTTPS usually TCP 443.

cards.front: Must data-plane forwarding occur in a hardware ASIC?
cards.back: No. Physical switches often accelerate it; virtual routers can forward in software.

cards.front: What does controller-based networking centralize?
cards.back: Some combination of network policy, management or control; device forwarding and protocols may remain distributed.

cards.front: Common SDN layers, bottom to top?
cards.back: Infrastructure, controller and applications.

cards.front: What is the northbound interface?
cards.back: The application-facing controller interface, often a REST API.

cards.front: What is the southbound interface?
cards.back: The controller's interface to infrastructure, using supported protocols such as NETCONF, RESTCONF or SSH.

cards.front: NETCONF versus RESTCONF at recognition level?
cards.back: NETCONF commonly uses SSH/XML RPCs; RESTCONF uses HTTP mechanisms with YANG-modeled JSON or XML.

cards.front: OpenFlow versus OpFlex, at recognition level?
cards.back: OpenFlow programs flow behavior; OpFlex distributes declarative policy in supported integrations.

cards.front: Does one enable command prove a device API is usable?
cards.back: No. Platform support, authentication, transport, authorization and an actual request must be verified.

cards.front: Underlay, overlay and fabric?
cards.back: Underlay supplies transport; overlay supplies logical connectivity; fabric names an integrated system or product-specific overlay.

cards.front: VXLAN's usual destination port and identifier size?
cards.back: UDP 4789; a 24-bit VNI. Encapsulation does not encrypt the payload.

cards.front: SD-Access management, endpoint control and forwarding examples?
cards.back: Catalyst Center management, LISP endpoint/location control and VXLAN forwarding.

cards.front: SD-Access edge, border, control-plane and intermediate roles?
cards.back: Attach endpoints; connect outside; maintain endpoint/location information; transport underlay packets.

cards.front: Endpoint identifier versus routing locator?
cards.back: The endpoint's identity/address versus the fabric attachment location used to reach it.

cards.front: What does APIC do in Cisco ACI?
cards.back: It manages fabric policy; switches perform normal application-traffic forwarding.

cards.front: SD-WAN Manager, Controller, Validator and edge roles?
cards.back: Management, control, onboarding/orchestration and forwarding, respectively.

cards.front: Can the five management approaches overlap?
cards.back: Yes. A cloud-hosted controller can be driven by automation using reviewed infrastructure-as-code definitions.

tickets.title: A controller loses SSH access after a management ACL change
tickets.scenario: The controller at 10.10.5.20 can ping SW3 10.10.0.13 but its new SSH connections time out. Users through SW3 still work. A console inspection confirms this ACL is applied inbound to every usable VTY range. These are authored diagnostic excerpts.

exhibits.title: SW3 VTY configuration
exhibits.text:
line vty 0 15
 access-class MGMT-IN in
 login local
 transport input ssh

exhibits.title: SW3 management ACL
exhibits.text:
Standard IP access list MGMT-IN
 10 permit 10.10.99.0 0.0.0.255
 20 deny any

tickets.question: Which mismatch is established by the configuration?
options: The controller's northbound token uses the wrong HTTP header.
The controller source is excluded from the VTY permit list.
The switch's user data must transit the controller before forwarding.
The OSPF neighbor table has no route to the controller's API.
tickets.explanation: 10.10.5.20 does not match the only permit and reaches deny any for VTY access. A VTY access-class does not apply to ordinary transit frames or prove that other management protocols are also blocked. The supplied source and ACL establish the SSH mismatch without attributing unrelated counters.
tickets.fix:
```ios
SW3# configure terminal
SW3(config)# ip access-list standard MGMT-IN
SW3(config-std-nacl)# 15 permit host 10.10.5.20
SW3(config-std-nacl)# end
SW3# show access-lists MGMT-IN
```
Retest a new SSH session from the controller's actual source and then its documented synchronization workflow.

tickets.title: The overlay path cannot carry the required packet size
tickets.scenario: A controlled VXLAN design carries a 1500-byte inner IP packet with 14 bytes inner Ethernet, 8 VXLAN, 8 UDP and 20 outer IPv4 bytes. No inner VLAN tag is retained. A replacement underlay interface has an effective IP MTU of 1500. The design requires an outer IP MTU of at least 1550 along this path.

exhibits.title: Representative path evidence
exhibits.text:
Small endpoint-locator ICMP tests: successful
1550-byte outer IPv4 test with DF: ICMP fragmentation-needed received
Reported next-hop MTU: 1500
Replacement interface effective IP MTU: 1500
Other tested path interfaces: effective IP MTU at least 1550

tickets.question: What established issue should the approved repair address?
options: The inventory application's controller token has expired.
The inner application must use a different VXLAN VNI.
The replacement interface's MTU is below the required outer IP size.
The tunnel endpoints have no small-packet IP reachability.
tickets.explanation: The required outer IP packet is 1500+14+8+8+20=1550 bytes. Explicit fragmentation-needed evidence and the replacement interface's effective MTU establish the size mismatch. This is stronger than inferring MTU solely from a stalled file copy.
tickets.fix: Use the replacement platform's documented MTU procedure to meet the approved end-to-end design, checking whether a reload or interface action is required. Do not blindly apply a system-wide command to an unspecified model. Recheck the effective MTU, repeat the 1550-byte DF test, and test the actual application and return direction.

JSON, XML and YAML side by side

lab.title: Read a local HTTP API and validate JSON
devices: One Windows, macOS or Linux computer
lab.intro: Run a small, supplied **teaching service** on your own computer. It returns deterministic inventory data and lets you distinguish 200, 401, 403 and 404 without a public sandbox. It is not a production controller, a full REST implementation or RESTCONF. Its fictional tokens protect no real resource. The service binds only to IPv4 loopback and intentionally uses HTTP; real credentials require authenticated HTTPS.

steps.title: Prepare a new folder and check tools
steps.body:
Create an empty folder named `ccna-api-lab` in your documents area and open two terminals in it. Use your text editor to save files as plain UTF-8. Do not place unrelated sensitive files in the folder.

On Windows PowerShell:

```powershell
python --version
curl.exe --version
```

On macOS/Linux:

```bash
python3 --version
curl --version
```

The remaining commands show Windows names; substitute `python3` and `curl` on macOS/Linux. If Windows uses the Python launcher, substitute `py -3` for `python`. If tools are absent, install Python from python.org and curl using its official platform instructions or your OS package manager, then reopen the terminal. No Python packages are needed.

:::expected
Python is version 3.9 or later and curl identifies itself. Windows PowerShell 5.1 may alias plain curl to another command, which is why `curl.exe` is explicit. If installation is unavailable, interpret the expected exchanges on paper and record that execution was not performed.
:::

steps.title: Create the teaching service
steps.body:
Save this complete code as `api_lab.py`. You need not memorize its implementation; the exercise is reading requests and responses.

```python
import json
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, HTTPServer
from urllib.parse import urlsplit, parse_qs

DEVICES = [
    {"id": "r1", "hostname": "R1", "enabled": True, "ports": 3},
    {"id": "r2", "hostname": "R2", "enabled": False, "ports": "3"},
]
ROLES = {"lab-read-token": "read", "lab-admin-token": "admin"}

class Handler(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def reply(self, status, body, challenge=False):
        data = json.dumps(body, allow_nan=False).encode("utf-8")
        self.send_response(status)
        self.send_header("Content-Type", "application/json")
        self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(data)))
        if challenge:
            self.send_header("WWW-Authenticate", 'Bearer realm="ccna-lab"')
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(data)

    def do_GET(self):
        scheme, _, token = self.headers.get("Authorization", "").partition(" ")
        role = ROLES.get(token) if scheme.lower() == "bearer" else None
        if role is None:
            self.reply(401, {"error": "valid lab token required"}, True)
            return
        target = urlsplit(self.path)
        if target.path == "/api/admin":
            if role != "admin":
                self.reply(403, {"error": "admin role required"})
            else:
                self.reply(200, {"role": role, "changed": False})
            return
        if target.path != "/api/devices":
            self.reply(404, {"error": "resource not found"})
            return
        name = parse_qs(target.query).get("hostname", [None])[0]
        matches = [d for d in DEVICES if name is None or d["hostname"] == name]
        self.reply(200, {"response": matches, "next": None})

    def log_message(self, message, *args):
        print(message % args)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    server = HTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 8765), Handler)
    print("Teaching service: http://127.0.0.1:8765 (Ctrl+C to stop)")
    try:
        server.serve_forever()
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        pass
    finally:
        server.server_close()
```

In Terminal A:

```powershell
python api_lab.py
```

:::expected
The service announces 127.0.0.1:8765 and stays running. If that port is already in use, stop only an earlier copy of this lab that you recognize, or choose a different unused port in the script and every later URL. Do not bind to 0.0.0.0 or publish this teaching service.
:::

steps.title: Read inventory with the supplied credential
steps.body:
In Terminal B:

```powershell
curl.exe -i -H "Authorization: Bearer lab-read-token" -H "Accept: application/json" http://127.0.0.1:8765/api/devices
```

:::expected
The response has status 200 and `Content-Type: application/json`. The body contains two records in `response` and `next: null`. Python's small server may use an HTTP/1.0 response line; that does not change these status or JSON meanings. `-i` prints response headers, not the outgoing request.
:::

steps.title: Observe missing authentication
steps.body:
Omit the credential:

```powershell
curl.exe -i http://127.0.0.1:8765/api/devices
```

Record the status, challenge header and body before repairing.

:::expected
401, a Bearer `WWW-Authenticate` challenge and the error `valid lab token required`. No inventory body is returned. This result follows the supplied service's contract, not an assumption that every network timeout means bad credentials.
:::

steps.title: Restore the credential
steps.body:
Repeat the successful Step 3 request unchanged.

:::expected
The status returns to 200. You changed the authentication context, not the path, protocol or stored device data.
:::

steps.title: Observe insufficient permission
steps.body:
Use the valid read credential on the restricted endpoint:

```powershell
curl.exe -i -H "Authorization: Bearer lab-read-token" http://127.0.0.1:8765/api/admin
```

:::expected
403 and `admin role required`. Here the code explicitly authenticated the supplied read token before denying its role. In an arbitrary API, 403 alone does not establish all of those internal steps.

steps.title: Use the correct fictional role
steps.body:
```powershell
curl.exe -i -H "Authorization: Bearer lab-admin-token" http://127.0.0.1:8765/api/admin
```

:::expected
200 with `{"role":"admin","changed":false}`, allowing for spaces. The name admin does not make GET a write operation; the endpoint reports a role and makes no change.
